items.title: Balming Tiger - Kinfolk
items.description: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
paragraphs: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
- Hair & Makeup Mahito Ohtani

My Zoom interview with Balming Tiger is chaotic. Five of the eleven members are on the call, each in a different location in Seoul. Omega Sapien is at a salon, dyeing his hair green for a music video. Leesuho is munching on a snack with a soda. Unsinkable is strumming a guitar, on mute. bj wnjn is lying in bed in sweatpants. Mudd the Student sits calmly, his long wavy hair dyed like a lion’s mane. There are multiple conversations all happening at once as we wait for the other members, some of whom never show up.

When the interview starts, however, the group is focused and attentive. A self-described “alternative K-pop group” from South Korea, Balming Tiger is composed of two women and nine men. They’ve been described by critics and fans as pioneering, experimental, an artist collective beyond music and, last but not least, “a group of hairstyles that elderly Koreans would definitely hate,” a running joke among fans online. In their two studio albums and a debut mixtape, released in 2018, they sing about alienation, absurdist humor, friendship and love, pigeons and frogs.
“We want Balming Tiger to be its own genre,” says Omega Sapien, a rapper and singer-songwriter, holding up the phone as his hair, now fluorescent green, is being rinsed out in the sink.

Ironically, Balming Tiger’s alternative identity depends on its proximity to South Korea’s best-known cultural export. K-pop, literally Korean popular music, is itself less of a distinctive genre than a cultural phenomenon. Within South Korea, it can refer to a wide variety of styles including ballads, EDM and hip-hop. Abroad, K-pop most often means idols: entertainers whose music and image are strictly produced by massive entertainment conglomerates, such as mega-groups like BTS and Blackpink, or soloists such as Somi and G-Dragon. However you define it, K-pop is a glittering symbol of Korean soft power. The stratospheric success of different Korean musicians in the past decade—especially BTS on the US charts—has catapulted K-pop into a household name everywhere.
“Honestly, we don’t really think about what genre we are, other than during interviews,” says Leesuho, one of Balming Tiger’s producers and video directors.

True as that may be, the label they have chosen—alternative K-pop—is a strategic choice, devised by the group’s founder and creative director, San Yawn. With K-pop’s international popularity, Balming Tiger has smartly positioned themselves as adjacent to something familiar to the global audience—giving themselves a wide playground to try anything and everything.

“It’s always more fun when the possibilities are open,” San Yawn later explains over email. “Whatever we are now won’t be ‘the final version’ of us. We have no idea what we’ll be in the future, but we want to continue to express the little joys of the world in our own language.”

It’s true that the structure of Balming Tiger is wildly different from a conventional K-pop idol act. Idols are usually conceptually defined by an agency, with clear roles differentiating members, for example “lead vocalist” or “lead dancer.” Idol wannabes train, sometimes for years, to audition for a role. Once the group is formed, the performers are the faces of a much larger and more intricate corporate structure.

There were no trainees in Balming Tiger. And no auditions—think more “Wanna join?” conversations at waffle houses and barbecue joints. Nor are all of Balming Tiger’s members performers—their 11 members include producers, photographers, music video directors, A&R managers and DJs. Some faces are more familiar, like those who sing, rap and dance in the music videos (usually Omega Sapien, bj wnjn, Mudd the Student and Sogumm, with cameos by others), but behind the scenes, everything is more collaborative and collective.

Balming Tiger can be seen as less a band with a signature sound than a creative universe, a rainforest of different species colliding and coexisting with each other. From their critically acclaimed debut mixtape, Homie304, to their first studio album in 2023, January Never Dies, to the 2026 album, Gongbu, Balming Tiger’s music defies classification—as does their creative direction. Their videos embrace Hong Kong noir (“SOS”), a ’90s boy band parody (“Big Butt”), and the industrial-era alleyways of the Euljiro neighborhood in Seoul (“Sexy Nukim,” featuring BTS member RM). Their sounds traverse old Korean pop, EDM, psychedelic rock and—of course—hip-hop, many of the members’ first love and forays into music.
“We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

The origins of Balming Tiger can be traced to Itaewon, one of the most culturally diverse neighborhoods in Seoul. It’s a place where the city’s only mosque towers over a hill, next to mom-and-pop stores and cockroach-filled villas, the US military base and ritzy alleyways that are home to the Samsung family and BTS members.

“Balming Tiger is basically a meeting of people that are full of holes,” San Yawn once said on the Korean talk show Moneygraphy. These “holes”—loneliness, for instance, and the desire to fill them through music and art—were what brought together this cacophonous collective through a random series of events starting in 2017, when San Yawn began looking for a crew.

They met at San Yawn’s home in Itaewon and spent much of their time together at Trans 201, on the second floor of a run-down villa in an area popularly known as Transgender Hill. The members started connecting in various ways: through friends of friends, an Instagram message, a chance listening to a future member’s SoundCloud account. “Trans 201 was Omega Sapien and bj wnjn’s house,” recalls Mudd the Student. “The space was very damp and full of dark energy.”

“After a heavy rain, the ceiling in my room was bulging with water, like a giant pimple,” Omega Sapien adds. “We had horrible mold problems. bj wnjn and I split the rent, which was like 600,000 won [approximately $400], and I didn’t even have that money, so my older sister helped pay half of my 300,000. It really was an awful time.”

“Not for me,” says bj wnjn, a vocalist, singer-songwriter and producer. “That space is one of the most memorable moments of my youth. Even with the cockroaches and all that noise from the clubs outside, there was a joy particular to that time.”

Memories like this are specific to Balming Tiger, to Seoul, and permeate their art in ways that can’t be manufactured. The evolving members remain consistently curious about their own experiences and the world around them. There have been some member changes over the years, including the exit of Byung Un, a beloved front man in the early years. But the joy—and the DNA—from that early, formative period is still alive, holding everyone together 10 years later. “There’s a childlike attitude that we never lost as a group,” Sogumm, a singer-songwriter and vocalist, says in an email. “A simplicity that feels honest.”

Often, Balming Tiger’s childlike experiments feel much deeper than mere fun and play, resonating like a sharp resistance against the norms imposed by others. Sometimes this critique feels particularly Korean—like in the 2023 music video of “Kamehameha,” where exhausted office workers are forced to drink with their superiors at a hoesik, an after-work company gathering notorious for heavy alcohol consumption. And at other times it feels fantastically delocalized, like in “UP!” where a cashier at a mega supermarket climbs up the mountain of objects he must clear, reaching for the sky.

“It’s different for me,” says Omega Sapien, who grew up in Korea, China, Japan and the US. “I’m not trying to be rebellious. But I do like provoking a sense of discomfort in others. I like creating differences of opinion through what we do.”

“I’m less interested in making others uncomfortable than in creating a sense of wonder,” says Mudd the Student, who is from Busan, down south. “I love art that makes me feel things for the first time. I suppose that can sometimes make people uncomfortable.”

Despite their almost tongue-in-cheek label as alternative K-pop, Balming Tiger is grateful to the K-pop industry for opening doors for other Korean musicians. The group has performed at major music festivals including SXSW in the US, Primavera Sound in Spain and Fuji Rock Festival in Japan. Their creative orbit is similarly wide-ranging: they’ve collaborated with artists including Japanese girl group ATARASHII GAKKO! and RM of BTS, while independently creating content celebrating figures they admire, such as Korean artist Lee Bul and Thai filmmaker Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Their music video with RM, “Sexy Nukim,” remains Balming Tiger’s most viewed, with 20 million views.

“People often think of idols as these puppets, who only do what they’re told,” says Omega Sapien. “But creative languages within the idol industry are changing too. I really love groups like CORTIS. I think their work is raw and fantastic.”

“I’m really interested in girl groups,” says Unsinkable, a producer and DJ. “These days we see groups that are more like crews, with more creative independence from their company. I sometimes wonder if new idol acts are inspired by what we do.”

In Gongbu, Balming Tiger explores themes of Korean and Asian identity. The single “Home” is absurdist and nostalgic, evoking Korean folk music while mixing synthesizers, rap and ritualistic chants. The music video is black and white, reminiscent of a Park Chan-wook film or a Lee Gap-chul photo. It’s inspired by the architecture of Kim Chung-up and the traditional marriage ritual hamjinabi.

“What does it mean to be Korean? To be Asian? When we were younger, we looked up to American hip-hop,” says Omega Sapien. “I wanted to be like J. Cole. But now I see that that’s his thing. We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

items.title: Taking Play Seriously - Kinfolk
items.description: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
paragraphs: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
A conversation with the National Institute for Play.

In 1966, psychiatrist Dr. Stuart Brown was appointed by the governor of Texas to investigate a mass shooting at the state university—at the time the deadliest in American history. Brown realized there could be a connection between the gunman’s actions and his oppressive childhood, which had been dominated by his controlling father. He would go on to spend the following decades showing that the need for play is biologically hardwired into the brain stem—the part of the nervous system that governs our essential functions like breathing and heart rate.

“When we’re deprived of play, it can be similar to being deprived of sleep and nutrition and connection—the things that fundamentally make us human,” explains Mia Sundstrom, Dr. Brown’s granddaughter and the CEO of the National Institute for Play—a nonprofit organization Brown established in 1994 to champion play as a public health necessity. “I grew up through play,” she says, “and have firsthand seen the benefits of it.”
Appointed to her role earlier this year, her mission at the institute is to show “how people can incorporate play into their lives to promote cognitive, social, emotional and physical health.”
Ellen Peirson-Hagger: Why is play important?

Mia Sundstrom: Here’s the paradox—and it’s why it’s so difficult to convince people that play matters: One of the core definitions of play is that it’s purposeless, that it’s not done for any specific outcome. Yet there’s a ton of purpose in the outcomes we get. We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.
EPH: What are the benefits of play?

MS: When we are in a state of play, it boosts the production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is the neuroplasticity protein that helps to create new neural connections and strengthen existing pathways. Play also calms down our amygdala—our emotional processing center—meaning it takes us out of a stress response, which is great for emotional regulation. And in the case of social play, our mirror neurons—which light up when we observe the motor activity of someone else—allow us to develop the basic foundation of attunement, which is the first seedling of connection with another human being, and which in time leads to trust, to community, to belonging. So on a neurobiological level, play promotes our cognitive health, our emotional resilience and our social competence.

Physical play is obviously good for us: Exercise is healthy, whether we enjoy it or not. But we’re a lot more likely to sustain it when it’s something we enjoy, so we might as well try and find a form of physical exercise that feels like play.
EPH: If we don’t play, are those things lost?

MS: When we’re play-deprived, there can be really severe consequences. It can lead to cognitive rigidity, which is when you can’t think outside the box and solve problems creatively. We have seen that a lack of play can lead to susceptibility for anxiety and depression, and toward addictive behaviors, because we try to find those things that we need from play in other forms—alcohol, drugs, social media, sugar—all these things that offer short-term relief rather than long-term benefit.

And then there’s social incompetence: As my grandpa’s research showed, when we don’t play it’s hard to build tolerance and empathy for each other because we miss that fundamental level of attunement. This leads to diminished well-being.
EPH: How does our need for play change as we become adults?

MS: There’s a misconception that it has to change like crazy, that what you do as a kid is not what you should do as an adult. But we don’t ever lose the desire to play, we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways. For example, as you go through grade school, the playgrounds change—there is no longer the opportunity to go down a slide at recess—and then all of a sudden you forget that you love to do that, and you might never do it again.

I don’t think adults should stop swinging, or playing at parks, or jumping on a trampoline in the backyard. We often think that we outgrow these things, but we really shouldn’t. Lego is a breaker of this rule: Lego adult sets are selling so well right now because of their connection to nostalgia and childhood. And what’s great about moving from childhood to adulthood is that the possibilities to play open up significantly: Instead of exploring your backyard with a stick and turning your cardboard box into a rocket ship, you have access to a car and a plane.
EPH: Is play different to different people?

MS: Everyone is born with a deep natural predilection for play, but that looks different for each of us. There are people who love to make things—art, music, building, tinkering with objects. There are people who love to dream or get lost in a book or movie and create imaginary worlds in their mind. There are people who love to compete, who play through mastering. There are people who love to organize—collecting new things, arranging social gatherings, even cleaning out a junk drawer. These are all different play styles, and one of the greatest gifts you can give a child is to notice what those natural tendencies are and help nourish them.
EPH: Do you think we need to take a broader view of what play is or can be?

MS: Yes! Most of the time, when I ask people “What is play to you?” they say “a board game” or “my kid’s sport.” We have confined play to this really narrow scope, when actually play is any activity that brings us into the play state, which is an altered state of being, almost dreamlike, that takes us out of the usual experience of time and space and evokes positive emotions like joy and awe. It is intrinsically motivated, not coerced, so it’s done for its own sake, and it’s self-reinforcing, so the benefits of a play state last beyond the time we’re playing.

Any activity that meets that criteria can be play—that could mean coding for someone who loves to code, or cooking for someone who loves to cook. Heck, that could even be cleaning if you put on a great song and you turn your broom into a microphone.
EPH: Why is society so resistant to play?

MS: Well, the psychologist and play researcher Peter Gray would answer by taking us back to the 16th century, when the Protestant Reformation taught us to believe in the moral virtue of work and that play, by contrast, is the breeding ground of sin. And then you throw capitalism into the mix which calls for more production, more consumption: that’s what defines success in the capitalist dream, right? Then you add in the compounding effects of automation and AI. Of course play isn’t celebrated in a world that prioritizes those things.
EPH: Has digitization played a role?

MS: We can’t prove causation, but our screens do seem to be factor in why we’re not playing. Scrolling on your screen disguises itself as play because you lose track of time, and it feels fun in the moment. But it has long-term detriments in terms of our attention span and our loneliness. If we’re scrolling, we’re not connecting with each other on a human level.
EPH: What kind of society would we have if we all played more?

MS: Play dissolves our differences and reminds us of what we have in common. Our world is so polarized, but play brings us together and is one of the most powerful ways to create a better society. Play lowers our inhibitions—I want to shout that from the rooftops. If you disagree with someone and go play with them, you’ll see the humanity in one other. It can also help combat the trends that we’re talking so much about right now—loneliness, disengagement, burnout—because play brings us back to that deep intrinsic drive to do something for a sustained period of time that makes the time pass more quickly.
EPH: What should adults do to help recover their love of play?

MS: We help adults rediscover their natural spark—their thing that makes them most curious and fully alive—and then think about small ways to reintegrate that into their life. The first step is to think back to your earliest memory of play: What was that thing you loved to do before the world told you who to be? Second, based on that, what do you love to do now—is there something that you’ve forgotten about and haven’t done for ages? Third, nothing ever works when we try to create massive changes all at once. So we say that 30 seconds is enough. See if you can add a burst of play into your morning or evening routine, based on those two things you reflected on. What’s great about play is that it’s self-reinforcing, so as soon as you give yourself that permission, it will keep you coming back for more.
“We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.”

items.title: Kyle Kuzma - Kinfolk
items.description: The NBA forward is playing the long game.
paragraphs: The NBA forward is playing the long game.

Kyle Kuzma is enjoying himself. He’s about to catch a flight for the south of France, where he’ll be attending the Cannes Film Festival, and is midway through the long, complex and, for him, extremely pleasurable process, of picking out what to wear. “If I’m going somewhere in three days, I may already be in my closet, just trying on clothes, seeing what I want to wear, thinking about what type of events I’m going to,” he says over a video call from his home in Miami. He’s planning ahead for the films, parties and red carpet events.

If a lot of this sounds like fun, Kuzma thinks so too. “Everything is play—unless, you know, it’s your profession,” he says. This is the challenge because Kuzma’s job is, after all, a form of play. He is in his 10th year in the NBA. A first-round draft pick in 2017, he’s currently a power forward for the Milwaukee Bucks; in 2020 he won the NBA national championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in only his third year in the league.

items.title: Sofia Coppola's New 'Marie Antoinette' Merch
items.description: words by DOUGLAS GREENWOOD
items.author: Douglas Greenwood
paragraphs: words by DOUGLAS GREENWOOD
product photography COURTESY OF MACK

The merch-ification of the movies we love is a fairly recent development, brought on by cult studios who know we like our cinephilia to be seen at all times. But if you go back further than five years, then original, director-approved t-shirts, sweatshirts, anything, is much harder to find. Die-hards will scroll on eBay looking for scant objects made as wrap gifts or for crew. But that’s about it! For Sofia Coppola fans—a director whose lore-steeped, decadently formed, insular worlds are catnip for aesthetes—we’ve mostly had to rely on fan created or bootleg stuff. That’s all about to change.

This year, to mark the 20th anniversary of Marie Antoinette, Coppola has unveiled a trio of projects. There’s a remastered cut of the film, a documentary about the film’s creation directed by her late mother Eleanor Coppola titled Making Marie Antoinette (out now via MUBI), and the release of its hardback companion by MACK and Coppola’s own imprint Important Flowers, comprised of pictures shot by Coppola’s long-time collaborator Andrew Durham. Durham’s pictures have carried their own special stories for Coppola fans; now, you can wear them, or carry them slung over your shoulder with some new Marie Antoinette merch, available on MACK’s website now.

To celebrate the confectionary-sweet moment, Coppola spoke to us about the film’s modern reassessment, the merch, and the crew t-shirt she’d love to own from one of her favorite films. She also sent us polaroids taken of the new merch.

DOUGLAS GREENWOOD: Seeing Marie Antoinette’s new life—through the anniversary, the documentary, and the book—must have been so beautiful. Where has it sat for you in your own filmography since it was shot?

SOFIA COPPOLA: Oh, I don’t revisit my films much, but I did when working on my book. I’ve always loved my friend Andrew Durham’s set photos. It was really nice to put them all together in a book, revisit that shoot with Kirsten [Dunst] and Jason [Schwartzman] at Versailles, and see the restored film on a big screen again after so long. I’ve never done that before; it was nice to get to celebrate a film that didn’t have much of a release at the time, and wasn’t loved when it came out. It’s fun to share in the enjoyment of it.
I feel like people are excited about Andrew’s work in your world. What’s it been like to share this journey of the film with a friend like that?
I love Andrew’s photos and everyone likes when he visits my set. He’s fun and easy to be around, so he’s able to get photos that no one else could. I love his eye.

I love the life that your films live after they’ve been released, like here in this collection of merch you’ve made with MACK and Important Flowers. Can you talk me through how these pieces came together?

I just thought it would be fun to make some merch because I love the images, and there had been some counterfeit ones using Andrew’s photos, so I thought people might like to have them, and it would be nice for Andrew to benefit from his images (even if it’s a small run).
Is there a film you love that you’d love to own something from? Or to wear a t-shirt adorned with the visuals of?

I was really excited to get a New Order crew t-shirt from when they played at Versailles! I love crew t-shirts. I still have my kid crew t-shirt from Apocalypse Now! And it’s fun to see friends of my kids wearing a Bling Ring crew sweatshirt or something. I would like to have a crew shirt from The Hunger.

items.title: i-D X New Balance, Straight-Up!
items.description: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheeseca
items.author: Tiffany Lai
paragraphs: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheesecake before the party continued downstairs at the Knave of Clubs for pub drinks and a boogie.

At 8 p.m., a new billboard was unveiled outside the pub, celebrating version 7 of New Balance’s iconic 990 silhouette, set to release globally on November 6. Made in the USA, the 990 has been a proud “dad shoe” since 1982, so naturally, we had to ask our guests: who is your favorite American? And which celebrity dad has the best style?

Who is your favorite American? Kim Kardashian or Adam Sandler. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Rey Mysterio from WWE. What’s an album that’s on repeat right now? The new Worldpeace DMT album. What are you doing this weekend? Spreading optimism and premature Christmas cheer!

What do you do? I’m a stylist. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Ford Bronco cars. What are you wearing today? Mules, which aren’t very practical for walking in the rain, an old pair of Our Legacy jeans, a cashmere jumper to keep me warm, and a vintage bomber. My hat is made by my friend Biddyish. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Brad Pitt.

What’s an item of clothing you’d never part with? My 1960s vintage McGregor jacket that I picked up in Paris a few years ago. What are you drinking tonight? Guinness. Who’s your favorite American? Jim Carrey. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My granddad, actually. What’s your favorite form of exercise? Running, because of the mental clarity and the long and steady journey I’ve had with New Balance.

What do you do? I’m a photographer, director, and DJ. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? A secondhand leather jacket from a market in Paris. What album is on repeat right now? Choke Enough by Oklou. What’s a color that you’d love to wear more of? Green.

What do you do? I make music, but I like saying my job is just connecting the dots because there’s no laws or limits to art. Tell us about your outfit. My outfit’s steady but also flex-y, smart-casual. What are you doing this weekend? I’m always creating. I’m working on some new music, shooting cool videos, fun stuff. Who first taught you to tie your shoes? My mum. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? I’m in a black era right now.

What do you do? We’re freelance stylists. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Jacob: Jeff Goldblum. His personality is the style. If you had to run between two Tube stops, which ones would you choose? Jacob: Bethnal Green and Mile End because they’re the closest ones together. Lauren: Custom House to Canning Town. Nice scenic run. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? Lauren: A big fur coat.

Who’s your favorite American? Fred Hampton. He was one of the leaders of the Black Panther Party. What’s your side hustle? I’m rebranding my friend’s fashion brand. Doesn’t mean I give it less attention than a main hustle, but that’s the thing that I’m supporting right now! What’s your favorite form of exercise and why? Push-ups and pull-ups at home. I hate going to the gym. What are you doing this weekend? I’m seeing my friend who’s leaving for Australia. I’ve got to sort his Moonpig out ASAP!

What do you do? I’m the editor-in-chief of i-D Magazine. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Me. Which celebrity dad has the best style? My dad. He’s modeled in the Chopova Lowena show, he wears New Balance 990s, and he loves a Ralph Lauren polo. Best grail? This Prada scarf. Who’s your favorite TV dad? Michael Bluth from Arrested Development.

What do you do? I’m a fashion designer. What’s an item of clothing you’ll never part with? This pair of jeans that my boyfriend gave me. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? Gray. What’s your favorite form of exercise? I go to the gym, but I want to pick up tennis.

What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Black music. What are you wearing tonight? Made in the USA 2040 V5 New Balance shoes, Supreme Made in Japan denim, and a Bleue Burnham ring. What are you drinking tonight? Chili margarita, some red wine, Guinness, and water. Got to stay hydrated. What are you doing this weekend? This weekend, it’s the Amsterdam Dance Event where I live. My partner’s going clubbing, so I’m taking care of the kids.

What do you do? I’m a musician, and I play the harp. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? My 1800s Victorian body that is falling apart, but I’ll never let her go. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My dad. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a cemetery walk date with my girlfriend in Abney Park. Who’s your favorite American? Lana Del Rey.

What are you wearing? Hysteric Glamour boots with pink studs, a skirt that my ex-boyfriend gave me, a nice, warm Supreme jacket, and a Goldwin jumper. What are you drinking tonight? Two spicy margaritas, a glass of white wine, and a glass of red wine. Who’s your favorite American? Martine Syms. I like her exhibition at Sadie Coles. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a first date to a wine bar in Hoxton. Do you have a side hustle? Hustling!

What do you do? I work for Homer Jewellery and Louise Konrad Jewellery. Who’s your favorite American? The Tiger King. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? My sweatpants. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Zendaya’s Mugler outfit for the Dune premiere. What are you drinking tonight? Vodka soda.

items.title: The Story of Cécred
items.description: photography BLAIR CALDWELL
items.author: Eni Subair
paragraphs: photography BLAIR CALDWELL
hair NEAL FARINAH FOR CÉCRED
colour direction MASON POOLE

Haircare was always one of the many ways Beyoncé’s family expressed love. Watching her mother Ms. Tina Knowles care for everyone from doctors and judges to the unhoused in her now-famous Houston salon Headliners, Beyoncé saw firsthand how hair can empower and instill confidence in others—and in herself. It was in Ms. Tina’s salon chair, at just 9 years old, where Beyoncé’s appreciation for haircare began.

Decades and dozens of House of Deréon looks later, Beyoncé and Ms. Tina decided to bring their love and appreciation for haircare to the world. In 2024, they turned their lifelong shared passion into Cécred, with Beyoncé as the sole investor, founder, and Chairwoman and Ms. Tina as Vice Chairwoman. Years in the making, the brand was an endeavour worth perfecting—with Beyoncé and Ms. Tina personally testing every product.
Limited copies of the zine are available here.
The quality speaks for itself: Take the Restoring Hair and Edge Drops, which has become the number one hair product in the United States, driven by hair growth testimonials all over social media.

Meanwhile, a heartwarming Father’s Day short film of JAŸ-Z’s loc takedown process, using the brand’s signature Detangling Spray, has offered an intimate glimpse into the family. The love poured into the products only amplifies the scientific truths: These serums, shampoos, and gels really work for you.
This autumn, Cécred jumped across the pond from Los Angeles to London, offering its wide range of products for us Brits at Space NK stores.

To celebrate the UK launch, Beyoncé and Ms. Tina opened up about their hair and their lives. It’s a full-circle moment for the mother-daughter duo, who are sharing the lessons in hair confidence passed down through generations with a whole new audience. For Beyoncé, it’s about more than hair. It’s about continuing her mother’s legacy and making sure everyone feels their best in their hair.
ENI SUBAIR: What has been the most rewarding part of building Cécred?
BEYONCÉ: My mother and I poured decades of experience, tradition, and love into Cécred, so seeing our community grow across every ethnicity, texture, generation, and gender is so fulfilling.

In the beginning, it took some conditioning from the world’s perception of how to launch a brand founded by someone like me. I’m the founder, visionary, and sole investor—not the face or model for this brand. I had a vision to build something that solved real problems and performed so incredibly that the people who can’t stand my music still use Cécred, haaaa! … because it works.
Cécred has been years in the making, so why did 2024 finally feel like the right time to launch?

MS. TINA: Well, we tried to launch it two years earlier, and Beyoncé, you know, she’s a perfectionist. So, with the products, I thought they were amazing, but then I would give them to her, and she would test them on herself, her friends, and her daughters. Then, if one person didn’t have an excellent experience, she would give it back to me. She drove us crazy, and the team was like, “Oh my God!” But I’m so happy that she was so picky about it because it just got better and better. And our testing, research, and development is where we put a lot of money. I was like, this is so crazy expensive because we’re researching and testing so much. We’ve tested on three continents to get all types of hair textures, to make sure that it works on all hair. I had a salon in the ’80s, and what I was told all the time was that our hair was strong because they think that because our hair is coarser, it is stronger. But that is a myth surrounding Black hair. It’s just the opposite. Our hair is the weakest, most fragile hair, and the curlier your hair is, the more texture you have.

And I’ve always studied the science of hair: what it was made of and what it needed. Even making sure to reduce the molecular weight of products so that it can get through the cuticle and build and strengthen the hair.
What lessons have you learned from your mum that have helped you on this journey?

BEYONCÉ: Growing up I saw my mom pour love into others at her salon, and she still does this every day. I love that she trusts that the world is for her. She trusts God. She approaches things with humanity and love. I love my mother’s rebellious spirit. She can spark an idea and make it come to life. She’s fearless and I get that from her. It was in her salon that I witnessed stylists transforming women and helping them get their confidence back and see their beautiful potential. It was more than just getting their hair done, it became a sacred space where they were cared for. That impact resonated so deeply, and I wanted that to be reflected in Cécred and the community we’re building. Your heart carries energy and wisdom from your fingertips.

Recently my mom decided to surprise me by visiting a hair salon in the UK. No calls ahead, no warning. She packed a bag of Cécred, got into the car, and showed up without any pre-planning. Even though one of the managers told her she couldn’t be there, she stuck around and made the owner come. She was determined to build a relationship with the salon owners and clients and ended up spending almost a whole day doing hair there, ha!
What’s your first memory of experimenting with your hair?

BEYONCÉ: One day I decided to cut my own hair. I think I may have cut the whole ponytail off and also cut bangs! I walked in with my ponytail and said, “Mom, put this back on please.” And she was like, “I can’t.” But I thought she could, because I’d seen her be such a hair magician, especially when she would bond hair. Those crazy memories were the foundation of my childhood.
Both you and your mum love Tottenham—where do you like to go? What are your favourite spots?

BEYONCÉ: One of my favourite things about London is the drive to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and passing through Seven Sisters. I love seeing all the communities with their kids, the barber shops, and all the culturally diverse restaurants. As I get closer to the stadium, I start to see the fans who put so much effort into attending the show, either dressed in metallic silver, glistening in the streets and sunshine, or in full cowboy gear, boas, and boots. I can spot my Hive from miles away. When I’m onstage and see all the ethnicities, all the beautiful and fabulous outfits and families, there’s no other experience like it. The melting pot of beautiful diversity in London, particularly at my shows, is something magical to witness.

I love the music scene in the UK. I’ve watched Sienna Spiro grow up from a beautiful young girl to an extraordinarily talented young woman. I’ve known her family well for quite some time. I heard her sing when she was a kid discovering her voice and I can’t articulate the pride she brings me. What a God-given talent! I’m also so proud of Raye, who wrote some of the songs on The Gift. She has had such an anointing. You hear the vulnerability and wisdom in her voice. I also love and respect Olivia Dean. These beautiful women are all kind, have grace, and write and produce their own music. It gives me goosebumps. I just burst with pride when I see them.
Looking back, what was your favourite hairstyle during the B’DAY era, and your favourite look created by your mum?

BEYONCÉ: My favorite hair look was the B’DAY cover updo. That’s stood the test of time and has had such a renaissance this year. I love seeing everyone’s interpretations, and videos and the evolution of the early 2000s look.

My favourite dress my mother designed was my wedding dress—it was gorgeously simple and made with her love. We had a very small wedding in our home. We told the guests we were having a party, and no one knew they were coming to our wedding but our parents and a few friends. Wearing a dress, she designed was very important to me, and more important than any designer dress.

You recently re-wore a House of Deréon top that you wore back in 2006 to mark 20 years of B’DAY. What did you love about House of Deréon then that you still love now? What can we find in your archive?

BEYONCÉ: Yes, haaaa! I pulled out the Deréon archive for the Hive for the B’DAY 20th Anniversary re-release. I also had so much fun recreating some of my and my mother’s designs. We brought back the Deréon hoodies and metallic Freakum dresses. I’ll never forget calling my mum the day before the “Freakum Dress” shoot, asking her to make more dresses in more colours because I envisioned match-cutting the colours during the choreography. She was frustrated that I tasked her with making them so last minute, but she and Ty (Tyrone Hunter) got it done. I’m so very thankful for her. I’m so excited to pass all my archives to my kids, especially now that they’re all discovering their own personal style. I’m going to enjoy seeing how they pull from their parents’ carpets and tours if they’re ever interested. Rumi’s favourite place to shop right now is Ross and TJ Maxx these days.

items.title: Tyra Banks Leapt Out of a Car to Help an Aspiring Model
items.description: Looks like Rihanna's little lookalike isn't the only aspiring model getting a little boost from supermodel and business mogul Tyra Banks.
items.author: Sandra Song
paragraphs: Looks like Rihanna's little lookalike isn't the only aspiring model getting a little boost from supermodel and business mogul Tyra Banks.
Over the weekend, Banks was at BeautyCon LA when she spotted beauty YouTuber Tatyana Ali in the middle of a curbside photo shoot. So, naturally, she leapt out of her car to assist.

Retelling the story via her Instagram earlier today, Banks shared her favorite shot of Ali, writing, "When you go to @beautycon and you're in your car leaving but you see a photo shoot happening that is kind of going in the wrong direction."

"What else do you do but put on your Super/Model/Hero cape, jump out of the car, grab the camera from the photographer and start clicking," Banks continued, before adding, "Maybe one day I'll jump out of the car to capture YOU. #TyraTaughtMe."
That said, Banks was quick to also acknowledge that the photographer eventually "took some amazing photos" after a quick five-minute lesson.

Not only that, but Ali also ended up posting a photo of Banks behind the camera, writing, "Soo today THEEE TYRA BANKS got out of her car to take photos of me. BASICALLY this is most iconic moment in my life." Ali then went on to joke, "Quick question though Tyra, can you just sign me?"
Check out her post, below.

items.title: Did Madonna Invent the Pop Star Remix Album?
items.description: After four months of nothing but Brat, Charli xcx decided it was time for more Brat.
items.author: Joan Summers
paragraphs: After four months of nothing but Brat, Charli xcx decided it was time for more Brat.

Specifically, the completely remixed version of the original LP (Brat and it’s completely different but also still brat), which flexed features from Bb trickz, Julian Casablancas, Ariana Grande, to reimagine the entire Brat tracklist. The result was pretty much a second Brat that also wasn’t Brat at all. The title didn’t lie.

Since then, it feels like every main pop girl has opted for a remix album instead of tacking a few new tracks onto a deluxe. Brat and its completely different broke through a ceiling in the slightly left-of-center pop mainstream, as if she reminded us and her contemporaries that full remix albums were even an option. We’ve since seen similar efforts from Rose Gray, PinkPantheress, and Smerz, and more are on the way, like Zara Larsson’s upcoming Girl’s Trip.
But by no means did Charli create the remix album.

Like most things pop culture, all remix album roads lead back to the Mothers: Madonna and Janet. On You Can Dance (1987), Madonna reimagined tracks from her first three albums, while janet. Remixed (1995) only features about half of the original janet. tracklist. Jennifer Lopez and Britney Spears would usher the trend into the 2000s with J to tha L-O! and the first volume of B in the Mix. Mariah Carey would similarly release the club classic The Remixes in 2003. But by the late 2000s, the remix album had largely given way to the bonus-track deluxe, especially as “mainstream” pop moved away from those gritty club tracks that could be more intuitively remixed. Think: Adele, Bruno Mars, Mumford & Sons.

Among all the big-name pop stars throughout the 2010s, like One Direction, Ariana Grande (My Everything), and especially Taylor Swift, deluxe editions would become defining parts of their catalogues. And the bonus-track deluxe is still kicking: Sabrina Carpenter’s Short n Sweet (Deluxe) and Olivia Rodrigo’s GUTS (spilled) are perfectly recent examples of what feels like the industry-standard deluxe form. Charli herself did it with Crash just two years before Brat, adding four new songs to the original tracklist while actively playing the Main Pop Girl game.

Even as mainstream pop battled between EDM and “ho-hey!” in the 2010s, remix albums persisted in the underground electronic and R&B spaces. Kelela has released top-to-bottom remix projects since the Cut 4 Me EP and her debut album Hallucinogen in 2015, getting renditions from artists like Kaytranada, Princess Nokia, and Yaeji. Kaytranada, specifically, has become a kind of cosigner in that pop-R&B-club space, with his remixes serving as a go-to bridge between scenes (Rochelle Jordan, Kali Uchis), ushering that ever-changing sonic spirit into the 2020s.

Into the late 2010s, pop remixes were mostly one-offs: Calvin Harris’ Funk Wav remix of SZA’s “The Weekend,” Lorde compiling the very-of-the-time group of Post Malone, SZA, and Khalid for a 2018-pilled “Homemade Dynamite.” Early in the Brat rollout, when we’d only heard the “Von dutch” remix with Addison Rae and A.G. Cook, this seemed the more likely route for Charli.

In the pandemic era, as pop turned back toward the dancefloor and artists had more time to experiment, Dua Lipa and Lady Gaga both released their own ravey dance-pop LPs (Future Nostalgia and Chromatica, respectively), each with a remixed counterpart. Dua went on to drop Club Future Nostalgia, a collab with The Blessed Madonna that evokes ‘90s British radio-DJ mixes, featuring remixes by Jayda G, Mark Ronson, and London disco mainstays Horse Meat Disco. Gaga recruited a grab-bag of hyperpop, triphop, and electronic artists for Dawn of Chromatica, with remixes and occasional verses from Ashnikko, Arca, Shygirl and Dorian Electra. Dawn, specifically, follows the same tracklist order as Chromatica, making it feel even more like an evil counterpart.

When Tame Impala’s Rushium tour was put on pause at the start of the pandemic, just weeks after he dropped his fourth full-length, The Slow Rush, Kevin Parker released The Slow Rush in an Imaginary Place. It’s less of an on-the-nose remix album than an environmental reinterpretation, with ambient crowd chatter and a faraway effect that sounds like the album is reverberating from the club across the street. This was also a less formal “drop” (released to SoundCloud and YouTube rather than an official streaming release), but it’s a reinterpretation that gets at the sonic malleability at the core of remix efforts, especially in the electro-pop space. And in that same vein, on the production side, Parker’s work with Dua Lipa on 2024’s Radical Optimism resulted in an extended cut of the LP that added 20 minutes of music to the original tracklist, offering a trancey counterpart to the original’s pure pop sensibilities.

This is to say that Charli xcx didn’t so much invent the remix album as she did reintroduce it to the masses. If anything, Charli’s roots in remix albums, specifically, lie with A.G. Cook’s PC Music label/collective, which gave rise to artists like Danny L Harle, SOPHIE, and EasyFun, who then utilized that ethos with artists outside the scene.
Brat and it’s completely different but also still Brat feels like the inflection point, where remix LPs were officially “back” for the mainstream listener.

The drop coincided with her midweek midday livestream listening party at an upstate New York art installation, Charli teasing songs in a similarly frenetic, Boiler Room-type energy. Some of her biggest features (Lorde, Billie Eilish, Troye Sivan) rolled out as a slow drip, holding us over for the summer. And those songs, with their underlying gossip and subsequently internet-combusting lyrics — Lorde’s “Girl, so confusing” verse, Eilish’s “Charli likes boys, but she knows I’d hit it” on “Guess” — landed as “moments” in their own right.

Part of what made Brat and it’s completely different feel so expansive in the mainstream was the way she thoroughly reworked most of the original material. Tracks became completely new compositions, with new elements and melody lines that changed the song’s original tone (see: “Talk talk featuring troye sivan” only building off the original’s bridge, or the “Owner of a Broken Heart” sample added to “Mean girls featuring julian casablancas”).

Since then, Rose Gray released A Little Louder, Please in October, the remix-deluxe (featuring JADE with remixes from Logic1000 and Alex Chapman) that built on the slow-burning hype the original fostered throughout the year. PinkPantheress more than quadrupled the Fancy That runtime with her three-disc behemoth, Fancy Some More?, which split the tracklist into a slew of features that leaned into each artist’s style and a separate set of remixes that showcased her UK underground inspirations. As if to say, “Yes, I’m giving you three versions of ‘Illegal’ and four versions of ‘Stateside,’ and you’re gonna listen to all of them!”

At the top of the year, Lily Allen teased a West End Girl remix LP in Interview at the top of the year, while Zara Larsson (who cited Charli as inspiration) confirmed a Midnight Sun remix album is imminent. Is everyone just playing catch-up? It feels like something of an expectation now: every pop album that makes a splash must reignite the conversation with a complete reinterpretation. Brat and it’s completely different still held the surprise and spectacle, but each one since then, regardless of how good some of the songs are, comes across as a box-checking obligation.
It also begs the question of when a remix album is and isn’t necessary.

Would the dancefloor underwhelm of Kiss All The Time. Disco, Occasionally benefit from a more balls-to-the-walls trance-house makeover? To me, yes. But is something like a Sabrina Carpenter feature on Lily Allen's "Tennis" going to hit the same as Pink and Zara's “Stateside”? Probably not. If everything is stage-setting for reinvention, then reinvention stops meaning anything at all.

items.title: Lil’ Kim on 30 Years Of Being Herself
items.description: When you hear the name Lil’ Kim, a variety of images come to mind. She’s forever known as the force of nature from Brooklyn who turned the music industry on its head when she entered the scene 30 years ago, and her bodacious lyrics and unique fashion sense hav
items.author: Kia D Goosby
paragraphs: When you hear the name Lil’ Kim, a variety of images come to mind. She’s forever known as the force of nature from Brooklyn who turned the music industry on its head when she entered the scene 30 years ago, and her bodacious lyrics and unique fashion sense have kept her as a source of inspiration on your favorite designer’s mood board ever since. On November 18 and 19, to celebrate the music that cemented her icon status, Lil’ Kim will perform in front of a symphony orchestra at the Kings Theatre in Brooklyn, not far from her humble beginnings.

Today she’s less interested in being in the spotlight and more focused on raising her 12-year-old daughter, Royal Reign. In between practices for her performances, Lil’ Kim spoke with Vanity Fair to reflect on her career, how she spends her days, and her standout looks.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Vanity Fair: What do you remember about putting your debut album, Hard Core, together?

Lil’ Kim: I remember Biggie and Un [Lance Rivera], who was the label owner that we had. I watched Un build a record label called Undeas, which [stood] for “Un ideas,” and then he finally sold it to Atlantic Records. At the time, we didn’t know the process, but we became Undeas-Atlantic. I remember Biggie having the idea of how he wanted my album to be red, and he explained it to me and Un. I was able to write according to how his idea was to present me, because when they met me, I was who I was—in high heels, jeans, motorcycle jackets, and furs at 13.
That’s incredible. It sounds like your fashion-icon status started very early. Was there anyone that you looked to back then? What inspired you to dress that way?

My mom was a big inspiration to me when it came to fashion, and so I looked to her for a lot of things. I used to wear her mink coat. She used to wear big sunglasses with her fur coats, with the diamonds and jewelry. She was always taking vacations and I would see her pack her stuff, and she would always have the cutest outfits. They were all matchy-matchy. It’s funny because she would have her outfit to go play tennis in and her outfit would match her tennis racket. So when I bought my big house, I bought a Chanel tennis outfit and I bought the racket to match it, because of my mom.
I love that. Do you keep up with tennis or specifically the ladies in tennis?
No, I haven’t in a while, but, of course, you know, Serena and Venus were like my heroes.
Well, maybe we need to see you on the court one day.
I know. I’m pretty sure I’m rusty, but I like to get out there, though. I used to beat my cousin’s butt back then.
How did the symphony performances come about?

My agents called me and they’re like, “Kim, what do you think?” And I was like, “That’s a freaking awesome idea.” I love performing with bands. And so I imagine that it could be very similar, if not very close. And I thought this could be something really different for me. Sometimes I even listen to classical music. I don’t have to know who the artist is, but I just put on a station and let it flow.
Do you have a favorite song from Hard Core?
I love “Queen Bitch”; it’s my favorite song. It’s still my favorite to perform. And “Crush on You.”
When it comes to fashion, you’re obviously on everyone’s mood board, from stylists to designers, so how important was fashion for you as part of the Lil’ Kim persona?
I just was being myself, honestly. When I first met Biggie, I was coming from my after-school job at Bloomingdale’s. I was probably 13 or 14 at the time, and they would let the teenagers work there.

But I had on a motorcycle jacket and high heels. And one of my best friends told Biggie, “You know, my girl can rap,” because we knew he was rapping around the way. And he was like, “I heard you can rap.” And I just laughed. He was like, “Yeah, see, I knew you didn’t know how to rap.” He was very condescending. He knew how to get you to do what you wanted to do, because I was really shy.

And then I started rapping, and he was blown away because I had on high heels. No one had ever seen someone just bust a rap in high heels. When Biggie, Un, and Jacob York started really talking to me, they didn’t want to change me because that was just what they were so blown away about. That was just who I was.
Do you think people ever misunderstood the way you presented yourself?

To be honest, I never really felt misunderstood by my hardcore fans—the kids my age and the younger kids, they totally got it. I think that’s why I had such a cult following and there was such pandemonium about me when I came out. They understood me. I think it was the older people and the politicians, those are the people who I think misunderstood me.
What did you think of the midterm elections and all of the women who broke barriers in the Senate and gubernatorial offices?
I’m going to be honest with you, I stay away from politics.

Are you keeping up with all of the changes within fashion today? When I listen to your music, you’ve mentioned so many designers and houses, and since then the creative directors have changed. Are you following all of the changes within fashion and seeing how you’re still a part of the conversation?

That’s what I’m trying to say. As a fashion icon, if you really her, and I’m considering myself really her, that’s never gonna change. That’s never going to change. I might put on a fur coat that my stylist or myself will get asked about, because I style myself a lot. And I was styling myself then.
What has motherhood been like for you?
Extremely rewarding. My daughter’s with me all the time. This world is so cruel and so evil; it’s so different. She’s my safe haven. I feel the extra need to keep her safe.
What does a regular day look like for you?
Lately, I’ve just been really getting into myself. I get up and go have a little spa day. I might take my daughter to go do whatever she wants.
How do you feel that we’re still talking about your MTV VMAs look in 1999?
I think it’s iconic and I love it. I love when they bring that up, because it was a fun day and it was so good to see people’s faces when they saw my outfit.
Are there any other looks that don’t get as much love as you wish that they did?

I don’t know, because most of the looks that I love, they get the love. There’s a look when I was on the cover of Nylon magazine and I had the teddy bear dress on; that’s one of my favorite looks. The Louis Vuitton look is one of my favorite looks; I love that look. A lot of the Chanel looks and the Versace and the Chanel in the hair.

items.title: Glenn Close Gets Teary-Eyed as She Finally Gets Her Oscar at the Governors Awards
items.description: The day before the Governors Awards, a studio executive who had attended the past few years told me that she often found herself crying at the star-studded gala. The annual awards ceremony, held by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, is often an e
items.author: Rebecca Ford
paragraphs: The day before the Governors Awards, a studio executive who had attended the past few years told me that she often found herself crying at the star-studded gala. The annual awards ceremony, held by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, is often an emotional event, with honorary Oscar statuettes bestowed on influential figures in the film industry. A tribute to Michael J. Fox in 2022 and a posthumous honor for Quincy Jones in 2024 left many guests misty-eyed.

At Sunday’s gala, that teary-eyed trend continued when Glenn Close finally got to hold her own Oscar, after eight nominations without a win. Others got emotional when Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, the independent producers from Killer Films, were honored for their tireless work making boundary-pushing and challenging movies. And when Floyd Norman, the 91-year-old artist who was the first Black animator to join Walt Disney Animation Studios, thanked his wife and five children, the crowd cheered along with him. Even though honoree Ridley Scott couldn’t attend, he dedicated his award to his late brother Tony Scott in a video message. “It is about time we all saw him with an Academy Award in his hand,” said Matt Damon in his remarks for Scott, who has been nominated for four Oscars but has never won competitively.

The presentation of honorary Oscars is often a way to correct Academy Award history, recognizing those who have been overlooked but deserve to be honored for their lifetime of dedication to storytelling and film. The Governors Awards ceremony is also a major stop on the Oscar season campaign trail, with a room packed full of stars and filmmakers from the year’s contenders.

This year that meant a surprising number of couple contenders, including Monica Barbaro and Andrew Garfield (who both star in Artificial), Carrie Coon and Tracy Letts (The Liberation), and Zendaya and Tom Holland. Though Zendaya and Holland arrived together and walked through the Ray Dolby Ballroom as a pair, they actually sat at different tables—Zendaya at the Dune table, with Timothée Chalamet and director Denis Villeneuve, and Holland at the Odyssey table, with director Christopher Nolan. Chalamet also made a date night out of the event, bringing Kylie Jenner with him.

The room held a mix of A-list Hollywood stars, like Tom Cruise (in support of Digger), Julianne Moore (The Debut), and Charlize Theron (The Odyssey), and breakout filmmakers of the year, like Obsession’s Curry Barker, La Bola Negra’s Los Javis, and Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman.

Another breakout of the season, La Bola Negra star Guitarricadelafuente, has been busy promoting the film as both an actor and a musician, having written the original song “La Nieve.” I wondered if he was exhausted from doing double duty. “I’m not tired,” he said with a smile, raving that he had enjoyed meeting many of the other songwriters in the race this year.

All four of the presenters who handed the Oscars to the honorees are also in the Oscar race this year. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother star Mahershala Ali honored Norman; Wild Horse Nine star John Malkovich honored his Dangerous Liaisons costar Close; Julianne Moore, teaming up with Todd Haynes, honored Vachon and Koffler; and Damon, the star of The Odyssey, honored Scott.

As Close took the stage to accept the award from Malkovich, she wiped tears away from her eyes. The star of films including Fatal Attraction, 101 Dalmatians, The Wife, Albert Nobbs, and The Big Chill spoke about being raised in a religious cult and how, in her childhood, animated films were her only escape. She also spoke about being nominated for eight Oscars over her career, insisting that it didn’t phase her not to emerge victorious. “As an outsider, I have never worried about whether I was going to win or not,” she says. “I have always felt that the great honor is to be in the room.”

She wrapped up her speech with a strong statement against AI. “The craft of acting and of great storytelling has never been more vital to the existence of our fragile, violent, but capable-of-transcendence species,” she said. “We are not machines. We are flawed. Our imperfections are our salvation.”

Vachon and Koffler have been making indie films through Killer Films since 1995, championing movies like Far From Heaven, Boys Don’t Cry, Kids, Carol, and Still Alice (which won Moore her Academy Award for lead actress). They dedicated their awards to the many people they’d worked with over the years, some of whom were in the room. “We have walked into propellers with you and what has resulted is usually a piece of work that has touched somebody. Sometimes it’s seen by millions of people and sometimes it’s seen by tens of people,” said Vachon. “But our movies came to life and made it to the screen because writers and directors trusted us with their stories and actors knew we were creating an environment that enabled them to give their best performance.”

Many of the honorees spoke about the mentors and industry giants who had helped them along the way. Close said she’d promised her World According to Garp director, George Roy Hill, that she’d thank him if she ever won an Oscar. “I never got the chance to thank the man who put me in my first movie. Now I can,” she said, holding her statuette up high. Scott, the director whose prolific career output includes Thelma & Louise, Gladiator, Black Hawk Down, Alien, Blade Runner, and The Martian, told a story in his video message about making his brother star in his very first project, the 1965 short film Boy and Bicycle. “I’m flattered and proud to accept this award, but I also accept it for Tony,” Scott said of his brother, who died in 2012. “His great work would certainly have earned this recognition.”

items.title: Zendaya “Felt Overwhelmed” on the Set of ‘The Odyssey.’ Luckily, Tom Holland Came to Support Her
items.description: On the set of The Odyssey, in which Zendaya plays the goddess Athena, there were some particularly challenging days, as the actor recalled during a recent special screening attended by the cast at Los Angeles’s Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. While filming
items.author: Alessandra De Tommasi
paragraphs: On the set of The Odyssey, in which Zendaya plays the goddess Athena, there were some particularly challenging days, as the actor recalled during a recent special screening attended by the cast at Los Angeles’s Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. While filming certain scenes—especially those with a crowd of extras—the 30-year-old actor felt “incredibly nervous,” she said.

How did she manage to keep the situation under control? Thank her husband, Tom Holland, whom Zendaya says went to set that day to cheer her up. Spider-Man: Brand New Day star Holland also appears in The Odyssey as Telemachus, son of Odysseus and Penelope. And although he wasn’t scheduled to work at that particular moment, he showed up anyway to support his wife.

“I felt overwhelmed, to say the least,” Zendaya said at the screening, as reported by the Daily Mail, with the actor looking stunning in her cream-colored one-shoulder dress, pixie cut, and Christian Louboutin stilettos. “It was interesting because I was on a night shoot, and I remember I came in and I was like, This is like, a pinch-me moment…. I’m in front of these people who I’ve admired, but I’m just like, I don’t want to mess this up.”

While she admitted that these emotions might have worked for her character, they were not so good for her state of mind: “I was incredibly nervous, which I guess is helpful for the scene, but there’s so many other background actors as well who are performing their hearts out—so many—stunt performers who are performing and giving the most beautiful performances.”

The turning point came when Holland stepped behind the scenes to encourage her. “It helped that Tom came to set that day, and he was, like, in the corner like, ‘You got this, you’re doing good.’” It was a team effort.

Zendaya and Holland are one of Hollywood’s most admired couples, not only for their discretion (they quietly married last August 4 in Surrey) but also for the care with which they address sensitive issues, such as mental health. Even in the cult series Euphoria, Zendaya’s character, Rue, grapples with psychological issues—in addition to addiction—as a way to raise public awareness and combat the stigma that often surrounds these kinds of situations.
Originally published in Vanity Fair Italia.

items.title: Billy Crystal Answers the Proust Questionnaire
items.description: What is your idea of perfect happiness?
items.author: BILLY CRYSTAL
paragraphs: What is your idea of perfect happiness?
120/80 and a steady stream.
What is your greatest fear?
How this is all going to end.
Which historical figure do you most identify with?
Which living person do you most admire?
My wife, Janice. Fearless, smart, optimistic, hilarious, loving…adored by all.
What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?
Self-doubt. Wait, now I’m not sure of the answer. Was that okay? Can we come back to that one?
What is the trait you most deplore in others?
What is your greatest extravagance?
My imagination. And I like clothes.
What is your favorite journey?
From my dressing room to backstage—standing alone in the dark, a deep breath, and then feeling it’s time and walking out into the light.
What do you consider the most overrated virtue?
On what occasion do you lie?
When there’s a gun pointed at me.
What do you dislike most about your appearance?
Which living person do you most despise?
I’d rather not say, and thank you for your attention to this matter!
Which words or phrases do you most overuse?
“Sorry, I didn’t see your text till now.”
What is your greatest regret?
That my father died when I was 15 and never got to see my family, my career, and the man I think I am.
What or who is the greatest love of your life?
When and where were you happiest?
In the hospital waiting room, when my girls were born, and the doctor said everyone was fine.
Which talent would you most like to have?
What is your current state of mind?
If you could change one thing about yourself, what would it be?
I’d stop worrying about everyone all the time.
If you could change one thing about your family, what would it be?
That they’d finally understand why I worry about everyone all the time
What do you consider your greatest achievement?
We raised two fantastic daughters who became good, hard-working, honest people and great spouses and mothers in the middle of this business.
If you were to die and come back as a person or thing, what do you think it would be?
A New York Yankee with a sense of humor.
If you could choose what to come back as, what would it be?
What is your most treasured possession?
I lost them all, so I’d have to say my memory.
What do you regard as the lowest depth of misery?
Where would you like to live?
In the beautiful state of clarity.
What is your favorite occupation?
What is your most marked characteristic?
Determination, focus, self-starting.
What do you most value in your friends?
Love, empathy, loyalty, a sense of humor, and a handful of quarters for the parking meters.
Who are your favorite writers?
Hemingway, David Sedaris, Neil Simon, Herb Gardner, Arthur Miller, Victor Hugo.
Who is your favorite hero of fiction?
Santiago, the fisherman in The Old Man and the Sea.
Who are your heroes in real life?

Picasso, Muhammad Ali, Mickey Mantle, Buster Keaton, Sid Caesar, Mel Brooks, JFK, Alan Shepard—and Jim Redmond, a father who ran out of the stands at the ’92 Olympics to help his son, Derek, who had torn a hamstring in his race and was struggling to stand up and continue. They held onto each other and crossed the finish line together. Perfect.
What are your favorite names?
What is it that you most dislike?
A port-a-potty on a hot day.
How would you like to die?
Holding Janice’s hand. Ready, not frightened, satisfied, and with a smile and a goodbye to my family. And if there’s a laugh, that’s the last thing I hear? That would be great.

items.title: THE BIRTH OF BOND | Vanity Fair
items.description: Half a century ago, at the dawn of the commercial-jet age, James Bond strode into movie history, to show audiences how stylish and thrilling life could be. But creating the cinematic Bond was fraught with peril, as best-selling author Ian Fleming discovered wh
items.author: David Kamp
paragraphs: Half a century ago, at the dawn of the commercial-jet age, James Bond strode into movie history, to show audiences how stylish and thrilling life could be. But creating the cinematic Bond was fraught with peril, as best-selling author Ian Fleming discovered when he first tried to take his hero to the screen. DAVID KAMP recalls the unlikely team—two small-time producers, a journeyman director, and a "rough diamond" of a star―behind 007's film debut, Dr. No,, the beginning of a $5 billion franchise
ORIGINALLY PUBLISHED IN OCTOBER 2012

nter Sean Connery, dark hair slicked with pomade, eyes locking hungrily upon a beautiful green-eyed girl. Her return glance leaves no doubt—the feeling is mutual. His slouch and casual banter exude languor and nonchalance, but there's an undercurrent of coiled menace to this man, as though he might, at any moment, spring into table-overturning, crockery-shattering action.

Except nothing of the sort happens. Instead, the other fellow in the scene cuts the tension by taking out his fiddle and favoring the room with a jaunty tune learned, he says in a stagy brogue, "in the old ruins on the top of Knocknasheega!"

This isn't a James Bond picture. It is 1959, and Connery is putting in time in a cornball live-action Disney feature called Darby O'Gill and the Little People. He's the second male lead, billed beneath not only Albert Sharpe, the elderly Irish character actor in the title role—a kindly farmhand who sees leprechauns—but also the greeneyed girl, the ingenue Janet Munro. Though verily pump-misting pheromonal musk into the air, to a degree unmatched before or since by any actor in a Disney family movie, Connery is still a jobbing scuffler, not a star. He has no idea of what lies in store for him.

The seventh of Ian Fleming's Bond novels, Goldfinger, has recently reached the shops. But there are no Bond pictures yet. In London, a Long Island-born film producer named Albert R. Broccoli, known as Cubby, is still lamenting that he blew his chance with Fleming. The previous year, Broccoli had set up a meeting with the English author and his representatives to talk about securing movie rights to the Bond series, only to miss the meeting to tend to his wife, who had recently been diagnosed with terminal cancer. In Broccoli's absence, his business partner, Irving Allen, let Fleming know that he didn't share his colleague's ardor. "In my opinion," Allen told Bond's creator, "these books are not even good enough for television."

This is an older, stiffer world, with Britain just five years removed from food rationing and America still in an era of Kramdens, Eisenhowers, and finned Caddies. It is a world unfamiliar with the catchphrases "Shaken, not stirred" and "Bond, James Bond," where no ears have ever heard Monty Norman's four-note Bond motif and no eyes have ever taken in Maurice Binder's amniotic credit sequences of lissome women undulating in silhouette to lavishly charted John Barry arrangements.

But it is also a world in transition. Transatlantic jet service is newly available to commercial passengers, thanks to the carriers B.O.A.C. and Pan American. G.D. Searle & Company, a pharmaceutical concern, is awaiting approval from the Food and Drug Administration to market one of its products, Enovid, as a birthcontrol pill for women. A scrubbed, fit group of U.S. military test pilots has just been introduced to the public as the Mercury Seven, America's first astronauts. And the undeclared Democratic frontrunner in the next presidential election is only 42 years old.

In March 1961, when he actually is the president, John F. Kennedy lists Fleming's fifth Bond novel, From Russia with Love, as one of his 10 current favorite reads in a Life magazine article. That same year, Broccoli, having parted ways with Allen and joined forces with another producer, a Canadian by the name of Harry Saltzman, finally gets the rights to turn Fleming's books into movies. After an arduous and seemingly fruitless search to find a lead actor mutually agreeable to the two producers and their studio benefactor, United Artists, Broccoli circles back to one of the lesser-knowns among the candidates: Sean Connery. To confirm his hunch that this tall, handsome Scotsman could be the guy, Broccoli, while in Hollywood, arranges for his new wife, Dana, to join him in a screening room at the Samuel Goldwyn Studio. There they watch the only Connery footage that Cubby has been able to rustle up: Darby OGill and the Little People. Dana Broccoli's response is instantaneous: "That's our Bond!"
And so on October 5,1962, at the London Pavilion theater, in Piccadilly Circus, Connery joins Fleming, Broccoli, and Saltzman on the red carpet for the world premiere of the first Bond film, Dr. No.

half-century later, even in an era inured to skin, gunplay, and wide-screen shots of tropical waterfalls, Dr. No remains exhilarating to watch. The azure brightness of Jamaica, with Connery striding purposefully through it; the seawater-salted flesh and ounces-light wardrobe of Ursula Andress; the modernist bachelor-pad fantasia that is the undersea lair of the titular doctor, played with cool reserve by Joseph Wiseman—it's all so fantastically stylish, racy, and forward-looking. So imagine what it must have been like for the people who actually saw the picture in a theater when it first came out.

Dr. No took just a few months in the U.K. to recoup its $1 million budget and ultimately made 20 times that amount in its initial release. Theater bookers in the U.S. hedged their bets at first, putting out the film "in the sticks," as a chagrined Broccoli noted, before allowing the sophisticates in New York and Los Angeles to see it. Nevertheless, the drumbeat had already begun, with North Carolina's Rocky Mount Telegram, for example, relishing how Connery "twists his supple body through a tiny aperture to potential freedom." The syndicated entertainment columnist Erskine Johnson suggested that "tawny 26-year-old Ursula Andress should have been billed not by her last name, but as 'Undress.' "

As it turned out, the coastal intelligentsia were pretty easily won over, too. "Oh, it was dazzling: Ursula coming out of the ocean, the brilliant art direction, straining your eyes to see the almost-nude women in the opening credits. They were cheap tricks, but good tricks," says Buck Henry, who, with Mel Brooks and the TV producer Daniel Melnick, was inspired in '65 to create the sitcom spoof Get Smart in homage. "It wasn't Brueghel," Henry says of the early Bond films, "but it was like the stuff that Lichtenstein and those other guys were doing—great Pop art carried into another medium."

Dr. No and its two follow-ups, From Russia with Love (1963) and Goldfinger (1964), are the cornerstones of Bond mania. Like the early Lennon-McCartney singles that spurred Beatlemania, they augured bigger, more elaborate things to come, but the sheer excitement they generated remains unsurpassable. Not only were these movies terrifically entertaining, they also delivered a sort of jet-age holodeck experience, granting regular folk an opportunity to glimpse the future awaiting them. As of 1960, fewer than 2 percent of all Americans had traveled internationally by air. So both Dr. No and From Russia with Love include what are essentially fetish shots of Pan Am jets landing on runways as air-traffic controllers announce their arrival. ("Hello, London, your flight PA1 just landed in Istanbul")

"It was a sense of 'Buy your ticket—we're going to take you places!' " says Guy Hamilton, the director of Goldfinger. He recalls the Broccoli-Saltzman attitude toward Bond transport as "Don't take a train when you can take a plane, and if you're going to take a plane, take the newest one around. And if you give Bond a car, don't show what's been seen—show what's not out yet." This is why, while Bond drives an Aston Martin DBIII in Goldfinger the novel, he drives a DB5 in Hamilton's movie, made five years later. It's also why, when Bond comes to after being knocked out with a tranquilizer gun in the same film, he is told, by no less than Honor Blackman's knockout aviatrix, Pussy Galore, that he is aboard "Mr. Goldfinger's Lockheed JetStar"—this at a time when the very concept of a private business jet was virtually unheard of. Even Bond's room-service breakfast order in From Russia with Love— "Green figs, yogurt, coffee, very black"—sounds ahead of its time.

Beyond the travelogue aspect, there was the sex aspect—another way, as it were, to hitch a ride with James Bond. "The actual film, to film, was sexy," says Shirley Eaton of her scenes with Connery in Goldfinger. Eaton is famous for being the blonde girl whose body is discovered nude, lifeless, and coated in gold paint—her death (by "skin suffocation," not a medical possibility in real life) a punishment by her boss, Auric Goldfinger, for switching to Bond's side.

But it's Eaton's first scene with Connery that packs the erotic wallop. Bond, poolside at Miami's Fontainebleau hotel, has worked out from which room Goldfinger's accomplice is spying on his opponent's cards, thereby allowing Goldfinger to cheat at his alfresco games of high-stakes gin rummy. Letting himself into the room, Bond discovers Eaton's Jill Masterson lying stomach-down in a black bikini on a balcony lounger, using binoculars and a radio set to convey the card info into Goldfinger's earpiece. Wearing a shorty jumpsuit of pale-blue terry cloth that only someone as masculine as Connery could pull off, Bond, grinning, simply lowers himself gently onto Jill, shrewdly opting for horizontal bodily contact rather than force to accomplish his mission.

Eaton, then 27, had been acting in movies since her teen years, "always playing the girl next door," she says, or a pretty thing to be ogled in one of Britain's low-budget Carry On comedies. "But this was entirely new," she says. "It was grown-up sexuality. Sean and I just fell into our natural sensuality without any rumpy-pumpy, and I think that's what made it so exciting."

Honor Blackman, likewise, had already established herself as the judo-chopping, leather-clad Dr. Cathy Gale on the British TV series The Avengers but found the Bond universe to have an altogether different dynamic. "Cathy Gale was a very proper lady, with collars up to the chin," she says, "whereas Pussy was supposed to match Bond's sexuality. She was a tough broad who also showed a fair amount of bosom." Johnny Carson, just a few years into hosting The Tonight Show, was so taken with the scene in which Pussy finally surrenders to Bond's charms (they trade martial-arts body flips in a hay-filled barn before falling into a love clutch) that "he badgered and badgered me—would I show him how it was done?" she says. Blackman feared injuring Carson, but she flew to New York to rehearse the bit with him, and when they performed it live "he passionately kissed me at the end, which wasn't planned. It was funny, but it also showed how much even someone like Johnny Carson wanted to be James Bond."

an Fleming had long been alert to the screen potential of his books, but realizing this potential proved to be something of a chore.
