- Jason Isbell and the 400 Unit, ‘Cumberland Gap’ (2017) Before his name became synonymous with the best in detail-rich Americana songwriting thanks to albums like his 2013 opus, Southeastern, Jason Isbell was one of the three singer-guitarists in this century’s top literate bar band, Drive-By Truckers. On this rocker from his 2017 LP, The Nashville Sound, Isbell showed how hard he could still bring it, singing about working-class angst and desperation in the heart of coal country over the roaring backing of his band the 400 Unit. “Maybe the Cumberland Gap just swallows you whole,” he wonders. That sense of fatalism is deep in his bones, but so is the dream of punching your way out. —J.D.

- At the Drive-In, ‘Arcarsenal’ (2000) At the Drive-In’s third album, Relationship of Command, truly felt like a band firing on all cylinders. Their sound was sharper, crisper, and more adrenaline-surged than ever — some of that a result of producer Ross Robinson finding ways to capture the musicians at their most heightened state. And the first song, “Arcarsenal,” offers the best introduction to the power coursing through the album, functioning as a forceful call to action to break from societal conformity. It’s also a solid example of Omar Rodríguez-López and Cedric Bixler-Zavala’s almost telepathic connection, with Bixler-Zavala howling out the lyrics (“I must have read a thousand faces”) to Rodríguez-López’s blistering riffs. —J.L.

- Louis XIV, ‘Finding Out True Love Is Blind’ (2005) Deliciously sexy and sleazy, this track epitomized why Louis XIV were once banned in Alabama. What other band can make “carrot juice” sound dirty? The standout on 2005’s The Best Little Secrets Are Kept, this song encapsulates a truly horny era replete with flat-ironed bangs, that first foray into skinny jeans, and a solid lacquering of eyeliner. The song may have an STD or two, but singer Jason Hill is an equal opportunity letch: smart girls, short girls, tough girls, girls of all races and creeds, he’s down to wind you up and make you crawl to him — even 20 years later. —B.E.

- Deerhunter, ‘Desire Lines’ (2010) On their space-rock epiphany “Desire Lines,” the Atlanta band Deerhunter found a happy place somewhere between moody Velvet Underground drone poetry and languid, stretched out, eat-a-peach transcendence. The peak moment on their great LP Halcyon Digest, the song begins as a hesitant reflection on twentysomething coming-of-age ambivalences, then lifts off into a mind-meld monster jam between guitarists Lockett Pundt and Bradford Cox, who make like shoegaze ninjas for three dazzling minutes. It’s a modern psychedelic bounty that brilliantly undercut trippy escapism with real-life ambivalence. —J.D.

- Sturgill Simpson, ‘Call to Arms’ (2016) After the release of his breakthrough album, Metamodern Sounds in Country Music, it was clear that Sturgill Simpson was in a category all his own, far beyond just the bounds of traditional country. He cemented that on 2016’s A Sailor’s Guide to Earth, which ends with the furious “Call to Arms,” where Simpson, alongside a wailing horn section, bemoans our modern discontents. “They serve up distractions and we eat ‘em with fries, until the bombs fall out of our fucking skies,” he sings. When Simpson appeared on Saturday Night Live, he finished the song with the ultimate rock star move: smashing his guitar.—Marissa R. Moss
- Ought, ‘Beautiful Blue Sky’ (2015)

The Montreal post-punk rebels Ought racked up a string of cerebral records in the 2010s, eventually evolving into the new band Cola, which put out one of 2026’s finest rock statements with Cost of Living Adjustment. “Beautiful Blue Sky” is a life-affirming staccato guitar groove, building under Tim Darcey’s acerbically witty voice, as he narrates another boring no

items.title: The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time
items.description: Editor’s note, February 2024: In the two and a half years since Rolling Stone rolled out the all-new, fully revamped version of our 500 Greatest Songs list in September 2021, artists like Beyonce, Lana Del Rey, and Taylor Swift have all released classic tracks
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: Editor’s note, February 2024: In the two and a half years since Rolling Stone rolled out the all-new, fully revamped version of our 500 Greatest Songs list in September 2021, artists like Beyonce, Lana Del Rey, and Taylor Swift have all released classic tracks. So we’ve updated the list. We kept the update light; the 2021 list covered many decades of popular music, and was the result of a vote among more than 300 artists, writers, producers and industry figures; this update covers three years, from 2021 to early 2024.

In 2004, Rolling Stone published its list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time. It’s one of the most widely read stories in our history, viewed hundreds of millions of times on this site. But a lot has changed since 2004; back then the iPod was relatively new, and Billie Eilish was three years old. So we’ve decided to give the list a total reboot. To create the new version of the RS 500 we convened a poll of more than 250 artists, musicians, and producers — from Angelique Kidjo to Zedd, Sam Smith to Megan Thee Stallion, M. Ward to Bill Ward — as well as figures from the music industry and leading critics and journalists. They each sent in a ranked list of their top 50 songs, and we tabulated the results.

Nearly 4,000 songs received votes. Where the 2004 version of the list was dominated by early rock and soul, the new edition contains more hip-hop, modern country, indie rock, Latin pop, reggae, and R&B. More than half the songs here weren’t present on the old list, including a third of the Top 100. The result is a more expansive, inclusive vision of pop, music that keeps rewriting its history with every beat.

- Harry Styles, ‘As It Was’ The lead single from Harry Styles’ third album balances its agitated inner monologue, where the shape-shifting pop star picks at the details of a relationship in crisis, with spun-sugar synths that give cover to his torment. From its playful opening — Styles’ goddaughter Ruby giggling “Go on, Harry, we want to say goodnight to you!” — to its singsong bridge, during which Styles’ thoughts are ping-ponging around his head at “high-speed internet” velocities, “As It Was” paints an unusually vivid picture. Everything might seem fine on first glance, but it all becomes more troubling (“What kind of pills are you on?”) with each repeated glimpse.

- Townes Van Zandt, ‘Pancho and Lefty’ An epic story-song about a bandit and the friend who betrays him, “Pancho and Lefty” became a country hit thanks to Willie Nelson and Merle Haggard’s 1983 duet. But it’s the songwriter’s own forlorn reading, on 1972’s The Late Great Townes Van Zandt, that best conveys the doomed fates of the main characters. It begins with what might be one of the most descriptive opening verses in the country-folk canon: “Living on the road my friend/was gonna keep you free and clean/now you wear your skin like iron/your breath as hard as kerosene.” “It’s hard to take credit for the writing,” Van Zandt said in 1984, “because it came from out of the blue.”

- Lizzo, ‘Truth Hurts’ “That song is my life and its words are my truth,” Lizzo wrote at the time. She had to tack on a writing credit to British singer Mina Lioness, who had tweeted its iconic line “I just took a DNA test, turns out I’m 100 percent that bitch,” but the power of this gale-force breakup banger was pure Lizzo, uproariously swaggering and endearingly soulful. “Truth Hurts” was originally released in 2017, but the song got a big boost two years later, when Gina Rodriguez day-drunkenly sang it in the Netflix show Someone Great, and it became Lizzo’s signature hit.

- Harry Nilsson, ‘Without You’ “We did it because my career was on the wane and we wanted something to make a hit,” Harry Nilsson bluntly told an interviewer when asked why he covered Badfinger’s near-despondent ballad: “I heard it and searched through every Beatles album for two and a half weeks, trying to find out which one of their tunes it was.” Producer Richard Perry agreed, piling on the strings to showcase Nilsson’s desperate lunge of a vocal. Both were right — the song went to Number One and earned a Grammy nomination for Record of the Year.

- Carly Simon, ‘You’re So Vain’ The holy mother of all diss tracks, “You’re So Vain” contains one of the most enduring musical mysteries of all time. Just who is so vain that he probably thinks the song is about him? Simon previously revealed that actor Warren Beatty inspired the second verse of the song (“Oh, you had me several years ago/When I was still naive”), but speculation abounds regarding the other man (or men) behind the ire. Either way, the track — boasting omnipresent Seventies arranger Paul Buckmaster’s orchestration and Mick Jagger’s background vocals — is pure soft-rock fire.

- Cyndi Lauper, ‘Time After Time’ Cyndi Lauper was nervous about “Time After Time” — the aching ballad she wrote in the studio with keyboardist Rob Hyman to finish off her blockbuster solo debut, She’s So Unusual. “I asked them to please not put ‘Time After Time’ out as the first single,” Lauper said. “People would never have accepted me. If you do a ballad first, and then a rocker, that doesn’t work.” Her instincts were right: Following the jaunty “Girls Just Want to Have Fun,” “Time” became her first Number One.

- The Pixies, ‘Where Is My Mind?’ No song typifies the freakish pop instincts that made the Pixies stand out in a sea of gloomy Reagan-era bands better than “Where Is My Mind?” Joey Santiago’s lead guitar is catchier than most Top 40 hooks, and by the time Fight Club made this song iconic a decade after its release, it had already formed part of the DNA of countless alternative-radio hits in the years between, from Nirvana to Korn. When an interviewer in 1988 asked about his unique ability to crank out great songs, Black Francis’ answer was typically cryptic: “It’s nice to have space. How much can one brain deal with?”

- Kanye West, ‘Stronger’ Explaining the tighter, broader-reaching songs on his third album, Graduation, Kanye West said, “I applied a lot of the things I learned on tour [in 2006] with U2 and the Rolling Stones, about songs that rock stadiums. And they worked!” West found the inspiration for his most grandiose statement to date from Daft Punk’s “Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger,” which he sampled and reshaped. West is a big fan of the French duo: “These guys really stick with the whole not-showing-their-faces thing. Just amazing discipline — that’s straight martial-arts status.”

- Miles Davis, ‘So What’ It’s likely that no song on this list has soundtracked more dinner parties than Kind of Blue’s warm, welcoming first track. But at the time it was a jarring departure, trading bebop chord changes for a more open-ended modal style. According to pianist Bill Evans, the trumpeter worked up his material just hours before recording dates, but the all-star band here sounds like it’s been living with “So What” for years: Saxophonists John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley turn in solos that have since become as iconic as any in jazz history, and the rhythm section of Evans, bassist Paul Chambers, and drummer Jimmy Cobb swings like it’s dancing on air.

- Bad Bunny, ‘Titi Me Pregunto’ “Tití Me Preguntó” is a showcase for Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny’s unbridled creativity and eccentric pop genius, mixing frantic dembow beats, a classy sample by bachata master Anthony Santos, and a coda with a dash of Latin psychedelia to the global mainstream. He does it all with panache and a healthy sense of humor. Using the archetype of the concerned Latin American aunt asking about her nephew’s potential girlfriends as a starting point, he launches into a hilarious tirade of salacious puns to a bouncy party vibe that — in typical Bad Bunny fashion — unexpectedly morphs into moody self-reflection.

- Lil Nas X, ‘Old Town Road’ Montero Hill was an Atlanta college dropout sleeping on his sister’s couch and looking to break into music when he came across a track he liked by a Dutch 19-year-old called YoungKio that was based around a banjo sample from a Nine Inch Nails track. “I was picturing, like, a loner cowboy runaway,” he told Rolling Stone. Within a year “Old Town Road” was the longest-running Number One song of all time, seeming to sum up eons of American cross-cultural love and theft in just one minute and 53 seconds.

- The Breeders, ‘Cannonball’ Notified by fax that her services in the Pixies were no longer required, Kim Deal called up her twin sister, Kelley, to be her new guitarist (never mind that she didn’t know how to play guitar) and had the last laugh when this absurdist gem became an MTV phenomenon in 1993. “When people were talking about the Breeders being a one-off,” Kelley told Rolling Stone, “I was like ‘No, actually … the Pixies are a side project.'” A little over a year later, the Breeders were on an extended break of their own, but the effortlessly fun trampoline bounce of “Cannonball” is one for all time.

- The Weeknd, ‘House of Balloons’ Far from the international superstar he’d become, Toronto singer-songwriter Abel Tesfaye didn’t even send out photos or do any interviews when he released the first Weeknd album. “The whole ‘enigmatic artist’ thing, I just ran with it,” he said. “No one could find pictures of me. It reminded me of some villain shit.” But the title track of House of Balloons nevertheless set the course for his career, both thematically — drugs and sex, meet depression — and musically, with its sample of Siouxsie and the Banshees’ “Happy House” announcing a new direction for R&B.

- Solange, ‘Cranes in the Sky’ In an interview with her sister Beyoncé, R&B innovator Solange Knowles described how this song was inspired, in part, by overzealous real estate development she noticed around Miami: “This idea of building up, up, up that was going on in our country at the time, all of this excessive building, and not really dealing with what was in front of us.” She turned the metaphor inward to examine her own feelings about change, self-doubt, and aspiration, finishing the song years after it was originally conceived with producer Raphael Saadiq to create a lavish moment of neo-soul introspection.

- Lil Wayne, ‘A Milli’ Producer Bangladesh looped the opening chords from Gladys Knight and the Pips’ “Don’t Burn Down the Bridge,” then segued to a drill-like volley of trap drums. He gave the beat to his friend Shanell — a onetime R&B singer on Wayne’s Young Money Entertainment — to pass along. Wayne initially had grand plans for “A Milli”: He wanted to use the instrumental as skits for rappers like Tyga, Hurricane Chris, Corey Gunz, and Lil Mama. In the end, though, “A Milli” is just Weezy solo, blacking out in the booth and dazzling everyone who hears him.

- Azealia Banks, ‘212’ In 2011, Azealia Banks was a teenage rapper-singer whose clear talent yielded a development deal with XL Recordings but little else. “She had been working on a collection of tracks and there was one Dutch house-sounding one that was just absolutely insane,” producer Jacques Greene recalled. Banks freestyled ferociously about her New York hometown and, uh, cunnilingus over the jittery beats of Belgian house duo’s Lazy Jay’s “Float My Boat.” Initially released in 2011 as a viral track, “212” was a hip-house banger that earned Banks a deal with Interscope and served notice that this uninhibited provocateur would not be constrained.

- Weezer, ‘Buddy Holly’ Never has geek been so chic as in Weezer’s 1994 breakout single, “Buddy Holly.” Written for frontman Rivers Cuomo’s girlfriend, the poppy ode to nerdy romance was almost left off the band’s self-titled debut, also known as the Blue Album, due to Cuomo and now-ex-member Matt Sharp’s reticence. “We had the sense that it could be taken as a novelty song, and people aren’t going to take the album seriously,” Sharp told Rolling Stone. After producer Ric Ocasek heard the receptionist at the recording studio humming it, he insisted they keep it in.

- The Four Tops, ‘I Can’t Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch)’ One of Motown’s most rousing anthems, “I Can’t Help Myself” was inspired by songwriter Lamont Dozier’s grandfather, who’d call the women his hairdresser wife fixed up “sugar pie” and “honey bunch.” During the recording, engineer Harold Taylor recalled, “People were banging on the door of the studio; they were so ecstatic about what they heard.” Nevertheless, Levi Stubbs asked Brian Holland if he could do another take. Holland promised him they’d do it soon — and Stubbs’ first pass hit Number One.

- Lady Gaga, ‘Bad Romance’ Shortly after Gaga had established herself as a star, she catapulted to a next level of weirdness with this Nadir “RedOne” Khayat production, which drew upon the electronic music Gaga had been inundated with while touring Europe. “I want the deepest, darkest, sickest parts of you that you are afraid to share with anyone because I love you that much” is how she summed up the idea behind the song. Fittingly, she debuted the hit-to-be at Alexander McQueen’s show at Paris Fashion Week.

- Robert Johnson, ‘Cross Road Blues’ The primal terror in the Mississippi bluesman’s voice, and his mystifying slide guitar playing, transfixed the Sixties generation of British rockers: “I could take the music only in very small measures because it was so intense,” said Eric Clapton. Recorded during a session at a San Antonio hotel room in 1936, two years before Johnson was murdered at 27, “Cross Road Blues” is a mythmaking statement of spiritual desolation and scorched-earth betrayal — even if the legend that it’s about Johnson selling his soul to the devil in exchange for his monster guitar chops is, as far as we know, apocryphal.

- Biz Markie, ‘Just a Friend’ Nobody beats the Biz (1964-2021), an impossibly good-natured DJ, rapper, producer, human beatboxer, and hip-hop personality who broke big with this ode to the friend zone off his second album. Built on a fat beat, plinking piano, and his charmingly off-key singing, “Just a Friend” interpolates Freddie Scott’s 1968 song “(You) Got What I Need” as Biz warbles about a love that will never come to pass. It was based on real life. As he told Rolling Stone in 2000, “I was talking to this girl from L.A., and every time I called her, this dude was at her house, and she’d say, ‘Oh, he’s just a friend.’ I hated that.”

- Santana, ‘Oye Como Va’ Growing up in San Francisco, Carlos Santana was shaped by the city’s psychedelic explosion. “You cannot take LSD and not find your voice,” he once claimed, “because there is nowhere to hide.” And while his early heroes were bluesmen, he changed history with this foundational Latin-rock reworking of a 1962 salsa number by Cuban percussionist Tito Puente. Santana kept the original’s cha-cha pulse but replaced its horns with Greg Rolie’s organ and Carlos’ lysergic guitar flares. Said Puente years later, “He put our music, Latin rock, around the world, man.”

- Juvenile feat. Lil Wayne and Mannie Fresh, ‘Back That Azz Up’ In the late Nineties, Mannie Fresh’s diamond-sharp productions for Cash Money Records helped put New Orleans in the center of the hip-hop map. The title of this hit was so reminiscent of local artist DJ Jubilee’s single “Back That Thang Up” that Jubilee sued (unsuccessfully) for infringement, and the beat rode the “Triggerman” rhythm that is foundational to New Orleans bounce. Juvenile freestyled his best shit-talking bounce rhymes, and Lil Wayne shut it down with a “drop it like it’s hot” hook. As Mannie said, “[He] immediately was just like, ‘Shit, I’m getting a piece of this.’”

- The Go-Gos, ‘Our Lips Are Sealed’ The radiant first hit of the Go-Go’s was influenced, according to writer Jane Wiedlin, by “the Buzzcocks and Sixties girl-group stuff.” It was also inspired by a clandestine relationship she was having with Terry Hall, of U.K. ska group the Specials, who got a co-writing credit because Wiedlin based the lyrics on some poetry he’d written her in a letter. “It was pretty personal,” Wiedlin recalled. “I mean he had a fiancee at the time — nowadays I wouldn’t touch that with a 10-foot pole, but I was 19, and I was like ‘fiancee shmiancee.’”

- Kris Kristofferson, ‘Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down’ The desolation of spirit in Kris Kristofferson’s “Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down” is so heavy, so apparent, that it’s almost hard to listen to. But that despair is exactly what drew Johnny Cash to sing it on his TV variety show in 1970. Kristofferson cut his own stunning studio version that same year for his debut album, Kristofferson. Cash’s interpretation, more shuffling and accessible, is the one most listeners turn to, but listen to them back-to-back if you can, and marvel at how Kristofferson’s lyrics about being hung over, alone, and desperate shake your soul.

- Janet Jackson, ‘Rhythm Nation’ Jackson’s socially conscious Number Two hit came together late in the sessions for her blockbuster LP Rhythm Nation 1814. Co-producer Jimmy Jam recalled being in the studio and “switching between MTV and CNN. Watching music videos on one side and watching atrocities on the other. Somehow they all merged together. The idea for ‘Rhythm Nation’ was you can dance, but we can also do something more intelligent.” When Jam heard Sly and the Family Stone’s “Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)” at a restaurant, he raced to the studio to sample it.

- Curtis Mayfield, ‘Move On Up’ Mayfield’s irresistible “Move On Up” was politically empowering, morally demanding, and effortlessly propulsive, powered by swinging horns and tangy congas — the nine-minute LP version, with its powerful drum break, laid a foundation for disco and hip-hop alike. Mayfield’s message was just as steadfast: that pride and dignity were paramount for Black America to rise. “I’m not trying to say anything to make you think, ‘Well, this is the way, this is the only way,'” Mayfield said. “I’m trying to cover the whole subject.”

- Tammy Wynette, ‘Stand by Your Man’ From the start, this pledge of wifely devotion, the first song Wynette ever co-wrote, was a cultural lightning rod. Feminists recoiled from its pledge of unquestioning fidelity in the Seventies, and Hillary Clinton defined herself a modern woman by slamming the song during Bill Clinton’s first presidential run. But the recording itself steamrolls over ideological objections, as the catch in Wynette’s voice on the verses gives way to a vocal swell that rises to meet the epic sweep of Billy Sherrill’s production.

- Peter Gabriel, ‘Solsbury Hill’ Shortly after Gabriel quit Genesis in 1975, he climbed to the top of Little Solsbury Hill in Somerset, England, to reflect on his life-changing decision. It inspired his debut solo song, in which he explained to fans why he felt the need to go out on his own. Musically, it was a departure too, a pastoral tune with a 12-string acoustic guitar lead that was pointedly different from Genesis’ prog-rock. The song has since become ubiquitous in movies and film trailers. “Maybe I’ve let it go too much,” he admitted to Rolling Stone in 2011.

- The Animals, ‘The House of the Rising Sun’ “We were looking for a song that would grab people’s attention,” said Animals singer Eric Burdon. They found it with the old American folk ballad “The House of the Rising Sun.” In 1962, Bob Dylan had sung this grim tale of a Southern girl trapped in a New Orleans whorehouse. The Animals, from the English coal town of Newcastle, changed the gender in the lyrics, and keyboardist Alan Price created the new arrangement (and grabbed a composer’s credit). Price also added an organ solo inspired by Jimmy Smith’s hit “Walk on the Wild Side.”

- Gladys Knight and the Pips, ‘Midnight Train to Georgia’ Songwriter Jim Weatherly originally composed this as “Midnight Plane to Houston,” only to change it for Cissy Houston (Whitney’s mom) to something “more R&B … in order to get it onto Black radio.” Weatherly had already penned “Neither One of Us,” Knight and the Pips’ Number Two hit, and when they heard “Midnight Train,” they took it to the top. “I never really imagined writing R&B songs,” Weatherly admitted. “I really thought I was writing country songs.” It reflected the times; the 1970s were the first decade since after World War I in which more African Americans were moving to the South than leaving it.

- Dixie Chicks, ‘Goodbye Earl’ A murder ballad with a modern, feminist twist, this jaunty song about poisoning an abusive husband spawned disparate reactions. Some stations banned it, apparently concerned that it would spawn a rash of hubby offings; others shared the number for domestic-abuse hotlines. When the label reps listened to the Chicks’ Fly album, though, they were more concerned with another song: “Sin Wagon,” with its reference to “mattress dancing.” “You can’t say [that],” Natalie Maines recalls their manager’s relayed message from the execs, “but they love the song about premeditated first-degree murder.”

- Mazzy Star, ‘Fade Into You’ Singer Hope Sandoval and guitarist Dave Roback, the prime movers behind Mazzy Star, were active in the 1980s neo-psychedelic Paisley Underground scene in Los Angeles. After Sandoval replaced singer Kendra Smith in the band Opal, David Roback and Sandoval reconstituted the band under the name Mazzy Star. Their second album yielded this spaced-out hit, perhaps dream pop’s ultimate statement of blurry desire. “We’re not so concerned about the outside world,” said Roback. “[Each song] is its own world unto itself.”

- Nirvana, ‘Come as You Are’ “It’s just about people and what they’re expected to act like,” Kurt Cobain said. “The lines in the song are really contradictory. They’re kind of a rebuttal to each other.” The song is driven by a simple riff that Butch Vig goosed with a flanged, subaquatic guitar effect. Cobain apparently lifted it from a 1984 song by U.K. art-metal band Killing Joke, who Dave Grohl paid back 12 years later by drumming on their 2003 album. In the wake of Cobain’s suicide, though, the most haunting lyric would become, “And I swear that I don’t have a gun.”

- Luther Vandross, ‘Never Too Much’ The Eighties’ major male R&B balladeer’s solo debut was financed in part from money he made singing jingles for KFC and 7UP. Vandross had been pushed to do his own thing by Roberta Flack, for whom he’d sung background. Said Vandross: “She said, ‘Luther, you’re too comfortable sitting on that stool singing “ooh and aaah.”‘ Roberta was single-handedly responsible for me starting my own career.” What pushed her was hearing the demo of “Never Too Much” — one of the most buoyant love songs of the Eighties, with Vandross’ high notes as delicate as soap bubbles.

- Daft Punk feat. Pharrell Williams, ‘Get Lucky’ When Pharrell Williams volunteered to appear on Daft Punk’s fourth album, he told them he’d been thinking about Chic legend Nile Rodgers musically; fortuitously, the French dance producers could play him a track they had on hand that they’d made with Rodgers himself. The result was “Get Lucky,” which, as the lead single from their disco-flavored album Random Access Memories, rose like a phoenix to become the song that defined its year. “I think the robots are leading,” Williams told Rolling Stone. “Daft Punk, they’re definitely leading.”

- Joni Mitchell, ‘Help Me’ Mitchell’s 1974 album, Court and Spark, her biggest-selling ever, was also the one that she held the tightest amount of musical control over to date. “I guided everything into place on Court and Spark — even though I didn’t play it, I sang it, and then they played it from that, and it was pretty much as writ,” she said. (Her next album, The Hissing of Summer Lawns, was looser and more jazz-oriented.) “Help Me,” recorded with the jazz group Tom Scott’s L.A. Express, features one of Mitchell’s sultriest vocals and most brocaded arrangements, inspiring Prince, 13 years later, to pay the song lyrical tribute in his “Ballad of Dorothy Parker.”

- John Lee Hooker, ‘Boom Boom’ Hooker, whose canny blues boogie became a root integer for early rock & roll, said this swinging, swaggering bit of primal thump was inspired by his inability to get to a regular gig on time. “There was a young lady named Luilla,” Hooker said. “She was a bartender [at the Apex Bar in Detroit]. I’d always be late, and whenever I’d come in she’d point at me and say, ‘Boom Boom, you’re late again.’ One night she said, ‘Boom boom, I’m gonna shoot you down.’ She gave me a song, but she didn’t know it.” Keith Richards said of Hooker, “Even Muddy Waters was sophisticated next to him.” That was a compliment.

- Van Morrison, ‘Into the Mystic’ Delectably arranged, transportingly sung, this may be the definitive Morrison song — an evocation of “the days of old” that feels like a lover’s whisper. The highlight of 1970’s classic Moondance, “Into the Mystic” benefited from a new, more organic way of recording for him: “It was more like working with an actual band rather than a bunch of session guys,” Morrison said. As for the lyrics, he’d admit, “So many of my songs from that Seventies period, I haven’t a clue what they’re about. A lot of the time, I was just picking up on a vibe.”

- Roy Orbison, ‘Crying’ Orbison said he wrote this lush, dreamy ballad after an encounter with an old flame: “Whether I was physically crying or just crying inside is the same thing.” His near-operatic performance culminated in a high, wailing note, which Orbison never lost the capacity to hit before his death, in 1988. “He sounded like he was singing from an Olympian mountaintop and he meant business,” Bob Dylan wrote in Chronicles. “He was now singing his compositions in three or four octaves that made you want to drive your car over a cliff. He sang like a professional criminal.”

- Steel Pulse, ‘Ku Klux Klan’ The first great British reggae band — and some of the style’s finest songwriters — made their Island Records debut with this incendiary look at the rising tide of racist violence in late-Seventies Britain: “The Ku Klux Klan/Here to stamp out Black man.” They underlined the lyric by actually performing the song live — including a memorable BBC appearance — wearing white Klan headgear. “The hoods seemed extreme at the time, but that’s what we are in a way,” vocalist Michael Riley said. “When we wore them, people started questioning what the song was about instead of just dancing to it.”

- Sade, ‘No Ordinary Love’ Helen Adu’s small but fully inhabited range has been her secret weapon from the beginning. “I decided that if I was gonna sing, I would sing how I speak, because it’s important to be yourself,” she said. Her voice cracks before she reaches the first chorus of this 1992 hit, playing up the romantic drama of the lyric. Even better, so does Stuart Matthewman’s guitar; in the middle of this otherwise mellow groove, he overdubs a seriously moody and low-key noisy part that gives the whole thing a welcome edge. Sade — it’s not just the singer’s name, it’s also a band.

- Beck, ‘Loser’ In 1992, 22-year-old Beck Hansen was scraping by as a video-store clerk while performing bizarro folk songs at L.A. coffeehouses. After friends offered to record some songs, Beck cut “Loser” in his producer’s kitchen. It became the centerpiece of the album Mellow Gold. At first people took “Loser” to be a mere novelty hit, but Beck knew better. “You’d have to be a total idiot to say, ‘I’m the slacker-generation guy. This is my generation.… we’re not gonna fuckin’ show up,'” he said. “I’d be laughed out of the room in an instant.”

- Bon Jovi, ‘Livin’ on a Prayer’ Like his New Jersey model Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi concentrates on working-class heroes and heroines. “Livin’ on a Prayer,” co-written with guitarist Richie Sambora, pumped the everyday struggles of Tommy and Gina full of grandeur — guitar-pick slides, dramatic pauses, the inevitable key change — and continues to resonate today. “It’s great that we wrote songs so long ago that people can still relate to,” Bon Jovi said in 2005. “When I hear ‘Livin’ on a Prayer,’ I think to myself, ‘We wrote that. That song has really made its mark. I guess that works.'”

- Lana Del Rey, ‘A&W’ “A&W” is maximum Lana Del Rey: a sweeping, seven-minute epic that follows the sunburned, SoCal folk rock she’s perfected on recent albums back to the hip-hop-inspired pop productions of her early discography. That musical scope is paired with a narrative that’s no less ambitious — vulnerable and lurid, nostalgic and hopeless, funny and utterly bleak. And the bow tying it all together? The name of classic root beer brand, “A&W” used as shorthand for “American Whore,” because no one bends American iconography to their will like Lana Del Rey.

- Jefferson Airplane, ‘White Rabbit’ The song that brought acid rock to Middle America was a heady rock bolero written by vocalist Slick, reportedly after taking LSD and listening to Miles Davis’ Sketches of Spain. She first recorded it with her earlier band, the Great Society, before rebooting it with the Airplane. “Our parents read us stories like Peter Pan, Alice in Wonderland, and The Wizard of Oz,” Slick said. “They all have a place where children get drugs, and are able to fly or see an Emerald City or experience extraordinary animals and people.… And our parents are suddenly saying, ‘Why are you taking drugs?’ Well, hello!”

- Sister Nancy, ‘Bam Bam’ Nancy (a.k.a. Ophlin Russell) was the DJ (mic controller) for Kingston’s Stereophonic sound system when she met reggae producer Winston Riley in the late Seventies. “I really admired how he took recording serious,” Nancy said. “You couldn’t go into his studio and do any foolishness.” Their peak, “Bam Bam,” is one of the great early dancehall anthems, booming but bright, tough but playful — and it’s been sampled extensively by everyone from Lauryn Hill to Kanye West.
- Missy Elliot, ‘The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)’ As producers, Elliott and Timbaland had already made their rhythmic impact on hip-hop and R&B before Missy’s first single. And some high-profile features

items.title: Dexter: Resurrection Recap: No Strings Attached
items.description: The downside of a show being as good as Dexter: Resurrection has been that a mostly solid episode — one significantly stronger than anything toward the tail end of Dexter’s original run — ends up feeling mid by comparison. After the thrilling reintroduction of
items.author: Louis Peitzman
paragraphs: The downside of a show being as good as Dexter: Resurrection has been that a mostly solid episode — one significantly stronger than anything toward the tail end of Dexter’s original run — ends up feeling mid by comparison. After the thrilling reintroduction of Charley last week, the third episode of the season is somewhat less dynamic. It doesn’t help that the theme being emphasized (we’re really hammering those home this year!) is a retread of ground we’ve already covered. Do we need Dexter philosophizing about how he once walked a lonely road but now understands the importance of having attachments? That’s what last season was for!

I guess with three other serial killers in the episode, it’s good to draw some contrasts. We open with the Five Borough Killer, who lures a maintenance worker named Trey up to the roof of a building. “I’ll let you in on a secret,” FBK says before shoving the man to his death (and ruining Dexter and Charley’s date). “Nobody cares.” That’s not entirely true — Dexter certainly does, and as we saw at the end of the last episode, he and FBK lock eyes post-kill. Dex races into the building to find him, but it’s hard to run up that many stairs in your 50s. While the two men see just enough of each other to cause problems down the line, Dexter is forced to abandon his pursuit so he can focus on the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger. Meanwhile, Harrison has arrived on the scene and thankfully sees his dad before anyone else does. Yes, Dex observed some new details about FBK that could help identify him, but he doesn’t want to put himself back on Wallace’s radar. It’s the first sensible choice he’s made recently.

We’ll get back to Dexter. For now, let’s follow FBK, who AirDrops his latest snuff film to a bunch of unsuspecting (and now traumatized) coffee-shop patrons from the subway station below. In addition to dispelling any theories that Trey’s death was an accident, it also helps Wallace profile FBK as a “power-control killer.” “Their pleasure is derived from the psychological torment of their victims,” she tells Oliva. In this case, the victims are the residents of New York City (hey, that’s me!), who now live in fear of a serial killer in smart glasses. Unfortunately, the NYPD has very little to go on, even as Wallace presses for useful fingerprints on the scene. And she has other problems to worry about. Across the street from the building where FBK pushed Trey to his death, Don Framt is watching Wallace work and singing a very familiar song. No, Brian Cox’s cover of “Stayin’ Alive” is not going to chart, but it triggers the hell out of Wallace, who angrily confronts him. As they face off, Framt backs up his wheelchair so it hits the curb, and he tumbles to the ground. Though his laughter makes it clear he’s uninjured, the damage is done.

To the many witnesses at the FBK crime scene, it sure looks like Wallace shoved an octogenarian, and that’s enough for him to sue the NYPD for harassment. Captain Mixon takes his most dogged detective off the New York Ripper case — adding insult to injury, he even takes down her murder board. (Please tell me I’m not the only person who remembers Trial & Error.) When Wallace tries to approach Mixon, Oliva wisely stops her and demands an explanation for her erratic behavior. It’s here that we get a “Stayin’ Alive” origin story that nobody asked for. Wallace explains that during her first week as an officer, she responded to a noise-code violation in an apartment building. What she found there was her first dead body: a woman torn to shreds by the Ripper. “Stayin’ Alive” was playing on repeat, but Wallace couldn’t turn it off for fear of tampering with the crime scene. The fact that Framt sang it to her is proof he was the man she brushed past in the stairwell that day, and had she stopped him, she could have saved 19 lives. Now she listens to the Bee Gees track so she’ll never forget. Sorry, but this doesn’t make any sense. Last season, it was simply her favorite song — remember how excitedly she ran to the dance floor at Prater’s gala? It’s hard to square that with the idea that “Stayin’ Alive” is a reminder of her foundational trauma.

I’m probably overthinking it. Let’s circle back to Dexter, who is texting his “love bug” Charley. Harry sees the way Dex is cozying up to his former enemy. “Don’t let your boundaries get confused, son,” he warns. “Things can get messy.” This is the downside of a life with attachments — and Dexter is reminded of that when he’s repeatedly interrupted en route to his date with the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger. First, Harrison shows up to get all the off-the-record intel he can about FBK. The most interesting detail Dex shares is that he spotted a wedding ring on FBK’s finger. Maybe this serial killer isn’t a loner either. The next interruption comes in the form of Quinn, who believes he’s found Prater. In fact, he’s discovered the brownstone where Dexter and Charley plan to dispatch the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger, having linked it to one of Prater’s secret Cayman Islands accounts. “When did Joey Quinn actually become good at this?” Dex wonders via voice-over. The only bright spot is that there are a few potential brownstones owned by the real-estate company connected to the account, so Quinn will have to investigate all of them. That should buy Dexter enough time. Maybe. Quinn also warns him to be on the lookout for Charley — she’s been cleared by the cops, but Quinn still has questions. Looks like he’s going to be at least as big a problem as Batista.

When Dexter finally arrives at the brownstone, he gets a pat down from Charley (kiss already!) and an introduction to the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger a.k.a. Ray Ballard, who is as devoid of charisma as expected. When Dex mentions being held up by family and friends, Ballard tells him, “I cut all of that shit out years ago. Other people just get in the way.” Yes, yes, we get it, attachments versus no attachments. I just feel like Dexter has already landed firmly on the side of keeping his loved ones close — insofar as he can truly love anyone — so I’m not sure why we’re spending so much of the episode on this. At least Dex isn’t wasting time with the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger, whom he invites to check out Prater’s secret wine stash downstairs (hint, hint). There’s just one problem. En route to the kill room, Ballard reveals that his share is a victim he intends to murder in front of Prater. He’s rented a U-Haul and stashed an actual live person in there; if Dexter kills Ballard, they’ll never be able to find poor George.

When Charley refuses to intervene because she doesn’t want to be involved with any actual killing, Dex points out they’d be saving a life, which nudges her toward helping. (I’m not sure I buy her complete personality transplant, but I suppose being rejected by your mother on her deathbed could mess you up.) Charley tells Ballard that Prater is now arriving that night and expects shares immediately, so the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger will have to change his plans. He speeds away to the parking lot where he’s hidden the U-Haul, with Dexter and Charley following in separate cars. As they tail Ballard, the two talk openly while admiring each other’s stalking skills. It has strong date vibes. “The few times I’ve worked with someone else, I was teaching them,” Dex’s voice-over notes. “This is … nice.” Whether or not he realizes it, our boy is down bad. Once they arrive at the parking lot, Charley distracts Ballard and Dexter comes up from behind to knock him out. They’ll meet back at the townhouse, but they have to evade Quinn and rescue George first. Credit to Dex for killing two birds with one stone here — he calls Quinn and says he saw a creepy guy loading a suspicious box into a U-Haul, then points him to the parking lot.

Back at the townhouse, Dexter hangs up victim photos in the kill room, prompting another heart-to-heart with Charley. “Is your thing more about the urge or vengeance?” she asks. It’s a valid question, especially as the show continues to paint Dex as a justice-seeking hero. He admits it’s a little of both, explaining that seeing his mother get chainsawed to death by the cartel as a child now makes him want to save innocent people. This is sort of a retcon — Dexter’s traumatic past has long been an explanation for his Dark Passenger, not why he wants to be a force for good. (And don’t get me started on the way the franchise has aged up shipping-container massacre Dexter. Thanks a lot, Original Sin.) I know this may sound minor, but I don’t love the way the series keeps pulling away from the moral gray area that defined the original run. What happened to the sociopath we all fell in love with?

Charley leaves Dexter to his dirty work, and we get a back-and-forth between Dex and the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger to further underline this week’s themes. He asks Ballard why he kills his victims with an ice pick to the back of the head while they’re sleeping — they die before they even know they’re in danger. Ballard says it’s more about the grief of the people they leave behind. “Everyone thinks that these relationships make their lives better, but it actually makes them weak, vulnerable,” he says. “I free them from that lie. It’s the gift I give all my victims.” This is nonsense, which Dexter calls him on before plunging a knife into his heart. Right on cue, Quinn calls to let Dex know they found the U-Haul and rescued the man inside. Dexter is killing it in both a literal and figurative sense, and he couldn’t have done it alone. As he’s disposing of the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger, he reflects, “No attachments felt simpler, cleaner, but my life has changed. Today would have been impossible without Charley, without Quinn. Maybe I need to resolve to not worry so much about that.” Again, I wasn’t clear on this being a current area of concern for him, but I’m glad he’s feeling so zen: Being in a good headspace is important with the Ripper and the Five Borough Killer still at large. Next up, however, is the JawSplitter, and I’m not looking forward to learning how he earned that name.
• Curious how other longtime Dexter fans feel about the current iteration of the character. Am I wrong that he’s gone too soft?

• Speaking of things I might be wrong about, I have an FBK theory. The wedding ring and Mr. and Mrs. mugs are clearly significant. I wonder if his wife was killed by another serial killer — maybe the Ripper — and the murder went unsolved. That’s why he feels like “nobody cares.”
• At the end of the episode, FBK tinkers with the cameras on the 4 train. His kills have felt a little muted, so I wonder if he’s planning something bigger next.
• Remember Blessing? The writers barely seem to. I know it’s hard to service every character, but he’s a total nonentity so far this season. Maybe Dexter will take him up on his church group invite.

• Fun little New Blood Easter egg: When Harrison thinks back to his first dead bodies, he remembers finding Molly Park. In the next scene, Dex is listening to Molly’s podcast, Merry Fucking Kill, to find out more about the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger.

items.title: The Great British Baking Show Recap: Do You Caramel
items.description: Do you remember the Warrant song “Cherry Pie?” I honestly hope that you don’t, but there’s a lyric from it that I think about all the time: “Tastes so good it makes a grown man cry. Sweet cherry pie.” He’s not, you know, actually talking about cherry pie. He’s
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: Do you remember the Warrant song “Cherry Pie?” I honestly hope that you don’t, but there’s a lyric from it that I think about all the time: “Tastes so good it makes a grown man cry. Sweet cherry pie.” He’s not, you know, actually talking about cherry pie. He’s talking about something else, but this episode reminded me of it. Not because they made cherry pie. In fact, it was Caramel Week, which has very little to do with cherries or pies, but because this episode was so delicious, it made a grown man cry. That grown man is me, and maybe you if you are a man. It also definitely made Moyin cry, and I think maybe, just maybe, we got a little drop melting out of Paul Hollywood’s icicle blue eyes.

Caramel Week starts with the bakers having to make a treacle tart, but the catch is that they have to make the golden syrup themselves. Treacle, where the tart gets its name from, is very similar to molasses, a by-product of the sugar-making process that was repurposed for other foods. (However, there was never a Great Treacle Flood.) Golden syrup, which is now used to make the dessert, doesn’t really have an American corollary, just like you can’t find construction paper in any store in the U.K. (How do English kids make birthday cards for their nans? Do they use paper plates?) It’s kind of like Karo corn syrup, but it’s not made out of corn; it’s made out of boiling sugar and water for a really long time, as the bakers demonstrate. While I like the idea of making a very traditional dessert, particularly because it plays to the strengths of more mature bakers like Connie, asking them to make the syrup is kinda silly. Everyone just buys it in the store. What’s next? Making them grow their own baking powder? Is that how you make baking powder? No clue. I’ve only ever bought it in the store. I guess, like Mo preparing for this challenge, I’ll just watch two (2) TikToks about it and call it a day.

A treacle tart, as Mo says, is the kind of medieval food that is a British staple from when they were known for having the most terrible cuisine on the planet, but they stick by it anyway. It combines breadcrumbs and golden syrup and, honestly, I’ve never eaten one because I think I would rather lick the underside of a boot. Most of the bakers do a great job. Tom turns his into a PB&J treacle tart, even though he eats his PB&Js with cherry conserve. I’m sorry. The PB&J Council of America specifies that our national delicacy should be made only with grape, raspberry, or strawberry jelly and never the kind where the peanut butter and the jelly come in the same jar. Paul says it tastes great and like something totally different. Yeah, that’s probably why they like it. Mo makes an apple crumble tart, and Nigella says that the apple flavor combines well with the traditional treacle, though his pastry is a bit too thin. Moyin made a sticky toffee pudding tart that combines Mary Berry and Paul Hollywood’s recipes, so it’s no wonder Paul loves it.

But Gabe and our girl Connie struggle. Gabe’s is orange and almond flavored, and you know as soon as he put extract in it that Paul will say that the almond flavor is too strong. Connie, while making the best-looking tart of the bunch, struggles in several ways, including the dreaded soggy bottom. She also can’t get her tart casing off of her bake. She shouts to Moyin, “I can’t get my bottom off!” That’s something my husband has been saying for years. Moyin rushes to help her, and Connie later rushes over to help him get his tart on its stand. Their relationship is so sweet, and we see it several times this episode. Combined with all the talk about how Moyin wants to win the whole show without winning Star Baker (which only happened once in season 10), it makes me think that this episode will end with Connie going home and Moyin winning Star Baker.

The technical is to make a millionaire’s shortbread, another British staple that is shortbread topped with a fat layer of caramel and chocolate on top. It’s basically a Twix bar, a whole slab instead of a tiny little finger (or two; don’t want to forget the left Twix). While this isn’t a terrible idea for a challenge, they didn’t give the bakers nearly enough time for the caramel to set before putting the chocolate on top, and most of the bakers turn in mushy messes with underbaked shortbread, unset chocolate, and caramel runnier than a 4-year-old’s nose. “At least it was better than Bread Week,” Nigella says. Um, both of these are a problem. I get that there needs to be a time crunch to make compelling television, at least in the minds of the producers, but setting our lovely bakers up to fail is not how it should go. The order from worst to least worst is Mo, Connie, Gabe, Moyin, and Tom, who is, of course, decent because he’s always decent.

The showstopper is based on the Hungarian dessert Grillázstorta, which sounds like a pie made out of gorillas. The bakers must make a structure out of nougatine with a praline-based cake inside of it. Ugh, nougatine. I have never ever in my life seen it outside of Baking Show. They used it even more frequently in Bake Off: The Professionals, where they have to make really elaborate structures that are entirely edible. Well, there is edible, and there is something you want to eat. Lint is, technically, edible, but do you actually want any? That’s how I feel about nougatine. You only have to learn how to make it and work with it to be on one of these shows, so why are we bothering?

During the challenge, Connie has too much to do and is starting to spiral. Paul Hollywood, of all people, gets down off his pedestal and tells Connie to go sit on the bridge and stare at the water for five minutes. I’ve never seen anything like that in the tent before. Could someone get her a five-minute YouTube meditation video to go along with it? When everyone finishes baking, Moyin goes to give her a big hug, and they talk about how special they are to each other. Oh yeah, he’s winning, and she’s going home.

Mo does a great job making a box for a baby shower complete with nougatine ribbons and adorable frosted teddy bears, and the cake is a coffee sponge with chocolate ganache that Nigella rips into with unreserved gusto that was shocking even to her. Moyin makes a crown with blue “sapphires” around it, inspired by a song that his grandmother made up about him. Inside there is an opera cake that looks absolutely immaculate. Nigella says it’s dainty but packs a whallop; Paul even manages to try the nougatine and says it’s great. Moyin, as predicted, wins.

Everyone else has a difficult time. Gabe makes a really cool-looking black sesame nougatine, so it’s black and in the shape of a boat on the waves. As cool as the outside looks, inside is a Genoise sponge with a blue mirror glaze that looks like an algae bloom that could bleach all the coral reefs. Paul says that there is no flavor to it at all. That’s not usually a problem for our Gabe. Tom makes a pub out of nougatine, and inside is a hazelnut praline cake that looks like the Wicked Witch of the West after she had water poured on her. It is just a chocolaty puddle. Paul says it’s “Not his best work.” For an English person to say that is like he just pulled down his trousers and slapped him in the face.

However, it is Connie who really struggles. She tries to make her husband Myke’s favorite kind of cake to thank him for all of his support while she’s been off in a tent in Berkshire every weekend. She takes way too long to make nougatine and barely gets her rudimentary box finished in time. Both judges love the light, creamy hazelnut cake inside, but the box literally falls apart when they open it. As predicted, Connie goes home. This is when Warrant sings “Cherry Pie” and we all sob. She and Moyin hug once again, and Moyin says that she means everything to him. She tells him that she’ll be with him every step of the way, but there are only two more episodes, so it’s not that long. But sweet, sweet wonderful Connie. She even has hugs and kisses for all of the crew on the way out. She was undone by some not-great challenges on an uneven week, but she managed to capture all of our hearts, which is like winning a whole different trophy.

items.title: Cupertino Recap: Fair Use and Foul Play
items.description: As I’ve mentioned before, the key to making a good courtroom drama — and Cupertino is on its way to being a great one — is to ensure that the lawyers facing off against our righteous heroes can make their own compelling cases. I firmly believe that strong argu
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: As I’ve mentioned before, the key to making a good courtroom drama — and Cupertino is on its way to being a great one — is to ensure that the lawyers facing off against our righteous heroes can make their own compelling cases. I firmly believe that strong arguments make for good television. But how can you do that when the opposition is defending AI slop?

In this week’s episode, an over-the-hill rapper who goes by the stage name Yungwood (Cliff “Method Man” Smith) comes to his old friend Michael Price for help with a lawsuit that is going nowhere. Yungwood relies on the income from streams of his old songs, but his numbers have dropped off precipitously ever since the major streaming services — represented here by the fictional Noisement — started hosting AI music that sounds almost identical to his. Yungwood first retained PSA’s enemy Ry Vance, who dropped the case as soon as the music-tech titans pushed back hard by hiring Bayard Diamond, Michael’s father.

There are red flags aplenty in this case for PSA. The firm still needs some quick and lucrative wins, and with the Yungwood lawsuit, they’ll be dealing with an unpredictable client who films himself nearly 24/7 for his social-media followers, making inflammatory comments that compare music-industry executives to slaveholders. They’re also up against a deep-pocketed opposition who can drain their coffers with motions and delays.

Still, a few episodes ago, Michael allowed Olivia to pursue her “crusade” against WorkSource in exchange for her promising to back some future crusade of his own. Now is the time for Michael’s crusade. Not against Noisement necessarily, but against Bayard.

The case itself provides some fantastic theater, and not just because father and son can’t stop themselves from making multiple petty objections, needling each other and infuriating the judge (Danny Burstein). No, what’s more fascinating about the way this lawsuit plays out is that it pushes the Cupertino viewers — who, I assume, are all inclined to think that AI ripoff artists are all lazy, parasitic scum — to think hard about what music is, who makes it, and who benefits from that work.

Let’s take this one by one, but out of order. First: Who makes it? On one side we have Yungwood, an artist well past his prime, whose declining streaming numbers could have just as much to do with a recent incident where he assaulted a man at a bar. But at least Yungwood can prove in court that he composes his songs himself, starting with a guitar that he actually plays. On the other side we have Purvis Beer (Amir Malaklou), who turned Yungwood’s biggest hit, “Booty Bass,” into the deceptively titled sound-alike “Bass Booty,” and who can’t even play a C chord on a piano, despite claiming to be a “born musician.”

Which raises the next question: What is music? And it’s here that this episode becomes genuinely challenging. Can Michael argue that what Yungwood does — deriving songs from a long tradition of folk music and spirituals, many of which melodically resemble “Booty Bass” — is wholly distinctive from Purvis Beer layering instrumental tracks using AI prompts? After all, both songwriters are relying on their tastes, their memory, and their relative facility with the musical tools at hand.

Of course, there has to be an end to this stalemate for the dramatic tension to resolve. And ideally it should be a break in favor of our side. So we come to the final question: Who benefits? This is where Noisement and the AI music producer Gold Artist Studio get kind of caught with their hands in the cookie jar. PSA is able to prove that Noisement is manipulating its algorithm to deprioritize Yungwood and other legacy artists in favor of the cheaper, more lucrative GAS knockoffs. When the judge pulls out his phone to listen to Jimmy Buffett and is directed toward some slop that sort of sounds like Jimmy Buffett, it’s game over for Noisement.

As has happened a couple of times in this first season, the ending is both satisfying and a bit abrupt. It feels like there’s more that could’ve been mined from this debate over musical authorship, which predates the AI boom. (But I did like that Yungwood uses the controversy to get famous again, in part by hiring a bot farm in Peru to goose his numbers.)

The biggest reason why the Yungwood story line feels curtailed is that about a third of the running time this week is dedicated to a subplot carried over from “Harper.” As Olivia suspected, her older brother, Jacob, is being scammed by a pig-butchering operation working out of Krakow. The most damning piece of evidence arrives when Jacob tries to help his “girlfriend” get through “customs” by providing personal banking information, which ends up compromising the Siffre family’s Christian publishing business.

There’s a twist here, and it’s a good one. While Olivia is working with “Josh Frank” from “One Coast Bank” to protect her parents’ accounts, she suddenly wonders if she herself is being played. If you’re the kind of person who reads every possible long-form article about frauds and swindles, you know that Olivia is right to be wary, because “saving you from a con artist” is also a common con. (Once again, there is a great New York Magazine article about this phenomenon from The Cut.)

Olivia gets Vik to help her scam the scammers, using what he calls a “beaconing payload” to track them down and infect their network with malware. Again, this is a satisfying outcome, if maybe too neat. But if I’m being honest, my biggest beef with how the One Coast subplot resolves is how dopey it looks. As the malware hits the Krakow office, all of the computers start making loud beeping noises and popping up big warning windows.
That’s the sort of thing you’d expect to see from a much cornier show, and not one as savvy about tech as Cupertino. It’s pretty sloppy … no offense to all the AI artists out there.

• We learn a bit more in this episode about Michael’s dead sister, Anna, who jumped off a balcony because she was tired of the pressure from their demanding father. She was apparently a Yungwood fan, which is another reason why Michael took this case.

• Natalia gets to put her law degree to use in this episode, filling in for Olivia in court, where she struggles to figure out how best to stand while questioning a witness. (The judge: “Try perching.”) She also laughs at Bayard when he accuses her of being a wannabe who “spread your legs for the third-richest man.” While smirking straight in his face, she whispers, “You shouldn’t drink before court.”

• Natalia makes Michael nervous by suggesting that she’s not as rich as she may need to be to keep the firm afloat. But when Michael is not around, she tells the people building her office that she needs to have her own shower and that she’ll be covering the expense from her personal account. Is Natalia making promises she can’t keep?
• A nice, realistic touch: Over the past few episodes, the cut that Olivia got on her cheek in “A.J. & Buddy” has gradually shrunk, until by the end of this episode she’s no longer wearing a bandage.

• Olivia is very flirty with Vik this week, and the episode ends with the two of them going out to dinner at a place Christy suggested — someplace very loud with a dance floor. It’s nice to see Christy enjoying herself, and yet I couldn’t help but notice that she’s still downing her booze pretty hard.

items.title: Southern Charm Season-Premiere Recap: Boys Will Be Boys
items.description: Well, we know that the season ends with Whitney asking all the guys who has a secret love child. Is it [dun, dun, DUNNNN], Austen, the lovable cad who has been dating all over Charleston; [dun, dun, DUNNNN] Craig, the unrepentant narcissist with a giant hole i
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: Well, we know that the season ends with Whitney asking all the guys who has a secret love child. Is it [dun, dun, DUNNNN], Austen, the lovable cad who has been dating all over Charleston; [dun, dun, DUNNNN] Craig, the unrepentant narcissist with a giant hole in his living room ceiling; [dun, dun, DUNNNN] Shep, the newly-bearded wastrel who just got back with his ex-girlfriend; or [dun, dun, DUNNNN] Whitner, the recently buff playboy and possible performative male? Tune in this season to Southern Charm, where all the answers are revealed, including just how cute the baby is. (The baby is reportedly very cute.) If I’m putting money on it now, I would say that it’s Whitner because there is no way that the other boys would have gotten someone knocked up and we wouldn’t have known. I love you, Whitner, but are you our main suspect or a red herring?

It’s going to take us three months to answer these questions. We’re not in Maui on a cast trip; we are in Charleston where everyone is goofing off with their pets and Miss Patricia is cleaning out her cabinet of dog clothes. Talk about relatable! JK. I do not have a dog, and that imaginary dog certainly does not have clothes. We also check in with everyone. Craig went to Switzerland, where he wanted to isolate himself so that he could learn how to be alone. He did this with a luxury ski vacation. Now that he’s back in Charleston, it seems like nothing has changed, including that his assistant, Jack, is still in love with him. Madison’s baby, Teddi, is not sleeping through the night, so Madison isn’t getting much rest and still manages to look absolutely amazing. What is wrong with the rest of us?

Venita and Salley are friends once again, and they’re FaceTiming in the morning while Salley sticks her face and her extra E in a bucket of ice water that her dogs, Kevin and Boots, have already been drinking out of. Molly broke up with her dude and is just hanging out lots with Whitner (as friends), who is sending out shirtless pics with the frequency and urgency of a gay man who just downloaded Sniffies. (Straight people, do not ask Claude or Gemini or Jeeves what that is.) Venita says she’s into Whitner and Molly is like, “Are you? Are you sure? Do you want to be? How about being into someone who is not on the show? I think that is much better for you.”

All of the budding relationships come together at Venita’s Garden of Eden But Don’t Spend Too Much on the Flowers party that she holds to kick off the season. Whitner shows up with all of his shirt buttons undone to show off all the work he has been doing at the gym. Much like Venita, I have fallen for it. Salley can have my old imaginary husband, Kyle Cooke, because I have a new imaginary husband, and his name is Whitner Moylan. Yes, he is taking my last name because I can neither spell nor say his. (Also, Moylan in Gaelic means “bald,” and it’s ironic because he’s so wonderfully hairy.) Anyway, Whitner has fallen for Allie, the new girl who is a 26-year-old model that Venita knew when she was 14, when she was a modeling coach, a job that she had to go through a six-year accreditation process to practice. Yes, because she is a 26-year-old model in an amazing dress and after my husband — I already hate her. He asks her out on a date, and she accepts. Can’t wait to vomit all over that.

There’s only one problem. She was going out with Austen for a bit. Shep and his new beard (no, not a fake girlfriend to hide that he’s gay, an actual beard) pull Allie aside and ask about the relationship. He says Austen told him that they went on two or three dates and she wanted to be exclusive before being “intimate,” and so Austen said, “Maybe this isn’t for me,” and called it off. She rolls her neck and is like, “No, girl. That is not what happened.” She says that they went on a few dates; he was calling her all the time, but she is the one who stopped calling him because the whole time Salley and her extra E were blowing up his phone, and everyone was telling her that they were dating. At the very end of the episode, Allie sits down to talk to Austen, and I’m sure next week will open with her blowing him into oblivion for putting his own spin on this tale.

Yes, that means we need to talk about Salley and Austen. Do you want the short version? Let’s start with the short version. Salley is in love with Austen, and he treats her like crap. When Austen is talking to Madison at the party about his relationship with Salley, Madison tells him to stop kissing this woman who “wants to be his lady.” Austen says he didn’t know that. What? How did he not know that? That’s like going through the Wendy’s drive-thru, eating a whole square hamburger, and then being like, “How did this grease get all over my fingers?” Salley has literally told him this, but Austen is pretending like he didn’t know so that he can keep the status quo, which wildly favors him. He wants to keep going out with Salley, get all the companionship and fun of having a girlfriend, the occasional makeout when they’re drunk, but still get to date and sleep with whomever he wants. Why would he want to change it?

Meanwhile, Salley is unhappy and uncomfortable. Oh, no. Not because of Austen. Because she is wearing the dumbest dress I have ever seen in my life. It’s like she took a white pillowcase, cut out a hole for her head, trimmed off the bottom so that her underboob and midriff would show, and then put it over her head so that she can’t move her arms higher than her waist without exposing everything between her navel and neck. Who designed this dress? A blind couturier with a humiliation kink?

She’s also upset because of Austen, whom she tells everyone who will listen that she wants to be his girlfriend, even while she knows he treats her like yesterday’s doo-doo. She’s angry that, at the reunion, he called her a “bar rat” and said that not only was her hair high body count, but that her whole existence was. This is literally the problem, but no one will tell Salley. Venita tells her that he doesn’t respect her because she doesn’t respect herself. She says that she makes herself too available to Austen and acts like his girlfriend when she’s not. This is all true, but that’s not the problem at all. Austen literally tells Madison that he would have dated her, but she’s been with too many other guys that he knows. The problem is, frankly, that Salley is a slut.

I say that word with pride. I am a slut, and I am a firm advocate for sluts’ rights. That Austen thinks this way is totally stupid and antiquated, and I hate it. I especially hate that he won’t just tell Salley that, put her out of her misery, and allow her to move on to falling in love with another man who is going to treat her horribly. (I mean, PK is available.) Instead, she gets upset that Austen was wining and dining Allie but didn’t do the same to her. It makes her wonder what Allie has that she doesn’t. Sally wants to know what is wrong with her. The answer is nothing. However, what Austen sees as wrong is that she has been too promiscuous, and that makes her tainted in his eyes. Yes, it’s ridiculous, but someone please tell Salley. Let her move on. Let Austen be the villain that he always will be.

She sits him down at the party to tell him that they need to have more boundaries in their friendship. Across the party, Craig, Madison, Molly, and Rod are trying to read their lips and see what they’re saying. Honestly, the conversation about their conversation is more interesting than the conversation itself because Austen won’t be truthful with Salley, and she can’t be respectful of herself. Salley says that her hard line is that they can’t be kissing or touching anymore. Wait, that’s it. I mean, that is the baseline. She needs to tell him: no kissing, no touching, no calling her and asking her to hang out, and her dropping everything to do so. No hanging out with him and his friends and then letting him hit on other girls in front of her. No more treating her like one of the guys. No more double standard about how he can sleep with every co-ed in town, but she’s too slutty to be his wife. No more texting her about his problems late at night. No more making her think that on one hot night when they’re both oppressed by the heat of summer that he’ll eventually wake up and figure out that she has been the one all along and he will run to her house, sweat dripping in dense rivulets down his back, and shout up at her window, “Salley! It was you! It was always you!” as she throws open the shutters and jumps down from the second floor in her white nightgown to land in his arms like a dandelion seed. None of that. No more. Forever.

items.title: War Recap: Man on a Mission
items.description: Well, it had to happen: Johnny’s cover is blown, and he has no one to blame but himself. This week’s episode is aptly titled: It is the juicy bit, and not just where the divorce is concerned but in terms of the narrative structure of the season. This is the mo
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Well, it had to happen: Johnny’s cover is blown, and he has no one to blame but himself. This week’s episode is aptly titled: It is the juicy bit, and not just where the divorce is concerned but in terms of the narrative structure of the season. This is the moment the story has been leading to: The firms’ respective reactions to the mole reveal will define what kind of lawyers they really are. All season long, Taylor & Byrne was positioned as “the good guys” and Cathcarts as “the bad guys,” but, perhaps as a reflection of our screwed-up world, the firms turn out to be two sides of the same self-preservationist, unscrupulous coin.

The firms cut a deal: If Taylor & Byrne agree to forget about Johnny, Cathcarts will agree to forget about Flora and the honey trap. This way, everyone leaves this infernal trial with their reputations intact. The deal is good for everyone except Johnny, who is left in the worst position imaginable. It goes without saying that he should have thought of that sooner. For most of this week’s episode — until the deal is made — he still believes he might have a shot at securing that job with Cathcarts, his only opportunity not to get the British equivalent of being disbarred. I still think he should have double-crossed, but obviously he hasn’t watched The Departed as many times as I have, so he scrambles in vain.

This week’s episode opens where we left off, with Serena realizing that Johnny is the mole. She whispers as much to Nick as soon as she gets a chance, but by that time, court is already in session. Nick and Serena are distracted as Prudence delivers her opening statement, in which she emphasizes Morgan’s visionary status and Carla’s middling acting career, and soon Smallwood becomes distracted too: Johnny texts him from his burner that he has “been rumbled.” Smallwood texts back that the job offer still stands if he can produce proof of the honey trap. I’m still caught up on how this evidence could possibly, legally be admitted in court. (I would love to hear from our helpful, informed readers on this point — sound off in the comments!)

Meanwhile, Nick and Serena try to decide what to do. Serena’s first instinct is to stop the proceedings and alert the judge that the trial has been compromised. That’s what they should do, but this is television, folks, and this episode still has 40 minutes to go. As Budgie charms the room with her opening statement — in which she encourages the judge to remember that Carla is a creative professional as they debate the creation of Zephyr — Johnny runs to the Taylor & Byrne offices hoping to get a copy of the receipt for the construction of the conservatory with which they paid off Flora, charged to Bernard’s card. He uses his make-women-stupid spell on Cleo, but it fades as the walls close in: Cleo questions the purchase of the conservatory; the ever-watchful Molly questions Johnny’s urgency; Michael questions why he wasn’t notified if there was a document needed in court; Bernard questions why he is up in his finances without asking. All this questioning happens while Johnny is literally in the elevator, and Michael snatches the receipt from his hand before the door closes.

Johnny briefly loses it in a great short montage that sees him squirm under pressure. He proceeds to Flora’s house, and on the way, calls Bella to propose a midweek getaway, since he won’t be needed in court the next day. Bella correctly identifies this as a weird suggestion to make on a Tuesday. Johnny tries to convince Flora to “do what’s right” and go to Cathcarts to confess about the conservatory, the NDA, the honey trap, everything. He tells her she has been used by Taylor & Byrne, just as he’s been used. But his desperate demeanor is sudden enough to raise Flora’s suspicion. After seven episodes of women being too easily manipulated by Johnny, they finally wake up and smell the rat.

At this point, Nick is looking for Johnny. Still in court, Nick and Serena agree that they need to speak with Bernard, and by the time they get him on the phone during recess, all the stuff with the receipt has already happened. They decide not to alert Budgie to the mole problem because there’s nothing she can do at present, and there’s nothing Johnny himself can do for Cathcarts while Budgie cross-examines Morgan. They also immediately agree that they should not tell Carla, though they might reconsider if they knew she was sleeping with the mole. I thought Johnny might try to use Carla somehow, but at least for now, he’s ignoring her calls. I fear we’re in for a soapy how could you do this to me confrontation in the finale.

The firms race to find Johnny. As Morgan worries about his performance on cross-examination (we’ll get to the trial itself after we have surveyed the depth of Johnny’s snafu), Smallwood instructs Schill to get to Johnny before “Singer,” who has disappeared from court, and offer Johnny a job lest the other side tries to “turn him” (Smallwood is familiar with The Departed). But Schill is too late; Nick has a few hours’ head start and gets to Johnny first. He waits for him in his apartment, where he threatens Johnny with criminal charges for corporate espionage and promises to ruin his career forever. When Schill calls the burner, it’s Nick who picks up (Schill hangs up right away). Nick also tells Bella everything, and she is actually mad for once. She leaves and tells Johnny to be gone when she returns. Johnny weakly apologizes to Nick, but I think the show is banking on a stronger emotional reaction for next week. Archie Renaux embodies Johnny’s desperation well; I’m eager to see him bring this character to resolution.

Nick’s brief phone call with Schill leads to the deal between the firms. Serena and Nick meet with Beatrice, Smallwood, and Schill at the Cathcarts office. At first, Cathcarts plays dumb, but when Nick assures them they have proof, they get to business. If each side can overlook their opponent’s trespasses, neither firm’s reputation will suffer and no client will have to know about anything. They come to a settlement number in about 30 seconds that will hopefully bring this God-forsaken trial to a close, so everyone can forget about honey traps and corporate spies and go have tea and shoot clay pigeons or whatever it is they do for fun. It was that easy!

This is all done without the knowledge of clients or barristers, who might be a little peeved to see their hard work so easily dismissed. Prudence and Budgie spend the day with Morgan on the stand. He oscillates between tenderness and hostility toward Carla, though he brings up her diminishing relevance as an actress as many times as possible. Prudence’s goal is to show that Carla doesn’t have any real professional involvement with Zephyr, while Budgie labors to prove that Zephyr would never have existed without Carla. Under Prudence’s examination, Morgan explains that Carla wasn’t present for most of Zephyr’s development, which took place largely in Palo Alto. By way of illustration, Prudence introduces a photo of Zephyr’s American launch party, which Carla didn’t attend because she was at the premiere of a film she wasn’t even in.

What Morgan forgets — and what evades Cathcarts’ research — is that this launch party took place on the eve of Morgan and Carla’s wedding anniversary, and that Morgan set the party date himself. Budgie argues that, knowing Carla would be at a friend’s premiere, and that their anniversary was on the next day, and that every other Zephyr executive was bringing their spouses to the function, Morgan picked a date Carla couldn’t make to purposefully exclude her and take all the credit for himself. Losing his patience, Morgan scoffs that it’s ridiculous he should have to give away “half of [his] life’s work” because he forgot an anniversary date.

But that’s not Budgie’s main point, anyway; she is only course correcting. The core of her argument is that Zephyr couldn’t have existed without Carla because the idea for Zephyr emerged in reaction to something that happened to Carla, when she was the target of a social-media pile-on and became a viral laughingstock. That was the reason Morgan and Carla went to the cottage in Normandy for a needed respite. Maintaining that Carla was a passive muse, “the Jane to his Serge,” Morgan exploited his wife’s suffering for his own gain.
