The truth is, he can’t recite the poem that gave Zephyr its name, which we’ve seen Carla recite by heart. He can’t even correctly remember the name of its author. If I ever need a lawyer, I’m calling Budgie.

Budgie’s perfect rhetoric puts Carla ahead, but a string of Zephyr employees — including Gillian, Eric, and an unnamed front-desk receptionist — testify in Morgan’s favor that Carla was never professionally involved with the company. Despite Serena’s encouragement that they’re still in a good position, these testimonies make Carla nervous. Morgan is thankful for his colleagues’ contributions, but he notices that Gillain seems “off.” Carla notices the same thing a bit earlier, when Gillian stops her in the hallway to offer her sympathy for how things turned out and promises to call her.

The weirdness that Morgan sensed in Gillian was nothing less than the turning gears of machination. Gillian does call Carla, as promised, and they meet covertly in Carla’s car. Gillian tells Carla about Ancker’s offer and proposes a plan: If Carla changes her strategy to go after Morgan’s Zephyr shares, rather than cash, Morgan would no longer be the majority shareholder and they could force the sale to Ancker. As a result, Carla would become a billionaire. On the stand, Gillian hinted at her intention — she testified that her contributions to the company have been reflected in her shares. With Carla, she works the overlooked-woman angle, hoping she can convince her to act out of wrath and greed. But Carla has been notoriously wishy-washy when it comes to those cardinal sins. She has gone from honey-trapping Morgan to wanting only “what’s fair”; earlier that same night, sharing an umbrella with her soon-to-be ex-husband, she almost looked wistful. Maybe this final decision will invest Carla’s character with some actual complexity and humanity, though I fear, with one episode left, it’s too late.
Representations and Acknowledgments

• With Morgan on the stand, we finally get a definition of what Zephyr actually is: “A social-media platform with strict community guidelines designed to promote positivity rather than division.” Still sounds like word salad to me, though. I can’t envision what a platform like this would actually look like, especially when a couple of episodes ago, Carla got a lot of heat on Zephyr for bombing her late-night appearance.

• At the trial, the press is present both inside and outside the courtroom. Given the prominent place the media has had in the unraveling of Carla and Morgan’s marriage, I suspect the journalists sitting in on the proceedings will play some role in the finale.

• Taylor & Byrne’s eagerness to make a deal with Cathcarts seemed anti-climactic to me. I understand they’re nervous the stuff with Flora will come out, but isn’t employing a corporate spy a much graver transgression? Is anything that happened with Flora straight-up illegal, or as illegal as planting a mole in the opponent’s firm? As Nick said last week, the espionage plot could ruin Cathcarts forever, while Taylor & Byrne established deniability about the honey trap from the get-go. I wanted to see Nick and Serena coming in for the kill. I’m hoping this isn’t the end of negotiations!

• Let’s place our bets on what will happen in the finale. I think Carla will take Gillian’s offer but backtrack at the last minute, thereby ensuring some kind of dignified ending for herself. I also think Saeed will return to the Taylor & Byrne offices and that we will finally learn what actually happened in New York, though I have very high hopes we won’t have to sit through a flashback sequence. I think we’ve seen the last of Bella, and Johnny will end up as all greedy, selfish men do: lonely and friendless. And I think Carla and Morgan will reconcile. Will we see Gabe again at all? What about Flora? Cast your predictions!

items.title: Robert Pattinson Is Officially James Bond: Meet the New 007 Actor
items.description: It’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson.
items.author: Jack Dunn; Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: It’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson.

The “Batman” and “Odyssey” star has officially been cast as the next James Bond, ending months of rabid speculation about which young actor Amazon MGM and director Denis Villeneuve would hand the keys to the Aston Martin.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Added Villeneuve, who recently directed Pattinson in the upcoming “Dune: Part Three”: “Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”

Amy Pascal, who has produced the “Spider-Man” franchise and several 007 films, and David Heyman, behind the “Harry Potter” series, are producing the new Bond film, with Tanya Lapointe executive producing. Steven Knight is writing the screenplay.

Pattinson picks up the 007 mantle after Daniel Craig’s five-movie run as the womanizing super spy, which began in 2006 with “Casino Royale.” Craig’s final turn was in 2021’s “No Time to Die,” which ends with Bond sacrificing himself to save the world from a secret global terrorist organization. “No Time to Die” was also the last film in the series released before longtime producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli sold creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM for $20 million.

Predictions about who would be the next James Bond had taken over media and the industry in the last month, and a shortlist of British actors took turns as the presumed favorite. Jacob Elordi was pegged for the role in the earliest days of swirling rumors, but reports since surfaced that the “Euphoria” star didn’t even screen test for the part. Jack Lowden seemed like another safe bet. In early September, his “Slow Horses” co-star Gary Oldman claimed Bond was already picked and cheekily added that his “fingers are crossed” for Lowden. However, Lowden’s run at the character was largely overshadowed by Callum Turner, who seemed like a sure pick until news of Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult’s auditions was revealed. At that point, it became anyone’s guess who would come out on top until Pattinson was ultimately chosen. Other actors in the mix included Josh O’Connor, Tom Francis, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and even Harry Styles.

It’s not hard to see from Amazon MGM’s perspective why Pattinson was the obvious choice. He is, almost unquestionably, 2026’s most in-demand movie star and has the box office record to show for it. With help from Zendaya, Pattinson drove A24’s “The Drama,” an intimate yet squirmy original dramedy, to $134 million worldwide from a budget of $28 million. “Primetime,” in which Pattinson starred as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, likewise hit big with $61 million globally against a slim $18 million budget. Pattinson also starred as the sniveling Antinous in “The Odyssey,” which did $1.8 billion, and is set to star in “Dune: Part Three” in December, which is sure to pull in the big bucks. (It’s very possible Pattinson earned the part after impressing Villeneuve on Arrakis).

Pattinson also has the big IP experience needed to lead a franchise like James Bond. In 2022, Pattinson debuted as the titular Caped Crusader in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman.” He is set to revisit Gotham for the sequel in 2028. Those doubting Pattinson would land 007 often pointed to his obligations to Bruce Wayne as a reason why he could never take on Bond. However, after several production delays with “The Batman Part II,” it seems Pattinson is ready for a new longterm relationship with another familiar big-screen icon.

“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” said producers Pascal and Heyman. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

items.title: BET Media Group President Louis Carr to Exit After 40 Years at the Company; New Structure to Be Announced Later
items.description: Louis Carr, who took over as president of BET Media Group last year after the departure of former president/CEO Scott Mills, is exiting. Carr had previously served as BET’s president of media sales but was elevated to president last December while maintaining
items.author: Michael Schneider
paragraphs: Louis Carr, who took over as president of BET Media Group last year after the departure of former president/CEO Scott Mills, is exiting. Carr had previously served as BET’s president of media sales but was elevated to president last December while maintaining his media sales role, reporting to George Cheeks, then chair of TV media at Paramount Skydance. Cheeks, now co-chair and chief content officer for Skydance TV, announced the exit on Monday.

“I’m deeply grateful to Louis,” Cheeks said in a memo to staff. “For four decades, he has been one of BET’s greatest champions, helping shape the brand, its business and its connection to Black audiences and culture. Louis built lasting partnerships with some of the world’s leading brands and helped cement BET as a cultural force. As President, he led BET with clarity and purpose, creating renewed momentum for the brand. His passion, vision and heart have been front and center in everything he does, and it has been a privilege to partner with him.”
Carr will remain through the end of the year. Cheeks didn’t immediately announce Carr’s replacement, but said “we will have more to share soon on BET leadership and structure.”

In his own memo to staff, Carr said: “For 40 years, I have had one of the best jobs in the media and entertainment industry. Having a position that gives one the opportunity to carry out a purpose that is bigger than oneself is a privilege. Working for a brand whose mission from day one was to uplift and empower the Black community is an honor I’ll never forget.”

“That said, even as I write this email, I wrestle with my decision that the time has come to make a transition. Based on recent events within our community and our country, I’ve decided to chart a new path and my last day will be December 31.”

Besides his four decades at BET, Carr founded the Louis Carr Internship Foundation to help improve diversity in corporate America through paid internships. He also wrote the book “Dirty Little Secrets” and “Little Black Book: Daily Motivations for Business and Personal Growth.” In 2023, Carr was inducted into the Advertising Hall of Fame and received the Chicago Advertising Federation Silver Medal Award.

Last year, Mills’ exit came after the acquisition of Paramount Global by David Ellison’s Skydance Media; similarly, Carr’s departure comes following the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. by Skydance.
Here is Cheeks’ memo to staff:
I wanted to share the note below from Louis Carr, who has decided to leave the company after an extraordinary career at BET.

I’m deeply grateful to Louis. For four decades, he has been one of BET’s greatest champions, helping shape the brand, its business and its connection to Black audiences and culture. Louis built lasting partnerships with some of the world’s leading brands and helped cement BET as a cultural force. As President, he led BET with clarity and purpose, creating renewed momentum for the brand. His passion, vision and heart have been front and center in everything he does, and it has been a privilege to partner with him.

BET is an iconic brand with a unique and important place in our industry. We believe deeply in BET, its mission and the community it serves. We are committed to BET’s future and to building on its legacy, ensuring the brand continues to grow, evolve and thrive.

Louis will be with us through the end of this year. We will have more to share soon on BET leadership and structure. In the meantime, please join me in thanking Louis for the lasting impact he’s made and in wishing him all the best in his next chapter.
And here is Carr’s memo to BET staffers:

For 40 years, I have had one of the best jobs in the media and entertainment industry. Having a position that gives one the opportunity to carry out a purpose that is bigger than oneself is a privilege. Working for a brand whose mission from day one was to uplift and empower the Black community is an honor I’ll never forget.

That said, even as I write this email, I wrestle with my decision that the time has come to make a transition. Based on recent events within our community and our country, I’ve decided to chart a new path and my last day will be December 31.

BET has never been just a job to me. It has been a community, a culture and a place to serve. When I reflect on this journey, I am incredibly proud of what we have accomplished together. Over the years, we helped transform the multicultural advertising landscape, built meaningful relationships with some of the world’s most recognized brands and served as the launching pad for today’s top Black creators. We demonstrated the undeniable value, influence, and purchasing power of Black consumers while helping companies better understand and invest in our communities.

I am particularly proud of the momentum we have created and the work we have undertaken to strengthen the brand, expand our business and reaffirm BET’s place at the center of Black culture. Stepping into the role of President gave me the opportunity to see just how much the BET brand is loved by our talent, our consumers and the next generation.

We established our brand positioning as “Something You Can Believe In,” reinforcing the trust, purpose, and cultural connection that have always defined BET. We established a trusted Board of Advisors, one that would be envied by any Fortune 500 company, to help inform our direction and ensure that the voices and perspectives of our community remain part of the conversation.
And that was just the beginning. In 2026 alone, we:
- Delivered the network’s highest television and digital ratings since 2019, with the 2026 BET Awards hosted by Druski.
- Brought back the Soul Train Awards after a three-year hiatus.

- Expanded our relationships with an impressive roster of Black creators such as Kev on Stage, Nick Cannon, Jason Lee, Manny Halley, Desmond Scott, Chris “CP” Powell, Ice Cube’s BIG 3, Kevin Frazier and Stephen A. Smith with HBCU Basketball and more.
- Expanded the global reach of Black content through multiplatform partnerships with creators such as Tyler Perry and Ms. Pat.
- Entered new content sectors and explored new ways to connect with audiences across platforms with the launch of our microdramas.
- Relaunched the iconic ComicView franchise.
- Launched a new social impact campaign “Get Your Mind Right,” focused on mental health to further support the communities we serve.
- Created a new financial model for programming spend that makes our content more aligned and efficient to our potential ratings.

The work of this incredible BET team has afforded me the opportunity to earn an abundance of professional accolades and recognition, including five Lifetime Achievement Awards, induction into the American Advertising Federation’s Advertising Hall of Fame, and more than 14 community awards. I have also been privileged to sit on board seats across the industry, including with the International Radio and Television Society (IRTS), the Advertising Council, and the American Advertising Federation (AAF). Additionally, I am proud to be the longest-serving board member of the Video Advertising Bureau (VAB).
Thank you for your partnership, your commitment, and, most importantly, for allowing me to be part of your journey. It has been one of the greatest honors of my life.
I am proud of what we have built and proud of what we have accomplished.

items.title: Grammy Nominations 2027: Raye Leads With 11 Noms as Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley and Other Female Artists Dominate
items.description: The full lineup of nominations for the 2027 Grammys was announced Monday morning, and most of the top artists that had been predicted to score big came through with impressive tallies. But one piece of the puzzle definitely did not go as foreseen — that it wou
items.author: Chris Willman
paragraphs: The full lineup of nominations for the 2027 Grammys was announced Monday morning, and most of the top artists that had been predicted to score big came through with impressive tallies. But one piece of the puzzle definitely did not go as foreseen — that it would end up being Raye leading the pack, and just how big her haul would be.

Raye leads all nominees with a startling 11 nods, followed by Rosalía with nine. Tied for seven nominations each are Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers. Following close behind with six nods each are Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and Olivia Dean.

It’s not necessarily a fresh angle to point out that the Grammys have been favoring female artists as of late, but the disparity in gender representation has never been as dramatic as it is this year. In the category of album of the year, which many consider the Grammys’ most prestigious award, the eight nominations boil down to seven women and just one man (Bruno Mars being the lucky exception in that bunch). The same seven-to-one split goes for song of the year. For record of the year, six of the eight nominations go to women artists, and even then, one of the other two is for a male group with a woman as the featured artist (Tame Impala featuring Jennie).

The album of the year category will see Raye’s “This Music May Contain Hope” and a deluxe edition of Rosalía’s “Lux” face off against Bridgers’ “Lost Weekend,” Dean’s “The Art of Loving,” Langley’s “Dandelion,” Mars’ “The Romantic,” Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” and Swift’s “The Life of a Showgirl.”

With her nod for “The Life of a Showgirl,” Swift has tied the record for the artist to have the most consecutive albums nominated for record of the year: five. Only Kendrick Lamar joins her in having had that many new albums in a row compete for the big prize.

This year, Swift claimed a total of five nominations, including entries in the top three categories — album, record and song of the year — plus pop duo/group performance and song written for a motion picture. She split her submissions for record and song, choosing “The Fate of Ophelia” for her entry in the former category and the Disney song “I Knew It, I Knew You” for the latter division, and that paid off with nominations for both. “I Knew It, I Knew You” is, of course, the song that’s up as a movie theme song, and the title track of “The Life of a Showgirl,” a duet with Sabrina Carpenter, made it into the duo/group division.

Mars also took a similar approach to Swift in submitting different songs for record and song of the year, and it also paid off for him, as his album’s biggest hit, “I Just Might,” scored a chance at record, while arguably the most beloved track from his project, “Risk It All,” got the song of the year nom.

Otherwise, most top artists submitted the same tune for record and song of the year, as reflected in the final nominations. The numbers nominated for both include Dean’s “Man I Need,” Langley’s record-breaking “Choosin’ Texas,” Raye’s “Where Is My Husband!,” Rodrigo’s “The Cure,” and Rosalía’s “Berghain.”

Only two artists managed to score a nod in either record of the year or song of the year but not both. Tame Impala and Jennie’s “Dracula” is up for record but not song, and conversely, Ariana Grande’s “Hate That I Made You Love Me” made it in for song but not record.

The eight nominees for best new artist include Langley, who has a rare shot at sweeping all four top general categories this year. The others are Angine de Poitrine, Geese, Slayyyter, Sienna Spiro and Don Toliver.
Hip-hop did not have a banner year as far as the Grammys are concerned, with Toliver’s best new artist nomination being the only representation for that genre in any of the top general categories.

Others having a less stellar Grammy year than predicted include Harry Styles, who was completely shut out of the nominations. Noah Kahan also defied expectations by only picing up one nomination; although he had only been nominated for a Grammy twice before, he was predicted to have a bigger look this year with his blockbuster album and ticket sales and a degree of critical praise.

Plenty of other artists besides the aforementioned nominees managed to rack up multiple nominations. There is a large crop of 18 artists, producers or songwriters that managed to tie with an impressive four nods apiece, including some established Grammy favorites: Angine de Poitrine, Jon Batiste, Cardi B, Brandi Carlile, Doechii, Ariana Grande, Madonna, Jake Miller, PJ Morton, Kacey Musgraves, Zach Nahome, Daniel Nigro, David Rodriguez, Slayyyter, Tame Impala, Joybeth Taylor, Tems and Dylan Wiggins.

The list of people who came in just behind that with three nominations each is too long to mention, at 29 names — but it’s worth mentioning that one of those triple-nominees is Dolly Parton, who has three posthumous nominations. The late superstar was nominated in the best audiobook field, for the audio memoir “Star of the Show: My Life on Stage,” and she will also compete against herself with two nominations in the best country duo/group performance category.
The 69th annual Grammys will air Sunday, Feb. 7, 2027, at 4 p.m. PT/7 p.m. ET on ABC and stream on Disney+ and Hulu. The show will go out live from Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.

items.title: In Choosing Robert Pattinson, Bond Producers Have Taken the Safe Bet — But Is It the Right One? (Opinion)
items.description: So much for the underdog. After the race to be the next James Bond was reported to be down to three on-the-rise Brits — Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner — Robert Pattinson crashed the conversation late in proceedings, hugely pulling focus in a matt
items.author: Guy Lodge
paragraphs: So much for the underdog. After the race to be the next James Bond was reported to be down to three on-the-rise Brits — Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner — Robert Pattinson crashed the conversation late in proceedings, hugely pulling focus in a matter of days.

Why wouldn’t he? Suddenly, a competition of next-big-things had a bona fide already-big-thing in the mix. 40 years old and known to multiplex audiences for almost half that lifetime, the Londoner is a household name who, even by his established standards, has been enjoying a banner year at the movies: sharing in the blockbuster glory of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” this summer, sandwiched by inspired star turns in two offbeat A24 projects, “The Drama” and “Primetime,” that both impressively overperformed at the box office. All that, and he’s still got “Dune: Part Three” coming up next month.

Adding James Bond to his roster feels almost like gilding the lily, which is one reason I was skeptical that he’d ultimately be picked: Wasn’t the announcement of Pattinson (along with Nicholas Hoult) as a contender just a glittery distraction to juice up public interest in a lower-profile selection process?

Shows what I know. In picking Pattinson as the next 007, the 64-year-old movie franchise is heading into unprecedented territory: Bond has traditionally been a star-making role, not one for a readymade movie star, and that has worked out more often than not. (George Lazenby, it simply wasn’t meant to be.) Sean Connery had played just one leading role before he was cast in 1962’s “Dr. No”; prior to donning the tux, Roger Moore and Pierce Brosnan had both found their signature roles on TV. Timothy Dalton, a reasonably seasoned and well-regarded actor when cast as Bond, never quite made the leap to stardom via the role; Daniel Craig, on the other hand, very much did.

Lowden, Turner and O’Connor all made perfect sense given this history, while Pattinson, already known to billions for playing Edward Cullen and Batman, brings associative celebrity baggage that Bond has never had to contend with before. Is that a problem? Not necessarily. Director Denis Villeneuve, a high-end, blue-chip blockbuster artist with a distinct stylistic signature, isn’t the typical choice of Bond helmer either — so if he’s going in his own prestigious direction with the series, it makes sense for him to take an equivalently A-list leading man (and one with whom he has an existing relationship, through “Dune: Part Three”) with him.

And yet there’s something about the choice, on paper at least, that doesn’t sit right with me. It seems a little too neat, too convenient, even a bit too risk-averse — the proven safe bet taken over the chance to mint a brand-new megastar. I have little doubt that Pattinson, a reliably terrific actor, will make a fine Bond: tall and elegant and angularly handsome, he certainly looks the part and he can project the balance of charm and chill needed to play a character who, in any incarnation, remains a suave killing machine.

Is he a little too good for the part, though? Perhaps. Pattinson’s reputation as a movie star rests on playing two darkly brooding mainstream heroes; his reputation as an actor, however, has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos: a hapless small-time criminal in the Safdie Brothers’ “Good Time”; a deranged, gull-mauling lighthouse keeper in “The Lighthouse”; a sniveling, pathetic read of Chris Hansen in “Primetime”; or whatever the hell he’s doing, multiple times over, in Bong Joon-ho’s loopy sci-fi “Mickey 17.” Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play: His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in “The Odyssey” is off on its own beam entirely.

I don’t know that James Bond is really the role to mine Pattinson’s most compelling eccentricities as an actor: The very point of the character, across 25 films, has been that he’s a well-dressed, tightly controlled cipher who has a sharp way with a one-liner. Perhaps Villeneuve and his chosen star have other ideas, but it’s hard to imagine the character straying too far from a failsafe template. One hopes instead that Pattinson is negotiating himself enough time between 007 shoots (and at least one more “The Batman” entry still on the docket) to do the odd auteur projects he clearly loves — and that adventurously chosen collaborators like Claire Denis (“High Life”) and Lynne Ramsay (“Die My Love”) can only benefit from his cachet.

In the meantime, spare a thought for the less famous guys who, for a moment there, thought they had a shot at being cinema’s longest-running action man. They’ll all be fine — I confess to some relief in particular that O’Connor, a superb and unusual hybrid of character actor and leading man, may have more time for the intrepid arthouse projects in which he thrives — and will doubtless each get some manner of boost for having been so prominently on the shortlist. Sometimes, however, the winner really does take it all in this business: For Pattinson, snagging the most in-demand role going just feels like a victory lap.

items.title: Is ‘Club Kid’ a ‘Conservative’ Movie? Only If You’re Still Living in the ’60s
items.description: One of the things I love about movies is how layered they are. When a film connects on a deep level, saying what it’s truly “about” may not be as simple as it sounds. Chasing down a movie’s inner meaning can lead you into the mystery of things. A great movie c
items.author: Owen Gleiberman
paragraphs: One of the things I love about movies is how layered they are. When a film connects on a deep level, saying what it’s truly “about” may not be as simple as it sounds. Chasing down a movie’s inner meaning can lead you into the mystery of things. A great movie can be “about” more than it seems.

Take “Club Kid.” Jordan Firstman’s ebullient and moving first feature tells a story that couldn’t be more straightforward — or, in a way, more traditional. Firstman, who gives a fantastic performance, plays Peter, a queer New York party promoter (a few decades ago we would have called him “downtown,” now he’s Brooklyn) who learns that he has a 10-year-old son, whom he fathered in a random three-way sexual encounter at one of his 4:00 a.m. club bacchanals. The kid, Arlo (Reggie Absolom), is sweet and curly-haired and British (he arrives with a chaperone from London); his mother, who raised him, recently committed suicide. The responsibility to take care of Arlo has suddenly dropped on Peter like a load of bricks. It’s something he doesn’t want and, for the time being, doesn’t have much choice about. But as he and the kid start to hang out, a tentative relationship forms, and the two begin to figure out what they might mean to each other.

What “Club Kid” is “about” is how Peter, a charming dissolute man-child, living an existence of unhinged hedonism, discovers that he wants to grow up and take care of someone besides himself. On that score, the drama is authentic and fully felt. In outline, though, it’s something we’ve seen many times before, in films from “About a Boy” to “Big Daddy.” Yet what makes “Club Kid” singular is that it’s about something larger than that.

As a filmmaker, Firstman plunges you into the world of queer club culture with a fervor and tumult and personality and lived-in detail that takes your breath away. He plunks the audience down in the middle of the shade-throwing nightbloom revels, the cocaine and ketamine binges, so that we experience the cathartic rush of drugged-out insolence, of heightened erotic excitement, of gender-flipping transgression. From the earliest days of gay liberation, the party scene was a core expression of queer freedom, and still is. What we call disco started in the underground gay clubs of the early ’70s, and part of Peter’s cachet as a promoter is that what’s he organizing is now a business, but it’s still underground. The staging of these scenes, and the acting in them, is extraordinary. Jordan Firstman makes us feel the life of the party.

And yet…he’s not merely celebrating it. Far from it. As authentic and scene-specific as they are, the party sequences in “Club Kid” signify as more than just a portrayal of the New York queer club scene. They’re also a larger snapshot of what party culture, out there in the world, has become: an arena of liberation that’s rooted in a place of physical and spiritual abandon that contains the seeds of destruction.

If you wanted to encapsulate the history of the last six decades in one sentence, you could do worse than this: Ever since the late ’60s, the party has never stopped. There are countless versions of the party, and we’ve all been to our own preferred versions. It might have been the singles bars of the disco age, or the frat-house benders that came to rule in the late ’70s — and have only grown more frenzied and predatory ever since. It might have been the industrial dance clubs of the ’80s or the raves of the ’90s. It might have been the suburban saturnalia of “Jersey Shore,” or the more contempo versions of that. It might have been the punk mosh pits, or the revels of Studio 54, or the back-to-the-underground scene of Basement. The music, the drugs, the alcohol, the hooking up, the vibe of orgiastic excess — for 60 years now, we’ve been a culture on the prowl.

In “Club Kid,” it’s not just Peter who starts to question the party culture that has fueled him. The film itself is questioning it. It’s asking, “Is this how we should be living?” And yet, because the movie dares to pose that question, there has been a backlash against it, with a chorus of voices damning the movie by branding it “conservative.” A certain number of people are looking at “Club Kid,” with its tale of a queer man who turns his back on his own personal decadence to embrace the call of family, as if it were a movie Nancy Reagan could love.

What I think the “conservative” slur misses is that Jordan Firstman, who came out of this scene, is not questioning it in a puritanical or moralistic way. He captures the honest vibrance of party culture. Yet he also captures — and this is what I think is brilliant about “Club Kid” — that whatever version of it floats your boat, the party that never stops, while rooted in a certain vibe of community, may be rooted even more deeply in the enticement we feel from getting high on ourselves. That’s the hidden seduction of party culture, the thrill and the beauty of it, and maybe the lie of it. The party doesn’t need to stop. But it might be time that we stopped seeing it as an uncut salvation without ever pausing to ask, as “Club Kid” does, what it’s doing to us.
