items.title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
items.description: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”
items.author: Jessica Hamzelou
paragraphs: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”

Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.

He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it.

The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough.

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”

In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition—an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.

The guidelines, published on Tuesday, lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”

As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.

The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants.

Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data. Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.

The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.
“It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”

The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago, he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.)

Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.

Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will—an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.

Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.

Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low. The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference.
“This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”

items.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
items.description: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook i
items.author: Aaron Zamost
paragraphs: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda.

Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers, the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs.

For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.

The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else.

In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die.

Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “violence and death to our enemies” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”?

I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand.

There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “masculine energy,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats.

In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.”

“Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida, they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones.

Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next.
Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

items.title: Could My Politics Survive the Strip Club?
items.description: When I began to consider stripping in 2007, I was taking a class on Marxism called “Reading Capital” and earning an annual $18,000 stipend from my Ph.D. program. Peanuts. To supplement this, I taught a political-science class each semester at Brooklyn College.
items.author: Azra Liaqat Khan
paragraphs: When I began to consider stripping in 2007, I was taking a class on Marxism called “Reading Capital” and earning an annual $18,000 stipend from my Ph.D. program. Peanuts. To supplement this, I taught a political-science class each semester at Brooklyn College. Though adjunct pay was also absolute shit, the job came with union-negotiated health insurance, reason enough to stick around. Still, adjuncting was its own racket. While the thin ranks of tenured faculty enjoyed research budgets, office space on campus, and a decent salary, they weren’t the ones doing the bulk of a university’s teaching. That was done by us — by adjuncts, who had no contract, no annual salary, and no clue whether our job would exist next semester.

Everywhere, I found proof of the lessons we were taught in Professor David Harvey’s midtown auditorium. My fellow graduate students and I would read about the ruling class hoarding Manhattan real estate and turning it into a speculative commodity, then fight other wretched renters for a rush-hour seat on the subway.

After class, I stepped into the 34 Street Macy’s. In the juniors’ section, I saw a tiny stretchy blue dress with a silver-sequined bodice. To me, it looked like something a stripper could wear. In case I ever decide to audition, I told myself. Treating the idea with whimsy rather than resolve was a familiar coping mechanism, like the time I visited a LASIK doctor believing I was only there to “get some questions answered.” It wasn’t until I smelled the burnt top layer of cornea that I admitted to myself I was actually going through with it.

I looked at the garment — miniscule, clingy — and noted the irony. Of late, I had been consumed with worry that my parents, Ammi and Abbu, might see the photo of me in a pencil skirt that had been posted on the Brooklyn College website. My God, if they saw that? They’d make me move back to my hometown, Charlotte, North Carolina, and it would be curtains for the Ph.D. student in the big city.

Even in my mid-20s, I remained under close parental supervision. My life was split into two halves: the debaucherous New York City Azra and the dutiful, modestly dressed Charlotte Azra. Ammi and Abbu’s precondition for letting me move away for grad school was that I fly home every time there was a long weekend, a family gathering, or a new potential husband to meet.

There was no way in hell I’d audition at a strip club. Dance naked? In front of strangers? For money? Me? I could barely fuck with the lights on for love. Most likely, I’d chicken out before I even auditioned. Besides, the manager might take one look at me and tell me not to bother.
And if by some miracle I was hired? I doubt I’d make any money at all.

Still, I went home, put on my new platform Pleasers, and did what I’d been doing since I began considering stripping to pay the credit-card debt from my round trips to Charlotte: I danced around the apartment. I did it while folding laundry or waiting for my eggs to boil, feeling more than a little silly dancing to a Justin Timberlake or 50 Cent song. But when I forgot how ridiculous this scene was, when I pictured myself strutting out onto a stage surrounded by gawking customers, I could dance. I could kitty crawl across a floor with my stomach tucked in, look back over my shoulder with a smoldering glance at an imaginary patron, and pop my ass or flip my hair just so.
In other words, I could strip.
CityScapes was mostly empty when I arrived just before happy hour. Three guys were scattered around the stage tipping with singles. I ordered a tequila soda at the bar and watched the girl onstage.
“Are you hiring?” I asked the bartender.
“We’re always hiring pretty girls,” she said.

I looked past her at my reflection on one of the mirrored walls that lined the club. I was wearing my street clothes (a checkered halter dress I’d gotten for a bargain at Century 21) and very little makeup, my hair tousled from the humidity of the train station.

Pretty girls, she’d said, as if it were entirely uncontroversial, a matter of fact and not opinion. Maybe, despite the conclusions reached by my grandmother (“This dark?” she exclaimed minutes after I was born) or my mother (“It’s too bad — Azra really could have been a boy!”), I was a pretty girl.
“Bill?” The bartender waved over the manager.

Bill was a mid-30s white guy and kind of attractive, like a young Edward Norton. He was a former homicide detective and, setting aside my feelings about cops and bosses, would prove to be a great club manager.
“I’d like to audition,” I told him, the words spilling out of their own accord.
“What’s your stage name?” he asked.

Damn. I’d found my ideal thong and the perfect Pleasers, planned out how I’d manage my mandatory nightly check-in call to Ammi and Abbu while working, and debated whether to wear a bold lipstick. But I hadn’t bothered to come up with a name.
“Mona?” I said, reaching for something ethnically ambiguous.
“Mona,” Bill asked, “what are you?”
Not an uncommon question on the streets of New York, where catcalls were both constant and ethnically inflected. “Indian,” I said.

“Never had one,” he said. “Go tell the DJ what you want to hear. Dressing room’s back there. He’ll call you to the stage when he’s ready. Come out, do three songs, we’ll see what you’re working with. Then we can talk.”
In the dressing room, several women primped and primed themselves, swabbing their pussies with baby wipes and spritzing themselves head to foot with cheap body sprays.
I got undressed. Bill entered the dressing room to ask for a copy of my ID.

“Mona?” he asked. Reflexively, my hands moved to cover myself, one across my tits, the other over my crotch. Bill and I locked eyes, tacitly acknowledging the absurdity of my Birth of Venus pose in a roomful of exposed strippers whose ranks I hoped to join.
“Up next, we have Mona,” the DJ announced.

I put on the dancer‑grade black G-string I’d bought at a midtown sex shop that had survived the Giuliani years, perhaps the most durable piece of clothing I would ever own. It stayed put, it didn’t slice my midsection into a muffin top, and it wouldn’t let an errant labia pop out. Somehow, even when I was naked, this itsy-bitsy garment flattered every curve and dip of my otherwise body. Then I stepped into my dress, the tiny blue number, and looked in the mirror. My waist looked small, my cleavage substantial. I looked hot and tacky. I looked like a stripper. I took a deep breath and walked through the dressing-room curtain onto the stage.
The first of the three songs in my set ended, and it was time to get naked.

As I reached for the tie behind my neck, I felt like a Western feminist’s wet dream. How tired. A repressed Muslim girl throws off the shackles of oppression to find sex and agency as a stripper in the big city. Isn’t this why Laura Bush claimed the U.S. needed to invade Afghanistan — so women wouldn’t have to cover their heads? Isn’t that why the U.S. military says it does anything — to liberate the world’s downtrodden women?

I brushed aside these thoughts and let the dress fall. Steadily, attempting gracefulness, I stepped out of the gown as one dance-hall number faded into the next. One guy shuffled a stack of singles in front of him, which I took as a cue to collect my first tips. He let his jaw hang as he studied my crotch eagerly, allowing his eyes to move up to the swell of my breast. There was no bashfulness, no averting of the gaze, and I didn’t recoil in disgust. The exchange was straightforward, transactional. A stranger had never looked at me like this, with no pretense of decorum. Here, between us, was a presumption of egalitarianism. I was to be ogled.

More customers filtered in as I returned to the stage for my final song. By now, seven minutes into my first-ever stage set, I was spinning around the pole and crawling across the stage, winking or smiling at the men who made eye contact. I felt like a natural.

I recalled a few months earlier, when my new friend Deepika had told me about her brief stint as an escort and the time she’d gone home with a guy for a few hundred bucks. In that instant, I realized, she had transformed in my eyes, crossing that irreversible line from woman to whore. Now, I’d undergone the same transformation: I had become a sex worker, and sex work is never just a thing one does, like bartending or adjuncting. It’s who one is. It’s a totalizing identity.
Naked onstage with dollar-bills tucked into my G-string, that identity was mine. There was no going back.

I didn’t get rich stripping. Getting rich was for people with investment portfolios, rental properties, and intergenerational wealth. For the rest of us, an unexpected $300 tip was enough to smooth out the rough edges of everyday life. I could afford to rent an apartment in a building with an elevator and laundry, book air travel to Charlotte, and spend an occasional $50 at Sephora. I bought a gym membership and had long-delayed dental work that wasn’t covered by my bare-bones insurance. For the first time since arriving in New York, I was paying down my credit-card balance, even putting money in a savings account.

I didn’t receive benefits as a stripper, never filled out a W‑2, and wasn’t eligible for paid sick days. I was an independent contractor but without the perks independent contractors are entitled to. The club forced us to work a minimum number of shifts per week, charged a hefty house fee for each one, and mandated buying certain outfits. (I’m still mad about having to wear a sluttified soccer jersey — I picked Honduras — during the entirety of the World Cup.) Such violations of labor law, the norm at strip clubs, are unthinkable elsewhere. Imagine charging your plumber $40 for being 20 minutes late to fix your sink and, while you’re at it, making him wear hot pink for the job. And if I happened to sell an hour in the VIP room to a customer, the club kept two-thirds of what the guy paid for privacy behind the beaded curtain. I spent thousands of dollars at the strip club, and that’s before accounting for taxis, gym memberships, makeup, and waxing.
It was highway robbery. I wondered what Harvey would have to say about that.

“How are sex workers any worse off than agricultural workers? No, really! Think about it for a second,” said Rachel from the podium. I was at a sex-worker-rights event in lower Manhattan, and Rachel, a longtime labor organizer, was presenting the argument that sex work is simply work and thus deserving of protections and oversight like any other job. She went on to enumerate the commonplace abuses suffered by farmworkers in the U.S., many of them undocumented. “And what about package delivery drivers? They fight with their bosses for the ‘luxury’ of air-conditioning in their trucks, even during heat waves. But berry pickers are never pitied for ‘selling their bodies,’ no nonprofit wants to ‘save’ your UPS driver, and I never saw a charity collect donations to help an adjunct professor quit a job that has them on food stamps. People just hate whores, that’s all.”

Several months into working at CityScapes, I knew my job was exploitative. I knew that, in this industry, management preferred more youthful dancers with lighter skin. Black dancers made less for the same work as their white counterparts, and how they wore their hair was strictly policed by house moms. There was also the fact of sexual violence on the job, sometimes at the hands of management or club staff. Add in the risk of raids, arrests, or police violence, plus all the fees we paid working there, and it would be foolish to claim stripping was uniformly empowering.

From the sex-worker-rights meeting, I went to CityScapes. As we prepared for the night shift, my co-workers Veronica and Rebecca engaged in a catty takedown of our other colleague Mariana, whom we all found obnoxious. But they didn’t drag her for approaching other girls’ regulars, irritating big spenders so much that they eventually got fed up and left the club, or even the lowest-hanging fruit — the annoying pitch of her voice. Instead, they went after her for selling “extras,” an industry term used to describe any formally prohibited acts between a dancer and customer (even if management turned a blind eye).
“Mariana’s cheap as shit,” said Veronica. “She sucks dick in VIP. We all see her going across the street to the hotel after work.”
“That’s how she makes her money,” said Rebecca. “That’s why you don’t see her working. She’s always sitting in the back, not selling dances or nothing.”

I noted the disconnect between the dressing-room chatter at CityScapes and the discourse at the workers’ rights meeting, where prostitution was granted a degree of legitimacy, even dignity. At the club, the stigma ran deep. Veronica and Rebecca, who I knew also sold extras, were going after Mariana for doing the same. Among my stripper co-workers, the assumption was that all of us would work somewhere else in a heartbeat if we could.
Away from the club, I encountered equally firm opinions about sex work, including by those outside the trade.

“I know that whole ‘Sex work is work’ argument,” my classmate Shreya said when I told her about Rachel’s speech. Shreya and I had met in Harvey’s class and, as brown girls are wont to do, found friendship in the hallways outside our seminar. Over lackluster sandwiches at a midtown Au Bon Pain, I told her about my new job at the strip club and the political organizing I was doing with other sex workers. She wasn’t the least bit moved by the UPS driver or farmworker analogies. Instead, she seemed annoyed.

“I don’t buy that,” she said. “The relationship between a john and a prostitute is exploitative. It’s uniquely exploitative. And in every instance, it’s an extension of patriarchy. The only real solution is abolition.”

“Abolition of … sex work?” I asked. It was the kind of thing I expected to hear from a nonprofit savior type, the kind of liberal who thought the U.N. should create a program to give all prostitutes sewing machines or something. But that’s not who Shreya was. She was a leftist and a sharp one at that. Like me, she hated the NGO-industrial complex, which equally kissed the asses of its donors and pitied the recipients of its services. She also shared my critiques of capitalism and modern policing. And she wanted to abolish sex work?

Yes, she did. While people like Rachel believed sex work should be regulated, destigmatized, and decriminalized as a form of legitimate labor, those like Shreya saw it as a product of patriarchy and the traffic in bodies.
“Of sex work,” she replied. “Of porn. Of all the industries that exploit women’s bodies.”

“Well, what about textile mills in Bangladesh, where Gap manufactures our clothing? Wouldn’t you agree that they exploit women’s bodies? And men’s? And probably kids’? How is the exploitation of prostitutes different from the exploitation of any other worker? Dicks and pussies? Nudity? That some of them are trafficked?”

“You’re being glib, Azra,” she replied. “I’ve met those sex-worker-rights advocates. They act like being an escort is liberating. That’s nonsense. If it’s liberating, tell me why sex workers are some 100 times more likely to be murdered than non–sex workers. And what about the wives of these men paying for sex? Do they figure at all in the ‘I was an escort and it allowed me to pay off my debt’ Ivy League girlboss discourse?”

I didn’t want to go toe-to-toe with Shreya the way our dads did when debating which part of the Indian subcontinent had the best mango. After all, there was an element of truth to what she was saying. I knew people in sex-work organizing who said idiotic things about sex work being emancipating, as if their experience as an escort or stripper had anything to do with the most vulnerable folks in the sex trade. Imagine calling both a handlebar-mustachioed Brooklyn community gardener and thousands of undocumented agricultural laborers “farmworkers.” What did I, broke by choice and rebellious by circumstance, have in common with the street workers in the late-night hours on Roosevelt Avenue? Other than selling our sexuality, what did we share? What did someone trafficked into the sex trade have in common with someone webcamming for extra cash after being laid off from an office job? What did someone who sold used underwear on the internet have in common with the “juicy girls” catering to U.S. troops in Korea, often victims of the sexual violence created by American militarism?
“I think we can agree,” I said, offering both an olive branch and a platitude, “as long as there’s capitalism, there will be exploited workers.”
“And it’s capitalism that needs to be abolished,” Shreya said.
“I’ll drink to that,” I said.

We raised our egg-salad sandwiches, pantomiming a toast, then ate. Still, the debate between Rachel and Shreya ping-ponged in my mind. They were both so firm, so unapologetic, in their convictions. Meanwhile, I shuffled between worlds — from meeting a would-be husband at Ammi and Abbu’s dining table to dancing in the lap of a groping customer, from the graduate seminar to the front of a Brooklyn classroom, from the pro-sex-work advocacy spaces to the stigma-ridden strip-club dressing room — never bothering to reconcile them.

I wasn’t unlike my customers in that regard: men who, sneaking around behind their wives’ backs and spending money from secret investment accounts, created intricate double lives for themselves. It was easy to critique the tangled webs they were weaving. It seemed to me inevitable that their secrecy would catch up to them, that eventually they’d buckle under the weight of their duplicity. But if I’d bothered to look past my customers seated around the stage, I’d have noticed the wall behind them was, at every one of these clubs, a mirror.

Adapted from Mona: An Immodest Memoir of Race and Rebellion, by Azra Liaqat Khan, to be published on November 17, 2026, by Tiny Reparations Books, an imprint of Penguin Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House LLC. Copyright © 2026 by Azra Liaqat Khan.

items.title: Dressing ‘Horny’ in My 40s
items.description: A few weeks ago, as I was getting ready to head out for dinner with some girlfriends, I caught my husband staring at me. Nearby, our two young daughters were playing “family,” the 6-year-old tucking the 4-year-old into a bed they’d made from a cardboard box. H
items.author: Meghan Nesmith
paragraphs: A few weeks ago, as I was getting ready to head out for dinner with some girlfriends, I caught my husband staring at me. Nearby, our two young daughters were playing “family,” the 6-year-old tucking the 4-year-old into a bed they’d made from a cardboard box. His brow was furrowed in an expression of mild confusion. I stared back at him.
He cleared his throat. “You look hot,” he said.

I was wearing a vintage dress I’d thrifted at Curator Consignment earlier this year on a girls trip to Maine: a silk floral with a drop waist and tiny buttons up the back; entirely sheer, underwear glaringly visible.
“Are you …” he said carefully, then trailed off. He tried again. “Are you going to wear a jacket?”
“I … no reason,” he said. He chewed his lip. Then, in a rush: “I’m not sure you should go out like that.”

It was cute, his feminism warring with whatever mammalian instincts a 45-year-old professor of moral philosophy possesses. I felt the way I had as a teenager, my mom’s eyes trailing me through the house, assessing my hemline, the cut of my shirt, fearing for — what, exactly? My safety? My virtue? “No one is looking at me,” I reassured my husband as I left the house, which is mostly true. At 42, I am largely invisible, my postpartum and perimenopausal body absolutely no one’s sexual ideal. I made it home without anyone giving me a second glance. (My girlfriends, though, thought I looked great.)

Twenty years ago, this layer of invisibility would’ve been crushing; a decade ago, looking “inappropriate” for my age would have left me feeling, as my mother often says, “like mutton dressed as lamb” (Britspeak for embarrassing yourself by dressing younger than your age). But my previous body disappeared somewhere between my two pregnancies, and when I stopped nursing just over a year ago, I confronted my now-unrecognizable body as an explorer discovering a new land. How to shop for this form? What clothing could possibly communicate the enormity of what I had done?

Focusing on how clothing feels, rather than looks, seemed the natural place to start. Sensual, after all, literally means the gratification of the senses. There’s a kind of forced bodily engagement that comes with pregnancy and nursing, and with this acute understanding of what my body had been through, I was unwilling to give it anything but the best.

I purged anything that felt too tight or low-cut, anything that reminded me of the way I used to move through the world: carefully, nearly unbearably self-conscious. I committed to thrifting most of my clothing, which forced me to pay attention to fabrics and feel. To get into my body, even when I might not know how. Gradually, a new wardrobe began to emerge: crop tops paired with vintage white bloomers. A ’90s Betsey Johnson butterfly skirt, just this side of translucent. Rachel Comey snakeskin platforms I scored for a steal on Poshmark. A tissue-thin lace shirt I might have worn to a rave as a teen, if I ever went to raves as a teen. These are clothes that display my body, all two kids’ worth of it. Clothes that express an unfocused feverish desire, albeit weirdly and slightly askew.

It isn’t what others might think of as sexy, not skintight or cleavage baring. It’s combative and aggressive, demanding attention long after society has deemed you worthy of it. Refusing, as a friend recently said, to go gently into that good night. I dress the way I often wish I could behave: I want things, and I want them now.

Laurel Pantin, owner of the L.A. boutique Earl IRL and author of the forthcoming What to Wear Every Day, calls it “horny dressing,” a term I read in her newsletter that rang clear as a bell. Horny dressing, first and foremost, “has nothing at all to do with sex.” This is a key, if slippery, distinction. Pantin, who is 40, has a very clear understanding of what makes her horny: her girlfriends; ordering (and eating) the plate of fries; being called “a broad”; clothing with a purpose that moves as though it was made for her. “I look for clothes that show my clavicles, that you can scrunch up around your arms, that have a tactile quality,” she tells me. These are clothes that you can throw on, wrap up, tie around your waist, and forget about.
“I want the fabrics to feel good, my skin to feel good, for everything to just make me feel really good in my body,” Pantin says. “It’s like a little kitty purr.”

I’ve seen a similar shift with my friends, too. My friend Eva piles gold necklaces under men’s silk shirts she leaves unbuttoned; Brook let her hair go gray and cut it into a severe bob that she pairs with feverish red lipstick. We’re stretching our wings, letting things go fuzzy around the edges. We’re meant to be heading into our Talbots era; instead, we’re dressing like the teens we didn’t have the courage to be.

“I want my clothes to push me a little past where I think I ‘should’ be dressing as an early 40s doctor and mom,” Carolyn says. The 42-year-old — who went through a “second puberty” at 40, getting a tattoo and nose piercing — sends me mirror selfies in her olive-green velvet minidress with fringed sleeves, braless in a black-and-white shift, a sheer polka-dot dress worn over bike shorts. “Divorcing really unlocked giving no fucks,” she tells me. “I’m an eldest daughter raised Catholic in the ’90s in the Midwest. I did everything right and my life still imploded. So that approach clearly didn’t work.” Whatever version of herself she thought she might be at her age had to go. “I was never going to be a Lululemon mom, but I’m thrilled not to want to or let myself disappear anymore. I’m horny for life.”

When she was younger, Justine, now 39 and the mother of two boys, imagined that at this age she’d look “a bit like Lily van der Woodsen.” Instead, she left her abusive partner and gave up the outfits that signified maturity and control. She’s since broken up with a man who once asked her, derisively, “Is that what you wore to drop your kids off?” and recently flew to Paris on a whim wearing a trench coat and lace stay-ups to meet her new lover. These days, she’s leaning into oversize men’s button-downs with boots and no bra. “I want to feel French,” she says — emphasis very much hers.

The deeper I get into my 40s, the more fascinated I am by this decade, the strange interregnum between postpartum and perimenopause, young enough to desire, too old to be categorically desirable. I know there’s an expiration date on this feeling, and that there will come a time when I feel less inclined to expose anything at all, let alone my entire midriff. At my age, my mom was wearing oversize skirt suits. I hope she felt powerful, but I can categorically say she didn’t feel horny.

For now, like Pantin, I’m reveling in pleasure. “Horny dressing has less to do with the clothes themselves than how my body feels in the clothes,” she says. It’s about “being out in the world,” which gives her the most pleasure of all. I’m doing the same, pairing a tiny sequined miniskirt and a One Direction tee with red jelly sandals for a Harry Styles concert where I danced harder than anyone with a 42-year-old pelvic floor really should. Choosing pleasure, as a woman, can often be a difficult and radical act. What’s hornier than that?

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Hopes You Won’t Hate Her New Project
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Angelina Chapin
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Jennifer Lawrence has been here before. At this exact same sort of restaurant, the kind where celebrities discreetly mingle (this time, Gemma, the Italian trattoria attached to the Bowery Hotel), in a booth that gives her some privacy but not so much that her publicist and assistant can’t keep a watchful eye and ear from a table nearby. There’s always a stranger sitting across from her scribbling down notes on what she orders (a cappuccino and avocado toast with a soft-boiled egg) and what she’s wearing (an oversize bright-red sweater and a small beaded turquoise necklace). This is her cue to rehash talking points about her chemistry with a co-star or reverence for a director.

But when we meet for breakfast in early October, something about the familiar scene is different; she’s slightly outside her comfort zone. “I’m in this interesting transition,” she says. “For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can’t let doubt in. Now I’m experiencing doubt.” Lawrence, whose blonde hair is wavy from sleeping in loose braids last night, says any movie release comes with nerves, which she can normally soothe by bingeing the latest season of Real Housewives. This morning, though, she’s not here to talk about developing a Miss Piggy feature, working on a rom-com, or shooting a sci-fi thriller next spring. Instead, for the first time in her 20-year career, the 36-year-old is debuting a project you won’t find in theaters or on Netflix. And she’s still figuring out how to talk about it. “I have to pretend I’ve made the greatest thing on earth,” she says, her hands fiddling with the salt and pepper shakers. “Otherwise it gets too scary. It’s a form of forced manifestation.”

That thing arrives on October 27, when Lawrence will officially join the oversaturated world of celebrity brands by launching Mes, a “biodesigned haircare” company that is selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. She’s partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can. That sounds great and all, but “what if nobody gets it?” she asks. “What if everybody hates it?”

Lawrence might seem like the type of actor who would roll her eyes at the celebrity–to–beauty brand pipeline. She has an Oscar and a production company and just shot a Martin Scorsese movie alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Why spend time shilling a volume mist? Her answer doesn’t involve cracking jokes about girlbosses making #OOTD videos, the brand of self-deprecating humor she used as armor earlier in her career. Instead, she’s taking it very seriously, speaking about Mes as a natural extension of her art. “There is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product,” she says, twisting up her hair into a bun. “I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.” Lawrence has made peace with the humiliation inherent in being a creative person forced to talk about their work and doesn’t need to turn herself into the punch line. The baby-faced 22-year-old who laughed off tripping on the stairs at the Academy Awards is now more than a decade older and a mother of two. I watch her arrange her delicate features into a thoughtful expression while telling me how creatively satisfying it felt to develop a brand. I know she’s a good actor, one of the best, but I believed her.

Lawrence has always been a “hair girl.” “I feel like if my hair looks okay, then nobody’s gonna notice anything else about my face, clothes, or body,” she says. “I also can find myself using it to hide.” As a child, her thick curls would puff up in the Kentucky humidity, and she slept in braids to control the “floof.” In her teenage years, she ceded control to stylists, who did whatever they needed to get her camera-ready. “When you are a new and upcoming actress, you can’t be like, ‘Don’t put that on my hair,’’’ she says. “You sit in the chair and you say ‘Thank you’ and you shut your mouth.” Her strands would smoke and sizzle when the hair spray hit the straightening iron; her hair was dyed four different colors in one day for an X-Men screen test. After shooting the second Hunger Games film in 2013, her hair was so fried that she chopped it off into a pixie cut, a style she thought at the time “looked dope.”

Soon, Lawrence had bought every new product on the market in a desperate search for anything that would style her hair without hot tools. She even met with scientists about developing new products, but she struggled to find a like-minded collaborator. That is until 2023, when she watched a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a chemical biological engineer with a shiny brown bob and a beauty company who spoke about creating products that would fundamentally change the makeup of hair rather than just coating it in products — the industry’s current approach. Lawrence got goosebumps and emailed Aganovic to set up a meeting in the fall, just as the actors’ strike was ending. “It just seemed like a new way of going about things,” she said. “This is what I’ve been waiting for.”

Aganovic was initially less enthusiastic about the partnership. She had already founded a company, Arcaea, that uses DNA sequencing and skin microbiology to make, among other things, perfumes that reimagine extinct flowers or the smell of clouds. And while she wasn’t blind to the attention Lawrence could shine on her life’s work, she worried it could also be a distraction. “One of my biggest fears is having my work be misinterpreted,” she says. “Jen came across as credible and curious, but you never know how much she had actually looked into the company.” After a Zoom call, Lawrence set out to prove she wouldn’t be the kind of business partner with “25 assistants rescheduling something.” Within a few weeks, she flew to Aganovic’s Boston lab, showed up without an entourage, and smelled the smelliest bacteria in the fridge. Aganovic was impressed. “Jen literally said, ‘If you want to do this in five years, I’ll still be here,’” Aganovic remembers. “And I think that took the pressure off. I was like, Oh wow, she’s really serious.”

By fall 2024, Aganovic’s team of scientists was working on formulas that would make hair healthier while cutting down on styling time, damage, and shampooing. Lawrence had very specific ideas for the products, like a hair mask that would go on dry hair (and that could double as a “wet look”), a serum that got rid of her “floofs” without leaving residue, and a volumizing spray that wasn’t crunchy and improved her scalp. To execute her vision, Aganovic’s scientists had to become experts in lipids, proteins, and the scalp’s microbiome and experiment with different techniques, including developing a proprietary ingredient to promote a balanced, less oily scalp. “Hair masks are not usually applied to dry hair,” says Aganovic, “which is why it’s very expensive to produce them this way, without water.” (A 150-milliliter bottle costs $52.) Lawrence’s head became the guinea pig. She tried the products on her naturally curly hair, which she says makes her look like Isaac Newton. She tested the serum while doing promo for Die My Love and used the volumizing mist on the set of What Happens at Night, the Scorsese film she shot earlier this year. Her dedication was total, and she sent the serum back to the lab almost 150 times. At one point, she started to smell like fish after leaving on an unscented version of the mask for four days. “My husband was like, ‘If you don’t wash your hair, you have to get a hotel room,’” she said. Lawrence held firm.

When she wasn’t filming, she spent hours on weekly calls about the business and focused on developing the look of Mes’ logo and bottles. “I knew I couldn’t miss a Zoom and that I’d need to look over every single letter on the website,” she says. Sometimes it was hard to juggle everything. During one call, Lawrence tells me she was bouncing on a yoga ball at nine months pregnant when it occurred to her she was only in a bra. “I just turned my camera off and said, ‘I’m so sorry. I realized that I’m not wearing a shirt,’” she says, “And then everybody pretended like they hadn’t noticed.” But she wanted to stay in the weeds of the business. Lawrence took nose-training classes to help develop Mes’ scent; she sent product samples to everyone in her group chat and asked them for their feedback on fonts. She got so involved in the design that she had a colleague fly out to the New England beach town where she was vacationing so she could hold the 3-D-printed models in her hands. “I wanted them to be pretty,” she says of the bottles, which look like modernist mini-vases. “Bathroom products are always out, and it’s like, Why is this ugly?”

Lawrence trusts her eye, she assures me during our post-breakfast tour of the artist Robert Rauschenberg’s former Noho studio, a place she wanted to visit because it’s up for sale and could soon be turned into luxury condos. “I am good at telling when something’s going to be hot,” she says, now wearing a black baseball cap from her husband’s art business, American Pictures. After looking at a small exhibition of work by the mid-20th-century multimedia icon — “he’s kind of hot,” she says under her breath as she stands in front of a photo of Rauschenberg smoking — we sit in a room with sun pouring in through arched windows while Lawrence tells me about the vibe she’s trying to create. Mes, which is pronounced Mess (the latter was already trademarked), is meant to capture the kind of girl (gender neutral) who leaves the house with dewy skin and a rumpled-in-a-chic-way button-down shirt. “The moment something was fussy, it was like ‘no,’” she says. “Avoiding pretentious words and pretentious font is big. Our girl is not that. But she appreciates beauty.” Lawrence’s personal ethos is also looking good with minimal effort, despite the fact that she’s had a boob job and one day plans to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she says. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.”

But don’t expect to see GRWM videos in her bathroom before taking her toddler to school. She had resisted creating an Instagram account for her entire career — she did, however, make a Finsta to share memes with her friends — in hopes of keeping a few shreds of life private. But Lawrence knew Instagram was a necessity for any founder in 2026 and a few months ago met with a social-media expert, who explained that Lawrence’s strategy didn’t need to involve constantly pumping out content or filming her home life. Instead, since officially joining the platform in September, she’s only posted to the grid three times — “If anyone says anything negative, I will quit,” she deadpanned in her first video — and already has more than 8 million followers. She plans to do minimal promo for Mes, including product tutorials she might film in a “public or hotel bathroom” to keep her own sink offline.

It’s a tough time to jump on the celebrity-beauty-brand bandwagon. Fans tend to view these companies cynically, as cringe cash grabs rather than genuine passion projects. And the bar for success is high: The products have to be good on their own merits, and the celebrity selling them has to make sense. People want Kylie Jenner’s lips and Hailey Bieber’s skin, but on Reddit threads speculating about Mes, commenters are already questioning whether Lawrence’s hair is a standout feature. When I ask Lawrence if she feels pressure to have aspirational hair, she says, “That didn’t even occur to me,” with a look of panic. “Is that something people think about?” In her fortress of positivity, she hasn’t dwelled on the criticisms that could be coming her way and seems genuinely caught off guard when I bring them up. Is she concerned a highbrow beauty product is at odds with the every-woman persona fans love? “I think about how excited people will be to have something so sculptural and beautiful!” she says. “My little bubble is about to be popped.”

While beauty brands have turned rich celebrities like Rihanna and Selena Gomez into filthy rich business moguls, Lawrence scoffs at the idea that Mes was conceived as a source of financial stability amid Hollywood’s decline. “A smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise,” she says. “Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door.” And anyway, worrying about the bottom line is not her strong suit. When talking about the look and feel of Mes, she adopts the self-seriousness of any artist talking about their craft. But when it comes to the more technical sides of the business, Lawrence falls back on her familiar brand of self-mockery. “If you put a gun to my head and were like, ‘What are the numbers we would need to reach in order for Mes to be a success?’ I would have no clue,” she says. “Numbers don’t stick in here. I’m dumb but cute!” When I ask if the company has investors, she whispers “I don’t know” and redirects me to her co-founder. (Aganovic says her original company, Arcaea, which has raised $78 million, is funding Mes.)

But the shtick isn’t working so well this time — which is a good thing. It felt charmingly authentic when, in 2012, the Kentucky-born ingénue told David Letterman, “I hate myself. Don’t go see the movie. I’m a troll.” But Lawrence is in a much different phase of life. She’s a mother married to a prominent art dealer and serves as the face of Dior. In Hollywood, she calls the shots, green-lighting movies with her own production company and fielding requests from the most in-demand directors while slamming the industry’s pay gap. Even if she can’t balance a spreadsheet, it’s hard to believe she’s a buffoon in the boardroom. “It’s funny that she describes herself as the creative needing the business counterpart,” says Justine Ciarrocchi, who runs a production company with Lawrence and is her friend of almost 20 years. “I think she has an incredible business intuition, and she’s fearless when she is sure of something.” Molly Howard, the CEO of La Ligne — a brand whose coveted wide-legged pants are a staple of Lawrence’s “momboy” aesthetic — says her friend already has the most important quality in a successful founder: the willingness to pore over the most boring details of the business, from learning about EBITA to testing a bottle’s seal. “The ambition is that this becomes a Fenty Beauty of hair care,” Howard says. “I really think this could be a Rhode.” Lawrence actually has an even more audacious North Star in mind, one she’s too embarrassed to name. “If I told you, you would be like ‘Hahaha,’” she says. “It is so big and so huge that I’m aware Mes will never get there.” I beg her a few more times, but all she’ll say is that the aspirational brand is not beauty-related. “If I was Taylor Swift, the people on Twitter would figure it out.”

Towards the end of October, I visit Lawrence at her office in Tribeca, a Federal-style townhouse with exposed brick and barnwood panels. There’s incense burning on the long wooden coffee table, and as she curls up on a rust-colored couch, asking me at one point if I’m bothered by her bare feet, Lawrence claims to be feeling more calm than when we first met. “I’m back to being utterly and completely positive,” she says, wearing a sequined brown wool cardigan and a long black skirt. “I can always fall back on the product. It’s just kind of like, Well, these are obviously really good.” If she’s stressed about anything today, it’s a recent haircut that left her with uneven bangs, which she’s repeatedly tried to fix. “No matter what I do, it flicks out,” she says, pointing to a strand on the left side of her head. “And I went into a meeting today as a hair authority.” Come to think of it, maybe she is a little nervous, mostly about the idea that people won’t have enough patience to stick with the products. “If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” she says. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.” She’s already dealt with a few emergencies, like the mask leaking during the ship test or the cap on the restyling serum squeaking. (“This isn’t luxury,” she remembers saying. “It sounds like I’m stepping on mice.”)

Earlier that day, the Mes landing page went live, featuring a video of Lawrence’s blonde waves bouncing as she dances in a red cardigan. She immediately texted her group chat asking for compliments, which includes Howard of La Ligne, Tracy Dubb of Isla Beauty, and two women she won’t name because they are “very private.” On October 27, the full website will roll out, and if all goes well, Mes bottles will start filling people’s bathroom cabinets.

In a material sense, whether Mes is a hit or not won’t have a big effect on Lawrence’s life. She’s already rich, and Paul Thomas Anderson probably wouldn’t blacklist an actor whose hair mask doesn’t sell. For Lawrence, the stakes are more personal. She has the antsy intensity of someone who’s desperate for people to join in their obsession rather than mock it, like a friend who’s become a javaphile and wants you to adopt a new coffee-brewing technique. “Tell me about your experience because the products take time,” she says, fixing me with an intense stare. “I can answer questions.” She’s itching to nerd out about the eccentricities of her creations, excited for people to log on to the website and see the microscopic images of how these products affect the scalp. As she’d told me during breakfast, “I’m nervous about someone putting on the restyling serum and being like, Oh my God, this went on really oily, without knowing that in 15 minutes, it’ll all dry.”

Toward the end of our talk, she catches her foot bouncing and says, “I think the nerves are in my body. I work really hard to keep my brain disciplined.” At some point, Lawrence knows someone from the Mes team will call and let her know if the sales numbers are good or bad. But the real risk is a bruised ego, the idea that people won’t like — or simply don’t care — about a product she’s devoted years of her life to perfecting. “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension,” she says. “I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 16, 2026
items.description: With Mars and Jupiter aligned in bold Leo, this should be a great day to put your extra confidence and energy to use. If you’ve been procrastinating on an intimidating task, now’s the perfect chance to take care of it. If you’ve been too nervous to express how
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: With Mars and Jupiter aligned in bold Leo, this should be a great day to put your extra confidence and energy to use. If you’ve been procrastinating on an intimidating task, now’s the perfect chance to take care of it. If you’ve been too nervous to express how you really feel, take this opportunity to open up. Of course you’re never guaranteed to get the response you want — but in general the outlook is optimistic, so do yourself a favor and try.

You don’t have any trouble being direct about what you want. The issue is that others don’t always respond the way you hope they will. Some seem to interpret your confidence as a challenge; they read your assertiveness as aggressiveness. But today, there’s no need to tone down your message. If anything, people will probably admire your willingness to simply tell them what you want, rather than playing games. They’ll appreciate knowing where they stand with you, and they’ll be honest with you in return.

Although you try to trust your gut, you’re easily confused when you can’t determine why you feel the way you do. If you vaguely distrust someone but they’ve never done anything clearly wrong, you may worry you’re being judgmental; if you want to take a chance with someone who’s not impressive on paper, you may imagine you’re being naïve. But today, your intuition is probably right, even if you don’t (yet!) have the hard data to back it up. Trust it.

Acting on impulse often leads to trouble. When you make snap decisions without fully considering the consequences, you can end up solving one problem while creating three new ones. But spontaneity isn’t always a bad thing. Today especially, your instincts are likely to be spot-on. Don’t take drastic action simply for its own sake, but if you truly sense a decision is the right one — even if it seems sudden and unexpected — then give it a shot.

Sometimes you worry you’re unlikable because you’re stubborn. You hold fast to your convictions. But sometimes that makes you feel as if you have to choose between your relationships and your values; you worry that expressing your opinions risks damaging your friendships. Today, though, the opposite is more likely to be true. This isn’t the time to meekly go along with the crowd: People will respect you more for being authentic and brave enough to say what you really think.

If you’ve been wanting to try something new, now is the time to go for it. If you’ve been waiting to get something off your chest, now is your opportunity to speak up. Whatever has been holding you back won’t feel quite so insurmountable right now, but it’s up to you to make the most of the moment. Just remember that this newfound sense of power and confidence doesn’t give you license to tell everyone else what to do. Let them make their own choices while you focus on yours.

Most of the time, self-promotion is necessary if you want your hard work to be recognized. People often won’t notice how much you contribute unless you go out of your way to show them. Today, however, could prove to be the exception to this rule. You don’t need to waste your energy trying to prove to anyone else that you’re capable of achieving great things — if you simply put your head down and focus on doing good work, you’ll soon get the praise you deserve.

When setting goals for yourself, you tend to prefer ones you know are in the realm of possibility. You would rather be pragmatic than dramatic, even if that means your plans are less exciting. You don’t want to get your hopes up about a future that’s ultimately too good to be true. But today, give yourself the freedom to truly dream big without worrying about what is and isn’t “realistic.” You’ll have plenty of time later to drill down into the details and make the practical decisions. For now, act from the assumption that anything may be possible.

Some people seem to brag about their big plans before they’ve actually accomplished anything. But you prefer to do the work quietly, announcing your ambitions to the world only after you’ve made them a reality. Today, though, don’t be so hesitant to tell your friends what you’re working toward. There’s no point in pretending to have modest goals if your real dreams are sky-high: Right now, especially, people will admire your boldness. It may even inspire them to start wanting more for themselves.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You have a strong need for interesting new experiences. But sometimes, you feel you have to tamp down this desire. You understand real life can’t always be exciting, and you do your best to resign yourself to the dull parts. Today, though, there’s no reason you must accept boredom. If you want to try something new or if you need an adventure, don’t wait for someone else to invite you. You can take it upon yourself to go out and make it happen.

Sometimes, good-natured arguments can be fun. The debate itself may get heated, but you both understand the matter at hand is ultimately trivial so nobody’s feelings get hurt. Lately, though, it’s possible you’ve been arguing about more consequential matters — and when your deeply held values and beliefs are on the table, arguing becomes much less enjoyable. Today, don’t back away from these uncomfortable topics: If you’re willing to face them and discuss them honestly, you may finally make some headway.

You’re good at talking yourself out of pursuing your dreams: You can come up with a hundred reasons why things would never work anyway so you’d be foolish to try. But today, stop getting in your own way. If you truly want something, you owe it to yourself to give it a good-faith effort. Maybe you’ll fail — but if you do, at least you’ll know you did everything you could. Right now, it’s much more likely that you’ll get further than you ever imagined. Don’t give up before you’ve even started.

If you aren’t careful, you can easily get lost in your thoughts. You spend all your energy dreaming up possible futures but never doing anything to bring them into being; you worry about worst-case scenarios but don’t take action to prevent them. Today, make an effort to get out of the brainstorming phase and into the real world. Your thoughts and dreams matter, but your actions matter too. You have a chance now to make a real difference, so don’t let it go to waste.
