items.title: Lindsay Clancy Will Face a Second Trial
items.description: On Monday, a judge said Lindsay Clancy will face a second trial this spring for the killing of her three young children, setting a retrial date for March 29.
items.author: Erica Schwiegershausen
paragraphs: On Monday, a judge said Lindsay Clancy will face a second trial this spring for the killing of her three young children, setting a retrial date for March 29.

Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her children with exercise bands before slitting her wrists and throwing herself out a second-floor window, was tried on first-degree murder charges earlier this year. While prosecutors argued that she carefully plotted the murder of her children, her defense said she was suffering from severe postpartum mental illness and should not be held criminally responsible for the deaths. The six-week trial — which sparked heated debates and conspiracy theories online — ended in a mistrial in September after jurors remained deadlocked with all but one voting that Clancy should be found not guilty by reason of insanity.

While prosecutors have not yet said what charges they’re planning to bring to trial, the fact that they agreed to a new date suggests they intend to retry her for first-degree murder, the New York Times reports. (If they had reduced the charges, Clancy could have avoided a second jury trial.) Clancy, who was paralyzed after her suicide attempt, remains in the custody of a state psychiatric hospital, where she’s been held since 2023. Following the mistrial in September, her defense attorney Kevin Reddington said he didn’t think she would be able to emotionally handle a second trial.

items.title: Exclusive: Aspyn Ovard Opens Up About Being In A Throuple On ‘Mormon Wives: OC’
items.description: Aspyn Ovard Doesn’t Need This
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Aspyn Ovard Doesn’t Need This
She was a social media star long before The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County came calling. With her sensitive home life in a new spotlight, can she deliver the drama and set her own terms?

When you’re famous enough to have your own dedicated snark Reddits, you get used to people asking questions — about your dating life, about the makeup you’re wearing, about how you’re raising your children. What Aspyn Ovard is less used to is having to answer back. The 30-year-old content creator has spent the past week running around Southern California for press events and interviews to promote The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, her first foray into reality TV and Hulu’s first spinoff of the Emmy-nominated phenomenon that made #MomTok a household name.

“I was very anxious,” Ovard admits over Zoom from the back of an Uber, palm trees whizzing by as she heads home to Orange County from Los Angeles, where she just recorded a podcast with her castmate and fellow influencer Avery Woods. “But I was lucky to be with the other girls for most of the stuff, so it’s nice that I didn’t have to be alone navigating it all for the first time.”

To most reality TV aficionados, Ovard is a newbie, but to the chronically online, she already has more lore than an average A-list celebrity. By 2014, before she even graduated high school, Ovard already had a million YouTube subscribers who tuned in to her lifestyle and beauty vlogs, watching her grow from a wide-eyed high schooler to a young wife and mom. She’s since expanded her platform to TikTok and Instagram, but she still doesn’t want to be called an influencer: “I usually say I’m a YouTuber if people ask, actually.”

A reality show is only as good as its cast, and Ovard resembles a producer’s dream, someone who’s already used to documenting themselves on camera and whose nontraditional romantic life — she is in a loving throuple — brings a built-in horde of curious viewers. Ovard admits she didn’t need reality TV to maintain her career, but she knew the power Mormon Wives holds as both a fan of the flagship series and a friend of some of the Utah stars. “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity even though I have had so much success on my own,” she says. “It would’ve felt crazy to say no.” But taking the leap also means she’d have to divulge details about her life she adamantly kept private until now.

Ovard was born in St. George, Utah, one of the epicenters of the Mormon Church. Her family is no longer religious, but in the early 2000s, she and her four siblings were steeped in Mormon culture. “I grew up going to church when I was little, and I did end up getting baptized when I was 9. The missionaries, they got me,” she says with a smirk.

Ovard dutifully hit all the traditional hallmarks of a young small-town Mormon woman: “I got married at 19” — to her high school sweetheart (and now ex) Parker Ferris — “pregnant at 22, and wanted to have four kids by my 30s.” But the online fame she found as a content creator was already starting to break her out of her bubble. “I didn’t go on a plane until a couple of days before my 16th birthday,” she recalls. “When we started getting opportunities to travel out of the country, you realize you think in such a small way when you come from a small town.”

Ovard’s social media made her the breadwinner as she and Ferris, 31, welcomed two daughters, 7-year-old Cove and 4-year-old Lola. The couple divorced in 2024 while she was pregnant with their third child, 2-year-old Elle, and relocating to Orange County for a fresh start. Ovard said in a video that she found out a “10-year secret” Ferris had been keeping, which set the subreddits ablaze. Looking back, she didn’t realize how ominous it sounded. “I’ve said in every interview that I think the 10-year secret will be pretty underwhelming to people,” she jokes.

On Mormon Wives O.C., she finally filled in the blanks, revealing that Ferris hid his alcohol use from her while they were married — a sensitive point for Ovard, whose father died due to complications associated with alcoholism. “We’re just not each other’s people. We love differently, so we’re definitely better off as friends,” she says. “But finding that out two months after my dad had died was definitely a lot. It’s not necessarily what he did, but knowing something was hidden from you was a hard pill to swallow.”

While the divorce provided enough fodder for followers, the exes were navigating unimaginable tragedy at home. Ovard confirms on the show that one of their young daughters received a terminal cancer diagnosis three years ago, and the family doesn’t know how long she has to live. (Suspecting fans had already noted that Ovard’s collaboration with Tarte Cosmetics last year donated all net proceeds to pediatric cancer research organizations.)
“We’ve been through a lot the last couple of years, and we haven’t had a lot of things to really look forward to.”

Ovard is careful not to reveal any specifics on-screen, including which child is navigating the disease, aside from saying she received a “stable” prognosis during a scan. However, she is candid about how her daughter’s health factored into her decision to do the show: Reality TV stardom is another source of income that lets her and Ferris, who also appears on camera, maximize family time. “We’ve been through a lot the last couple of years, and we haven’t had a lot of things to really look forward to,” she tells me. “Parker being able to look at this as a career opportunity is a helpful thing for him, so we came to an agreement that we would both do the show and on the things we would share.” Regardless, Ovard won’t let the show invade her children’s privacy, blurring their faces if they appear on-screen, and her reps asked outlets to refrain from questions about how her daughter is doing.

“I was hoping my boundaries would be followed with certain things that I did not want to talk about, and it was, thankfully,” she says, then quips: “Most people just wanted to ask me about being in a throuple.”

In March of this year — before the spinoff was announced — Ovard hard-launched her relationship with a married couple, Briana “Bri” and Billy Davis. Her newfound throuple status threw everyone in her life for a loop — including herself. “There was never a moment of coming out for me,” she says. “I just kept saying, ‘Oh, you’ll never see me with a man again’ to my friends or family as I was going through the divorce process. Obviously, I was wrong. There are good ones out there.”

Ovard had been interested in dating women after her marriage ended, and she connected with Bri through Instagram in late 2024. (She prefers not to put a label on her sexuality: “Sexuality is so fluid, and I love not feeling the pressure to label mine.”) In their first conversation, Bri shared that she’s ethically nonmonogamous. “I was not in a place of looking for anything serious at all, so it didn’t really make a difference to me that she was married,” Ovard says. Despite being long-distance, things got serious quickly, with Ovard regularly flying to Bri’s home in New Jersey. “After I was with her, I was like, ‘Oh, wow. I can’t imagine ever wanting anything to do with a man,’” she recalls. “We connect on so many things. Loving a woman and being loved by a woman is so special and such a beautiful, different type of love that I’m so grateful I get to experience.”

But after a month of dating, Ovard decided she wanted to meet Billy. “I was like, ‘If he’s good enough for her, he is good enough for me,’” she says, laughing. “They were always so respectful. If I changed my mind and didn’t want to hang out with both of them, that was totally OK.”

Last fall, Bri and Billy moved across the country to Orange County to live with Ovard and her children, with whom she shares custody with Ferris. (Her ex wasn’t a huge fan of this idea at first — as seen on Mormon Wives O.C. — though she says he’s slowly starting to come around.)
“People expect it to be a lot more salacious than it is.”

Any concerns Ovard had about living as a throuple vanished upon move-in. “I didn’t have a lot of conflict resolution skills, so getting a front-row seat to two people who do have those skills has accelerated my growth in that way,” she says. “When we get asked, ‘Do you ever feel attacked by the third?’ We’re like, ‘You shouldn’t ever feel attacked by your partner.’ But we’ve all learned if it is two against one, you really have to take a look at yourself, and odds are you probably are the one in the wrong.”

She is, however, still figuring out what being a prominent face of nonmonogamy requires of her. She’s happy to dispel stereotypes by inviting cameras into her home and showcasing their love, though open discussions of their sex lives are a touchy subject. “I love to talk about that with friends because it’s a fun topic, but I’m only going to share so much,” she warns. “We get a lot of questions like, ‘Oh, would you ever add another one?’ Imagine how weird [it’d be] if I asked someone that as a hetero person in a straight relationship. People expect it to be a lot more salacious than it is, but they meet us and are like, ‘Oh, wait, they’re pretty normal.’”

Tell that to her costars. Since the first day of production, Ovard’s relationship has been a hot topic, especially among the castmates she hadn’t even met yet. Jen Affleck, a star of the flagship Mormon Wives series, moved to Orange County and leads the spinoff, which follows two polar-opposite friend groups: Ovard was already close with Woods, Bobbi Althoff, and Salomé Andrea — women with more progressive values and years of influencing experience — but wasn’t as familiar with Affleck’s friends who are still devout members of the Mormon Church: Ashleigh Pease, Madison Bontempo, Jordan McClanahan, and McCall DaPron (the older sister of OG star Mayci Neeley), who are oft referred to as “Molly Mormons.”

Within the expanded friend group, Ovard emerges as fiery and outspoken, unafraid to put herself on the front lines when culture clashes come to the forefront. During a cast trip to Palm Springs, Ovard confronted DaPron and McClanahan about their resistance to explicitly say they supported “gay rights” in spite of the Mormon Church’s practices. “We talked about politics a lot in that conversation, and that was cut out from the show. That’s Disney for you, I guess,” she says with a shrug. “I wasn’t looking for them to just say they support my relationship. I want the people I surround myself with to be aligned with supporting human rights. It’s a hill I will die on. It was hard at that moment because I don’t feel like they were understanding exactly what I was asking, but I know they were trying and have kept trying.”

Ovard isn’t that worried about all the new eyeballs she’ll get from Mormon Wives O.C. You don’t become a teen YouTube star without learning to deal with a fiery comments section. “I feel like I’ve always had thick skin doing this job,” she says. “There’s a screenshot from years ago: Someone commented on my video saying my hair was really curly, and the comment was like, ‘You don’t look good with curly hair.’ And I replied, ‘Yeah, I do.’” She’s more concerned about what her less experienced castmates are in store for: “It’s a bigger adjustment for them to go from sharing nothing to sharing everything on your socials and reality TV,” she says.

Still, when the show premieres, Ovard will be on vacation in Mexico with Bri, Billy, and her children, with plans to turn off her phone and lie on the beach. Oh, and Ferris is joining them, too. “We’re in a pretty good spot right now,” she tells me happily, as her car gets closer to home. “It’s definitely a unique relationship, but all three of us are willing to do anything we can to make him feel more comfortable and good with the situation that we’re in.”

The Mormon Wives franchise has already proved itself to be an effective star-launching vehicle: Just ask Whitney Leavitt, who leveraged her participation into starring roles on Broadway. But with everything her family’s going through, Ovard isn’t interested in a career change or world domination: “I’ve done this for 16 years now, and I’m transparently looking to keep this going for as long as I can,” she says. “I just want to spend time with my kids and be able to work the least amount possible.”

But like a great reality star, she knows how to keep you watching: “I feel like I’m slowly gathering the strength to be the person that I want to be again, and to show up for friends and myself,” she says, as we talk about what viewers might see on a potential second season. “Even getting through these press days, I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, I did it.’ I can do hard things.”

items.title: Your Horoscope For The Week Of November 16 - 22
items.description: It’s been one hell of a Scorpio season, and the final week of the sun’s journey through this deep water sign feels just as emotionally charged as the rest — despite both Mercury and Venus having finally ended their retrogrades. As this week begins, everyone is
items.author: Nina Kahn
paragraphs: It’s been one hell of a Scorpio season, and the final week of the sun’s journey through this deep water sign feels just as emotionally charged as the rest — despite both Mercury and Venus having finally ended their retrogrades. As this week begins, everyone is still wading through the strange but cleansing vibes of the triple conjunction involving Mars, Jupiter, and the release-oriented South Node. Go-getter Mars and Midas-touch Jupiter officially link up in ego-driven Leo early on Monday morning, giving each of your actions a greater range of impact. Are your current endeavors deserving of the amount of energy you’re pouring into them? The ripple effect is real. Use it wisely!

While this particular planetary pile-up began activating last week, its intensity is still building up, as the sun will square off with these three celestial players from Tuesday through Thursday. You’re being challenged to level up your game, own the consequences of your actions, and expand beyond your comfort zone in ways that feel — you guessed it — uncomfortable! Instead of shining your light in hopes of simply being seen, can you learn to beam your brightness for the sake of illuminating the world around you?

This dramatic and red-hot energy dominates these last days of Scorpio season — but by the wee hours of Sunday morning (or late-night on Saturday, for those on Pacific time), it’ll be time to bid the cosmic scorpion adieu. That’s when the sun enters party-hardy Sagittarius, kicking off the free-spirited and celebratory season of the zodiac’s mutable fire sign. This is exactly the type of spontaneous and fun-loving vibe needed to counter balance the emotional rawness of Scorpio season, so get ready to aim for the stars and chase some rainbows.
Here’s each zodiac sign’s horoscope for the week ahead.

If you know deep down you haven’t been doing the things you’re passionate about, you’ll probably feel something gnawing at you from the inside out this week. What fears are you carrying when it comes to pursuing your creative visions and putting yourself out there? Dreams aren’t meant to be kept on a shelf.

Watch the way you act and react within your relationships this week. Could some of your behavior be driven by a past version of yourself — a version that hasn’t fully healed from their experiences? Everyone’s got baggage, but you don’t need to carry it with you to every future destination.

You’ve got no shortage of things to share or possibilities to mull over, but do you have enough hours in the day to see these ideas through to their full potential? You’ll need to find a way to align what’s on your mind with what’s on your calendar if you want to put some actual plans into motion.

It’s hard to put a price on passion, but unless you have infinite resources, you have to make some decisions about what endeavors are truly worth your time. If you can learn to discern between fleeting momentary indulgences and genuine desires, then you can always feel good about your investments.

Many people feel confident when looking at themselves in a very particular light — but does the facade crumble when they step into the sightline of someone who knew a past version of them? Focus on finding ways to integrate all of your evolutions into your current state. Your growth arc is something to be proud of, not to downplay.

If you’re willing to look at your own reflection, then the whole world can become your mirror. Pay attention to the subtle feelings and reactions that get triggered in you when interacting with others or just going about your day. This kind of attentiveness gives you the opportunity to see into your own motivations more clearly.

Building community may feel especially important to you right now, but make sure you’re not compromising your personal values in order to feel like part of the crew. You have a natural inclination toward being diplomatic and trying to keep the peace, but it should never be at the expense of your own truth. It’s time for a vibe check.

Some professional ambitions could be reignited this week, but it’s important to check in with yourself honestly about where your motivations lie. Are you being driven toward your current career goals by a desire to impress someone else, or are you genuinely fueled by your passion and purpose? Either way is OK, but awareness is key.
Sagittarius (Nov. 22-Dec. 21)

The world is your oyster, and you’re discovering more and more corners of it that pique your interest and expand your perspective. Of course, that doesn’t mean you have to have it all figured out! It’s normal to question your beliefs and challenge your own dogmas as you gain more experience in life. Be OK with the fact that you’re always changing.
Capricorn (Dec. 22-Jan. 19)

When you’re craving true intimacy and emotional depth, it can be frustrating to have to engage with shallow or casual connections — but there’s an appropriate time for everything. So you may not want to pile complicated feelings onto an acquaintance, but you can certainly make an effort to embody vulnerability in your closer relationships.
Aquarius (Jan. 20-Feb. 18)

Life is life, so sometimes personal circumstances can shape or interact with your professional endeavors and vice versa. Right now, you may find that your closest relationships can be a huge asset when it comes to making career moves. Align on shared goals with a lover or get serious about a business partnership with a trusted friend.

Your sparkliest goals may feel like nothing more than a fantasy when dealing with the mundane and unglamorous details of your daily life. But perhaps there’s a way to start bridging the gap between your dreams and your reality. What are some tangible steps you can take to actualize your highest aspirations? Work that into your routine.

items.title: Exclusive: Mckenna Grace Says There’s A ‘Hunger Games’ Easter Egg Everyone Missed
items.description: You Actually Missed One Of Mckenna Grace’s Press Tour Easter Eggs
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: You Actually Missed One Of Mckenna Grace’s Press Tour Easter Eggs
The actor unpacks the hidden meaning in one of her Hunger Games premiere ’fits.

Mckenna Grace is turning her press tour for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping into a master class in Panem-inspired fashion. Joining method-dressing icons like Zendaya and Jenna Ortega, the 20-year-old actor — and franchise superfan (remember her viral Peeta Mellark edits?) — has been serving nod after nod to the OG trilogy, proving she knows the lore by heart.

With the help of her stylist Molly Dickson, Grace has already channeled Katniss Everdeen, Effie Trinket, Lucy Gray Baird, and even the second Quarter Quell arena. While fans have been quick to decode nearly every Easter egg, one major reference flew completely under the radar — and it happens to be the one closest to home.

At last month’s Sydney premiere, Grace stepped out in a custom lavender mermaid gown by Vera Wang HAUTE, crafted from decadent macramé lace and featuring oversize, hand-cut silk organza flowers blooming over one shoulder strap. Fans immediately flooded the label’s comments, comparing her to Rapunzel and begging Disney to cast her as the live-action princess, while others guessed it was an Effie nod. Plot twist: The real inspo was her own SOTR character, Maysilee Donner. Grace herself confirms it.

“Most days I have, like, birds or butterflies or flowers in my hair,” she tells Bustle, before singling out her Sydney look as an extra-special Easter egg. “One thing I was excited about was ... I wore this purple dress in Australia that was a nod to Maysilee.”

Eagle-eyed fans who’ve watched the official trailers might already recognize the palette. In the footage, Maysilee is reaped wearing a lavender minidress — fittingly elevated for a District 12 merchant’s daughter — complete with an A-line silhouette, a contrasting floral collar, and a bow-clad belt.

But the color wasn’t the only Maysilee-coded detail — the flowers adorning her Vera Wang gown were a nod to her character too. During the reaping, Maysilee accessorized by stacking necklaces with floral pendants and pinning a chamomile flower onto her lapel. (She’s a known accessory girlie. According to SOTR lore, she was the OG owner of the Mockingjay pin Katniss eventually inherited.)

To bring that floral motif to life on the red carpet, Grace went all in. “All the flowers in my hair were real flowers, which was really fun,” she says, adding, “At the end of the night, I was picking them all out. In the morning, I had all these wilted flowers on my floor.”

Still, thanks to the butterfly clip in her hair and the gown’s voluminous strap, Grace agrees that those Effie theories weren’t totally off base. “It also did remind me of Effie a bit,” she admits. Two Panem icons in one look? Truly Capitol-worthy.

items.title: Uma Thurman Doesn’t Believe In ‘Work-Life Balance’: ‘No Thanks’
items.description: The Dexter: Resurrection star has always sliced her own path through Hollywood (even if she’s secretly a softie). Now, with her kids mostly grown and a slate full of big-swing roles, she’s going “full throttle.”
items.author: Maggie Bullock
paragraphs: The Dexter: Resurrection star has always sliced her own path through Hollywood (even if she’s secretly a softie). Now, with her kids mostly grown and a slate full of big-swing roles, she’s going “full throttle.”

Uma Thurman was still a young child when she became fixated on the idea that she needed to formulate a life plan. The daughter of a Buddhist scholar and a former model turned psychotherapist, she grew up in a household where the intellectual stakes were high, and an independent streak was encouraged. “Both my parents were and are, in their own ways, very remarkable… unique, self-created individuals,” she says.

“I just had a sense that I was going to be providing for myself, and that there was no net,” Thurman says, with a shrug. “You know how kids get a bug in their head? I got a bug in my head. Like, ‘Oh, this isn’t going to last forever. I’ll make a move. I’ll do something.’”

Within three minutes of logging into our Zoom call, it is clear that Thurman is not one to linger on the surface of things. Sitting in her home office in Manhattan surrounded by framed black and white images, silver tchotchkes, and bookshelves that look like they’re actually in use, she is fresh from a shower, with combed-back wet hair and skin that looks fresh-scrubbed, save lingering traces of black eyeliner. As she talks, she gestures with her famously attenuated hands, revealing nails that are cut short and varnished a color that — even if it wasn’t being worn by Uma Thurman herself — many of us still think of as a Mia Wallace-esque noir.

At 56, the mother of three (her youngest is a high school freshman, while 24-year-old Levon and 28-year-old Maya Hawke are actors in their own right) has a slight gravelly edge to her once-flutelike voice, and an earned wisdom to her gaze. Otherwise, though, Thurman appears to be aging exactly the way one might expect from a bona fide movie star with her genetic advantages. Which is to say barely at all.

It’s hard not to feel a little starstruck by her presence, even when, technically, you’re only looking at her face, with its instantly recognizable features, on a computer screen. “There’s nobody who doesn’t know who she is,” says Clyde Phillips, the veteran TV creator behind the original Dexter and its reboot, currently featuring Thurman in her latest role, that of an ice-cold henchwoman in Season 2 of Dexter: Resurrection. “She’s iconic.”

On the show’s set, Thurman’s icon power took some getting used to. Dexter himself, Michael C. Hall — a TV icon in his own right — recalls comparing notes with Season 1 co-star Krysten Ritter “about our struggle to get over the fact that Uma Thurman was there.” Even Phillips, who recruited her to the show and, after two seasons working together now considers Thurman a good buddy, says he still has to pinch himself on occasion. At a large, complicated shoot in Times Square earlier this year, he remembers people “walking by going, ‘Holy sh*t, that’s Uma Thurman!’” He understands the feeling. “I was at her birthday party, and I’m thinking, ‘Holy sh*t! I’m in Uma Thurman’s house.’”
“I was missing in action with focus on the home front for the last 28 years. Now, my children are still in first position, but they can share the stage a little.”

Regarding that grand childhood plan of hers: Thurman’s father, Robert Thurman, who died at age 84 in June this year, was a Harvard Phd who became a professor at Amherst College in leafy western Massachusetts, where Thurman and her three brothers largely grew up. He went on to found the Tibet House — an organization dedicated to preserving Tibetan culture — alongside Richard Gere and Philip Glass. Suffice it to say that the family as a whole was academic, progressive, formidable. “Everybody was brilliant and getting, like, perfect SAT scores,” she says.

Thurman didn’t feel brilliant. It wasn’t until well into motherhood, when she was filling out a form about her own educational development in service of one of her kids, that she realized she hadn’t been able to read “a book with more words than pictures” until fourth grade. It was “a funny light bulb,” she says. “I was absolutely dyslexic.” Eventually, she says, “a dyslexic will crack the code, and years later, missing foundational pieces, they will read,” she says. Today, she loves reading. But she still experiences dysgraphia (the transposition of letters) and has difficulty with spelling and grammar. “It chases you all the way.”

As a kid, this left her frustrated and confused. She was obviously intelligent. “I could understand everything,” she says, “until you took the sound away, or the visual cue.” This left her with an “early feeling of being stupid.” That’s the kind of idea that leaves a mark. Convinced that she “couldn’t shine academically,” she knew that her big plan, whatever it may be, was going to have to be something totally different from her family background.

At 15, she left her Massachusetts boarding school on her own for New York City, where she moved into a studio apartment and started modeling. (This wasn’t as controversial on the home front as you might imagine, since it was something of a family tradition: Thurman’s mother had left home at 16 to pursue her own modeling career.) Modeling was not the grand plan: It was always intended to be a brief stepping stone to acting, and that’s what it became.

By the time her high school classmates were packing up their lava lamps for college, Thurman was playing Cécile, the porcelain-skinned virgin deflowered — and seriously turned on — by a scheming John Malkovich in Dangerous Liaisons. At 20, she played the wife of Henry Miller and the lover of his lover, Anaïs Nin, steaming up 1930s Paris in Henry & June, a movie that made history as the first ever to receive an NC-17 rating.

From the jump, Thurman displayed both a stunning willingness to go there and an innate onscreen magnetism that went beyond her unusual looks — the deep-spaced Bambi eyes and lit-from-within golden coloring. No matter the role, the co-star, or the genre, when Thurman is onscreen, it’s hard to look at anything else. For Hall, this je ne sais quoi is Thurman’s ability to “achieve dynamic movement in the middle of absolute stillness,” he says. “Where there’s nothing demonstrably happening, and yet so much seems to be going on.”
Imagine a light bulb, Hall continues: “Even though its light seems kind of static, there’s a lot going on to make it shine. She’s just got that thing.”
“I wasn’t looking to Xerox an archetypal woman for people. I wanted to be an actor who explored different things.”

She was just 23 when she joined forces with the creative partner of a lifetime, Quentin Tarantino, in the role of a lifetime. As Pulp Fiction’s aforementioned dark-fingernailed heroine, she drank milkshakes and did the twist, cool as a cucumber opposite John Travolta, a movie veteran who had made his name sliding across light-up dance floors. This past August, Mia Wallace’s white button-down shirt and black flares — the simplest, chicest costume ever to make it into the Halloween hall of fame — sold at auction for $64,000, more than twice its estimated pre-auction value.

Tarantino worked for a decade on the follow-up, centered on a character they created together. As The Bride, she swashbuckled her way through Kill Bill Vol.1 and 2. If Pulp Fiction made her a movie star, Kill Bill cemented her legacy, making her the female action hero of a generation. Years later, her cinematic descendant, Charlize Theron — equally tall, equally golden, equally badass — would tell Jimmy Kimmel that Thurman was the “OG” of the genre — the “sensei.”
Kimmel eagerly agreed: “She should have won the Academy Award for Kill Bill, right?”
Theron’s reply: “A hundred percent. Men get a lot of credit for these movies.”

What Uma Thurman did to prepare for Kill Bill was herculean in a way that, like so much of her early work, hits different circa 2026. Not only did she train for months to swing katanas, shoot guns, and perform three different styles of martial arts — she did it all starting when her son, Levon, was just 8 weeks old.

Thurman trained with “a master who you actually called master,” she recalls. The first time she walked into the training gym, infant son in one arm, his team stared at “this out-of-shape mother standing in front of them,” she says. “They had this kind of oh-my-God reaction — like, we have to work to work with that?” Among action-movie heads, the film’s biggest fight scene is canon. In the long, bloody sword battle sequence known as the “Crazy 88,” Thurman single handedly eviscerated an army of at least 40 stuntmen. All while taking breaks to breastfeed. (When I marvel at this physical feat — how did she do that? — she demurs. Tarantino, after all, had created the movie around her and then timed the shoot around her pregnancy — of course she was going to do whatever it took to live up to the role. And besides, “People are nursing in flooding tents. Is what I did anything special? No.”)

Given all that, it may surprise you to learn that Thurman is secretly a bit of a softie. More than anything, she says, she loves romantic comedies. She’s read all of Nora Ephron’s books, and when she discovered that Ephron recorded the audio for a lot of them, she listened to them, too. “I’m sad that I’ve already listened to them, and I don’t have them to look forward to,” she says. “I know this makes me seem very corny and sentimental.”

There are few true romantic comedies on Thurman’s resume. One is 2005’s underrated Prime, in which she plays the “older” love interest of the son of her own therapist (played by Meryl Streep). Then there’s 1996’s The Truth About Cats & Dogs, in which she plays the obstacle, not the lead: In a Cyrano-esque spin, she’s the Helen of Troy who turns Ben Chaplin’s head away from “regular woman” Janeane Garofalo. Thurman is matter of fact about why she wasn’t cast in more rom-coms: At 5-foot-11, she did not fit the mold. “Leading ladies couldn’t be taller than leading men. You would not be considered, bottom line.” (She’s too polite to specify which projects she lost out on because of stature.)

There was an upside to not being, as she puts it, “a typeable type.” It forced her to become versatile, which ultimately defined her career. “Also, I wasn’t looking to Xerox an archetypal woman for people,” she says. “I wanted to be an actor who explored different things.” If her resume runs the gamut — from art house films to popcorn movies to serious theater, action to drama and back again — she says that’s very much by design.

Last year, no one knew whether Dexter, the serial killer drama that refuses to die, could or should be revived. The original show ended in 2013 after eight seasons; since then, the franchise has given us a prequel (Dexter: Original Sin) and a sequel (Dexter: New Blood). Still, Hall thought his “killer with a conscience” had work left to do. And Showtime, for which Dexter: New Blood had turned out to be the most-watched show in the network’s history, was ready to roll the dice.

To up the ante, Phillips and longtime co-writer Scott Reynolds assembled a murderer’s row of co-stars, including the aforementioned Ritter, plus Neil Patrick Harris, Eric Stonestreet, and Peter Dinklage. The latter played a twisted billionaire tech wizard (timely) whose dirty secret is a basement museum in which he stores his passion project: collecting the gory “trophies” of noted serial killers.

Phillips says that in addition to trying to keep Dexter dangerous, funny, and vulnerable, he always wants to keep its audience “leaning forward,” which meant bringing a certain icon into the fold. Over Zoom, he demonstrates, bringing his face 2 inches closer to the screen, as if to get a better look. “When I see Uma Thurman in a television show, I go like this. I lean forward. I pay attention.”

The definitional quality of Dexter Morgan is that he’s a serial killer who is not a lunatic — he operates by a strict code, plying his craft, so to speak, only on evildoers he thinks deserve to die. He’s the Robin Hood of serial killers. Which doesn’t mean he doesn’t relish the job.

As Hall puts it, Thurman naturally “presided over” every scene as Charlotte “Charley” Brown, a character who was introduced last season as the terrifyingly composed body woman of Dinklage’s billionaire. She’s a decorated former Ranger in the U.S. Army with a law degree from Harvard and, in Season 1 at least, a ruthlessly sleek blond bob. (Phillips and Reynolds are diehard Tarantino fans, but it was total coincidence that the show’s costume designer happens to be Cat Thomas, the same person who came up with The Bride’s indelible yellow tracksuit.) As Thurman sees it, Charley is “a highly trained professional warrior” who has “done bad in service of her country,” and then, in retirement, found herself in the unfortunate position of being the right-hand woman of a raging psycho — who happens to be paying top dollar for her invalid mother’s medical care. (Talk about golden handcuffs.)

“Charley’s job turned into this toxic, dark, sick thing that she’s locked into by financial need,” Thurman says. “And she hates herself for it.” But like Dexter, she also seems to take a certain job satisfaction in, say, deftly bludgeoning a guy with a nail-studded baseball bat, just because he touched her shoulder.

It’s delicious to watch Charley doing dirty work of her own while maintaining a withering disdain for the bloodthirsty killers in her midst — exhibiting a glamorous chill that even Dexter can’t resist. “In spite of himself, Dexter is captivated by her,” says Hall. “That’s not something I had to manufacture. I just sort of… rest in the tractor beam.”
“People who are obsessed with ‘work-life’ balance — no thanks. I want to be fulfilled in action, and I want to be comfortable at rest.”

Online, the only audible complaint about Thurman’s performance in Season 1 was that there wasn’t enough of it. The part was mostly written by the time Thurman signed on, and while Phillips was able to work a little more backstory into the part once she was on board — close viewers might even catch a nod to her hometown of Amherst — for Thurman fans, it was a bit of tease: Why hire Uma if you’re only going to give her a few minutes of screen time per episode?

Thurman, too, had doubts initially about whether there would be enough for her to do in Season 1. The whole season’s worth of scripts were largely stitched up by the time she read them, which Phillips says is part of his strategy: In the hiring process, it is much easier to sign legends like John Lithgow on to your serial killer project if they know “exactly where their character is going, and that we’re not going to f*ck them over in the end.” Thurman says being able to see the whole arc of Season 1 allowed her to recognize how good the show could be. The structure wasn’t just locked, she says. It was “perfect.”

“It’s funny, for someone who struggled with reading,” she says, to have become “a worshipper of writing.” With the benefit of a long career, she has learned that “so many times you get seduced by ‘Oh, it’s the creator of X,’ and you throw your piece of the puzzle at it. But it is the quality of the writing that creates the product. Period.”

Season 1 was widely received as a triumph. Season 2 debuted Oct. 30, cannily timed to spooky season, with episodes dropping weekly. One thing is clear so far: There’s much more Uma this time around. (It helps that most of her fellow shiny co-stars, Dinklage included, had been killed off by the end of Season 1.) Having snuck a peek at a couple of early episodes of Season 2, I tell Thurman that I still can’t tell if Charley is a force for good or for evil. Is she about to decapitate Dexter… or bed him? “Could really go either way,” the actor says with a small, wicked smile.

Every time Thurman’s name is announced in a new project, there is a little ripple of online excitement: Where has she been? But the idea that she has taken a long break is a misconception. Her IMDb page shows that she never stopped working.

That said, for a very long time, she’s also had another big job to manage. “Until two years ago,” she says, “I had a child under 12 in my home. I was sort of missing in action with focus on the home front for the last 28 years — trying to continue getting some work in for myself, and not let my career die.” For nearly three decades, she says, her career wasn’t in first position; her kids were. And now? “Now, my children are still in first position, but they can share the stage a little.”

Within the last year, Thurman passed two major milestones in any woman’s life — defining moments as a daughter and as a mother that occurred only months apart. She said goodbye to her father, and she watched her daughter get married. On Valentine’s Day, Stranger Things alum Maya married her longtime beau, musician Christian Lee Hutson, in a true winter-white New York City affair. “I enjoyed every part of it,” Thurman says, grinning. The bride wore custom Prada, a nod that seemed to recall her mother’s long history with the fashion house. One of Thurman’s own most iconic fashion moments was standing on the Oscars stage in 1995, luminous in a pale lilac Prada column with a single strand of diamonds glinting around her neck. For fashion history types, the moment is seminal: The unfussy look defined the minimalism of the era, and Thurman was one of the first stars to put Prada on that grandest of stages. (“Mrs. P is an icon,” Thurman says, who has “done more than most people on the planet for artists and artisans. She is a cultural institution in loafers.”)

Today, Thurman says she’s enjoying a sort of rebirth that may sound familiar to other women her age, even ones who aren’t movie stars. She’s finding liberation in “letting go of… expectations that younger women and actresses have to carry.”

This doesn’t mean she’s looking to take it easy. “I want to go back to it with full throttle,” she says. Thurman has always had what she calls an “old-growth hardworking mentality. I’m happier if I’m working harder.” These days, in some ways, she finds herself working even harder than ever, putting energy into being ultra-prepared, but approaching projects with a lighter touch: “I work harder but easier.”

She gently rolls her eyes at “people who are obsessed with ‘work-life’ balance,” she says. “To me, they’re, like, New Agey. Like, no thanks.” Woo-woo is not for her. “I want to be fulfilled in action, and I want to be comfortable at rest.”

Given her Buddhist roots, one might expect Thurman to be somewhat New Age-y herself. “You would think so,” she acknowledges, a little sardonically. “But you might also think that I would have a little bit of a New Age phobia.”

A new sense of freedom seems to have come with an increased willingness to take swings on surprising projects, ones that aren’t always quite as gilded as her earlier fare, maybe, but have the potential to be even more fun. Dexter is one example. “I was late to TV,” she says. Now she’s making up for lost time.

Next up, she’ll reprise her role in the follow-up to Prime’s smash gay rom-com Red, White & Royal Blue, in which she plays against her own untypable type, as an American president with a go-big-or-go-home Southern accent. “She’s very nice, Ellen,” Thurman says — making the point, with a note of irony, that not all of her characters are mercenary killers. “She’s just a really great mother and a very kind-hearted president. Totally different flavor.” Listening to Thurman drawllll out Ellen’s syllables, it’s easy to see what she means about enjoying a new kind of freedom.

As a young superstar, with the eyes of the world on her every move, award season always pending, and studio honchos counting every dollar she brought in, “I used to apply so much pressure on myself,” she says. “Nothing was ever good enough.” She knows that’s normal at that stage of life; nevertheless, “it’s kind of unbearable to be like that.” Today, she says, “I feel freed up.”

items.title: Hayley Atwell Of 'Much Ado About Nothing' On Her 4 Favorite Plays & Musicals
items.description: Callback With Hayley Atwell
items.author: Christina Amoroso
paragraphs: Callback With Hayley Atwell
Ahead of her Broadway debut opposite Tom Hiddleston, the actor reflects on the magic of live theater and the performances that have made her fall in love with it.

Hayley Atwell is an accomplished veteran of the London stage, but now, the actor — perhaps best known for her portrayal of Agent Peggy Carter in the Marvel Cinematic Universe — is making her Broadway debut, and she’s ready to party. Or at least throw a damn good one.

“We’re here to essentially host the audience in having an amazing party,” the actor, 44, says of the Shakespearean comedy Much Ado About Nothing, which opens Nov. 19 at the Winter Garden Theatre after a successful West End run. “We get to do it again, but in this completely different environment and a different kind of audience, which I expect will be even more raucous than in London.”

Co-starring fellow MCU star Tom Hiddleston as Benedick, the play is directed by Jamie Lloyd, who has been praised for his reimagining of works including Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Sunset Blvd. and Evita, the latter of which moves into the Winter Garden after Much Ado wraps up on Jan. 10. Much Ado received accolades in London for its high-energy campiness (picture lots of pink confetti and strobe lights) — something Atwell is here for.

She describes the production as “visceral, juicy, and gorgeous” while remaining rooted in the text. “The way [Jamie Lloyd] pitched it to me when he first offered me the role was, ‘It’s a massive party,’” she says. “Everyone’s having a great time. Some people drink a little bit too much. They stay a little bit too long. They have some feelings. Someone takes things too personally. Arguments break out. Confusions occur. We flirt with the wrong person.”

She’s also heartened by what she sees as a growing desire for the collective experience that you can only get by attending live events like a Broadway play. “When you have human beings in a room, it feels different. We can get more of a sense of each other when we’re sharing body language and just the molecules in the room changing because someone new has walked in or walked out,” she says. “That makes plays a very visceral, kind of immersive experience.
“I want to feel more alive and more connected and less numbed out from the sort of content that can kind of bore into my eyeballs that I realize I didn’t really consciously consent to.”
Ahead, Atwell shares five plays and musicals that have done just that for her.
Her first selection is August Osage County, Tracy Letts’ 2008 Pulitzer-winning dark comedy. The play follows a fractured Oklahoma family that is forced to reunite when their patriarch goes missing.

“I love plays that have a really strong ensemble, and there is a sense of real company on stage that have worked together intimately, intricately over a rehearsal period to understand the heart of the play,” she says. “But also understand their own dynamics within each other and how you always have to keep the ball in the air, and that the performance is only as strong as the people that you play with.”

Atwell learned the power of a strong ensemble during a run of Dry Powder in London. Her character, a private equity partner, often had to interrupt her casemates. “I remember coming in really hot, beginning a monologue and then realizing within about the first three lines of dialogue that I’d skipped three pages. And my fellow actors are looking at me and the terror in their eyes,” she says. “I had to keep on going and get to the end of my monologue and then try and work out what we needed to then improvise to backtrack to make sure the audience were at the same place in the script that we were.”
Sunday in the Park with George

Her second pick is Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s 1984 musical Sunday in the Park with George, which follows a fictionalized Georges Seurat. Atwell first saw the play in the West End revival starring Daniel Evans and Jenna Russell nearly 20 years ago.

“That musical encapsulates the creative process, the struggle for an artist’s identity, the struggle to have an artistic career and to maintain personal relationships. You can be selfish and also generous and fully focused on a creative career, and yet the cost of that can sometimes mean that personal relationships. In this musical, that’s where they start to falter,” she says. “And I find the tension of that really beautiful.”

Her third show is The Rocky Horror Show, the 1973 cult-classic rock musical by Richard O’Brien. “I saw it first when I was a child, probably way too young, didn’t really understand a lot of the ideas behind it, but I just loved the energy and I loved particularly Tim Curry’s performance — so magnetic,” she says. “And for me, it was about freedom. And although it’s also like a homage to the B movies and sci-fi films of back in the day, it’s very camp and it’s ridiculous and it’s silly and it’s weird and it’s bizarre.”

Her fourth selection is Shakespeare’s Hamlet, which Atwell fell in love with during a 2018 Robert Icke adaptation starring Andrew Scott. “I saw Andrew Scott playing Hamlet four times — in a play I know very well! And yet when I saw Andrew do it, I felt like I was hearing it for the first time and I felt like I was hearing it made up then and there,” she says. “He talked so openly to the audience. He felt like he was talking to every single individual in the auditorium.”

Her final pick is Medea, which Atwell saw starring Helen McCrory at the National Theatre in 2014. The play, written by Euripides in 431 BCE, tells the story of Medea, a sorceress who sacrifices her children in an act of revenge against her husband.

“Medea I think is one of the hardest roles in the canon for women to play because I think it’s one of the major taboos of our world and our society,” she says. “The idea that a woman could harm her child or her children — and how to have that as your protagonist, how a woman has to portray someone who does the absolute unspeakable, unthinkable, and that we’re having to want to engage with that feels an impossible task.”

Atwell feels McCrory handled the responsibility of Medea with grace. “Helen had, for me, as an actor such formidable courage in exposing human failings and human pain,” she says, “and how great pain and things being done to an individual can have such a devastating effect on the psyche, that then they become capable of doing the unspeakable.”

items.title: Your Horoscope This Week: November 15 To 21
items.description: R29 babes, welcome to the first week in November where it finally feels like things are moving forward again! With Mercury and Venus having officially ended their retrogrades in Scorpio and Libra, respectively, the second half of November is shaping up to have
items.author: Dossé-Via Trenou
paragraphs: R29 babes, welcome to the first week in November where it finally feels like things are moving forward again! With Mercury and Venus having officially ended their retrogrades in Scorpio and Libra, respectively, the second half of November is shaping up to have a considerably different flavor than the first. We’re entering the final week of Scorpio Season with greater clarity, passion, momentum, and sensitivity to what we truly want. After spending the past month and a half reviewing our values, relationships, and needs from every possible angle, we can finally start putting those realizations into practice. There’s a sense of relief in the air, even if we’re still figuring out exactly what comes next.

As the week begins, the moon is in Aquarius, offering us a healthy dose of emotional detachment after all the deep-diving Scorpio Season has encouraged us to do. We may find it easier to look at our circumstances objectively, laugh at situations we were taking a little too seriously, or simply enjoy being in the present moment. Then, on November 17th, the moon enters sensitive Pisces, eventually harmonizing with the Scorpio Sun on the 19th. This watery energy encourages us to be more vulnerable and honest about the realizations we’ve had throughout Mercury and Venus retrograde. Now that both planets are direct, it may feel easier to express our truth with grace and sensitivity while remaining open to hearing someone else’s perspective. Conversations that once felt intimidating could become surprisingly healing, especially when we approach them with curiosity rather than assumptions.

By the weekend, the moon enters fiery Aries just as Scorpio Season prepares to come to a close, giving us a particularly Martian burst of energy. Both Aries and Scorpio are ruled by Mars, which is currently moving through bold, expressive Leo. Translation? We may suddenly feel ready to put ourselves out there after weeks of being more introspective than usual. Maybe you finally post that photo you’ve been sitting on, experiment with a new look, tell your crush how you feel, or shoot your shot with a creative opportunity. Whatever form it takes, this weekend encourages us to embrace a little more courage, spontaneity, and visibility. We’ve spent plenty of time getting to know ourselves on a deeper level this Scorpio Season. Now it’s time to let the world see more of who we’ve become.
Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

Aries, now that Mercury and Venus are both moving forward, you may be surprised by how much easier it feels to get people on the same page. With Mercury direct in your shared-resources realm and Venus direct in your partnership zone, the first full week of both planets moving forward is ideal for strengthening the relationships that help you thrive. Perhaps you and a romantic partner are finally figuring out how to divide responsibilities more fairly, or you’re discovering that a professional collaboration works best when everyone brings something different to the table. There’s also an opportunity to become more comfortable receiving support, whether that’s financial, emotional, or practical. You don’t always have to be the one figuring everything out, Aries. Let yourself experience what happens when other people show up for you, too.

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, you may feel increasingly aware of how much your priorities have evolved since late October. Rather than spending another week analyzing every emotion, take advantage of the Aquarius moon early in the week to reconnect with friends, exchange ideas, and enjoy experiences that get you out of your own head. By the weekend, the moon enters your sign, giving you an extra boost of confidence and spontaneity. With your ruling planet Mars in Leo energizing your creativity and pleasure zone, this could be the perfect time to make a bold first move,  attend an exciting event, or share something you’ve been working on. End Scorpio Season by reminding yourself how good it feels to have fun, Aries. You’ve earned it.

Taurus, your calendar may be filling up again, but this time you’re getting a lot more selective about what deserves a spot on it. With Mercury now direct in your partnership zone and your ruling planet Venus moving forward in your work and wellness realm, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring a refreshing shift in how you manage your commitments. Maybe you’re establishing better boundaries with clients, delegating tasks to a colleague, or realizing that a professional relationship could become much more productive with a few adjustments. You may also find yourself enjoying your daily routine more, especially if you’ve been experimenting with a new fitness class, co-working space, or work schedule. The goal is to create a lifestyle that actually feels good to live, Taurus. Being booked and busy is only cute when you’re enjoying yourself.

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon highlights your career and public-image zone, making the beginning of the week especially promising for professional visibility. This could be a great time to present an idea, update your portfolio, or reach out to someone whose work you admire. Then, as the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your social life gets a boost, and you may find yourself making spontaneous plans with friends or meeting people who share your interests. By the weekend, the Aries Moon encourages you to slow down and recharge behind the scenes. You’ve got plenty of exciting things brewing, Taurus, but you don’t need to attend every function or respond to every invitation. A little JOMO (joy of missing out) might be exactly what you need before Sag Season begins.

Gemini, your work-life balance is getting a much-needed software update, and this version might actually be worth keeping. With your ruling planet Mercury now direct in  Scorpio and Venus moving forward in Libra, the first full week of both planets being direct brings a refreshing combination of productivity and pleasure. You may notice that your relationships with coworkers are improving, that you’re getting more recognition for your contributions, or that a project you’ve been working on is finally becoming enjoyable again. Venus in your creativity and romance zone could also inspire you to bring more personality into your professional life, whether that’s pitching an unconventional idea, adding humor to your content, or connecting with colleagues outside the usual work setting. Who says being productive has to be boring, Gemini? You might accomplish more when you’re actually having fun.

As Scorpio Season comes to a close, the Aquarius Moon at the beginning of the week activates your travel and adventure realm, making this an excellent time to explore something outside your usual routine. You could discover a fascinating podcast, sign up for a workshop, or start planning a trip that gives you something exciting to look forward to. When the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your career takes center stage, and you may find yourself receiving attention from someone influential or feeling inspired to take on more responsibility. Then the Aries Moon over the weekend  energizes your friendship zone, making it a great time to organize a gathering or reconnect with people who bring out your adventurous side. Let curiosity lead the way. You never know which conversation could open your next door.

Cancer, your main-character energy is making a comeback, and this time you’ve got the confidence to back it up. With Mercury now direct in your creativity and fame zone and Venus moving forward in your home realm, you may feel increasingly comfortable  sharing more of your personality with the world. Perhaps you’re ready to film that video you’ve been overthinking, submit your work to a publication, or invite friends over for a gathering that shows off your hosting skills. You could also find inspiration in your family history, childhood memories, or cultural roots and incorporate those influences into something creative. There’s something powerful about letting people experience your perspective, Cancer, especially when you’ve spent so much time keeping your best ideas to yourself.

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon activates your intimacy and shared-resources zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for tackling practical matters involving joint finances, subscriptions, or financial commitments. Then, when the moon enters fellow Water sign Pisces on the 17th, your appetite for adventure grows. You may feel inspired to research a destination you’ve always wanted to visit, explore a new neighborhood, or connect with someone from a different cultural background. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your career sector, giving you the courage to take a professional risk. Whether you’re pitching yourself for an opportunity, reaching out to a potential mentor, or announcing an exciting project, don’t underestimate how far a little initiative could take you. The spotlight looks good on you, Cancer.

Leo, the cosmic traffic jam is finally clearing, and you’re ready to get back in the driver’s seat. With Mercury now direct in your home zone and Venus moving forward in your communication realm, the first full week of both planets being direct brings a welcome sense of ease to your everyday interactions. You may find yourself laughing more with relatives, making exciting plans with siblings, or finally enjoying a living space you’ve spent weeks trying to organize. This could also be a great time to host a dinner party, explore a new neighborhood, or invite someone over who’s been asking to see you. After all the retrograde back-and-forth, there’s something refreshing about making plans without needing a Plan B, C, and D. Let yourself enjoy the simpler pleasures of life, Leo.

As Scorpio Season enters its final stretch, the Aquarius Moon highlights your partnership zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for quality time with someone special or an exciting one-on-one collaboration. Then, when the Moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your intimacy realm gets activated, encouraging deeper conversations about your desires, finances, or future plans. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your travel and adventure zone, and with Mars in your sign, you may feel an irresistible  urge to get out of town, try something spontaneous, or say yes to an experience you’d usually overthink. A last-minute getaway or an unexpected invitation could be exactly the change of scenery you need.

Congratulations, Virgo — your ruling planet Mercury is finally behaving again! With  Mercury moving forward in Scorpio and Venus direct in Libra, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring a noticeable improvement to your communication and financial affairs. Maybe an overdue payment finally arrives, a client responds to your proposal, or a conversation that previously went in circles suddenly becomes productive. You may also feel more confident promoting your work, reaching out to potential customers, or sharing your expertise with people who could benefit from it. If you’ve been considering teaching a class, offering a service, or monetizing a skill, this is an encouraging time to test the waters. Your ideas have value, Virgo, and people may be more receptive to them than you expect.

As Scorpio Season winds down, the Aquarius Moon energizes your work and wellness zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for trying a new productivity tool, switching up your workout routine, or finding a more enjoyable rhythm with your responsibilities. When the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your partnership realm takes center stage, and you may find yourself feeling especially appreciative of the people who make your life easier. Plan a date, celebrate a friend’s accomplishment, or spend quality time with someone whose company you genuinely enjoy. Then the Aries  Moon over the weekend activates your intimacy zone, potentially inspiring a bold conversation about a joint goal or financial commitment. You’ve spent enough time analyzing every possibility, Virgo. Give yourself permission to enjoy the progress you’re making.

Libra, your magnetism is back, your confidence is rising, and the universe may finally be ready to give you your flowers. After weeks of Venus retrograde in your sign testing your patience, the first full week of your ruling planet moving direct could feel like a breath of fresh air. You may notice people being more receptive to your ideas, compliments coming your way, or opportunities that previously seemed out of reach suddenly becoming available. With Mercury also direct in your money and self-worth zone, this could be an especially promising time to negotiate a raise, attract new clients, or treat yourself to something you’ve been saving up for. If you’ve been feeling overlooked or under-appreciated lately, the tide may be turning in your favor. Enjoy being pursued, celebrated, and recognized for everything you bring to the table.

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon activates your romance, creativity, and pleasure zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for flirting,  socializing, or getting back into a hobby that makes you feel alive. Then, when the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your wellness and daily-routine realm gets a boost, encouraging you to find a healthier balance between productivity and play. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your partnership zone, potentially bringing an exciting date, a spontaneous invitation, or a breakthrough in a close relationship. With  Mars in Leo energizing your friendship realm, someone in your social circle could even play matchmaker. Say yes to being seen, Libra. Your charm is doing some serious overtime this week.

Scorpio, is it just us, or does it feel like your birthday season is finally hitting its stride?  With Mercury now direct in your sign and Venus moving forward in Libra, this could be the most energized and confident you’ve felt all Scorpio Season. After weeks of second-guessing your decisions or feeling like you had to explain yourself a hundred different ways, you may find that trusting your instincts comes naturally again. You could feel inspired to refresh your appearance, announce a personal project, or make a decision you’ve been sitting on for far too long. Venus direct in your spirituality and solitude realm also brings a welcome sense of emotional ease, helping you feel more comfortable with where you are in life. There’s something incredibly attractive about someone who knows what they want, Scorpio, and that energy is radiating from you right now.

As your season approaches its grand finale, the Aquarius Moon begins the week in your home and family zone, making it a great time to celebrate with loved ones or enjoy the comforts of your personal sanctuary. Then, when the Moon enters fellow Water sign Pisces on the 17th, your romance, creativity, and pleasure realm comes alive. A flirtatious encounter, artistic breakthrough, or spontaneous celebration could remind you just how much fun life can be. By the weekend, the Aries Moon energizes your wellness zone, while Mars in Leo lights up your career realm. You may feel motivated to make a bold professional move, share an accomplishment, or step into the spotlight in a way that feels long overdue. End your season with a bang, Scorpio. The world is ready for more of you!

Sag, your birthday season is just one week away, and you’ve hit the cosmic jackpot by getting to experience it with both Mercury and Venus direct! After weeks of retrograde reflection, the universe is practically rolling out the red carpet for your comeback. With Mercury moving forward in your spirituality realm and Venus direct in your friendship zone, you may already notice your enthusiasm for life returning. Friends could start reaching out with invitations, exciting group plans may come together, or you might find yourself dreaming up a birthday celebration that’s a little extra this year. And why shouldn’t it be? This is your cosmic pregame, Sag! Enjoy reconnecting with your favorite people, making plans for the adventures ahead, and feeling that familiar spark of optimism returning.

As Scorpio Season wraps up, however, there’s still something delicious about enjoying a little hibernation before the festivities begin. The Aquarius Moon early in the week activates your communication zone, making it a great time to clear your inbox, organize your space, or handle errands you’ve been postponing. Then, when the moon enters  Pisces on the 17th, your home and family realm takes center stage, encouraging you to rest, enjoy homemade meals, or spend quality time with loved ones. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your romance and pleasure zone, giving you an early taste of the fiery energy that’s about to define your season. You might feel inspired to dress up, flirt, dance, or do something spontaneous just because you can. Your birthday season is almost here, Sag. Get your beauty sleep now, because things are about to get exciting!

Capricorn, the universe is finally returning your calls, and some of them could lead to opportunities worth celebrating. With Mercury now direct in your friendship zone and Venus moving forward in your career realm, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring a refreshing wave of professional and social momentum. Perhaps a former colleague reaches out with an opportunity, someone recommends you for a project, or a connection you’ve been nurturing finally leads to something tangible. Venus direct in Libra can also make it easier to win people over professionally, especially if you’re presenting an idea, interviewing for a position, or building relationships with influential people. You’ve spent enough time waiting for the right moment. Your reputation and connections could be opening doors for you now, so enjoy the recognition!

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon activates your money and self-worth zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for reviewing your financial progress or rewarding yourself for a recent accomplishment. When the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your communication realm gets a boost, and you may find yourself enjoying spontaneous conversations, neighborhood outings, or an invitation to connect with someone interesting. Then the Aries Moon over the weekend lights up your home and family zone, inspiring you to refresh your living space, host a gathering, or tackle a domestic project you’ve been putting off. With Mars in Leo energizing your shared resources realm, you might even find a creative way to split costs or make a home improvement more affordable. Let yourself enjoy the fruits of your labor, Capricorn. Life can be productive and pleasurable at the same time.

Aquarius, your comeback era is looking pretty promising, and people are starting to take notice. With Mercury now direct in your career zone and Venus moving forward in your travel and expansion realm, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring exciting opportunities to broaden your horizons. Perhaps you’re invited to speak at an event, collaborate with someone overseas, or share your expertise with an audience you hadn’t previously considered. If you’ve been dreaming of working remotely from another country, applying for a fellowship, or taking your career in a more adventurous direction, you may feel increasingly optimistic about your options. Venus direct in fellow Air sign Libra also makes networking across cultures and communities especially rewarding. Your world is getting bigger, Aquarius, and your talents deserve to travel far!

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the moon begins in your sign, giving you an extra boost of confidence, charisma, and emotional clarity. This is a great time to prioritize yourself, refresh your look, or initiate something you’ve been excited about. When the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your money and self-worth zone gets activated, encouraging you to explore ways to make your talents more profitable or celebrate a recent financial win. By the weekend, the Aries Moon energizes your communication realm, making it a fantastic time for spontaneous outings, lively conversations, or sharing something bold on social media. With Mars in Leo activating your partnership zone, someone special could even encourage you to take a leap you wouldn’t have considered on your own. Let yourself be seen, Aquarius. You have plenty worth celebrating!

Pisces, the universe is finally giving you the green light to explore, expand, and enjoy  yourself again. With Mercury now direct in your travel and adventure zone and Venus moving forward in your intimacy realm, the first full week of both planets being direct could make some of your bigger dreams feel more attainable. Maybe you’re discovering a scholarship, finding a more affordable way to travel, or receiving financial support that helps you pursue an exciting opportunity. You could also feel more comfortable discussing money with a partner or exploring ways to combine resources toward a shared goal. After weeks of reviewing your options, there’s something refreshing about realizing you have more possibilities than you initially thought. Dream big, Pisces. You may be pleasantly surprised by how much support is available when you ask for it.

As Scorpio Season comes to a close, the Aquarius Moon begins the week in your solitude and spirituality zone, encouraging you to recharge your batteries and enjoy some peaceful time away from the noise. Then, when the moon enters your sign on the 17th, the energy shifts beautifully in your favor. You may feel more magnetic, emotionally connected, and inspired to do something special for yourself, whether that’s booking a massage, going on a date, or spending time near the water. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your money and self-worth realm, potentially inspiring a spontaneous purchase, a new income idea, or the confidence to ask for  what you deserve. With Mars in Leo energizing your work and wellness zone, you could also feel motivated to invest in something that makes your everyday life more enjoyable. You’ve spent enough time weighing every possibility, Pisces. Let yourself experience some of the joy you’ve been planning for!

In today’s episode, we talk about how early-2000s YouTube and Teen Vogue Fashion University shaped her style education, how she built an audience by refusing to be precious about digging through other people's old underwear, and why she thinks clothing quality has gone downhill.

Macy also walks us through her new book, Second Chances: The Ultimate Guide to Thrifting, Sustainable Style and Expressing Your Authentic Self, including her two-page spread of extinct Y2K mall brands. I have a confession to make: I've been thinking about cheating on my Christmas tree this year. Not with another full-sized fir, but with a growing collection of miniature, colorful, and delightfully unconventional alternatives that have absolutely no business being this cute. And judging by the number of faux trees currently occupying my online shopping carts, this might be getting out of hand.

Don't get me wrong. I love traditional Christmas trees as much as the next person (and there are some ahead!). The twinkling lights, the sentimental ornaments, the excuse to rearrange your entire living room around a seven-foot centerpiece? I'm here for all of it. But somewhere between discovering a wicker tree dressed up in oversized velvet bows and a sparkly little number that looks like it belongs in a disco, I realized that holiday decorating doesn't have to be quite so serious.
In fact, the more personality, the better.

This year's faux Christmas trees are making a compelling case for abandoning the rule book altogether. We're talking sculptural silhouettes, unexpected textures, candy-colored branches, and designs that could easily double as art installations. Some are charmingly understated while others look like they were dreamed up by someone who considers more is more a personal philosophy. Naturally, I want both.

And here's the beauty of going faux: You can skip the falling needles, forget about watering anything, and keep your festive masterpiece looking fabulous year after year. Plus, who says you have to stop at one? A petite tree on your nightstand, a statement-making creation in the entryway, and something wonderfully ridiculous on your mantel sound like a perfectly reasonable decorating strategy to me.

Whether you're working with a tiny apartment, looking to give your usual holiday setup a little personality, or simply can't resist something shiny, I've rounded up the faux Christmas trees that deserve a spot on your nice list.
Fair warning: Your traditional tree might get a little jealous.

items.title: Everything We Know About Adults Season 3
items.description: Adults has officially been renewed for Season 3 at FX and Hulu. That's not all: the studio has ordered 16 episodes for the next season. Seasons 1 and 2 only had eight episodes each, so this is a true blessing. We'll be reunited with Samir (Malik Essal), Billie
items.author: Simran Pasricha
paragraphs: Adults has officially been renewed for Season 3 at FX and Hulu. That's not all: the studio has ordered 16 episodes for the next season. Seasons 1 and 2 only had eight episodes each, so this is a true blessing. We'll be reunited with Samir (Malik Essal), Billie (Lucy Freyer), Issa (Amita Rao), Anton (Owen Thiele) and Paul Baker (Jack Innanen).

Specific plot details haven’t been announced. For now, the premise remains five twenty-somethings living in Samir’s childhood home in New York, trying to navigate work, relationships, family and the delicate business of being in each other’s space constantly.

Main cast members Malik Elassal, Lucy Freyer, Jack Innanen, Amita Rao and Owen Thiele are coming back. No guest stars or recurring stars have been announced, but we will likely see Issa's new love interest, the librarian played by Mia Fowler.

n 3, according to Freyer. "[Fox]was like, 'I wanna come back next season, and the season you don’t bring me back is the season you’re gonna get cancelled,'" she told Refinery29 Australia. "And I was like, she put a curse on us, and I believe it. And now, she has to be in every season of the show for as long as it runs. And I'm like, 'OK!'"

Behind the scenes, Kronengold and Shaw remain the creators, showrunners and executive producers. Their statement about the new FX deal also acknowledged a particularly important figure in this whole operation. "We started working with FX over six years ago, back when Paul Baker was but a twinkle in all of our eyes," they joked.
Not yet, but we will update this article once there is.

The audience has grown, which is reassuring news for anyone who has been personally campaigning for their friends to watch. According to FX, Season 2 viewership increased by 60% compared with Season 1 across Hulu and Disney+ globally over its first five weeks. International viewership doubled. The network didn’t release actual audience totals, so we don't know exactly how many people joined the household.

FX Entertainment president Nick Grad also credited the show’s devoted following. "Ben and Rebecca have elevated Adults in every way, earning critical praise and a legion of devoted fans who have embraced the friend group as their own," he said in a statement.
There’s no announced release date for season three yet, but in the meantime, Australians can watch the first two seasons on Disney+.
