items.author: Susan Hornik
paragraphs: Last year, I sold my parents’ co-op apartment in Queens, after holding on to it for two decades and paying the monthly maintenance fees – even though I lived 2,500 miles away in Los Angeles. I grew up there; those three-and-a-half rooms, overstuffed with modest furniture and childhood souvenirs, were imprinted on my skin. During infrequent trips east, sitting on one of the cozy cream couches in the living room of my inherited New York sanctuary – with its 40-year-old cupboards and old-fashioned bathroom mirror – I could almost feel my parents’ presence.

I never got to say goodbye, but if I close my eyes tight, I can still see my beautiful train wrecks – aka, my parents – on vacation with me in Playa del Carmen, south of Cancún, on 10 December 2004. They are sitting in the back of our rental car, dusty but cheerful, on the way to the Tulum ruins. My so-not-thin father, Karl, is hungry, for a change. My mother, Violet, is impatient from the suffocating Mexican heat. So rather than listen to them argue, I pull over to the side of the road. It is scorchingly dry. My mind, too, is parched and dull from their nonstop pestering. But I am used to it: arguing is their love language.

The locals tell me el restaurante is across the road, so I start the car back up, go to the worn Stop sign, then move behind a large truck, thinking the driver is about to make what they call a retorno, or U-turn.

But the truck doesn’t move. Why is it just sitting in the middle of the road? We are in the middle of the road and he’s not turning. My brain is in slow motion when I notice a taxi speeding toward us, so close, so fast.
I went to one hospital, and Ma and Pa to others

Why am I crushed between the seatbelt and the car door? Why is my ma unconscious? Her owl-like glasses crushed against her sweet, soft face, which had amazingly few wrinkles for a woman in her 70s. Why is my father screaming: ‘Violet, wake up!’

I reach the hospital and am put in a wheelchair. Those who speak English tell me Mexico is a poor country, ambulances need the business, so the drivers were fighting with each other over who to take where – and that’s why I went to one hospital, and Ma and Pa to others.
My hospital bed is near the taxi guy who hit our car. The doctors tell me the driver will be OK, just shards of glass in his face. He cries, knowing I am near him.

‘Please help me stand up so I can find my parents,’ I say. But the rude nurse tells me: ‘You could go to jail if you don’t cooperate’ and ‘Sit still, we need to monitor you.’ Then the US Consulate calls. My ma is dead.

The nurses feed me papaya slices because, in my basic high-school Spanish, I asked for fruit and they thought I wanted only that for every meal. I notice irony, like the fact that my parents loved fried foods and I would scold them about eating healthy. Yet now Ma is dead; she could have eaten anything she wanted. And there was a beautiful serendipity with my orthopaedic doctor, who holds my hand and tells me, in broken English, that he was on call at my mother’s hospital. He tried everything to help her, but for her frail, petite body, a massive haemorrhage was too much. At least she did not die alone.

Initially, the police are puzzled: why was my car in the middle of the road, and did I even know my passengers? When the policewoman and detective visit my hospital room, I tearfully explain. My passengers were my parents. With their round bellies after retirement, they had protested wearing seatbelts, so I put them in the back.

As I tell them about the retorno lane, where the truck blocked our way forward, leaving us in the path of the speeding taxi, the policewoman starts crying. She knows the area and knew the truck had been abandoned. I was at the wrong place, wrong time.
Back home, the tumour is taken out, but he’s a vegetable

So… good news, I am no longer blamed for the accident or facing Cancún jail. The US Consulate helps free me from the Mexican police, who return my mother’s rings. And I’ve no broken bones, just contusions; give it a few months and I’ll be able to walk with a cane.

Worse news, my father is acting strangely. They’ve found a large non-cancerous brain tumour, growing in his head for 20 years and no one knew. Yet it made sense. He is more forgetful, no longer enjoying the use of forks and knives. One afternoon, in Queens, he’d brought down my luggage and stood holding my computer in the pouring rain, no umbrella, until the taxi came.

I beg his insurance to medevac us to New York City, and they do. The triumph is short lived. Back home, the tumour is taken out, but he’s a vegetable. They move him to a nursing home, and he’s too sick even for a place like that. Three months later, he’s dead, too.

That moment when I touched his cheek in the funeral home will always stay with me. Refrigerated, his skin was cold. You look good, Daddy, I half-smiled inside to myself. My ma, on the other hand, had to be embalmed to fly back to New York. She looked jarringly unreal, like a doll.
But our old apartment was the coziest, safest place in the world. In recent years, my cousin lectured me about the financial cost: ‘You do know they are never coming back, right?’

I was distracted by the frayed photobooks Ma kept crammed in the fake-wood bookcases. I found myself lingering, squeezing long-forgotten memories back into my brain. Checking the pockets of my father’s large winter coats, I found one of the many square handkerchiefs my ma would stuff into them. Still neatly folded, yellowed in spots from old snot, it was a joy to clutch in my hands.

Seeing the photos documenting my life, I was grateful to my ma, who commanded my father and me to take hundreds of them. In one of my favourites, Ma wears a cream-coloured Mexican dress with a colourful fabric trim she’d bought on a previous trip to Playa del Carmen. Then there was the photo with her blue floppy hat and double-breasted bathing suit. Next to her, my father, holding in his stomach at her request – maybe he wouldn’t look so fat.
That divine Italian tomato sauce could melt in my mouth whenever I was back in town
Now, when I remember my parents, I think of… food. How they had dessert even with breakfast. My father’s love of pizza had him consuming a slice from Gaby’s down the hill every single day.

Maybe that’s another reason why I held on to the apartment, so that divine Italian tomato sauce could melt in my mouth whenever I was back in town. Miraculously, Gaby’s has lasted for decades and it’s a beautiful thing to eat something I’ve loved since I was 10 years old.

Still, I listed the apartment in January 2025. ‘Beautiful grounds, well maintained elevator building, Very Large 1 king size bedroom with two double closets, EIK fits table and chairs, Dining room living room very spacious,’ the ad on Zillow read. Months later, it was sold.
As much as I wanted to savour more than the two big boxes I was shipping back to my tiny guest house in California, I threw away so much… what remained was just a glimmer of who they were.

If only I had a time machine to go back to our days on Francis Lewis Boulevard, in the kitchen where she’d talk to me: ‘Suzie dolly, you are home!’ I grew up trying to adjust to the high anxiety she lived with. It was a good day when we weren’t fighting about, well, everything.

Sometimes, I would do just about anything to get away from her shrill Brooklynese, or beg my father to please share some of the burden – so that maybe he could be bothered by her too, just for a bit. Now, I long to hear her Jewish momma voice. I can hear it exasperating me.
She worried endlessly about me, because she had lost my older brother, her only son

I could taste her temper from a mile away. Her rage was black, like the colour of her permed wavy hair, and when she wasn’t hitting me, I grappled with her fear of what could happen when I walked out the door.
You could die or get stabbed.
You could get mugged on the train.
‘Ma, that’s not goin’ to happen.’

She worried endlessly about me, because she had lost my older brother, her only son, Michael Stuart, who lived for only three weeks before dying in the Brooklyn hospital. I tried to reassure her, bringing flowers and chocolate. But I could not escape.

And yet I missed her scent: a mix of baby powder and Jean Naté. (If you don’t know Jean Naté, go to a drugstore, and look at the bottom shelf, with the cheap imitation perfumes. I’m sure you’ll find a bottle.)

Of course, it was better than the smell of the mothballs she’d put in everything – something her Jewish mothers’ generation was hip to at the time. These were chemical pesticides that a child should never even be near! Did we live in the jungle? Were we being plagued by moths? Every spring, I’d reach into my pockets and find myself still touching a bunch of these balls she’d forgotten to take out.
Argument #20,124: ‘Get rid of the mothballs, Ma.’
Why does it bother you so much?!
‘Because they fucking smell, Ma.’
Don’t use that language with me.
‘Well, you taught it to me.’
In her later years, she realised those mothballs weren’t necessary, but she still didn’t trust me.
Together we would laugh so much… as if we had a secret language no one else shared
‘Ma, let me cook you dinner.’
No, that’s OK, we can eat out.
‘Why do you say that, Ma?!’

I was the better cook. Well, at least I knew how to read a recipe. I never did develop a taste for her boiled chicken. She kept all of her mother’s handwritten recipes. I promised to rewrite and save them for her but I never did. I still have every fragment of yellowing pages.

While I tried to talk with her about our oft-antagonistic relationship, she seemed to be mostly unaware of all the times that she’d hit me or called me names. And yet, we were still best friends when she died. I adored teasing her; together we would laugh so much… as if we had a secret language no one else shared.

If she were still alive, I’d want to ask her: ‘Why’d you piss me off so fucking much, Ma?’ I wish we could sit here and eat your favourite tea cookies. I look for you in my dreams. You elicited such intensity, Ma.
It wasn’t that bad, she would say of my childhood.

And sure, that’s true. I did look cute in those black patent-leather shoes, and we did enjoy that slice of blackberry pie to celebrate sixth-grade graduation. I don’t fault you for the bad perm you had me get. Or for throwing out my three-foot-tall Rosie doll after your screaming fit.

It’s just that when you tried to hang me outside the second-storey window to teach me a lesson, you never thought it could trash my soul. There was something wrong with you, Ma. I should have realised that, but I was so small.

What the fuck, Ma. We both should have been better to each other. Why am I alive and you dead? Why did I drive the car that accidentally killed you? After being evacuated twice during the Los Angeles wildfires, what was I holding on to? I could no longer clearly see my Ma standing outside the apartment door, wearing her owl-spectacle glasses, permed black Brillo hair and faded frock, waiting to hug me as I got off the elevator. My parents don’t live in Queens anymore.

items.title: What does motherhood look like without my best friend? | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: On page five of an eight-page letter dated 3 September 2019, my friend – whom I will call Naaz – wrote to me:
items.author: Ashwaq Masoodi
paragraphs: On page five of an eight-page letter dated 3 September 2019, my friend – whom I will call Naaz – wrote to me:

I always pray that nothing in this world may ever blur your vision of your own self. Not people, not your circumstances. One must not be delusional, but one should also never lose the grip of one’s essence. Never forget who you are, what all you have achieved, how hard you worked to be where you are today.

Naaz had never written to me before – not a note, not a postcard. We were on each other’s speed dial for as long as I could remember. But that August, the Indian state had revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status and, anticipating blowback, had throttled internet broadband, cable TV, landlines and mobile networks. Even postal services were disrupted; Naaz planned to hand-deliver her letter. Another letter tells me that on 11 August she knocked on my door for a long time. But I had already left for New Delhi, and would soon be halfway across the world.

In Kashmir, we are used to uncertainty but, in those days, it was dialled all the way up. When I left, I did not know when I would be able to speak with my parents again. We seemed to have collectively tumbled back in time to the 1990s, when separatist conflict was at its peak and, with it, the Indian state’s iron-fist policy to counter it. I was leaving for a year-long journalism fellowship at Harvard, and wracked with guilt and self-doubt: guilt over leaving when so many others could not, self-doubt over whether I would live up to the opportunity. Perhaps Naaz sensed my ambivalence, which is why she wrote those lines. She knew I might need the reminder.

Naaz first knew me as a bushy-browed teenager, travelling 110 km each day to study journalism in Baramulla, a small town in Kashmir. We met on a bus, in the spring of 2005. She was in a three-seater near the middle, in a white crewneck sweater with a Fair Isle pattern around the neckline. I took the seat beside her. I remember what she wore because my mother knit sweaters for me in that pattern, too. Within minutes, we were exchanging names, then places, then families. My mother was from the same area as her. My naanu had taught Naaz’s father. Her father had taught mine. Our meeting felt both serendipitous and predetermined.

She was seven years older than me, a science teacher, a lover of poetry. In a society steeped in existential despair, she took her vocation seriously. ‘We are the builders of Kashmir,’ she’d say. Growing up, I’d seldom encountered older people who weren’t in survival mode, always braced for the next loss or threat, who were able to support those dreaming of lives larger than the ones they’d inherited. Perhaps that’s why Naaz – thoughtful, curious, never infantilising – was so easy to like.
My friendship with Naaz quickly deepened into something closer to sisterhood

I dreamed of being a reporter. A few years after meeting Naaz, I would join a workshop led by one of Kashmir’s finest journalists. Every Sunday, at 9 am, a group of us – the youngest in their teens, the oldest in their 40s – gathered in his tiny apartment in Srinagar, thick with the smell of old books and cigarettes. We read Ryszard Kapuściński’s dispatches and watched The Battle of Algiers.
‘If we don’t tell our story, someone else will,’ he would often remind us.

My friendship with Naaz quickly deepened into something closer to sisterhood. Even when I moved away, for further studies or for work, we spoke almost daily. We would fall asleep on the phone, only to wake when the phones slipped and knocked against our faces. When I visited, we would take boat rides on Dal Lake, stroll aimlessly through the Mughal Gardens, go on long drives around Srinagar, never running out of conversation. Two young men might be construed as a security threat and attract state surveillance; a young man and woman might be seen as romantically involved and draw social scrutiny. Female friendship, on the other hand, could occupy public space more freely, without constantly defending its right to exist.

Naaz and I often joked that our ‘halal:haram’ ratio was almost identical, a way of saying we drew a similar line between the permissible and the forbidden, with many of the same compromises and contradictions. And yet we were utterly different in other ways. She would not undo what she had already done. If she left the house with her hair tied, she would keep it tied, even if it no longer made sense to do so. Whereas I agonised over everything. Naaz was surprised I could put myself in all sorts of situations as a journalist – interviewing human traffickers, reporting from conflict zones – and yet be so internally unanchored. I was driven but also anxious: I wanted professional success but, when it came, I knew only how to move past it, towards the next milestone. Naaz would shake me lightly, yanking me back to the present.
‘Can you be proud of yourself? Can you accept that you are good?’

When I returned to Kashmir after my fellowship ended, we met at her wedding. The happiest bride I have ever seen, when she saw me, she held my hands and pulled me into a tight embrace. Within months, I too was married. Despite our age difference, it felt as if something larger was aligning our lives. We became pregnant within months of each other, our conversations turning to baby names, nausea, exhaustion.
‘What do you want,’ I asked her once, ‘a girl or a boy?’
‘It doesn’t matter,’ she said. ‘I just hope the baby survives. I hope I survive.’

I remember feeling a flicker of irritation when she said that. Doom-mongering was what I did. And why would anything go wrong? Yes, she was in her late 30s, but she was healthier than most 20-somethings. Meanwhile, I fretted over how motherhood would alter the life I’d carefully built for myself, the five-year plans that I worried would now be upended. It didn’t help that my partner and I would be moving to Germany soon.
Each time I visited Kashmir, my heart clenched – that unmistakable giggle was gone

Naaz gave birth in September. Days later, she suffered an intracerebral haemorrhage – a brain bleed caused by a ruptured blood vessel, the risk of which is three times higher among women during pregnancy and in the weeks following delivery. She was the one who messaged to tell me. I should keep a tab on my vitals, she added, and not stress out over small things while pregnant. Soon after, she slipped into a coma.

A month passed before Naaz regained consciousness. Even though there were times when she seemed to be improving, the things that distinguished her began slipping away. Among the first women in her village to drive, she could no longer hold the movement of a car. A poet, she could no longer read or write. Each time I visited Kashmir, my heart clenched – that unmistakable giggle was gone, as was the way she tucked loose strands of her hair, behind her right ear specifically. Once, when I went to see her, I noticed how her dupatta, which she typically flung around her neck, was spread out over her chest. She would never wear it that way, I kept thinking to myself. As terrifying as it was to witness her suffering, so was the dissipation of things that make a person: language, memory, skill.

For more than two years, Naaz fought bravely. She passed away in March 2024 – typically, a month of birthdays in my family. That year, all through March and April, my toddler played Zum Geburtstag viel Glück in an endless loop on her music box – Happy Birthday in German, the soundtrack to my grief.

It was early morning in Berlin when I received the news. When I read the message – N is no more – I collapsed onto the prayer rug, crying into my breath so I wouldn’t wake my two-year-old. Later, when my daughter stirred, expecting me beside her as always, I moved toward her, my body performing the choreography of care as if nothing had happened. As if the mountain hadn’t fallen over me.

In Kashmir, we are used to untimely death. But how to grieve the loss of your best friend, so young, so vividly alive? And how to grieve with a two-year-old at close hand, amid meals NOW, baths NOW, nappy change NOW, tantrums NOW?
Grief, in a sense, has become intertwined with motherhood

I had known motherhood would unsettle my sense of self – what I never imagined was that it would also take away the person who held my story alongside me. In narrative psychology, identity is theorised as what Dan P McAdams calls an ‘evolving story of the self’ – an integration of one’s reconstructed past, perceived present and imagined future. This story has multiple authors. We come to know who we are through conversation, through shared recollection, through being witnessed: by our parents, our siblings, our partners, our best friends. Each holds a fragment of us, reflecting the person we are and the person we once were. Those shared memories become the story we tell ourselves about our own life. That story is never fixed. It changes as we change, and as the people who hold pieces of it enter and leave our lives. With Naaz’s death, parts of my past lost their primary witness just as motherhood began shaking the very roots of who I was.

Kashmir – my home, my muse – has changed, too. Since 2019, dissent of any sort is promptly quashed. The graffiti proclaiming azadi, freedom, has disappeared from the walls as has any public expression of separatist sentiment. Local journalists are asked to sign pledges vowing not to ‘disturb the peace’. Most of our writing group has drifted into PR or fiction; one of the youngest members was recently released after two years in prison. Like people, places also need someone to hold on to their stories. In Kashmir, bearing witness now comes at a cost.

Two years ago, I became pregnant again. As I gave birth the second time, memories from the days after Naaz’s death started playing on a loop. Grief, in a sense, has become intertwined with motherhood. It is there when I lift my son, when I chase him down the hallway. I hear his laughter and think of Naaz’s. She should have lived to experience this: the chaos, the beauty, the bone-deep exhaustion that is now my everyday.

Occasionally, in a note jotted in the margin of a book, on a walk by myself in the park, in the sheaf of letters that eventually made their way into my hands, I catch a glimpse of my earlier self: the journalist, Naaz’s best girl. I have taken to telling my daughter stories from that time, as if piecing together a self she has never known. For now, the only one she remembers is about the time a jellyfish stung me on a beach in Miami. ‘Once more… only one,’ she says, asking me again and again to act out the moment the jellyfish stung me. I oblige every time.

items.title: The ex-cop on a mission to see fortune-tellers arrested | Psyche Portraits
items.description: In 2008, Bob Nygaard sat on a stool at the Neighborhood Sports Bar and Grill in Boca Raton, Florida, just before 5 pm. It was Wednesday, a night with generous happy-hour deals and the possibility of taking someone home by last call. Nygaard, a tall and brawny
items.author: Shayla Love
paragraphs: In 2008, Bob Nygaard sat on a stool at the Neighborhood Sports Bar and Grill in Boca Raton, Florida, just before 5 pm. It was Wednesday, a night with generous happy-hour deals and the possibility of taking someone home by last call. Nygaard, a tall and brawny man with a disarmingly goofy smile, had the strongest New York accent for miles. He had recently retired from a 21-year-long career as an NYPD officer. At 46, he got out when his pension kicked in, and moved down to Florida to relax.
Except he wasn’t relaxed. He was bored.

Nygaard had been a high-energy cop who didn’t get along with fellow officers because of how doggedly he pursued arrests. He probably should have known that he wouldn’t adjust to sipping Mai Tais and sitting on the beach. Shortly after arriving in Florida, he got a private investigator’s licence, using it to track down missing money or catch cheating husbands. Neither was satisfying.

He ordered a rum and Coke. He had become friendly with the bartender, who introduced him to two women sitting at the end of the bar, a nurse and a doctor. They had dinner together, swapping stories about working in medicine and the police force. Nygaard gave both women his card. Ten minutes later, his phone rang. It was the doctor. Could they meet up nearby, on a street corner outside a Chevron station? Nygaard thought she was hoping to hook up.

When she pulled up and rolled down the window, her face was half-covered in shadows. ‘I’ve never been able to tell anyone this before,’ she said from the driver’s seat. ‘I’m a medical doctor and I fell for a psychic.’ She had given more than $12,000 to a woman she met through her hairdresser. The psychic said someone had put a curse on the doctor: it explained why she was having issues with her immigration papers, and why her love life was ruined. For enough money, the curse could be lifted. Now, the doctor realised she’d been had. Nygaard had arrested conmen before. Could he help her?

From that moment on, Nygaard was never bored again. He became a PI who specialises in helping victims of psychics. And he didn’t settle cases out of court – he went after arrests to get as much money back for his clients as possible. Through word of mouth, psychic victims all over the country have sought him out. Since his first case, Nygaard has helped recover more than $5 million.

I first heard about Nygaard around a year ago, through a news article about a psychic’s arrest he had orchestrated in Philadelphia. I thought of him as part fictional detective Sherlock Holmes, part real-life Harry Houdini, who spent his later years exposing mediums. When I initially reached out over email, Nygaard didn’t respond. But after I sent a follow-up, I got a call from an unknown number a few days later. It was Nygaard: ‘I like when people don’t give up,’ he told me. He started talking fast, recounting his recent cases. What drives a retired cop, someone who busted drug dealers and burglars, to focus only on this fringe sect of society – psychics? And why was he so good at it? We made plans to meet up in the city.

On a below-freezing day in early February, I turned a narrow corner in lower Manhattan and saw a figure wearing a beige trench coat and fedora standing under the granite arch of the historic Life and Trust Bank. In my memory, steam started to rise up from the sidewalk grates, and the deserted street became the spot for a clandestine midnight meet-up. In truth, it was a clear sunny morning and Nygaard was politely waiting for me outside, but every minute spent with him can make you feel like you’re acting out a scene from a movie set in old New York. The former bank now houses a coffee shop. We walked into the cavernous lobby and ordered drinks where the bank tellers once sat.

I expected to meet a hardened law-enforcement officer with a dark past. Maybe he, or someone he loved, had been wronged by a psychic, and he had a score to settle. Or maybe he was a rationalist – someone so dedicated to an evidence-based view of the world that he wouldn’t stand for anyone proposing they could break the laws of nature.

But as we settled down with our hot drinks, I learned that Nygaard hadn’t thought about psychics at all until later in life. He had a happy, grounded childhood, he told me. He was born in Queens in 1961, and moved to New Hyde Park, Long Island, when he was four. His mother was 20 when she had him, his father only a few years older. The family, including his younger brother, ate dinner together every evening.
‘Knowing how to deal with the raccoon also helps you deal with the person’

They were a hard-working and proud unit. The family would put on their best clothes to go to the Howard Johnson’s on Jericho Turnpike for fish and chips. Nygaard was taught to always be ‘squared away’. He made his bed in the morning. His hair was always combed. ‘You pay attention to the details, to the little things,’ he said. ‘You’re clean, well dressed, polite, you’re on time.’ Even though his apartment was just around the corner from the café where we sat, he had arrived nearly 20 minutes early to make sure he wasn’t late. (Nygaard now splits his time between Florida and New York, based largely on when the New York Rangers are playing; he has season tickets.)

His sense of justice also seems to have started early. If Nygaard came home and said that all the kids were picking on someone in the schoolyard – ‘knocking them on the ground, calling him four-eyes’ – Nygaard’s father would counter: ‘You didn’t sit there and watch, did you?’

Nygaard spent summers in northeast Pennsylvania, where his grandfather had bought an old farmhouse with no running water or electricity; it relied on kerosene lamps and a well. The property reminded his grandfather of Norway. When Nygaard brought out his friends, brothers called Tommy and Richy Gambino, they had never seen a cow before. Once, they tricked another visiting city kid by telling him that chocolate milk came out of the brown cows’ udders.

In the countryside, Nygaard fostered compassion for other living things. When he was around six, he had a BB gun to shoot at cans. One day, he saw a bird, aimed his gun at it, and shot it out of a tree. Nygaard looked at it up close, examining the pellet in its belly. It wasn’t dead, but it was suffering. He killed it, to put it out of its misery, and then felt sick. ‘I never killed again,’ he told me. Yet, he also gained insights into the animalistic side of humans. When he saw a raccoon trapped inside the barn, he later recognised similar responses in perps with a warrant on them, cornered on a subway platform. ‘Knowing how to deal with the raccoon also helps you deal with the person,’ he said.

It was Nygaard’s father who wanted him to be a police officer. When Nygaard was 17, he took the police test. The job came with a pension and healthcare, Nygaard’s father would say. Plus, he could help people. But Nygaard went to college in Texas, at Southern Methodist University, majoring in business – thinking he would join the family flooring company. Then he got called to the police academy at 23.
He asked if the psychic’s last name was Marks. Stunned, the doctor asked how he had known. ‘I’m psychic,’ he joked

Police work matched his philosophy of justice: when someone broke the law, there were consequences, and it was his job to deliver them. He became obsessive about making arrests, so much so that he chafed against the other cops. When he was an officer on Long Island, there were unspoken rules about how proactive or ambitious to be, he said. Others would accuse him of creating too much paperwork. Supervisors punished him by putting him on desk duty. Yet he still managed to make arrests without leaving the station, remembering passersby with outstanding warrants, and once discovering drugs in someone’s purse. He memorised the penal code, so that he could always justify what he was doing, including a New York State law that fortune-telling was a crime.

One of Nygaard’s few police mentors was the late Jon Grow, a detective at the Baltimore Police Department. Grow co-founded the National Association of Bunco Investigators, a non-profit that helped law-enforcement officers share information about fraudsters and scams around the country. Grow passed Nygaard names and photos of scammers who had hit nearby cities. But it ‘wasn’t until that woman in that bar [in Florida] … that all of that knowledge from those years came into play,’ he said.

When the doctor asked Nygaard to help her, he asked if the psychic’s last name was Marks. Stunned, the doctor asked how he had known. ‘I’m psychic,’ he joked. Actually, the psychic in question was Gina Marie Marks, a serial offender whose last name Nygaard remembered from his conversations with Grow.

Nygaard had one stipulation for taking the doctor’s case: she would pursue an arrest no matter how much money the psychic offered her to settle. Then he found four more women who were Marks’s victims, and gathered evidence from all of them. Eventually, Marks was arrested, and the doctor got her money back.

Marks was his first psychic arrest, and that was the moment the disparate pieces of his life clicked into place. ‘All of those years, all that aggravation … fighting with the bosses … having to know the law – I never understood what it was forging me for,’ he said. ‘It was forging me for this fight.’

In early March, Nygaard and I ate dinner at a corner table at P J Clarke’s in midtown Manhattan. He was telling me about another case: in June 2010, a young woman – let’s use the name Vivian – was walking in New York City when she was approached by a woman who called herself Sarah. Sarah said she sensed an energy from Vivian and that something bad was happening in her life. Indeed, Vivian had recently been discharged from Army Officer Candidate School after an injury, and was going through a divorce.

Sarah and Vivian exchanged numbers, and Sarah later told her that she needed $90 for crystals to figure out where the negativity was coming from. By the end of the month, Sarah said she had figured it out: someone had placed a curse on Vivian, probably her stepmother. Vivian should take out $2,700 and put the money, along with rose petals and tree leaves, under her mattress and sleep on it.

Later, Sarah contacted Vivian to confirm it was her stepmother who had placed the curse. To lift it, she would have to sacrifice the $2,700. Vivian needed to bring the money, a jar, and a pair of white underwear to her apartment. Sarah filled the jar with water, wrapped an egg in the underwear, and rubbed it over Vivian’s body. In the dramatic finale of the ritual, the egg cracked open, and a dead baby corn snake fell out. The water had turned a deep, bloody red.
Psychic tricks haven’t changed much, Nygaard said. Needles emerge from a tomato. An egg cracks, and blood or dead animals spill out

Over the succeeding months, Sarah asked Vivian to send more money. In October 2013, Sarah said ‘the church’ needed $10,800, and Vivian went to the bank and took out a $12,000 loan. Vivian followed instructions to send Sarah a Cartier watch and Saks Fifth Avenue gift cards, though she was unsuccessful in leasing a Mercedes. By the time Vivian contacted Nygaard, she had lost more than $30,000.

Nygaard took Vivian’s case to the NYPD, where he was turned away. But Nygaard knew that Sarah had asked Vivian to send a watch to her address in Florida. If any part of a crime happens out of state, the whole crime can be prosecuted in that jurisdiction. Nygaard flew there to speak to a detective who agreed to help. His accumulation of evidence led to Sarah’s arrest, and Vivian’s money was returned.

Psychic tricks haven’t changed much, Nygaard told me. Needles emerge from a tomato. Something ominous comes out of a grapefruit. An egg cracks, and blood or dead animals spill out. ‘A lot of the newer ones, they stay away from that stuff, but when they want to really go for it, they go old school,’ Nygaard said.
As Nygaard ate his burger, I shared a case of my own: I had gone to see Sarah, who now goes by Emma, a couple weeks earlier, for a psychic reading. Nygaard perked up: ‘Oh, you did?’

I had nervously walked down 12th Street in the East Village until I arrived at a storefront with a green sign. I had wondered if Emma would try to scare me with a curse or some other tactic to get more money from me. I asked for a full-life reading for $150. I didn’t want to lie to be a better mark, so I brought up the most vulnerable topic I had on hand: whether my husband and I should try to have a baby. Emma looked carefully at me while I sat somewhat awkwardly in a large, velvet throne-like chair.

She asked some leading questions about my family (‘there is one family member you’re not as close to, there’s some pain there’) and my husband (‘you’re not spending as much time together these days’). Her first insight was universally obvious, and the second was untrue. I tried to keep the conversation going, but we naturally petered out around 25 minutes later. Emma asked if I would like to have my aura cleansed, because she saw I had two dark spots; it would cost an additional $250. I had budgeted only $300. I declined. Looking a little bored, Emma ended the session.

I found the interaction unimpressive, and, as I left, my sympathy for Nygaard’s clients wavered. The experience didn’t feel like a film noir; I wasn’t caught up in a seedy underbelly world of conmen who were experts at deception. The storefront space had been dumpy, and I was embarrassed to be there. I was even embarrassed for Emma, who was barefoot, possibly wearing a nightgown, and had put no effort into the reading. There were clearly children hiding behind a curtain, attempting to be quiet while their mom worked.

As a journalist who writes about science, I have covered my share of health scams. Throughout my career, I’ve spent hours carefully explaining in articles why certain wellness products don’t work and are a waste of money. There’s no scarcity of psychic scams either. Recent surveys suggest that four in 10 US adults believe in psychics, and as of 2022 the industry makes around $2 billion a year. After a few years of debunking, I accepted that scams were like a hydra’s heads: cut one off, and two more grew in its place.
Walking down the sidewalk, I hardened against the people who could fall for what I’d just experienced. If people could get tricked by that, what good was it to help them?

Across the street from P J Clarke’s, at the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, I had tickets to a one-night-only performance of Houdini Speaks to the Living, a play based on letters between Harry Houdini and Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. Nygaard and I crossed the street into a packed auditorium, finding two empty seats near the back. The lights dimmed, and two actors walked on stage, one representing Doyle, and the other Houdini.

Doyle had dreamed up Sherlock Holmes, the ultimate logician who solved crimes by piecing together clues in ingenious ways. But Doyle was an advocate of Spiritualism, the belief that mediums could communicate with the dead, while Houdini (who once brought tricks based on the idea to his performance) came to believe that the profession was poison. In 1926, Houdini testified before the US Congress for a law that would criminalise fortune-telling. Elected officials didn’t feel it was necessarily their responsibility to help those who were duped. (Did I relate?) Ralph Gilbert, the representative for Kentucky, said that Houdini was ‘taking the matter entirely too seriously’.

The play dramatised Doyle’s attempts to convince Houdini that some mediums were credible. Houdini rebutted with counter-Spiritualism screeds, revealing how the mediums’ tricks work. He was harsh, and came across as a self-righteous know-it-all. Doyle and Houdini’s friendship ended, and they never spoke again.

At the end of the show, Nygaard was animated. I expected him to align with Houdini, especially after my encounter with Emma. Nygaard had seemed like an obvious reincarnation of the magician and his undertaking. Others think so too – Nygaard was recently invited to the Society of American Magicians’ Paranormal Investigations Committee, and regularly speaks at sceptic societies.
‘When the right con artist comes along and uses the right techniques on you … It can be more powerful than a gun’

But Nygaard felt conflicted. ‘My investigations are really not about supernatural ability,’ he said. He doesn’t care whether people can see the future. ‘I’ve never gone after a psychic and said … they should be arrested because they say they’re psychic,’ he said. He busts people for lying about what they say they’re doing with their clients’ money: buying cars and watches instead of casting spells.

We left the theatre and walked through a cold wind towards the 1 Train. ‘I’m going to take you out [to] the left field,’ he said. Nygaard told me he’s had experiences that have made him wonder about the supernatural. Sometimes, when driving a police car, he felt like the universe was taking the wheel. Once, while searching for a stolen briefcase, Nygaard heard a voice that told him to look up. He was passing by a deli, and stopped to check if the briefcase was on the roof; it was. In another instance, he was at the Chinese restaurant Wo Hop in Chinatown at 2 am when he saw, written on a dollar bill stuck to the wall, the nickname of a person who was connected to a crime he was investigating. ‘I have asked for help, and I’ve gotten answers, and I know those answers came from the universe,’ he said.

Nygaard had deep empathy for Doyle, who had lost a son in the war and wanted to speak to him again. Doyle’s grief fuelled his myopia when it came to a medium’s tricks, and when Houdini showed him it was all an illusion, it served as a reminder that his son would never return. For Nygaard, it was a perfect example of how ‘all of that learning, all of that knowledge, could go right out the window when the right con artist comes along and uses the right techniques on you … that’s how scary it is, how words can be so deceptive. It can be more powerful than a gun.’

I suddenly felt ashamed of how I felt when I left Emma. My attention had been misdirected, I realised. In being so judgmental about how someone could succumb to a bad trick, I had forgotten how much power the deceiver had.

Even Houdini remained vulnerable to wondering what if. He told his wife Bess that, if it was possible to send a message from the beyond, he would do so. For a decade, she held a seance on Halloween (the day he died) and waited. On the last one, Bess announced:

I do not believe that Houdini can come back to me, or to anyone … I do not believe that ghosts or spirits exist. The Houdini shrine has burned for 10 years … I now reverently turn out the light. It is finished. Good night, Harry.
The final moments of the show played recorded audio of Bess’s shaky voice. My stomach had tangled up into knots.
In May, Nygaard and I sat outside the Fanelli Cafe in SoHo, sharing a plate of fries in the afternoon sun.

I asked about his future. He works mostly by himself and has more cases than he can handle. He doesn’t think he could train someone to do what he does. Others might have the same investigative skills, but no one else would give psychic victims their all. He flies to other states to see clients or track psychics at the drop of a hat. He pressures police officers and prosecutors, and isn’t afraid to get in their face. His forcefulness has had consequences: in 2019, the National Association of Bunco Investigators rescinded his membership after his criticism of police handling of psychic fraud.

His dedication has required sacrifices. ‘I always did want a family, but I think what I do came at a cost,’ he said. When he was a cop, he was once on call with an officer who didn’t want to pursue an arrest because he would be late to his children’s dentist appointment. Nygaard responded: ‘Well, I guess your kids aren’t going to the dentist.’
‘You can’t have that attitude and have a relationship,’ he told me.
‘I was sitting all by myself in Florida contemplating on whether I have chosen the correct path in life’

Had I seen the movie Heat (1995), he asked, with Robert De Niro as a thief and Al Pacino as a cop? The two men are locked in a cat-and-mouse game. Near the end of the movie, they sit in a diner, comparing their lives.
‘So you never wanted a regular-type life?’ Pacino asks. He himself barely sees his family because he spends ‘all my time chasing guys like you around the block.’
De Niro replies: ‘A guy told me one time, don’t let yourself get attached to anything you are not willing to walk out on in 30 seconds flat if you feel the heat around a corner.’
That’s how Nygaard felt: ‘You want it, but you want the other thing more.’

Around a month later, on Father’s Day, I thought about Nygaard. I wondered if comparing his life with film characters who had simplistic moral drives was masking a deeper, more complex loss. The next day, I got a text from him. After spending Father’s Day alone, he had pondered the same: ‘I was sitting all by myself in Florida contemplating on whether I have chosen the correct path in life,’ he wrote. Was it all worth it?

Then, he received a message from a former client. ‘I don’t recall if you have children, but today I wanted to honour you all the same,’ she wrote. ‘You came into my life at such a strange time and the strength you provided, the direction, and how much you believed in me really made a difference and a massive impact on my life.’ Her text felt like a divine signal, he told me. ‘I felt like, through her, God was telling me: “Don’t doubt for a minute the path you have taken,”’ he wrote, ‘“because it’s the right one.”’

items.title: The origins of the state are not agrarian but pastoralist | Aeon Essays
items.description: Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mob
items.author: Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene
paragraphs: Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mobility. Halting all oil supplies paralyses virtually all transport, communication and supply lines: cities collapse, states disintegrate, societies break down and populations die off, throwing humanity back to the pre-industrial age. Without transport animals, humanity would still be back in the Stone Age.

No city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources. No transportation means no extrahuman transportation, leaving walking and carrying as the only means of transit. This baseline determined the size and structure of human communities. Production was limited to what could be carried home, circumscribing the areas where humans could settle and colonise. Production capacity and resource availability kept communities small, forcing them to split and disperse. Because size dictates structure, small meant undifferentiated and egalitarian. Ultimately, the inherent limit of the physical capability of travel and portage formed a natural immunity to inequality: it kept communities small, egalitarian and autonomous, leaving their lands beyond conquest.

As long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the New Guinea Highlands. The domestication of animals and the invention of boats liberated humanity, making long-distance mobilisation possible. With this newfound capacity, communities no longer needed to fit their immediate environments; instead, they could build cities and integrate expansive areas – all roads lead to Rome. Transportation – not grain – is what brought the state and civilisation into existence, and what continues to maintain them. Let’s examine this power by looking from the present back to the origin of the state.

Whoever rules the waves rules the world! Without its navy and air force, the United States cannot command global reach or project power worldwide. The same was true of European colonial empires; ultimately, warships and gunboats forged them. In earlier periods, Vikings built their empire on longships, Aztecs on canoes, Egyptians on riverboats, and Romans, Greeks and Phoenicians on galleys.

Conquering the world on horseback is easy, as the saying goes. On land, equids – donkeys and horses – forged states and civilisations, while the llama did the same for the Inkas. Ur’s kunga chariots project the military might of Mesopotamian cities, and the Abydos donkeys demonstrate their vital role in early Egyptian kingship. By the end of the 3rd millennium BCE, Central Eurasian nomads were entombing entire horse chariots – the high-tech, high-value war machines of their time – to honour their kings in Sintashta. Horse chariots later symbolised the power of the Shang and the Zhou; the latter deployed 4,000 chariots to overwhelm the former in 1046 BCE.
Building a state does not require grain, but does demand extrahuman transportation

‘The rider appears on the stage of history like a new breed of man’ – a centaur, as the German sociologist Alexander Rüstow put it in the 1950s. Eurasian nomads had long bred their mounts into the modern domestic horse, paving the way for an age of empires that would fundamentally reshape the world. Horses dominated human history for nearly four millennia. Even for maritime powers, horses remained key to conquest; from Carthage to the British, all relied on horses for inland expansion. Francisco Pizarro’s conquest of the Inkas is a prime illustration of the power of horses against an essentially pedestrian empire built on llama transportation. Horses also enabled the Comanche in North America to forge their empire and compete with European powers for nearly a century.

The Comanche Empire? Did they actually have grain to build a state? No, they had no grain – nor any agriculture, for that matter. Horse husbandry and bison hunting sustained their livelihood. In fact, all the Eurasian steppe powers – including the Mongols – relied on pastoralism. What they enjoyed most was an abundance of extrahuman transportation; what they lacked most was agricultural produce. Ultimately, building a state does not require grain, but it does demand extrahuman transportation.

Look at the political geography of the Roman and Mongol empires: the Romans could reach where ships could reach, and the Mongols could reach where horses could reach. The same is true of European colonial empires; it all comes down to the power of extrahuman transportation. Donkeys, horses and all other herd animals are the creations of pastoralists. Extrahuman transportation made the state and civilisation possible; this places pastoralism at the origin of the state and civilisation, and the Eurasian steppe at the centre of human history.

Yet the Sinocentric paradigm – the predominant vision of human history and civilisation with China at its centre – structurally erases extrahuman transportation and, with it, pastoralism, steppe empires and charisma from state formation, thereby negating the Eurasian steppe as the prime centre of human history. This framework shapes our current understanding of world history, leaving us with a view defined by entrapment, doom and despair. Becoming aware of this paradigm is essential if we are to break free from this bleak outlook, better comprehend the world we live in, and chart a brighter future.

While scholars critique world history for its Eurocentric bias, its conceptual framework and narrative are profoundly Sinocentric. This is because the origin of the state – and consequently the birth of civilisation – is the question that shapes our vision of world history. The latest authoritative iteration of this view is James C Scott’s Against the Grain: A Deep History of the Earliest States (2017), along with his The Art of Not Being Governed (2009). ‘The Origin of the State: Land Productivity or Appropriability’ by Joram Mayshar and colleagues is its economic restatement. Scott, readers might counter, focuses almost exclusively on Mesopotamia and rarely mentions China. Yet his underlying framework actually rearticulates the paradigm established by the American Orientalist Owen Lattimore’s influential work, Inner Asian Frontiers of China (1940). Precisely for this reason, Scott not only frequently mentions ‘the loess soils along the Yellow River’, but also, directly quoting Lattimore, claims that ‘irrigation was spectacularly rewarding in the loess core of ancient China’.

Lattimore sought to legitimise the Republic of China’s claims over Mongolia, Manchukuo, Tibet and Eastern Turkestan. To this end, he advanced the grain thesis to locate the origins of statehood and civilisation in the Yellow River Valley, positioning China as the Cradle of the East. By mapping Frederick Jackson Turner’s American frontier thesis onto the region, Lattimore framed China as the civilised centre and reduced the aforementioned territories to ‘Inner Asia’ – a mere geohistorical frontier akin to the American West. In doing so, Lattimore abandoned the traditional conquest theory – a framework he had previously espoused – which held that both China’s early states and most of its subsequent empires were forged by Eurasian nomadic conquerors rather than indigenous dynamics. The rejection of the conquest theory was a repudiation of extrahuman transportation and pastoralism as forces that led to statehood, and an exaltation of sedentism and grain agriculture instead.
The paradigm owes its formation to Cold War politics and is at odds with archaeological evidence

The theory that entrenched Lattimore’s thesis in academia is Robert Carneiro’s circumscription hypothesis, published in the journal Science as ‘A Theory of the Origin of the State’ (1970). Not just conventional narratives, but a wide array of prominent thinkers – including Michael Mann, Jared Diamond, Francis Fukuyama and Yuval Noah Harari – popularised Carneiro’s theory in different guises. Even David Graeber and David Wengrow ultimately remain within this framework.

Drawing on Carneiro’s concept of circumscribed agricultural land, Mann’s The Sources of Social Power (1986) posits ecological and social cages with no ‘escape route’, while Diamond’s Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997) similarly focuses on regions with ‘nowhere to flee’ to isolate the environmental conditions that generate the population pressure needed for the rise of the state. Fukuyama’s The Origins of Political Order (2011), however, is far more direct in delineating the primary conditions for pristine state formation: ‘that population needs to be physically constrained so that it increases in density’ and ‘that subjects cannot run away when coerced’. When Diamond wrote in Nature in 2002 that agricultural storable food surpluses ‘led to social stratification, political centralisation and standing armies’, he was merely rationalising the Lattimore-Carneiro population-pressure dogma as an ‘autocatalytic’ process. Harari’s Sapiens (2011), with its disease-ridden ‘luxury trap’, Scott’s The Art of Not Being Governed, along with his Against the Grain, and Graeber and Wengrow’s lamentation that ours is a species ‘enslaved to its crops’ all ultimately stem from the same grain thesis.

Indeed, the Lattimore-Carneiro framework relied on a population-pressure model, arguing that agriculture and sedentism triggered overpopulation, forcing the creation of hierarchies and states. However, Carneiro’s circumscription thesis required areas such as Mesopotamia, the Nile Valley and the Peruvian coast to be entirely overcrowded. Instead, empirical settlement surveys revealed that these areas lacked the demographic density to exhaust arable land, with some even experiencing depopulation during early state-formation. Because no population pressure existed to catalyse state formation, archaeological findings invalidated Carneiro’s theory.

Scott’s novelty lies neither in his rhetoric of ‘political crops’, nor in his laser-focused ‘circumscribed ecological niches’ of ‘alluvial or loess soils’, but rather in his theoretical sleight of hand: dynamic climatic circumscription. His fertile alluvial or loess soils mirror Carneiro’s circumscribed agricultural land, though on a minuscule scale, engineered by a millennium-long drought rather than geographic barriers. Ultimately, Scott repurposes Carneiro’s model of resource concentration – a resource-rich habitat that draws people from surrounding regions – yet he supercharges it with the driving force of drought. In sum, drought – simultaneously reconfiguring the physical terrain into a localised cage and driving populations inward – enables Scott to isolate the minuscule, 250-hectare footprint of Uruk as the circumscribed agricultural land. Scott’s model here is a clever manoeuvre to salvage the Sinocentric paradigm. That paradigm, as we shall see, owes its formation to Cold War politics and is at odds with archaeological evidence.

Whether climatic or geographical, the agricultural cage is inherently an anti-mobility framing that structurally erases pastoralism from the formation of the state. This erasure is, however, not just a conceptual flaw; it is written into the paradigm’s DNA, as the framework is fundamentally built against mobility, and actively argues for its exclusion. The erasure takes the form of epistemic theft by way of attributing the authorship of domestication of livestock and pastoralism to farmers, delaying the date of the advent of pastoralism through hyper-restrictive definitions, and relying on exclusionary framing. While the initial framework was a politically motivated, instrumental scheme, subsequent models have resulted from paradigmatic biases.

The question that led to this erasive framing was not the origin of the state in general, but its emergence in what is now China – specifically, whether it was indigenous or born of nomadic conquest. This issue was linked to a raging political dilemma: did Manchuria, and by extension the Daiching Empire (also known as the Qing dynasty), constitute a Chinese or an Inner Asian empire? This debate was a political question concerning the definition of China and the delineation of its territory. Specifically, should China be defined as ‘China proper’, restricted to the Ming provinces, or as ‘China imperial’, encompassing the domains of the Daiching Empire.

The controversy escalated into a heightened political crisis with the declaration of Manchukuo. Japanese scholarship argued that the Daiching Empire was an Inner Asian state that had conquered China, and that the Manchus were a distinct people deserving independence. The Chinese nationalist regime and its scholarship countered, arguing that the empire was inherently Chinese, and that Manchuria had been an integral part of China since antiquity. Meanwhile, contemporary critical scholarship essentially agreed with the Japanese view; the dominant framework for the origins of the state in China was the invasion theory, which argued that early Chinese states, as well as many subsequent empires, were forged by Eurasian nomadic conquerors. Crucially, until then, Lattimore himself had been a proponent of this theory.

The Republic of China was a legal fiction enabled by the Open Door policy (authored by US diplomats in 1899). Yet, this very regime claimed sovereignty over Mongolia, Manchuria, Eastern Turkestan and Tibet. By the 1930s, however, the Open Door order was in tatters: Outer Mongolia had declared independence in 1911, Tibet in 1912, and Manchukuo had broken away in 1932, absorbing Eastern Inner Mongolia. The rest of Inner Mongolia was ruled by a Japanese-allied government, while Eastern Turkestan declared independence in 1933.
Had Mongolia and the others remained states, they could not have been conceptualised as frontiers, but rather as independent neighbours

Recognising the Daiching Empire as an Inner Asian state meant forfeiting China’s claim over all of these regions, stripping the regime of what Lattimore estimated at nearly two-thirds of its claimed territory. Worse still for the West, the Soviet Union was poised to become the ultimate beneficiary – an outcome the regime and its primary architect, the US, were determined to prevent. The regime had to ensure that its territory emerged as inherently Chinese, and scholarship was needed to substantiate this claim. This required refuting the invasion theory and reframing China as the Cradle of the East. Lattimore’s book, Inner Asian Frontiers of China, accomplished precisely this.

Executing a complete about-face from his earlier position, building on Chinese nationalist scholarship, and drawing on Turner’s American frontier thesis, Lattimore reframed Mongolia, Manchuria, Chinese Turkistan (today’s Xinjiang) and Tibet as the frontiers of China. Reducing these territories to a mere geographic area – Inner Asia – and rebranding them as mere frontiers required rendering the region stateless, tribal and barbarian. Had Mongolia and the others remained states, they could not have been conceptualised as frontiers, but rather as independent neighbours; his framework thus demanded a terra nullius.

Refuting the invasion theory required disarming it of its most potent weapon of conquest – mobility – and supplanting it with an alternative framework. Lattimore accomplished this by casting mobility as an anti-state force, substituting the invasion thesis with evolutionary materialism. Inverting his earlier argument that mobility provided a ‘snowball’ effect to Mongol political organisation, Lattimore was the first to equate mobility with dispersal. He thereby transformed what was previously understood as the ultimate mobilising and concentrating mechanism into an inherently dispersive element. This reframing neutralised conquest theory, turning its defining weapon into an anti-state force.

Furthermore, by establishing mobility as the defining feature of pastoralism, and immobility as that of irrigated agriculture, Lattimore posited both a positive correlation between wealth and power and a negative one between mobility and wealth/power, thus advancing his ‘wealth versus mobility’ thesis. And by asserting that ‘grain, accumulated and stored, was beyond question the standard of real wealth in essentials’, he guaranteed ‘the ascendancy of wealth over mobility’. In this manner, Lattimore not only erased mobility as the state-making force but also established grain as that very force. In fact, Lattimore is the author of the grain thesis, and in his framework, the state emerges as a grain store.

Mobility, thus, emerged not merely as dispersal, but as a mechanism of destitution, rather than a driver of state-building. While Lattimore declared that ‘it is the poor nomad who is pure nomad,’ intellectual successors like the cultural anthropologist Marshall Sahlins observed that a nomad’s wealth ‘is a burden’ that ‘soon poses a contradiction to his mobility.’ Anatoly Khazanov pushed this thesis further, arguing that pastoralism is inherently non-self-sufficient (non-autarkic) or even anti-autarkic, thereby rendering it fundamentally incapable of producing a state.

At the same time, by mapping environmentally determined societies – specifically, forest-hunting clans, steppe-pastoral tribes, and loess-agricultural states – and adding extensive and intensive dimensions, Lattimore established population pressure as the primary catalyst for state-formation. While agriculture in general emerged as uniquely capable of generating a state, irrigated agriculture was intensive enough to trigger severe demographic strain. Identifying a continuous agricultural expanse enclosed by ‘an immense mass of inhospitable terrain’ – namely, ‘the bleak highlands’ and ‘the Inner Asian barrier lands’ on one side, and the Pacific Ocean on the other – Lattimore mapped China as a circumscribed agricultural land.

To cast China as the Cradle of the East and claim Inner Asia as a Chinese frontier, Lattimore framed Inner Asian pastoralism as a byproduct of agricultural expansion, attributing all historical agency to farmers. By claiming pastoralists were ‘akin by culture and probably by blood to the early Chinese’, he cast both populations as homologous. Dating steppe pastoralism to the 4th century BCE – as an offshoot of intensive Chinese agriculture – allowed Lattimore to monopolise the state-formation timeline and neutralise the invasion theory.

To stall the timeline of pastoralism’s emergence, he devised a hyper-restrictive definition: dismissing categories like ‘true’, ‘strict’ or ‘normal’ as overly broad, he defined ‘pastoral nomadism’ exclusively as ‘the extreme of nomadism’ or ‘the strict or extreme phases of steppe nomadism’. This framework equates pastoralism with the advent of horseback riding and, in effect, with the rise of cavalry.

To be sure, all of these claims conflicted with contemporary scholarly knowledge, including archaeology and linguistics. Back then, archaeology had shown that horse-riding nomadism and animal art emerged around 1500 BCE in the Black Sea region before spreading eastward through Mongolia to Ordos – a fact Lattimore was aware of. Similarly, linguists such as Henri Maspero had shown that the Chinese language ‘has no relation whatever, not even a distant connection with’ Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic languages. Nonetheless, Lattimore’s attribution of pastoral animal domestication to farmers and his hyper-restrictive definition of pastoralism became paradigmatic in the field. Khazanov cemented Lattimore’s thesis: he claimed that only sedentary groups with definite vegetable surpluses could domesticate animals, and characterised ‘pure pastoral nomadism’ as ‘the most extreme form’ of nomadism. In this manner, mobility and pastoralism were written out of the state-formation process.

However, modern scholarship by Melinda Zeder shows that ‘plant and animal domestication occurred at roughly the same time, with signs of initial management … reaching back to at least 11,500 cal BP [ie, 9550 BCE], if not earlier.’ Furthermore, we now know that early animal domestication ‘only took place within a subset of the geographical distribution of the wild ancestors’, unfolding ‘often in regions distant from centres of plant domestication.’ Critically, while most herd animals were domesticated via the prey pathway rather than a commensal one, pastoralists domesticated equids – donkeys and horses – via a directed pathway. Yet, by claiming that ‘specialised pastoralism, seen as an outgrowth of agriculture’ confronts the state with a ‘problem of dispersal and mobility’, Scott continues to perpetuate Lattimore’s delayed timeline and restrictive definition – even while acknowledging that agriculture and pastoralism emerged concurrently roughly 12,000 years ago.
Mobility, pastoralism and tribalism were essentially conflated

By the 1970s, Lattimore’s framework had become the dominant orthodoxy. Elman Service, a leading neo-evolutionist, hailed it as ‘the pathfinding ecological theory’, while Morton Fried acknowledged that Lattimore ‘proposed a theory that stimulated my own’. Ultimately, neo-evolutionism displaced conquest theory as the mainstream paradigm. By positioning intensive agriculture as the sole economic foundation capable of sustaining the state, Fried’s social stratification scheme (egalitarian, rank, stratified, and state) and Service’s sociopolitical typology (band, tribe, chiefdom, and state) reinforced Lattimore’s irrigated agriculture thesis while anchoring evolutionary materialism. Consequently, the state – either as an instrument of the upper class or as a managerial institution – emerges fundamentally as an economic instrument and an evolutionary product.

By deriving the state from either social or functional differentiation, both Fried and Service rejected conquest theory. Whereas Service’s model is basically a refinement of 19th-century bourgeois materialism, Fried’s framework aligns with the Marxist model by emphasising conflict driven by internal economic differentiation. Carneiro likewise rejected conquest theory; despite his incorporating warfare and coercion, his model remains an elaboration of Fried’s framework. As one of the most influential models of neo-evolutionary thought, Carneiro’s framework was a direct product of this paradigmatic bias, and it effectively resulted in the global scaling of Lattimore’s framework. China was established as the Cradle of the East, while Inner Asia was relegated to a tribal world and ‘the barbarian “outer darkness”’. Mobility, pastoralism and tribalism were essentially conflated until Caroline Humphrey and David Sneath deconstructed the category of ‘nomadism’ and the myth of the wandering nomad in 1999, paving the way for Sneath to later debunk the tribal model as a complete misrepresentation. Meanwhile, in a corpus of historical scholarship utilising primary sources, Christopher P Atwood compellingly demonstrates that the tribal model is untenable.

However, Scott not only resurrects Lattimore’s framework in its entirety along with its long-refuted theories but also repackages it to fit his own anarchist project. Following Lattimore, Scott maintains that Inner Asian pastoralism – along with its population – was merely a byproduct of Chinese agricultural expansion. His assertion that the Great Wall was built as much to contain Chinese taxpayers as to repel external invasions likewise mirrors Lattimore’s position. Scott’s most spectacular move is his elevation of mobility into a primary form of freedom. Lattimore’s notion of free nomads – with their ‘idea of freedom, free movement, free migration’ – nicely dovetailed with Scott’s anarchist thesis, prompting him to valorise mobility as a freedom-preserving force and recast it as the fundamental state-preventing strategy.

This conceptualisation clearly finds its echo in The Dawn of Everything (2021), where Graeber and Wengrow theorise ‘the freedom to move’ as one of the ‘fundamental, even primary, forms of freedom’. At the same time, Scott’s grain thesis, in particular, and agricultural paradigm, in general, powerfully guide our thinking, leading the two authors to declare in despair that ‘we got stuck’ and that ‘ours is a species that has become enslaved to its crops.’ Mobility thus emerged as a fundamentally anti-state, anti-domination and freedom-preserving force, albeit one that proved impotent against the all-powerful grain to which we, along with all our extrahuman transportation, are enslaved. This is how the Sinocentric paradigm was devised and how it erases pastoralism from state-formation. The objective of this paradigm is to eliminate mobility, and its theoretical frameworks inherently structure scholarly thinking and enquiry against pastoralism. Ultimately, this is how the Sinocentric paradigm traps us intellectually.

With the erasure of mobility and pastoralism and the relegation of Inner Asia into tribal barbarity, the Sinocentric paradigm monopolised state-formation in China for the Chinese while establishing China as the sole empire and civilisation within the former Daiching domain. However, there were Inner Asian empires – especially the Daiching Empire – on whose identification the integrity of the regime’s claim over Inner Asia depended. This demanded their total erasure. The method – as Lattimore himself observed in 1934 while depicting the grim reality that the Open Door policy had imposed upon the Mongols, the Manchus, the Uighurs and the Tibetans – was to ‘deny their history and surrender their national and racial identities’ and, ultimately, to conquer them conceptually. Notably, this is the exact policy that the current Chinese administration pursues today.

This meant the appropriation of all the empires that conquered China as inherently Chinese, and the construction of an everlasting Chinese empire. To achieve this, two problems had to be solved: the reality of conquests and the distinct identity of the conquering empires. Because these conquests were not isolated incidents but occurred in overwhelming numbers, a sophisticated framework had to be devised.

To appropriate Inner Asian empires, Lattimore devised the theory of Chinese dynastic cycles, a teleological device that powerfully legitimises Chinese nationalist claims through a veneer of deterministic, historical law. By reducing all empires to mere dynasties, this cycle creates the illusion of an enduring Chinese state where successive dynasties simply replace one another. Conquests are thus erased as mere changes in ruling houses while the empire itself remains intact. Consequently, the Chinese empire emerges as uniquely endless – an everlasting polity standing in stark contrast to the mortal trajectories of all other historical powers, including the Roman Empire.

To make this everlasting empire inherently Chinese and to deny the identity of the conquering empires – in contrast to British ‘accumulative’ and Russian ‘incorporative’ models – Lattimore forged ‘the third great type’: the Chinese ‘absorptive’ empire. Unlike ‘conquest’ empires, this was a ‘defensive empire’ – one that did not conquer but was conquered, yet remained Chinese by absorbing its conquerors. Consequently, the polity emerged not as a conquering political power, but as a cultural community predicated on assimilation. Furthermore, as China was established as civilisation itself, and Inner Asia was reduced to barbarity, all Inner Asian conquests represented a barbarian advancement toward civilisation. Sinicisation was a ‘standing offer of the opportunity to become civilised, to any individual or group interested in progress’ – the civilising mission.
China was reified as an everlasting empire, and its history emerged as unbroken dynastic cycles

However, Lattimore’s highly idiosyncratic conceptualisations invert reality. Empire, by definition, is an expansionist, incorporative polity; what defines an empire is expansion, and what drives it is conquest. It is also anything but culturally homogeneous; its very nature is all-encompassing, hierarchical and heterogeneous. Thus, Lattimore’s Chinese absorptive empire is a veritable anomaly. Moreover, with hundreds of mutually unintelligible varieties divided across at least eight major language groups, even the Sinitic group – let alone China as a whole – represents immense cultural diversity.

In fact, Lattimore’s ‘absorptive’ empire was the political embodiment of the Chinese nationalist narrative of assimilative power, depicting China as a solid, homogenising mass, ‘homogeneous in race, language, and culture’, where the ‘barbarians were all absorbed by the Chinese; they became Chinese like any other Chinese.’ Hence, the Manchus were all assimilated by the Chinese and became Chinese like any other; therefore, the Manchu empire was a Chinese dynasty like any other. Had all the Mongols shared the Manchu fate, the Chinese empire would have been the largest contiguous land empire the world had ever seen; then, what June Teufel Dreyer called the ‘tianxia trope’ – the idea that a Sinocentric world is the better one – would have possessed a formidable precedent.

Nevertheless, Lattimore’s framework immediately became hegemonic. China was reified as an everlasting empire, and its history emerged as unbroken dynastic cycles with a predictable Sinicisation pattern. Paired with the Chinese world order, the paradigm crystallised into unchallenged dogma. Lattimore emerged ‘as the intellectual godfather of all historians of China’ (as the sinologist Mark C Elliott put it), and the founder of Chinese frontier studies. Only in the 1990s did scholars like Pamela Crossley, Evelyn Rawski and Elliott finally break ranks to challenge the Sinicisation thesis, instigating what would become the New Qin

items.title: Sometimes, you ‘just know’ something’s off – but how? | Aeon Essays
items.description: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
items.author: Marc A Moffett
paragraphs: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
‘This seems like phishing. I wouldn’t click that link.’
‘Something about this deal feels off. Walk away.’

When people say such things, they are not typically drawing conclusions from a chain of reasoning. The person who avoids getting in the stranger’s car is not thinking: ‘He displayed these three behavioural cues and, therefore, he poses a risk.’ The email isn’t flagged by going through an explicit checklist. The deal doesn’t announce its flaws through a formal audit. In each case, something is simply presented as having a certain character: the man as creepy, the email as fraudulent, the deal as suspect. And yet, acting on these intuitions seems not merely excusable but entirely reasonable. If the man really does strike you as creepy, staying out of his car was probably the smart call – even if you can’t say why.

Despite this, ‘vibes’ and ‘intuitions’ are often dismissed both in daily life and in academic enquiry as irrational or merely heuristic devices. And while we cannot always trust such reactions, they are central, indeed indispensable, to our ability to rationally navigate the world. Philosophers, however, have done surprisingly little to illuminate the rational credentials of these ordinary kinds of intuitions. Instead, they have focused the bulk of their attention on a much more rarefied kind of intuition called rational intuition, which is taken to function primarily in the a priori disciplines of philosophy, logic and mathematics.

My objective is to explain why our everyday intuitive reactions can have such rational force. The key is to see that intuition works in much the same way as perception, in that both can directly present something to us as actual. Once we understand what gives perception this feature, we can see why intuitions might involve exercising the same basic kind of cognitive capacity.

A standard way of characterising rational intuition is in terms of seemings, by analogy with perception. Just as it perceptually seems to you that there is a car in the garage, so it can intellectually seem to you that 2 + 2 = 4 – the former presenting a physical fact, the latter a conceptual one. But rational intuition and the everyday intuition at work when you decline to get in a stranger’s car are not as far apart as this rarefied example suggests: the philosopher’s intuition is, at bottom, a highly specialised version of the same basic capacity.

To draw these two capacities together, let’s consider a favourite pastime of philosophers: the thought experiment. Philosophers have a penchant for exotica, which is never more clearly on display than in their invocation of thought experiments. Consider two cases that have occupied philosophers for decades – one from ethics, one from the theory of knowledge.

In the trolley problem, the philosophers Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson imagined a runaway trolley hurtling toward five people tied to the track. You are standing on a bridge above, next to another bystander. The only way to stop the trolley and save the five is to push the bystander off the bridge. If you do, his body will halt the trolley, but he will die as a result. Many people feel, immediately and forcefully, that pushing him is wrong, even if it saves five lives. But why?
We routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life

Or consider Carl Ginet’s case involving fake barns. Imagine you are driving through the countryside and see a barn. It looks exactly like a barn; you’re paying attention, the light is good. You form the perfectly reasonable belief that this is a barn. What you don’t know is that you’re in ‘fake-barn country’: the region is dotted with elaborate barn facades, indistinguishable from real barns when viewed from the road. You happen to be looking at the one real barn in this area. Your belief is true, and it seems justified. And yet almost everyone who considers this case has the immediate, firm sense that you don’t really know it’s a barn. But why not?

To sceptics and the uninitiated, these thought experiments can seem fantastical. Because we encounter them in their most dramatic forms, like runaway trolleys and fake barns, thought experiments seem exotic. But properly understood, these imaginative episodes are important tools for sharpening our grasp of key concepts. In fact, their functioning is continuous with something far more familiar: the way we routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life, wondering what might happen if we take one path rather than another in the proverbial fork in the road.

These imaginings are just thought experiments as they appear in everyday life. Imagine you are deciding whether to tell a friend that his husband has been unfaithful. You picture the conversation, the shock, the hurt that registers on his face.
