Slender and tall, with cropped hair and wearing a crisp black button-down, he went on, “When I’m working on something, I’m, like, ‘Is anyone going to hear this?’ I sort of don’t expect anything. I’m just trying to put notes in the right places.” In part because of “Daylight,” Richter became the best-selling living artist on the classical label Deutsche Grammophon.

Measured and not easily ruffled, Richter comes across like the human version of a beta-blocker. His vocal cadence is similar to his music—lulling and copacetic, with a tendency to repeat. Normal frustrations don’t seem to stick with him. He had recently experienced a disruptive tech issue during a show in North Carolina. “It was the keyboard—it broke in such a wonderful way,” he said. “I stood up and it was still going, and it turned into this blur of noise. Audiences kind of like that stuff, because it’s human, isn’t it?”

For the past two years, Richter has been on tour with two of his albums, “In a Landscape” (2024) and the omnipresent “Blue Notebooks.” He considers them both ever relevant. “ ‘In a Landscape’ is an attempt to model an ideal society,” he told me. “It’s a piece about the world we’re living in, and I suppose every time we think it cannot get crazier, it keeps getting crazier.” “Blue Notebooks” features text from Franz Kafka’s “The Blue Octavo Notebooks,” read aloud by Tilda Swinton. On the first track, which sets a two-note figure reminiscent of Debussy’s “Des pas sur la neige” against typewriter clacks, Swinton muses portentously on “the rattling of a mirror not quite firmly fastened to the wall.” The record was conceived as a protest against the Iraq War, an urge for peace amid conflict. “And here we are again,” Richter said.

“Here we are again” is an ethos for Richter. His music is defined by simple, repetitive figures, set in simple, repetitive progressions. It is immediately understandable—there’s never a need to guess what you should be feeling, for better or worse. “A lot of my work is trying to make things land in a very direct way,” he said. “So that you have a situation where if you move a single note it wouldn’t be as good.”

This directness has made him popular in the streaming era—his stuff is easy to put on as background music. “Most musical artists, their streams go up on the weekends, and during the week they’re played less,” Richter told me. “Mine is exactly the opposite.” His fans listen at home or at work, filling the gap in our brains that finds silence intolerable—while cooking, cleaning, studying, reading. “It’s a private, intentional situation,” he said. I listened to it while putting together a wedding speech for a friend and while brushing up on “Music in the Late Twentieth Century,” by Richard Taruskin. I listened to it while writing this sentence. “It’s not up to me,” Richter said. “I don’t want to prescribe how people encounter the material. To me, making a piece of music is about asking a question: What about this?”

The musicologist William Robin told me, “The music’s adaptability is key to how it serves listeners. Whether Richter does it better or worse than other ambient figures, I don’t know. But the way ambient listening has taken off since the pandemic is certainly related to his success.” Richter bristles at the “ambient” label and instead refers to himself as “post-classical,” a term he coined half jokingly. “Talking about it has always been a bit of a problem,” he said. “I don’t really believe in categories.”

Since 2002, Richter has released dozens of albums, some of which are retooled versions of his own music—or of other people’s. “Intertextuality is pretty fundamental to what I do,” he said. After “Blue Notebooks,” listeners may know him from “Recomposed: Vivaldi’s Four Seasons” (2012), which extracts swatches of Antonio Vivaldi’s concertos and re-stitches them together with Richterian threads: crescendos surging to a sudden stop, recurring gestures of a measure or two, low strings drawn out like molasses. (At one point, the chords below the sprightly violins of the track “Spring 1” even contour through the same circular four-note figure that is in the opening of “On the Nature of Daylight.”)

“I had fallen in love with Vivaldi as a tiny kid, but grew to hate it as an adult because you hear it in insurance adverts or when you’re on hold, or whatever. So I wanted to get that out of my system,” Richter said. “I assumed I was going to be destroyed for it—the end of my career. But it’s not like I really had a career.” The record topped classical charts in twenty-two countries. Two years later, Richter came out with a follow-up, a spoken-word album, his mellow voice explaining each piece on the record, DVD-extra style. (Track 9: “ ‘Autumn 1’ is pretty much the original Vivaldi for quite a long time, except I’ve sort of sliced it up and cut holes in it.”) Then, in 2022, he released “The New Four Seasons: Vivaldi Recomposed,” which is the same music, this time made with era-accurate strings, plus one of many Moog synthesizers he owns. “I heard a performance on period instruments and just thought, This is brilliant,” he said. “I thought it was a nice learning journey. A three-hundred-and-sixty-degree project.” His label extended the journey three years later, with “Vivaldi by Max Richter,” which includes tracks from both versions of “Recomposed.” Perhaps a person might save some time by simply listening to Vivaldi.

The masses swooned over the project, but it irritated many musicians. “The way ‘The Four Seasons’ was adopted by the Pottery Barn Muzak crowd already harmed Vivaldi’s status as a serious composer,” Ethan Iverson, a critic and composer, told me. Richter’s own “defanging,” he said, “suggests a future where nobody knows anything about anything: we are all senseless drones, oblivious to the mystery and magic of tonal harmony.”

Not long ago, an A.I. company approached Richter about a potential collaboration. “Their pitch to me was ‘Hey, Max, say you’re writing a song and you get stuck. You’ve got the beginning and you’ve got the end. That’s where we come in. You click this and it’ll fix that for you.’ But that bit is what I live for. That’s where I learn stuff.” He has advocated before British Parliament on the need to protect artists and regulate A.I. Has that been successful? “No, in short.”

Richter believably insists that the art must always come first. “As far as I know, I’m the biggest seller on D.G., but I see that as kind of their problem, not mine,” he said. “I’m very hazy on the commercial side. I don’t love sitting in meetings. The only thing I can control is where I put the notes on the page.”

Richter was born in 1966, in Hamelin, Germany. “It’s where the Pied Piper came from—that’s the only reason anyone knows it,” he said. When he was three, his family moved to Bedford, England, after his father, an electrical engineer, was posted there. His mother, who eventually ran a health-food shop, was an amateur pianist. At age five, Richter started piano lessons: “My teacher was a very lovely elderly woman named Mrs. Hart. If you played a wrong note, she’d hit you with a ruler.”

During Richter’s childhood, the classical world was in the midst of a counterstrike against modernist complexity, which had become an academic norm. In the nineteen-twenties, Arnold Schoenberg had pioneered the twelve-tone method, rejecting the idea of a central key. After the Second World War, this musical language, which yielded a lot of atonal work, became more widely accepted and was further developed by figures like the French serialist composer Pierre Boulez. Artists began to push back against what Richter described as a “modernist hangover,” stripping away the elaborate status quo. In 1964, the composer Terry Riley put out the groundbreaking piece “In C,” which consists of a high C being pinged to eternity for forty minutes, against pulsing instrumentation. Riley’s friend, the New York City-born composer Steve Reich, had suggested the idea of an eighth-note heartbeat—one of many stamps Reich left on the contemporary scene, including “Clapping Music.” Philip Glass, who had studied at Juilliard before doing a Fulbright with the composer Nadia Boulanger, knew Reich and was paring back his own compositions. He soon established the Philip Glass Ensemble for experimental work.

When Richter was twelve, his family milkman offered a portal into this burgeoning new world called minimalism. “He’d be hearing me doing my Mozart, and he took me on as kind of a project,” Richter said. “For me at that time, new music was Stravinsky. But the milkman was a jazz musician, and he had gone to New York and picked up Chatham Square Philip Glass records and Terry Riley. And he would just drop them off with the milk in the mornings. I was hearing it, going, ‘What is this even?’ ” It became an unquenchable fascination. Richter began, in his words, “scribbling.”

In secondary school, music continued to be a vehicle for his curiosity. “It was an insurgency against a very normalizing, conforming over-all project in the Margaret Thatcher–Ronald Reagan era,” he said. “Really, all I wanted to do was sit around in cafés reading French novels and smoking cigarettes. I stopped going to classes, and they kicked me out.” After completing his A-levels at a training college that had a robust music program, he enrolled at the University of Edinburgh, then transferred to the Royal Academy of Music to study composition. At RAM, modernism was still going strong. “If you were writing tonal music, it just meant that you were an idiot,” he said. They wanted him to write “post-Boulez,” Richter said. “I did that for a while. I wrote very complicated pieces.” But he was drawn back to the intelligibility of minimalism. “The real world makes no sense at all, but a piece of music is a place where things can make sense,” Richter said. “It’s a way of talking about things. And, therefore, I just took everything away. Simplify, simplify, simplify.”

After RAM, Richter moved to Florence to study with Luciano Berio, a pupil of Boulez’s Darmstadt School who later also taught Reich. “Although he was very much a modernist figurehead, Berio was into folk music, historical materials, working with history rather than trying to erase it,” Richter said. “His music was really omnivorous.” (Some people I talked to were surprised that Richter was Berio’s student, but the signs are there: Berio’s “Sinfonia” repurposes Mahler’s Symphony No. 2, serving as an inspiration for Richter’s Vivaldi project.) While working with Berio, Richter engaged with new ideas coming out of the Baltics. “I had heard the very beginning of Arvo Pärt happening,” he said, of the Estonian composer. Pärt developed “tintinnabuli,” a style of two-voice minimalist composition. “I went to his concerts and I said, ‘Hang on, this is amazing.’ So there was lots of stuff that punctured that sort of modernist brain.”

Richter’s style is, no doubt, descended from Pärt. But, in considering Richter’s path, a closer parallel might be Glass—a composer who, despite the judgment of some people in the classical world, made the journey from post-modernist enfant terrible to well-known creator of scores for blockbuster movies (he has been nominated for three Academy Awards, including for “The Hours”). Nico Muhly, a composer who worked closely with Glass, told me that, decades ago, “if you mentioned Philip Glass’s name in academia, it was, like, horses whinny, thunderclaps, lightning strikes. It was some Wicked Witch of the West shit. Nobody was in dialogue with that music. People were actively hostile.” Glass’s crossover into the mainstream, although reviled by certain purists, was momentous. William Robin, the musicologist, said, “When Glass began writing scores, in the eighties, it set a new kind of standard for film, TV, and commercials to have music that is very generic and also emotionally powerful. Richter is doing a similar thing.” On top of the umpteen uses of “Daylight,” Richter has scored countless pieces of media, including “The Leftovers,” “The Veil,” “Spaceman,” and “Ad Astra.” His professional success would not exist without the efforts of Glass.

But Glass, Reich, and Pärt tend to ask more of listeners than Richter does. Their work feels easier to actively engage with, rather than passively absorb. They employ microevolutions—changes of rhythm or placement that make it harder to predict what the ear will catch, despite the cyclicality. As Glass explained in his memoir, “It never repeated all the time, for if it had, it would have been unlistenable.” Richter’s work is not unlistenable. On the contrary: it’s so listenable that you can sometimes forget to listen. When he does make subtle changes—and he does—the impact isn’t as evident. Take “Daylight.” The violin’s floating seesaw melody switches up its suspensions, sometimes holding a note over a measure and sometimes playing it on the downbeat. But it’s loyal to the same type of disruption, and the ear comes to expect it as if it were the norm all along. Perhaps that’s part of his point in the quest to be intelligible, and there are certainly other undercurrent changes that the listener won’t register. But that ultimately means they’re missable.

“If you listen to Max, there are some pieces where there’s a really explicit Glass influence,” Muhly said. “You see that in ‘Vladimir’s Blues,’ ”—a track off of “Blue Notebooks.” He continued, “But, to me, its relationship to Glass is cosmetic,” not structural.

Richter isn’t shy about Glass’s influence, but he skirted the suggestion that his work is derivative of him. “The thing that Glass’s music did for me is it gave permission,” he said. “He brings repetition into the foreground as a somatic idea.” He added, “All music is, in a way, about other music. But repetition is in everything. You know, Chopin’s studies are minimal.” Richter doesn’t have a relationship with Glass (“Our paths have never crossed”), but he’s open to meeting: “Why not? I’m sure he’s a fascinating guy.”

The influence of Richter’s minimalist forebears aside, his project falls more in the comfortable pocket of pop music. (He is planning a show at the Sphere, in Las Vegas, with Oprah Winfrey.) He serves as a gateway for non-musicians to safely enter the classical space. One young composer who has worked with Richter told me, “I used to feel very hostile toward his music. I remember playing this three-hour show, and I was, like, People are sitting through three hours of the same chord progression developing over every minute, going up a fifth every five minutes? This is exhausting for me, and I can’t imagine sitting in the audience listening to it. But people were weeping.” She added, “The market is the market. Maybe there’s something we can learn from that.”

In early September, I visited Richter’s studio, behind an automatic gate in a thirty-one-acre spread near the village of Charlbury, in England. A light rain—rare, after the summer’s heat wave—misted the triangular structure, dappling a glass wall decaled with the letters “SRM”: Studio Richter Mahr. “A big part of this building is about creative community, so we’ve embedded that in the architecture,” Richter explained, standing by an open kitchen in a clinically white foyer. “We’ve got the café in the center, which was very deliberate because it’s a shared space.” Every sound seemed to both echo and disappear instantly. An aide named Joe, who introduced himself as “Mr. Assistant,” brought Richter a small cup of black coffee. (The espresso machine is a La Marzocco Linea PB, which costs as much as a car. Richter said, “I remember in that meeting with the architects, they thought I was joking when I walked in with a brochure for this thing.”)

Richter wore a white shirt rather than his usual black, because, he said, “I’m a bit sleepy this morning.” He’d accessorized with a “Peanuts” watch. “Schroeder’s my guy. He’ll just have a bar of Beethoven in a speech bubble,” he said. “He’s such a pianist.” He led me past a few analog recording machines into the control room—a production area with knobs and screens, and a window onto an open studio. “This room is the end point of the workflow. The whole building is conceived as a kind of an instrument,” he said. “It’s a Henry Ford thing, we’ve got the means of production.” He walked into the recording room. “Oak,” he said, of the walls. “This all comes from a forest in Germany, which has been managed by the same family for two hundred years.” A Steinway D automatic Spirio sat in one corner. A Hammond M102 organ was against the opposite wall. “It’s the same kind of Hammond that Billy Preston played on ‘Abbey Road,’ ” he said. “When I watched that eight-hour documentary, I was just, like, ‘That’s it. I’ve got to have it.’ ” He pointed out the serial number, which dated it to 1967. “The one he plays was lost, and no one knows where it is,” he said, dropping his voice low. “So this could be the one.”

The studio is where Richter created his new album, “While The Flood Rages.” Revision: the music is not exactly new—it’s drawn from his score for a 2022 ballet, “MADDADDAM,” based on a series of post-apocalyptic books by Margaret Atwood. The ballet translates the tale of the rebirth of society after a horrific disaster into egg-forward visuals: egg-headed figures, a giant egg displaying black-and-white footage of industrial cityscapes, interpretive dancing in egg-shaped costumes.

Richter and the director Wayne McGregor began collaborating on “MADDADDAM” in 2019. “The record is not the ballet,” Richter said. “I made some architectural decisions.” He uses his reliable muses—strings, morose bass lines—to represent the harmonious characters known as the Children of Crake. “They’re sort of these synthetic creatures. Genetically, they’re manufactured in a lab,” he explained. “They inherit the Earth from humanity, but that’s a good thing because they’re nonviolent.” The theme closes out each third of the record, including the first single, “Now We Can Sing”—a Pachelbel’s Canon-esque chord cycle, topped by a falling B-major melody that feels a bit like an ear-training interval exercise. It is, in Richter’s words, “existentially safe,” as opposed to a jittering, electronic track called “Data Ballistics,” which sounds, refreshingly, like it could be played at a techno club. To coincide with the album, he released a limited-edition book of crosswords: “1. Broadcast from Howard Stern, e.g.”; “8. Mountain range on the Europe/Asia border.”

Richter introduced me to his wife, the visual artist Yulia Mahr. Her workspace was as white as the foyer. “These guys are tempestuous,” Mahr said, gesturing to a line of ceramic arm sculptures she had made, marbled with dirt and dried weeds, lying on the floor. “They won’t do what they’re asked to do.” Petite and sparkly-eyed, she and Richter first met at the Edinburgh Festival, in the late eighties. “We’ve always just talked ideas,” Richter said. Their partnership brims with creative support—she wears his custom-made Comme des Garçons perfume, which sells for a hundred and sixty-five dollars a bottle and is called “Max Richter 01.” (“We used all the source materials that I work with,” Richter said. “Piano-soundboard wood, rosin, magnetic tape, the insides of synthesizers, the forest.”) Mahr helped come up with the idea for his 2015 album “Sleep,” which was the first classical album to exceed two billion streams across all platforms. It stayed on the Billboard Classical chart for three hundred and fifty-nine weeks. It’s no mystery why: “Sleep” is an eight-and-a-half-hour, two-hundred-and-four-track concept album that you put on before you go to bed. Richter worked with the neuroscientist David Eagleman to learn about the brain during rest, and the record is an ambient—sorry, post-classical—cloud of cyclicality. Richter has described it, as he does “Blue Notebooks,” as “protest music.”

Others might wonder if it’s a gimmick, a ploy to increase streaming numbers masquerading as art. (It does bring to mind Justin Bieber’s desperate attempt to put his song “Yummy” at the top of the charts, in 2020, by urging fans to “create a playlist with ‘Yummy’ on repeat” and “let it play while you sleep.” The song reached No. 2.)

Richter once described “Sleep” as music for when “your conscious mind is on holiday.” He has performed the work live twenty-eight times—the lights are dim, the audience are in beds instead of seats, and the musicians take staggered breaks. Ben Russell, a violinist who often performs with Richter, told me, “You have to really time things and keep your mind interested, otherwise you start to drift. I’ve definitely had some very slow blinks happen during that concert.” Backstage, Richter provides cots and snacks. “You grab a little sushi,” Russell said. “There’s coffee, and even wine helps if you use it judiciously. So sushi, coffee, wine, sushi, coffee, wine.”

One night, I decided to sleep to “Sleep.” I settled into bed around 11 P.M., queued up the first track, and was greeted by pulsing chords on soft keys. I was playing it from my phone, which I imagine most people do, so the low values in each track got lost in the mix, and I found myself being kept alert by the high-end sounds—violins, or a soprano. My conscious mind was not on holiday.

Maybe I would have had a better time napping to the hour-long “From Sleep” (2015), or the slightly longer “Sleep (Remixes)” (2016), or the thirty-minute, electronic-forward “Sleep: Tranquility Base” (2023). Or perhaps I should try a whole night again with “Sleep (Faded)” (2018), which is the same eight and a half hours of music, but with each track fading out at the end. I’ll think it over more, once I finish watching the 2021 documentary “Max Richter’s Sleep,” about Max Richter’s “Sleep.”

Deep in the S.R.M. property, past a large crow-inspired art work by Mahr, there is a secluded patch of trees. “All right, my dears, settle down!” Richter called, by a fence. The dears were his three alpacas—“Paddington, Finn, and . . . I’ve forgotten his name”—who were trying to kick one another in the head. “They’ve gotten frisky with the rain,” he said, beaming. “The dynamics change constantly. It’s the three-alpaca problem.”

The drizzle pattered on his umbrella. “I come out here every day,” he said. “I really enjoy the effect on your thinking, being in the green.” He walked past a row of short dog hurdles set out for his Labrador, Haku, named after a character from “Spirited Away.” “If I’m working on something, I’m here,” he said. “I’ve written movies in hotel rooms, but it’s a pretty torrid experience.” In fact, he wrote a third of the score to “Hamnet” in one.

The project didn’t originally include “On the Nature of Daylight.” “I wrote a different cue for the ending of ‘Hamnet,’ ” he said. “But ‘On the Nature of Daylight’ really got under the skin of the film.” He sounded defeated. “They played it on set, for hours and hours and hours.” The director and co-writer, Chloé Zhao, hadn’t yet finalized the end of the movie, and Jessie Buckley, who starred as Agnes, Hamnet’s mother, sent her “Daylight.” When Zhao listened to it, she had an epiphany about how to wrap up the story—the hands of the audience reaching onto the stage at the Globe Theatre, set to the strains of the twenty-year-old song.

“We had a lot of conversations where I was saying, ‘Look, it’s been in loads of films. I think we need an original score,’ ” Richter said. “It was quite an intense back-and-forth.” (Zhao told IndieWire, in 2025, “We live in a culture that is so afraid not to generate new things.”) Richter went on, “But, ultimately, it’s the director’s baby. Even though I’d written some other music which I personally prefer.”

That piece, called “Of the undiscovered country,” wound up being shovelled to the film’s end credits. I overlaid the final scene with the song, and found myself undistracted by familiarity. As Agnes mourned her son and forgave her husband, the music—high, pearly voices; deep, sombre strings—became a buttress rather than an engine. It allowed the scene to be.

Richter told me that he turns down licensing offers for “Daylight” all the time now, and doesn’t know if he wants it to appear anywhere in the future. “It’s problematic,” he said. “I’m cautious about it because I think it hijacks a movie.” Part of the issue is that British licensing laws allow national TV broadcasts to use the piece without his permission. “So, to some extent, you can’t control it,” he said. He quickly added, “But I’m very grateful.” With thirty-one acres, three alpacas, and a perfume, how could he not be?

One evening, I travelled to Newark, New Jersey, in a downpour to see Richter perform on tour. The PATH train was dotted with flight attendants and World Cup fans. Despite the weather, the New Jersey Performing Arts Center was packed, and Richter’s mass appeal was on full display. A guy downing a Miller Lite sat near a woman in an evening gown. “I listen to him a lot when I read,” a young woman with glasses and a slicked-back ponytail said. This was her first time seeing his music live.

Since Richter emerged as a commercial success, services like Spotify have been flooded with imitators, compiled on such playlists as “Peaceful Strings” (five thousand saves), “Focus Piano” (four hundred thousand saves), and “Peaceful Piano” (nearly eight million saves). In the streaming era, how we consume music has become less intentional—we’re fed what the machine thinks we’ll like, and then more of it. Richter is a cross-genre artist who could lead a listener into the world of classical music, which, in an ever-struggling industry, is a phenomenal contribution. But chances are that an algorithm will feed Richter fans the music of Hans Zimmer or Ludovico Einaudi, and not Dvořák or Messiaen or Fauré. The gateway becomes less of a gateway than an echo chamber.

Blue stage lights dimmed, and Richter, in chunky black glasses and a black shirt, walked out with his ensemble. A rectangular spotlight appeared center stage, like sun coming in from the small window of a stone church. The ensemble began playing “In a Landscape.” Fog-machine smoke billowed across the stage, choreography to the looping bass line.

After intermission, it was finally time for “On the Nature of Daylight.” Slow string notes blossomed out, and the fog wafted into the audience. A couple in front of me huddled closer together. Maybe it was the rain. Maybe I was thinking about dead little Hamnet. Maybe it was because, three nights earlier, my boyfriend had said he wasn’t in love with me. Somewhat against my will, I started to cry. After the piece ended, several people headed toward the exits—they had gotten what they came for. ♦

items.title: Gifts for Cats (and Their Owners) That Are Worth Knocking Off the Table
items.description: Cats: what would we do without them? To the cat agnostics, not to mention the cat haters, I say: don’t answer that! (Also, what’s wrong with you?) But to the cat lovers, my intended interlocutors here, I say: no need to answer, either. We both know. A catless
items.author: Naomi Fry
paragraphs: Cats: what would we do without them? To the cat agnostics, not to mention the cat haters, I say: don’t answer that! (Also, what’s wrong with you?) But to the cat lovers, my intended interlocutors here, I say: no need to answer, either. We both know. A catless world is a terrible thing to contemplate. No lap snuggles? No headbutts? No slow blinks? No raising of the rump to welcome a wealth of scritches? No occasional, inexplicable biting? We’d truly be lost without our fuzzy, innocent but knowing friends.

A catless world would also be devoid of a whole slew of objects and accoutrements, gadgets and doodads—some meant for cats and some for the humans obsessed with them—that turn a house into a home, or, in some cases, a living room into a giant obstacle course. There are two things I can’t resist: any item that might improve or enrich my two cats’ lives in some way (even if that perceived improvement is a pathetic fallacy that exists purely in my own mind); and any item that captures, for me, the half-sweet, half-tart character of the feline species. If there’s a special cat fanatic in your life (or a special cat!), why not treat them, this holiday season, to one of the below?
Children’s Books About Cats

It’s never too early for the cat-loving parent to Stockholm syndrome their kids into becoming cat lovers, too, a process that might begin with stuffing the proverbial stocking with a nice cat-centric book. My daughter is now past the age of picture books, but one of her favorites, and mine, used to be “Rich Cat, Poor Cat” ($21), by the magnificent Bernard Waber (best known for his Lyle the Crocodile series), in which a scraggly street cat named Scat finds a home. Other picture books we never tired of were Jenni Desmond’s “Red Cat, Blue Cat” ($14), about two feline frenemies; “No Kiss for Mother” ($51), by Tomi Ungerer, in which a young kit refuses to play nice; and Judith Kerr’s Mog the Cat series ($36 for eight of the books). For the slightly older child, I’d suggest either Esther Averill’s fantastic “Jenny and the Cat Club” collection ($22), about the shy black cat Jenny Linsky and her community of cat friends in nineteen-forties Greenwich Village, or Ursula K. Le Guin’s “Catwings” series ($28), about a litter of flying cats. Finally, a book for adults that kids will also enjoy leafing through is “The Encyclopedia of Movie Cats” ($50), from A24.

The best gift for an actual cat is almost undoubtedly the gift of play. I love watching my cats go nuts for catnip, and these knitted cigarette-shaped catnip toys ($15 for three), for the bad-boy feline about town, are super cute. (For a healthier-looking playtime option, these felted vegetable toys, for $6, are also terrific.) Feather wands ($6) can help the rotund cat get her jumps in, but if she prefers a more brainteasing kind of exercise this tri-tier ball tower ($12) will keep her occupied. Finally, a clicker toy ($28) is my own cats’ personal favorite. Hours of fun following that little red dot . . . if only all of us were so easily amused.
Cat Furniture and Homeware for Cats

Let’s face it, neither a cat tree nor a scratcher is likely to stop your cat from shedding on your furniture, or destroying it (and I have the totally clawed-down Design Within Reach sofa to prove it). Still, it’s nice to make them feel like they have their own little domain, and if this domain is aesthetically pleasing, so much the better. This rustic pearwood-and-sisal cat tree-cum-scratcher (£90) will make one’s cat look like Robinson Crusoe sleeping in a tree; this fun cherry-shaped cat tree ($136) is very Claes Oldenburg; and this mid-century-modern scratching chair ($47) will class up any joint. A plush window perch ($23) will allow a bored house cat a view of the outdoors. (I always think of this kind of contraption as a public service, since there’s nothing that makes my heart beat faster than spotting an indoor cat lounging on one while walking down the street.) And, perhaps most useful, this techy litter robot ($599) will keep one’s home odor-free.
Cat-Themed Clothes, Accessories, and Homeware

I know, I know. Feline-themed clothing and paraphernalia can easily veer corny or “crazy cat lady,” but there’s some cool stuff out there that avoids these pitfalls. I, for one, always enjoy a good vintage Kliban shirt ($48). This nineteen-seventies Danish cat tapestry ($404) is giving Ingmar Bergman’s “Scenes from a Marriage” décor (in a good way), and drinking coffee out of this William Steig New Yorker-cover cat mug ($24) could turn a terrible morning into a good one. The cat bus from Miyazaki’s “My Neighbor Totoro” always gives me a warm, happy feeling, so falling asleep in a room illuminated by this night light ($55) seems very soothing. Another famous cartoon cat that I’m obsessed with is, of course, Garfield, and this vintage ceramic figurine ($35) takes me straight back to 1981.

There’s never enough support for the people and organizations that are helping to save cats from the mean streets of America’s cities. I live in Brooklyn, and I adopted my extremely soft black-and-white cat, Gully, from Bushwick Street Cats, a nonprofit doing fantastic work with stray cats in the area. (They also helped neuter my other cat, the grumpy but loving Gingy.) Two other great organizations near me are Flatbush Cats and Brooklyn Animal Action. I can’t imagine a nicer gift than making a donation in someone’s name to one of these charities, or the cat charity of your choice, wherever you live.
And . . . a Bone for the Dog Lovers

Believe it or not, I love dogs, too (though maybe not as passionately as I love cats), so I was delighted to take my editor’s note and add a few choice finds for our canine friends. Since my knowledge of dogs is much less intimate, however, I solicited the assistance of two friends. Susan Korn, who owns both an accessories brand called Susan Alexandra and a gentle senior chihuahua named Pigeon, makes fabulous hand-beaded leashes ($155) and collars ($98). Pigeon, meanwhile, recommends this dog shampoo ($98) and this human-grade dog food (a basic plan starts at roughly $1 per meal). My friend Claire Jarvis has recently found herself the owner of a large, Marmaduke-like setter named Frankie, who’s been enjoying this wand toy ($32) and this harness ($40). He’ll also “walk on water” for these freeze-dried elk treats ($30). ♦
The art accompanying this article was changed after publication.

items.title: Tech Gifts That Won’t Rot Their Brains
items.description: Binge-watching. Doomscrolling. Rabbit-holing. Brain-rotting. These, it seems, are the behaviors encouraged by our computers and digital devices—intoxicating masterworks of engineering that we stumble away from, glassy-eyed. It’s a sad state of affairs, especia
items.author: Joshua Rothman
paragraphs: Binge-watching. Doomscrolling. Rabbit-holing. Brain-rotting. These, it seems, are the behaviors encouraged by our computers and digital devices—intoxicating masterworks of engineering that we stumble away from, glassy-eyed. It’s a sad state of affairs, especially if, like me, you grew up in the nineteen-eighties and nineties, when digital technology was exciting and liberatory. Back then, Steve Jobs called the computer a “bicycle for the mind”; parents bought PCs hoping that their kids would become “computer whizzes.” The idea was that circuits and software could unleash our potential.

Today, of course, we associate screens with mindlessness, and computers with distraction and drudgery. But it doesn’t have to be that way. Gadgets are still great, and computers remain delightful. In fact, it’s easy to turn your personal tech dystopia into a utopia: all you have to do is shift from being a consumer to becoming a creator. We live in a golden age of digital creativity. Forget A.I.: you, yourself, can record an album from your sofa, or curate a photo-essay on the train. In that spirit, here are some of my favorite creative digital tools.

Perhaps you’ve seen, on YouTube, videos of “infinite sketchbooks”—digital drawings that can be zoomed into seemingly forever, revealing worlds within worlds. It turns out that tablets aren’t just for Netflix: even a small model, like the iPad Mini ($699), can open up onto endless vistas when it’s equipped with a digital pencil ($124) and an app like Endless Paper (free). Tablets are always getting slimmer and lighter, making them better for watching than for drawing. But turning a tablet into an ergonomic drawing surface is simple: just get a drawing board ($45)—one of those slanted wooden surfaces that illustrators use. Add a book stand and a copy of “Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain” ($24).

If a tablet is too distracting, there are other ways to make digital art. For years, I’ve been doing a lot of my writing and sketching using e-ink tablets made by reMarkable, a Norwegian company. The deluxe version, the Paper Pro ($629), has a big screen and can be expanded with a keyboard. But the Paper Pro Move ($449) is the size of a pocket notebook and lets you sketch in color. There’s no e-mail, web browsing, or social media on these—only a Kindle-esque e-ink display that feels paperlike beneath your stylus. (When my eight-year-old son and I are bored, I sometimes make sketches so that he can color them in and add to them.) I also find that writing in longhand on an e-ink device can loosen up one’s brain, and I’ve written many articles—including this one—on my reMarkable, eventually using the device’s handwriting-recognition feature to transform my scrawls into editable text. For those who like writing but want to get away from their work computer, this sort of freestanding writing device can be a godsend. The BYOK ($199) is a little portable screen that’s made entirely for writing; as its name suggests, you should bring your own keyboard, and a tiny, pleasantly clicky model like the Keychron K2 ($60) would be a good choice. The Freewrite Alpha ($349) is like a digital typewriter, and includes its own keyboard.

I was in college when the iPod appeared. In the two decades since, dedicated music players have almost completely disappeared. And yet, beneath the radar, music-making devices have proliferated. Today, there are zillions of cool little synthesizers and “grooveboxes” on the market, and they’re not at all difficult to use.

You can make beats with a Teenage Engineering Pocket Operator ($59), which is about the size of a deck of cards. You can compose lovely melodies and soundscapes with the Roland P-6 ($229), a sampler the size of a paperback book, with rechargeable batteries so that you can use it on the go. (The P-6 can be hooked up to its siblings, which include a synth, for $230, and a drum machine, also for $230, to form a synth-pop band.) Bigger units let you build whole tracks, with different parts playing in parallel. The Elektron Model:Cycles ($349) offers modern sounds and medical-device chic; the Sonicware Deconstruct ($399) lets you pretend your living room is Berghain. The most elegant grooveboxes are probably the Teenage Engineering OP-1 Field ($1,999) and OP-XY ($2,299), which are like scaled-down music studios with Apple-calibre designs and batteries that last all day; the Field is better for keyboard players, while the XY works best for purely electronic music.

A computer or a tablet can, itself, become a musical gadget, with the addition of the right piano-style keyboard. The Arturia MiniLab 3 ($119) is a compact model that connects to your computer and lets you play, compose, and record in apps like GarageBand, which contain hundreds of free synthesized instruments. You can listen through the lightweight, comfortable Koss PortaPro headphones ($50), which weigh nothing but sound gorgeous, and record your songs with a phone app like Tape It, for listening on the go. If you know a lapsed musician, any of these tools could help get them back up and running—especially in combination with a lesson or two from an online instructor. I’m hoping to learn more about my synthesizers from Jeremy, at Red Means Recording, this winter.
Photography and Filmmaking

Everyone has a smartphone, and every smartphone has a camera; this means that everyone is just a step away from becoming a hobby photographer. Doing so is partly a matter of self-perception—you have to look at your pictures with a critical, artistic eye—but it also has to do with equipment. The Canon Selphy Printer ($159), which allows you to effortlessly print four-by-six photographs at home, can help bridge the gap between taking pictures and making photographs to keep. The Aura Carver Frame ($149), which can rotate through pictures you select, creates a place for your best digital pictures to live.

Giving someone a dedicated camera is like giving them a new form of self-expression. There are all sorts of cameras, and they suit different kinds of photographers—but don’t overthink it, since people can grow into the tools they happen to have. The Insta360 Go Retro Bundle ($299) contains an action camera (great for filming daredevilry and dynamic exploits) that can also be used as a pocketable point-and-shoot. The Polaroid Now ($120) is a stylish instant camera perfect for social butterflies. The Lomography MC-A ($549) is a 35-mm. film camera with autofocus. And the Panasonic Lumix L10 ($1,498) is a discreet but powerful model with a built-in zoom lens and options for “color-grading”—that is, giving photos or footage a professional, cinematic look.

Writing, drawing, music-making—an art form that combines them all is game design. Earlier this year, I bought our family a Playdate ($229), a handheld video-game console with its own easy-to-use game-creation tool, which runs in a web browser. My son and I had fun making a little game; we even moved beyond the browser-based editor, writing our own code directly (with a little help from Claude). And we also played Big Walk ($20), an unforgettable adventure from a game studio called House House. In Big Walk, you play together but on separate screens—I used a Nintendo Switch, he used his computer—solving puzzles while communicating almost entirely through systems of symbol and gesture that you improvise. It’s a video game that brings out new aspects of your own creativity and ingenuity—a perfect example of how humanizing technology can be. ♦

items.title: The Best Gifts for Kids Are Small. Or Big. Or Lots. Or Stomp
items.description: When you are a kid, time can seem to organize itself around occasions for receiving treats—and, above all, presents. This is not because children are materialistic monsters (mostly) but because they have a limited ability to treat themselves. Generally speakin
items.author: Molly Fischer
paragraphs: When you are a kid, time can seem to organize itself around occasions for receiving treats—and, above all, presents. This is not because children are materialistic monsters (mostly) but because they have a limited ability to treat themselves. Generally speaking, an eight-year-old cannot reward herself, at the end of a tough week, by doing a little window-shopping and deciding that she deserves a cute bag, or its third-grade equivalent (glowing slime?). The calendar can become a series of buildups and letdowns around the prospect of surprise delights. This is the golden age of gift-getting. No one cares as much about presents as kids do. No pressure!

Fortunately, choosing a gift for a child comes with fewer shades of social nuance than picking something for an adult. The goal is pure pleasure, not a statement or message; the worst-case scenario is indifference or mild disappointment—not, say, horror at your fundamental misunderstanding of a long-standing personal relationship. You are going for FUN. Think about the experience of seeing the present and opening the present, and about whom the present is actually going to please.

If you are buying a present for a person who lacks object permanence, that present is for their parents. Shop with this fact in mind. Clothes are an excellent gift, in a way that they won’t be again until the child’s adolescence—here is your chance to jazz up the Center of the Universe. Buy something that’s more expensive than anyone thinking about the cost of child care could justify buying themselves, but that’s still functional enough for everyday use. No to tiny buttons, the color white, and lace; yes to $64 balloon pants. Yes to leopard-print anything. (It’ll hide stains!) Yes to seasonally appropriate comical hats ($55-$99).

Parents spend a lot of time gazing upon their babies (how would the Center of the Universe look in pink sunglasses?), and they also spend a lot of time reading to their babies, at least if they are overachieving millennials who have imbibed the requisite parenting expertise. It is important that they have books to read aloud that are not bad. My husband, a bookseller, often notes that most books are bad, and this may be doubly true for children’s books, whose brevity leads foolhardy would-be authors to underestimate the difficulty of their task. Before you give a children’s book, think: Is this book fun to read aloud? Will it be fun to read aloud twelve million times? Rhythm counts for everything, subject matter for almost nothing. Babies do not care about “art” or “science,” and you can’t make them. What you’re after here is fluid prose and pictures that contain lots of interesting items to identify and talk about. There’s a reason everyone already has “Goodnight Moon.” Instead, consider “The House in the Night,” by Susan Marie Swanson, or “All the World,” by Liz Garton Scanlon, both sold in chompable board-book editions. Richard Scarry’s “I Am a Bunny,” though not explicitly bedtime-oriented, is another durable hit. (If you want to give a new parent something to read to themselves, consider “And Now We Have Everything,” by Meaghan O’Connell, a funny and unsparing account of parenthood’s earliest days.) ($9-$40)

As for toys: true infants are scarcely capable of “play” in any sense that requires accessories or equipment; they’re still realizing that they have hands. Something with fabric that produces a crinkly sound ($10) when pawed inexpertly is pretty much the upper limit of possibility.

Not long ago, my husband and I asked our three-and-a-half-year-old what we should get his grandfather as an eightieth-birthday present. “Cars and cars and cars and cars and cars,” he replied. It was an instructive answer: the sorts of gifts that people imagine giving others are a good indication of the gifts that they themselves enjoy receiving. In general, I’m all for quality, but when attempting to please a small child there’s something to be said for quantity. Sheer, dazzling quantity: cars and cars and cars and cars and cars ($7-$30). Present them loose in a bag or in a box; remember that it’s always nice to have spares to lose, or for a visitor to take home.

By a similar token, stickers and stickers and stickers and stickers and stickers ($9-$31). The recipient can stick them on a giant roll of paper ($33) (how giant? That’s up to you), taped out on the floor. The effect is something like an off-season approximation of a sidewalk, and, your winter climate permitting, sidewalk chalk (tons of it, for $18) is another good option. And books are not excluded from the thrill of scale. Richard Scarry’s “Biggest Word Book Ever!” ($45)—about twenty-four by thirty-two inches when wide open—is irresistibly grand, full of many quintessentially busy Scarry characters, and large enough for a small reader to literally climb inside.

The appeal of something to climb inside is a valuable reminder of another language that kid gifts can speak: the charm of little. It can be fun to be small and to feel small, and this is why it is nice to build forts. Technically, doing so only requires a blanket, but you don’t need a gift guide to direct you to your linen closet. Expand your household’s fort horizons with the Nugget ($249-$299), a “play couch” made of sturdy, rearrangeable cushions that can be used to construct cozy reading corners and nooks for playing pretend. (A chair called the Smore, at $199-$239, from the same company, offers a similar concept, with a smaller footprint.)

It is also fun simply to think about small things. And so, to stock the fort’s library: the author and illustrator Phoebe Wahl produces books full of magical tiny beings, stories that are beautiful and sweet without being precious or twee. “Little Witch Hazel: A Year in the Forest” ($20) collects four stories—one for each season—about a witch who lives in a mossy stump and is small enough to ride on the back of an owl. Her friends and neighbors include the Mole Sisters, Mousepappa, and a frog named Wendell (who might plausibly have been named for Wendell Berry). Wahl’s “Backyard Fairies” ($19) depicts a kid who is sure that there are fairies just out of sight, in the woods behind her house, and tries to find them. For children inclined to such expeditions—or who just want to read in a dark spot—a camping headlamp ($35) makes an inexhaustibly useful accessory.

Becoming a parent, and shopping for a child, is a constant reminder that everything and nothing changes. I can easily recall the joy of forts; I would have loved “Backyard Fairies.” Yet certain stalwart kid pleasures have been reimagined in the intervening decades. Take training wheels and tricycles: they’re out. Now children have balance bikes, which are two-wheelers without pedals—an arrangement that supposedly makes for an easier transition to riding the real thing. Based on the anecdotal evidence of my local playground, I’m convinced. The little guys get good at gliding, fast. These new versions of that classic Big Present, a bike, can be procured from such manufacturers as Guardian ($169) and Woom ($249) (branding keyed to a target market of anxious parents).

Even crayon technology has somehow improved in the years since I was coloring. Have you tried gel crayons ($20)? Instead of hard and waxy, they’re as soft as oil pastels, but miraculously smudge-proof once dry, with colors bright and opaque enough to draw on dark construction paper. And, for kids approaching the age of phones, Tin Can ($100) has given the humble landline a contemporary reinvention: it permits calls to preselected phone numbers using home Wi-Fi, and has (yes) a cord.

When I set out to make a list of gifts for kids, there was only one thing I was sure I wanted to include. If you take nothing else from this guide, know this: a Stomp Rocket ($30) is the perfect present.

One kid can have fun with a Stomp Rocket; two kids can execute some impressive teamwork; three or four kids can share effortlessly. The learning curve is nonexistent. The payoff is immediate. The only way to improve it is to buy extra rockets ($10), which you should do. (And do not go off-brand with these—you want genuine Stomp product. Amazon imitations can get stuck on the launch tube, an unacceptable defect, and one that I discovered the hard way.) I have never seen a group of children get bored of a Stomp Rocket. I have seen a group of adults sipping early-evening drinks on a patio, idly Stomping and chatting, enjoying the beginning of a spring thaw and the return of sunlight. ♦

items.title: Gifts for Discerning Design Lovers
items.description: In Vincenzo Latronico’s novella “Perfection” (originally published by Fitzcarraldo, and, in the U.S., by New York Review of Books), Tom and Anna, two young digital creatives, aspire to an idealized life plucked from discerning social feeds: modernist seating i
items.author: Nicholas Blechman
paragraphs: In Vincenzo Latronico’s novella “Perfection” (originally published by Fitzcarraldo, and, in the U.S., by New York Review of Books), Tom and Anna, two young digital creatives, aspire to an idealized life plucked from discerning social feeds: modernist seating in an industrial urban loft, a black metal side table with the latest issue of Monocle, an Anglepoise lamp with house plants positioned just so to look like the pages of Apartamento. The writing is deliberately superficial and deeply relatable—a painfully accurate depiction of a curated life that feels only ever quasi-real. What are the things that become meaningful over time, and that last? Which objects do I like enough to give to the people I love? The objects listed here come from the studios of friends, designers, illustrators, and makers I admire. They follow some of Dieter Rams’s principles of good design: they are utilitarian, durable, minimalist, and aesthetic.

Warning: some of the items are made in limited quantities and will sell out quickly, but I encourage you to browse the sites they are listed on. Labour and Wait, Best Made, Wms & Co., and Florentine are among my favorite sources for gift-giving.

The most prominent object on our kitchen table is an analog calendar. Filling out my family’s daily pursuits (Ultimate Frisbee practice, choir lessons, dinners out) is a family ritual. Manufactum sells a minimalist weekly calendar ($19) that is our organizational bible. Crispin Finn makes a wall calendar ($39) for the entire year that’s aesthetic enough to function as a poster. Seeing the whole year at once is a wonderful way to visualize time. John Lennon was a devout user of the New Yorker Desk Diary ($60), which includes cartoons and covers of the magazine, in addition to a monthly planner. Best Made, which began as a shop centered on high-end painted axes, sells a traditional Japanese daily calendar ($68) that includes the lunar phases and zodiac signs; it’s screen-printed by hand, with bold typography on a semitransparent vellum. You can see the next day underneath, as if peering into the future. Or, instead of starting each day with a number, begin with an image—a watercolor landscape, or a witty drawing—with the illustrator Christoph Niemann’s new calendar Every Day ($52). The celebrated Dutch designer Karel Martens uses metal shapes and found objects to create abstract and colorful numerals in Every Day Is a New Day ($45).

Designers tend to be obsessed with watches because they are both aesthetic and utilitarian, equal parts form and function. The legendary graphic designer Tibor Kalman (who created Colors magazine) designed a collection of watches in the nineties that are now being reissued as they were originally produced, by M & Co Labs ($250). One of the watch designs, Askew, playfully scrambles the positions of the numbers; Onomatopoeia replaces numerals for tiny spot drawings; and the most minimal design, 10-1-4, in a classic exercise of the design mantra “Less is more,” uses only three numbers. (It’s in the MOMA design collection.) No watch is coveted by designers as much as the Max Bill watch ($1,030). Bill, a Bauhaus-trained Swiss designer with work in the permanent collection of MOMA, created this piece for the German company Junghans, in 1960. It is exceptionally elegant and restrained, with every line and mark carefully considered. I’ve always loved military watches for their no-nonsense design and easy-to-read numerals knocking out of a black background, like the instruments in the cockpit of an old airplane, and my favorite on the market is made by the Canadian company Marathon ($575). One thing that makes military watches so fun is that you can demilitarize them by customizing the bands with bright colors through the Strap Tailor ($37). On a larger scale, Mondaine makes an iconic wall clock ($345) using a design developed for the Swiss Railways. Mine hangs on the kitchen wall and keeps my family on track. In an expression of Swiss precision, the red second hand is the most prominent element. If you are not really in it to tell time, the German artist Sarah Illenberger makes Slowlex ($845). It’s a piece of jewelry disguised as a watch, and completely nonfunctional. It’s subversive, sexy, and literally timeless.

My favorite kinds of gifts, to receive and to offer, are from art-supply stores. The Toronto Ink Company offers handmade inks ($25-$32) using elements from the urban environment: rich hues of blue from oxidized metals, and old railway spikes foraged from the streets of Toronto. Sample color swatches, called “test prints,” are works of art in themselves. Inks are useless without paper, and I always have a few sketchbooks stacked on my desk ready for use. My favorite is a German Pasteboard sketchbook ($20-$40), made with a blank chipboard cover, a bright cloth spine in a selection of Bauhaus colors (red, yellow, and blue), and natural white paper suitable for ink drawing. Because of the cloth binding, it opens flat. The typesetter in me loves the Japanese rubber-stamp set ($147), possibly drawn by hand in a serif font similar to Cheltenham Condensed, sold by Wms & Co. Beyond the creative potential (think of the rubber-stamp drawings of Saul Steinberg), it would make an eye-catching object on your shelf or desk. Another printmaking gift is a mini linocut set ($41), sold at the British home-goods store Labour and Wait. It has everything you need to print multiple editions of whatever you design. Create your own holiday card! The holy grail of mini ballpoint pens is the Lamy Pico ($39), available in neon colors, and half the size of a normal pen, with a sleek design and an ingenious telescopic mechanism for releasing the tip. Pantone, a universal system for accurately specifying colors, and worshipped by designers and printers around the world, sells a straightforward ruler ($29). It comes in a variety of colors (of course), and would look great on any desk; my favorites are Red 2035 and Yellow 012.

For most of the nineties, my wardrobe was black (with the occasional navy so dark that it might as well have been black). Since then, I’ve been on a mission to bring more color into my life. One of the most stunning pieces of product design I’ve come across is the Tex-Lock ($169), a cloth-covered bicycle lock designed by art students in Leipzig. It’s theft-proof: saw blades get ensnared in the fabric covering, and clippers can’t cut through the fibres. The lock comes in bright orange and looks good looped around your neck during transit.

Anticipating the colder weather about to descend on New York, you might check out the Dutch furnishing brand Suite702’s reinvention of the hot-water bottle ($62). The unique rounded-rectangle shape, with bold colors and racing stripes, may just make you want to hibernate. But, if you decide to brave the elements, keep in mind the German proverb “There is no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing.” Lloyd’s made-to-order Canadian-fleece toque with a massive brim ($62) will make you feel invincible. My favorite colors are red and “epoca” blue. To fill in awkward silences at holiday cocktail parties, the San Francisco artist Tucker Nichols created a set of hand-lettered napkins ($36), printed in pink and red, on linen, with suggested topics of conversation: “Where birds go in big storms,” “fear of escalators,” “smog v. fog.” As a companion piece, he designed subjects to avoid: “Root Canals,” “When was the last time you wore that sweater,” “Cloth diapers.” I was happy to discover that Karel Martens also collaborated, with Suite702, on a series of modernist towels with bold stripes and blocks of color ($28-$229), inspired by the colors on the beach in Le Havre, France. On the other side of the Channel, in Cornwall, the illustrator Tabby Booth designed the Odessa throw ($250), for Slowdown Studio, depicting a mermaid staring at a red fish. It’s remarkably primitive, and powerful.

To draw, I need a really good light. Anglepoise invented the now ubiquitous and widely imitated adjustable-spring desk lamp in the nineteen-thirties. Paul Smith refreshed the design by introducing primary colors to the steel arms of the Type 75 Mini Desk Lamp ($370). This simple design move transforms an understated lamp into a fun object. Another great use of color can be found in the Dutch coffee-brewing machines made by Moccamaster ($369). Designed in the nineteen-sixties to bring high-quality brewing to Scandinavian homes, the red, orange, yellow, and green machines are surely intended as an antidote to the monochromatic, dark Nordic winters. They remind me of the colorful houses often seen in traditional Scandinavian towns. For those who drink tea, the Japanese enamel kettle Noda Horo ($41), with its simple forms and bright colors, is another design classic. If you want to make this gift more special, pair it with Taiwanese tea ($8-$46) from Té Company, a shop in the West Village. Florentine sells an affordable designer butter knife ($35) engraved with an abstract illustration by Oded Webman, which transforms a mundane kitchen utensil into a small work of art. Its dull edge and playful motif make it suitable for children. The Kiridashi knife ($128), sold through Best Made, looks more dangerous. Unlike a jackknife, it has a penlike cap (also known as a scabbard cap). Made of steel, iron, and magnolia wood, the knife has an elemental quality, and adheres to Rams’s principle “Good design is as little design as possible.”

After my cloth pencil cases deteriorated, owing to wear and tear and leaking black ink, I upgraded to a steel box ($39) from Toyo. I pack pens, brushes, erasers, inks, pencils, and earbuds in this box, but it can hold anything, and versatility is one of its virtues. It’s also lightweight and durable. (I’ve had mine for two years, and it does not have a scratch.) The box comes in a variety of colors and sizes, and is handcrafted in Japan in a retro style. As someone who tends to lose art supplies, I can tell you that this inexpensive item has improved my life. Another Japanese steel company, Nakamura Seiko, makes a beautifully proportioned toolbox ($48). Not as bulky as those from heavy-duty American brands such as Stanley, it comes in bright powder-coated red, green, and blue. Conceal a bottle of locally distilled Kings County Bourbon ($23-$84) inside for a bonus surprise.

The extra-large River Café tote bag ($54), from Ruthie Rogers’s legendary London restaurant, is the perfect urban bag for running errands. Whether Yves Klein blue or bright yellow, this bag radiates joy. Ruthie’s late husband, the architect Richard Rogers, incorporated color into all of his buildings, notably the Pompidou Center, and I can’t help but think that his ethos is woven into the fabric of this bag. The designer Deborah Ehrlich, known for her exquisitely sculpted handblown glassware, released a super-light travel bag ($750) made of reused sails. Because sails are made to withstand gale-force winds, the bag is structurally strong, yet looks light and luminous. Ehrlich is not the first to make bags from old sails, but she is the first to make them this refined. They’re handcrafted in Florence with sustainably made materials, including leather from Blue Hill at Stone Barns. ♦
An earlier version of this article included an inaccurate price for the watches sold by M & Co Labs.

items.title: 20 Ways to Think About Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Mess
items.description: It’s been a roller coaster of a week for Nvidia and its now-departed co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. It’s also been an overwhelming week for anybody trying to follow this fast-moving, multifaceted story of sex, espionage, White House intrigue, AI dominance, i
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: It’s been a roller coaster of a week for Nvidia and its now-departed co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. It’s also been an overwhelming week for anybody trying to follow this fast-moving, multifaceted story of sex, espionage, White House intrigue, AI dominance, investor panic, and a growing number of ill-advised affairs. There have also been a lot of twists and turns and takes. Just in case you’re having trouble keeping up, here’s a collection of additional ways to think about this megascandal and its impact on, well, everything.
AI is helping us put Huang’s absurdly stupid situation in context
By which we mean AI-generated parodies:
Maybe these guys shouldn’t be masters of the universe
Gary Sernovitz writes about how Huang and the ten other tech emperors have proven they are not responsible enough to have so much concentrated power:

For years, there have been no consequences as the emperors’ lives got wackier, sometimes grosser, and always more known. Most of us can recite a few facts about each emperor’s love life without quite trying — or wanting — to. The impunity of the emperors’ carelessness and misdeeds coincided with a period in which they have become richer, louder, coarser, more visible, more Florida, and more right-wing. The emperors don’t all share the same politics, but they have grown comfortable with the sense of all of us as passive participants in their vision of the future. They like nothing more than to scold the scolds: the small thinkers, the enemies of progress, the pearl-clutching moralists. Theirs is the rhetoric of conquerors and commanders. It’s not the rhetoric of people in happy, committed relationships. They can do whatever they want.
Maybe, just maybe, the resignation of Jensen Huang is another sign that all of us have had enough of this rhetoric. And of the men behind it.
There may be some internal groundswell for Huang’s return
Wired notes that some Nvidia staffers don’t think Huang should have been ousted and want him reinstated, but it’s not clear from the report how widespread that sentiment is:

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.
“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.

One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”
There’s probably more ugliness to come
At the New York Times, Huang’s biographer, Stephen Witt, explains why he knows the tech mogul’s humble public persona was all an act:

I started hearing rumors of Mr. Huang’s infidelities earlier this year, but was unable to confirm them. Inside Nvidia, there was a culture of omertà that was difficult to break, and this enabled Mr. Huang to be his worst self. I sensed this deference, at times, in the sycophantic laughter of his subordinates when he was around, and the little things they muttered once he left the room. Ultimately, it took government intelligence to pierce Nvidia’s culture of silence — along with the reporters at this newspaper. But now that containment is shattered, and I will not be surprised if more women come forward. No one will be surprised. …

In truth, Mr. Huang was quite arrogant. He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash.”
Nvidia’s downturn could be an investment opportunity

As of Thursday afternoon, the fallout from the Huang spy and employee affairs has erased about $500 billion of Nvidia’s market value, but that’s actually up from the roughly $1 trillion it was down after the company’s stock crashed 16 percent on Thursday morning, and really up from the $1.7 trillion it was down after news of Huang’s spy-lover news first broke.
Nvidia’s sudden downturn has also prompted a lively discourse among investors as to whether now is the perfect time to buy the dip, as CNBC notes:

“The premise here is that there is no successor to a generational founder,” says Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, which invests in founder-led companies. “It’s that they’re one of one, and what they bring from a vision, execution and grit standpoint is not replaceable.”

While some investors are exiting Nvidia positions based on that premise — Monaghan’s fund must, per its prospectus — others will see the slip in Nvidia’s price as an opportunity to buy a great stock on proverbial sale, he says.

Looking purely at the numbers, the opportunity to buy a stock with Nvidia’s prodigious projected growth at its current depressed price “happens once a decade, maybe once in a career as an investor,” he says.
The take from JPMorgan analysts, per NBC News:
“We expect the [Nvidia] team to maintain its leadership in AI,” JPMorgan’s team said, while cautioning that “history has shown that one execution misstep often leads to more.”
“Maintaining flawless execution” will be critical to Nvidia and the sector going forward, they said.
The leather jackets were a tell
Our Cut colleague Emma Childs writes:

A $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution. That’s a man in a midlife crisis with an active Raya profile and a Harley in the garage. If someone had consulted me years ago, I’d have said Huang is clearly someone who drinks wine with his mistress in the middle of the day. (The Times uncovered a 2023 photo of Jensen appearing to do exactly that at a luncheon in Shanghai with Alice.)
But pity other leather-jacket lovers
At the New York Times, Anand Giridharadas decries how uncool Huang’s leather jackets have been for the leather-jacket-wearing community:

We may have undiagnosed issues with vulnerability (as reflected in our need for a supplemental dermis), but we’re not stupid. Did we acquire multiple jackets that our spouses smeared as “identical to the last one”? Yes. But a lot of our spouses don’t know the difference between a 1.5-ounce leather and a three-ounce leather, which is like not knowing the difference between Texas and cheese. This was our thing, OK?

Then Mr. Huang, with his own penchant for black leather jackets, had to go and become a household name, the pillar of artificial intelligence, and the man, we were told, without whom the future itself might vanish and the world regress to however it got things done in 2022.

It was annoying to watch a billionaire cosplaying as a rebel, perhaps in order to mask his extraordinary power. Here he was boasting in interviews of not even knowing where his jackets came from, saying his wife and daughter bought them for him, when we in the community could tell you what we ate for dinner any of those fateful days when a new jacket came into our lives. Leather jackets are for people with chips on their shoulders, not microchips in their palms.
And never forget what Charles de Gaulle probably never said
Per former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein:
(As Quote Investigator has concluded, there’s little to no evidence that de Gaulle ever actually said that.)
And never forget this was the beginning of the end
Or as SemiAnalysis posits:

We aren’t ones for conspiracy theories, but a few events around the same time seem to create a narrative that is hard to ignore. The intelligence community had much to gain. The second New York Times story on the topic explicitly states (five times) that the basis for its reporting is the U.S. intelligence community. Trump, Rubio and Lutnick have known about all of this since before their trip to China in May. What’s more is that there is reporting that Lutnick stalled the Chinese chip crackdown. Something has shifted in that relationship, and now the wind is blowing in the other direction.
Seriously, think about all the things we still don’t know
The Verge’s Elizabeth Lopatto wants to know how high it all goes:

Huang has insisted that Nvidia has seen “no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” He’s been pretty emphatic on that point, actually. I am now wondering if that is even a little bit true. If the board is cutting Huang loose, there’s probably more on chip smuggling allegations coming. More substantively, Nvidia reportedly intervened in a 2025 Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed, which was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips — halting the investigation. Since the scandal broke, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick appears to have become the fall guy for this, with Axios reporting that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent “confronted” him about failing to note Megaspeed as a national security concern and Politico saying “more than half a dozen Republicans have demanded answers” from him. …

Come January, Elizabeth Warren will be able to send subpoenas in her role as the chair of the Senate Banking Committee. And wouldn’t you know, she seems to be pretty interested. Democrats will control both the House and the Senate. Their voters have given them a mandate to root out corruption. And boy howdy, does Nvidia look like a sitting duck right now. If Huang knew chips were being diverted — or had reason to know that — and tried to ensure their sales anyway, he may have committed actual crimes (bribery, espionage, smuggling, whatever) and, under a functioning legal system, could actually go to jail. Nvidia dispensing with its indispensable CEO is the company reducing its risk of getting roped into Huang’s drama.
And this saga has inspired a lot of overlong tweets
We won’t share any in their entirety because nobody should be forced to read a superlong tweet, but here’s how one begins:
Infidelity is obviously bad
But his contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated
We believe Jensen Huang is an irreplaceable part of Nvidia and the AI Revolution more broadly.
Once the dust settles, firing Jensen Huang would prove to be a costly mistake.
It is time to pause and consult your shareholders.
Huang didn’t just torch market value
Politico points out the terrible position Huang put his company in:

Trump has stuck with Huang. But the scandal is draining the company of the political capital that its CEO had accumulated during the Trump 2.0 era, according to more than a dozen lobbyists, executives, former administration officials and industry analysts who were interviewed for this story.

“If you have a personal brand that’s tied to the corporate brand, you have to think about: ‘What’s my bench look like? Who’s gonna be ready to step up into the spotlight?’” said Brett Bruen, a former diplomat and adviser to President Barack Obama who now runs the public affairs and crisis communications firm the Global Situation Room. “The fact that Nvidia apparently had none of this in place is both shocking and incredibly stupid.”
“Not only did they lose share value. They have lost and — in some cases — done irreparable harm to their relationship with the government, with clients and with investors,” Bruen added.
The second chances are already on offer
Professional scandal surfer Elon Musk is ready to give Huang one:
And armchair CEO Donald Trump is ready to give one to Tim Apple:
The scandal has (at least briefly) shattered a glass ceiling

Nvidia’s new interim CEO is the company’s longtime CFO Colette Kress, which instantly makes her the most powerful woman in tech, in the AI industry, and in the business world, overall, since she now runs one of the world’s three most valuable companies.
However, Huang overlooked Kress when Wired asked him to name the most powerful women in AI earlier this year:

Notably, Huang didn’t mention the highest-ranking woman executive in his own company, someone who joins him on nearly every quarterly earnings call and has deeper knowledge of Nvidia’s finances than probably anyone else in the world. As CFO, Kress was an integral part of one of the most valuable companies in the world—one of the most powerful women in tech by any measure.

As interim CEO, Kress now sits atop the bedrock of the entire AI industry at its most precarious moment. The choices she makes while in this role will reverberate across tech, geopolitics, and the broader economy.
Regardless of whether that promotion becomes permanent, we now know just how powerful Kress is in the tech industry—and that her omission from Huang’s list was just one in a long line of bad calls.
But beware the “web of financial dependencies”
The Financial Times warns that Huang’s resignation “threatens to unravel a web of financial dependencies that binds the AI ecosystem together”:

Huang has made Nvidia the AI industry’s backer of last resort — and he did much of the dealmaking himself. Despite having dozens of direct reports, he was personally involved in many of its investments worth billions of dollars, according to company founders who have received money from Nvidia.

When CoreWeave, the neocloud and prodigious buyer of Nvidia chips, saw its IPO falter last year, Huang led Nvidia to step in with an anchor order. When OpenAI needed support to build a massive data centre campus in Ohio, Huang had Nvidia guarantee up to $105bn of its lease and power payments.

He then worked with Wall Street groups on a plan to use Nvidia’s balance sheet to mobilise more than $500bn of outside capital for chip financing. Several deals are under way, people familiar with the matter said. Nvidia is planning to invest $10bn in Anthropic in a private placement alongside the Claude maker’s initial public offering next week.
And never underestimate the “dangers of lust”
YouTuber Asian Dad Energy’s takeaway:

I think what happened to Jensen over here, it’s a clear example of the dangers of lust. Lust is so dangerous that it can destroy the smartest, the most powerful of men. Yet despite the danger, it is so very appealing. And that’s because lust, it’s a part of man’s nature. …

I believe that most men, maybe even the vast majority of men, they have never experienced what it’s like to be pursued aggressively by a beautiful woman. It’s absolutely exhilarating, maybe even intoxicating to feel so wanted without having to ask.
Zuck is now big tech’s only remaining wife guy
Futurism’s Maggie Harrison Dupré makes her case, now that Jensen’s hidden life as an affair guy has been exposed:

[I]f there’s one tech industry wife guy to rule them all, it has to be Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. The Facebook founder and his wife, Priscilla Chan, met as students at Harvard University. In 2024, to celebrate his love for his wife, Zuckerberg recorded a cover of T-Pain’s “Get Low,” which was apparently playing when they first met. Zuckerberg also built a 7-foot-tall statue of Chan, and implored others to join him in bringing back the “Roman tradition of making statues for your wife.” Chan, meanwhile, has stuck by Zuck through Congressional hearings, lawsuits, local jiu jitsu tournaments, and his blinged out fashion rebrand. They share two children and recently went as “burger night” for Halloween, which we have to admit was fun.
And maybe actions will have consequences again
This post has been updated.
- Big Tech’s ‘Soulless’ Reaction to the Jensen Huang Scandal
- What Happens to All the Jensen Huang Buildings Now?
- Bessent Throws Lutnick Under Nvidia Bus on Live TV

items.title: You don’t have to be mean to get ahead. As it turns out, nice guys can have their cake and eat it too
items.description: I like an orderly queue. But this morning, the staff checking passports and tickets at the gate seemed keen to spice things up by starting a human stampede. Group-five passengers were allowed to shove in front of group-one folk (the injustice!). Seizing the op
items.author: Andrew Tuck; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: I like an orderly queue. But this morning, the staff checking passports and tickets at the gate seemed keen to spice things up by starting a human stampede. Group-five passengers were allowed to shove in front of group-one folk (the injustice!). Seizing the opportunity, a group of older ladies with sharp elbows came out of nowhere in a bid to insert themselves in prime boarding positions. As another one of their troupe started pushing beside me, I edged my suitcase forward a few strategic inches to repel her attack.

“Oh, you’ll let everyone else in but not me,” she responded a little too vocally for comfort. “It’s like we are back in England already,” she said, trying to rally people to her cause. “Are you happy now?” she added like a child robbed of its inheritance by a wicked uncle.
