I assured her that I was, even if I might have begun to perspire just a little. Guess what? We were seat neighbours. Squeezed-in-economy-seat neighbours. Elbows-touching neighbours.

In future, I am going to try and be a little more James Talarico in my dealings with opportunistic queue jumpers. Because, while watching the campaigning and subsequent victory of the Texas senator-elect, I was struck not just by his youthfulness and integrity but the fact that he’s, well, a nice man.

“Nice” is a funny word. Indeed I remember our English-language teachers telling us to avoid its use, to search for richer, more evocative adjectives. “Nice”, we were told, hinted at something mediocre, pleasant but a little bland. I disagree. Nice is calm, enduring, welcoming, a safe haven. And after years of meanness and political egoism run amok, I would argue that nice is having a bit of a moment. Talarico certainly does nice very well; the new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, seems nice; Mark Carney is definitely nice. Let’s see – but I have a feeling that the nice guy might be back.

Recently, on The Urbanist, I interviewed Amanprit Arnold, an activist for deaf people who is campaigning to open Deafcity Hub, London’s first cultural and business centre for her community. I liked talking to her, listening to how she believes that good design can ensure that deaf people are not isolated (echoey restaurants, for example, cause mayhem for people who wear aids, while large computer screens in offices make lipreading impossible).

One of the reasons that her work resonated is because I had an aunt, long gone, who was in a building struck by a Luftwaffe bomb during the Second World War. She survived but, in the years that followed, her hearing increasingly deserted her. At first there were hearing aids that fixed things but, in old age, she struggled. She was surrounded by a wall of silence. And that’s when the dementia struck.

This is why I have long understood the dangers of such isolation and believed that rich friendships, conversation and community are key to defending our cognitive abilities. We are going to pick up this theme in Monocle’s December/January issue, where we meet a man who has researched this very link and found places where dementia is rare. Beyond community, he also believes that you need to eat a vegetable-rich protein diet to keep your brain running smoothly. And avoid processed food.

On Thursday, I had lunch with a woman who I have known all my working life and who was instrumental in helping me find the confidence to be a journalist. She’s unchanged: funny, sharp, editing a new magazine. She told me that she’s reading a recipe book on the very topic of brain health and that, apparently, we need to eat 10 different vegetables a day. It seems a lot, unless you are a pet rabbit. But after our little Scandi lunch, I saw her scanning the now-empty plates. “We might have done 10,” she said rather confidently. It seemed her forensic veg audit included the carrot in the delicious cake that we had devoured.

Being generous to pushy fellow travellers and hitting this new veg target feels like a lot of self-improvement targets to embrace. But I’ll try my best and my new daily rallying call is going to be: “nice guys eat cake”. Who’s with me?
To read more columns by Andrew Tuck, click here.

items.title: Are we entering a new golden age of car design?
items.description: For the better part of a decade, cookie-cutter, identikit design and Chinese copycats have made the automotive market particularly bland. But in the past couple of weeks, off the back of major industry fairs such as the Mondial de l’Auto – or Paris Motor Show
items.author: Adam Workman; Chloe Lake
paragraphs: For the better part of a decade, cookie-cutter, identikit design and Chinese copycats have made the automotive market particularly bland. But in the past couple of weeks, off the back of major industry fairs such as the Mondial de l’Auto – or Paris Motor Show – has brought forth a glut of inspiring new designs. Are we entering a brave new era for automotive eye candy? The evidence suggests so.

Tesla grabbed headlines with its new Roadster that can (almost) fly – capable of performing short hops, leaps and mid-air manoeuvres. Whatever you think about the electric-carmaker’s enfant terrible in chief, Elon Musk, he’s rather good at a few things: namely putting on a show and turning out remarkable, narrative-shifting motors. The long-mooted Roadster’s space-age, wedge-like form variously brings to mind 1970s icons such as the Lamborghini Miura by Italian coachbuilder Bertone and the submersible Lotus Esprit piloted by James Bond in The Spy Who Loved Me. Almost 20 years on from its original pocket-rocket Roadster, it appears that Tesla has set another benchmark.

On the opposite shores of the Atlantic, the French have been hard at work bringing the nation’s trademark brand of idiosyncratic design back to life by drawing inspiration from decades past. Admittedly, two of the best examples, under the Renault umbrella, are in concept-car form. The new Alpine 310 Vision reanimates the original 310, an American muscle car-adjacent thing of brutalist beauty from 1971 and the last model conceived by the brand’s founder, Jean Rédélé. The result is a blueprint for how an electric car should look in Q2 of the 21st century. The Renault 8 Gordini Concept, meanwhile, is an electric two-seater that builds upon the 1964 model of the same name and continues a rich seam of aesthetically rear-gazing, technologically future-facing work.

Perhaps the most promising, however, is Citroën’s 2CV reboot, which drags the Gallic classic from 1948 into the modern day with an electric version. Yes, it looks like a Tonka toy model of what is arguably France’s greatest ever motoring export but the starting price is mooted to be similarly junior. At €15,000, it could be about to break the mould for electric-car pricing and usher in a new era of mass consumption for all – à la sea change created by its forebear.

Not to be outdone by its neighbour, the Italians also have some sleek new additions to the global garage. Alfa Romeo’s sumptuous Cuorerosso (for once, the English translation – Red Heart – doesn’t entirely ruin the mystique; we’re looking at you, Maserati Four-Door…sorry, Quattroporte). The sleek four-seater coupé is, again, only at concept stage for now but in terms of embodying Alfa Romeo’s design philosophy of bellezza necessaria (necessary beauty), it fulfils the brief and then some.

An honourable mention also goes to the Porsche Mission S, which injects charisma into the Stuttgart maker’s overarching visual language. And Jaguar’s mad, mega-bonneted Type 01 has been in the public domain for a while but it was only properly launched this month, warranting a hat tip. Nobody would argue that it looks like anything else, meaning that it’s a design that we’ll likely still be talking about in 50 years.

It has been almost a running joke that people who care little about automotive design can only differentiate cars by colour. But until now, the idea that tones had become the only identifying factors in a scene dominated by dull designs wasn’t that far off the mark. Thank goodness, then, that you will be needing more than a Pantone swatch to get to grips with the latest generation of automotive innovations as the industry forges ahead into 2027.

items.title: Who will be the next UN secretary-general? Ecuador’s María Fernanda Espinosa makes her case
items.description: Seven candidates are vying to become the next UN secretary-general at a time when the organisation appears to be in great peril. Trust is haemorrhaging among member states and the general public, and multilateralism is in retreat. The job of whoever succeeds t
items.author: Charlotte McDonald-Gibson; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Seven candidates are vying to become the next UN secretary-general at a time when the organisation appears to be in great peril. Trust is haemorrhaging among member states and the general public, and multilateralism is in retreat. The job of whoever succeeds the outgoing António Guterres, whose term ends in December, will be nothing less than to overhaul the entire institution.

Guterres is stepping down after a tenure that has seen huge global upheaval, including the coronavirus pandemic, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Hamas’s 7 October attack and the ensuing war in Gaza, and the re-election of Donald Trump. Though viewed as a competent administrator, he has lacked the global profile of predecessors such as Kofi Annan and Ban Ki-moon, and has chosen a low-key approach at odds with seismic geopolitical events.

The candidates to replace him must strike a delicate balance. Though US scepticism about the size, budget and role of the UN means that the new secretary-general will need to signal a willingness to change, too much reforming zeal will not be popular with the five permanent members (P5) of the Security Council – the UK, US, France, Russia and China – that jealously guard their veto power. To be elected, candidates take part in a series of straw polls, in which the P5 and the 10 non-permanent Security Council members cast ballots encouraging, discouraging or giving no opinion on the candidates. Once one of them has the support of at least nine Security Council members and no veto from a P5 member, they go to a full vote at the 193-member General Assembly, which traditionally backs the recommendation.

Conventional wisdom holds that a candidate from Latin America should prevail, given that just one of the previous nine secretaries-general, Javier Pérez de Cuéllar, has come from the region. There’s also a feeling that it’s time for a woman to take the helm. María Fernanda Espinosa, a former Ecuadorean defence minister and a former president of the UN General Assembly, is one of the four female aspirants. Monocle sat down with Espinosa to find out about her plans for the body.
What do people want from the next UN secretary-general?

As a citizen, you want to see the secretary-general up there sitting at the table – sometimes leading but sometimes supporting too. We have seen that this is perfectly doable. All of this will be possible with a renewed, strong leadership. It’s really an advantage to know the system well but not be captured by it.

I have full respect for the main asset of the organisation, which is the very committed, high-quality staff that it has. But you cannot continue to operate under 40,000 mandates [Since 1946, more than 40,000 resolutions, decisions and presidential statements have been adopted across key UN bodies] in times when, frankly, the UN will be getting not more money but less.
What differentiates you from other candidates?

I have touched on all of the spaces and places where the UN operates. I have seen it from the perspective of a high-level government official and also been on the receiving end, negotiating national co-operation frameworks with UN teams at the country level. But I have never worked for the UN so my impulse is not to preserve the status quo. It’s to change it. I was responsible for reforming the armed forces of my country. I had to make very structural, profound changes and wasn’t afraid to do so. I received the highest decoration that the Ecuadorian armed forces provide to a non-military person. I understood that it was best for them to modernise, to change the institutional culture.
Is multilateralism really in retreat?

If you look around, everybody wants more international co-operation. It’s inevitable: we are living in times of radical interdependence. We learnt that the hard way during the coronavirus pandemic and are learning it again with the Strait of Hormuz situation. It’s impossible to say that we are on our own. The national interest is connected to our common interest and everybody understands that, at some point, we need to co-operate with each other.
How important will receiving the backing of the US be for the next secretary-general?

Persuading the US to support – and not veto – your candidacy is not just a formality. I see America as a critical partner for the future of the UN. The US is a founding member. The country has contributed the most to the UN financially. It is responsible for 20 per cent of the overall budget and more than 20 per cent of the peacekeeping operations. So it’s not only about the US being the funder of the UN. It was there at the origins of the organisation and plays a very crucial role in the three pillars of peace and security, development and human rights. So it’s symbolically, financially and politically vital to have the trust and the backing of the US.
How would you rebuild trust among citizens?

It’s true that sometimes people don’t trust what the UN is doing or what its leaders are discussing or agreeing to. That is a response to a very divided, polarised world. When I say that I will be a leader who rebuilds trust, I understand that it isn’t just something that’s declared in a memo. You have to earn it. And I think that people will trust a leadership or a leader that is seen as impartial, as not having any alignments, as faithful to the UN Charter and to international law. A person who everybody can believe in is predictable. They abide by the rules and treat everyone equally. That is very important, especially in the present times.
Why do you want to be UN secretary-general at a time like this, when the organisation is facing huge challenges?

I have something to contribute when it comes to making the organisation better and more effective. I believe that the UN has a lot more to give and has a responsibility to modernise and to revitalise itself. And this is not done by magic. It is done by putting in some hard work and by having a deep knowledge of the organisation without being captured by it. My experience of it has been more from the member-state side, from the government side. So I know what the UN can do, the frustrations that it can create, and I understand very well what the role of the secretary-general should be. I’m a reformist. I like a challenge and think I can do it.
The other runners and riders
Rebeca Grynspan, Costa Rica

Taking special leave from her role as secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, economist Rebeca Grynspan emerged as an early frontrunner. The vice-president of Costa Rica from 1994 to 1998, Grynspan moved into UN roles and has held senior positions in trade and development. This gives her an insider perspective – her vision statement promises to make the world body “more useful, more agile and more accountable to the governments and people it serves”. With a strong track record in multilateralism, she’s seen as a safe establishment candidate and has the backing of senior figures.
Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Guyana

Guyana’s current permanent representative to the UN and its former minister of foreign affairs, Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett has extensive experience in government and a deep understanding of the UN’s workings. She has also impressed in debates with UN staff and civil-society representatives. Though she has a relatively low international profile, this could work in her favour, because world powers are not looking for a big personality but rather a competent administrator and quiet reformer.

Once a leading contender, Rafael Grossi might have hurt his chances by not taking a leave of absence from his role as director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency while campaigning. With Iran’s nuclear programme in the headlines, he has been busy with global diplomacy, which might have affected his ability to travel and lobby for the UN position. But he has been at the heart of some of the most pressing issues today and, should there be a breakthrough with Iran, he could claim some credit. But Grossi was nominated by Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, whose recent sabre-rattling about the Falkland Islands could make the veto-wielding UK apprehensive.
The high-profile candidate

The president of Senegal from 2012 to 2024 and a former chair of the African Union (AU), Macky Sall is well versed in international diplomacy. Devolving some of the UN’s mandates to regional bodies such as the AU could be part of the streamlining process that many nations are demanding, so his experience will be an advantage. However, Sall’s vision might be at odds with those of some of the permanent Security Council members: he has called the body “the last vestige of a bygone world order”. While reforming the Security Council is a popular sentiment among the UN’s 193 member states, the prospect of a major overhaul is less welcome among the five permanent members, who prize their veto power.

A veteran of Ugandan politics who served as UN under-secretary-general for Kofi Annan, 76-year-old Olara Otunnu strikes a good balance between governmental and institutional experience. His candidacy has gained traction between the first few rounds of polling. He served as Uganda’s foreign affairs minister and its permanent representative to the UN, and is a respected diplomat with a good contacts book. He has campaigned on a promise of focusing on multilateral regulation of AI. If he can leverage panicked headlines about the technology into actionable talking points among the Security Council members, that could give his campaign added traction. But he could be foiled by his nominating government, which has faced criticism from UN bodies over its record on human and LGBT+ rights.

Another Ecuadorian candidate, Ivonne A-Baki also has Lebanese heritage and served as her country’s ambassador to the US, France and Qatar. She claims close ties to Donald Trump, a relationship that she traces back to 2004, when she helped him bring Miss Universe to Ecuador. Being a Trump whisperer could be useful, given his withdrawal of the US from 31 UN entities and his threats to the body’s funding. But touting a special relationship with any one government is a risky strategy – Russia and China also have veto powers and will not want to hand the role to anyone tied to a rival. A-Baki’s candidacy is also viewed as an anomaly because she was not nominated by her home country but by tiny Polynesian nation Tonga – and she has not performed well in straw polls so far.

The opening of Frieze London is casting the world’s art market in a positive light – and catching the eye of eager buyers.
Forget the usual business books. If you really want to get ahead, take some advice from Cruella de Vil, Tom Ripley and other entrepreneurial characters from the world of fiction.
Part workspace, part residence, the communal facility by Jan Garde and Henning Weiss is bringing people in all stages of life together in style.
This month’s highlights include an irreverent novel about contemporary art, an exhibition of one of today’s most exciting fashion photographers and a Tom Cruise disaster movie.
To help you pick the right books for your summer reading list, we asked an array of cultural figures to share the titles old and new that have inspired them.
The preview week of the world’s most prestigious exhibition of contemporary art was an unruly spectacle – charged by political dissent, moments of beauty and works shining brightly through the chaos.
In recent years the art world’s largest commercial fair has painted itself into a corner. But satellite shows and new initiatives at this year’s event are helping to offer fresh perspectives.
The world’s biggest space dedicated to illustration has opened in London. Can it help to protect the art amid rising threats from AI?
There’s more to collecting than following markets and speculating on value appreciation. We meet the people at the heart of the action, from a veteran auctioneer to a design-fair director.

items.title: Kate Middleton Announces First Major Trip Since Her Cancer Diagnosis
items.description: In unexpected news, Kensington Palace has just announced that Kate Middleton will accompany Prince William on his upcoming three-day official visit to Mumbai, India. The trip, which commences on Monday, will mark their first joint tour outside the United Kingd
items.author: Diego Parrado
paragraphs: In unexpected news, Kensington Palace has just announced that Kate Middleton will accompany Prince William on his upcoming three-day official visit to Mumbai, India. The trip, which commences on Monday, will mark their first joint tour outside the United Kingdom in the past four years and represents a new milestone in Kate Middleton’s gradual return to public duties since she was diagnosed with cancer in early 2024 and began scaling back her official engagements.

Last May, the princess made a brief solo trip to Italy to learn about early childhood development, but this trip to India (a nine-hour flight from London) represents her first long-distance journey and her highest-profile diplomatic engagement since the Caribbean tour she undertook in 2022 and the Earthshot Awards gala she attended in Boston that same year.

"So proud, I'm very, very proud. She's been amazing. She's been through so much in the last couple of years, particularly," William shared on UK radio show Heart Breakfast in May, pleased to see that Kate was “gradually resuming” her travels. Still, the heir to the throne wanted to be cautious and warned that these visits are very taxing. "Away trips like that take a lot out of you," he explained. "So we have to balance that, make sure she's, she's OK and rested, but she's in good form."

The reason for the visit is the sixth edition of the Earthshot Prize, an initiative spearheaded by the heir to the British throne that each year awards one million pounds (about $1,323,249) to five innovative environmental projects and which, after making stops in other cities abroad such as Singapore, Cape Town, and Rio de Janeiro, is now taking place in the country that has produced the most finalists and winners in the competition’s history.

Standout finalists this year include Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, for its fleet of electric motorcycle taxis designed to reduce urban pollution, and Mahila Housing Trust, which installs reflective roofs capable of lowering the temperature inside homes by up to five degrees during extreme heat. The awards ceremony will be held this Tuesday evening at the Jio World Centre in Mumbai and will feature a performance by the band Take That and be attended by celebrities such as actor Rami Malek.

Hours before the main event, the Prince and Princess of Wales will also preside over the first edition of the Earthshot Children’s Awards, a competition in which 15,000 schools from 24 Indian states have participated with environmental proposals designed by young people aged 9 to 17. The itinerary also includes a solo appearance by Kate Middleton, meetings with the Bollywood film industry, cricket-related celebrations, and a possible meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

In addition to being a positive sign regarding the princess’s health, this return to India holds strong symbolic significance for the couple, who last visited the country in April 2016. On that occasion, the then-Duke and Duchess of Cambridge visited the Taj Mahal and posed on the same white marble bench where Princess Diana was photographed alone in 1992—an image that has gone down in history as a reflection of the breakdown of her marriage to the now-King Charles III.
Originally published by Vanity Fair Spain

items.title: Zara Tindall Shows Cheltenham Why She's The Queen of Race Day Dressing
items.description: Zara Tindall didn’t let the cold snap stop her from enjoying a day at the races on Friday. Accompanied by her close friend Dolly Maude and country-set favorite fashion designer Jade Holland Cooper, the daughter of Princess Anne and granddaughter of Queen Eliza
items.author: Ben Jureidini
paragraphs: Zara Tindall didn’t let the cold snap stop her from enjoying a day at the races on Friday. Accompanied by her close friend Dolly Maude and country-set favorite fashion designer Jade Holland Cooper, the daughter of Princess Anne and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II brought a dash of regal glamour to the proceedings following a glitzy night out in support of Prince William.

And while the sun may have been out, the Olympic equestrian still needed to wrap up against the chill. Tindall opted for a long plaid coat from L'Agence, a Purdey roll-neck jumper in brown, and a fascinator from Sally-Ann Provan. She accessorized with a new pair of Hector Lion earrings, a new Fairfax & Favor handbag, and completed the look with leather boots, also from Fairfax & Favor.
Dolly, on the other hand, wore an avant-garde feather coat with knee-high boots and what looked to be a pair of emerald tights.

The pair were last spotted together in October, when they attended the William Hill Showcase Meeting at Cheltenham, but their friendship goes way back. Long considered Zara’s best friend, Dolly became Princess Anne’s lady-in-waiting in 2024. A former NHS midwife, she helped to deliver Zara’s third child, Lucas Tindall, on the floor of Zara’s bathroom at Gatcombe Park after the plan for the birth went awry in 2021.

But Dolly’s bond with the niece of King Charles III goes back long before that. (Not for nothing did Zara’s husband, Mike Tindall, joke that the 53-year-old is “more important than I am.”) Dolly was Zara’s maid of honor when the pair tied the knot, and when Zara split from her then-fiancé, jockey Richard Johnson, in 2003, the pair moved in together—they still live close by in the Cotswolds.

Having worked as a maternity practitioner in the NHS in Gloucestershire for 13 years, Dolly also did some philanthropic work using her maternity expertise, working in the unit of a hospital in Kambia, Sierra Leone for a month in 2013. At Kambia, she taught staff basic nursing skills. Before qualifying as a nurse, Dolly studied fashion and Cordon Bleu cookery at Eastbourne College of Food and Fashion, graduating in 1989.

Dolly Maude is known for her love of horses—a passion she shares with Zara and Princess Anne—and is often seen in Ascot’s royal box alongside the Princess Royal. In March 2024, she made her first official appearance as the Princess Royal’s lady-in-waiting, a momentous occasion that marked a new phase of her enduring bond with the royal family.
The royal confidant has four children with her husband Chris: Billy, who studied at Swansea University; Nell, who trained at the Central School of Ballet; a keen skier, Ted; and Mary.

Concerning Dolly’s appointment, another friend of Mrs. Maude's told The Telegraph, “She’s such a great girl. For the Princess Royal, it’s a perfect fit because of their shared love of dogs and horses. She’s not only extremely close to Zara, she also gets on brilliantly with the Princess. She’s fiercely loyal and discreet. It’s a great match.”

While much of Zara Tindall’s time this season has been spent touring the country’s most prestigious racing meets, she still found time to support her cousin, Prince William, at one of his treasured annual traditions. The Prince of Wales helped to put together the Tusk Conservation Awards at Raffles on Wednesday night and invited Zara to the celebration of conservation, alongside Lady Amelia and Lady Eliza Spencer and the Marchioness of Bath.

Zara showcased her characteristically elegant style, donning a sapphire-blue Rebecca Vallance short-sleeved midi number, aptly named the “Crown Jewel” dress, which she paired with Kiki McDonough earrings. It is not the first time that the royal has lent her support to Prince William’s second-longest patronage: she also joined the crowd at the Tusk Awards in 2025, donning Rebecca Vallance again, and tearing up at the Prince of Wales’ speech in honor of those who gave their lives as rangers.
Originally published in Tatler

items.title: Avril Lavigne Welcomes Her First Child At Age 42
items.description: Avril Lavigne is now a mom. The 42-year-old Canadian might count songs like "Here's to Never Growing Up" among her hits, but in news posted to Instagram Friday, Avril Lavigne revealed a very grown-up milestone.
items.author: Alessandra De Tommasi
paragraphs: Avril Lavigne is now a mom. The 42-year-old Canadian might count songs like "Here's to Never Growing Up" among her hits, but in news posted to Instagram Friday, Avril Lavigne revealed a very grown-up milestone.

Beneath a carousel of three black-and-white photos, Lavigne wrote “Our Mini Fucking Princess has arrived,” followed by emojis depicting a baby bottle, a crown, and a pink heart and bow. One photo shows Lavigne cradling an infant dressed in an animal-print onesie and matching headband, while another shows three pairs of Vans on a skateboard. No other details, including information on the baby's name or if Lavigne has a co-parent, were provided.
A spokesperson for the singer told People that “Avril has been enjoying time with her family while working on her new album and wants to thank the fans for all of their love!”

Lavigne has been married twice: once to Canadian guitarist Deryck Whibley and then to Chad Kroeger, the Canadian frontman of the band Nickelback. That latter partnership ended in 2018, but in 2022 she almost tied the knot a third time, with rapper Mod Sun. That relationship ended in 2023.

One constant in Lavigne's life has been strong bond she shares with her parents. When, in May 2025, she brought her mother on stage at Madison Square Garden, she wrote on social media: “Ever since I was a little girl, both my mom and dad saw something in me and encouraged me to practice very hard and pursue my dream of becoming a singer/ musician. They made a lot of sacrifices for me and I could not be where I am today without them.”
Continuing, she wrote, “I am grateful to both my parents. Thank you for everything, I love you both!”

Lavigne was still a teenager when her parents allowed her to leave high school to pursue her dream, and her debut at age 17 was a smash hit. Her success continued with singles including 2002's chart-topper “Complicated" and 2021 song “Bite Me.”

Though Friday's announcement was a surprise to most, Lavigne has never been quiet about her desire to become a mom when the time is right. Speaking with E! News in 2013, she laid out her plan: "I want one or two [kids], but not right now," the then-29-year old said. "Like, in the future. Eventually."
Originally published by Vanity Fair Italy

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Potentially Seismic Art Retreat
items.description: Welcome to True Colors. I’m in Manhattan. Lots to get into this week. There’s the matter of what to do about a major new San Francisco arts institution that was set to be named after Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang. Understandably, it’s a question whethe
items.author: Nate Freeman
paragraphs: Welcome to True Colors. I’m in Manhattan. Lots to get into this week. There’s the matter of what to do about a major new San Francisco arts institution that was set to be named after Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang. Understandably, it’s a question whether that renaming will still happen given…everything. There’s my ode to the death of the Cybertruck. And there’s all the details from the star-studded MoMA Film Benefit honoring Steven Spielberg. Tom Cruise shocked the crowd with surprise remarks, and Bruce Springsteen roasted the director. It was a whole night.

MENTIONED IN THIS ISSUE: Donald Trump, Jason Calacanis, Brendan Dugan, Siniša Mačković, David Zwirner, Lorenzo Amos, Kate Capshaw, Zohran Mamdani, Jessica Craig-Martin, Dean & DeLuca, Indochine, Stanley Whitney, Marina Adams, Will Whitney, The Beverly Hills Hotel, Elon Musk, Lana Del Rey, Grimes, Travis Scott, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, Tyler, the Creator, Bad Bunny, Julia Wachtel, Todd von Ammon, Frieda Toranzo Jaeger.
The major arts institution named for Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, appears to be—shocker!—very much in jeopardy.

Just months ago, Huang was getting a phone call from President Trump while onstage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles. “I’m here with the besties, Mr. President,” a laughing Huang said, putting his phone up to the mic. “Tell him I say hi!” said All-In cohost Jason Calacanis.

But Huang’s recent weeks have not been marked by good times with the besties. First, the Democrats took over Congress, throttling all the goodwill he built with the administration. Then he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by the US to be a Chinese spy—and then news of another affair, this time allegedly with a subordinate, came via a shocking New York Times bombshell. Amid rumors that yet another affair would soon break, he stepped down as CEO and, according to Forbes, has watched nearly $20 billion of his estimated net worth vaporize since Monday.

What’s unknown is the current state of his relationship with his wife, Lori Huang—and their ambitious plans for an arts organization that was set to bear their name. Earlier this year, the Huangs pledged $75 million to Vanderbilt University in order to help transform the soon-to-be-closed legendary San Francisco art school California College of the Arts into part of Vanderbilt’s SF campus. Vanderbilt announced that it planned to name a portion of its SF campus the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design.

Which is now a bit awkward, given the multiple alleged affairs, and the whole Chinese-spy thing. Plus, Huang is no longer affiliated with Nvidia, which teamed up with CCA in 2025 to form the CCA-Nvidia Incubator for Creative Intelligence. Will Jensen and Lori Huang still put their names together on arts organizations after all that’s happened? And if there is no Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design, what will happen to Vanderbilt’s SF campus when it opens next year?
The CCA was started in 1907, and Huang and his wife were expected to support its transition to a new chapter. It would be a shame if this is how it ends. Reps at Vanderbilt didn’t get back to me.

It’s a new era in Tribeca. Tonight, Karma, a burgeoning mega-gallery with spaces in New York’s Chelsea and LA’s Hollywood, opens its new gallery at 38 White Street. Founder Brendan Dugan and director Siniša Mačković took me on a tour earlier this week, and it’s easily one of the most generous spaces anywhere in the neighborhood. Plus, an outpost of Karma Bookstore—a much needed bookstore for a neighborhood shockingly lacking in one—is coming in right across the street.

This will be the latest big-tent blue chipper to take a space in the Triangle Below Canal, as they used to call this neighborhood. Something to consider: In the last few years, mega-galleries such as David Zwirner and Hauser & Wirth have shut their uptown townhouses and opened downtown.

Also opening tonight is a White Street outpost of Gratin gallery, which has a roster of incredibly exciting young stars, including Lorenzo Amos (whom we wrote about a year ago). I’m hearing about other younger dealers grabbing spaces in the neighborhood. The art market isn’t exactly on fire, but dealers are betting on one thing: the enduring power and capital of New York City.

Speaking of New York, guess who’s lived here full-time for almost a year? Steven Spielberg, that’s who. On New Year’s Day 2026, the GOAT American director—who is married to the artist Kate Capshaw—moved his official residence from California to New York, and has made the apartment in the San Remo his home base. You will not be surprised to hear that, post-move, Spielberg is doing extremely cool stuff in town. He’s walking around with a script and a Tracy Kidder book while slugging down an iced McCafé. He’s getting lunch at Benvenuto Cafe. He’s having Mayor Zohran Mamdani over to the crib.

The only thing left was for one of the city’s great museums to throw a big party for the Hollywood-royalty-gone-Gotham. Last night, Spielberg got just that: He was honored at the MoMA Film Benefit, sponsored by Chanel. I was there. Read the full report—with fun pictures!—here.

Also on VF this week: an exclusive excerpt from an uproarious new memoir by artist Jessica Craig-Martin, I Regret I am Able to Attend. Craig-Martin is a real treasure of the art world, a great photographer—and, as it turns out, a hell of a writer. The whole book is a compulsively readable blast. The chapter where Craig-Martin recalls working as an extremely inexperienced, occasionally larcenous teller at Dean & DeLuca is one of the funniest, most satisfying New York vignettes I’ve read this year. And of course, all the scuttlebutt from the ’80s art scene is fabulous. Read the excerpt, in which our narrator spills all the tea—and, um, stuff stronger than tea—about working as a waitress when Indochine opened.

Happy 80th birthday to the great painter Stanley Whitney. His wife, the artist Marina Adams, and son, dealer Will Whitney, threw Stanley a party to celebrate his octogenarian status on Nine Orchard’s roof, overlooking Dimes Square. Writers, artists, dealers, old heads, everyone was there. A fabulous Wednesday night.

items.title: Paapa Essiedu, Harry Potter’s New Snape, Is Ready for Questions
items.description: When Paapa Essiedu was just 25 years old, he was cast as Hamlet by the Royal Shakespeare Company. In an instant, he joined the ranks of all-time greats like Ben Kingsley, Kenneth Branagh, and Mark Rylance. “I still remember the day that my agent rang me up and
items.author: Chris Murphy; William Waterworth
paragraphs: When Paapa Essiedu was just 25 years old, he was cast as Hamlet by the Royal Shakespeare Company. In an instant, he joined the ranks of all-time greats like Ben Kingsley, Kenneth Branagh, and Mark Rylance. “I still remember the day that my agent rang me up and told me I’d got that job,” he says 11 years later. “I was gassed about it for about three seconds. And then I was like, ‘Fuck, what have I done?’”

Critics loved Essiedu as the Danish prince. “It was good,” he says casually of his star-making performance. Yet his casting provoked headlines for another reason: He was the first Black actor to play Hamlet at the RSC. “There was this—not even fascination—this obsession with the fact that I was a Black person who was doing it,” he recalls.

The Olivier-winning, Emmy-nominated performer now views that stint as a dry run for the most high-profile role of his career: potions professor Severus Snape in HBO’s highly anticipated and deeply polarizing Harry Potter television series. “I kind of draw a small pathway in comparison to the freeway that I’m on now,” he says.

There is likely not a soul alive who isn’t familiar with J.K. Rowling’s multibillion-dollar franchise about a boy wizard. After seven primary books, a variety of secondary volumes, eight feature films, multiple spin-offs, a Broadway play, and rides and shops at six Universal theme parks worldwide, Harry Potter arguably has name recognition rivaling that of Hamlet, or Jesus. Though “don’t let my auntie hear you comparing Harry Potter to the Bible,” says Essiedu. “Trust me, she can shut down the whole of Vanity Fair like that.” He flicks his wrist. “On the record, I’m not agreeing with this here, just in case.”

Essiedu was raised in the east London neighborhood of Walthamstow by his mother, who never imagined her son might have a career as a professional actor. “Single Ghanaian woman parent?” he says. “It was not on the top-five list of jobs that were made available.” His father, who lived back in Ghana with Essiedu’s half-siblings, died when Essiedu was 14. “He was there, but he wasn’t there,” Essiedu says.

The 36-year-old describes his childhood as “fully millennial”: “Slap-bang in the middle, pre-internet, pre-fucking-Netflix, on-demand television, just barely dealing with Game Boy Colors. Life was analog,” he says. But while many his age are predisposed to wax poetic about life in the ’90s, Essiedu doesn’t see it with entirely rose-colored glasses. “In many ways, it was fucking boring,” he says with a laugh. “There was a lot of just staring out the window and hoping some shit was going to happen.”

Reading became “something that was quite crucial to stop me from eating my own hands,” he says—including the Harry Potter books, which “were coming out regularly at the precise time that I was starting to develop my taste for literature…. The world that was created was so full. Can you imagine, like, 12-year-old boys, 13-year-old boys reading 600-page books, 700-page books about wizards? We’re meant to be out here in the streets playing football, basketball, whatever. I’m like, ‘I’m going home. I’m reading the book. I’m inside.’”

When he was 18, Essiedu joined the National Youth Theatre—a selective performing arts training center in London where actors like Daniel Day-Lewis, Helen Mirren, and Daniel Craig honed their craft. Essiedu auditioned for a distinctly teenage reason: “Let’s just say there was someone that I wanted to be around who was also going to National Youth Theatre,” he says cheekily. After getting accepted, Essiedu raised the money he needed to attend, going around his school asking friends and acquaintances for donations. The crush might not have lasted—“let’s say the person who I was supposedly following disappeared”—but a lifelong passion for performing developed.

“I found myself just in this room surrounded by people who were talking about Shakespeare and talking about Harold Pinter and Jez Butterworth,” he says. “By luck, really, I found myself in a room that gave me the idea to basically burn down all of my mother’s ambitions for myself and go in a different direction. Arguably, it turned out okay.”

After his star turn as Hamlet, Essiedu got an Emmy nomination for his supporting role in Michaela Coel’s I May Destroy You. He wasn’t surprised when the show made a recent New York Times list of 100 best TV shows of the 21st century: “Of course it was on that list,” he says. “I think it was a phenomenally singular and confident and brave and unprecedented piece of work.”

Then Francesca Gardiner and Mark Mylod—a pair of Emmy-winning Succession alums—reached out to let him know they were interested in him for the new Harry Potter. Snape was the only part he wanted, though the role was a bit of a reality check: “They’re considering me for a teacher. That means I’m fucking old now. When you’re a kid, teachers don’t even have ages. They’re just old.”

Essiedu put his pride aside and met with Gardiner and Mylod. Much to his surprise, after a two-hour chat about the show, Essiedu found out he had the part. “Professor Snape requires an extraordinary actor,” Gardiner tells VF via email. “He has to be intimidating, dangerous, sometimes very funny, but there’s also an enormous amount that he’s concealing. You need someone who can make you feel that there’s a whole other story unfolding beneath the one you’re watching. Someone who can convey depth and complexity without necessarily saying a word. Someone with real intensity. Paapa is one of those rare actors who can do all of that.”

Acting stalwart John Lithgow stars opposite Essiedu as Hogwarts headmaster Albus Dumbledore. Over the phone, the veteran says he’s never acted with anyone quite like Essiedu. “He is so focused and intense, and yet there’s an ease to his acting,” says Lithgow. “He just has a great sense of how mysterious he is, which is what makes him so compelling as Snape in Harry Potter.”
“We simply needed one of the greatest actors in Britain to do it justice,” agrees Mylod, also via email. Essiedu “has extraordinary range, and I always, always believe him.”

In April 2025, HBO announced that Essiedu had won the role of Snape—played with an inimitable snarl in the film franchise by the late great Alan Rickman. Essiedu read the books to prepare, but opted not to watch the movies. “To be honest, I never watched the movies when I was younger,” he says. “I still don’t think I really know what happens in Deathly Hallows because I read it so quickly that it didn’t really seep in. I was like, ‘This shit is complicated as hell, man. Dumbledore’s dead? What the fuck?’”

But even if he only has passing familiarity with Rickman’s take on the character, Essiedu says he’s not focused on trying to reinvent Snape or make people forget about his predecessor’s work. “The guy is an icon. He’s a legend,” Essiedu says of Rickman. “Anyone who’s ever met Alan or spoken to him or been friends with him have all reached out to me and spoken about what Alan would’ve thought about my casting. There’s so much goodwill, and I really feel him with me.”

The public’s reaction was decidedly more complex. After Essiedu’s casting was announced, the internet erupted, with certain corners deeply upset that a Black man was stepping into the role. In March, Essiedu told The Times of London that he’d received death threats from so-called Harry Potter fans: “Quit or I’ll murder you,” one said.

Essiedu doesn’t have a problem with good-faith criticism. “There’s some people who are just like, ‘I’ve done my research, and I know what kind of actor you are, and you suck.’ And they’re totally entitled to their opinion,” he says. “Then there are the people who are like, ‘You are bad because you are Black’—which, to me, is racist.” He stops to reconsider his words for a moment. “Well, actually not ‘You’re bad because you are Black.’ But there is a racially driven animosity.”

In the final weeks before the series premiere, though, Essiedu is most concerned with a third group, one he has real empathy for. “There are people who have got such a tight and deeply felt connection to something that they believe is theirs, and it feels like somebody is trying to take their thing and break their thing,” he says. Essiedu has a message for that cohort: “I know that’s not what I’m trying to do. I’m not trying to break anybody’s nothing. After this, we’re not going to burn the books. We’re not going to remove the DVDs of the films. It’s not the end of that. That all still exists.”
And Essiedu is quick to point out that the vitriol hasn’t been universal: “I got a lot of love as well,” he says. “That really fuels me as much as the hate.”

He’s also aware that he could avoid much of the bad stuff by staying offline—if only it were that easy. “You’ve got your DMs, and then there’s the bit where it says ‘request’ or ‘hidden,’” he says. “You know you shouldn’t go in there. You know you don’t need to scratch that itch. But you can’t stop yourself from doing it. You want to know what the face of the monster looks like.”

Essiedu’s showrunner, at least, has his back. “It’s appalling that anyone should be subjected to that kind of abuse in any circumstances,” writes Gardiner. “He has handled it with incredible grace, and I have nothing but the greatest respect for him…. Paapa has absolutely nailed the role, and it is that performance that deserves our attention.”

Although I've been sworn to secrecy, it seems to me that the only major difference between the Harry Potter from yore and the new series is Essiedu’s casting. Though the plot unfolds more slowly—the show has approximately eight hours to fill, after all, rather than two—the world of the series looks more or less the same as the one in the original films, from Hogwarts to Diagon Alley to the Dursleys’ house. Dominic McLaughlin, Arabella Stanton, and Alastair Stout, who play Harry, Hermione, and Ron, respectively, bear a striking resemblance to their forebears, Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson, and Rupert Grint—particularly McLaughlin. In this milieu, Essiedu’s dreadlocked Snape stands out—which has potentially given the trolls more ammo.

Essiedu says he’s “very clear-minded in my head about what I want to do and what I’m trying to achieve, and the potential of it.” Having more time to tell the story means “hopefully I get the opportunity to pull the contradictions and the unexpected masks of Severus so that eventually we get a human being that is fully fleshed [out] and living and breathing. That was my ambition, and is my ambition. And you can judge me sometime—in 2039 or whatever it is—as to whether it’s been successful or not.”

There’s another reason one might have some trepidation about joining the staff of Hogwarts at this particular moment. In the past decade, J.K. Rowling—the mastermind behind Harry Potter—has descended into what her critics characterize as anti-transgender activism, using her apparently endless supply of cash to support gender-essentialist policies in the UK. While Rowling is adamant that she is not anti-trans, some, like The Matrix director Lilly Wachowski, have said that anyone who supports the Harry Potter franchise is “supporting trans genocide.”

Shortly after he was cast in the series, Essiedu signed an open letter in support of the transgender, nonbinary, and intersex community. Rowling then made a post on X saying that she does not have the power to fire him from the show—but wouldn’t even if she could.

“I have been super clear about my position on this topic, and that is the reason why she spoke out about me,” says Essiedu. “I’m really keen not to make a kind of ‘them and us’ dynamic here. I’m not really here to speak about Jo’s politics or to be a mouthpiece for her. I can only be really, really clear about what I believe and be consistent with that.”

So, what does he believe? After a bit of equivocating (“I don’t want to talk about Jo at all,” he repeats), Essiedu says the following with his chest: “I believe, in my bones, that trans people, queer people, people of all creeds and color have got the right to be treated with respect and dignity and safety at all times—whether they’re in the workplace, whether they’re at home or in the street, whatever. That’s what I believe, and that’s the way that I choose to live my life. That’s the creed by which I live.”

Perhaps that statement presents an inherent contradiction. Rowling is actively involved with the new series and will generate income from it that she could then use to fund her pet causes. But Essiedu believes Rowling’s books—rather than her politics—prove why it’s important to tell Harry’s story again for a new generation.

“When I come back to this story—this actual story—I’m thinking about the themes that it explores,” he says. “Themes of forgiveness, and good triumphing over evil, and of accepting people for who they are and allowing people to really be themselves within a world where anything is possible. I feel like there is something at the center of the story that we own, at least as much as anybody else, that still has the potential to do really, really, really beautiful things.”
