items.title: Slayer's Tom Araya Pauses Concert to Reprimand Unruly Fans: 'Maintain Yourself'
items.description: Slayer’s concert Saturday at Los Angeles’ Kia Forum was paused mid-show so singer Tom Araya could reprimand some unruly fans in the crowd.
items.author: Daniel Kreps
paragraphs: Slayer’s concert Saturday at Los Angeles’ Kia Forum was paused mid-show so singer Tom Araya could reprimand some unruly fans in the crowd.

“The fire marshal said we’re gonna pause. We’re gonna pause until you guys get your shit and your act together,” Araya told the fans in the arena seats. “There’s no one to blame but you. You know who I’m talking about.”

The admonishment came just seven songs into Slayer’s North American tour-ending performance; after dusting off tracks like “God Send Death,” “Bloodline” and “The Antichrist” for the first time live in nearly a decade, Slayer fans apparently got too hyped, which sparked safety concerns and a five-minute cool-off.

It was during that timeout that Araya addressed the audience. “Quiet! I just need your attention. I don’t know how many times I had this conversation when we first started playing fucking huge places, I kept telling everybody, ‘Man, you gotta fucking maintain yourself. You can’t start destroying shit, because they’ll shut this shit down,’” he said.

“Listen, if you guys wanna have fun, you have fun right down here in front of us. Do it over here where there’s nothing you can destroy except each other. When you start doing shit on the outside of the line over there, they’re gonna shut the place down.”
“The line,” as Araya suggested, was the arena seating area, where the more casual fans were likely sitting, and where moshing and body-slamming is probably unsafe.

“You guys get so fucking crazy you start hurting each other,” Araya said. “I know it’s hard to fucking contain yourself, it’s hard to fucking maintain yourself, I know that. But you have to be respectful of the people around you, especially if you’re sitting in fucking seats.”
Araya also suggested that some fans were destroying the arena, and — when it comes time to pay for the repairs — it’s the band that foots that bill.

“We’re in a time when there’s no consequences for the shit you fucking do. We need consequences. If you guys keep that shit up, we’re gonna go home, and hope you guys don’t do it next time we come,” Araya warned.
“Have you ever heard me talk to you like this? So you need to get your fucking heads on straight and behave like human fucking beings unless you’re in this fucking area in the front.”

Thankfully, despite the initial round of boos and chants of “Ole, ole,” the crowd respected Araya’s call for chilling out, and the Slayer concert continued without incident, including a show-closing performance of Reign in Blood in full and a “Black Magic” encore.

items.title: Watch Stephen Wilson Jr. Interpret 'Wonderwall' for Oasis at Rock Hall Induction
items.description: At first glance, Stephen Wilson Jr. may look like a left-field choice to sing for Oasis at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony. But the Nashville singer-guitarist has carved out a unique lane for himself by blending alt-rock with country music
items.author: Joseph Hudak
paragraphs: At first glance, Stephen Wilson Jr. may look like a left-field choice to sing for Oasis at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony. But the Nashville singer-guitarist has carved out a unique lane for himself by blending alt-rock with country music for a sound he often describes as “Death Cab for Country.” Even some of that era’s defining voices have taken notice: In September, Pearl Jam’s Eddie Vedder joined Wilson onstage to perform Temple of the Dog’s “Hunger Strike.”

On Saturday, however, he had the unenviable task of performing one of the most over-performed songs of the modern era, “Wonderwall.” Armed only with his acoustic guitar and pedalboard, Wilson put his own spin on the ballad, off Oasis’s 1995 U.S. breakthrough (What’s the Story) Morning Glory?, offering a growling, deep-voiced version that was in stark contrast to Liam Gallagher’s keening whine. It may not have been what the Oasis faithful were expecting, but it reinforced Wilson’s skill in interpreting classic songs (see: his viral version of Ben E. King’s “Stand by Me.”)

Neither Liam nor Noel Gallagher chose to attend Oasis’s induction, joining other no-shows like Sade and Iron Maiden. The Britpop kings will, however, return to the road in 2027, playing dates across the U.K., Europe, and two select cities — Las Vegas and Boston — in the U.S.

Wilson, meanwhile, is gearing up for a big week in Nashville. He’s a multiple nominee at Wednesday’s CMA Awards, including nominations for New Artist of the Year and Song of the Year for his solo composition “Gary.” Wilson is also set to perform, taking the stage with Chris Stapleton to presumably recreate their collab “I’m a Song,” the studio version of which drops on Monday.

items.title: St. Vincent and Metallica Honor Iron Maiden at Rock Hall (With a Jack Black Assist)
items.description: A supergroup featuring members of Metallica, Rage Against the Machine, and St. Vincent honored Iron Maiden with a thrilling rendition of “The Trooper” at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony.
items.author: Jon Blistein
paragraphs: A supergroup featuring members of Metallica, Rage Against the Machine, and St. Vincent honored Iron Maiden with a thrilling rendition of “The Trooper” at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony.

St. Vincent’s Annie Clark, who once played the 1983 classic on bass at a middle school talent show, led the group, which also featured Metallica’s Kirk Hammett on guitar and Robert Trujillo on bass. The band was rounded out by Rage Against the Machine drummer Brad Wilk and metal guitarist John 5.

While that quintet honored Iron Maiden with plenty of firepower and shredding, Clark got an extra assist on vocals from Jack Black, who bounded onto the stage to help belt that classic Iron Maiden “Oh oh oh” refrain.

Black also inducted Iron Maiden during the ceremony, positing at one point: “Has there ever been a band that has rocked this hard for this long? The answer is ‘No.’ In fact, they’re not even here tonight because they’re rocking halfway around the world.”

Indeed, Iron Maiden chose not to attend the 2026 Induction Ceremony because it conflicted with a slate of previously scheduled Australian tour dates. As the band’s manager stated earlier this year, “In accepting, Iron Maiden made it very clear to the R&R HoF that the fans always come first and that the shows will of course go on.”

Iron Maiden were finally inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame after being eligible for more than two decades, going back to 2005. They were joined in the performer class by Phil Collins, Billy Idol, Joy Division/New Order, Oasis, Sade, Luther Vandross, and Wu-Tang Clan. Elsewhere, Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti, Queen Latifah, MC Lyte, and Gram Parsons received the Early Influence Award; Rick Rubin, Philly soul songwriter Linda Creed, producer Arif Mardin, producer Jimmy Miller were honored with the Musical Excellence Award; and Ed Sullivan was given the Ahmet Ertegun Award.

items.title: Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Big Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony
items.description: Cynthia Erivo and Blink-182’s Travis Barker took the stage at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony to pay tribute to one of this year’s honorees, Phil Collins.
items.author: Jon Blistein
paragraphs: Cynthia Erivo and Blink-182’s Travis Barker took the stage at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony to pay tribute to one of this year’s honorees, Phil Collins.

Though the pairing of Erivo and Barker may seem unlikely on paper, it proved to be an inspired choice as they performed Collins’ timeless 1980 hit, “In the Air Tonight.” Erivo delivered the song with the perfect amount of drama and bravado, while Barker pummeled his kit with precision when it came time for that all-important drum fill.

Along with performing “In the Air Tonight,” Barker delivered Collin’s induction speech. He recalled the massive influence Collins had on him as a drummer and singer-songwriter, calling hits like “Sussudio,” “Take Me Home,” “Easy Lover,” and “Against All Odds” the “soundtrack to my childhood.” As for “In the Air Tonight,” Barker said the song had “arguably the most badass drum fill of all time. You don’t even have to be a drummer to know that fill. When that part comes on, everybody plays air drums.”

Inducted this year as a solo artist, Collins previously entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2010 as a member of Genesis. The musician declined the opportunity to perform himself, admitting in an interview earlier this year, that he wasn’t “match fit.” (Collins hasn’t played live since March 2022 and has faced several health challenges since then.)
But during his own speech at the ceremony last night, Collins told the crowd, “You haven’t heard the last of me. I promise you that.”

Along with Collins, the Rock Hall’s 2026 performer class included Billy Idol, Iron Maiden, Joy Division/New Order, Oasis, Sade, Luther Vandross, and Wu-Tang Clan. Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti, Queen Latifah, MC Lyte, and Gram Parsons received the Early Influence Award; Rick Rubin, Philly Soul songwriter Linda Creed, producer Arif Mardin, producer Jimmy Miller were honored with the Musical Excellence Award; and Ed Sullivan was given the Ahmet Ertegun Award.

items.title: Red Hot Chili Peppers Donned Their Bushiest Rick Rubin Beards for Wild Rock Hall Performance
items.description: The Red Hot Chili Peppers honored 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Musical Excellence Award recipient Rick Rubin by playing one of the biggest songs they made together, and dressing up like the legendary producer.
items.author: Jon Blistein
paragraphs: The Red Hot Chili Peppers honored 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Musical Excellence Award recipient Rick Rubin by playing one of the biggest songs they made together, and dressing up like the legendary producer.

Taking the concept of “imitation is the sincerest form of flattery” to its funniest possible conclusion, all four members of RHCP took the stage at Saturday night’s Induction Ceremony in Los Angeles wearing ludicrously big, bushy white beards and wigs. They also all sported some very Rubin-esque orange-tinted sunglasses, while drummer Chad Smith played a special drum kit with a portrait of Rubin emblazoned on his bass drum.

For the performance, the Chili Peppers ripped through “Give It Away,” off 1991’s Blood Sugar Sex Magik, the first album Rubin produced for the band. (Since then, he’s produced all the band’s albums except 2016’s The Getaway, which Danger Mouse helmed.) Some technical difficulties with Flea’s bass caused an initial hiccup, but the band easily recovered after starting the song over, their fake beards bouncing wildly as they ran around the stage.
As for Rubin, he accepted his Musical Excellence Award with a short, but powerful speech. Taking the stage, he held up his prize and stated simply, “Can’t kill rock & roll.”

Along with Rubin, the Rock Hall’s 2026 Musical Excellence Award was given to Philly soul songwriter Linda Creed, producer Arif Mardin and producer Jimmy Miller. In the performer category, the 2026 class boasted Phil Collins, Billy Idol, Iron Maiden, Joy Division/New Order, Oasis, Sade, Luther Vandross, and Wu-Tang Clan. Meanwhile, Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti, Queen Latifah, MC Lyte, and Gram Parsons received the Early Influence Award, while Ed Sullivan was honored with the Ahmet Ertegun Award.

items.title: The Traitors: New Blood Recap: Follow the Teeny Traitor
items.description: They got a Traitor at the last roundtable, and now the players are riding that high. It only took them weeks and weeks of blindly groping in the dark before chance finally gave them a win. That, and Victor’s incessant harping. Now we’re at the next roundtable,
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: They got a Traitor at the last roundtable, and now the players are riding that high. It only took them weeks and weeks of blindly groping in the dark before chance finally gave them a win. That, and Victor’s incessant harping. Now we’re at the next roundtable, and Victor is coming for Joe. Oh, Joe. You seem pretty good. I’m sorry about your fate.

Kriste kicks things off by accusing Wyatt. She thinks there’s someone young in the turret. Shane thinks it’s too on the nose for Abbey to have accused Wyatt and then get murdered, and Kriste calls out the men’s clique at the table. Yeah! How many women are left now? Three. Three women and seven men, and of the ten people left at the start of the episode, eight are white. Were players commenting on this and we’re just not seeing it? This is seriously so egregious and so embarrassing for the players. Now there’s a clique of men who sway all the votes, and no thanks, everyone can experience that in real life readily enough.

It’s not just that they’re a clique; it’s how they revel in both their in-group status and their voting power. You are grown men. Grow the fuck up, stop fawning over Victor, and stop acting like you’re in a fraternity. You’re making me prefer Jay. JAY.

At the roundtable, Victor starts coming after Joe. Joe doesn’t think he has anything but the fruit idea, which seems right? When Joe asks if anyone saw him interacting strongly with Tomica, no one has anything to say. And this is yet another reason this season is so infuriating. Based on this discussion, it seems really weird for people to vote for Joe, other than Victor having been right before. But when it comes time to vote, it goes: Joe (Wyatt), Wyatt (Joe), Jay (Joe), Shane (Kriste), Kriste (Wyatt), Katie (Wyatt), Victor (Joe), Abby (Joe), Clyde (Joe), Ben (Joe). So clearly, the men’s clique (plus Jay and Abby) agreed to vote for Joe beforehand, and/or there was more compelling evidence presented that we did not see. These votes are baffling because we’re missing so much context. Also, Jay cries when he votes for Joe, and everyone is suspicious of this.

Joe has the most votes, so he stands before them all and says, “My headstone will read: Here lies Joe, proud father, beloved husband, trrrrrrruly a great friend, and Traitor.” That “truly” was very fun, Joe. True dad energy.

So now it’s just Katie holding things down for the Traitors. She pulls Victor to chat since he has this huge voting bloc, and we learn that he is leaning toward Kriste or Jay. Wyatt and Ben are also thinking Jay, due to the crying. Okay, guys. With Katie right there, everyone speculates about her being a Traitor, just in case the Traitors have someone young. Ben asks Katie not to kill him tonight, which is kind of a joke, but also not, since Ben thinks it’s Katie. Before everyone leaves for the night, Victor pulls Shane aside and tells him he has a shield and he’s going to spread the rumor that Shane has one so Shane won’t get murdered. That’s a solid move, Victor.

Unfortunately, it’s recruitment night, and Katie has picked Shane. She debated choosing Victor, but there’s like a 90 percent possibility that Victor would turn on her. When Shane sees it’s Katie, he laughs really hard. He was totally set on Kriste and Jay! The visual of Shane and Katie as Traitors is excellent. They should cast more things by height difference. He’s so tall and she’s so wee! Shane accepts Katie’s offer and becomes a Traitor, making them (per Katie) the teeny Traitor and the mega Traitor. “Let’s hood up,” she says. I don’t know about that phrase, Katie.

Shane immediately has to help murder someone that night. He discloses that Victor has a shield (so much for trust, am I right, Victor?), and they decide that it’s between Ben, Clyde, and Abbey. I really thought Ben was out of the running since he’s been saying Katie’s name, but the next morning, who has been murdered but our Ben Platt look-alike, Rodeo Ben. Should I even mention the continued idiocy of trying to guess whether a knock is a “girl knock” or a “boy knock,” per Victor and Wyatt? And how they are consistently wrong about this? Players have also done this in previous seasons, and they were almost always wrong.

The mission today involves puzzle building. It’s a little Survivor-y, but with a Traitors twist. Every player has to search a trough for puzzle pieces to complete their own three-dimensional shield puzzle. If their shield puzzle is complete by the end of the mission, they are protected from that night’s murder. But the Traitors will also be completing a shield puzzle, only using pieces from other players’ puzzles. If their puzzle is completed, $26,000 will be added to the prize total. When the castle bells chime, everyone must pause, put on a visor, and the Traitors have one minute to steal pieces from other players’ puzzles. The mission ends when the Traitors’ shield is completed, or after four rounds.

Shane is rightfully concerned about stealthiness, as he is a friendly giant with a size-16 shoe. Victor hears floorboards creaking by him and tells us it can only be one person: Kriste. Amazing. Shout-out to Alan’s Victor/Victoria headpiece. Teeny Traitor and Mega Traitor creep around as best they can, trying to complete their puzzle. Clyde is getting suspicious. He was already suspicious of Katie, but he hears heavy footsteps, so he knows if Katie is a Traitor, there’s one more. When you look at the people remaining, he says, there are only a couple of people who could have such heavy footsteps. He hears Shane’s puzzle fall and now is considering Shane for the very first time.

It feels like the players are being given more opportunities to identify Traitors than in other seasons. Or maybe the Traitors aren’t great at this, but are saved by the players also being terrible at guessing. Except for Victor. Somehow. Can you imagine Lisa Rinna being given the fruit task? She would have crushed it.

Next week is the finale, if you can believe it. Really rooting for Katie and Shane, or at least Shane, if Katie can’t make it. Shane wants to support his family and provide some more financial stability for them! Which, again, should be a function of our government and not an NBC game show, but this is the society in which we live.

Who would I vote for on Traitors? It’s hard to judge what one would do without having the insider knowledge, because who knows the full context of what’s happening in that castle, but based on what’s presented, here are my picks:

No Insider Knowledge: I think I would have voted for Wyatt, but I’m interested in why Jay voted for Joe. We don’t really know why, which, again, is something aggravating about this season and its shortened format. If something compelling were brought up about Joe, then maybe! But Wyatt’s name has been thrown around long enough that I think I would go with Wyatt, due to building suspicions.
Yes Insider Knowledge: Victor has a shield, so I’m gonna also pick Wyatt here, if only because of him saying, “They’re clocking cliques. They know we’re boys.” How would anyone not know that, Wyatt?

items.title: Governors Awards 2026: Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and More Receive Honorary Oscars From The Academy (Live Updates)
items.description: After a weekend of flight delays, Hollywood’s 2027 awards season is finally ready for take-off.
items.author: Antonio Ferme Social Media Editor
paragraphs: After a weekend of flight delays, Hollywood’s 2027 awards season is finally ready for take-off.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences is kicking off the Oscars race in Los Angeles with its 17th Governors Awards, a major campaign stop for contenders looking to mingle with Academy governors representing its 19 branches. Creatives behind sweeping spectacles like “The Odyssey” and “La Bola Negra” to intimate dramas like “Wild Horse Nine” and “The Debut” will walk the red carpet before the star-studded ceremony, where some of Hollywood’s most accomplished veterans will receive long-overdue accolades from their peers.

Glenn Close, who has earned eight competitive acting nominations over her career (four for Best Actress, another four for Best Supporting Actress), will finally receive an Oscar recognizing her decades of awards-caliber performances. Ridley Scott, a three-time Best Director nominee for “Thelma & Louise,” “Gladiator” and “Black Hawk Down,” will not attend in person but will accept his honorary Oscar through a prerecorded video.

Also receiving an honorary Oscar is animator Floyd Norman, best known for his work on Disney classics including “The Jungle Book” and “Sleeping Beauty,” while Killer Films producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler will receive the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award.

Here, Variety’s Antonio Ferme will be live-blogging all the biggest moments from tonight’s festivities, from glamorous red carpet looks and candid celebrity interviews to the evening’s most memorable speeches and exclusive behind-the-scenes details from reporters inside the ceremony.

items.title: Box Office: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to No. 1 With $19 Million, ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Stumbles With $5 Million Debut
items.description: Johnny Depp returned to the top of box office charts as “Ebenezer,” his new take on “A Christmas Carol,” collected a decent $19 million from 3,535 North American theaters in its opening weekend.
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: Johnny Depp returned to the top of box office charts as “Ebenezer,” his new take on “A Christmas Carol,” collected a decent $19 million from 3,535 North American theaters in its opening weekend.
Overseas, the PG-13 adaptation of the Charles Dickens classic has generated $23 million from 63 markets for a global start of $42 million.

“Ebenezer” is notable as Depp’s first major movie role in eight years, since 2018’s “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald.” His career in Hollywood began to unravel in 2020 after allegations of domestic abuse leveled by his ex-wife Amber Heard (which he has denied) resulted in two costly, high-profile defamation trials. Although his acting roles mostly dried up, a study conducted by the National Research Group in April 2026 indicated that Depp remained a popular figure across the globe. Participants ranked him among the top 10 actors — ahead of Tom Hanks and behind Margot Robbie — who “would make you most interested in seeing a new movie in a cinema in the future.”

So how did that enthusiasm translate to “Ebenezer” in its first weekend of release? Analysts say tickets didn’t signal a resounding embrace amid Depp’s return to studio fare. However, the movie delivered a nice boost to theater owners ahead of Thanksgiving and looks to provide a sizable return on investment for Paramount. Given the uncertainty around Depp, the studio cautiously spent $38 million to produce the film. Depp was paid $5 million, a fraction of what he’s earned on prior studio movies, with the promise of bonuses tied to box office performance.

“This is a solid opening for a Christmas-themed movie,” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “Johnny Depp remains a major celebrity around the world, and director Ti West brings some edge.”

Directed by West, known for the “X” horror trilogy, “Ebenezer” spins the oft-told tale of the cold-hearted businessman known as Scrooge as he’s visited by the ghosts of Christmas past, present and future. Though critics were harsh (it holds a 53% on Rotten Tomatoes), audiences awarded the movie a positive “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls. Ticket buyers were mostly older white women; audiences were 52% female and 58% Caucasian while 59% were aged 30 or older. The movie performed best in the south, per the studio. Around 50% of moviegoers cited Depp as a reason for attending, making him the film’s top attendance driver, according to PostTrak data.

In the wake of “Ebenezer,” box office watchers believe the town will be more willing to work with Depp. His next film is Lionsgate’s 2027 action thriller “Day Drinker,” co-starring Penélope Cruz. Meanwhile Disney has been contemplating another “Pirates of the Caribbean” movie. Depp has said he’s open to returning to the franchise as the chaotic Captain Jack Sparrow, but he noted “the only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.”

“With the No. 1 film in the marketplace, and his image and likeness splashed all over the marketing material, Johnny Depp’s Hollywood exile is effectively over,” says Jeff Bock, an analyst with Exhibitor Relations. “This benchmark tells the industry that Depp is once again castable, marketable and capable of opening a studio movie. Captain Jack Sparrow — it’s time to set sail again.”
Two other movies, Amazon MGM’s caper “How to Rob a Bank” and Sony’s action thriller “Ghost Soldier,” starring Jim Caviezel, opened nationwide to mixed results.

“How to Rob a Bank” didn’t make bank, stumbling at No. 7 with $5 million from 2,810 theaters in its debut. It also struggled internationally with $5.1 million from 73 territories, bringing its global total to a soft $10.3 million. The heist comedy, starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Pete Davidson, was produced for more than $40 million, and cinema operators keep about half of ticket sales. What’s troubling is neither critics nor audiences were receptive to the film, which landed a “B-” grade on CinemaScore and tepid 33% on Rotten Tomatoes. David Leitch directed the R-rated movie, which follows a crew of social media-savvy bank robbers who broadcast their daring heists, unaware their viral fame has caught the attention of the feds.
“This is a weak opening for an original action comedy,” says Gross. “With limited business overseas, the movie is going to fall short of recouping its investment.”

“Ghost Soldier” was just ahead on box office charts, in sixth place with $5.2 million over the traditional weekend and $8.3 million through its first five days of release. There’s no CinemaScore, so it’s unclear how audiences felt about the movie; reviews were negative, with a 36% on Rotten Tomatoes. “Ghost Soldier,” featuring Caviezel as a former American Special Forces soldier, carries a lean $18 million production budget.
“How to Rob a Bank” and “Ghost Solider” opened behind several holdovers, including Warner Bros. Animation’s “The Cat in the Hat” and Gkids action sequel “Godzilla Minus Zero.”

“The Cat in the Hat” remained in second place with $11 million from 4,003 theaters in its sophomore outing, a 45% decline from its debut. So far, the animated family film has earned $36.7 million domestically and just $55 million globally, a disappointing tally against a $92 million budget.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” slid to No. 3 after leading box office charts last weekend. The kaiju sequel earned $8.31 million from 3,264 locations, a harsh 75% drop from its opening. Despite a big decline, “Godzilla Minus Zero” has been a hit in North America with $48.1 million to date.

In fifth place, A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” brought in $5.4 million from 1,845 screens in its fifth weekend of release. The buzzy movie, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, has been a huge draw with $89 million and will soon clear the $100 million mark in North America. That’s a rare box office milestone for any documentary — especially one that’s nearly three hours long.

At No. 8, Searchlight’s dark comedy “Wild Horse Nine” added $4.6 million while expanding to 2,175 theaters. The Oscar hopeful, starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell and directed by Martin McDonagh, has grossed $13.3 million in North America and $28 million worldwide after two weekends in theaters. McDonagh’s prior film, 2022’s “The Banshees of Inisherin,” ended its run with $10.5 million domestically and $50 million globally.
Among specialty releases, A24’s heartwarming comedy “Club Kid” and Amazon MGM’s drama “I Play Rocky” attempted to sustain momentum in limited release.

“Club Kid” stayed strong with $756,060 on 27 screens, translating to $28,002 per screen and boosting its tally to $1.45 million. About 80% of audiences were under 35, according to PostTrak. Jordan Firstman wrote, directed and stars in the film, which revolves around a hard-partying club promoter who finds out he has a 10-year-old son.

“I Play Rocky” captured $503,818 from 29 venues, averaging $17,373 per location. Directed by Peter Farrelly, the movie depicts the real-life story of Sylvester Stallone bringing the 1976 classic “Rocky” to the big screen. Both films will expand nationwide around Thanksgiving.

Neon’s period drama “Paper Tiger” opened to $215,009 from six screens, averaging $35,835 per location. By comparison, “Club Kid” earned $65,097 per location and “I Play Rocky” captured $49,200 per location last weekend from similar theater counts. James Gray directed the film, in which Adam Driver and Miles Teller portray brothers Irwin and Gary Pearl, whose get-rich-quick scheme to help clean up the Gowanus Canal lands them in the crosshairs of the Russian mafia.

Overall, the box office is 20% ahead of the same point last year, and exhibitors are optimistic about the rest of November. Next weekend brings Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” which is tracking to open above $100 million. Then Turkey Day will bring Universal’s comedy “Focker in Law,” with Ariana Grande joining Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, and Disney’s animated “Hexed.”

These movies are “setting the table for what promises to be an exciting Thanksgiving frame,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “With the holiday moviegoing season getting underway, the industry has a great opportunity to build momentum heading into the final weeks of the year.”

items.title: Governors Awards 2026 Red Carpet Photos: Zendaya, Inde Navarrette, Timothée Chalamet and More
items.description: The red carpet for the Academy’s 2026 Governors Awards is now open.
items.author: Marc Malkin; Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: The red carpet for the Academy’s 2026 Governors Awards is now open.
Inde Navarrette, Jaafar Jackson, Andrew Garfield, Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder are just a few of the Oscar contenders who have arrived for the 17th gala at the Ray Dolby Ballroom in Hollywood.

This year’s program will present honorary Oscars to Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Disney’s first Black animator Floyd Norman. Scott previously announced that he is unable to make it to Los Angeles to accept the award in person.
Killer Films co-founders Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler will receive the Irving G. Thalberg, making them the first female producing team and first independent producers to earn the honor.
The Governors Awards are considered the first for the year’s Oscar contenders, allowing nominee hopefuls to shake hands and schmooze with hundreds of voting members of the Academy.
The evening is produced by Jennifer Todd and presented in partnership with Rolex.
Check out the best red carpet pics from the Governors Awards below.

items.title: Billy Evans Addresses Amanda Seyfried’s Portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in ‘You Can See Everything’: She Was ‘Eager’ to ‘Play a Character’
items.description: Billy Evans is finally weighing in on Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in “You Can See Everything.”
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: Billy Evans is finally weighing in on Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in “You Can See Everything.”

In his first interview since the A24 documentary’s release last month, released Sunday morning, Holmes’ partner sat down with CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman to discuss how, exactly, he feels about the film. When asked what he thought about Seyfriend’s role, Evans responded: “I’m really glad that they included her because it shows what a difference there is between the real thing and how eager she was to play a character.”

Gutman then followed up by questioning if the actress played the role of the disgraced tech founder well, to which Evans said that he was “glad Nathan was there to help her.” “Doesn’t seem like you hold very high opinion of her acting, or of her as a person,” noted Gutman.
Evans concluded: “Matt, I’m gonna do my best not to speak poorly about other people right now, because I’ve had a lot of people do that about me recently, and I know how it feels.”

Seyfriend also recently told all about her experience filming “You Can See Everything” in a new interview with Rolling Stone, including that she didn’t tell her agents about the project and had “no approval” over filming. She also noted that her opinion of Evans “only got worse” as filming went on, and she felt he “disrespected” her during that tense dinner table conversation.

Before hitting theaters on Oct. 16, the buzzy doc had been quietly in the works from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim for more than three years. The doc offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score. Seyfried, who appears as herself while also reprising her Emmy-winning turn as Holmes from “The Dropout,” will be campaigned in the supporting actress category.

items.title: John Mulaney Mocks Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in ‘SNL’ Monologue: ‘No One Likes Him. You Dumbass … Your Thing Can’t Be the Measles!’
items.description: John Mulaney‘s opening monologue on this week’s “Saturday Night Live” took an unexpected turn when he mocked controversial U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
items.author: William Earl
paragraphs: John Mulaney‘s opening monologue on this week’s “Saturday Night Live” took an unexpected turn when he mocked controversial U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The comic started by impersonating Kennedy, saying, “‘My father was a good man, and I’m a lousy man, but I have the same name. Am I good if I have the same name as my father? No, please, let me be in charge of your bones and your tummy. Please allow me to control how your blood feels in your butt and everywhere. Stop the science … Robitussin, when taken during menstruation, will cause telekinesis. This is clear from the pamphlets in my rental car.’”
Mulaney then slammed Kennedy’s vaccine skepticism, saying, “No one likes him. You dumbass … your thing can’t be the measles!”
He then mocked Kennedy’s previous occupation as an environmental lawyer, saying, “He would just join cases late if they were about to be successful. ‘Are you about to win? I’m part of this too.’”
Mulaney then described how he interacted with the politician by performing comedy at benefits for Kennedy’s Riverkeepers organization.

“They were in charge of keeping the Hudson River in New York City clean,” Mulaney said. “That was his job. That’s how good he is at jobs. His old job was keeping the Hudson River, whose native fish are tied-off used condoms, clean. Now he’s in charge of all of our tummies.”
The Nov. 14 episode was Mulaney’s seventh as host. His monologue also touched on family issues and children whose deep, scratchy voices remind him of Kennedy.

items.title: Governors Awards: Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman Accept Honorary Oscars, Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler Receive Thalberg Award
items.description: Five giants of the global film community were feted on Sunday night at the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ 17th annual Governors Awards: actress Glenn Close, animator Floyd Norman and — in absentia due to a recent medical procedure — director/prod
items.author: Scott Feinberg; Brande Victorian
paragraphs: Five giants of the global film community were feted on Sunday night at the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ 17th annual Governors Awards: actress Glenn Close, animator Floyd Norman and — in absentia due to a recent medical procedure — director/producer Ridley Scott with bestowed honorary Oscars, and longtime indie producing partners Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award, which recognizes “creative producers whose bodies of work reflect a consistently high quality of motion picture production.”

The black-tie gathering, which took place inside the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood, was, as always, packed with Academy members — including most of the 55 members of the organization’s board of governors, who host the event — and dozens of current Oscar contenders. Among them: You Can See Everything’s Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, The Odyssey’s Christopher Nolan, Zendaya, Tom Holland and Charlize Theron, The Debut’s Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti and Emma Stone, Obsession’s Curry Barker and Inde Navarrette, La Bola Negra’s Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, Elsinore’s Andrew Scott, The Invite’s Olivia Wilde and Penélope Cruz, Wild Horse Nine’s John Malkovich, Artificial’s Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, and Dune: Part Three’s Timothée Chalamet, accompanied by Kylie Jenner.
Seated with Scott were his family, along with Lucy Fisher, Doug Wick, Jim Gianopulos, Tom Rothman, Richard Lovett, Simon Halls, Steve Asbell, Matt Damon and Jerry Bruckheimer, while

Norman was notably joined by Marlon West and Travon Free. Close’s table consisted of Malkovich, Kevin Huvane, Franklin Latt, Rodrigo Garcia and Ram Bergman. Vachon and Koffler were accompanied by John Sloss, Wash Westmoreland, Marcus Hu and Liz Karlsen.

The first awardee was Norman, 91, who began his career in 1956 at Walt Disney Animation Studios as the company’s first Black animator. He contributed to numerous Disney classics including Sleeping Beauty, The Sword in the Stone, Mary Poppins, The Jungle Book and Robin Hood, as well as other notable films made outside of the Mouse House including The Hunchback of Notre Dame, Mulan, Monsters, Inc. and Toy Story 2. A friend and mentor to younger animators and storyboard artists, he was the subject of a 2016 documentary feature, Floyd Norman: An Animated Life.

The presentation of the honorary Oscar to Norman — only the fourth animator to ever receive that accolade, after Walter Lantz, Chuck Jones and Hayao Miyazaki — was led by Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother star Mahershala Ali, who stated, “Floyd has played a pivotal role in our lives without any of us even realizing it, one [animation] cel at a time.”

In his acceptance speech, Norman reflected on his beginnings in the industry, offering “a special thank you to the best mentor a filmmaker could ever have, Walt Disney.” He concluded his speech remarking, “On occasion, even movies have a happy ending. This special evening? Here’s my happy ending.”

The evening’s next honoree was Close, one of the great stars and character actresses of the past 50 years. The 79-year-old has received eight Oscar nominations, four for leading performances (1987’s Fatal Attraction, 1988’s Dangerous Liaisons, 2011’s Albert Nobbs and 2018’s The Wife) and four for supporting turns (1982’s The World According to Garp, 1983’s The Big Chill, 1984’s The Natural and 2020’s Hillbilly Elegy). She could just as easily have been nominated for 1985’s Jagged Edge and Maxie, 1990’s Reversal of Fortune, 1994’s The Paper, 1996’s 101 Dalmatians and 1997’s Air Force One.

Close’s tally of eight noms for performances is higher than that of all but three other actresses, dead or alive — Meryl Streep (21), Katharine Hepburn (12) and Bette Davis (11), each of whom won multiple times — and more than any other living man or woman (Peter O’Toole, who died in 2013, also went 0-for-eight and received an honorary Oscar).

The presentation of the honorary Oscar to Close — who previously presented honorary Oscars to the National Endowment for the Arts in 1985, Deborah Kerr in 1994 and Carol Littleton in 2023 — was kicked off by John Malkovich, who described her as “my friend and treasured colleague.” Close’s Dangerous Liaisons co-star then went on to state, “She is a true master… she’s got the goods, she can do the big stuff, the little stuff, and everything in between… Glenn is unafraid to ‘go there,’ and I love that about her,” Malkovich added. “She loves the world, she is relentless, very smart, a little cagey and a great actress who knows exactly what she’s doing and gives it 100 percent every single time.”

Following a lengthy standing ovation, Close, who dedicated the award to her daughter, Annie, declared: “As an outsider, I have never worried about whether I was going to win or not, though some years I thought I might have a chance. I have always felt that the great honor is to be in the room. Over the past 43 years, I’ve been in the room eight times… so to be in this room tonight, embraced by the people who have consistently inspired me, whose work has sustained and challenged me and only made me want to be better is the greatest honor of all.”

Next up was Scott, whose films, collectively, have been nominated for 45 Oscars and won nine, but who himself has never won a competitive Oscar. The 88-year-old, who was nearly 40 when he made his directorial debut, has made up — and continues to make up — for lost time, consistently pumping out action-packed blockbusters, many now considered landmarks of cinematic achievement.

Indeed, he is behind two of the most significant sci-fi films of all time, 1979’s Alien and 1982’s Blade Runner, as well as 1991’s Thelma & Louise (for which he received a best director Oscar nom), 2000’s Gladiator (which won the best picture Oscar, while he lost best director), 2001’s Black Hawk Down (for which he received his most recent best director Oscar nom) and 2015’s The Martian. He has also produced many of his films, as well as a ton of TV series.

The presentation of the honorary Oscar to Scott was led by Matt Damon, who described him as “a master at the helm” of two films they’ve made together, The Martian and The Last Duel, stating, “Thank you to the Academy on behalf of everyone who has ever worked with Ridley Scott. It is about time we all saw him with an Academy Award in his hand.” Scott accepted his Oscar via a pre-recorded video from London, which included a clip from his first movie, Boy in a Bicycle, featuring his late brother, Tony, in which the narrator states, “I’ll remember this moment when I’m 80, and it’ll all seem like yesterday.”

“That was a moment for both of us,” Scott stated. “Now I’m well past 80, and I’ve thought about those days and moments. It does resonate just like yesterday. Both of us sharing our first film together that led to 20 years of advertising, five decades of filmmaking… I’m flattered and proud to accept this award, but I also accept it for Tony. His great work would certainly have earned this recognition.”

The final awardees of the night were Vachon, 63, and Koffler, 60, two of the most important producers in the history of American independent film. The co-founders of New York-based Killer Films have guided to fruition all 10 of Todd Haynes’ features — including Poison (1991), Safe (1995), Far from Heaven (2002) and Carol (2015) — plus Larry Clark’s Kids (1995), Todd Solondz’s Happiness (1998), Kimberly Peirce’s Boys Don’t Cry (1999), John Cameron Mitchell’s Hedwig and the Angry Inch (2001), Wash Westmoreland and Richard Glatzer’s Still Alice (2014) and Celine Song’s Past Lives (2023, for which they received their sole Oscar noms).

Vachon, the more public-facing of the duo, has been nicknamed “the Queen of New Queer Cinema” and is such a fixture of the indie scene that she was affectionately referenced alongside Spike Lee, Michael Moore and Richard Linklater in the title of the classic 1996 tome Spike, Mike, Slackers, & Dykes: A Guided Tour Across a Decade of American Independent Cinema. Her own 2006 book A Killer Life, which she co-wrote with Austin Bunn, was included on The Hollywood Reporter‘s 2023 list of the 100 greatest film books of all time.

The presentation of the Thalberg to Vachon and Koffler was kicked off by Neil Patrick Harris with a performance from Hedwig and the Angry Inch, which Vachon and Koffler produced. Todd Haynes and Julianne Moore then conducted the actual handoff of the statuettes, with Haynes saying, “From the outside, they couldn’t see more different, and of course they are. But the ways they trade and riff off each other, divide and share their unique abilities. It’s a shimmering example of how the world might actually be if it were run by adults, otherwise known as women.”

Added Moore, “These women have never been driven by profit and even recently admitted to me that no matter how hard they tried to be commercial, they’ve had to make peace of the fact that they’re just not. That doesn’t mean that they haven’t had commercial success. They are just not driven by it. They are interested in radical voices, queer voices, new voices, personal points of view.”

Vachon, in her acceptance speech, dedicated the pair’s honor to their “fellow hardworking producers,” stating, as she recalled a recent interaction, “A producer came up to me in New York and said, ‘I know this is really your Oscar, but it kind of feels like all of ours,’ And it is.”

items.title: Next Gen 2026: 35 Rising Hollywood Executives Under 35
items.description: Nobody ever said that Hollywood careers come easy. But right now, with consolidation and layoffs decimating the middle rungs of entertainment’s steep corporate ladder and studio remits changing with each earnings report, dream jobs have never been more difficu
items.author: Winston Cho; Aaron Couch; Caitlin Huston; Mia Galuppo; Ryan Gajewski; Katie Kilkenny; Borys Kit; Lacey Rose
paragraphs: Nobody ever said that Hollywood careers come easy. But right now, with consolidation and layoffs decimating the middle rungs of entertainment’s steep corporate ladder and studio remits changing with each earnings report, dream jobs have never been more difficult to land, much less retain.

Such trends aren’t slowing the ascent of THR’s Next Gen class of 2026, who join such illustrious alumni as Donna Langley, Ari Emanuel, Kevin Feige and Peter Rice. In fact, this group is too busy forging new paths through the chaos — whether that’s bringing Gen Z back to cinemas (as indie producer Christian Vazquez did with both Primetime and You Can See Everything) or fortifying the streaming ecosystem amid endless churn (see Claudia Shin and Louie Hayes, behind the Apple TV Emmy darling Widow’s Bay and the Prime Video breakout Sterling Point, respectively.)
Meet the 35 executives and reps, each of them 35 years old or younger, who should be atop your call list, if they aren’t already.

- Alyssa Altman, 35 RK Films, senior vp LOGLINE Championing rom-coms like Anyone But You and Netflix’s upcoming 13 Going on 30 update. THE ARC Altman got a unique view of the industry when she would join her father, Steve, who rented out lighting, camera and grip equipment: “I grew up doing my homework in grip trucks, and I just loved being on set.” Her dad’s rom-com adoration rubbed off during their weekly trips to the movies, where films like Love Actually made an early impression. Altman studied journalism at Emerson but caught the producing bug while moonlighting on college TV projects. After time at Gersh, she became then-Universal exec Jeff Kirschenbaum’s assistant and followed him to RK Films. While the company focused on bigger IP plays, she endorsed the script for Anyone But You (“That was my baby”), Sony’s Sydney Sweeney-Glen Powell feature that became a rare theatrical comedy hit. Up next: Amazon MGM’s tennis rom-com Love Love and Netflix’s Millie Bobby Brown-led Just Picture It. PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Andy Cohen. My favorite way to de-stress after a long day is to watch and listen to the soothing sound of people fighting on Bravo.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “The fact that movies geared towards women do great theatrically. Every time it happens, people act like it’s an anomaly. Women are starved for content and it’s not a coincidence.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I was an assistant at Universal, we set up a screening for an A-list star who specifically requested popcorn from the Universal Studios theme park. I had to sneak into the park through the back lot and bring it back before he arrived.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Sally Albright from When Harry Met Sally. She isn’t afraid to speak her mind, is a hopeless romantic, and has strong opinions on how she orders her food.”

- Jenna Berger, 35 Marvel Studios, director of production development LOGLINE Berger is serving as co-producer, and Kevin Feige’s right hand, on Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars. ’Nuff said. THE ARC An L.A. native with industry parents, Berger grew up wanting to make movies. “I had this theory that everybody who didn’t want to make movies was lying to themselves and secretly did,” she says. So, shortly after graduating from University of Pennsylvania with a double major in English and film, she landed a gig at The Mark Gordon Co. Still, it was Marvel that was making some of her favorite films — she saw Spider-Man: Homecoming four times in the theater — but the company felt impenetrable … until it wasn’t. In 2019, Berger scored a position, rising to junior exec before finding herself the solo exec on the Marvel TV series Ms. Marvel, where she earned a supervising producer credit and honed her creative leadership, talent development and production expertise. “It was the best crash course in figuring out how this company worked and making something worthy of the Marvel name,” she says. The higher-ups took note, which is why Berger now oversees some of the studio’s most ambitious films. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kermit the Frog. Because my job is to bring amazingly talented people together to make something special amid total chaos … which sometimes means convincing everyone the show must go on before the set falls down around us.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “David Heyman. To get to work on Bond and Harry Potter?! A dream. Would love to trade places for a day … or forever.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Having a sneeze attack while leaving a voicemail for Aaron Sorkin on behalf of my boss.”

- Natalie Berkus, 35 LuckyChap, senior vp TV LOGLINE Developing (and producing) your future TV obsessions, including Andrew Garfield’sWild Things. THE ARC Rather than follow her agent dad and comedy writer mom into the business, Berkus arrived at University of Michigan eager to be a lawyer. “Then I rushed the law fraternity and didn’t get in,” she says. “I mean, I whiffed it and was like, ‘Shit, now what do I do?’ ” The answer, it turns out, was to parlay her love of TV into a series of PA gigs on shows like The Mindy Project before talking her way into a job as the writers assistant on Girls and, later, with Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner’s company. From there, she logged six years at Imagine Entertainment, where she was intimately involved in a slate that included The ’Burbs and the upcoming Siegfried and Roy series starring Garfield and Jude Law for Apple TV. But LuckyChap came calling a year ago, and the L.A. native and new mom to daughter Roonie jumped at the opportunity to work at the Margot Robbie-led hit factory. In that time, she has built a roster of 10 to 15 projects, including a Life Is Strange series for Amazon Prime Video. Still, Berkus doesn’t take herself too seriously. “If I had to brand myself, I’d say I like to bring a levity to this business,” she says, “because I think sometimes, especially now, things can get really stressful and we lose sight of the fact that ultimately this is just one big party.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Nina Rosenstein, who does all of the HBO comedy specials. We’ve never met, but Nina, girl, if you’re reading this, let’s link and get our Freaky Friday moment started!” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “That having unapproachable girlboss ‘I’m smarter than you’ energy is cool. It’s not, it’s lame! Normalize the quiet power in validating others and having a fun vibe.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Nowhere are you crazy!! No more of these!!”

- Mandi Brooksbank, 34 Netflix, senior manager, business affairs, scripted series LOGLINE Helps mold Netflix’s scripted slate, brokering deals with top talent like Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media. THE ARC As a kid in Reno, Nevada, Brooksbank figured she was destined for Broadway. While most her age were on the playground, she was busy with casino shows, doing dinner theater (and playing the harp) in vintage Hollywood glam. “It was entertainment or bust,” she recalls with a laugh. Later, she’d speedrun undergrad at USC and law school at Southwestern, finishing both in five years. Since then, she’s built a Hollywood résumé that includes stints at CAA, Donaldson Callif Perez and eOne. Now in her fifth year at Netflix, Brooksbank helps steer the streamer’s scripted series unit, striking deal after deal with TV’s biggest names. It’s a high volume affair, with Brooksbank managing a slate that includes The Altruists, Ransom Canyon and Sirens, among many others. “I’m the third child in a family of six,” she says of her negotiating chops. “They all have big personalities, so they prepared me well for Hollywood.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Miss Piggy.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Women directors’ second and third films. We talk about breaking through, but what about career longevity?” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “When I was considering law school, Patti Felker encouraged me to see being a woman as an advantage in negotiations, particularly the ability to read people, adapt and adjust your approach to the person across the table without losing sight of what you’re there to accomplish.”

- Barry Buren, 35 CAA, TV talent agent LOGLINE Makes deals for A-listers including Pedro Pascal, Matthew Rhys, Steven Yeun and Eddie Redmayne. THE ARC Hollywood has Orlando’s Central Florida Talent agency to thank for putting Buren on his path. After the New Jersey native graduated a semester early from nearby Rollins College, he picked up a gig at the model/talent agency to stay near friends who were still in school. Though he imagined he might become an engineer someday, he accepted an L.A.-based relative’s offer to live with her while giving Hollywood a try. As luck would have it, agenting stuck, and after a stint at Gersh, the avid golfer joined CAA in 2014. Today, the married rep is entrusted by actors including Josh Hartnett, Charlie Hunnam and Hannah Waddingham. Earlier this fall, client (and double Emmy winner) Rhys gave Buren a shout-out from the Emmy stage. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Serving coffee to people in an order determined by seniority and annual earnings. It was my first introduction to the Hollywood hierarchy, and I learned very quickly that even caffeine has a pecking order.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being on a call with 15 people to schedule another call with 15 people, only to discover that the one person who actually needed to be there wasn’t invited.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Lorne Michaels. To have spent five decades at the intersection of comedy, culture, and discovering talent is pretty remarkable.”

- Winnie Carrillo Montiel, 35 Amazon MGM, film executive, production & development LOGLINE Oversees films that range from bro-y actioners (The Wrecking Crew) to weepy love stories (Honeymoon With Harry). THE ARC Carrillo Montiel’s career in entertainment began with a clerical error. As an Emerson undergrad, she was mistakenly admitted as a screenwriting major instead of the literature and publishing program she had applied to. She ended up staying the course, eventually doubling down by attending graduate school at USC’s famed Peter Stark Producing Program. While there, she landed a temp job in MGM’s film group, which she did by day, leaving classes for night. Ultimately, it was the studio’s then-president Jonathan Glickman who helped push through the Guatemala City native’s visa sponsorship to land her her first full-time Hollywood gig. “He just made me promise that I wouldn’t get my green card and leave,” she remembers. “This was almost a decade ago and I’m still here. So, I really kept my promise.” Carrillo Montiel has since survived several regime changes, not to mention an acquisition, to land at her current spot on Amazon MGM’s film team, where she has overseen such films as The Sheep Detectives and an upcoming slate with projects from Dan Fogelman (Honeymoon) and Michael Showalter (a Serendipity reimagining). One of her proudest accomplishments is shepherding Angel Manuel Soto’sThe Wrecking Crew, explaining, “Latinos are often put in a very specific box, and we are only hired to tell Latino-specific stories. I’m always looking for opportunities to elevate talent that I think are just great filmmakers.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Unlimited budgets.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “I was advised to look for an American husband as I was told it would be impossible for me to earn a work visa in this industry.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Cold calling very specific animal experts in Russia and Brazil to attempt to track down recent sightings of extremely large species of bears and snakes.”

- Margaret Clark, 32 20th Television, director of development LOGLINE Manages a roster of overall deals (Liz Meriwether, Drew Goddard) and development projects, including the Hulu hit Furious. THE ARC Technically speaking, Clark was discovered at the Panera on South Beverly Drive. At least, that’s where a guy from APA overheard her during an informational coffee with a fellow University of Virginia alum and offered to pass along her résumé to his agency mailroom. She was hired the following week. “I treated it like my grad school,” Clark says of her agency stint. By late 2017, the Virginia native and onetime theater kid had jumped to 20th Television, where she eventually found her way to Dana Walden’s desk for three pivotal years. In that time, she gained both a high-level education and a top-tier mentor. These days, Clark’s back on the 20th team, punching above her weight as she manages a slate of projects and the studio’s IP pipeline. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Jennifer Lopez in The Wedding Planner.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Buying a single old-fashioned donut for the CEO on Friday mornings. It had to be from Winchell’s. I wasn’t his assistant.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “The National Theater in London. Or the ABC Riverside Starbucks.”

- Sarah Colvin, 30 Neon, senior vp acquisitions LOGLINE Keeps Neon supplied with art house favorites and horror standouts, including The Secret Agent, Leviticus and All of a Sudden. THE ARC Colvin spends a good chunk of her year traveling to Sundance, Berlin, SXSW, Cannes and beyond in the name of supplying Neon’s film slate with titles that will soon be Letterboxd’s new obsession (see: Oliver Laxe’s Sirāt and the long-awaited doc Once Upon a Time in Harlem). Raised in New Mexico by artist parents, young Colvin would spend whatever free time she had with friends at Santa Fe’s one art house cinema. She laughs, “We thought we were so highbrow.” But she took that passion to NYU, where her professor, indie producer David Hinojosa, helped her land an internship at Neon, right as the then-upstart distributor was releasing its first success, I, Tonya. “There was no formal end date to the internship,” she says. “Eventually, Tom [Quinn] was like, ‘You should probably have a job here, then.’ ” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “A blend of PeeWee Herman and Griffin Mill from The Player.” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Wile E Coyote.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The great equalizer that is the valet stand after the Academy Awards.”

- Dylan Conklin, 34 Entertainment 360, manager LOGLINE Guides the careers of clients like Kaia Gerber and Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story star Ella Beatty. THE ARC Conklin was studying international business in China for a summer when he realized the path wasn’t for him. Fortunately, a TV class with guests from Breaking Bad and Mad Men opened his eyes to a career in the entertainment field instead. Following a stint as an assistant to producer Tripp Vinson and some good advice from mentor attorney Howard Weitzman, he landed at 360 in 2016. A decade later, the dad of two has an impressive roster of talent clients, including Costa D’Angelo, for whom he’s lined up back-to-back shows (East of Eden, The Sticks, We Were Liars), Ji-young Yoo, whose post-KPop Demon Hunters path includes a Paramount movie and Presumed Innocent season two, and Colin Woodell, who toplines as the title character in Myron Bolitar, a series based on the Harlan Coben books. BEST ADVICE ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Don’t chase hits. Champion exceptional artists, nurture their talent, and the hits will follow.” IT WAS FROM… “Mo Ostin.” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Danny DeVito.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Making PB&J sandwiches in the office kitchen with Jennifer Garner.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “Jerry Bruckheimer.”

- Kai Dolbashian, 33 1.21, Film & TV development head LOGLINE Identified filmmaker Michael Shanks and helped develop Together from script to splashy Sundance sale. THE ARC While attending Chapman’s film school, Dolbashian landed an internship at MGM TV. The problem: The job was an hour away on a good day, and he had no car. Though he racked up credit card bills renting Zipcars, the bet paid off. He scored a post-grad gig and found a mentor in producer Andrew Mittman. And when Mittman launched his own banner in 2020, he was there on day one. Now, as the company’s head of film and TV development, Dolbashian has a slew of projects in development, including Warner Bros.’ remake of Attack of the 50 Foot Woman with Margot Robbie and Tim Burton. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Arno from Uncut Gems. We’re both impatient Armenians and both desperately want to do business with Adam Sandler.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The first time I had lunch with Christoph Waltz, he cut and ate his strudel exactly the way his infamous character Hans Landa does in Inglourious Basterds. Thankfully, unlike Hans, Christoph is one of the nicest human beings.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Bill Hader. There is literally no one else who could write and direct that epic motorcycle chase and shootout from season three of Barry, yet also perfectly embody the unhinged role of Officer Slater in Superbad.”

- Carly Elter, 32 Hidden Pictures, senior vp film and TV LOGLINE The architect behind The Housemaid is also behind lit-centric packages based on best-sellers from Rebecca Yarros and V. E. Schwab. THE ARC When Elter first walked into the house at the center of her 2025 movie The Housemaid, she cried. “It was such a surreal moment,” she says. “In my apartment, I read a book that I thought was a good idea for a movie, and now we have 100 people-plus employed making that movie.” Elter sold the film adaptation when it was self-published by author Freida McFadden; it would later land a publishing deal and sell 6 million copies, while the movie earned more than $400 million and quickly scored a sequel, which is in production. It’s not the married New Jersey native’s only claim to fame. While still an assistant — with stints at WME, Pascal Pictures and Mandeville — she also founded Women Wednesdays (now The Real Champions), where she’d screen films from women and nonbinary filmmakers for fellow assistants with the goal of getting the directors studio jobs. Later, Elter — who lives in Playa Vista with her husband and mutt Archie and also counts TV as a part of her remit with MGM+’s Robin Hood — started a mentorship program that’s helped place over 150 people into jobs. MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being approached by a famous actor on a red carpet who told me he was a huge fan of mine. Turns out he thought I was Alana Haim.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Amanda Seyfried. She has built a life where she makes incredible movies and TV shows and then goes home to her farm to hang out with goats and emus. She’s cracked the code.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “You have to work hard to build the version of Hollywood you want to be a part of.” IT WAS FROM “Sara Scott.”

- Anna Flickinger, 34 UTA, motion picture lit agent LOGLINE From Mary Beth Barone to Sterling Point producer Raffi Donatich, she gets funny women’s work to screen. THE ARC “I read these goddamn think pieces like, ‘Comedy’s dead,’ ” says Flickinger, whose response is often: “Really?! There’s always going to be a big theatrical comedy that gets people back in the seats.” She saw it happen firsthand when writer client Ilana Wolpert’s Anyone But You made over $200 million at the box office. Initially, the Chicago native and oldest of eight thought she’d pursue a career in politics, but after interning in the office of Sen. Dick Durbin (“loveliest man in America”) and a DC lobbying firm (“fucking depressing”), she realized her love of The West Wing was more about an interest in entertainment than government. After temping her way around L.A., she landed at UTA, where she ultimately found a home in the motion picture lit group. Now, Flickinger, who lives with her husband and their Rottweiler and Chihuahua, guides clients like Sammi Cohen (You Are So Not Invited to My Bar Mitzvah) and Barone, who’s writing and starring in her own rom-com. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “C.J. Cregg sun, Josh Lyman rising, Toby Ziegler moon.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “The public transit infrastructure of New York in L.A.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Why it takes women making their first, second, third and fourth movie to get the compensation and resources that men get to make their second movie.”

- Carly Frankel, 32 WME, digital agent LOGLINE Brokers deals for top podcasts, including Giggly Squad’s nine-figure pact with SiriusXM. THE ARC An L.A. native, Frankel got an early taste of agency life while booking comedy shows, including Chelsea Peretti’s, as an undergrad at UC Berkeley. It led to an assistant gig in UTA’s comedy touring department, then another at then-podcasting startup Wondery. But after greenlighting Wondery shows including Baby, This Is Keke Palmer, Frankel was called back to the agency side at WME, where she’s helped Maria Sharapova launch a podcast with Vox Media and brokered Tinx’s deal with SiriusXM and Dr. Mary Claire Haver’s deal with Audacy. As more and more people consider starting a podcast, Frankel advises talent about the hard work required, including recording a minimum of 45 episodes a year. “I think the number one thing is someone who is genuinely enthusiastic about it,” she said. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Chasing comedians down Melrose to introduce myself after their stand-up sets. Saying hi on behalf of the agency was my cardio.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Truly anywhere that offers a 16-ounce cup. The ‘default 10-ounce latte’ trend is killing me.”
BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Your reputation is your greatest currency. Work hard and be kind.”

- Katie Giarla, 35 Cut To, founding member/partner LOGLINE Building a slate of hot projects, including the upcoming Elle Fanning-Nicole Kidman legal thriller Discretion, for the A24-based company. THE ARC Raised by a psychologist and a lawyer in Pittsburgh, Giarla’s only link to the entertainment business was her childhood birthday parties at the local movie theater. “I thought I’d be a lawyer,” she says, “and then I did some internships in law and realized I could make money and I would hate my life.” Upon graduating from University of Pennsylvania, Giarla parlayed her love of reading into a gig in the books department at WME. The trouble, she’d soon learn, was that she was more interested in the books than the dealmaking. So, she shifted groups before segueing to Endeavor Content (later, Fifth Season), where she championed projects including East of Eden as a series for Netflix. Giarla would later jump with boss Joe Hipps to Cut To, a red-hot company that will soon have more shows than executives. Among its recent sales, all of which prompted frenzied bidding wars: the Joel Edgerton-led crime drama Trigger Point and a two-season order for a Gwyneth Paltrow drama. At press time, however, Giarla was more focused on her other major project, her newborn son, with whom she’s now home on maternity leave. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Lady Olenna Tyrell. I’ve been rewatching GoT on maternity leave. She’s inquisitive, sharp-tongued and loyal to a fault.“ MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I realized there was a typo on a deck that my boss was en route to present to Obama — at the White House. That was a crazy two hours.”
PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “Andy Cohen. The writers’ strike was in full swing when Scandoval hit, which gave me way too much downtime to stumble into the Bravoverse.”

- Jordan Gorelick, 34 UTA, talent agent LOGLINE Steers the career of rising stars Odessa A’zion and Alien: Earth lead Sydney Chandler. THE ARC As an undergrad at Colgate, Gorelick had his sights set on a career in screenwriting. The dream shifted, however, once he stumbled upon HBO’s Hollywood show Entourage and David Rensin’s book The Mailroom: Hollywood History From the Bottom Up. Suddenly, agenting was the goal, which led to an early gig in UTA’s mailroom. It was everything Gorelick had hoped for: “Watching the agents, the intensity, being a 21-year-old kid and driving around Hollywood and seeing the billboards on the Sunset Strip — I loved being in it.” Eleven years on, he’s constructing a list of rising stars (Nicholas Braun, Ray Nicholson, Lili Reinhart) and helping craft the next stage for established actors (Lizzy Caplan, Adam Scott, Timothy Olyphant, Paul Bettany). He feels his abandoned writing ambitions are actually key to his success. “The way I analyze and interpret and discuss material, that comes from a writer’s perspective and has set me apart in the way I work with actors.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kevin McCallister eating that cheese pizza in the stretch limo.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Buddy from Air Bud.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Driving a young Chalamet to general meetings.”

- Angie Haney, 31 Netflix, director, film LOGLINE Supplies Netflix with rom-com hits like Voicemails From Isabelle and People We Meet on Vacation. THE ARC Haney was outside the Vatican on vacation when she saw two girls filming themselves doing a choreographed dance featured in her latest movie, Voicemails for Isabelle. “I was like, ‘There’s no way that’s what they’re doing!’” She approached the girls in St. Peter’s Square and that was exactly what they were doing. While Haney is now Netflix’s romantic comedy whisperer, she grew up envisioning a career in politics. In high school, the L.A. native and future Columbia poli-sci major was a congressional intern for outgoing L.A. Mayor Karen Bass. But a series of entertainment internships — not to mention a childhood watching classics like Singin’ in the Rain with her voiceover actress mom, theater director dad and screenwriter twin brother — prompted a change of heart. After a cold email led to a stint at Disney, she landed a job as the assistant to then-Lucasfilm head Kathleen Kennedy as the Star Wars series were starting to populate Disney+. She’d later jump to Netflix, where she has found success with rom-coms and coming-of-age films. Up next: a reimagining of 13 Going on 30. “I’ve heard it said before that we should all make movies for our 12-year-old self,” she says, “And that is very true for me.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Watching George Lucas meet Grogu on the set of The Mandalorian.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR “Nora Ephron to have written 20 more movies.”

- Louie Hayes, 35 LuckyChap, vp TV LOGLINE The on-set producer for the summer smash Sterling Point. THE ARC Hayes’ family moved half a dozen times before he left for college. The constant in his home growing up was TV, which he claims he watched “an unhealthy amount of.” Eager to put down roots after graduating from Northwestern, he settled in L.A. with some college buddies. “At the time, everyone started at a talent agency,” he says, so he dutifully lined up a gig at Gersh. And while agenting wasn’t Hayes’ calling, it was there that he’d meet his future wife (and fellow Next Gen honoree), Samantha Militante, who’d later follow him to FX. But after nearly a decade as a buyer — working on hits like Dave and Alien: Earth — he jumped to LuckyChap, where he’s built an impressive roster. In fact, one of Hayes’ very first projects at the uber-successful Margot Robbie outfit was the runaway hit Sterling Point, which he was intimately involved with every step of the way. Up next: series Sex Criminals, from Kumail Nanjiani and Emily Gordon, and an adaptation of The Retrievals from Molly Smith Metzler. PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Jeff Probst. I consider Survivor America’s fifth major sport, and I have some ideas.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Arnold from Hey Arnold! An idealist with an oversized head and a compulsive need to help.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Don’t date anyone in the industry. My wife is on this list.”

- Julia Iglesias, 34 Focus Features, VP LOGLINE Shepherds artistic films including Sense and Sensibility and Nosferatu, along with the upcoming Werwulf and the adaptation of The Bell Jar. THE ARC Growing up in South Florida, Iglesias would regularly make her little sister act in her home movies. It wasn’t until she landed at Boston University that she learned how to turn her passion for storytelling into a career. “I did tons of internships,” she says, “and took all of the screenwriting and production classes I could get my hands on.” After a brief, post-grad stint as an unscripted postproduction coordinator at Relativity Media, she landed at NBCUniversal. A job working for then-Universal Filmed Entertainment Group chairman Jeff Shell turned into a gig at Focus Features, where Iglesias has been ever since. Now, the newly engaged exec — her fiancé proposed at this year’s Sundance Film Festival — cherishes seeing projects through to the end with auteurs like Sarah Polley and Robert Eggers. BEST ADVICE ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Pick your boss, not your job.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “The dog handler on Sense and Sensibility.”
THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Somewhere neither person has to valet.”

- Ben Iguchi, 32 Netflix, manager, original series, live-action comedy LOGLINE Champions buzzy comedies including Cobra Kai and Doozer Productions’ upcoming I Suck at Girls and Nick Kroll’s A Hundred Percent for Netflix. THE ARC Iguchi can’t remember a time when comedy wasn’t a central focus in his life. As he tells it, his Ph.D. dad had proposed to his dancer mom during an episode of The Golden Girls, and every memory in his childhood home seems to feature a sitcom of some kind. In fact, by the time Iguchi turned 13, Jewish comedy became his bar mitzvah theme. “It definitely was not cool,” he jokes as he recounts the Groucho Marx gla
