items.title: ‘I Love My Boyfriend — But Is He Rich Enough?’
items.description: I’m 28, and I’ve been dating my boyfriend, who’s 38, for about a month. Somehow, I’ve already found myself in an inconvenient place where I genuinely love him (which I know is absolutely insane to say a month in, but let me explain) — while simultaneously wond
items.author: Amy Rose Spiegel
paragraphs: I’m 28, and I’ve been dating my boyfriend, who’s 38, for about a month. Somehow, I’ve already found myself in an inconvenient place where I genuinely love him (which I know is absolutely insane to say a month in, but let me explain) — while simultaneously wondering if I should walk away.

I recently went through aggressive cancer treatment. I’m in remission now, so thank God I’m back to man problems and not “am I going to live” problems. Still, I lost my hair and have a lot of residual health issues. He’s more understanding about them than I ever could have imagined. Also, he’s sweet, funny, affectionate, and very into me. He makes me feel cared for in a way nobody else has. The sex is out of this world. We have an incredible connection, and he’s been very clear that he wants a wife and children someday. I can picture a version of my future with him. But there are some things I can’t stop thinking about.

I’ve come to the extremely ugly realization that, while I love my boyfriend, I want to marry someone richer. I’m not looking for someone to fund my life. I’m ambitious and independent; I have my own money and career. But I want a partner whose financial situation makes me feel secure and whose lifestyle is closer to the one I envision for myself. My boyfriend has a normal income and is still living with his mother, partly because he helps care for her. (He’s also slightly shorter than me, which bugs me a little.) Even writing this makes me feel like the worst person on earth.

After my health scare, I told myself I would set extremely high standards, especially because my last boyfriend abandoned me during the hardest moments of my life. So that part of me thinks that I’m only one month into this relationship and I’m already doing an enormous amount of mental gymnastics to justify it when I barely know the guy. But I also don’t want to waste his time when I know, long-term, he’ll probably want to put a ring on my finger.

The most conflicting part: Despite all of this, I don’t actually want to break up with him right now, no matter what I ultimately decide. I want to keep dating him. I love him. I’m attracted to him. I have fun with him. I have great sex with him. I want to see where this goes. And I wonder whether the desire to be with a well-off man is actually mine, or whether I learned it in a previous relationship where money and financial security were constantly emphasized. But I also don’t want to stay because I’m afraid I’ll never find someone better. I’ve worked very hard to build the life I want, and after my cancer changed my perspective on life, I’ve become more determined not to settle.
Am I making a mistake by continuing to date someone who, on paper, makes me question whether I could marry him? Or is it completely reasonable to keep dating while I discover more about who he is?
Most important: Is “I love him, but I want someone richer” a legitimate relationship incompatibility? Or am I being an asshole? I’d love an honest answer, even if the answer is that I’m the problem.

Hey, Healthy Perspective. I’m so glad to hear you’re in remission, though sorry to hear you are such an asshole. Just kidding! I’m not shocked or appalled by anything in your letter. There’s nothing amoral in wondering, post-chemo at 28, how to reconfigure your newly updated understanding of stability. Nor is it wrong to wonder if your age-gap sweetheart is The One, even if it’s only been a calendar month, even if he only has a “normal income.” (I laughed. I like you!)

Still, and I hate to tell you this: I really tried to write a few answers that zeroed in on this 38-year-old newcomer’s place in your life. All of them ultimately struck me as dishonest. I don’t think your letter is about your monthlong boyfriend’s net worth, like, at all. It’s irritating to dwell on cancer when you’d prefer to move back to man problems, but they’re linked. I promise I don’t want to simper to you about how you’re a survivor and we’re going to hear you roar! Illness and treatment have changed your perspective. You’re figuring out how, next, to live. While this is never easy, it at least used to be semiautomatic.

Maybe getting into a relationship not long after such a major life event feels like nailing down the furniture before another big one hits. Especially considering you felt abandoned by your last boyfriend and you’re anxious — and that would be true no matter how lovely this new guy is. Life is an ambush. Of course you’re inclined to ask, Does this man have enough money to keep me safe? Even when you are safe, and you have enough money to support yourself. Writing checklists about your perfect husband can feel like protection against dread. But you’re wise to wonder, too, if it’s possible all you’re protecting yourself from is falling in love with a worthy person.

I hope I can stretch a hand back through the past few years for you to hold. I was diagnosed with cancer at 31. It’s well-managed four years later. We’ve doubtlessly had different experiences; all people do. I never went through chemo or lost my hair, and I’m sorry you did. But for all we don’t have in common, you and I still know things others can’t, including that sex and romance remain priorities for career women such as ourselves, even when you’re hanging out in the hospital a lot.

Early on, my oncologist told me the cancer I have isn’t environmental. I didn’t smoke too much or not eat enough blueberries, thus, bam, fatal outcome. Nor is what I have a hereditary family heirloom, passed down like my Italo-shtetl nose through an odd combo of recessive genes. “It’s random, like God took a little segment of your genome and pinched it,” the doctor said, making a twisting motion with his index finger and thumb. No one could have prevented it, there is no cure, it might get worse. Interesting. So what could I control? And how fast? This is my fight song!!!

Even though embracing nihilism was seriously right there, I instead became dictatorial about what would happen next. Pre-diagnosis, I thought marriage was insane. After, I was certain it was the rational next step with my boyfriend, with whom I shared an apartment and a profound, impossible-to-articulate mutual unease. I reasoned that relationships were about compromise. Time to be mature. Because what if I got really sick?

All the while, I was obsessive about employment in the signature key of Americans who need “yes, forever” medications. (Mine is an interferon that reduces the risk of my cancer progressing into leukemia. Its sticker price is $20,000 per monthly dose. I only recently stopped rationing injections, just in case.) I walked around my workplace and heard its noises differently. Did everyone overdoing the professional jargon secretly have cancer? Death’s call rang out in every desperate, assimilating “circle back.” No, yeah, this email does find me — for now! Ha ha ha.

I wasn’t going to panic out loud, though. I was seriously going to be so okay. I urgently searched for cancer’s big important lessons, then rushed to apply them. Possibly like you, I knew intellectually that the nobility and profundity of cancer was a fable about a notoriously complicated group of illnesses. Still, I preferred this interpretation to other popular favorites, including, “You die, horribly for you and everyone you love” or rubber bracelets stamped #BadAssSurvivorChica.

Unlike death’s vast morass and #WarriorBitchLikeAGirl, “I’m learning big beautiful lessons!” is a workable approach, aesthetically and practically, when you’re about 30. It’s similar to the script we’re already fed: You’ve reached the knowing age. You’ve figured out your ethical belief systems, not to mention what hairstyles actually flatter your face. Maybe you can afford to live on your own, given your diligence at work. Life is coalescing!

Healthy Perspective, nothing could have interrupted my self-actualization reverie. Was it like that for you? Oh, my body is overdoing it, to a potentially fatal degree, cell-division-wise? Just another story to pluckily locate a moral for! You’ve partially built the stability you have, I bet, through dogged optimism. Me too. It’s fab! But it can make me too hasty to decipher the promise in every heartbreak. Death is, by definition, not just another amazing new opportunity for your future.

Plus, cancer warps and rarefies time. It’s whiplash inducing. Out of nowhere, you maybe don’t have a future? Then you access treatment, and there it is, once more. You’re not going to idly take it for granted this time! You’ve Learned From Cancer. So you make lists about money. You will not be caught unawares again.

Treatment is only the start. From there, whenever I talked or wrote in my journal about what I wanted from marriage, it felt like repeating the promise that I was becoming healthier. It was not ever about love. More so, it was about worthiness and a sort of gameness toward what “rationally” came next in life. I insisted I wasn’t afraid. I was making a plan. I wanted to get wifed up by a heterosexual office job because I thought it would help, in some way, to keep me alive.

But I was already alive. The “survivor” mind-set is a boondoggle even if you’re positive you’re too smart for it, badass chica! When I came to my senses and broke up with my then-boyfriend because he was a broke bitch — I’m just playing; he was great, but we weren’t compatible, which got too sad to ignore — he thought I was out of my mind. How could I leave, given how nice he was to me about my cancer? He pointed out that he had been there for me throughout all the hard times.
“That’s absolutely true, and I’m grateful,” I said. “But shouldn’t there also be good times?”

You’re having them. You’re in your late 20s, excited by someone who’s been consistently kind for the 30 days you’ve known him. Incredible! You already know this is the answer, per the end of your letter. Yes, it’s fine to step back and see what happens now. (Especially when you’re still sorting out how you feel after your last breakup.) Keep your standards in mind, but don’t rule out revisions at the expense of your happiness.

Also? The “big lessons” of cancer are very, very boring in the end. Always the same texture-free bromides about strength and, also, the power of being strong. More interesting is individuated, ambiguous self-discovery. Great news, my diva: It seems like that means continuing to have hot sex with your short boyfriend, just for now, just to see.

I understand and think it’s fair if you’re annoyed that I made your new-boyfriend letter about cancer. I would have been. But my gut tells me that, thanks to your ex, you already know that money alone doesn’t fortify a relationship, unless that’s most or all of what you’re looking for. Either way, I trust your discernment.

You seem to need me, instead, to say: Even if — when! — life ambushes you again, you’ll know what to do. Real stability means not jumping to decisions out of insecurity, whether you’re feeling it about death or love or anything else. You’re capable of changing your mind, come what may with this boyfriend of 30 days.

Please actively try to reorient your sense of time. Feel your way through each arriving day, the only one like it. In “On the Shortness of Life,” Seneca wrote, “The greatest obstacle to living is expectancy, which hangs upon tomorrow and loses today.” (Was Seneca a hot woman of about 30 with cancer? Historians of Roman Stoicism, weigh in.) Turning toward the present is about all there is to conclude, big lessons-wise. I think? Unless I missed the entire point of cancer? It’s possible! I have time to find out. Maybe. I’m choosing to think that I do.

You do too. When you get antsy, put $10 in your 401(k) and think, I throw my head back and laugh at Death! Read this poem about being 28 years old and observing the sunlight in your yard. The person who wrote it is now dead. Still, you can tell the warmth wasn’t wasted when the light washed over him. X ARS

items.title: Birth Rates Are Down. Give Party Dads a Chance.
items.description: You’ve probably heard that young Americans are experiencing an unparalleled parenting crisis. The surgeon general declared parenting a nationwide health emergency. Birth rates have steadily declined for two decades. Sam Altman thinks AI chatbots should prep ki
items.author: Sarah Wheeler
paragraphs: You’ve probably heard that young Americans are experiencing an unparalleled parenting crisis. The surgeon general declared parenting a nationwide health emergency. Birth rates have steadily declined for two decades. Sam Altman thinks AI chatbots should prep kids for their days on the drive to school.

In the midst of all this comes Jordan Firstman’s filmmaking debut, Club Kid, a laugh-a-minute, cry-into-your-popcorn banger of a movie that is small in scale but big in feeling. It makes a strong case for the positive impact of children on the sometimes directionless lives of adults. When queer party promoter Peter learns he made a baby the one time he accidentally slept with a woman (yes, it’s medically possible; yes, it’s a movie), he has to transition quickly from coke on the coffee table to caring for another human — 10-year-old Arlo. Can a wayward gay with a few thousand bucks in his bank account handle the responsibility of a child? Some of Peter’s friends clearly think absolutely not. But what does a child really need from an adult, anyway?

Many have compared Club Kid to Adam Sandler’s 1999 movie, Big Daddy, where, in a much more cis, straight world, Sandler’s character adopts a kid to win back the affections of a woman who has deemed him too immature. The plots are eerily similar, but — maybe this is my hetero-pessimism talking — the vibes couldn’t be more different. To use Club Kid’s parlance, while the film does “give” Big Daddy, it’s more spiritually related to Mike Mills’s tremendous 2021 film, C’mon C’mon, which starred Joaquin Phoenix as a bachelor uncle who gets stuck with his sister’s kid for a while and whose heart grows three sizes in the process.

As in C’mon C’mon, the chemistry between Firstman’s Peter and the outstanding Reggie Absolom’s Arlo is as palpable as an EDM beat, and the audience finds itself wishing someone would look at us the way these two look at each other. Despite his precocious taste in music (“But I like Björk!”), Arlo is not an unrealistic child. He comes close to but never quite crosses that cringey “Curly Sue” rubicon wherein a magical child turns a bad adult (usually a straight white man) good with sheer pluck and probing truisms. Sure, he is eager to please and strangely comfortable with grown-ups, but many parentified children adopt these traits as a matter of survival. (We learn throughout the film that Arlo’s mother was not capable of keeping him safe, even if she did love him very much.)

Anyone with children in their lives can feel how grounded the impact of Arlo on Peter truly is in the film. The love he builds is almost painfully tender, like the ache I feel when I watch my daughter’s sleeping face after she has called me the worst mom in the world for making a spicy dinner. I know she doesn’t mean it, that being a child in an adult world is strange and cruel and sacred. “He’s cleaner than me,” Peter says of his son. Cue the tears.

How does one become a good dad? Peter doesn’t quite seem to know, but loving Arlo lets him love himself, and we watch that growth over the span of a tight two-hour run time in surprisingly authentic beats for a somewhat hackneyed premise (see Big Daddy, above). In one tense scene, Peter is torn about whether to put Arlo in a very adult situation that he and others are counting on. As a parent myself, who wasn’t exactly fucking strangers on “G” when my kids were born but who has grown up considerably over the decade since, it was a revelation to watch Peter learn to define the boundaries that needed to be created between his child and the world, and realizing, not without horror, that he is the one who has to set them. You may hold your breath at this point in the film because you are scared for Arlo, but perhaps also because you are bearing witness to the uneven, messy metamorphosis we humans undergo when tasked with the care of other people.

Arlo doesn’t judge Peter’s queer community, and they, in turn, don’t judge him. They know how shitty the world can be, and they let him have fun in it, get angry in it, whatever he needs to do. There is no pathologizing here. Besides, plenty of kids growing up in two-parent heterosexual homes have it pretty bad. What could be so horrible about giving a single gay man in active ketamine withdrawal a chance?

Peter is not alone in his initial confusion around what purpose a child could possibly fill in his life: Published just a few months ago, journalist Anna Louie Sussman’s Inconceivable: The Impossibility of Family in an Age of Uncertainty laid out the endless reasons (family-last policy, crap economy, lack of community) that we don’t want or can’t have kids. In 2024’s What Are Children For?, by philosophers Anastasia Berg and Rachel Wiseman, an entire book is made out of the ambivalence that Millennials and Gen Z have towards child-rearing. Last year’s If I Had Legs I’d Kick You, a very different movie that encapsulated, importantly, the rough side of parenting that elder Millennials have perhaps emphasized too much, was unwatchable for some (not me!) for this reason. Watching Club Kid, I feared that some viewers might be too uncomfortable with the casual references to Arlo’s past and future trauma, or the precarious situations Peter puts him in (these are not treated casually, though, despite being filled with humor). Sadly, we do live in a society that takes terrible care of children. Over 10 million children in the US live in poverty. One in seven experience abuse or neglect. At least 200,000 have had a parent detained by immigration in the past two years. Club Kid hurts for Arlo, and leads the audience to wish for him to have a parent who has their shit together. But it respects the reality of childhood by not glossing over how hard childhood actually is for most kids.

Another fall film about the way children can alter the paths of their fathers in interesting new ways is the standout Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which stars Mahershala Ali as a hit man named Latif whose wife dies and leaves him to care for his three children while trying to get himself out of a job he doesn’t want to do. Just like Club Kid’s Peter, the juxtapositions between Latif’s lifestyle and his parenting never get old, and YMYMYM treats us to the most edge-of-your-seat breastfeeding scene you never knew you needed. It’s a premise that is perhaps a tad more far-fetched than a gay man’s onetime vaginal ejaculation turning up a decade later, but great writing and acting (and a jaw-dropping breakout performance from Adia as Latif’s teenage daughter, Fatiha) keep the parent-child relationships grounded.

There’s some killer swordwork in YMYMYM, but it’s ultimately a story about how the love for your children saves you — from inertia and grief and, most important, yourself. In making YMYMYM, the film’s writer and director, Bassam Tariq, a father of two, wanted to explore what happens when children see the worst parts of their father, the “monster side.” His thesis, in life and in the film, is that as long as you keep showing up authentically for your children, they will love you no matter what. Maybe there are, and should be, a few exceptions to this rule, but despite not considering myself a pro-natalist, I can’t help but pitch this as one of the most powerful reasons to procreate.

We know what these films think children are for, but what are adults for, especially at a time when it’s hard for them to get jobs or homes, or when a global pandemic fucked the rythm of their young adulthood and they are still stuck six years later? Firstman, 35, hasn’t had children yet, though he did donate sperm for his sister’s partner’s baby, becoming an uncle for the first time on the last day of filming Club Kid. He has said, though, that the process of making this movie forced him to grow up. “I needed to change and I didn’t know how,” he’s told crowds at Club Kid screenings. Luckily for him, he was able to knock out some self-transformation while making a hell of a film. For the rest of us, there’s always parenting.

items.title: Exclusive: Jesse Kove Teases Whitney Leavitt’s “Raw Talent” In Her 1st Movie Role
items.description: Keeping up with Whitney Leavitt’s post-#MomTok resume feels like you’re making a list and checking it twice. Her last year was a dizzying run from Dancing with the Stars to Broadway, The Traitors, and her own forthcoming reality show. This holiday season, the
items.author: Grace Wehniainen
paragraphs: Keeping up with Whitney Leavitt’s post-#MomTok resume feels like you’re making a list and checking it twice. Her last year was a dizzying run from Dancing with the Stars to Broadway, The Traitors, and her own forthcoming reality show. This holiday season, the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star is putting her own spin on a beloved pop-culture tradition: the holiday rom-com.

All for Christmas stars Leavitt and Jesse Kove as Winona and Luke, a podcaster and craftsman who work together on a renovation project — as seen in Bustle’s exclusive behind-the-scenes images ahead. At first, Winona doesn’t quite see Luke as romance material. But unbeknownst to her, he’s the very same man she just matched with through a dating-app partnership.
Beyond that delightful You’ve Got Mail-esque twist, Kove tells Bustle the movie “feels like one of those warm-hearted ’90s rom-coms.”

Before filming, Kove wasn’t too familiar with Leavitt’s work on The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives. But the actor — whose own resume spans action, romance, and beyond — had previously worked with director and producer Jake Helgren on projects such as The Holiday Proposal Plan, and welcomed the opportunity to star opposite Leavitt in her first film role.

“Whitney has so much raw talent. She was able to put all that energy into this project,” Kove says, noting that even though Leavitt had just come from the rigorous competition of Dancing with the Stars, she was more than game for the festive film at hand. “She was so looking forward to showing up and being there for the crew, and also for her character. She and I did a lot of laughing along the way.”
Indeed, practical jokes abounded. The pair filmed each other in playfully off-guard moments, and Kove was sure to bring up Leavitt’s DWTS run while filming a dance scene.

For Kove, Leavitt’s sense of humor was one of the gifts of working together — something he’s definitely down to do again. “I was so delightfully surprised at her attention to detail and how funny she is,” he says. “She’s so quirky and silly, which I didn’t expect.”

Expect that feeling to translate on screen when All for Christmas streams Nov. 24 on Netflix. “I want viewers to feel joy when they watch this movie because it is filled with a lot of love,” Kove says. “It’s also about giving people second chances, which is a great aspect of the movie as well.”

And that’s coming from a certified rom-com fan — as Kove names Love Actually, The Holiday, and How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days as just a few of his favorite titles. His only tip for watching this one? “Make sure when you do, that you’re all snuggled up under a blanket,” he says. “And you get some candles, maybe a glass of wine, and just enjoy.”

items.title: Refinery29 Loves: Our Favorite Fashion & Beauty Buys From October
items.description: Refinery29 Loves: Our Favorite Fashion & Beauty Buys From October
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: Refinery29 Loves: Our Favorite Fashion & Beauty Buys From October
Cécred Temple Oud Hair Perfume

"As soon as I tried Cécred, I fell in love with how it made my hair feel, but what I loved even more was how it made my hair smell. The signature Temple Oud scent is this beautiful blend of bergamot, night-blooming jasmine, rich oud, and warm sandalwood. So when they launched it as a hair perfume, I was immediately sold. The lightweight mist refreshes my hair without weighing it down, and because hair naturally holds onto fragrance, the scent lingers throughout the day. It’s my favorite way to elevate my everyday routine with a spritz of fragrance that follows me wherever I go." — Brooke DeVard, Chief Content Officer
Stila All Fire Liquid Eye Shadow & Kajal Eye Liner Duo

"As a die-hard Hunger Games girlie, I'm already counting down the days until Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters. So when one of my longtime favorite makeup brands, Stila, unveiled a collaboration inspired by the upcoming film, I had to get my hands on it. My standout pick from the collection is the All Fire Liquid Eye Shadow & Kajal Eye Liner Duo, featuring a shimmery bronze liquid eyeshadow and a smoky black eye pencil. (Fun fact: The name is a nod to Haymitch's romance with his District 12 sweetheart, Lenore Dove.) Together, they make the easiest two-step eye look: I sweep a wash of bronze across my lids and tightline my upper waterline for an effortlessly pretty daytime look, then build up the shimmer and intensity for date night." — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer
Bath & Body Works Worth Wanting Eau de Parfum

"I'll always have a soft spot for Bath & Body Works. While the brand usually scratches a nostalgic itch for me, its new Everyday Luxuries collection — a lineup of fragrances inspired by designer scents — has seriously impressed me as a perfume snob. Dare I say, some of these affordable alternatives might even beat their high-end counterparts? My favorite of the bunch is Worth Wanting, which has quickly become my signature scent for fall. With notes of juicy stone fruits, delicate lily, and whipped honey, it's fruity, cozy, and just the right amount of indulgent. Despite its decadent-sounding notes, the fragrance feels surprisingly fresh and airy, making it just as lovely worn solo as it is layered with something woodier for a more earthy, grounded vibe. Proof that smelling expensive doesn't have to be." — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer
Lounge ContourSoft Cinch Zip-Up Jacket

"The weather is dropping below 70 degrees, which means I’m swapping my tank-and-shorts activewear for warmer sets. Right now, I'm reaching for Lounge's ContourSoft sets. The buttery-soft fabric of these fitted leggings keeps my legs covered but not constricted. Meanwhile, the cinch zip-up jacket allows me to cover up or remove layers depending on fall’s unpredictable temperature changes. I’ve been wearing the set in the shade of dark chocolate, but I’m seriously eyeing cherry lacquer, too." — Raquel Reichard, Somos, Deputy Director
Dr. Loretta Barrier Enhancing Milky Essence

"As someone with dry skin, I’m forever chasing that juicy, dewy glow, especially during the fall and winter months when my skin wants to drink up every ounce of moisture it can get. This milky essence from Dr. Loretta has quickly become my favorite part of my morning skincare routine. I love pressing it into my skin before sunscreen for an instant hit of hydration that leaves my complexion looking plump, bouncy, and deliciously dewy. It’s packed with skin-loving ingredients like niacinamide, ectoin, and glycerin to support the skin barrier, lock in moisture, and soothe irritation. It’s lightweight, layers beautifully, and gives me that fresh, hydrated glow I’m always trying to achieve without a drop of makeup." — Brooke DeVard, Chief Content Officer
Reformation Clara Cashmere Crew Cardigan

"If you haven’t heard, purple is trending right now, and I’ve jumped on the bandwagon with this cute cashmere cardigan from Reformation. I love Reformation’s sweaters, and this is the perfect layering piece dressed down with sweats and a tee or to add some color to one of my all-black outfits." — Lisa Dionisio, Homepage & Newsletter Director
Salon Perfect Chill Short Square Press-On Nails

"I've always had a love-hate relationship with press-on nails. In theory, salon-worthy designs without the appointment, dry time, or hefty price tag sound like a dream. In reality? I've had nails pop off within hours of application. (Opening a can of soda? Forget about it.) So when I didn't have time for a manicure before an out-of-town wedding, I tossed a pack of these champagne cat-eye Salon Perfect press-ons into my carry-on and hoped for the best. Not only did they survive a night of dinner and dancing, but they stayed put for nearly two weeks. I'm not exaggerating: It took a full 14 days for a single nail to jump ship, at which point I finally removed the set. Since then, I've tried several more designs — including a fall-inspired ombré set I'm wearing as I type this — and the staying power continues to blow me away. At just $8 a pack, consider me a press-on convert." — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer
PS Goodnight Printed Ruffle Short Sleeve Pajama Set

"Walking into my home feels like I'm entering the set of my favorite period dramas, just with some Puerto Rican banderas sprinkled in. I've mixed second-hand, vintage trinkets with new furniture inspired by a previous epoch to curate a home that would belong to a Latina Jane Austen. Well, everything except for my jammies. I'm trying to change that, trying to have my nightwear reflect the mood I’ve set for other parts of my home life. And I'm starting with PS Goodnight's Printed Ruffle Short Sleeve Pajama set, a baby-blue printed lightweight woven fabric set with short puff sleeves and ruffled trimming. I’m loving it!" — Raquel Reichard, Somos, Deputy Director
Goldie Tees Audrey Cardigan

"Cardigan season is my favorite (it’s also a great Taylor Swift song!). What I love about cardigans is that they're timeless, so investing in quality styles won't just last for years to come but will look great however they're worn with changing trends. My black Goldie Tee’s Audrey Cardigan is lightweight, has some stretch, and is made from ribbed knit fabric, so it pairs beautifully with denim pants, fitted skirts, or just sweatpants during cool, cozy days indoors." — Raquel Reichard, Somos, Deputy Director
YSL Loveshine Plumping Lip Oil

"I first discovered YSL's Loveshine Plumping Lip Oil last year during a trip to Marrakech with the brand, where I got to see the chili peppers and ginger used in the formula growing in the brand’s own community gardens. Fast-forward to this fall, when YSL unveiled a coffee-inspired collection featuring new shades of the glossy lip treatment. My favorite? Cold Brew Craze, a sheer, caramel-brown hue that's basically cozy season in lip gloss form. You can definitely feel a subtle warming sensation from the peppers, but it's far from uncomfortable — and the plumping effect is noticeable without leaving your lips looking overly red or swollen. I've been layering it over my go-to nude lip liner for the ultimate cozy-girl lip combo, and suffice it to say, I'm obsessed." — Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer

"During a recent press trip to Germany, I was told a day before my flight that I’d be attending a ball and needed to pack a gown. Where was I going to find a dress after work that was appropriate for a European-style ball? Turns out there was one hanging in my closet. I was already planning on wearing JJ's House's Felia dress for my friend's wedding, but its floor-length, mermaid silhouette, ruffle chiffon slit, and deep burgundy shade made it equally perfect for a fancy dance. With some makeup and accessory changes, I felt beautiful and comfortable both days, in the same affordable gown, just styled slightly differently." — Raquel Reichard, Somos, Deputy Director
Anastasia Beverly Hills Genesis Eyeshadow Palette

"It’s been a minute since I’ve had an Anastasia Beverly Hills palette, but full glam is back and so is ABH. As I lean into my pale girl era for winter, I keep reaching for these soft taupes and dusty roses that don’t pull too warm on my neutral skin tone. They make for a gorgeous everyday blush-toned look, and the generous mirror is the cherry on top for travel. I keep getting compliments every time I pair it with a super cool-toned pink blush." — Taylor Loren, Social Media Director
Live Tinted Magic Blur Primer Stick

"As someone with large pores and texture, I’m a bit of a primer enthusiast, and I can honestly say this is the best one I’ve ever used. I don’t know what kind of magic makes it glide onto my skin like that (I’m not the beauty editor on our team!), but the application feels so nice, and my makeup looks so much better with it. Plus, the stick format just makes sense: no primer-covered hands, just a smooth, beautiful base. I’m obsessed and telling everyone!" — Taylor Loren, Social Media Director
Mario Badescu Hydrogel Under Eye Patches

"Okay, these eye patches aren’t new, but they were new to me, so I had to shout them out. I’ve never been a huge fan of eye patches because I thought they were all a scam, but these ones have been a lifesaver as the weather gets colder and my skin gets drier (in fact, I’m wearing them as I write this!). It always shocks me just how cooling they are. Plus, I love the thin jelly consistency. After use, I notice that my under-eye area is a bit less puffy, a bit brighter, and my fine lines aren’t as noticeable thanks to them being soaked in hyaluronic acid and niacinamide goodness." — Taylor Loren, Social Media Director
Charlotte Tilbury Exagger-Eyes Waterproof Eyeshadow Stick

"I’m someone who typically uses my bronzer and blush as my eyeshadow (because I’m usually lazy), but when I tried this eyeshadow stick at a Charlotte Tilbury masterclass, I was converted. The crayon shape and creamy formula make it so easy and quick to swipe over my eyelids. I have a few sparkly shades now, and they make the perfect no-muss, no-fuss eye (and highlighter if you have a shade light enough) for glam makeup looks. I’m excited to use them during the holidays for an extra festive touch." — Victoria Montalti, Senior Fashion Commerce Writer
Gola Classics Women's Corva Snake Sneakers

"I own a few Gola sneakers, and the newest addition to my collection is the green snakeskin print Corva shoes. I wear a lot of green and animal prints are basically neutrals at this point, so this pick was a no-brainer. They’re a great (surprisingly versatile) fall sneaker, but I can see myself wearing them cross-seasonally too." — Victoria Montalti, Senior Fashion Commerce Writer
Damson Madder Alphia Neck Tie Alpaca Blend Jumper

"Another Damson Madder piece has entered the chat. While I purchased a reversible Damson Madder jacket last month, I was gifted this sweater-and-scarf combo this month. The bright berry color is so striking and cheerful (and got me lots of compliments). I love that there’s a slit in the neckline for the scarf to slip into and stay in place all day, sans constant fidgeting. The wool is a bit more coarse than I had imagined because it looks fuzzy in photos, so I’ve simply added a short-sleeve top underneath for extra comfort." — Victoria Montalti, Senior Fashion Commerce Writer

items.title: Shunning people who ‘look homeless’ is an aesthetic injustice | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Being homeless is an unjust social condition. Unhoused individuals not only lack the resources necessary to satisfy their basic needs, but they are also excluded from the rest of society. They have little access to healthy food, to security, to the requirement
items.author: Giacomo Floris
paragraphs: Being homeless is an unjust social condition. Unhoused individuals not only lack the resources necessary to satisfy their basic needs, but they are also excluded from the rest of society. They have little access to healthy food, to security, to the requirements of good health. They are unable to fit in and participate in the normal activities of society, such as getting a job, and they are pushed to live in dangerous and socially deprived areas. But material deprivation and social exclusion are not the only injustices suffered by unhoused individuals. They also face aesthetic injustice. This is a widely neglected source of harm associated with homelessness, which seriously impedes the ability of unhoused people to live a life of dignity and to better their circumstances.

To understand the nature of aesthetic injustice, it will be helpful to start with the more general notion of justice. Justice concerns how people should be treated, and political philosophers often say that justice requires everyone to be treated with equal respect and concern. ‘Each person,’ wrote the philosopher John Rawls in A Theory of Justice (1971), ‘possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.’ An injustice, therefore, occurs when an individual is treated in a way that is incompatible with the respect and concern that is owed to them as an equal. Harming someone is unjust because it fails to express appropriate concern for their wellbeing. Exercising arbitrary power over an individual is unjust because it violates the equal freedom that everyone is entitled to.

Aesthetic injustice is a specific kind of injustice: it consists in the wrongful treatment of individuals based on how they look. In our society, many people benefit or suffer from aesthetic injustice. As the economist Daniel Hamermesh argued in his book Beauty Pays (2011), individuals perceived as physically attractive typically command higher salaries and occupy more prestigious positions. He estimated that the best-looking people, over the course of their careers, make around $250,000 more than their less attractive colleagues. Similarly, as Sean Talamas and colleagues found, attractiveness is strongly correlated with perceived competence and intelligence – despite bearing almost no relationship to actual performance. And as the philosopher Kate Manne showed in Unshrinking (2024), fat people are often bullied, discriminated against and marginalised. These are all instances of aesthetic injustice: individuals are treated as more or less worthy of respect and concern by virtue of their outward appearance.

The outward appearance of unhoused individuals is often a reflection of their social condition. Due to the lack of sufficient resources and reliable shelter, unhoused individuals typically display signs of deterioration, such as unkempt hair and damaged skin. Their clothing is frequently dirty and ill-fitting. Additionally, many unhoused individuals exhibit visible signs of substance use disorders, such as track marks on the arms and dilated blood vessels. In the sociologist Erving Goffman’s classic study Stigma (1963), he names these aesthetic traits ‘stigma symbols’. A stigma, for Goffman, is ‘an attribute that is deeply discrediting’. By possessing these aesthetic stigmas, unhoused individuals are placed at the very bottom of the aesthetic hierarchy. They are regarded as disgusting elements of the urban landscape, whose presence in prime urban areas – areas that are desirable due to their location or historical significance – is unacceptable.

To appreciate this, consider the wide range of strategies that are adopted by many cities in order to exclude unhoused individuals from prime urban areas, such as anti-homelessness laws and ‘hostile’ architecture. Unhoused individuals are likely to be fined for loitering in commercial districts, while they are permitted to remain in socially deprived neighbourhoods. As the legal scholar Robert Ellickson put it, ‘[a] bum on a Skid Row sidewalk would never hear [“move along”] because he was exactly where the cop wanted him’ – that is, away from profitable business districts or valuable residential areas. Similarly, ‘anti-sleep’ benches and ‘ground spikes’ are widespread in parks and main commercial streets, whereas they are nowhere to be found in socially deprived areas. These measures illustrate how negative aesthetic judgments about unhoused individuals are institutionalised through public policy and urban design.

Aesthetic injustice against unhoused people is sustained and compounded by the fact that they are deprived of their capacity for self-presentation, that is, the ability to exercise reasonable control over how they present themselves to others. This is because unhoused individuals lack ‘aesthetic resources’: the materials, tools and conditions that either directly contribute to a person’s aesthetic properties or are constitutive components of them. Without access to showers, unhoused individuals are unable to maintain personal cleanliness. Without grooming products, such as soap and razors, they’re unable to keep tidy their hair, skin and facial features. As a result, unhoused people cannot shape how they present themselves to others. They cannot but look homeless.

The deprivation of the capacity for self-presentation is unjust for two reasons. First, it reinforces the social exclusion of unhoused individuals. Employers typically screen out candidates whose appearance departs from the aesthetic norms of a ‘serious’ candidate – unkempt hair, wrinkled or dirty clothing, the absence of basic grooming – whatever their actual qualifications. The injustice is therefore doubled: unhoused individuals are denied the resources needed to present themselves as employable and are then penalised for lacking a presentation they were never given the means to produce.
They cannot choose which aspects of their appearance to reveal or withhold

The philosopher Andrea Sangiovanni points to the second reason it is unjust. In his book Humanity without Dignity (2017), he contends that developing and maintaining an integral sense of self requires the fundamental ability to exercise some degree of control over how we are perceived. That is, we need to be able to manage ‘what is inner and what is outer, what is presented and what is hidden’. In intimate relationships, for example, we may choose to reveal personal vulnerabilities, while professional relationships usually demand a more formal, public-facing image.

It’s morally necessary that we have the means of choosing what to reveal, and to whom, and how to present ourselves. Wearing a suit conveys professionalism, while casual clothing indicates approachability. Wearing a kippah represents an individual’s affiliation with the Jewish community, while wearing a hijab is associated with Muslim identity. Due to the lack of adequate aesthetic resources, unhoused individuals cannot shape and control how they present themselves to others. They cannot choose which aspects of their appearance to reveal or withhold, as most people routinely do. The inability to determine one’s outward appearance is, therefore, a violation of unhoused individuals’ status as equal, self-presenting persons – in Sangiovanni’s words, ‘as beings who have a say in how [they] are to be seen by others’.

How should a just society address the aesthetic injustices suffered by unhoused individuals? To start with, the social norms of respectable appearance – that is, the aesthetic standards that determine what counts as an acceptable way of presenting oneself in public spaces – should be revised. This is not to say, of course, that all people must be regarded as equally beautiful. Rather, it is to say that no one should be excluded from prime public spaces based solely on their appearance (provided that they satisfy very minimal aesthetic standards, such as covering their genitalia). This would involve abolishing beautification projects aimed at removing unhoused individuals from public spaces. For example, in Ottawa, Canada, officers of the National Capital Commission (NCC) are authorised to remove unhoused individuals from parks and confiscate their belongings on the grounds that they are in violation of ‘beautification goals’. As one study reports, NCC conservation officers often ‘approach homeless people as garbage and do not distinguish between homeless people and their belongings as objects for removal from parks’. No one should be denied access to and enjoyment of public spaces because they are perceived as ugly.

However, revising social norms of respectable appearance is not sufficient. A just society should ensure not only that unhoused individuals have the right to live and exist in prime urban areas, but also that they have the resources necessary to exercise some control over how they appear to others. It is not enough to grant unhoused people access to public spaces independently of their appearance – it is also necessary to provide them with the opportunity to shape and control their appearance as a matter of respect for their status as self-presenting persons. In pursuit of this goal, there are many charities providing free haircuts to unhoused people and programmes offering new and gently used clothes, including business attire. These are the kinds of social initiatives that society should actively promote as a matter of justice rather than as a matter of charity, since everyone has the right to the resources necessary to determine how they appear to others, at least to some extent.

Hardly anyone denies that being homeless is an unjust social condition characterised by material deprivation and social exclusion. But this doesn’t capture the entirety of the injustice that unhoused people suffer. Part of the burden of being homeless is to be regarded as a disgusting element of the urban landscape whose presence in public areas is unacceptable. That burden is badly compounded by the denial of aesthetic resources. Without a shower, a razor, a change of clean clothes, unhoused individuals are denied what those lucky enough to be housed take for granted: a say in how to appear to the world. A just society owes the unhoused the right to be looked at without disgust, and the resources to decide, for themselves, how they wish to be seen.

items.title: Those forced to cross borders are imagining a radical new world | Aeon Essays
items.description: In 1986, I was 19 and behind bars in a small prison on the border between Iran and Pakistan. I had been arrested while attempting to cross the border irregularly into Pakistan. Everyone I met in that prison had been detained in connection with the border. It w
items.author: Shahram Khosravi
paragraphs: In 1986, I was 19 and behind bars in a small prison on the border between Iran and Pakistan. I had been arrested while attempting to cross the border irregularly into Pakistan. Everyone I met in that prison had been detained in connection with the border. It was a small space, the cells overcrowded and unsanitary, but it held an extraordinary diversity of people: local smugglers, large-scale drug-traffickers, undocumented migrant workers, and refugees; Iranians, Afghans, Pakistanis, as well as Baluch men whose communities had crossed these lands freely for generations but who were now being punished for violating the territorial order of the nation-state. Multiple languages were spoken at once. Different histories, geographies and ways of inhabiting the world converged within the same confined space.

Yet we all shared one thing. We had refused, for different reasons, to respect the border. The state saw us through a single imaginary: as criminals, trespassers or illegal bodies to be contained. We, however, were animated by different imaginations. Each of us had imagined a life that exceeded the border and acted upon that imagination. In that sense, the prison did not simply contain border-crossers; it brought together people whose aspirations had collided with the territorial imaginary of the nation-state.

That prison experience was perhaps one reason I became a scholar of borders. It remains, even today, the most important school of border studies I have ever attended. The conversations in the cells and during brief moments in the prison yard revolved around borders; how they operated, how they were enforced and, above all, how they might be circumvented. The prison became an unlikely site of knowledge-production: not simply the sharing of survival strategies but the enactment of an imagination that paid no heed to prison walls or state borders.

Many years later, in a prison north of Stockholm, I interviewed a human smuggler who told me he saw himself as an architect: ‘I design a journey, like an architect designs a building,’ he said. The comparison stayed with me. Architects imagine and design structures that do not yet exist. Their work begins with the capacity to visualise what is not yet visible. In a similar way, smugglers design border crossings that, from the perspective of the state, would be impossible. A smuggler’s work consists of imagining routes where borders appear closed, creating connections where states impose separation, and envisioning possibilities for mobility when people are immobilised by borders. A smuggler speculates on possibilities in seemingly impossible situations. Seen this way, the smuggler’s ‘architecture’ is an enactment of an imagination that refuses the state imaginary expressed through borders.

The parallels between human smuggling and architecture helped me understand the relationship between imagination, fugitivity and knowledge-production. While fugitivity and imagination are oriented toward the future, toward not-yet-realised possibilities, state power often relies on backward-looking imaginaries grounded in myths of shared blood, origin and belonging. States are hostile to this relationship because it exposes borders as political constructions that can be reimagined, negotiated and crossed. Like capitalism, the nation-state depends upon such imaginaries to stabilise its claims to totality, making it difficult to imagine a world beyond capitalism and the nation-state system.
Precisely because imagination opens the possibility of other worlds, states often regard it as a threat

All around us, across the world, people are being confined, displaced, silenced and rendered disposable, in service of imaginaries that seek to define the limits of life, mobility and freedom. We live in a conjunctural moment shaped by the convergence of two dark forces: borderless wars that destroy lives, produce death and generate displacement, and endless borders that deny mobility to those seeking survival. Together, they produce fugitive lives and fugitive bodies. But they also produce fugitive imagination, the irreducible capacity to envision and enact life beyond the worlds that seek to contain it.

Philosophers often define imagination as the capacity to hold present in the mind what is absent from sensory perception. It is also the capacity to envision alternative ways of organising social reality. Precisely because imagination opens the possibility of other worlds, states often regard it as a threat. The state-centric imaginary presents history as coherent, and intact through symbols, narratives and rituals. The capacity to disrupt the hegemony of state imaginaries is therefore criminalised, suppressed and persecuted. In this sense, fugitivity is inseparable from imagination.

A fugitive is someone fleeing harsh institutions and conditions. The fugitive is an outlaw: a person hiding from a hostile law. Historically, the term referred to enslaved people’s resistance to slavery, its dehumanising logic, and the political economy built upon the extraction of uncompensated labour to maximise profits from cash crops like cotton, tobacco and sugar. Fugitivity was a response to captivity and, as such, an act of liberation, not only from the brutal material conditions of enslavement, but also from the imposed image of the enslaved subject produced by racist ideology. Fugitivity is a way of escaping and a way of knowing.

When Frederick Douglass, one of the most important figures in the 19th-century struggle for African American freedom and civil rights, began learning to read, his enslaver Hugh Auld forbade it, declaring that, if Douglass learned to read, ‘there would be no keeping him’. Once capable of reading, Auld argued, Douglass would inevitably desire to write, and ‘this accomplished, he will be running away with himself.’

This phrase is striking. It suggests a distinction between the enslaved person and the enslaved body. To ‘run away with oneself’ is not simply to flee physically; it is to reclaim one’s imagination and humanity. Under slavery, where Black bodies were turned into capital, fugitivity was criminalised as theft. The fugitive was pursued by law because they were perceived to have stolen property from their enslaver: their own body. In reality, they were reclaiming what had first been stolen from them. If the captivity of the body depends upon the captivity of the mind, then the emancipation of consciousness becomes a precondition for bodily liberation. Such emancipation engenders new subjectivities and creates the conditions for imagining what previously appeared impossible: life beyond chains, borders and confinement. Auld’s anxiety over Douglass’s literacy reflected precisely this logic. His fear was not simply the loss of labour, but the emergence of a subject who would not obey the racial imaginary; ‘he will be running away with himself.’
Literacy was inseparable from emancipation, whereas pedagogy became fugitive

The condition of fugitivity emerged from a radical imagination capable of envisioning existence beyond oppression. As a refusal of captivity, it entailed an inner transformation – a reorientation of consciousness that makes escape conceivable in the first place. This is the transformative power of imagination: it enables subjects to perceive possibilities beyond the limits imposed by domination. As Frantz Fanon reminds us in The Wretched of the Earth (1961), resistance opens a path toward liberation through a radical transformation of consciousness. Fugitivity is therefore a refusal to be objectified, categorised and reduced to the singular identities imposed by colonial imaginaries. The passage from subjection to freedom, from a colonial imaginary to a fugitive imagination, is thus a process of self-actualisation and the cultivation of what might be called a consciousness of refusal.

Despite prohibition and danger, Douglass pursued literacy covertly. Reading and writing eventually enabled him to forge passes for himself and others and to flee bondage. Literacy was thus inseparable from emancipation, whereas pedagogy became fugitive in two senses: first, because it was concerned with experiences of flight, concealment and resistance; and, second, because it was itself practised under conditions of flight and opacity.

Knowing the emancipatory power of education, many enslaved people continued to learn despite violent restrictions and anti-literacy laws. In Fugitive Pedagogy: Carter G Woodson and the Art of Black Teaching (2021), the historian Jarvis Givens traces the history of criminalised Black education in the United States, documenting the struggles of Black educators and students against centuries of anti-literacy laws and racist policing. The struggle surrounding Black education did not end with slavery, continuing instead through the era of racial segregation under Jim Crow and into the present. Contemporary attacks on Black studies and critical race theory in the US are among the latest examples of hostility toward forms of knowledge that expose structures of racial subordination.

In recent years, operations by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to arrest undocumented migrants have often been conducted near schools, where parents drop off and pick up their children. Such practices have deterred many parents from sending their children to school for fear of detention and deportation. One of the consequences of these enforcement strategies is that they undermine access to education and disrupt the pedagogical conditions. A study of five California school districts found a 22 per cent increase in daily student absences following ICE raids conducted in early 2025.

The situation is not much different in Europe. Universities are increasingly shaped by hostile political climates in which curricula are regulated, funding is reduced, and critical fields of enquiry are delegitimised. In such contexts, critical knowledge itself becomes fugitive. For example, Sweden recently proposed a controversial law requiring state employees, including teachers and university professors, to report undocumented migrants to the police; following protests, the law was amended to exclude teachers and doctors, but tax officers and insurance agents must still ‘snitch’ on the undocumented.

Across different historical periods and geographical contexts, we see attempts to control or criminalise education in order to reproduce the state imaginary and suppress any stirrings of a fugitive imagination.

Palestine offers a striking example of the relationship between imagination, knowledge and fugitivity. Palestinian resistance is sustained by a fugitive imagination of freedom beyond colonial domination. Israel’s continued imposition of its colonial imaginary through occupation, genocide and scholasticide therefore targets not only Palestinian bodies and institutions but also the spaces in which alternative futures are imagined. (‘Scholasticide’ describes the systematic destruction of educational institutions and schools in Palestine by Israel.) This is why schools, universities and cultural institutions have repeatedly become targets of repression.

Since the start of the recent genocide in Gaza, more than 95 per cent of schools have been damaged or destroyed, disrupting the education of nearly 700,000 students. All 19 of Gaza’s recognised higher education institutions, including 12 universities, have been destroyed, and approximately 100 university professors have been killed. Yet attacks on Palestinian education did not begin with the current war.
Called ‘cells of illegal education’ by the Israeli authorities, underground schools were frequently raided

Systematic destruction of educational infrastructures has been part of the war against Palestine since the early 1970s when the first higher education institutions emerged. Birzeit University, one of the most important centres of Palestinian intellectual life, was repeatedly closed by Israeli authorities. Between 1973 and 1992, the university was shut down 15 times, including a closure of almost four and a half years during the First Intifada. Starting in 1987, this period saw Palestinian education literally criminalised; repression only intensified. All six universities, 13 colleges and approximately 1,200 schools were closed.

Yet the suppression of formal education also generated fugitive pedagogical practices. As schools and universities were closed, teaching moved into homes, churches and mosques. Called ‘cells of illegal education’ by the Israeli authorities, these underground schools were frequently raided. ‘Soldiers would throw teargas grenades into the room to force all the students out, then split up so one group could arrest those who fled while the other would destroy science equipment or photocopiers and, later on, computers,’ writes Gabi Baramki in Peaceful Resistance: Building a Palestinian University Under Occupation (2009). Students escaped through windows or across roofs. Teachers and students who got arrested for organising and attending ‘cells of illegal education’ were charged with a ‘public order offence’.

The Palestinian case demonstrates that education is never merely about knowledge. It is also a site of political struggle because it cultivates the fugitive imagination, the capacity to envision freedom beyond the colonial imaginaries that sustain occupation.

Since the Taliban regained control of Afghanistan in August 2021, they have systematically restricted the rights and freedoms of women and girls. One of their earliest targets was female education. In March 2022, the Taliban banned girls and women from attending secondary schools and universities. According to UNESCO, by August 2025 nearly 2.2 million Afghan girls were barred from education beyond the primary level.

The criminalisation of female education has, however, generated resistance. Across Afghanistan, underground educational initiatives have emerged to challenge these restrictions. In parts of Kabul, local networks have organised clandestine schools hidden from the authorities. Living rooms, basements and private halls have been transformed into classrooms where small groups of girls continue to learn, despite the risks involved. If fugitivity in relation to education was historically shaped by race in the US, in Afghanistan it is profoundly shaped by gender. The struggle over women’s education is about regulation of who may know and imagine otherwise. What the Taliban fear is not women’s education but the fugitive imagination it cultivates. The Taliban know that literacy transforms consciousness. It enables women to refuse the patriarchal imaginary and to imagine lives beyond the confines it imposes.

The Taliban’s fear echoes Auld’s reaction to Douglass’s literacy. Auld warned that if an enslaved person learned to read, ‘he would at once become unmanageable’. The Taliban’s concern follows the same logic: a woman who acquires knowledge runs away with herself.

The history of fugitivity is deeply entangled with the history of modernity itself, a modernity grounded in racial capitalism and constituted through colonialism and the nation-state system. This connection can be seen in the continuity between enslaved people fleeing plantations and refugees crossing contemporary state borders – indeed, the words ‘refugee’ and ‘fugitive’ share the same etymological root in the Latin fugere, meaning ‘to flee’. So, it makes sense that Moria Camp on the Greek island of Lesvos, once the largest and most notorious refugee camp in Europe, offers another insight into how fugitivity and imagination are interlinked.

Set up in January 2013, the camp’s harsh militarised regulation, spatial design and material conditions produced what might be called a camp imaginary, an expression of Europe’s border regime and its political desires, positioning refugees as unwanted, unfree and disposable subjects. Yet Moria was also a site where refugees created alternative spaces of learning, artistic expression and collective care. Through education, music, art and everyday acts of mutual support, they generated conditions that made survival possible. As Yannis Hamilakis demonstrated in his archaeological study of Moria, refugees created spaces for imagining precisely what the camp sought to render impossible: life beyond its spatial and political boundaries. In this sense, the camp was not only a space of confinement but also a site of fugitive imagination.

The final act of this fugitivity came in 2020: after years of overcrowding and unsafe conditions, the camp burned down. Yet the most enduring expression of fugitive imagination was not the end of the camp itself but the lives that emerged from it. Many former residents became filmmakers, musicians, poets, researchers and activists, demonstrating that, while the camp sought to contain people physically, it could not extinguish their capacity to imagine and create otherwise.
A fugitive imagination emerges through the practical and intellectual labour of navigating violence

Survival under conditions of violence requires an intimate knowledge of violence – its logics, structures and repetitions. Such knowledge is necessary not only to endure violence but also to resist the imaginaries that sustain it. Drawing upon the idea of ‘borderland thinking’ – a concept originating from the Chicana scholar and poet Gloria Anzaldúa, which centres knowledge produced through the lived experience of physical and cultural borders – I think of fugitive imagination as a form of situated knowledge produced by people who must survive systems of capture, confinement and bordering. Anzaldúa, who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas, on the US-Mexico border, conceptualised the borderlands as a space of imagination through what she called la facultad:

… the capacity to see in surface phenomena the meaning of deeper realities, to see the deep structure below the surface … When we’re up against the wall, when we have all sorts of oppressions coming at us, we are forced to develop this faculty so that we’ll know when the next person is going to slap us or lock us away.

For people of the borderlands, la facultad is both a method of knowledge-production and a vital survival skill; it emerges not despite conditions of vulnerability and violence but through them. In the same manner, a fugitive imagination emerges through the practical and intellectual labour of navigating violence, even as it envisions possibilities beyond it.

To gain access to imagination, to learn how to cultivate and enact it, is to break with the imaginaries that make every future appear the same. It is to create, within the present, the conditions for something that does not yet exist. Politics, then, is not only a struggle over power. It is also a struggle over images, imaginaries and imagination itself. It is a battle over what can be thought, what can be desired, and what can still be made possible.

Earlier this year, I received a WhatsApp call from a childhood friend. We had grown up together in a small village in southwestern Iran, and it was the first call I had received from Iran in more than three months. The latest dreadful period had begun in December 2025 with the violent suppression of public protests; initially sparked by frustration over an economic crisis, they’d soon developed into a broad uprising. The Iranian state’s response was brutal. Thousands of people were killed and many more arrested. The state had cut off not only internet access but also much of the country’s telecommunications infrastructure. Iranians were still in shock from the militarised crackdown when an intense US-Israel war with Iran began on the last day of February 2026, bringing even more death and silence.

When my friend’s name appeared on my screen, I hesitated before answering. I felt ashamed: I did not know how to speak to someone who had lived through so much violence while I remained safe. I called him back later that day, after collecting myself. The connection was poor and our conversation fragmented: a word here, a phrase there, only occasionally a complete sentence. But I was surprised – unsettled, in fact – by what I was able to piece together. Spring, I heard him say, had brought abundant rain. Alongside bombs and bullets, rain had fallen, more than in previous years. What arrived through his fragmented voice was not words but imagination.

I imagined the mountains saturated with water, the springs running full, the wheat fields nourished and waiting to be harvested. Even as US bombs materialised a colonial imaginary that sought to reorder the world according to imperial logics of domination, people continued to imagine rain, harvests, seasons. To look toward the sky and see rain falling alongside bombs was a refusal of the imperial imaginary – an imagination of life, despite everything, an imagination that cannot be killed, bombed, stolen or abducted, and from which the seeds of an alternative future might emerge.

From the plantation to the border, from the genocide in Palestine to the Taliban’s war on women, and from refugee camps to the war on Iran, we encounter recurring attempts to preserve regimes of truth and imaginaries that seek to define the limits of life, mobility and freedom. Yet these projects of domination continually generate their own negation. Wherever people are confined, displaced, silenced or rendered disposable, fugitive forms of knowledge, pedagogy and imagination emerge. This is why history never ends.
Author’s note: a version of this essay’s opening story appears in my book ‘Illegal Traveller’: An Auto-Ethnography of Borders (2010) and in The Funambulist magazine.
This essay is supported by a grant from the Open Society Foundations.

items.title: The politics of masculinity at the end of the Roman republic | Aeon Essays
items.description: What does it mean to be a man? In the early 21st century, masculinity is contested and fraught with anxiety; influencers offer models of manliness involving fast cars, sexual conquests, and building up muscle. Before the rise of feminism, they suggest, in some
items.author: Catharine Edwards
paragraphs: What does it mean to be a man? In the early 21st century, masculinity is contested and fraught with anxiety; influencers offer models of manliness involving fast cars, sexual conquests, and building up muscle. Before the rise of feminism, they suggest, in some supposed Golden Age, everyone had a shared sense of what it meant to be a man – and being a man was unproblematically good. The Roman Empire, in their view, offers men today an inspirational example of power, hierarchy and achievement, which is why men think about it so much – unlike women, who are too immersed in their feelings…

Manliness certainly was celebrated in the works of Cicero, republican Rome’s most eloquent statesman. In the mid-1st century BCE, his persuasive powers in the law courts and the senate were second to none; his speeches went on to inspire would-be orators well into the 20th century. He is often seen as the very embodiment of the Roman republic. The political world in which he flourished was a self-consciously masculine one; to be accused of acting like a woman was, for a Roman man, a grievous insult. Yet in Cicero’s writing we can find other strains too.

For Roman men, anything labelled feminine was necessarily to be avoided, something to be ashamed of. But what exactly did it mean to act like a man? Ancient Rome in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE saw the rise of a succession of military leaders who were promoted as masculine role models. The great general Marius won a series of victories in Spain, North Africa and on Italy’s northern frontier. For several years in a row, he was elected consul, one of Rome’s two chief executive officers. Unlike many other Roman politicians, he didn’t have an aristocratic background. One Roman writer imagines Marius fending off accusations that he was coarse in his manners:
elegance is becoming to women but toil to men. All virtuous men ought to have more fame than riches. Arms, not fine trappings, bring glory.
– from The War Against Jugurtha by Sallust
(All translations are adapted from the Loeb Classical Library.)
Here was a model of manliness forged on the battlefield.

Given the military might of ancient Rome, it is surely unsurprising that Romans often associated masculinity with courage in battle. The word virtus, a term cognate with the Roman vir (meaning man as opposed to woman), clearly means ‘courage in war’ when it is first recorded in the mid-5th century BCE. Courage in battle could be taken as the foremost manifestation of Roman masculinity. The historian Sallust, writing in the 40s BCE, praises earlier generations of Romans for their pre-eminent manliness in war: ‘whenever their virtus repelled dangers, they rendered aid to their allies and friends.’ And yet, while Rome continued to boast ever more notable military successes in the middle and later republic (from the 3rd to the 1st century BCE), the battlefield was by no means the only arena in which Roman masculinity might be put to the test.

When Cicero was 16, like others of his social standing, his transition to adulthood was marked by a special ceremony, most likely at the feast of the Liberalia in 90 BCE. This was the moment when he first put on the toga of manhood, a cumbersome length of woollen fabric worn by Roman citizen men, a garment associated with civilian as opposed to military life. Years later, as consul in 63 BCE, Cicero played a leading role in uncovering and suppressing a conspiracy against the Roman state, and boasted that this was a victory won by ‘citizens in togas’. It was his speeches that had convinced his fellow senators and the Roman people of the dangers posed by Catiline’s conspiracy, leading to decisive action against those involved. Cicero had used his voice as consul to save Rome, he declared in a speech a few years later. Throughout his life, he insisted his victory was comparable to those of Rome’s greatest generals. Masculine achievements weren’t confined to the battlefield; rhetoric and oratory could also conquer.

By the time he secured the consulship, Cicero was regarded as Rome’s top orator. Public speaking was highly prized by members of Rome’s governing elite. Its end result mattered hugely – winning over one’s listeners. But the way Rome’s politicians spoke and even how they dressed could also serve to demonstrate their manliness. Codes of civilian masculinity governed behaviour in public spaces such as the Forum, the law-courts and the senate. Markers of manliness in this sphere were subject to relentless public scrutiny. As the later expert on oratory Quintilian put it, the orator’s dress needs to be ‘resplendent and manly: for when it comes to one’s toga and shoes and hair, excessive care as well as negligence are equally blameable’. The toga, for instance, must be correctly draped; he notes a little later, ‘throwing back the fold from its bottom onto the right shoulder is foppish and effeminate’.

Orators were alert to the niceties of their own – and one another’s – masculine self-fashioning. In the cacophonous world of the Roman republic, politicians, advocates and those aspiring to a public role exchanged no-holds-barred insults. Often, they cast aspersions on one another’s masculinity, with disparaging comments on an opponent’s way of speaking, his gestures, the way he wore his toga – as well as his sexual behaviour. Orators would be praised for speaking in a ‘manly’ way. And they were robustly attacked for any ‘effeminate’ deviations in their style and manner of speech. Some orators favoured a more elaborate style fashionable in the long-established rhetorical schools of the eastern Mediterranean, the zone the Romans called Asia. Contrasts were drawn between ‘Asian’ style and the plainer style associated with Athenian rhetorical tradition. The Asian style was regularly denigrated as ‘effeminate’. Yet too ‘unpolished’ a style could seem old-fashioned, even coarse. Moderation was itself celebrated as a quintessentially masculine quality. But where to draw the line?
Quintilian criticised rhetoric teachers who encourage their students to show off

In the late republic, attempts were made to codify guidance to aspiring orators. An anonymous treatise on rhetoric addressed To Herennius promises to help its reader present himself as a proper man through training in public speech. The author advises, for instance, against any sharp exclamation that ‘injures the voice and likewise jars the hearer, for it has about it something ignoble, suited rather to feminine outcry than to manly dignity in speaking.’ In On the Orator, Cicero has a character emphasise the importance of appropriate gestures in seeking to arouse particular emotions in one’s listeners: ‘all these emotions must be accompanied by gesture – … with this vigorous manly throwing out of the chest, borrowed not from the stage and the theatrical profession but from the parade ground or even from wrestling.’ The theatre had morally dubious associations; actors were often branded effeminate. Performer though he was, an orator would do well to cultivate a more military aura and disguise the degree to which his art drew on dramatic technique.

Writing a century after Cicero, Quintilian was a huge admirer of his work, regarding him as the ideal model for the aspiring public speaker. In Quintilian’s wide-ranging treatise on the education of the ideal orator, sound ethical character but also manliness are presented as essential qualifications: ‘I am training the consummate orator, a figure whose existence is predicated on his being a good man [vir bonus].’ Quintilian expresses his disapproval of speeches composed merely for display, a widespread practice in his day, criticising teachers of rhetoric who encourage their students to show off:

The teachers, I feel bound to say, have been guilty of the same offence as slave dealers who castrate boys to increase their attractions. As those dealers think there is no beauty in strength or in a muscular arm, and certainly not in a beard and the other natural endowments of the male, and so take what might, if left alone, have developed into sturdiness and soften its supposed hardness – so do we cover up the manly form of eloquence and the power of lean and vigorous speech with a delicate veneer of style, and think effectiveness of no importance, so long as everything is smooth and polished.

This simile – shocking in multiple ways to a modern reader – aligns the recommended mode of speech with the embodiment characteristic of the free, adult, bodily intact male. Indeed, the right kind of speech makes clear the laudable moral character and manliness of the speaker: ‘I decline to regard as eloquence in any sense something which shows no trace at all of a normal male, let alone of a man of weight and integrity,’ Quintilian continues.

But there was of course a paradox in all this effort focused on generating an impression of authentic masculinity, a paradox apparent in the advice in To Herennius to ‘make everything seem straight from the heart’. The artifice required to generate authentic-seeming masculinity was all too evident. We can see this as a symptom of the ongoing challenge of justifying male supremacy, through assertions of the ‘natural’ superiority of men to women (and indeed of free men to enslaved ones). What exactly was ‘masculine’ rhetorical style? Opinions could differ significantly. But masculinity itself was always a positive term. And giving effective speeches in Rome’s public spaces was an ideal way to communicate one’s specifically masculine virtue.

What happened, though, when a member of Rome’s elite, once renowned for his eloquence, found himself cut off from the Forum and the senate? Cicero’s role in the punishment of those who had conspired with Catiline was controversial; Roman citizens had been executed without trial – a breach of the rights of the Roman people. In 58 BCE, following the manoeuvrings of his political enemy Clodius, Cicero was unceremoniously exiled. He languished far from Rome for 16 months, often fearing for his life, separated from family and friends – but also from access to the public arena where he’d held his own for so long. His letters home are full of lamentation. To his old friend Atticus, Cicero communicates his utter misery and despair. He often wishes he were dead. Reflecting on his losses felt like tearing open a wound: ‘I mourn the loss not only of the things and persons that were mine but of my very self. What am I now?’

Cicero was criticised by his contemporaries (and by later commentators) for his emotional reaction to exile. Should he have adopted a Stoic stiff upper lip, perhaps? To have been unaffected by this experience would have been inhuman rather than manly, he asserts in a speech given after his return in 57 BCE:
