I could not now describe my action as praiseworthy or say that I was the source of any benefit to the republic, if I had but abandoned, for the republic’s sake, what I felt no pang at losing; I should hold that such mental apathy, like the physical apathy which does not feel the sting of fire, was brute insensibility rather than bravery [virtus].
In his own way, he claimed, even his retreat into exile, and even his frequent complaints, had shown bravery – manliness.
Cicero, eloquent exponent of Roman republican values, struggled to articulate his political disappointment

Back in Rome, however, Cicero remained anxious. Generals in command of large armies – Julius Caesar, above all – asserted their dominance over the state. Rome’s senate felt increasingly powerless. ‘The republic is an empty husk,’ Cicero lamented in a letter to Atticus in 54 BCE. Another celebrated general, Pompey, eventually led the challenge to bring Caesar under control. Yet, even if this was an attempt to shore up traditional modes of government where the senate exercised greatest authority, it ended in failure – and there were also doubts about Pompey’s intentions. Was he too, perhaps, aiming at one-man rule? Following a bitter civil war lasting from 49 to 45 BCE, a victorious Julius Caesar ruled the Roman world as dictator. Cicero, Rome’s foremost orator and long at the centre of its political life, was in despair. Throughout his career, he had championed a traditional political order in which Rome’s elite competed against one another in elections and took collective decisions in the senate. This was above all a culture of robust debate, in which persuasive speech played a critical role. But now the Forum was silent. In the senate, no one dared speak against Caesar.

Cicero, most eloquent exponent of Roman republican values, struggled to articulate his profound political disappointment. This was an experience compounded by devastating personal bereavement. In 45 BCE, shortly after giving birth to a little boy, Cicero’s daughter Tullia died. He was knocked sideways. Friends wrote letters of consolation. A long letter from one, Servius Sulpicius Rufus, observed that at least Tullia, dying when she did, avoided witnessing the end of the republic. In an equally lengthy reply, Cicero acknowledged his friend’s kindness – but disputed the claim that any comfort might be found in the timing of Tullia’s death. He contrasted his own situation with that of earlier Roman public figures, who had managed to avoid giving in to personal griefs by devoting themselves to public service: ‘the high standing they derived from public life soothed their mourning’. In current political circumstances, Cicero no longer had a part in public life. He couldn’t bear even the sight of the senate – the scene of his former triumphs. In these wretched political times, it was Tullia who had been Cicero’s one source of comfort. She was ‘a haven of refuge and repose, one in whose conversation and sweet ways I put aside all cares and sorrows.’ And now she was gone.

The collapse of the Roman state in its traditional form was something Cicero had been lamenting, at least on and off, for some years. He often used the language of death, bereavement and mourning in relation to the political situation. ‘For a long time it has been my part to mourn our liberties,’ he wrote to his old friend Atticus. Just a short while before Tullia’s death, he wrote to another friend: ‘I have already grieved for the state more deeply and longer than any mother for her only child.’ It is impossible to disentangle Cicero’s devastation at the loss of his daughter from his feelings of loss at the drastic transformation of Rome’s political landscape. The one loss intensified his grief at the other. And as Cicero’s words comparing himself to a bereaved mother suggest, he experienced both the loss and the intense grief it provoked as profoundly emasculating. He could no longer be the man he once was.

And yet perhaps another sphere of activity might offer scope for a new kind of self-actualisation, a new way for a man of Cicero’s extraordinary talents to win fame through service to the state and his fellow Romans. Even before Tullia’s death, Cicero had been increasingly immersing himself in philosophy. In 46 BCE, he had written to Sulpicius of his retreat from public-speaking: ‘seeing there is no further place in the Senate House or Forum for the craft which I have studied, I have devoted all my time and attention to philosophy.’ In changed political circumstances, with the dictator Caesar as Rome’s sole ruler, philosophy felt like a kind of salvation.

Cicero’s focus in his writings of these years was on a range of mainly ethical issues, particularly the nature of virtus – now taken in a sense much closer to the English term ‘virtue’ or ‘moral excellence’. A particular concern was the management of emotions in the pursuit of spiritual wellbeing. This was an issue of pressing personal significance to Cicero following his family bereavement but also of broader relevance to those who mourned the political changes in Rome.
It is about what it means to be a man and how manhood can be forged in – and by – challenging circumstances

Cicero (and other Roman writers), influenced by Greek philosophical explorations of virtue, might sometimes attribute to women virtue of a more generalised kind. But the Latin term virtus never completely lost its association with masculinity. Noting the word’s derivation, Cicero observes in his treatise on the management of emotions, the Tusculan Disputations:
the proper virtue of a man is above all courage, whose particular functions are contempt for death and pain. We must exercise these qualities if we wish to be virtuous, indeed if we wish to be men.

Closely concerned with philosophical approaches to dealing with grief and the fear of death, this treatise is also about what it means to be a man and how manhood can be forged in – and by – challenging circumstances. ‘For surely virtue [virtus] gives sufficient to make us live bravely; if bravely, sufficient too to make us high-souled and in fact never appalled by any event and always undefeated,’ he asserts. Similar concerns surface in other works he wrote around this time: in On Ends, he stresses the importance of self-control – which he defines as avoiding behaviour that’s ‘unmanly’ – parum virile.

Cicero’s philosophical writings were themselves an act of public service, he insisted. Through setting out philosophical ideas in Latin, he was offering a way for his fellow citizens to encounter the highest kind of learning. It was a particular comfort for Cicero in a time of deep political crisis, he declared, that this moment might see the birth of philosophy in Latin.

Cicero did return, albeit briefly, to the public arena in the last year of his life. Following Caesar’s assassination, his erstwhile deputy Mark Antony manoeuvred to take over Caesar’s following and resources. Cicero thought he too was aiming at dictatorship, and gave a series of speeches, attempting to rally his fellow senators behind the ‘liberators’ and against Antony. These speeches, known as the Philippics, were a dazzling return to form.

In the second Philippic, Cicero insisted at length and in colourful detail on the ways in which Antony was a slave to bodily pleasures – a man with no capacity for self-control. Cicero dredged up a story from years previously alleging Antony had had a homosexual affair with another Roman elite man, Curio, a relationship in which Antony willingly played a ‘passive’ role: ‘No slave boy bought to satisfy lust was ever so completely in his master’s power as you were in Curio’s,’ he fulminated. The lust here is implicitly Curio’s, not Antony’s – but this willingness to subordinate himself revealed Antony’s ‘slavish’ disposition. Such sexual ‘passivity’ in an elite male – taking what was seen as a ‘feminine’, receptive sexual role – was deeply shocking for Romans. It is notable that in his swansong Cicero does his utmost to paint Antony as a man of ‘unmanly’ sexual habits, addicted to pleasure and with no sense of masculine moderation. Cicero, ever the rhetorician out to win the argument, was quite prepared to exploit his audience’s masculinist prejudices to demean an enemy.

With these speeches, Cicero managed to rally his fellow senators, at least for a time, but, in the end, the power of those who commanded the legions was unstoppable. In 43 BCE, Antony eventually joined forces with Julius Caesar’s great-nephew and heir, Octavian. They rapidly gained control of the Roman Empire – and engineered the deaths of prominent opponents, among them Cicero. When a posse of legionaries finally caught up with him, Cicero is said to have offered them his neck, meeting his end with great bravery.

Military might prevailed for the time being, underpinning the regime of Rome’s emperors which was established a few years after Cicero’s death. Yet long after the Roman empire had fallen, his writings and reflections on the nature of educated masculinity would continue to influence European elites. While masculinity in Cicero’s world – and that of many of his later readers – is always a positive term, it’s also clear that its precise significance was just as contested then, albeit in different ways, and within different limits, as it is in the early 21st century. And just occasionally Cicero himself reveals the conscious effort involved in putting on a performance of authentic manliness.

items.title: AnOther Man Launches Its Pieter Hugo and Adidas Originals Cover at DSM
items.description: For the latest issue of AnOther Man, Pieter Hugo photographs Grace Wales Bonner’s Autumn/Winter 2026 collection with Adidas Originals in Nature’s Valley on coast of South Africa. The cover launched last week with a celebration at Dover Street Market
items.author: Another Man
paragraphs: For the latest issue of AnOther Man, Pieter Hugo photographs Grace Wales Bonner’s Autumn/Winter 2026 collection with Adidas Originals in Nature’s Valley on coast of South Africa. The cover launched last week with a celebration at Dover Street Market

Pieter Hugo was celebrating his 50th birthday the night he and AnOther Man launched their photo story, shot in South Africa with stylist Akeem Smith for the magazine’s Winter/Spring 27 issue. The event, which took place at Dover Street Market last week, was co-hosted by Hugo, and AnOther Man’s editor-in-chief Ellie Grace Cumming and art director Jonny Lu.

Continuing his longstanding exploration of place, identity and representation, for this story the artist honed in on Nature’s Valley on South Africa’s southern coast. Speaking to AnOther Man’s contributing editor Lucy Kumara Moore for the edition, Hugo reflected on the area’s personal significance: “[When I spoke to Ellie and Jonny about a shoot for the edition], I happened to be at a house my family has on the south coast of South Africa. It’s in the middle of a nature reserve. It’s incredibly wild, very small and quite isolated. I’ve been going there for many years, always thinking about photography – making mental notes of locations and what looks great at what time of the day. I’ve shot a lot of personal work there.”

Moving between the city and its surrounding landscape, Hugo brought his distinctive documentary-style approach to Grace Wales Bonner’s Autumn/Winter 2026 collection, including her collaboration with Adidas Originals. The casting brought together Cape Town-based models and individuals street-cast in nearby villages. Typical of his approach, the story offers a portrait of a place and the people who inhabit it, touching on the visual codes of cinema, fashion and documentary.

“A big part of my practice, even though it’s concerned with portraiture, is often responding to an environment,” Hugo said. “I was seeing how one could fit together these three components: Grace’s fashion, my portraiture, and the environment I’d proposed.”

More than 200 guests enjoyed the cover’s launch party, celebrated with an evening of drinks and food, provided by Rose Bakery at Dover Street Market. Attendees, intersecting the worlds of fashion, music, filmmaking and art, included Tallulah Harlech, Isaac Benigson, Ancuta Sarca, Birgita Toyoda, Jerry Stafford, Denzel Himself, Piotr Chamier, Ella Ezekiel, Casper Sejersen, Reuben Esser, SJ Todd, Liberty Joy, Simon Parris, Raphael Hirsch and Manu Loca.

Opening the celebrations to the public, AnOther Man invited readers and members of the wider Dazed audience to attend, registering through the Dazed Club app. Guests left with posters signed by Hugo – a limited-edition keepsake from the evening, and the issue.

items.title: The art of Japanese confectionery
items.description: Japan's sweets span an expansive spectrum, from traditional creations known as wagashi to Western-inspired yogashi treats. Be it a jelly-like yokan in a neat rectangular block, a sweet bean-filled mochi in the form of a flower or tiny white sugar balls, Japane
items.author: Danielle Demetriou
paragraphs: Japan's sweets span an expansive spectrum, from traditional creations known as wagashi to Western-inspired yogashi treats. Be it a jelly-like yokan in a neat rectangular block, a sweet bean-filled mochi in the form of a flower or tiny white sugar balls, Japanese confectionery is conventionally rooted in time and place. The centuries-old flowering of confectionery craftsmanship is closely linked to the rise of the tea world, with a single sweet presented before drinking a bowl of matcha during a tea ceremony.

Today, Japan's train stations heave with boxes of exquisitely wrapped treats, often tied to microseasonal flavours, local ingredients, nature-mirroring shapes and old pilgrim routes – reflecting the nation's thriving omiyage (souvenir) culture, as well as its love of sweets. Numerous confectioners can still be found across the country – from the big names, such as Toraya (with its serene architect-designed flagships) and designer Shinichiro Ogata's Higashiya, to family-run shops dating back generations. Here we have picked out a few that hit our sweet spot.

Toraya A red circle of sun sinking into the sea against a blazing sky: this image is embodied in this sweet – with graphic lines, curves and colours shaping both the packaging and the confectionery itself. Called Umi (‘Sea'), it's among a series of seasonal yokan – a traditional sweet bean jelly treat – made by Toraya, one of Japan's best-known confectioners. With roots dating back more than five centuries and longstanding Imperial ties, the company also has contemporary flagship confectionery spaces, designed by architect Hiroshi Naito, in Kyoto and Tokyo. toraya-group.co.jp

Shioyoshiken Small but perfectly formed white balls that melt on the tongue are among countless handmade treats sold at this family-run sweetmaker, based out of an old wooden house on a quiet street in Kyoto's historic Nishijin textile district. Made from wasanbon sugar with a small amount of natto (savoury fermented soybeans) from the nearby Daitokuji temple, the kogoh rakugan also feature a small red dot – symbolising a courtly female mouth – as a delicate finishing touch. The rakugan are sold either in small white paper boxes, or in light sugi cedar boxes, wrapped in paper with a pine tree motif and a small auspicious decoration by a local artisan. kyogashi.com

Higashiya Kelp, black sesame, white sesame, yuzu pepper, plum: an array of flavours define these mamegashi bean and nut sweets, crafted by Tokyo- based brand Higashiya. Created by Shinichiro Ogata, of design studio Simplicity, its season-mirroring treats come in pared-back minimalist packaging. Ogata is also behind Saboe, a network of tea spaces across Japan, as well as Ogata at The Shinmonzen in Kyoto and, for those outside Japan, Ogata Paris. higashiya.com

Uchu Wagashi This modern Kyoto brand, set up by graphic designer-turned-sweetmaker Katsuya Kimoto, features playfully contemporary packaging with graphic patterns and rainbow-toned motifs, from animals to acorns. The sweets mirror their packaging in form and shades, yet are crafted using traditional handmaking techniques and ingredients, from wooden moulds to wasanbon sugar. The main store, on the eastern edge of the Imperial Palace park, is also home to a peaceful café. uchu-wagashi.jp

Opposite, clockwise from top left, Umi seasonal yokan by Toraya and roasted green tea yokan by Irodori; crane-inspired Tsuruyado wasanbon sugar tea cakes by Tsuruya Yoshinobu; Hoshi Kohaku kohakutou jelly candies by Kyoto Tsuraya; kohakutou amber candy sticks by Irodori
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Tsuruya Yoshinobu For more than 200 years, this confectionery brand has been renowned in Kyoto for its wagashi, with a history rooted in the Imperial family and the tea world. Today, the Nishijin flagship store sells an array of crafted treats (there is also a tea room upstairs, where an expert wagashi artisan can shape and mould the sweet of your choice at the counter, to be enjoyed alongside whisked matcha). A highlight are Tsuruyado – dry white sugar sweets inspired by a red-crowned crane (a symbol of longevity, good fortune and happiness) – presented in small wrapped paper boxes. tsuruyayoshinobu.jp

Irodori An offshoot of historic Kyoto brand Tsuruya Yoshinobu (see above), Irodori offers a modern interpretation of Japan's sweets world. Its signature creations are the colourful stick versions of the traditional crystal-like amber candy known as kohakutou. Smoothly presented in clear modern packaging, the colourful light-filtering sweets come in five aromatic flavours: lavender, mint, rose, camomile and jasmine. tsuruyayoshinobu.jp

Satoya Founded in 1821, and the oldest sweetmakers in Yamagata City, northern Japan, Satoya has long been famed for its tangy plum noshi-ume sweets. Another highlight are its layered blocks of plum jelly, presented in painterly paper wrapping decorated with calligraphic abstractions of waves beneath the moon. satoya-matsubei.com

Toshoan Picture perfectly cubed paper boxes in modern monotones. And inside are cookies, with a Japanese twist – the soft wagashi-like texture made by mixing red bean paste, known as an, into the gluten-free dough. An de cookie – in an array of flavours (and coloured boxes), from framboise and kinako (roasted soybean) to matcha and cherry blossom – are popular modern treats dreamt up by Toshoan, a decades-old Kyoto bean paste company. toshoan.com

Kyoto Tsuruya A sky scattered with stars is the inspiration behind Hoshi Kohaku, the kohakutou sweets in jewel-bright shades of yellow, green and pink, made by confectioner Kyoto Tsuruya. Made with Tanba thread agar and sugar, the candies are slightly crystalline in form yet soft and jelly-like to bite into. Packaged in simple clear boxes, the colourful, fragmented form of the sweets shine brightly. kyototsuruya.co.jp

Noake Tokyo Origami-like paper folds, meticulously wrapped around a circular tin, instantly root this product in the world of Japanese confectionery. Upon unwrapping and opening it, however, the contents are something of a surprise: the freezable popsicles, called Candy Frappé – which come in flavours ranging from strawberry and rose to mandarin and osmanthus – sport striking labels with minimalist typography. The candies are the creation of Noake Tokyo, a popular sweetmaker known for its inventive flavours and modern riffs on traditional confectionery. noake.jp
Photos: Joana Gauer. Set design: Johanne Mills

Danielle Demetriou is a Contributing Editor at Wallpaper*. The British writer and editor moved from London to Japan in 2007 and writes about Japanese design, architecture and culture for newspapers, magazines and books. She lives in a machiya townhouse in an old textile district in Kyoto.
Instagram - @danielleinjapan

items.title: The past and future intertwine at this stunning museum dedicated to the history of brocade
items.description: The Shu Brocade Culture Museum is Chengdu's latest landmark. The Chinese city has been historically known as the 'City of Brocade,' making this new institution a vital element in its cultural identity - designed to showcase the famous fabric technique's origin
items.author: Ellie Stathaki
paragraphs: The Shu Brocade Culture Museum is Chengdu's latest landmark. The Chinese city has been historically known as the 'City of Brocade,' making this new institution a vital element in its cultural identity - designed to showcase the famous fabric technique's origins, craft and future for locals and visitors alike.

The architecture studio behind the new building, ARCHSTUDIO, is a local practice led by Han Wenqiang. It worked on transforming an existing structure – a disused agricultural machinery factory – into a 21st-century destination.
Explore the Shu Brocade Culture Museum in China

The project is situated in a dedicated park as part of a special initiative by the Sichuan Provincial Department of Culture and Tourism. The broader area is titled the Shu Brocade Heritage Cultural & Creative Park and is located in the city's Banqiao Village. It is a dedicated gesture that aims to both preserve the region's precious heritage in the craft and promote urban revitalisation through activities that bring together exhibitions, events and educational programming. The park also includes several smaller brocade workshops, which surround the museum.

The existing buildings were derelict when the project began. The architects worked with the simple, orthogonal brick structures, from which only the walls remained, and added new roofing. At the same time, the new design aims to retain the memory and feel of the factory – the building's original use – merging old and new. Meanwhile, the site includes a series of outdoor areas, in the form of gardens and courtyards, populated with plants traditionally used for dyeing fabrics.

Inside, the project contains spaces for temporary and permanent displays, as well as a digital archive of Shu brocade techniques - one of the most well-known, high-quality Chinese silk weaving methods.

Wood and intersecting steel beams define the interior, in particular the new roof, nodding conceptually to the shape of the brocade loom. At the same time, undulations in the facade and internal surfaces reference the elegant folds of brocade textiles. This also creates a balanced dynamism in the otherwise solid-feeling structure.
In a similar way, perforated bricks and calculated openings bring to mind brocade patterns and the soft folds of fabric. The terrazzo floor is similarly intricate, using reclaimed brick.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

'The Shu Brocade Culture Museum offers a model for industrial heritage revitalisation, the continuation of intangible cultural heritage, and rural renewal. It breathes new life into the former factory while translating Shu brocade culture into a tangible, immersive spatial experience,' say the architects in a design statement.

'Open to public life, the museum becomes a place where people, traditional craft and everyday life connect. Here, past and future intertwine, and tradition takes root anew in contemporary life,' they add.

Ellie Stathaki is the Architecture & Environment Director at Wallpaper*. She trained as an architect at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and studied architectural history at the Bartlett in London. Now an established journalist, she has been a member of the Wallpaper* team since 2006, visiting buildings across the globe and interviewing leading architects such as Tadao Ando and Rem Koolhaas. Ellie has also taken part in judging panels, moderated events, curated shows and contributed in books, such as The Contemporary House (Thames & Hudson, 2018), Glenn Sestig Architecture Diary (2020) and House London (2022).

items.title: ALVARO BARRINGTON - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: Fifteen takes on Alvaro Barrington.
paragraphs: Fifteen takes on Alvaro Barrington.
From Fantastic Man n° 38 — 2024
Photography by ROBBIE LAWRENCE

Subjects the artist Alvaro Barrington feels comfortable talking about include 1990s hip-hop, the art of Jeff Koons, the novel ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’, the concept of community, the TV series ‘Sex and the City’, the Harlem Renaissance, the European Renaissance, the sport of basketball, Hieronymus Bosch, and the notion of the Baroque. Alvaro considers himself a painter and much of his work does indeed involve the application of paint, but quite often it also involves materials like yarn, concrete, steel chains, brooms, tyres, and patterned leather. Nor is it limited to flat rectangular spaces: he will sometimes create entire environments that are at once settings for and part of the work. From the end of May a newly commissioned work by Alvaro will inhabit the vast Duveen Galleries at Tate Britain. What will he do? He’s not willing to say yet, though he does observe that “this is the first year that I’m starting to really think about work that is about the future” and he says he is thinking a lot about “the idea of duality.” Alvaro declared not that long ago that “every exhibition is autobiographical,” and it’s true that his projects tend to represent his life in many ways, but they are also densely packed with references of both an art-historical and a pop-cultural nature, smashing them together with a Cern-like zeal. Whatever he does at the Tate will surely only amplify his status as one of the world’s most talked-about artists.

Alvaro is 41. He was born in Caracas, Venezuela, on 1 February 1983 to parents from the Caribbean. Popular songs released that month include ‘Little Red Corvette’ by Prince and ‘Total Eclipse of the Heart’ by Bonnie Tyler. Millions of people born in the 19th century were still alive that year; none are now. Several of Alvaro’s artistic heroes, such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Louise Bourgeois and Tupac Shakur, were alive then. Alvaro grew up between Grenada and New York City and graduated from the Slade School of Fine Art, London, in 2017.

Alvaro is wearing a grey-green sweatshirt and has a black beanie quite high on his head. He is in his studio in Hackney, London. Shortly after our video call begins, he apologises and leaves to deal with a delivery.

I examine the room in his absence. Alvaro’s empty seat has a slightly curved backrest made from dark wood, quite similar in colour to a cabinet and bookshelf elsewhere in the room. In conjunction with the blueness of the carpet, the plain whiteness of the wall and the beadedness of the plastic cord that opens the window blind, it makes this room (which is clearly part of a larger complex) seem less like an artist’s studio than an office in a university or museum.

What it doesn’t resemble is the studio which the artist recreated in a ground-floor room at MoMA PS1 gallery in Queens, New York, for ‘Alvaro Barrington’, his first solo exhibition after graduating. As well as the paintings of hibiscus flowers that would become a signature motif, the show included Alvaro’s work desk and a number of handwritten notes containing various prompts-to-self such as “What is the next obvious but unexpected move?”

One of the books in the room I’m observing is called ‘Jamaica Vibes’. I look it up: a glorious large-format volume by Lisa Lovatt-Smith and Novia McDonald-Whyte, published last year. More books and papers are stacked on the flat surface below the shelf. At the other side of the room is a single kick drum. When Alvaro comes back, I ask him about it and he explains that, having used the drum as the basis for a sculpture, he’s been finding it useful in other ways. “You grow up with the drums as a symbol for so many things, and so I’m just keeping it around me, just helping me figure some stuff out,” he says. Alvaro is thoughtful and doesn’t take much shit. He will often think for a while in response to a question before setting off on a circuitous monologue that at some point nails the point from an unexpected direction.
In lieu of an official biography, Alvaro often provides an extensive text, the status of which — Poem? Song? Ready-made? — remains ambiguous. This is an excerpt:
You’re the most insecure person I know and it’s disgusting/
We have to be gentle with each other’s hearts
I Like America and America likes me
If you were them, You would be them/
“You’ve got to give them something special, you got to give them you, what you do, what you represent”
New women, old ways, Gotta Keep a Balance/
I don’t want my work to be some fucking free zone associations/

Alvaro places himself outside the conventional system where an artist is represented by a very small group of commercial galleries on an exclusive basis. Instead, he has developed what’s been called a non-monogamous arrangement, meaning any of the below should be able to field an enquiry on his work.
2727 South La Cienega Boulevard
1a Kempsford Road (off Wincott Street)
The Lazarus Building, 1 Holywell Lane

Emelda, Alvaro’s mother, was from Grenada. She died from cancer in 1993. She was a teenager when Alvaro was born, and then moved to New York. Alvaro lived with his grandmother for a time, only moving to Brooklyn to join his mother two years before her death. As well as naming his Notting Hill Carnival stage after her (more on that next), he is working on turning a building in Whitechapel into a hybrid art space called Emelda’s. His beguiling website, a hybrid of portfolio and e-shop — as well as displaying his work, it offers aromatherapy products from the London brand Cremate — is located at the URL emeldaart.net. “I only knew her as the person she knew I needed, and so in a way, she’s only the person that I need,” he says. “When I chose to be an artist, she was the reason. She’s just someone that I project my needs on. I allow myself to go down that road with a joy knowing that that is my safety.”

When he was a young child, Alvaro’s cousins took him to J’ouvert, the day of festivities that serves as an unofficial start to carnival in the Caribbean. He climbed on top of a sound system and promptly fell asleep. In 2022, the experience inspired a pavilion at the Notting Hill Carnival, created by Alvaro and the architect Sumayya Vally, where people were invited to take some downtime from the action elsewhere. The following year he created a stage for the carnival called Emelda’s Junction, which was in Powis Square. He held an exhibition to coincide with it, which was at 62 Kingly Street, an address you probably remember from section 5 (Polycule) above.
8. SADIE COLES DESCRIBES A SHOW

Affable gallerist Sadie Coles was instrumental in the Young British Artists movement of the ’80s and ’90s. Her gallery represents 52 artists, including Matthew Barney, Ugo Rondinone and Martine Syms. She would normally never work with someone right after graduation, but with Alvaro it was different. “He was such a standout,” she says. “Alvaro’s use of materials is so very particular.” In a late-afternoon call she describes his show that evolved from Emelda’s Junction: “The exhibition was called ‘Grandma’s Land’. The paintings that we showed in the gallery were the stage flats for the sound stage, at Powis Square. They were literally on stage and then at the end of the carnival they were rolled up and came into the gallery and were put into frames. So there was a very, very strong connection to his Caribbean ancestry.

The show had three structures in it, and they were referencing his grandma’s house, his uncle’s house, and his auntie’s house. So it felt like a village situation. Each of the structures had a painting on the side of the building, and his works were on the outside of them.
On the inside of the structures, he was hosting another artist, which is typical of Alvaro’s inclusive generosity. He’s often doing projects where he brings other people into them.

And we were lucky enough that we had Sonia Gomes in the grandma’s house, we had Paul Anthony Smith in the auntie’s house, and Akinola Davies Jr. had a film of the carnival that we were also showing, so it really felt like Alvaro was hosting other artists within his show, which was very nice.” This year’s Notting Hill Carnival will take place 25–26 August in west London.
9. THREE AMERICAN CHAIN STORES
— Bob’s Discount Furniture. Co-founded in 1991 by Bob Kaufman (now owned by a private investment firm).
— Circuit City. “Where the streets are paved with bargains,” went the slogan for this consumer electronics chain until its bankruptcy.
— P.C. Richard & Son. Televisions, appliances, mattresses. Distinctive jingle.

“My friends don’t necessarily go to galleries,” says Alvaro, who spent time on the payrolls of all of the above, back when he was living in New York and had yet to achieve the success that awaited him in London. “When I worked retail, more of my friends would come to visit me, because everybody bought a TV. Everybody wanted to have a TV. So now it’s just, ‘How do I make my art world into a place, like, where everybody comes to buy a TV?’”

For a recent Paris exhibition, ‘They Got Time: YOU BELONG TO THE CITY’, Alvaro mined memories of New York via a three-part installation. Staged at the Thaddaeus Ropac gallery’s space in the suburb of Pantin were a series of imitation shop fronts (a reference was Walter Benjamin’s unfinished book ‘The Arcades Project’, a sprawling work of cultural criticism largely concerned with the shopping arcades of 19th-century Paris). Alongside Alvaro’s retail-based interventions were works featuring figures such as Andy Warhol, Mary J. Blige and Tupac Shakur, the latter re-enacting a 1996 photograph by David LaChapelle in which the rapper (who would be killed in a drive-by shooting later that year) is lying in a bathtub covered in gold jewellery. Alvaro has described Tupac as the most significant artist of his lifetime, and his 2021 painting ‘They have They Cant’ pays tribute accordingly. Lyrics from the song ‘Keep Ya Head Up’ are stitched in yarn across a canvas of spray-painted concrete. Draped below it, bunting-like, are patterned bandanas, each a different colour.

“The quality of light by which we scrutinise our lives has direct bearing upon the product which we live, and upon the changes which we hope to bring about through those lives,” writes self-described “black, lesbian, feminist, socialist, mother, warrior, poet” Audre Lorde in the essay ‘Poetry Is Not a Luxury’. Alvaro has cited it as a formative inspiration. “It is within this light that we form those ideas by which we pursue our magic and make it realised. This is poetry as illumination, for it is through poetry that we give name to those ideas which are, until the poem, nameless and formless — about to be birthed, but already felt. That distillation of experience from which true poetry springs births thought as dream births concept, as feeling births idea, as knowledge births (precedes) understanding.”

The Tate’s collection includes Alvaro’s piece ‘Street Dreams are Made of Basketball’, in which a basketball sits on a block of concrete, which is in a milk crate, which is itself on top of a wooden frame stretched with hessian, which in turn has been laced with plastic ropes. These ropes adhere to an orange, yellow and lilac colour scheme inspired by Josef Albers, a favourite artist of Alvaro’s.

Basketball is a frequent motif in Alvaro’s work. In 2022 he created a functional court in Bethnal Green, east London, in collaboration with organisations including the Serpentine Gallery, Tower Hamlets Council and the basketball team London Lions (by far the winners of the 2022–23 British Basketball League season, with 64 points to the second-placed Leicester Riders’ 50).

The blue, khaki and green court can be found at the north-eastern corner of Weavers Fields. Alvaro described it as being at once a working recreational facility and “a map that represents both migration and athleticism.” The free-throw circles, he said, double as suns setting in distinct lands, the triangles on the sidelines as mountains and valleys. The inspirations at play included the work of pop artist Bridget Riley, video artist Arthur Jafa, and the celebrated creations of the Gee’s Bend quilt movement.
A conversation fragment in which Alvaro considers how — depending on the city in which he is painting — an identical object ends up being represented differently:

If I paint two hibiscus flowers, one in London and one in New York, it’s the same subject but it’s so different. I did a show at Nicola Vassell [2023’s ‘Island Life’, named after the Grace Jones album], and the flowers needed to be so much wider, but yet so much more radiant and bright and in your face. And it happened because I was dealing with New York.
How might the London hibiscus flower be by comparison?

Well, I did one series of flowers here. It was much thinner. It was much more intimate. It was much lighter. Whereas in New York, it had so much more saturation of colour. And I remember that after a couple washes and a couple of gestures, it felt finished a lot quicker, and in New York, it felt finished only after days of just pushing through it.
Then the hibiscus flower itself, it’s from the Caribbean, right? Is it associated with one of the other places you’ve lived in, aside from those two cities?

Yeah, although the first hibiscus I drew was in New York, because it was by the playground by my parents’ house, next to a mural of Marcus Garvey. I remember painting it and bringing it to my stepdad because they had these hibiscus flowers in their garden as well. And so even though I really first met it in the Caribbean, the first time I engaged with it in a real way was in New York.
14. BREAKFAST AT TIFFANY’S

As a kind of appendix to the Pantin show, Alvaro created a playlist of 45 songs which, thanks to the underrated magic of QR codes, was available to listen to as visitors pondered the work in situ or as they reflected on it afterwards. Various hip-hop artists are present in the playlist, which includes two tracks by DMX (‘How’s it Goin’ Down’ and ‘Slippin’’) and ‘Jesus Walks’ from Kanye West’s 2004 album ‘The College Dropout’, for example.

Perhaps most characteristically, it begins with three separate interpretations of the same pop-cultural artefact, namely ‘Moon River’, a song whose overfamiliarity never seems to nullify its impact of making the listener temporarily imagine themselves as the star of a movie. There’s the sparkling original by Audrey Hepburn from the soundtrack to the film ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’; there’s Frank Sinatra’s crooned one; and there’s Frank Ocean’s rendition, released as a single on Valentine’s Day 2018, turning an otherwise wistful and nostalgic number into something more assertive and forward-looking.

It’s the Hepburn, says Alvaro, that really moves him, and indeed the show took its inspiration from Truman Capote’s novel: “One day I picked up ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’ at Strand Book Store in Union Square and I realised the NYC I was experiencing in the ’90/2000s was what Truman Capote wrote about in ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’.”

That’s from a statement Alvaro released with the exhibition. Can he elaborate? “It was mostly about what I thought of as an end of a New York that I think of as being between ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’ and ‘Sex and the City’. It’s a very particular New York. How do you go from being a gay guy in the middle of Pennsylvania who’s deeply religious, socially awkward at best, and imagine yourself to be Andy Warhol? Or your Notorious B.I.G. or your Jay-Z? There was a New York that was about how — no matter where you started — you could get to this impossible thing that was only limited by your imagination.”

The Duveen Galleries at Tate Britain are 300 feet long. Over a million people pass through them each year. The most recent commission to fill the galleries was by Hew Locke and was called ‘The Procession’, back in 2022. Alvaro Barrington’s project will run from 29 May until 26 January 2025.
Styling by Stuart Williamson. Fashion by Bottega Veneta. Photographic assistance by Andy Moores. Styling assistance by Helly Pringle. Production by Fiona Percival and Phoebe Clothier.

items.title: Tiffany Day Will Tell You Everything
items.description: Hoodie and skirt MEMORY NYC, shoes FANCI CLUB
items.author: Steffi Cao
paragraphs: Hoodie and skirt MEMORY NYC, shoes FANCI CLUB

It’s 2023, and I’m standing on the sloping floor of Gramercy Theater in Manhattan watching indie musician Tiffany Day do something very vulnerable. In the middle of a series of viral bedroom pop singles — sugary-sweet melodies laid out over titles like “IF I DON’T TEXT YOU FIRST” and “I’M OVERDRAMATIC AND I MISS YOU” — she breaks into a 10-minute dubstep set.

I cannot emphasize enough that this set is hella random. Not the music itself — it’s a great selection, and Day’s stage presence is infectious — but the way she drops smack into the run of her first-ever headlining show. The reaction of the crowd, predominantly underage and sitting around the 5’2” mark, is mixed. Some people bob their heads in a vague appreciation, others look around to see if we should all be dancing to it or not. But this looks like the most fun Day has had on stage all night. She’s bouncing around, smiling, space buns vibrating.

It’s no surprise that, three years later, electronic music is the foundation of Day’s sophomore breakout album, Halo — a project that put her on the US Billboard Top Dance Albums chart, broke one million streams the day of its release, and inspired her first sold-out headlining tour. This year, Day has played Boiler Room in London, opened for Illennium at Red Rocks and Skrillex in Chicago, and reached over 1.6 million monthly listeners on Spotify. Three years ago, I think I paid less than $20 for my ticket; the only way I could get into the Halo tour was on the press list.

On night one of her three-night run in New York City, amid the sweaty haze of Elsewhere in Brooklyn, fans were craning to get a good look at Day, a gentle mosh was undulating in the center of the dance floor, and neon 21+ bands flashed against a giant projection of Cinnamoroll. It was a very different crowd from the one I was a part of in 2023. But a lot of things are different now for Tiffany Day. When we meet at her hotel the next afternoon, the 26-year-old just woken up; she was up late playing the afters for her own concert as her DJ alter ego, Bass Fluff. It’s exciting, all this new audience energy. There are boys in the crowd now. There are moshers and budding degenerates and a new throng of ravers. “A lot of this tour was very much a huge expansion of my brain,” she says. “I poured everything into it.”
Jacket, brooch, necklace COACH

In person, Day is not the anxiety-riddled thought daughter that she is in her lyrics (“If this is everything I’ve ever wanted / Why does it feel like something’s missing? / God I question, is this actually real?”). She’s energetic and inquisitive and funny. She talks with her hands in long, unbroken trains of thought. We have some of the same tattoos, she points out: a tiger and Chinese folk-style clouds on our forearms (she likes mine better, I like hers better, isn’t that life); she and her family play a lot of Mario Party; did I know that she cried within the first five minutes of watching the Mario movie? Not the new one, though; fun fact: she tolerates the heat and humidity of shows by imagining she’s in a Corepower Yoga class. Is she talking too much? Feel free to cut her the fuck off.
“Can I feel your shoes?” she asks me maybe 60 seconds after we meet. “They look like they feel cool.” I tell her of course, and she puts a finger on my crinkled silver tabi flats. “Whoa.”
That’s what’s so compelling about Tiffany Day: She invites you inside of her mind without hesitation. “I can’t be mysterious,” she says. “I love talking.”

Like most of the post-internet generation of musicians, Day’s entire life can be traced online. Born in Toronto and raised in Wichita, Kansas, Day (whose given name is Tiffany Ruan) grew a YouTube following of 500,000 by posting covers to Top 40 songs like “Breakeven” by The Script and Justin Bieber’s “Love Yourself.” She was also on Vine where a video of her singing into an Italian well went viral, temporarily turning her into a meme. She uploaded remixes to SoundCloud, posting edits and satire raps.
Top vintage from ETCETERA, shorts ASHLEY WILLIAMS from RETAIL PHARMACY, socks CALZEDONIA
Dress JENNY FAX, socks FALKE

The social media launchpad allowed Day to start releasing a series of singles. Her 2024 debut album, Lover Tofu Fruit, earned her a modest 10-city headlining tour. It was nothing to sneeze at, but it also came at great personal cost. The Gratitude Tour was entirely self-funded and self-produced, and it put her into $10,000 of credit card debt — something she has spoken openly about on social media.

Worse, Lover Tofu Fruit wasn’t the artistic thesis that Day had hoped her debut album would be. Day took a year off after first tour, which she officially said was to rest, but candidly, she tells me, was also and largely because she couldn’t get work. “No one booked me,” she says. “It was a mixture of, I feel like the world will never see me as someone who belongs to anything. Also, I’m running out of money. Also, my fans expect one thing from me, but I don’t want to give it to them because I feel like I’ve outgrown it. It was all these things mixed together where I just felt so heavy.”
Dress JENNY FAX, socks FALKE

She was ready to give it up, blow the dust off her biomedical engineering degree from Loyola Marymount, and get started on a civilian life. It was hard not to compare her standing to that of everyone else her age. “I had just graduated from college,” she recalls. “All my friends started their 9-to-5 jobs. These bitches were shopping at Aritzia, and I was like, ‘I feel so much FOMO. I want a desk, I want snacks in the kitchen.’ And I was like, ‘Maybe this is it for me.’ I genuinely was very much thinking about stopping my music career.”

Race also played a part in her career crisis. The mid-2010s saw a small boom of guitar- and ukulele-strumming Asian lo-fi girls achieve niche internet success: beabadoobee, mxmtoon, NIKI, Lyn Lapid, Luna Li, Stephanie Poetri, Alex Porat. Some of them managed to break out into the mainstream as standalone indie pop artists, but a large number of them saw their Asianness become a part of their artistry, like it or not. Both the music industry and consumers have certain ideas about the kinds of artists who should be making certain genres of music. And when an artist doesn’t match those stereotypes, they’re often excluded, their work corralled into “identity” playlists and heritage-month posts.

Day herself moved away from the overt Asian signals in her projects, with Lover Tofu Fruit giving way to Halo, Monolid metastasizing into Bass Fluff. I ask if she ever felt as though her race walked in the door before her work, in a way that felt more limiting than empowering. “Now that you say it, hell yeah!” she says. “One hundred percent. It’s more freeing to be considered a genre artist. Subconsciously, at the time, I probably couldn’t even understand what was going on. But it seemed like no one could break out [of the labels].”

It’s not that Day hated indie pop as a concept. But after a while, it felt like she wasn’t allowed to turn anywhere else. It wasn’t until 2020 that she connected with producer Jack Hallenback, who worked across both Lover Tofu Fruit and Halo, that she realized she was allowed to try other things. “He’s the one who made me realize I love writing and making things that feel a little more electronic-inspired. It was hard because I was dropping singles here and there that were kind of—” she waves her hands “—hyper-pop-y, the Gex sort of sound. And nobody fucked with it. I was like, ‘Oh, these stream like shit.’”

They did, at first. Even her lead single off Halo, “AMERICAN GIRL,” underwhelmed. Day says it was the worst streaming debut of her career (now, it’s the most-streamed song on the album). No one seemed to understand it. “I went back to indie pop because it was like, ‘I guess that’s what people want from me,’” she says. “It went on for so long that I became miserable because all of the singles I was releasing, I hated.”

Should we name the songs she hated? Day laughs, takes a breath, pulls out a hand to count them on her fingers, but her team jumps in. (Doing interviews with Gen Z artists, you learn that at some point, the team will jump in. I am told it wasn’t always this way.)

They’re new, Day’s team. Some of them, anyway. Her manager, Sammy Seaver, and creative director, Ally Wei, are longstanding friends and collaborators, but there are a lot of new faces, new resources pouring into this project of Tiffany Day. Still, Day herself is actively involved in pretty much everything. She gave notes on the lighting cues for this tour, spent two weeks editing the concert visuals at her parents’ kitchen table in Kansas, and even drove around to different merchandise suppliers in Los Angeles and tried on hoodie samples to find the perfect batwing sleeve for her tour merch — the ultimate hoodie that hoodies. (Yes, Day says, she’s seen that viral TikTok). “It’s the most amount of money I’m making from a tour, however, it’s also the most amount of money we’re spending on a tour,” she tells me. “But Halo was really special, and I wanted to make sure the tour was just as special.” And after years doing everything on her own, she says, letting go even a little bit is “very scary.”

To be fair, Day also thought that, given its initial reception, Halo would be her last project. Wei, 26, tells me that Day approached the album and the tour with a new clarity. “Tiff definitely had more of a vision for what she wanted the project to look like,” she says as we sit on the carpeted floor of a prop rental studio in Ridgewood. “It was a very Hail Mary type, ‘We're gonna go out with a bang.’” Wei and Day dreamed up their vision of “Tiffland” for the tour, a candy-colored Y2K world of Sanrio characters and early-internet tabs and angels. It was in the same colorway as Day’s previous bedroom pop projects, with the same bright hues and cartoon characters, but with a bit of Von Dutch edge.

Wei and Day first became friends in 2021, after Wei DM’d Day on Instagram suggesting they shoot sometime. They quickly started working together. Halo, Wei says, is a little outside of her personal style, so this era has become more of a collaboration. “The partnership we have is so special that sometimes people ask me, ‘How do I find that?’ And I’m like, ‘I don’t know; it just kind of happened.’ I can’t imagine doing what I do for her for anyone else. The friendship element makes the project stronger.”

It’s deeply ironic that the project that finally made Day feel like herself drew so many allegations of trend-hopping. It is true that this is a new sound for Day. It is true that electronic music is on the rise; data shared with me by Spotify shows that streaming numbers for electronic music were in decline until 2024, when they sharply reversed course, with US-based searches for genres like house growing 1,500% over the past six years. It’s a genre that, like many others, comes with a highly territorial fanbase and is skeptical of newcomers.

I ask Day how she feels about the discourse that clouded part of Halo’s release. In her open-book way, she nods. “I can understand that, as an avid person in your niche, it might feel like I’ve infiltrated,” she says. “But the reality is that I love your niche, I respect it, and I’m also very much a listener and a consumer. I’m not just gonna see something and be like, ‘Oh, that's trending, let me hop on that.’ The biggest misconception online is how people say, ‘Tiffany Day is a LARPer because she jumped into electronic music when it was trendy.’ It’s not their fault. It’s just that they probably don’t have enough time to do research on me.”

Artists almost always face backlash for changing their sound. Even if most of the critics weren’t at Gramercy Theater in 2023, or following Day’s middle-school SoundCloud, where she was uploading anime edits. And the truth is, the fact that it took Day a while to get here is the whole point. “It almost feels like artists are spawning with everything planned out. And it took me six, seven, eight years to find who I was, or at least who I want to be,” she says. “The world literally saw how I grew up and changed and developed. The way I did it is honestly, not to toot my own horn, but I feel like it was brave.” She pauses for a second to double-check with herself, then throws up her hands. “Yeah! It was very brave of me to do that!”
Hoodie and skirt MEMORY NYC, shoes FANCI CLUB

Anyway, she’s past trying to prove anything to anyone else. This is about making something she’s proud of. About getting on Ableton again without wanting to throw up. “I’ve really just brushed it off my shoulder because it’s like, what are you gonna do? Change Betty03’s mind by replying back to her? That’s not happening,” she says.

At Elsewhere, you can feel that return to self in the air. Day leaps around on stage, beaming and warning the boy sitting on another boy’s shoulders in the back to please be careful, please don’t make her liable for some bullshit. Everyone jumps when the lights start to flash, everyone goes pin drop-quiet during the tender moments. Nothing feels random, and no one is confused. Everyone’s into it, excited for this era of Tiffany Day.
