Velvet is also a signature. That duality of color and texture, and also a bit of a historical Victorian sensibility.
Where do you think that interest in Victorian garments comes from?

There’s an emotional, aesthetic love for it. There’s a bit of a groundedness and a weight to it, and a bit of that period of time was quite spiritual thinking about the afterlife and death, but there was a sense of romance around that that I think really seeped into the clothes in a way that I don’t know if other periods of time really reflect. On the other side of it, it isn’t Victorian specifically, but a lot of historical dress for women is incredible tailoring—thinking about those bodice jackets that have a lot of tiny little panels with lots of little grosgrain finishing on the seams on the inside—and it’s all about molding to the female body. As a menswear designer, I love wearing men’s clothes and wearing a tailored jacket, but I think that the idea of having that sensibility and also reflecting femininity is the perfect storm for me. A lot of that just got lost in a certain period of time once women were able to wear pants, and in the transition of women being able to access menswear, women’s tailoring never got back to that sort of technical level of fitting the body or the female form.
You’ve never done a runway show, which is something that many young designers feel signals their arrival. Why is that?

I love fashion and wanted to work in fashion because I loved watching fashion shows. And specifically, I loved shows that were immersive. I always go back to [Alexander] McQueen [that signaled] fashion is more than product. It is this world-building, cinematic performance art, and you can take it just so much further emotionally. If I’m going to do a show, I want it to carry that level of weight. For me, at my scale, it just feels like the most manageable way to encapsulate a sense of emotion is to do it through a [photo] shoot and showroom appointments for now, just in truly a practical sense. But it is my dream, and I’m working towards having a show. But when I do it, I want it to feel special.
What does this recognition mean to you?

It’s a bit surreal, in a way. It’s especially cool that it’s voted by the industry, and it sounds maybe kind of cheesy, but I do just feel like that is the best reward. That all these people that I’ve worked with are acknowledging [me]. It feels solidifying, grounding. It feels like I’ve been doing this forever, and it’s also going by so fast at the same exact time. It lets me be present and acknowledge myself for how much work has been put into it and that I did it and it’s real and it’s something I dreamed about for so long.
Do you feel like a fashion-industry darling?

[Laugh] Oh my God, how does one answer that question? Gosh, I think that three years ago I was entering these rooms knowing absolutely no one... I think the showroom has actually really fostered real relationships and friendships in the industry, and a sense of community that just feels really good. I work as hard as I can to support whatever the stylists are doing or the editors, I’m always physically running around to make sure that they get the clothes because I love what they do. I love that I know the photographer and the stylist and all the people, and know that if my clothes are in it, it will be amazing for me and they made the effort to reach out to me, to include me in it. The word darling is such an ick word [laugh]. I feel like the word I want to say is camaraderie, because everyone just works so hard. Nobody is flouncing around being a darling. We are all hustling together, and if I can support your hustle and you support mine, that’s the best thing. And when it works, it’s just so satisfying.

Tim Burton, iconoclast filmmaker extraordinaire, has a new capsule with Loewe, which has recreated characters and vignettes from The Nightmare Before Christmas as bags and charms. These kinds of collabs were a staple when Jonathan Anderson was at the brand, and Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez seem to be game to keep them coming with the same endearing whimsy.

In the age of artificial intelligence, the film has become a symbol of human craft and ingenuity. “The more it keeps going that way,” Burton told me yesterday, calling from London and answering a question about the proliferation of AI in film, “the more I appreciate [the human] side of it. I think it’s something that’s very important to keep in the world, the tactile, not being on a screen all the time and doing all that sort of thing. To me, [humanity] is very important to life and art and anything, really.” We also spoke about his collaboration with A$AP Rocky and whether he’d ever do a live-action remake of 2005’s Corpse Bride.
To subscribe to José Criales-Unzueta's weekly Fit Check newsletter, click here.

items.title: “I Hate My Fucking Life Right Now”: A Night Out With DC Republicans as the Blue Wave Crashed Down
items.description: It’s not easy to throw an election night party in Washington when your side is bracing for a wipeout. But at Butterworth’s, the bistro that has been a hub of MAGA Washington in Donald Trump’s second term, the DC Republicans were intent on trying. Women in busi
items.author: Aidan McLaughlin
paragraphs: It’s not easy to throw an election night party in Washington when your side is bracing for a wipeout. But at Butterworth’s, the bistro that has been a hub of MAGA Washington in Donald Trump’s second term, the DC Republicans were intent on trying. Women in business casual and men in the party uniform—blue suits, white shirts, and red ties taut to the collar—drank specialty cocktails including “The Elephant in the Room” and “The Senate Majority Martini.” The bar might have been busy, but the mood was precarious. As Dua Lipa blasted from the speakers inside, a man on a smoke break out on the street took big gulps of a pint of lager and stared down at his phone. “Darline Graham just plummeted on Polymarket,” he said, exhaling from his cigarette. “I hate my fucking life right now. Everything just sucks. Jesus Christ, we’re gonna lose it all.” A car drove past Butterworth’s with the windows down. A woman leaning out of an open window screamed, “Oh yeah, Democrats!”

Inside, at first, revelers were upbeat. It was early enough that the rising of the blue tide had yet to inspire fear—to an extent. A man waiting for drinks at the bar monitored the results in Florida, one of the few bright spots for Republicans. When informed that Senate candidate Ken Paxton and incumbent governor Greg Abbott were down bad in Texas, he clutched his head dramatically. “Oh my God! I just got here. I need to go home.” He looked at his phone in anguish. Within minutes, he darted for the door. A White House staffer wearing a red hat emblazoned with “45/47” on the side and “WINNING” on the front made the rounds. “Optimistic? I was a lot more earlier,” he said. “If we lose Texas, it’s a catastrophe.” Minutes later, Decision Desk called Texas for James Talarico, the first Democrat to be elected to the Senate in the Lone Star State since 1988.

As Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” blared through the speakers, two men at the bar lamented the cruel irony of the song playing as Talarico’s comfortable lead expanded over Paxton, his Republican challenger.

“I’m not trying to crash out,” said one of the men, a Republican volunteer. “But we nominated Hitler with Down syndrome. And guess what?! He lost! He lost! And now we lose a Supreme Court justice. It is a fucking disaster.”

It was a fucking disaster indeed. Republicans lost almost every Senate seat that mattered, with the small consolation of Florida quickly washed away by the titanic loss of South Carolina. Trump had spent the election telling voters, “Pretend that I’m on the ballot.” By all measures, they had. By 10:40 p.m., Trump offered his verdict on the night: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

Trump only has himself to blame for the Republican wipeout. The executive decisions that have defined his second administration were like something cooked up in #Resistance laboratories to alienate the vast majority of Americans from his political project. The candidates he backed in these midterm elections, against the wishes of the Republican establishment, are those who wiped out the hardest. Darline Graham, the political-neophyte sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general whom Trump backed in the primary against incumbent senator John Cornyn, lost to young Democrat James Talarico.
“We got SMOKED. BIGLY,” one source close to Trump texted me. “He’s not the kingmaker he was, or still thinks he is. This is a referendum on him.”

In the 1994 midterms, when Bill Clinton’s presidency was bludgeoned half to death by the Newt Gingrich revolution, The New Yorker’s Michael Kelly described the punch-drunk shock inside the White House. “No one can be expected to grasp immediately the full implications of being struck between the eyes by a two-by-four,” he wrote in the wake of the Gingrichian curb stomp, “so it was not surprising that the initial White House response to what had happened, and why it had happened, contained an element of stunned denial.”

The train that flattened Trump and Republicans this year had been barreling down the track for some time. No one could claim to be blindsided. Never in history has a party tethered itself so helplessly to one man, much less such a historically unpopular one. In December of last year, The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance invited a conservative pollster to the White House to deliver an urgent message to the president: Americans don’t feel like you are fighting for them, Mark Mitchell of Rasmussen Reports explained as Trump ate a crab cake lunch. Mitchell urged him to focus on a message of “pragmatic economic populism.”

Trump ignored all that. Soon after the meeting, he started a war with Iran that triggered a global energy shock and by one study’s estimate has cost the average American household $2,000. “The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least,” pro-Trump pundit Matt Walsh wrote on X. “A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles.”

A year after the calamity he dubbed “Liberation Day,” Trump conjured up a new plot to liberate Americans from economic security: an escalated trade war with Canada that battered states in the upper Midwest that Republicans needed to hold the Senate. All the while, the president dismissed concerns about the cost of living in his public statements. He referred to “affordability” as a hoax, and fixated on lavish renovation projects, like the $600 million ballroom and the messy renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The pool, of all things, ended up anchoring Trump’s closing argument. In a press conference held there on Monday, Trump spent more than 20 minutes regaling reporters with war stories from his summer campaign against algae. “They’re brand-new pipes put in, and the pipes being very important in terms of the algae and other things,” he said sternly, brandishing a poster board with photos of the pool base. The next day, gasoline and diesel prices hit their highest national average in history. The president’s approval ratings sat firmly at a record bottom. “I don’t think Trump cares,” said the source close to Trump.

The White House line on these elections is that Trump did all he could to help the party, holding a blitz of rallies in the run-up to Election Day and deploying more than $350 million of his sizable MAGA Inc. war chest to boost Republican candidates. The money might have helped, but it isn’t clear that the rallying did. Trump’s unpopularity is now seismic, and there’s a growing feeling that his movement, after a decade of dominating the frontal lobe of the American mind, is petering out. Even the president’s very generous offer to every American—$5,000 each if Republicans held both chambers of Congress—didn’t seem to sway our particularly plutomanic populace. Seventy-one percent of Americans, according to one poll, said they didn’t believe they would ever receive the money.

Trump’s approval among young men, a key voting bloc that ensured his return to power, has plummeted, and popular podcasters who cater to a younger audience have abandoned him. CNN’s exit poll on Election Day found Democrats won young white men by 17 points, two years after Trump won the same group by 28 points. “We all have to move to Florida,” said a dejected young Republican wearing a tie covered in elephants at Butterworth’s. “It’s a disaster.” Doja Cat’s “Paint the Town Red” was blasting.

Around 20 minutes north, at Metrobar, a few hundred Democrats assembled in the garden for a victory party. Emerging from a taxi, I was met with the roar of the crowd. NBC News had just announced that Democrats had won the Senate. As Steve Kornacki broke down the results from Ohio on a jumbotron erected in the garden of the bar, the crowd chanted, “USA!”

Michelle Meoh, a young Democratic volunteer, told me the night had gone “extremely well” for her party. “Basically every race, even races that I hadn’t thought would go in our favor, were wins.” What does she want Democrats to do with their newfound power? “I guess show that we’re worthy of the trust that the voters are placing in us. I want us to prove that we’re tapped into the feelings of ordinary Americans and that we really do feel their pain. And that we don’t take that support for granted.”
Two burly men embraced. “Susan Collins is fucking gone!” one shouted.

I made my way to the exit as the hysterical celebrations died down, and Kornacki on the jumbotron read the latest results in Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed held a narrow lead over Republican Mike Rogers. “How am I feeling?!” asked a visibly overserved woman. I hadn’t asked. “Fucking great!”
This story has been updated.

items.title: The Curious Case of Olivia Reingold’s AI Photo at a Democratic Victory Party: Valentino, Chanel, and a Free Press Mystery
items.description: On Monday night, the eve of the 2026 midterm elections, the fashion crowd celebrated at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, colloquially referred to as the Oscars of American fashion. Tory Burch was honored with the Positive Change Award, which was presented to her
items.author: José Criales-Unzueta
paragraphs: On Monday night, the eve of the 2026 midterm elections, the fashion crowd celebrated at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, colloquially referred to as the Oscars of American fashion. Tory Burch was honored with the Positive Change Award, which was presented to her by Anna Wintour, the global editorial director of Vogue and chief content officer of Condé Nast. In her remarks, Wintour made the evening’s only direct reference to the midterms, reminiscing about attending a fundraising event for James Talarico, who successfully flipped Texas in the race for the Senate last night, alongside Burch. After applause from the audience, Wintour, a prolific Democratic fundraiser herself, looked up and addressed the room: “Let’s hope all of Texas feels the way you do,” she said.

The American fashion crowd has largely distanced itself from politics since the 2024 election. During their time in the White House as first ladies, Michelle Obama and Jill Biden were staunch supporters of the American fashion industry, often wearing American designers for public appearances. Melania Trump, in contrast, has more often preferred European labels. It’s an MO that trickles down into the political parties they represent.

There were many headlines that came out of last night’s midterms: Talarico flipped Texas, Annie Andrews flipped South Carolina, New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas became the first out gay man to be elected to the Senate, and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia and Deb Haaland of New Mexico became the first Black and Native American women, respectively, to be elected governor in the history of the US.

And yet it wasn’t just good news (and many great memes) that circulated in my group chats last night; there were also some fashion choices worth noting. First, the most pressing: Where were Steve Kornacki’s khakis? And what was the reasoning behind Haley Stevens’s ludicrously capacious hat? Some questions in life simply go unanswered.

Kornacki, a national political correspondent for NBC News, does not make his political affiliations public. But men in his age range (he is 47) and in the generations that follow—millennials and Gen Z—have been contending with what formalwear means and signals today.

Democratic men have been hard at work on their public image since the 2024 election, largely distancing themselves from the MAGA look and its too-large suits and extra-wide ties. In separating themselves from the manosphere, men like Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Senate race in Michigan, and Jon Ossoff, who was reelected to the Senate in Georgia, have been dressing more like the less buttoned up, progressive men they represent and less like the old establishment politicians on both the right and the left.

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed often sported tees and sweaters rather than button-downs and ties, frequently wearing taut sweaters and henleys under his suit jacket, while Ossoff largely opted for rolled cuffs and no jacket. As the two delivered victory speeches last night, they each wore a tailored suit—a little too tight in the arms; these are men who seem to eat their fair share of protein—and ditched their tie.

It’s a familiar image of a more laid-back look, but one in stark contrast to that of the faces of the right: Donald Trump, JD Vance, et al. Ossoff and El-Sayed, similarly to Kamala Harris during her presidential bid, also leaned into what was happening on the internet. These days, netizens are happy to objectify men and christen a new internet boyfriend every week. Ossoff’s and El-Sayed’s campaigns seemed to understand the power of thirst—that their suits were too tight was most likely not completely intentional, but it did help underscore a simple fact: that they are fit, and that their virility can be both attractive and nonthreatening all at once.

It is worth noting, however, that there are some men further to the left, both in politics and around it, who have reembraced the suit: Zohran Mamdani and Hasan Piker. On one hand, this has served a similar purpose as Ossoff’s and El-Sayed’s choices: It has distanced them from looksmaxxers and other conservative-leaning young men. On the other hand, a suit for Mamdani and Piker signifies what suits have always represented: that these are grown men doing important things.

The men are not the full story, however. Bottoms and Haaland came as they are, nodding to the communities they represent. The former wore a bright fuchsia suit and matching blouse, a callback to the lively and monochromatic dressing that is a deeply embedded and celebrated tradition in Black church culture. Haaland’s jewelry—firefly earrings and a beaded necklace—nodded at the style of accessories that is representative of Native style and fashion. If there is something that fashion clearly signifies, it’s community and belonging.

It is a running punch line that the left is more closely connected to fashion—it’s the wine-and-cheese crowd, the elites. (Hillary Clinton, during her bid for the presidency in 2016, was dragged online and by the press for wearing an Armani jacket that reportedly retailed for some $12,000 while delivering a speech that touched on income inequality.) While it’s true that fashion designers are often more enthusiastic about dressing progressives than they are about dressing conservatives, in the era of Trump and the MAGA look, this has become a half-baked story.

Olivia Reingold, a staff writer at The Free Press, made a post on X last night while reporting from an event for the Michigan Democratic Party. “So far at Abdul El-Sayed’s election night event I’ve spotted, Valentino heels, a Chanel bag, a Moncler jacket, Rolex watches, and a YSL bag among other designer items,” Reingold wrote, captioning an image of a woman holding a gold quilted Chanel handbag and a pair of Valentino Rockstud leather pumps.

When one takes a closer look, however, the image has several discrepancies. The style and make of the Chanel Flap bag is inconsistent with others the brand has sold, and the Valentino shoes in question appear askew in proportion; their straps have several punched holes that the authentic Valentino style does not. This could mean that the products in the image are not authentic, but there is another suggestive tell: The bottom strap on the left shoe appears to cut through its connecting strap rather than around, a classic mistake made when artificial intelligence is used to create or alter an image. A run of the image through several AI detectors, including SynthID, a digital watermarking approach created by Google DeepMind that detects media generated by OpenAI, Google, Nvidia, and Kakao, suggests the use of AI. SynthID detected that “this media was made or edited with OpenAI.” (Vanity Fair has reached out to Chanel and Valentino to advise on the authenticity of the products.)

Reingold did not reply to a request for comment, but on Thursday afternoon followed up with a new post on X, admitting to using AI “to brighten and sharpen an image of a woman in Valentino shoes and a Chanel bag.”

It’s become too easy to try to make a point about the left’s fashion choices: that Rama Duwaji, wife of Mamdani, should not wear pricey shoes, even if borrowed, because of her political beliefs; or that Democratic women should not carry Valentino or Chanel and vote for a candidate seeking to tax the wealthy. Therein lies the crux of the argument: Does this mean that luxury shoppers should align themselves with MAGA because it’s a party associated with billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos and logo-clad celebs like Nicki Minaj, who wore Chanel to the polls in New Hampshire? The answer is simple: no.

Our fashion choices say much about our values, identity, and aspirations. And while politicians have oftentimes utilized fashion to align themselves with specific groups or appear friendly to voters, they, in broad strokes, do not define our political affiliations. A Chanel bag does not make a Democrat, just as a red tie does not make a Republican.
This story has been updated.

items.title: Gay People (Mostly) Explain Gay Halloween
items.description: When you see a post that begins with “I hate gay Halloween, what do you mean you’re dressed as…” you know you’re in for a good laugh, or perhaps the feeling that you’re completely out of the loop. Trick-or-treating isn’t until this weekend, but in the age of s
items.author: José Criales-Unzueta
paragraphs: When you see a post that begins with “I hate gay Halloween, what do you mean you’re dressed as…” you know you’re in for a good laugh, or perhaps the feeling that you’re completely out of the loop. Trick-or-treating isn’t until this weekend, but in the age of social media the day itself has taken the back seat—it’s online where the battle for the best costumes takes place, and it’s happening earlier every year.

The trend began taking shape in the late 2010s and gained strength during the pandemic: celebrities—most notably the Kardashian-Jenner clan—began re-creating memorable moments from pop culture, mostly old film posters or iconic music album covers, and staging elaborate costume shoots for their Instagrams. The closer the re-creation would get to the original the better—and worthier of likes.

The idea of gay Halloween exists somewhere in this realm, though it’s inevitably more lo-fi, and the most successful looks aim for laughs rather than mere online clout. Plainly, it’s when people—mostly gay men—pick a niche pop culture moment or meme and re-create it in a costume. Forget witches and Scream masks. In 2004, Mean Girls declared, “In girl world, Halloween is the one night of the year when a girl can dress like a total slut and no other girls can say anything about it.” The 2026 equivalent is less about horny devils. Halloween is now the one night of the year when you can let out your inner freak or geek: Now you can be the breakup Post-it from a 2003 episode of Sex and the City, or Marc Jacobs when he wore a neck brace. Two years ago, a friend dressed as Antonio, a character played by Ariana Grande on Saturday Night Live. Another at the same party went as Rihanna as a nun for an Interview magazine cover.

Once upon a time, Halloween was about being as frightening as possible. Sure, there is something indeed terrifying about being broken up with via Post-it, and some less-online people are still attached to the classics—a zombie, a devil, et cetera—but Halloween has been co-opted by the internet, and by celebrity culture, in a way that has made it entirely self-indulgent.

Consider Heidi Klum’s famous annual Halloween bash, which she started in 2000. Early on, her costumes evolved from classic (a dominatrix the first year, a vampire in 2005) to more complex (a skinless person in 2011) to complete cosplay. In 2015, Klum appeared as Jessica Rabbit; in 2018, as the ogre version of Fiona from Shrek. Last year, she was a Medusa, and her husband, Tom Kaulitz, a hoplite turned into stone. There are Hollywood-level prosthetics, and, largely, it appears as if her costumes are made more for an image than for a party. Klum, in this space, is both the trendsetter and the shining example of the way our collective take on the holiday has evolved to adjust to our online-first lifestyles.

“Someone I just started working with recently said, ‘We live in a reference economy,’” says stylist Ron Hartleben, who works with Camila Cabello and Tyla, among others. “That really struck me,” he says. “Everything has been done. Everyone has access to all the same images now.” So much so that people in the queer community “have gone about seeking the most niche, obscure reference from a show or pop culture moment and making that their Halloween costume” so that a mere mortal, in this case a cis, heterosexual person, may not understand it. “Gay Halloween is exploiting that obscure moment in pop culture and running with it to create one of the most stupid and entertaining outfits imaginable,” Hartleben says. “As long as you think it’s funny and you get it, you’re doing gay Halloween right.” Consider Benito Skinner and Mary Beth Barone’s costume this year as a shining example of gay Halloween: they dressed as Dakota Johnson and Ellen DeGeneres and even recreated their infamous, viral interview about the actor’s birthday party.

But gay Halloween has now broken past its own internet bubble. Celebrities and straight normies alike have adopted the reference-first language popular in queer and adjacent subcultures—from drag to ballroom and beyond—and made it mainstream to come off as more in-the-know.

Last year, Mandy Lee, a trend forecaster known as @oldloserinbrooklyn on TikTok and Instagram, dressed as Jonathan Anderson smoking a cigarette by the Seine, a video she reposted this year next to the original clip of Anderson to much online buzz (hers was taken by the Gowanus Canal in Brooklyn). “It’s a format that works particularly well online versus IRL because you’re able to [have] text onscreen or even throw up reference images to make it click,” Lee says. She categorizes her costumes as “fashion Halloween,” which she says lives under the same umbrella as gay Halloween. She’s dressed as Lynn Yaeger and Miuccia Prada before, and also the “tabi swiper.” The trick is that they are, as she says, “low effort.” They’re costumes that rely on what’s already in Lee’s closet—no production value, just a sense of humor. “It’s just fun to get hyper specific and granular,” Lee says. “[The costumes] are also not for everyone; they are for fashion people, and that’s what makes it fun.”

Earlier this week, stylist and creative director Chris Horan, who works with the likes of Charli xcx, Demi Lovato, and Christina Aguilera, reposted clips he’d been tagged in on Instagram of fans dressed as Adéla, for whom he is both stylist and creative director. “I obviously love when people dress up or reference any of the looks we’ve worked on,” Horan says. “It takes a lot of effort to make any sort of look on our part or [the fans’], so it always makes me happy to see it.”

Last year Horan worked with Lovato on her costume, for which she dressed as Poot Lovato, her fictional twin sister that originated from a Tumblr post in 2015. Poot had long been a gay Halloween staple, but her fans would have never imagined that Lovato herself would bring her back to the forefront in such a way. Horan thinks these costumes also speak to something bigger: “I don’t think you’re really hitting as a pop star if you don’t have an immediately identifiable look.”

The internet has changed the way we do most things, particularly getting dressed, so it’s no surprise that it would affect how we get dressed up. We do things not just for ourselves, or even the people who will see the costume IRL, but for our circles, or “followers,” to congratulate us. Social media may not have ruined Halloween—it’s made it funnier and perhaps less spooky—but it’s altered its spirit.

items.title: As “Black October” Comes to a Close, the Cybersecurity World Is on Edge
items.description: For months, the heads of frontier AI labs have been warning us that incidents like this summer’s Hugging Face hack could represent “early warning shots” before more menacing attacks in the years to come. Equipped with their own doomsday bunkers, some CEOs have
items.author: Julia Black
paragraphs: For months, the heads of frontier AI labs have been warning us that incidents like this summer’s Hugging Face hack could represent “early warning shots” before more menacing attacks in the years to come. Equipped with their own doomsday bunkers, some CEOs have begun instructing their teams to run preparedness scenarios for the day after a “catastrophic AI incident.”

“We are willing to accept some things going wrong,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Vanity Fair’s global editorial director, Mark Guiducci, last month, adding that “there is a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems that are going to come from these open-source models.”

Just in time for spooky season, those warning shots got a little louder. On Wednesday, October 21, two serious security vulnerabilities were revealed in PHP, the programming language behind more than 70% of the internet’s web pages. Some cybersecurity professionals have already begun to call this “Black October,” thanks to the unprecedented spate of hacks across the globe.

AI did play a role in all this—but perhaps not the one you’d expect. Security researchers had actually used tools developed by OpenAI to discover the bugs months ago—and had been rushing to patch them up before they got into the hands of bad actors. Unfortunately, those vulnerabilities leaked last week, sending governments and businesses scrambling to protect their websites before hackers—perhaps armed with some of the very same AI tools as those defending against them—moved in.

Yet even the frontier labs’ ability to keep pace was called into question on Monday morning, when The Washington Post published a story about how Cathedral, a new cybersecurity company founded by four ex-DOGE staffers, successfully infiltrated some of Anthropic’s internal systems in just 12 hours. The article dropped just hours before Anthropic filed pre-IPO documentation detailing the potential risks to its own revenues and the world at large if its cybersecurity game were found to be lacking.

To the cybersecurity community, this was just the latest in a series of startling escalations. Joshua Achiam, who resigned from his post as OpenAI’s chief futurist this summer after nine years at the company, wrote on X: “Feels like March 1, 2020 for Cyber. Not normal, something is happening. Internet lockdowns in a couple of months?”

While these anxieties may not have reached your average American yet, business leaders have been growing increasingly concerned. In mid-September, executives from some of the world’s largest companies gathered for a special meeting of the Partnership for New York City. Their special guests that day were Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon and former Department of Defense official Mark Beall, who had come to warn them about the threats posed by emerging AI capabilities.

The co-chairs, Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla and Tishman Speyer CEO Rob Speyer, looked out at their screens full of anxious CEOs from hedge funds and banks, as well as insurance, real estate, and pharmaceutical companies, and noted that it was one of their largest gatherings in years. One big topic on the minds of those gathered: AI-enabled cyberattacks.

During the Q&A portion of the talk, a representative from Coinbase raised his hand to ask what companies like his could do to combat the threat of “open-weight models in the hands of bad actors,” from cybercriminals to nation-states. (Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, meanwhile, has been one of the more outspoken advocates of deregulated, open-source AI.)

Earlier this month, Japan declared a “state of emergency” following sweeping cyberattacks on more than 20 major companies, from financial firms to rail operators. French authorities are still piecing together the mystery of how and why hackers targeted supermarket refrigerators around the country, spoiling millions of euros’ worth of food. Meanwhile, a new report from CrowdStrike suggests that recent attacks on South Korea’s financial sector were allegedly carried out by a single 26-year-old in China using an open-source AI tool.

Even here, cyberattacks have become so commonplace that you may have missed them in the flurry of headlines. (Did you catch this month’s massive breach of FBI employees’ personal details? Iran’s hit on more than 30 water systems in Minnesota this summer? And that’s to say nothing of mounting efforts by Russia to influence the midterm elections.)
“Feels like March 1, 2020 for Cyber.”

I was surprised to learn that the concerns of most cybersecurity experts are both less apocalyptic and more present than the kinds of visions filling the heads of AI CEOs. In short, they believe that AI systems haven’t yet caused a paradigm shift in terms of the scale of damage they can inflict. What increased access to AI tools has done is lower the barrier to entry for even unskilled hackers to target low-hanging fruit.

“Over the coming weeks and months, the more likely scenario is a local hospital network in Ohio losing power and patients on life support dying as a result; a utility network in Texas taken offline; the lights going out across half of Wisconsin,” says Hamza Chaudhry, the AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute.

“We’re just in an exceptionally unresilient moment, coming up against systems which are designed to exploit that lack of resilience,” he tells me. “The largest providers,” however, “also have the most resources to defend themselves, including early access to frontier AI models for defense.”
He concedes that there is one more scenario that is keeping him up at night. “I’m very concerned about the so-called geopolitical Hugging Face moment.”

At the Munich Security Conference earlier this year, his group ran a simulation for an audience of national security officials from across the West: Imagine China develops a Mythos-level cyber-capability, which then gets into the hands of the mercenaries at the Wagner Group, who deploy it in Mali to target French military infrastructure. Then, much like in the Hugging Face incident, the agents go on an unintended side quest and attack mainland military infrastructure inside Europe. And that’s when things spiral out of control. “There was a real chance that Article 5 would be invoked and NATO would declare war on Russia” in this simulation, Chaudhry tells me.

A high-level executive at one of the world’s largest energy suppliers tells me he’s been losing sleep over aging infrastructure, budget cuts, and staffing shortages. Small utilities, he says, are plagued by “patches that might be easy to fix given the resources necessary.” But for now, “operators are running on Windows NT,” he says, referring to Microsoft’s 1990s operating system. New infrastructure coming online to support data center buildouts isn’t much better off. This infrastructure is “being built at such a speed [that] there’s no regulation and there are no hard standards,” says the energy executive. “Security is an afterthought, and that scares me a whole lot.”

This is the part of the story where I’d love to reassure you that the powers that be have been hard at work bolstering our defensive systems. The reality is, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has lost nearly a third of its workforce and hundreds of millions of dollars in funding, and it has failed to appoint an official director to lead the agency since the Trump administration took office in January of last year. But things at the state and local levels are what really worry the experts I spoke with. A recent Deloitte survey of state chief information security officers (CISOs) found that their budgets are failing to keep pace with growing threats—and have even faced cuts in 16% of the country.
“For some reason, amidst increasing cyber-capabilities, our defenders are running out of money,” Soham Mehta, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, tells me. “Great.”
“Security is an afterthought, and that scares me a whole lot.”

There is at least some indication that authorities are beginning to wake up. Earlier this month, the new White House AI task force met for the first time to discuss cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection, among other topics. Many are hopeful that frontier AI will do more to help companies and governments defend themselves than it will to help their attackers—as in the case of OpenAI’s assistance in discovering the PHP flaws. In a survey of more than a hundred national security officials last month, 81% said that defensive capabilities are very likely to improve with the help of AI.

None of the experts I spoke with advised me to load up the bug-out bag just yet. For now, our fate is largely in the hands of the government officials and executives who have to make the choice to invest in updated security systems.

They largely gave the same advice I’ve been working off for years. Set up a password manager, as well as two-factor authentication wherever it’s available. Beware of any unusual messages, and don’t drop your credit card details into any suspicious websites. And perhaps most importantly: Contact your local representatives to nudge them on updating that 1990s software.

items.title: 'SNL': Watch Phoebe Bridgers Perform 'Bobby,' 'Still Standing'
items.description: Phoebe Bridgers performed two tracks from her acclaimed album, Lost Weekend, Saturday on SNL.
items.author: William Vaillancourt
paragraphs: Phoebe Bridgers performed two tracks from her acclaimed album, Lost Weekend, Saturday on SNL.
Bridgers opened with “Bobby,” a reflection on her relationship with comedian Bo Burnham, who co-wrote and sings on the track.

Other contributors to the 16-song album include fellow Boygenius members Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus, as well as Jack Antonoff and Geese frontman Cameron Winter. The finished product is the 32-year-old singer-songwriter’s “longest and most daring record yet, a tour de force in the art of disappearing, falling in love, and feeling grief so deeply that waking up every day kind of sucks,” Rolling Stone‘s Angie Martoccio wrote in a review. It reached the top spot on several charts, including Billboard’s top Independent Albums in the U.S.
Bridgers’ second performance was of “Still Standing,” a response to the loss of her father in 2023.
Bridgers’ SNL appearance comes a few days after she released her “Live at Madison Square Garden” EP, featuring five songs from Lost Weekend.

Later this month, Bridgers begins an eight-country European tour in support of Lost Weekend. Next year, The Lost Tour 2027 in North America runs from February through May, and includes two weekends at Coachella in April. She will also be a headliner at Iowa’s three-day Hinterland Music Festival in late July.

Bridgers debuted on SNL in February 2021, playing “Kyoto” and “I Know the End” from Punisher, which earned the 10th spot on Rolling Stone‘s list of the best albums of 2020. Bridgers returned in November 2023 when Boygenius performed two tracks from their debut studio album, The Record, an instant classic.

items.title: 'SNL': Hippie John Mulaney Has Some Very Unhip Thoughts at Woodstock
items.description: On Saturday Night Live, Woodstock attendee John Mulaney shared with his hippie friends some very uncool ideas about how their generation should live when they’re older.
items.author: William Vaillancourt
paragraphs: On Saturday Night Live, Woodstock attendee John Mulaney shared with his hippie friends some very uncool ideas about how their generation should live when they’re older.
While listening to Sly and the Family Stone at the 1969 music festival, Mulaney suddenly blurts out to his pals an odd suggestion: “Hey, when we get older, I think we should buy all the houses.”

When a friend (Andrew Dismukes) expresses confusion, Mulaney explains: “Our generation, the baby boomers, when we get older, I think we should just buy as many houses as we can get, and just like, have them.”
“Also, we should have all the money,” he goes on.

His freinds (Sarah Sherman, Kenan Thompson and Mikey Day) are skeptical, while Mulaney insists that their spirit of generosity should flip “in fifteen years, like 1985 or so.” Then, he says, “we should become ruthless corporate climbers that absolutely fetishize money in an almost pornographic way. Far out, right?”
After he’s offered marijuana, Mulaney has another idea: “We should scare our kids about this stuff.”

The group objects, prompting Mulaney to explain: “I feel like in 1985—hey, there’s that year again, feel like it’s going to be a big year for us—we should tell our kids if they smoke weed even once, it’ll ruin their lives. And not just weed, everything.”
“Everything we should enjoy, we tell our kids that it will kill them stone-ass dead,” he says.

When a friend relies that only hard drugs should come with a warning, Mulaney responds: “No, we should make our kids do speed: ritalin, adderall, just shove it down their throats their entire childhood so they can get into college.”
After a friend notes how easy it is to get into college, Mulaney advises: “We should change that a lot.”
After a lull in the music, Mulaney’s next remark draws even more backlash: “Hey, I think we should be Republicans.”
He follows that up with: “I don’t think we should die.”

His final plan for the future: “Even though it’s cold, and we can’t hear any of the bands, and we’re standing in mud and feces, I think we should say this concert was like incredible and life-changing.”

items.title: 'SNL' Weekend Update Roasts Trump Admin Over Grounded Flights, Jensen Huang Affairs
items.description: Saturday Night Live‘s Weekend Update took aim at the Trump administration’s explanation for grounding all flights for hours on Friday, and questioned what the president knew about ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
items.author: William Vaillancourt
paragraphs: Saturday Night Live‘s Weekend Update took aim at the Trump administration’s explanation for grounding all flights for hours on Friday, and questioned what the president knew about ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“The scariest part about all these flights getting grounded was the messaging from the normally dependable Trump administration,” Colin Jost began. “First, they said it was a ‘telecommunications outage, as of now.’ Why add ‘as of now?’ No one wants to hear: ‘Your child is safe, as of now.'”

“Then, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the whole situation was the result of a contractor upgrading copper wire to fiberoptic cable. So, one guy switched out one wire and took out all planes? I think that’s literally a scene from the movie, ‘Airplane!'” Jost joked.
Co-anchor Michael Che turned to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin telling reporters in the early stage of the incident that it was not a 9/11-type situation.
“Which he knew, because Rudy Giuliani didn’t see his shadow,” he joked.

Jost then addressed ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affairs, some reportedly with his subordinates and one with a suspected Chinese spy. The news has caused stocks to fall, since the company’s A.I. chips are shouldering a large part of the U.S. economy.
“Jensen Huang had a midlife crisis so bad, you might lose your house in his divorce,” he joked.
Jost then addressed the uncertainty about what Donald Trump knew about Huang potentially being taken advantage of and when he knew it.

“Insiders are also saying that despite Trump’s claim that he didn’t know about the Nvidia CEO’s relationship with a Chinese spy, he was actually briefed about it on a trip to China in May,” Jost said. “So this concludes yet another game of ‘Dementia or Lying?’
“Turns out it’s a trick question,” he added. “Because it’s always both.”
Additional topics Weekend Update covered included the surprising Senate win in Mississippi by Democrat Scott Colom over incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
“Or, as it was reported in Mississippi: ‘Black Man Savagely Beats White Woman,'” Che joked.

items.title: The Lowdown Recap: Vote for Family
items.description: Alone together on Oklahoma’s wide-open highways, Lee Raybons Jr. and Sr. inch their way toward mutual understanding. The pair are heading to Frog’s old storage unit, the one he keeps in the podunk town where Frog and Lee Jr.’s mom, Helen Francis, grew up. Trap
items.author: Amanda Whiting
paragraphs: Alone together on Oklahoma’s wide-open highways, Lee Raybons Jr. and Sr. inch their way toward mutual understanding. The pair are heading to Frog’s old storage unit, the one he keeps in the podunk town where Frog and Lee Jr.’s mom, Helen Francis, grew up. Trapped in the small cab of Lee’s van for hours, their only options are music or conversation. Unsurprisingly, the men can’t agree on a radio station.

For all their idiosyncrasies, the fault lines between father and son are refreshingly obvious. Despite their estrangement, Frog believes that he understands his adult son — that what is essential about Lee Jr.’s character was knowable from birth and maybe even before. In our blood. Lee Jr. has committed a related fallacy — mistaking the story he’s been telling about his dad for his dad’s actual story.

Before they set out, Frog assures Lee that he’ll leave Tulsa if his son does him this one last favor. Maybe it’s the promise of his dad’s absence that allows Lee to meaningfully engage with the man he’s dismissed all season as a liar and a fake. There’s really only one question a neglected kid ever wants to ask their neglectful parent, and halfway through their road trip, Lee braves it: Why wasn’t I worth sticking around for?

“Well, we’re always leaving and coming back … aren’t we? I mean, that’s what we do,” Frog tells him vaguely. He is 80 years old, sitting in the diner where he wooed Lee’s mother when she was a 16-year-old waitress. All the versions of himself that ever existed are suddenly nearby again, and he still doesn’t know the answer to his only son’s simple question. Frog continues: “Isn’t that what you do? Leave, come back? Leave and come back?”

The first time I watched the diner scene, I heard Frog’s rhetorical questions as both a rationalization and an accusation against his son, who says nothing in response, just purses his lips and lightly shakes his head. The second time I watched it, though, I started to think Frog was sincerely confused about human nature. Isn’t everyone always leaving and coming back? No. Isn’t the inability to stay put a universal condition? Not really. But Frog has a tendency to locate the root cause of his bad behavior outside himself. Earlier in the episode, for example, Frog tells Lee that his love of chasing women is a heritable trait. But Frog doesn’t know anything about Lee’s love life. He’s talking about himself — the narrative he’s invented to justify his own habits.

Still, no one is wrong all the time. When Frog tells Lee his problem is that he wants to control the world rather than “adapt” to it, he’s onto something about his son’s self-righteousness. Later, he’ll direct Lee to pull over the van in front of a derelict white bungalow that Lee doesn’t remember. It’s the house he grew up in before the family moved to Tulsa. When the Raybons lived there, the house had a porch swing. Frog may have left, but he did not forget, and that’s worth something.

Eventually, the men make it to the storage unit. What did Frog, a sham preacher who was always coming and going, decide was worth holding onto? Not much. There’s a painted upright piano and a yo-yo. There’s a spring-suspended toy horse, not unlike the toy horse Lee couldn’t resist mounting at Jed Sallsman’s ranch. Frog doesn’t seem overly interested in the jetsam of his life. He finds the small gift he promised his granddaughter, grabs an ancient bag of weed, and heads back out. It’s Lee who lingers, discovering a Vietnam field jacket among the clutter; Lee always thought his dad was lying about his war service. Before he pulls the roller door shut on his dad’s history, Lee tucks one of Frog’s old journals in his back pocket.

The Lee Raybons share a joint against the fading light of a long day before getting back on the road. There is no big showdown between them. There are no tears and shockingly few recriminations. They figure out how to be quiet with each other. Over the course of season two, Lee has continually defended his decision to have Frog committed 20 years ago. When the men pull over for a final refueling outside Tulsa, Frog tells his son that his stay in the psychiatric hospital wasn’t that bad. Actually, when Frog thinks about it, he really did need some rest back then.

The signs that something is up with Frog’s health have been accumulating since the cops found him wandering in his red cap (like he’d just stepped out of the title sequence of the ultimate road movie, Paris, Texas). There’s his persistent, ugly cough. Occasionally, Frog seems confused, unable to recall what happened when. In “Leaving and Coming Back,” he falls asleep in the van despite the fact that it’s only mid-morning. He’s nostalgic for the past, as well as the present. He hasn’t taken off that “Grandpa” bowling shirt since Francis gave it to him. But the biggest clue that Frog is dying is that he’s boomeranged back to Tulsa at all.

He came to town wearing a trucker hat emblazoned with “Psalm 107:29.” In the truck stop mini-mart where Lee is paying for 15 bucks’ worth of gas — incidentally, a very teenage boy amount — we see the same hat for sale on the counter. He stilled the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed. It’s an appeal for divine comfort or maybe intervention. Frog crying for help.

With his son inside, the older Lee Raybon closes his eyes against the neon lights of the gas station and opens them to find kids playing with bubbles, bubbles climbing dreamily skyward. Yesterday, he took Francis to the movies (Tulsa’s Circle Cinema) and told her to live her own life, to go to college if she wants. Since we’ve known Francis, all she’s wanted was to be treated like a grown-up, and Frog is the one to finally do it. Today, Frog got to ride shotgun with his son, singing along to “Polk Salad Annie” and laughing.

When Lee gets back to the van, his dad has passed away, and the immensity of it is too much for his body to bear. He finds himself sitting on the sill of the passenger side, absorbing the loss of a father who was never around anyway. A man he thought he knew better than he ever did.

Other stuff happens in “Leaving and Coming Back,” all of it prior to Lee and Frog’s road trip. Judge Jed, currently running for reelection under the banner “Vote for Family,” chastises Vela for arresting the governor’s close, personal journalist friend, then assures the sheriff that he’s seduced Lee into submission. Not one to be cowed, Vela issues a warning of her own: Her and Bobby’s cut of the Fresh Start profits is starting to look pretty meager compared to what Jed is pulling in.

It’s no idle threat. We learn in this episode that without the cooperation of Vela and her cousin, Johnny McMann, Fresh Start couldn’t operate. See, when Jed told Lee that the prison diversion program didn’t employ guards, he was telling a half-truth. He doesn’t need to employ guards because, with the help of McMann, he’s been able to borrow violent offenders from Boontill who do the work for free. That’s what Mekko was doing at Fresh Start, at least according to spineless Lonnie, who Ginger is able to flip from her kidnapper to her co-conspirator over the course of a three-minute conversation.

Convinced that Vela and McMann will eventually turn on him, Lonnie helps Ginger escape from McMann’s cabin, where she’s been held for the last few hours since they abducted her. Lonnie accidentally hits McMann with his car as they flee, which should give the pair a decent head start. We don’t find out where Lonnie runs to, but Ginger heads to Lee’s place, where she feels safe enough to break down. She thought she knew Mekko, but according to McMann, Mekko showed the prison guard her sexts. According to Lonnie, the client she risked her career to be with is the same man who murdered Nathan Spence. Understandably, Ginger feels like a fool.

But Lee is there for her. He’s actually really good at making people feel safe. Heard. You can’t be embarrassed in front of Lee. You can’t make a mistake that he can’t top. After Ginger showers off the aroma of Vienna sausages, which is McMann’s signature scent, Lee breaks them into Sweet Emily’s in the middle of the night, where they raid the whiskey. They’re drinking to get drunk enough to make the “bad” decision they already want to make. Lee has been calling Ginger his girlfriend despite the fact they’ve barely touched. Ginger is eager to admit she’s into this kind and reckless man-child who uses sheets for window blinds, keeps a garden of empty liquor bottles, and likes the smell of his own toe jam.

After a few shots, they hook up at the Sweet Emily’s soda fountain, or maybe they do it in one of the booths; we can’t be sure. Ginger must leave in the night, but Lee is still asleep on the floor when Western comes in to open the diner. In fact, Lee’s on his walk of shame home from Sweet Emily’s when he runs into Frog, who asks him to take him to the storage unit. There’s something in there that he wants to give Francis for her birthday, and he needs his son’s help.

We never quite see the birthday present. It looks like a small wooden box, which Frog pops into the chest pocket of his Grandpa shirt. Presumably, it’s still in his pocket as Lee drives his dad’s body back to Tulsa. As he sits behind the wheel, “Oo-De-Lally” from Disney’s Robin Hood plays, a jaunty sing-along song that undercuts and enhances the gravity of what’s happened. Frog stole from the rich, but did he ever give to the poor? Across his life, he was a fake preacher, a cartoon hero, a Peter Pan dad. Born and raised in Oklahoma, Frog (maybe) ran away from home at an early age and (maybe) spent his teenage years in Mexico, working odd jobs. He answered the call to serve his country, including a deployment in Vietnam. After returning home, Frog started a family and moved to the city. He was always leaving and coming back, which he attributed to his fundamental nature.

Lee “Frog” Raybon Sr. was preceded in death by his wife, Helen Francis Raybon. He is survived by an adoring granddaughter (Francis), a befuddled son (Lee Jr.), and a rich legacy comprised of outrageous lies and true stories so wild they sound like lies.

items.title: Survivor Recap: It Takes Two
items.description: I know I do a lot of bitching about the New Era of Survivor (honestly, seven tenths of these recaps are just dick jokes and vitriol), but if we’re going to take one thing with us into the Open Era, I think it might be voting out a pair. It’s an innovation I do
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: I know I do a lot of bitching about the New Era of Survivor (honestly, seven tenths of these recaps are just dick jokes and vitriol), but if we’re going to take one thing with us into the Open Era, I think it might be voting out a pair. It’s an innovation I don’t hate, but that mostly has to do with how this chaos-prone group of contestants decided to play the game. Yes, this episode convinced me. Let’s put one in the win column for Jeffrey Lee Probst.

The beginning of the episode expertly sets up everything about to happen, starting with everyone hating on Mike, a tray of sliced turkey club wraps at a shareholders’ meeting that no one ever bothers to take the cover off of. He sits down with Maggie and tells her the reason he flipped the vote to Brady last episode was that he was last in on the plan to get rid of Kristin, like he’s last in on every vote. She tells him exactly what he needs to hear, “If I was the last person to get information, maybe you should ask yourself why people don’t trust you.” Okay. Great. Now he knows. But what is he going to do about it?

The other consequential thing is Carter’s Salty and Sweet Alliance. He’s sick of all the plans going totally haywire, and he wants a group that is going to stick to a plan no matter what. Dude, don’t you realize you’re in the Open Era where Jeff’s motto is “No Fear!” Wait, that’s the wrong bumper sticker. Don’t you know his motto is, “[Calvin pissing on a Chevy logo.]” Nope, also the wrong sticker. Don’t you know his motto is “permanent uncertainty”? How are you going to stick to plans when everything is uncertain? Anyway, he gets together Kilby, Lewis, Cristian, Maggie, and Thien An and calls it the Salt Alliance because his favorite movie is the 2010 Angelina Jolie action-mystery film, Salt. No, it’s because they’re supposed to be the salt of the earth or something. To solidify this alliance with Cristian, he shows off his hidden immunity idol that he inherited from Rob, who quit on day six because he only got on the show so that his wife would be cast on The Real Housewives of Rhode Island.

As soon as the salt is on the pretzel, they get all twisted up. Everyone is going to be competing in pairs in the next immunity challenge. Yeah, how is that sticking to the plan? What I like about this is that they allow the players to decide what the pairs are going to be and don’t leave it up to chance. They are all unsure whether the pair will be voted out or will be fighting against each other, so they take a very interesting approach to forming the groups. Mike chooses Maggie, thinking that she’s well connected, so if they’re sending the group home, he might get spared because people don’t want to oust her. Carter and Cristian pair up because no one knows they’re working together. Devin and Jelly are bound together by a curse as ancient as the whale immunity idol that they dug up from the seabed. But other than them, most of the other pairs are unlikely and spread across alliances. Kilby and Kristin get together, as do Eric and Thien An and Lewis and Sharonda.

They get to the challenge, and Jeff shares some news. Our Brody Brady decided that he wanted to go home to tend to his thumb (which he partially cut off opening coconuts) and will no longer be on the jury. Are we sure that’s why? I don’t know; this whole stunt smells like the potent cologne of sour grapes. It’s like earlier this season when Jonathan had to leave because he had an owie. I would assume our Brody Brady is not used to losing and was like, “Brody. If this Brody can’t be the $1 million Brody, then this Brody is going home to Brody hospital to get his Brody thumb Brodied back onto his Brody body Brody. I mean, fuck this game, Brody. Don’t they know that I’m Brady the Brody?” And then they put him in the back of a van and drove him to the airport, where he just unceasingly said, “Brody” in different inflections for the entire ride.

Jeff tells everyone that they will be competing in pairs, winning immunity in pairs, and that a pair of players will be going home; however, everyone will be voting as individuals. He also says that immunity idols or other advantages, like Shots in the Dark, if played for one player, work on the whole pair, ensuring both players’ safety.

The challenge happens in three phases, with a pair of two being eliminated at each leg. The first challenge is to stand there and endure Eric’s incessant chattering about The Sopranos, spaghetti (which is the reward), and his fiancé the longest. At one point, Carter even says, “Can we focus up down there?” Kristin and Kilby are eliminated first, along with Maggie and Mike. There is also an advantage for the second part of the challenge for the people who listen to Eric the longest. (JK. They have to balance a ball on a plank.) Lewis and Sharonda make the only smart decision and throw the rest of the challenge, figuring that the energy they save by stepping down is better than whatever they might get from the advantage. This ends up being wise because, just as Carter and Cristian are about to win the whole damn thing by stacking a bunch of puzzle pieces, their stack falls to the ground, opening the door for Lewis and Sharonda to win. See, maybe if they didn’t stay listening to Eric for as long as they did, they might have come through when they needed it.

As they’re getting their necklaces from Jeff, Lewis tells Sharonda that he saw fire in her on day one, and when she was eliminated first in last week’s challenge, he knew that fire was back. Is this an unlikely alliance that is going to grow legs? I sure hope so, particularly because Sharonda has quite the week, as we’ll get to in a minute.

Lewis and Sharonda also have to send someone on a journey, and they choose Cristian. When the boat lands in the middle of the ocean, Cristian reads that he lost his vote, and if he gets a clue on the island, he might win it back but also win an extra vote for tonight. At first it doesn’t really make sense, but then he cuts a rope and a trough full of buoys empties out into the ocean. He soon realizes that some of them have letters on them and collects them all up to figure out what they say: “Dig Under Treemail.” He then leaves all the buoys and goes back to camp. Cristian comes back, tells everyone the truth, goes and digs up his vote and extra vote, with Mike watching over him like the corporate overlord he is.

Now the castaways have to select a pair who is going home, and this is where some deft selection comes into play. Everyone is tired of Mike for never saying anything of note and Eric for chattering more than a set of dentures on a roller coaster. However, no one wants Maggie or Thien An to go home, so both of those pairs are out, as are Lewis and Sharonda, who are immune, leaving only Carter and Cristian, Devin and Jelly, or Kilby and Kristen. Carter is whipping votes against Devin and Jelly for obvious reasons: they’re a close duo who everyone knows is working together. As Jelly accurately points out at tribal, it’s not like they win challenges or have lots of influence; it’s just that they’re clearly besties. Also, if Carter can get rid of both of them, then the Salt fan club has the majority and can coast the rest of the game. Devin and Jelly are going for Carter and Cristian, saying they’re both players no one has a problem with, and that is dangerous. When Carter hears this, he sits down with them and says that the vote is Kristin and they should just go for her. Jelly loves this idea because it means she can hold on to her extra vote and her idol for another week.

This is where our girl Sharonda comes in. She’s sitting down with Thien An and says, “We never talk game, but who are you voting for?” T&A Music Factory tells her Devin and Jelly. Sharonda has been working with both of them; she knows about Jelly’s idol, and she is skeptical of this plan. She doesn’t rat it out, but she tells Devin, “You need to come up with a game plan.” She asks Jelly who she is voting for, and Jelly tells her that everyone told her to vote for Kristin. Sharonda tells her, “That’s just a smoke screen.” This is what we would call on Real Housewives a “sniper from the side.” Sharonda is not trying to get into the mess, but she is trying to use a bit of influence to make sure exactly what she wants to happen happens. As we’re leaving camp for Tribal Council, the edit sets it up as Carter and Cristian versus Devin and Jelly, and whoever plays their idol is going to win.

At Tribal, it’s another live one with lots of whispers and gossiping and everyone not being sure what the plan is and who they can rely on. I usually hate a live tribal, but I’m kind of loving the vibes this season. Is it casting? Did they make this happen by getting us a bunch of nutcases who don’t know what they’re doing? Or is this Jeff’s “No Fear Chevy Peeing Constant Uncertainty” actually doing what it’s supposed to be doing? At one point, as everyone is chattering, he asks Maggie if she even hears the whispers anymore because they’re so constant. She’s basically like, “Jeff, STFU. I can’t hear the 14 different conversations happening around me.” The only thing of consequence that happens is that Christian goes to Eric and gives him his extra vote, saying he loses it if he uses his SITD and wants Eric to play it for Devin and Jelly.

The players are ready to vote, and Kilby, as he has at every Tribal, runs up to the voting booth with his arms outstretched like he’s just been cursed by the witch in Weapons. When Eric votes, he says that he knows this vote expires tonight, but they should have enough of a majority that he doesn’t need to use it. Dude! What is wrong with you? Use it! It’s like if you have a bunch of brown bananas on the counter that you know are going bad, do you just throw them away or do you make banana bread? You get out the walnuts, the chocolate chips, the Pam spray, and you Betty that M-er F-er Crocker. Why let a vote go to waste?

Before Jeff can tally the votes, a lot of advantages have to be played. Kristin tries her SITD, and it comes up “Not Safe.” Cristian was being paranoid all afternoon, and I was readying my whole monologue about how SITD is stupid, and he shouldn’t even think about it or waste his time going for it, and then it comes up SAFE, and he and Carter are protected. Monologue cancelled, I guess. Then Jelly plays her idol to everyone’s surprise, and it is on like Brody Kong. (That is the video game Brady played on the plane ride home while he sulked.)

Every vote comes up Devin and Jelly until the very end, with Jelly even cackling, “You tried it,” as Jeff keeps saying the votes don’t count. There is one vote for Carter and Cristian that also doesn’t count, and one vote left. It’s Kilby and Kristin, and that’s what Kilby gets for being possessed by a witch. We lose two excellent characters and one great player (no, Kilby, it’s not you) in one fell swoop. I feel kind of bad for them, but all in all it is an excellent episode, and that is much more important than keeping either of them around. As we watch the votes during the credits, a few things become clear: Sharonda, still sniping from the side, voted for Devin and Jelly just so she’d be in the majority in case Jelly was too stupid to play her idol. She got what she wanted and is still undercover. Also, Devin and Jelly were smart enough to split their votes in case one of the other pairs had some kind of advantage, which is exactly what happened, making sure that they were the ones choosing who went home no matter the outcome. A fantastic outcome for fans and a great night for the helicopter alliance, which is currently flying high over the rest of the competition.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City Recap: Swimming With the Sharks
items.description: If you thought last week’s exchange between Angie and Mary was painful, buckle up, because this show isn’t giving us a reprieve just yet. This week’s episode kicks off with yet another scene uncomfortable enough to make you crawl out of your skin, in which Bro
items.author: Tom Smyth
paragraphs: If you thought last week’s exchange between Angie and Mary was painful, buckle up, because this show isn’t giving us a reprieve just yet. This week’s episode kicks off with yet another scene uncomfortable enough to make you crawl out of your skin, in which Bronwyn introduces her fetal boyfriend, Brandon, to her mother, Muzzy, who has no interest in this sit-down whatsoever. And being that she’s Muzzy, she says that outright. Do you think if we banded together, there could be a class action lawsuit against Bravo for emotional distress for making us bear witness to this?

In all honesty, at the beginning of the season, when Muzzy seemed to be changing her ways after dealing with all the backlash she got as last season aired, I sympathized with her, because the ire of the Bravo fandom is no easy burden to bear. But this scene was a great reminder that she is, in fact, a nightmare. Before Brandon even arrives, she’s chiding him and expressing her disdain to Bronwyn at even having to meet him, and things only get worse when he gets there. Somehow she finds a way to blame him for the bad weather, tells him outright that she’s not happy about their relationship because she liked Todd (probably because they could reminisce together about FDR’s fireside chats), and says that she’s only there because she has to give him a chance in order to have a relationship with her daughter. Kudos to Brandon, because I would never be able to forgive or date anybody who would make me spend a single minute with this woman.

And why is this even happening so soon to begin with? Bronwyn notes that her daughter, Gwen, who apparently is the only sensible person in the family, said she won’t meet him until they’ve been dating for at least six months — so why rush to throw Muzzy into the mix? Well, Bronwyn notes in her confessional that she almost wishes the other women were there to see this because it would prove this wasn’t a publicity stunt. Ah, there’s our answer. This cursed meeting is a rebuttal to the PR relationship claims, but doing it on-camera kind of undoes the intended purpose and makes the whole thing seem even more fake. And speaking of falsities, as they leave, Brandon says to Muzzy, “You are such a joy; you are a fun time.” A damning lie that could only have been solicited via a hearty check or Zelle.

Meanwhile, Whitney and Justin have yet another sit-down about the state of their relationship without any real answers. Whitney says that sleeping apart has been an improvement but is still confused as to where she stands with the relationship, whereas Justin is simply standing by, waiting for a verdict. He says he’s very patient, but eventually needs her to make a decision because until then he’s just stuck in this odd marriage limbo. It’s not typical to see a marriage devolve like this on these shows, where there’s no one inciting event or tangible thing to point to, because as far as we’ve been able to tell, things between them are fine. We’re not seeing fighting or infidelity, or even Beador-esque tension. But the dissolution of a relationship doesn’t always come with all of that, and it’s compelling watching Whitney have to navigate and explain the intangible like this — all while planning a shark-themed Sweet Sixteen for her daughter.

Finally, we get to check in with Angie after last week’s blowup. She’s at the park with Heather and Lisa (who remain my favorite duo on this show, may the Good Weather never stop), and they’re both eager to chat with her now that the dust has settled and Angie has been able to process exactly how that fight played out.

“I said something that I will never be able to take back,” she says. “I regret it; I will never forgive myself, and Mary may never forgive me.” She admits to them that she’s been a ticking time bomb, and she now realizes that if she had been acknowledging her feelings rather than burying them, explosions like that wouldn’t have been happening. That was clearly Angie’s big error going into this season; she was hiding the diagnosis (her marital problems) while the symptoms were still on full display, and she repressed those emotions until they were uncontrollable. Learning from that, she’s now telling Lisa about her troubles with Shawn, and Lisa turns out to be the perfect person to confide in because she went through the same thing with John last season, and they ended up bouncing back. It’s not a guarantee that Angie and Shawn will, too, but Lisa is at least proof of that being a possibility.

As for Mary, Angie reached out to apologize, but she’s not responding, which doesn’t come as any big surprise. Mary will cut someone off for life over something as minor as stealing some flowers, so naturally something as big as this is going to be tough — if not impossible — to bounce back from. While Mary naturally deserves all the grace in the world this season, she hasn’t historically been a kind friend to Angie even in the best of times, so at this point I wouldn’t actually mind seeing Angie finally be freed from this roller coaster. They’ve long had this Gretchen Wieners and Regina George dynamic that can’t possibly be healthy for Angie.

We get to hear more from Mary at the tasting Meredith is throwing for her new lounge space, which looks like a desolate parking garage or a parody of an art gallery. If Meredith Marks invited me to an address and I showed up to that abandoned warehouse, I’d be certain she was going to kill me. I spent the entire event waiting for her to press a trap door button or shout, “Release the hounds.” But alas, it was just for caviar, and the event space will be named Perhaps, not to be confused with Premiere, which is Lisa’s event space across the street. All of the other women correctly point out that if this were anybody besides the two of them, these dueling lounges would result in a bloodbath.

Mary says that while she didn’t initially plan to do so, she ended up telling Robert Sr. — her step-grandfather and husband — about what Angie said, and naturally he didn’t take it well. The other women ask if she’s reached out, but Mary says she doesn’t know because she blocked her, which is a great representation of how Mary handles conflict with even the people closest to her. She also says that a big problem was that Angie didn’t realize what she said in the moment after she said it, which is a little confusing, because we did see Angie try to apologize right then and there, but Mary rebuffed it and stormed off. But the most shocking development is Mary saying that she’s now in a space to hear her apology, as long as it’s on her terms and face-to-face.

Quai has to leave early to head over to Bobbie’s birthday party, offending Meredith, who is apparently willing to have beef with a 16-year-old now, but who can blame Quai? Bobbie’s shark party is way cooler … and actually a party. Angie has an awkward encounter with Bronwyn there, but they both agree that it isn’t the time or place to hash things out. Something I do find promising is that Bronwyn isn’t reveling in or stoking the flames of Angie’s problems with Mary, but rather hopes to see the situation resolve. But speaking of awkward encounters, when Angie and Heather are chatting with and complimenting Justin, Angie jokes that he should call them up “if your wife ever dumps ya.” Heather recoils, since she’s the only one who knows that is exactly what’s happening.

Finally, Bobbie arrives, and they all surprise her before Whitney and Justin gift her with a brand-new car. But I don’t get any enjoyment from seeing children be surprised with cars in this (or any) economy, even children who seem totally great like Bobbie. The one exception to this is, of course, when Vicki Gunvalson surprised her daughter Briana with a car and excitedly told her that Briana was the one who was going to be making the payments. That is where this trope peaked, and we can leave it there.

The one positive of these two dueling events is having Quai zip between them like a carrier pigeon and filling in Angie about the conversation that happened over in Meredith’s abandoned garage turned lounge. She tells them all that Mary told Robert Sr. about the comments, that she blocked Angie and thus hasn’t received the apology, and that she rebuffed the suggestion that Angie loves her. The latter is what hurts Angie the most, but the good news comes when Quai informs her that she’s willing to hear her out in person. Normally, Mary is such a stone wall that it wouldn’t have been surprising if we never saw the two of them in the same room ever again, so this points to the potential of rebuilding some kind of connection. Now we just need to get Britani back into the mix.

items.title: Bowen Yang Returns to ‘SNL’ as Jensen Huang as John Mulaney’s Cold Open Mocks Nvidia Scandal, National Ground Stop and Outlook Outage
items.description: Bowen Yang made a surprise return to “Saturday Night Live” in the cold open, playing the disgraced tech mogul Jensen Huang as host John Mulaney led a group of tech billionaires through a CIA class on how to recognize female spies.
items.author: Cynthia Littleton
paragraphs: Bowen Yang made a surprise return to “Saturday Night Live” in the cold open, playing the disgraced tech mogul Jensen Huang as host John Mulaney led a group of tech billionaires through a CIA class on how to recognize female spies.

The cold open featured Mulaney as a CIA agent who gathered ultra-rich tech moguls at the agency’s headquarters for a crash course on how to recognize a classic espionage honeytrap, a nod to the Nvidia scandal that has rocked the business world. In the closing moments of the sketch, former “SNL” trouper Yang walked in delivering a pitch-perfect spoof of Huang, who was forced under pressure to resign on Nov. 12 from the Silicon Valley giant that he built for more than 30 years amid a growing sex scandal.

Yang introduced himself as “Jensen Hide-Your-Wife Huang.” Yang, as Huang, lamented that “women don’t like guys like us. That’s how we became guys like us,” after Mulaney’s CIA agent flashes him Venn diagram charts showing no overlap between beautiful women and tech billionaires. Yang also quipped that when Huang comes into the room, “You know what’s about to go down — the S&P 500.” And in a nod to Nvidia’s heft in the stock market, he added: “That’s right — I’m into BTSM: Breaking the stock market.”

The sketch featured “SNL regulars playing the tech billionaires who have flexed so much power over politics and culture in recent years. James Austin Johnson played Peter Thiel, Andrew Dismukes limned Mark Zuckerberg, Jane Wickline played Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane inhabited Elon Musk and Ben Marshall spoofed OpenAI chief Sam Altman.
