In a CIA conference room setting, Mulaney’s CIA agent used a pointer and monitor to flash Venn diagram graphics to school the billionaires in the difference between “Woman who would actually want to have sex with you” and “A woman who is clearly a spy.” The sketch turned on the story that has made global headlines as Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman believed to be a spy for China. In the days since the scandal broke, allegations surfaced that Huang, who is married, also had relationships with two other Nvidia employees.
“Never date a human woman,” Dismukes, as Zuckerberg, said, of the lesson to draw from the Nvidia scandal. “Never date anyone lest they become the antichrist,” Johnson, as Thiel, offered.

Thiel defended the contributions of tech billionaires to the greater good and asked Mulaney to “name one time when technology has let us down?” Mulaney cited this week’s one-two punch of the massive disruptions that exposed the vulnerabilities of our wired world: The five-hour national ground stop on air travel on Friday and Microsoft’s widely used email platform Outlook experiencing a global outage for nearly 24 hours.
“Like yesterday when every plane was grounded? Or the day before when Microsoft Outlook went dark?” Mulaney said.
Altman questioned whether he and Thiel, who are gay, needed the training to detect female spies. Johnson, as Thiel, added, “and we are both bears in the sense that we’ve killed a lot of hikers.”

Mulaney is notching his seventh time as host of “SNL,” after working on the show as a writer from 2008 to He’s in the midst of a push for Amazon Prime Video’s John Madden biopic “Madden,” which bows on the streamer and in limited theatrical release on Nov. 18. He’s also touring at present on his “Mister Whatever” stand-up tour. Mulaney most recently took the helm in November 2024.
Phoebe Bridgers performed as an “SNL” musical guest for the second time Saturday. She’s currently on tour with her newest album “Lost Weekend.”

items.title: How ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Pulled Off the Impossible With Latest Milestone: ‘It Will Never Happen Again’
items.description: “Some partnerships don’t end.”
items.author: Emily Longeretta
paragraphs: “Some partnerships don’t end.”
It’s a quote Ice-T’s Fin said during the 600th episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” on Thursday night — and one that means so much more than just the partnership between Benson and Stabler.

The same could be said about Mariska Hargitay and Dick Wolf. The pair have been working together since the show debuted in 1999. “People throw around the word ‘family,'” Hargitay says. But for the “SVU” cast and crew, many who have been there from the start, it’s true. “To like them, to love them… I go to work and we hug, and it’s real. It feels like you’re going to a good dinner party when you go to work on Monday.”

After the 600th episode of the Universal Television series wrapped, Wolf gathered the cast and crew for an actual dinner party, including the current cast and crew, Wolf COO Peter Jankowski and Christopher Meloni. Wolf made a speech at the beginning of the night, standing to tell the group, “This has never happened, and it will never happen again.”

In a time when a show hitting 100 episodes is a major accomplishment, Hargitay never saw a world in which the NBC show would reach 600. But Wolf did, she says. And it was part of the speech she gave that night to her “SVU” family.

“It really doesn’t feel totally real, which, in a way, is exactly how it should feel, because it’s as if we all get to live in this dream of what you thought might be possible someday. You’ve shown that it’s not only possible, but it’s so much better than anyone could have imagined,” she told Wolf. “If somebody told me that there was a show that’s been on the air for 600 episodes, I would say, ‘Really?’ That’s got to be tired. It’s got to be wheezing along. Must be running on fumes, or they’re catering to some mindless audience that just keeps coming back for some unknown reason. But here we are with a show that is healthy, that’s muscular, that’s fresh, smart, honest, and just so damn important. And yes, people keep coming back, but not for some unknown reason.”
She continued, “They keep coming back because you started something very special that we’ve all had the great privilege of carrying forward for all these years.”

For Hargitay, she can’t help but get emotional thinking about the love and respect the group has for one another, and for the set environment they’ve all created. It’s an environment guest stars thrive in — just look at the roster of them over the last 600 episodes — and always compliment when they arrive and leave the show.

“People are happy to be there. I love making a space that’s conducive to creating, and I love making a space where people feel safe enough to try, to risk, to play, and to hunker down, and know that we’re not playing around here,” she says. “This is someone’s life. This is serious, and these are important stories. I’m so grateful.”

For the milestone episode, written by showrunner Michele Fazekas and directed by Brenna Malloy, jury consultant Gwen Sharpe (J. Smith-Cameron) convinces Benson to take another look at an old case that put a man in prison for a 1998 rape and murder. When Benson revisits it, she realizes that she worked the case with Stabler (Christopher Meloni). Hesitant at first — since he failed to follow up on leads that could have revealed the truth and cut Benson out of the interrogation — Stabler ultimately joins Benson to help.

While they haven’t worked together in years, he’s eager to join her on a road trip to dig deeper and put the right person behind bars. Captain Renee Curry steps in, saying, “With respect, Captain, he’s not your partner anymore. You don’t need his buy-in.” Fin quickly responds, “It doesn’t matter. Some partnerships don’t end, even when they do.”

The storyline stirs up complicated feelings for both Benson and Stabler, as she realizes (and tells him), “I let you shut me out… I have to live with the fact that I didn’t do the right thing because I was new, that I didn’t follow my instinct because I thought you knew better.”

For the first time with him, she really uses her voice with him as she discovers how different they both are from who they used to be when they worked together. And that’s ok — because that partnership is forever.

The episode came in nearly 12 minutes over time, says Hargitay. “This was a big one. We were writing and rewriting and playing, and we had to shoot some scenes before we knew exactly what a scene was going to be, so there were a lot of different ways it could go. But it’s an embarrassment of riches.”

items.title: Adam Driver Says Disney Killing ‘The Hunt for Ben Solo’ Felt ‘Criminal’: ‘Steven Soderbergh Wants to Make a “Star Wars” Movie. What Are We Debating?’
items.description: Adam Driver continues to express his dissatisfaction with Disney over the decision to kill his “Star Wars” sequel movie “The Hunt for Ben Solo,” which he spent two-and-a-half years developing with director Steven Soderbergh. In a new interview with The Associa
items.author: Zack Sharf
paragraphs: Adam Driver continues to express his dissatisfaction with Disney over the decision to kill his “Star Wars” sequel movie “The Hunt for Ben Solo,” which he spent two-and-a-half years developing with director Steven Soderbergh. In a new interview with The Associated Press on his “Paper Tiger” press tour, the Oscar nominee said he was surprised Soderbergh’s involvement alone didn’t have the studio jumping at the chance to make the movie.

“For me it was: Steven Soderbergh wants to make a ‘Star Wars’ film. What are we debating?” Driver said. “It’s what it is. It’s criminal. Or it felt criminal. We’re all moving on. On to the next. And Steven already has something else that’s one of the best things he’s ever written.”

Driver revealed the existence of “The Hunt for Ben Solo” in an Oct. 2025 interview with The Associated Press, explaining how Disney executives pulled the plug on the project because they couldn’t wrap their heads around the character coming back after he presumably died in 2019’s “Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker.”

“I always was interested in doing another ‘Star Wars,’” Driver said at the time. “I had been talking about doing another one since 2021. Kathleen [Kennedy] had reached out. I always said: ‘With a great director and a great story, I’d be there in a second.’ I loved that character and loved playing him.”

The mere existence of “The Hunt for Ben Solo” instantly mobilized “Star Wars” fans on social media into calling for Disney to reverse its decision and put the “Star Wars” project back in development. A group of “Star Wars” fans even paid for a plane to fly a banner reading “Save ‘The Hunt for Ben Solo’” over Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, Calif. Even Daisy Ridley, who starred opposite Driver as Rey in the most “Star Wars” sequel trilogy, championed fans for their support of “The Hunt for Ben Solo.”

“I was blown away by the response to it,” Driver told the AP in his latest interview. “In no way did I think there would be billboards in Times Square. It’s so moving. It did feel like we were all at the bar having a conversation about the films we wanted to see.”

Earlier in his “Paper Tiger” press tour, Driver said on “The Rich Eisen Show” that his time playing Kylo Ren/Ben Solo is officially over now that “The Hunt for Ben Solo” is dead and gone. The actor said: “If they wanted to, fine. But we’re not … It’s not our call. I think the ship has sailed though.”

items.title: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Unwraps $19M to Win Weekend in Box Office Return
items.description: Ebenezer unwrapped $19 million domestically as star Johnny Depp‘s studio comeback vehicle opened in first place at the domestic box office.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: Ebenezer unwrapped $19 million domestically as star Johnny Depp‘s studio comeback vehicle opened in first place at the domestic box office.

Paramount Pictures released director Ti West‘s horror-tinged adaptation of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol in 3,535 North American theaters this weekend and landed an A- CinemaScore from audiences. Of the opening Thursday night audience, 62 percent of the crowd was over age 30, suggesting that the film was especially appealing for those who likely have positive associations with seeing Depp’s work throughout the decades. Ebenezer earned 4.5 out of 5 stars on PostTrak, with 50 percent of guests citing Depp as their reason for seeing the movie.
It took in $23 million from international markets for a global start of $42 million.

Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley and Ian McKellen round out the cast for the $38 million-budgeted feature that stars Depp as the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge who is visited by three spirits. Ebenezer marks Depp’s first studio project since 2018’s Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald, as he took a hiatus from high-profile work following abuse allegations from ex-wife Amber Heard that Depp has denied, in addition to negative headlines amid his and Heard’s 2022 defamation trial.

Paramount had been pleased with data suggesting that audiences want Depp back and that he still holds wide appeal, with the marketing including the actor appearing in character as Scrooge to remind fans of other transformative roles like Captain Jack Sparrow and Willy Wonka. Ebenezer has a PG-13 rating but is still geared toward the family crowd. Critics have been split on Ebenezer, as it holds a 53 percent approval rating from Rotten Tomatoes reviewers. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter, critic Frank Scheck declares that the film “fulfills its ostensible goal of restoring the actor to A-list status.”

Among other new arrivals, Sony Pictures released Ghost Soldier in 2,558 North American locations on Wednesday, with director William Eubank’s action movie grossing around $5.2 million for the three-day frame and a $8.3 million domestic cume. Jim Caviezel plays a former Green Beret who must defend his Wyoming community against a corporate threat. Hailing from Mandalay Pictures, Ghost Soldier holds a 42 percent score from Rotten Tomatoes critics and a 90 percent from audiences.

Not bagging much of a haul is Amazon MGM Studios’ How to Rob a Bank, director David Leitch‘s heist movie, also grossing $5.2 million for the frame. Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Anna Sawai star in the $40 million-budgeted ensemble film about a group of bank robbers who document their exploits on social media. It has taken $10.3 million globally.

How to Rob a Bank is opening well below Leitch’s recent work, including 2022’s Bullet Train ($30 million domestic debut) and 2024’s The Fall Guy ($27.7 million domestic debut), although those featured more proven box office draws in Brad Pitt and Ryan Gosling, respectively. The new movie, which earned a B- CinemaScore, has come up a bit empty with critics. It holds a 33 percent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes and an 80 percent audience score, with THR chief film critic David Rooney noting in his review that “the fun wears a bit thin.”

Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat is set to pounce on second place in its sophomore frame, grossing roughly $10 million domestically for the weekend to bring its North American sum to $36.7 million for a respectable decline of around 50 percent. Bill Hader voices the titular unpredictable feline in directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni’s animated retelling of Dr. Seuss’ classic children’s book.

Overall, the domestic marketplace collected $90 million for the quiet frame, down 25.9 percent from last weekend, although it was up 18.4 percent from the comparable 2025 weekend. The domestic total for 2026 hits $8.768 billion through Sunday.

After debuting in the top spot last weekend, Godzilla Minus Zero heads to third place with an estimated $7.5 million domestically for its sophomore frame as its North American cume is expected to hit $48.1 million. Filmmaker Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to 2023’s Godzilla Minus One looks to have a sizable decline of around 75 percent.

Sony Pictures’ Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is likely to notch $5.4 million in its second weekend for a domestic total of roughly $24 million through Sunday and a pleasing 38 percent drop. Its cume would rank director Nitesh Tiwari’s religious epic as the second-highest-grossing Indian feature ever at the U.S. box office. The two-part movie project carries a production budget reported at $420 million and beyond.

Likely to close out the top five when final numbers are reported is A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, which continues its impressive run into its fifth weekend with around $5.1 million for the frame and a domestic total of $88.6 million. With an enviable decline of around 37 percent so deep into the run, the buzzy feature from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim continues to build awards momentum.

Among the weekend’s debuts in limited release, Neon launched James Gray’s Paper Tiger in six theaters in Los Angeles and New York, with the crime drama heading to an estimated $203,000 for the frame, averaging $33,884 per screen. Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller star in the feature that Rooney’s review praised as “a drama of almost overwhelming power.”
Next weekend sees the arrival of Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, expected to become one of the fall’s top-grossing titles.
The story was first published on Nov. 14 at 8:33 a.m.

items.title: Inside the Plane Where Simple Plan, Hoobastank and More Performed Mid-Flight as Planes Were Grounded Across the U.S.
items.description: Have you ever been serenaded at 35,000 feet by Hoobastank? We’re betting that answer is no.
items.author: Kimberly Nordyke
paragraphs: Have you ever been serenaded at 35,000 feet by Hoobastank? We’re betting that answer is no.
But about 125 lucky Southwest Airline passengers got that opportunity on Friday on a charted Southwest Airlines flight from Los Angeles to headed to the Vans Warped Tour in Orlando.

The festivities actually kicked off that morning in Terminal 1 of LAX. At the gate, guests — who were mostly dressed in black, rock-themed attire, with plenty donning sort of Vans apparel, from shoes to purses to hats — were greeted with a rock music playlist as passengers had the opportunity to perform their favorites. (Shout-out to the woman named Gianna who gave a high-energy performance of Fall Out Boy’s “Sugar, We’re Goin Down.”) Then they were invited to a meet-and-greet with recording artists Lolo, Simple Plan, Hoobastank and The Used, all of whom are were on the Vans Warped Tour lineup.

What some of the passengers — who included fans, influences and journalists — didn’t realize is that all four acts were going to perform on the flight to Orlando. The initiative is part of the airline’s Live at 35, an in-flight entertainment program — celebrating its 15th anniversary this year — that surprises passengers with live pop-up music performances and events at 35,000 feet.

Once in the air, singer Lolo kicked things off somewhere over Texas with a four-song set. At one point, Lolo shared that she “almost didn’t take the gig because I’m a nervous flier and this is the longest I’ve gone without wearing a seat belt.” (Incidentally, the flight took off about an hour before the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all U.S. flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” The buzz on the plane was that our flight was likely one of very few planes in the air at the time.)

The aforementioned Hoobastank performed a trio of sings, culminating with their 2004 smash hit “The Reason.” During that song, lead singer Doug Robb asked the flight staff to turn off all the lights and the passengers to turn on their cell flashlights, upping the concert vibe inside the aircraft. The passengers also took part in a rousing sing-along to the tune.

“Is this the most annoying flight you’ve ever been on?” Robb joked. Walking through the plane, he swiped an iPad from a passenger who was evidently doing some online shopping. “I think you should buy that,” he joked.

During his set, The Used frontman Bert McCracken noted the unusual “venue” as the flight was passing over New Orleans. “This is the weirdest fucking shit I’ve ever done in my life,” he quipped. The band played four songs, and also turned “The Taste of Ink” into a sing-along. (“Everyone knows the lyrics to this song. It’s called ‘The Reason,'” McCracken joked in a callback to Hoobastank’s crowd-participation performance.)

Simple Plan’s Pierre Bouvier took the stage — floor? aisle? — last, performing songs including “I’d Do Anything.” After the song, he joked, “Give it up for Mark Hoppus,” the Blink-182 singer-bassist who is featured on the song. (Hoppus was not present.)

Bouvier joked it was “super awkward” to perform on a plane, even changing the lyrics to “I’d do anything for you, Vans Warped Tour,” before giving a knowing look and quipping, “Really, anything.” Bouvier also sang “I’m Just a Kid,” noting that it went viral on social media several years after its release as part of the #ImJustAKidChallenge Challenge, where users re-created childhood photographs as adults or adolescents.
As the plane began descending, Bouvier asked the flight crew to turn down the lights, quipping that “the flight crew didn’t know they were going to become the light crew.”

Markus Lloyd is the host for these events, which have featured acts including Julian Marley (son of Bob), the Plain White T’s, Magic!, Shane Smith & The Saints, Barenaked Ladies, Imagine Dragons, Chris Young and Cassidy Pope. “What’s fun” about these experiences, he told THR, “is that when we’re heading someplace fun, like the Vans Warped Tour, or Vegas, the plane has already kind of turned up a bit. And so when you tell them they’re getting this extra thing, it’s like they won the lottery. They’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, I’m going to Vegas AND I get a concert in the place? And that’s when we go, ‘You can’t get this anywhere besides Southwest.'”
For an encore on Friday’s flight, Hoobastank got up to perform one last song just moments before the flight landed safely in Orlando.

items.title: 21 Spring 2027 Runway Looks We Want to See at the Met Gala
items.description: The 2027 Met Gala has a new theme, meaning any guests who were planning a look around the now-canceled John Galliano affair will need to return to the drawing board. The Met announced last week that next year, instead of centering Galliano, the Costume Institu
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: The 2027 Met Gala has a new theme, meaning any guests who were planning a look around the now-canceled John Galliano affair will need to return to the drawing board. The Met announced last week that next year, instead of centering Galliano, the Costume Institute will celebrate everyday clothing and the ordinary objects made extraordinary by talented craftspeople.

“ExtraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” will definitely look different compared to any Met Gala we’ve seen in recent history. An official dress code for the event has yet to be announced, but Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute’s curator in charge, has already revealed his hopes for guests to attend in their versions of jeans, T-shirts, and puffers. It’s a unique request for one of the most glamorous red carpets of the year, but fortunately, this past season provided tons of options for those lucky enough to ascend the Met steps on May 3. Perhaps some good inspiration will convince attendees to ditch the gowns and opt for pieces that truly put the ordinary in extraordinary, and mix it up this year while the opportunity presents itself.

Stockings have been an integral part of women’s wardrobes for centuries, so this bodysuit Colleen Allen developed with the help of Swedish Stockings would make for a unique option for the 2027 Met Gala. Plus, it still falls into the sheer ensemble category, which is always popular at the Met.

Matthieu Blazy was inspired by the varied eras of Coco Chanel’s life for his Chanel spring 2027 collection, beginning with the Edwardian corsetry of her childhood and through her innovations in suiting. The latter informed several sets, freshly rendered in smocked tweed, a new invention that echoes the tweed of yore, but with more stretch. It’s a Chanel performance fabric, if you will. This play on a classic, made modern with a new fabric and an updated silhouette, perfectly encapsulates the theme of the Met Gala.

The party dress is quintessential, and Stuart Vevers embraced the most archetypal (and fabulous) version of it for the Coach spring 2027 show. Of course, the wearer must also go for the party hat, wrapped present, and sprinkled confetti. They complete the look.

For Gucci spring 2027, Demna looked at client archetypes, specifically those of a bygone era, like the mid 2010s, when indie sleaze gave way to a prep resurgence. While these looks may not come as expected, everyday ensembles for 2027, they represent a merging of the present and recent past that plays on the theme in an interesting way.

Not every Met Gala look has to be over-the-top, especially if it has something to say. This past season, Nicolas Ghesquière kicked off the Louis Vuitton show with a simple, sleeveless white shift dress. “Pieces perceived as structureless are in actuality complex topographies, composed of different surface tensions that mirror the body inside,” the show notes read. “Cloth or leathers are laid against the wearer, resembling a second skin not in appearance but through sensation and function.”

A good suit is, of course, a wardrobe essential, so hopefully someone will bring it to the Met in 2027. And no, we’re not talking about a man showing up in a boring tux, but a woman wearing something like this Ralph Lauren spring 2027 suit. It doesn’t hug any curve, taper in even an inch, or provide hints of overt femininity. It’s just a good suit.

For those seeking something more girlish, there’s the Dior spring 2027 collection, where Jonathan Anderson continued his exploration of bar jackets and circle skirts—brand signatures since 1947. Anderson has continuously updated the silhouettes, and this time, he loosened them up considerably with flowing mini skirts topped by breezy chiffon blazers.

The more courageous may consider Rei Kawakubo’s latest collection for Comme des Garçons, which saw the designer use her usual avant-garde approach to explore the concept of royalty. A good chunk of the show featured denim pieces, such as this structured skirt cut to almost resemble a pair of barrel-leg jeans. The inclusion of hair at the waist coincides with the Gala theme’s survey of unconventional materials in fashion.

It seems like denim is going to be a major material in the Costume Institute’s exhibition, so we hope to see some on the red carpet. But we’re talking about, you know, dressed-up jeans, like a pair worn with a superluxe fur coat à la Dolce & Gabbana.

Speaking of fur coats, it’s possible guests will have a bit of fun with the staple and attend, say, wearing the Hugh Hefner housecoat-adjacent piece from Phoebe Philo’s recent collection (leather slippers are a must, too).

Gorpcore needs to make its way onto the Met carpet. Is it too much to ask that someone attend in the shocking orange Mulberry parka, zipped all the way to the top? Worn without pants, it’s basically a mini dress, right?

If a guest is interested in the performancewear route, but has the desire to dress it up a bit, there’s a perfect look from Sandy Liang’s spring 2027 show. Liang sent a model down the runway in a ski jacket paired with a tulle skirt and oversize bow—a gorpcore red carpet moment if we’ve ever seen one.

The Prada spring 2027 show was made for the new Met Gala theme. Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons focused the collection “on an interrogation of this single, universal garment,” the skirt. And what is even more ubiquitous than the skirt but the bra? This look from the Prada show combines two of the most necessary parts of a closet.
Everyday essentials can also take the form of an accessory (like the hat) or a pattern (like animal print) both of which are considered and hyperbolized in this look from Torishéju spring 2027.

This may be the only Met Gala we’ve ever seen (and possibly will ever see) where one can prioritize comfort on the red carpet. An attendee could, perhaps, embrace the knit sweater, and we mean really embrace the knit sweater. See: this oversize crocheted top presented by Louise Trotter for Bottega Veneta, which could even be worn as a dress.

What is truly the most important piece of any wardrobe? The wardrobe itself, of course. And this minidress from Yuhan Wang allows the wearer to celebrate the true hero of every closet—the drawers holding their belongings.

We’re expecting many unconventional materials on the red carpet, which will likely be some of the most fun of the Met Gala. For example, if someone arrives in the Area jumprope dress, they will be the whimsical belle of the ball in our eyes.

Those wanting something with a little more of a traditional foundation should look no further than the silver-adorned Maison Margiela dress from this season. The piece features a vest of compressed plates, urns, and drinkware topping an otherwise simple white gown.

Some less obviously unconventional options come from The Row’s spring 2027 collection, which saw tablecloth linens, doilies, and vintage lace combined to create tops and dresses perfect for those wanting to make a more subdued—but still on theme—statement at the Gala.

And we cannot forget about the men, who, in our opinion, should consider Willy Chavarria’s spring 2027 show when choosing their Met Gala getups. Over the past few years, Chavarria has cemented many brand signatures, one of them being his boxer shorts, which feel appropriately on-theme. The rest of the outfit is similarly comprised of closet must-haves: the leather bomber, tube socks, and loafers. Why wear one essential when you can wear them all at once?

items.title: Turns Out Aspyn Ovard Is Perfect for Reality TV
items.description: The following contains spoilers for the first season of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.
items.author: Allie Jones
paragraphs: The following contains spoilers for the first season of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

Few people are better at the internet than Aspyn Ovard. The 30-year-old influencer has been creating “content” — chatty day-in-the-life videos about everything from her nose job to the births of her children — since she was 14 and today has over 5 million followers across YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok. In a way, she’s been making her own show about herself since she was basically a tween, which is more than any of the other Mormon and Mormon-adjacent women who appear on The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County (premiering on Hulu today) can say.

Ovard does not identify as Mormon, but she grew up in St. George, Utah, and got married at 19 years old, which she admits is pretty culturally Mormon. Two years ago, however, her content took a turn: After fans discovered that she had filed for divorce from her husband, Parker Ferris, on the day she gave birth to the couple’s third child, she created a whole new narrative, posting about the breakup, her discovery that she’d rather date women, and her new relationship, which happens to be a “throuple” with another married couple.

On SLOMW: OC, Ovard reveals even more, like the “ten-year secret” that contributed to her decision to file for divorce. (Spoiler: Ferris was drinking and hiding it from her.) She also lets the audience in on a personal matter she has thus far declined to share online: One of her daughters has been diagnosed with terminal cancer. (Through Hulu, Ovard asked not to discuss her daughter’s health during this interview. We agreed.)

Ahead of making her streaming-TV debut, Ovard chatted about filming as a throuple, supporting her friend and castmate Jen Affleck in her divorce, and why there is — blessedly — no DadTok on this iteration of Mormon Wives.
With YouTube and TikTok, you’re choosing what to film and how to edit it. What was it like stepping into reality TV and ceding some of that control?

It was actually kind of nice. I’m used to doing 100 percent of the work. I mean, I’ve had editors or people help me film, but when you produce your own content, you really do 100 percent of the work a lot of the time. So it was really nice to just get to show up — I was literally just existing, living my life, and having fun most of the time.
Was there anything that surprised you about the filming process?

How much goes into the backend. I think that you may assume that on reality TV, they’re just following you around with a camera all the time, but this was so streamlined and organized. At the same time, you’re still able to be real and authentic. That’s just a cool mix to see, especially as someone who has done content for the past 16 years. It’s a very different process.

You started talking about your divorce online a couple of years ago, and fans were very invested in finding out what happened. Can you talk about your decision to hold back the big reason for the divorce until the show?

Well, that wasn’t actually the reason that I got divorced. I think people are looking for one big thing or one big event that happened, but we just are not each other’s people. We got married very young, and I obviously still have so much love for Parker, and he’s the father of my kids. Being from Utah and being from such a small town and thinking it’s normal to get married at 19 to your first boyfriend … It’s interesting how even though I’m not actually Mormon, that culture still has really shaped my life so much.

But yeah, the ten-year-secret thing wasn’t even really the reason that I got divorced. I wasn’t really aware of what went on in my marriage until I was already in that divorce process. Parker himself was willing to talk about it, so that’s why it ended up being on the show. People would’ve been disappointed if we hadn’t included it, just because there’s so much curiosity.

People are also curious about your new relationship, and there’s a lot that’s been made of it in the show’s trailer and the first couple of episodes. Over the course of the season, though, it comes across as one of the most stable, drama-free relationships on the show. Why do you think that is?

We do have a pretty stable relationship, and I have heard that comment from other people that we are one of the more stable relationships that you see on the show. I think that so many people have questions about just the dynamic and how it works. Even if I ever see another throuple, I have all the same questions. I’m like, “How does that work? What’s the dynamic?” But I mean, my relationship is so healthy and fulfilling and just healing and amazing, so I think that it’s really special to get to just show up authentically as ourselves.

There were a few different discussions with some of the more conservative Mormon women about your relationship on the show about whether they supported it and gay rights in general. Did you feel satisfied with those conversations?

We definitely have talked about it, and I know that they’re very supportive of my relationship and just me as a person. I think as we’ve all gotten to know each other better, you just have less questions about where people stand with things. But I mean, the Mormon church itself does not support or recognize or perform gay marriage, so it is kind of interesting to navigate friendships with very devout Mormons when that’s what the church stands for, but then they’re saying that they stand for something else. But I mean, I choose to believe them.

In the original Mormon Wives show, there’s this DadTok contingent, where the cameras are following just the guys, and that’s refreshingly not present on your show. Was that something you talked about as a cast or with producers?

Everyone had their own individual conversations with their partners and kind of decided what worked for them or what didn’t. Production did have the feedback from the other show that people didn’t like DadTok, so that was not something that they pushed on us. But I think most of the husbands just didn’t want to be on the show, or they support their wives doing it, but they don’t want to be on camera themselves. I don’t think we need more DadTok.

The news just broke that Jen Affleck filed for divorce. On the show, we actually see you visit a divorce attorney with her and help her through that. What was it like supporting someone through something so similar to your own experience?

I love Jen so much. I feel for her. As hard as it is to show up for other people sometimes with everything I have going on, I was so just honored to be able to be there for Jen in this situation. Divorce is so lonely, and divorce while pregnant is even lonelier. So I was just very happy to get to be there for her.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: 'm 25, I Make $145K & I Feel Like I Would Be A Child Bride If I Got Engaged Or Married Anytime Soon
items.description: A Week In New York, NY On A $145,000 Salary
items.author: R
paragraphs: A Week In New York, NY On A $145,000 Salary
This week: An associate working in finance who makes $145,000 per year and spends it on her $40 Spotify "family" plan.

If you'd like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we're not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.
Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We'd love to hear your thoughts here.
Editor's Note: This is a follow-up diary. Read the previous one here.
Joint Income/Financial Setup: My boyfriend, J. makes $80,000 per year, but we don't combine finances. I pay 60% of the rent, and we split everything else 50/50.
Assets: These are only my assets — I don't have a clear view of my partner's finances.
401(k) (mostly Roth, some traditional): $33,359.25
Brokerage account: $28,434.90
Debt: About $10K on my credit cards this month, which I will pay in full when they are due.
Paycheck Amount (monthly): $7014.72
Housing Costs: $2,500 (I live with J. in a studio and he pays $1,500)
Internet: $59.99 (split with J.)
Electricity: ~$100 (on average, split with J.)
Phone: $0 (my work pays for it)
Lifetime membership: $123.97
Healthcare copay: $15 (comes out of my gross paycheck)
Brokerage investment: $550
Roth IRA investment: $1000 (once I hit the cap, this is being re-directed to brokerage)
Renters insurance: $146 (split with J.)
Amazon Prime Young Adult: $73.14
Capital One Venture X: $395
Amex Gold: $325 (for the past two years, I've gotten $100 off for having a corporate Amex)
Chase Sapphire Reserve: $795 (in theory I have renewed, but I think I'm downgrading to the Preferred, which is $95 per year)
YNAB: $115.54 (I share with J. but I don't charge him).
Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?

Yes, 100%. Both of my parents have advanced degrees and were the first in their families to attend higher education, so it wasn't a question of whether or not I would attend university, but where. They attended school outside the US, so their ability to help me through the college application process was limited. Luckily, I attended an excellent public school and had incredibly pushy parents. My parents started saving for school in a 529 plan when I was born, and my university provided ample need-based financial aid. Since my parents made undergraduate education (at the best schools we could get into) an expectation in our house, they felt responsible for paying for our degrees after any scholarships and aid we received. If I have a family, I will do the exact same thing because it allowed me and my brother to shoot for the stars when it came to colleges. Both of my parents have PhDs, so their expectation was actually that I also get a JD, MD, or PhD of some kind. They were the ones who pushed me to do the Master's when I was on the fence about it, as I mentioned in my previous Money Diary.
Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?

My parents have always been very frugal people, so most of our conversations about money revolved around saving money for emergencies. I didn't receive much of an education about finances directly, but I was aware that my parents had things like a mortgage, retirement accounts, and life insurance. I'm really interested in personal finance, so before starting college, I did an entire course to educate myself and be as set up for living on my own as I could be.
What was your first job and why did you get it?

My first real W-2 job was an internship within my state's judicial system. It was pretty basic office work, but I got to listen to a lot of podcasts and music on the job! Where I went to school, families were optimizing their kids' résumés from birth, so I got this summer job to improve my own résumé. My parents didn't actually give me access to any of the money I earned from my summer jobs until I got to college, which I have mixed feelings about, but this probably ensured I didn't waste all my money on fast food and clothes (which I did during undergrad anyways).
Did you worry about money growing up?

Yes and no. My father grew up in poverty, and that mindset was reflected in our household. He would always compare how much things would cost to how many loaves of bread he could buy with that amount (with one loaf somehow remaining constantly at $1 to this day). I was told “no” all the time for things like snacks and toys, though my mother would occasionally go shopping with me and hide purchases from my father. This kind of restriction, though, meant that when one of my parents lost their job during the recession, I didn't feel the impact. We would visit one of my parent's home countries every year, which I later found out was paid for by my mom's family during some difficult times. Ultimately, there was always money for necessities, school activities, and anything my parents thought would help my brother and I academically, so I never felt worried.
Do you worry about money now?

Not really. I opened a Roth IRA when I was 18 and have been pretty savvy with savings and things like credit card points. The problem for me is that I'm a big saver who also likes to spend, especially on little treats, and now that I have a big girl salary, the treats aren't so little. I always hit my savings goals every month, but I always think that I could and should be saving more of my salary for things like a wedding or a down payment on a house. This is mostly because I have friends already doing both of these things and other friends working at crazy startups and making a ton of money when they IPO. I know the mindset of comparison isn't healthy or reasonable, but it's hard to stop these pretty ingrained habits.
At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?

I would say I became completely financially responsible for myself this year when my job started paying for my phone plan, and the last financial tie to my parents fell away. While I'm technically on their health insurance, I have been using my own insurance through work since I moved to New York two years ago. My parents will probably always be my financial safety net, and maybe even J.'s if we get married, but my parents would never think of making me feel bad about it. I think they know that if I needed their help, it would be because something truly bad happened rather than me being irresponsible with money given my saving habits.
Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.

In my last Money Diary, I was given a "loan" from my parents for my Master's degree. After half a year of payments, they decided to forgive the loan on the condition that I put the same amount of money monthly ($1,000) into retirement or other investments. They reasoned that my brother's undergraduate education cost the same as my undergraduate education, plus my Master's, and they wanted to be fair to us. They don't check on this, but I'm very diligent about it. I guess my parents "forgiving" their loan to me for my Master's program might count, but otherwise, no. It will hopefully be a long time until my parents pass, and any inheritance from any of my grandparents would go to my parents directly.

I definitely had some high-ticket items this week, but I think the other spending is pretty in line with regular weeks for me. Unfortunately, that's not a great thing because I always exceed the budget I give myself for dining out and groceries. I need to either learn to say no a bit more or be more thoughtful about buying snacks and drinks ahead of time, rather than making impulse purchases.
The first step to getting your financial life in order is tracking what you spend — to try on your own, check out our guide to managing your money every day. For more Money Diaries, click here.

items.title: The Other Room: Hanna Moon and Moffy Gathorne-Hardy’s New Creative Agency
items.description: As the photographer and writer launch their women-only agency The Other Room, they discuss the importance of transgression, financial freedom and rebelling against the system
items.author: Violet Conroy
paragraphs: As the photographer and writer launch their women-only agency The Other Room, they discuss the importance of transgression, financial freedom and rebelling against the system

Although photographer Hanna Moon insists she is averse to the term ‘female gaze’, much of her creative work focuses on what it means to be a female artist. After coming across an introspective Dorothea Tanning self-portrait at a Tate retrospective in 2019, Moon became “interested in how the social and physical status of being female affects female artists’ work.” Feeling inspired, she revived her student publishing project A Nice Magazine, releasing a third issue in February 2025 devoted to the work of women photographers including Jet Swan, Momo Okabe, Rosie Marks, Julie Greve and Moon herself.

It’s an ethos that carries through to her latest endeavour, The Other Room – a new agency representing exclusively women: photographers Sandy Kim, Leigh Johnson, Donna Trope, Moon herself, and artist Frances Waite. Co-founded with Moon’s best friend, the writer and model Moffy Gathorne-Hardy, The Other Room takes a radical stance in its mission to facilitate artists’ creative freedom through financial stability. Most talent agencies operating in the fashion industry do not have a tone of voice or perspective per se, and not many are female-only; The Other Room is a welcome anomaly. A concurrent editorial platform, The Other Times, will expound upon the founding principles of the agency, publishing interviews, essays, articles and show reviews.

The Other Room takes its name from Virginia Woolf’s seminal 1929 essay A Room of One’s Own, a feminist polemic about women’s need for financial independence and intellectual freedom. Meanwhile, the design of the agency’s website lifts from the DIY, Xeroxed aesthetic of the Guerrilla Girls and feminist publications and posters from the 1970s and 1980s, with artists’ work showcased in a purposefully non-hierarchical manner. So, is there a uniting aesthetic that binds the work of these female artists? “There’s an inherent quality of resilience in women’s work because you have to go through so much shit, like having kids or people patronising you,” says Moon. “If you manage to actually have a voice as an artist, that’s already a huge achievement.”
Violet Conroy How did you two first meet?

Moffy Gathorne-Hardy I was a model when I was younger, and Hanna was on set as a photographer’s assistant on my first ever modelling job. She wanted to shoot me for something, so she asked the photographer for my number.

Hanna Moon I’ve always been interested in this weird or extraordinary kind of beauty. I was interested in Moffy because she was so awkward, and she came in with this book under her arm. I probably sensed something real in her, and then it was also her crossed eyes. [Laughs]. It’s quite hard to come across someone who fully embraces themselves in a fashion context.
VC How did your creative relationship unfold from there?

HM As well as photographing her, I commissioned Moffy to write things for my student magazine, A Nice Magazine, and I realised how intelligent she was. A sense of rebelliousness is the common thing for us. I also loved that Moffy doesn’t care about being naked in front of the camera. We’re very aligned: there’s a sense of transgression in our work but at the same time, it’s not serious.
MGH It always felt like our primary aim was just to have fun, and be cheeky in our work.
VC When did you start thinking about launching an agency together?

MGH We really wanted to do something creative together that felt like more of a long-form project, instead of Hanna just taking photos and me writing about them. Initially, we wanted to write a semi-autobiographical film loosely based on our friendship, then we thought we’d do a gallery. Then we landed on the idea of an agency. It felt like a structure we could use to fuck about with pre-existing structures.

HM I know what the agency world is like, so it made sense. It’s a bit naive to walk into a completely new system, like the art world, that you don’t really know how to navigate. In our relationship, Moffy is about thinking, ideas and feeling, whereas I’m very practical, like a bulldozer. I make things happen and I’m very decisive. We work well as a duo in that sense – it’s all about balance. We can operate in the current system with a touch of rebelliousness. But we are very serious about the business side of this project.
VC Why did you decide to represent only women artists? It’s quite radical.

HM It means there’s a clear starting point. The third issue of A Nice Magazine was female-only. It was inspired by a self-portrait by Dorothea Tanning, which made me cry. I wasn’t specifically focusing on gender, but the things Dorothea went through as a woman artist really resonated with me. There’s also a humour and lightness to her work that I love, despite the fact that the world wasn’t fair to her as an artist.

I hate the term ‘female gaze’, so I didn’t want it to be about that. But there’s an inherent quality of resilience in women’s work because you have to go through so much shit, like having kids or people patronising you. If you manage to have a voice as an artist, that’s already a huge achievement.
VC Tell me about your roster of artists.

HM We represent five artists, including me. There’s Sandy Kim, Leigh Johnson, Donna Trope and Frances Waite. Donna is from the older generation, but there’s a contemporariness to her work. There’s a certain freedom, confidence and provocation there. I first saw Sandy’s work when I was a student, and it was her nude self-portraits. I was quite shocked that she was an Asian girl doing that kind of work. It was ballsy and powerful. There’s an emotional and human quality to her work. Leigh bridges the worlds of art and fashion on her own terms. She’s primarily interested in sex and death. Frances is a visual artist who does pencil drawings. I saw the potential of how that could work in a commercial fashion context. She didn’t only want to belong in a traditional art space, and doesn’t care about labels. Her mentality aligned with ours.
VC I’m intrigued by the branding and design of The Other Room. It feels more editorial and conceptual than most agencies.

HM We want to be rebellious, but at the same time, we have to navigate the system and survive. We added a green filter on everything, which is an aesthetic from feminist publications and posters from the 1970s and 80s. The design is almost like an Easter egg: if you know, you know. If you’re interested in the sort of activism or feminism that we reference, it will resonate. The website homepage presentation is non-hierarchical and democratic. We also don’t want a news page, because the idea of constantly having to produce new work is just another pressure for artists.
VC How else is The Other Room different from other agencies?

HM We want to tackle all these traditional ideas, and the artist bio is one of them. What is the role of the bio? When you read the bio, it should be personal and make you feel the urge to look at their work.

MGH The thing I noticed when I did my own research on agency websites was that the focus was always on gallery names or big designers artists had worked with. That really detracted from the artists themselves because it was borrowing hype from other institutions. We do have client lists at the end of our bios though, because you need to in order to survive in the current climate.
VC Tell me about The Other Times, the editorial platform that runs alongside the agency.

MGH It’s making room for conversations and ideas that are being generated by the work that we’re doing at The Other Room. We’re going to do interviews, essays, articles, show reviews. The Xeroxed effect on the homepage was also a nod to the Guerrilla Girls and the DIY aesthetic. Alongside digital articles, we’re going to make physical newsletters that people can subscribe to.
VC Hanna, you’ve spoken about the importance of financial stability for female artists in the industry. Tell me about your own journey as a photographer?

HM As a student, I printed the first version of A Nice Magazine in Brighton on the cheapest paper. But I printed the most recent issue [in 2025] in Japan. When you have more financial freedom, it opens doors. You can have more power, a bigger platform, and most importantly, freedom. I managed to establish stability for myself as an artist via my work as a fashion photographer, and do multiple things at the same time. Having your own platform gives you freedom of speech.
VC How do you navigate that relationship between your editorial or personal work and your commercial work?

HM I think there almost shouldn’t be a separation. But if you work more, you have less focus on your personal projects. I’m not trying to criticise everything because I think any industry in the world is like that. I love fashion and I want to stick with it. But to do that, I shouldn’t feel bored in it. That’s why I’m trying to do something more meaningful with The Other Room. For me to have more passion, I just had to think about my value system and what really works for me.
VC Moffy, could you talk about your relationship to modelling and writing?

MGH I’m lucky in the sense that my experience of being a model hasn’t traumatised or disturbed me to the extent that it has lots of other people. But it has inserted itself into my experience of my own femininity and my own body. The fashion industry does this thing where it forces us to project ourselves into potential future aspirational states of being, like being thin or finally owning a certain handbag. By definition, having to project yourself into that potential state makes the current version of you ‘less than’. There’s also this idea that when you’re 30, 35, 40 – if we’re being generous – your life as a woman is also seen to be over. The whole experience of being a woman and being allowed to experience pleasure is really bookended. Writing is the antidote to that. And this project with Hanna feels like an antidote to that.
Learn more about The Other Room here

items.title: John Goldberger’s ‘100 Superlative Rolex Watches’ Returns in a Fully Revised Edition
items.description: John Goldberger’s 100 Superlative Rolex Watches returns in a fully revised edition.
items.author: Zoe Leung
paragraphs: John Goldberger’s 100 Superlative Rolex Watches returns in a fully revised edition.
New photography and updated research spotlight 100 of the rarest Rolex references.
Physical copies will hit European stores in December, followed by the rest of the world in Spring 2027.

Nearly two decades after its original 2008 debut helped establish the modern blueprint for vintage Rolex scholarship, Damiani Books is releasing a completely revised edition of John Goldberger’s landmark reference volume, 100 Superlative Rolex Watches.

Featuring an introduction by Giampiero Negretti, the updated 280-page edition brings together 100 of the rarest and most historically significant Rolex timepieces ever produced, spanning early Oyster models, cloisonné enamel dials, and military-issue Submariners to complicated moonphases and Paul Newman Cosmograph Daytonas. Developed in collaboration with some of the world’s foremost collectors, the volume pairs newly commissioned high-resolution photography with updated archival research and previously unseen historical material, examining why vintage Rolex continues to serve as the benchmark at the intersection of luxury, design, and collectibility.

Printed in Italy , the new edition runs to 280 pages and comes as an eco-leather hardcover with a slipcase, measuring 24.2 by 28.5 cm. It’s available to order from Damiani Books, retailing at €240 EUR (approx. $265 USD). Physical copies will officially arrive in European bookstores starting December 1, 2026, followed by a wider release across the US and worldwide in Spring 2027.

items.title: KidSuper and Mercedes-Benz Have Football Fever
items.description: KidSuper and Mercedes-Benz celebrate seven World Cup-winning nations with a 17-piece collection connecting football and automotive history.
items.author: Hypebeast Newsroom
paragraphs: KidSuper and Mercedes-Benz celebrate seven World Cup-winning nations with a 17-piece collection connecting football and automotive history.
The collection pairs iconic Mercedes-Benz vehicles with national team colors, historic victories, and football-inspired designs.
Priced from $125 to $595 USD, the collection launches November 14 alongside a special event at KidSuper Studios in Brooklyn.

KidSuper and Mercedes-Benz are bringing football history to the forefront of their latest collaboration. First previewed during KidSuper’s Spring/Summer 2027 runway show in Miami, the collection celebrates seven World Cup-winning nations by pairing their football heritage with iconic Mercedes-Benz vehicles.

Marking 140 years of Mercedes-Benz, the collaboration takes inspiration from the stars found above national team crests, each representing a World Cup victory. For KidSuper founder Colm Dillane, the symbol serves as a connection between generations of football fans, with each country’s sporting achievements paired with a Mercedes-Benz model from a corresponding era.

Spanning 17 pieces, the collection brings together football jerseys, tracksuits, tailoring, knitwear, and accessories, incorporating national colors, historic dates, and automotive references throughout.

Brazil’s football legacy is reimagined through a tailored jacket inspired by the Mercedes-Benz 220 SE, while Uruguay’s history informs a navy crochet polo referencing the SSK. Germany’s 300 SL Coupé appears on a black zip-up jacket, while Argentina’s 450 SEL 6.9 inspires a printed shirt and leather-trimmed bag.

Elsewhere, France’s G 500 is referenced through a blue workwear set, Spain’s SLS AMG Coupé Electric Drive Concept inspires a colorful football jersey, and England’s Mercedes-Benz 600 is translated into a burgundy tracksuit.

Throughout the collection, KidSuper reworks the Mercedes-Benz three-pointed star alongside football iconography, combining the visual language of vintage sportswear, automotive memorabilia, and national team merchandise.

The KidSuper x Mercedes-Benz collection is available from today, with prices ranging from $125 USD to $595 USD. Available in store and online at KidSuper, alongside select global retailers, the release will also be celebrated with a public event at KidSuper Studios in Williamsburg, featuring a display of Mercedes-Benz vehicles, music, food, and drinks.

items.title: Siegelman Stable's Holiday Homecoming Takes Over SoHo
items.description: Siegelman Stable returns to SoHo for the holidays with a six-week pop-up featuring exclusive drops, coveted restocks, and its FW26 collection.
items.author: Hypebeast Newsroom
paragraphs: Siegelman Stable returns to SoHo for the holidays with a six-week pop-up featuring exclusive drops, coveted restocks, and its FW26 collection.
The space features an Almost Home coffee bar, lounge, and interiors inspired by the late 1980s.
In partnership with Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business, the brand will host special events and programming for New York's entrepreneurial community.

Siegelman Stable is back in New York City for the holidays. Following previous pop-ups in SoHo, East Hampton, and Chicago, the brand returns to its hometown with a new retail space at 430 W Broadway, open through December 23.

Presented in partnership with Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business, the holiday pop-up will feature exclusive releases, restocks of some of the brand’s most sought-after pieces, and its latest Fall/Winter 2026 collection. While Siegelman Stable has become known for its signature headwear, the space will also highlight its growing ready-to-wear offering, including an expanded selection of knitwear.

Designed by ForEveryday.Life alongside creative director Karoline Spenning, the store takes inspiration from the late 1980s, with rich blue walls, velvet curtains, suede finishes, and plush carpeting. An Almost Home coffee bar and lounge at the back of the space offer visitors somewhere to unwind between shopping.

Beyond retail, Siegelman Stable is making room for New York’s entrepreneurial community. Throughout the pop-up, the brand and Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business will host special programming, including a founder’s roundtable focused on navigating the holiday season as a business owner, alongside dedicated early shopping hours.

“We’ve had our biggest growth year to date, and now we have to pop up at home in NYC and show who we are as a brand in person,” said founder Max Siegelman, emphasizing the importance of creating physical experiences as the brand continues to grow.

Siegelman Stable’s holiday pop-up is now open at 430 W Broadway in SoHo through December 23, with prices ranging from $38 USD to $2,200 USD. Additional exclusive drops and special events will be announced throughout its run.

items.title: Vincent Tsang Brings Quiet Luxury to the Fairway With PIERRE
items.description: Dime artistic director Vincent Tsang serves as artistic director for PIERRE, a new golf-inspired luxury apparel label
items.author: Joyce Li
paragraphs: Dime artistic director Vincent Tsang serves as artistic director for PIERRE, a new golf-inspired luxury apparel label
Designed in Montréal and manufactured in Japan, the brand crafts garments from silk and premium materials without loud logos
The official website is now live with all products available to purchase via pierre.golf

PIERRE is a newly introduced luxury apparel label with Dime artistic director Vincent Tsang serving as its artistic director, built on the core belief that true luxury is felt before it is seen. Designed in Montréal and meticulously manufactured in Japan, the newly minted golf lifestyle and apparel brand blends thoughtful Montréal design with the precision and craftsmanship of Japanese manufacturing to establish an understated wardrobe for those who value quality over spectacle.

Drawing direct inspiration from golf’s enduring relationship with nature, PIERRE celebrates patience, presence, and the beauty of moving at a slower pace. Rather than chasing fleeting trends or relying on loud logos, the imprint creates garments that honor both the natural rhythm of the game and the landscapes it inhabits. Through this measured approach, each piece is conceived to embody quiet confidence, timeless style, and lasting comfort.

Materiality and tailoring sit at the center of the label’s creative direction. Placing uncompromising fabric and considered fit at the forefront of every garment, PIERRE crafts its pieces from a refined mix of silk and other premium materials. Engineered to move effortlessly between the golf course and everyday life, the resulting wardrobe offers versatile, tactile staples defined by subtle luxury and enduring wearability.

items.title: Alessio Ascari on What Lasts Once the Hype Dies Down
items.description: As the founder of KALEIDOSCOPE and Capsule, Alessio Ascari is one of the few figures in design publishing who translates ideas into physical spaces—from Spazio Maiocchi in Milan and Manifesto in Paris to the annual roaming event Capsule Plaza. This month, Caps
items.author: Yumiko Zhao
paragraphs: As the founder of KALEIDOSCOPE and Capsule, Alessio Ascari is one of the few figures in design publishing who translates ideas into physical spaces—from Spazio Maiocchi in Milan and Manifesto in Paris to the annual roaming event Capsule Plaza. This month, Capsule Plaza touches down in Shanghai for the first time, taking over IYOUTH STUDIO from November 10 to 15. Taking advantage of the occasion, Hypebeast sat down with Alessio for an exclusive conversation, spanning his recent observations of Shanghai’s design scene, the changing relationship between younger generations and design, and his take on the true motives behind the industry’s “crossover” frenzy—ultimately asking: when the hype fades, what is worth holding onto?
The Shanghai Design Landscape

You’ve visited Shanghai frequently recently to prepare for this Capsule Plaza. What excites you most about the current design ecosystem here? Specifically, what shifts are happening that the outside world might not fully realize yet?

I really love the energy of Shanghai. What excites me most is the collision between tradition and innovation: cultural heritage and craftsmanship on one side, technological advancement and forward-thinking on the other. There’s also a subcultural and experimental side to Shanghai’s creative scene that outsiders might not be familiar with, but it’s incredibly cool and dynamic. Youth culture is strong here, and people have an international, open mindset, which fills the city with possibilities.

Beyond fairs, auctions, and gallery openings, where do you think the most interesting design discussions in Shanghai are happening right now? Could you talk about specific studios, neighborhoods, or individuals?

I’m paying close attention to what young creators in Shanghai are doing, especially in design and architecture, where many practice outside the mainstream through independent studios. Mario Tsai is a great example. Seeing an industrial designer like him open his own space to build a platform for his work and ideas is thrilling. I’m also very interested in Atelier Guo and their architectural approach.

On the institutional side, I love the cultural programming Prada Rong Zhai is doing; the building itself is stunning. I’ve also been following the work of curator X Zhu-Nowell at the Rockbund Art Museum (RAM), and David Chipperfield’s renovation of the architecture is spot-on.
From Milan to Tokyo and Now Shanghai

Capsule Plaza has been held in Milan four times, is heading to Tokyo in 2025, and has now landed in Shanghai. How has your understanding of “design” shifted across these different cities? Placed side-by-side, where does Shanghai sit?

The design histories of Milan and Tokyo have many intersections. Especially in the 1980s, as the postmodernist movement evolved, there was a brilliant dialogue between the two cities, which the Memphis Group embodied most vividly.

The exchange between Chinese and Italian design and fashion has a similarly long history—take the influence of Chinese aesthetics on Giorgio Armani’s collections in the 1980s and 1990s, for example. Today, we are witnessing a new chapter in this cultural exchange, and I hope Capsule Plaza can be part of it.

You’ve mentioned that the Capsule model can travel anywhere, but the content is tailored to the location. Bringing it to Shanghai, what are you trying to do differently than in Milan? Facing the need to localize, what elements do you insist on keeping intact?

If you think of the Milan edition as the “motherboard,” the Shanghai edition is a more compact version—smaller in scale and more agile in its lineup. But our ambition is the same: to connect different fields through interiors, architecture, music, cultural talks, and publishing.

Stone Island’s “NO SEASONS” is one of the core threads of this exhibition, featuring an installation by Milanese design studio NM3. Music runs through the entire space, including live DJ sets curated by independent Shanghai radio station BYYB.RADIO. We’ve also invited two contemporary artists to present sculptures exploring the tension between the natural and the artificial, and set up an art gift shop showcasing several design brands and publications from China, Italy, and beyond.

But for me, the most important thing is always that “collision and intersection”—bringing people, ideas, and objects that would never normally share a room into the same physical space. The format can adapt to the city, but that core remains unchanged.

Milan Design Week is backed by deep historical roots and a mature institutional system, whereas Shanghai is still writing its own design narrative. Does this give you more creative freedom, or does it mean more pressure?

Shanghai’s creative forces are booming across multiple dimensions, from projects driven by large cultural institutions to fiercely independent cultural initiatives led by the younger generation. It’s exhilarating to be here at this moment because everything is still full of undefined potential.

This openness gives us room to experiment, but it also means we need to connect more deeply with the existing local cultural ecosystem. I want Capsule Plaza to be more than just a showcase; I want it to build bridges, sparking collaborations between local and international creators, brands, and cultural institutions. We brought a format that developed elsewhere, but we want it to engage in Shanghai’s local conversations and grow through that exchange.

You chose IYOUTH STUDIO in Changning, deliberately avoiding the West Bund art hub. What is the logic behind this location choice, and how does it reflect the way you want audiences to encounter Capsule Plaza? What does the surrounding environment add to the experience you’re trying to create?

What drew us to IYOUTH STUDIO was its ability to bring furniture, art, fashion, and contemporary culture together without being confined to any single field. Their aesthetic and way of perceiving things are very close to ours.

I love staging Capsule Plaza in a place like this: it inherently flows between different creative fields. Art installations, a professional sound system, DJ performances, cultural talks, a café, and a magazine shop come together to form a complete ecosystem where people can stumble upon unexpected delights.

Being away from the core circuit of traditional art fairs gives the venue a completely different rhythm. Visitors can enter through any thread—an installation, music, or a talk—and find their own path of exploration. I love when a project unfolds naturally like that.
Cross-Disciplinary Intersections

When we spoke in Milan in 2024, you mentioned that the younger generation was rediscovering design. Two years later, has this trend matured, splintered, or evolved into a new form? What is it becoming?

I think people’s connection to design is becoming more personal, even intimate. The pandemic was a major catalyst: it changed our relationship with domestic life and forced us to reexamine the objects and spaces we live with every day.
At the same time, vintage culture continues to rise. The younger generation is looking back at the past, discovering its objects and aesthetics, and reinterpreting them in their own way.

Design is becoming a way for people to express themselves, build a personal aesthetic, and connect with the things around them. I think this shift goes beyond simply following a trend or collecting a specific piece.

The intersection of design, art, architecture, and fashion is practically the norm today. In your view, where is the next truly worthwhile intersection to explore? Are there any directions that haven’t yet been named or widely recognized?

I think the hospitality and resort sector is undergoing a transformation. A hotel, a resort, or even an entire travel destination can become a natural meeting point for design, art, architecture, fashion, and food. More and more cultural institutions and brands are doubling down on these spaces, which reflects what people want right now: human connection, a sense of belonging, and the memories formed between people and places.
I don’t really like the word “experience” because it’s a bit overused. But one thing is clearer than ever: more than material things, time is the ultimate luxury.

You once curated a major exhibition about Virgil Abloh and Gucci. From your perspective, how much of the constantly referenced “crossover” stems from an organic flow between cultures, and how much is just brand marketing disguised as creativity?

I can’t imagine being confined to a single framework or field. The people who inspire me most creatively are usually true polymaths. They navigate different dimensions with ease, bringing ideas from one world into another.
For me, true cross-disciplinary thinking starts with curiosity and a genuine urge to explore, rather than setting out with a predetermined goal to connect different industries.
Of course, brands are getting better at leveraging these intersections strategically. But when the connection itself is authentic, it can still spark a chemistry that transcends the sum of its parts.

You helm Capsule, Kaleidoscope, Spazio Maiocchi, Manifesto in Paris, and Capsule Plaza—what is the core thread tying all these projects together? And what is the biggest tension you have to navigate between them?

I’m interested in building cultural platforms rather than staying confined to a single field. Every project has its own unique identity and audience, but they all stem from the same curiosity, pointing toward art, design, fashion, music, and contemporary culture in the broadest sense.

Kaleidoscope started in publishing, Spazio Maiocchi is a physical space, and Capsule spans both print and offline events. They each have their own way of operating, but I see them as complementary parts of the same ecosystem, not isolated projects. The biggest challenge is letting each project grow naturally along its own trajectory while maintaining the perspective that connects them. I’ve never had any interest in creating cookie-cutter, interchangeable templates; every project must have an irreplaceable reason to exist.

Over the past five years, the design industry has expanded rapidly: fairs are denser, collectible design auctions are breaking records, cross-brand collaborations are endless, and budgets and expectations are skyrocketing. From an operational or cultural logic standpoint, what cognitive biases or misconceptions do you think still exist in the industry today?

I think this industry sometimes confuses visibility with cultural value. True, there are more platforms, collaborations, and opportunities now than ever before, but that doesn’t mean we’re creating work with deeper value. We should give things the time they need to develop fully, rather than rushing toward the next launch or the next fleeting trend. Not every collaboration needs to exist, and not every object has to be a collectible.

What interests me is getting the right people together for the right reasons, and giving them enough space to make something neither side could achieve alone. I care more about the quality of the ideas themselves than the scale, and what stays with people long after the hype fades.
Personal Interests and the Future
Lately, what has excited you that lies outside design and its adjacent fields, beyond the usual talking points, yet is quietly influencing your thinking?

Sound is vital to me. It’s the energy and inspiration that runs through my day, helping me shift between different moods and atmospheres. I listen to music constantly, and lately, I’ve been digging back into the catalog of the German label ECM; it builds an incredibly nuanced world of jazz and ambient music. I’ve also been revisiting reggae and dub classics from Wackies, as well as quintessential street rap from Griselda.

I’m also almost obsessively collecting out-of-print vintage books and independent magazines. Wherever I go, I seek out indie bookstores, publishers, and rare editions. I’m building my own private library, and I go back there every day to find references, organize my thoughts, or, more often than not, just immerse myself completely.

items.title: Белый дом подтвердил планы встречи Трампа, Путина и Си Цзиньпина
items.description: Белый дом подтвердил планы встречи Трампа, Путина и Си Цзиньпина
items.author: Иван Адоньев
paragraphs: Белый дом подтвердил планы встречи Трампа, Путина и Си Цзиньпина

Трёхстороннюю встречу Дональда Трампа, Владимира Путина и Си Цзиньпина планируют провести 19 ноября на полях саммита Азиатско-Тихоокеанского экономического сотрудничества (АТЭС) в китайском Шэньчжэне. Подготовку переговоров Белый дом подтвердил в пятницу, сообщило Associated Press.

По словам высокопоставленного представителя администрации США, Вашингтон рассчитывает начать разговор о ядерном разоружении трёх стран. Объявления каких-либо соглашений по итогам встречи в Белом доме не ожидают.
Собеседник агентства также сообщил, что Трамп не планирует обсуждать Украину на этих переговорах.

В феврале истёк срок действия российско-американского договора о сокращении стратегических наступательных вооружений (ДСНВ). После этого Трамп выступил за новое соглашение, в котором участвовал бы и Китай. Как отмечает AP, Пекин пока проявлял мало интереса к такому договору.

items.title: В США на несколько часов запретили вылеты из всех аэропортов
items.description: В США на несколько часов запретили вылеты из всех аэропортов
items.author: Иван Адоньев
paragraphs: В США на несколько часов запретили вылеты из всех аэропортов

Федеральное управление гражданской авиации США (FAA) 13 ноября временно приостановило вылеты по всей стране из соображений безопасности. Запрет действовал несколько часов, после чего авиакомпаниям разрешили постепенно возобновить вылеты, сообщило Associated Press.

По словам министра внутренней безопасности США Маркуэйна Маллина, новое оборудование перегрузило устаревшую систему управления воздушным движением. Это привело к перебоям со связью и радиолокационным наблюдением. На момент брифинга власти не обнаружили признаков кибератаки.

Аэропорты продолжали принимать самолёты, которые уже находились в воздухе. По данным аналитической компании Cirium, не менее 827 рейсов изменили маршрут. Из них 670 вернулись в аэропорты вылета, ещё 157 перенаправили в другие аэропорты.

Запрет сняли в ночь на 14 ноября по московскому времени. Восстановление расписания может занять несколько дней, поскольку часть самолётов и экипажей оказалась вне запланированных аэропортов. Предыдущую общенациональную приостановку вылетов в США вводили в январе 2023 года из-за сбоя в системе оповещения пилотов.

items.title: Авангард, современное искусство и ржаные блинчики: зачем ехать в Иваново
items.description: Иваново не похоже на Ярославль, Кострому и другие приволжские города Золотого кольца. Здесь почти нет старинных церквей и золоченых куполов, зато много архитектурного авангарда. В 1920-е годы советская власть хотела сделать из Иваново-Вознесенска образцово-пок
items.author: Афиша Daily
paragraphs: Иваново не похоже на Ярославль, Кострому и другие приволжские города Золотого кольца. Здесь почти нет старинных церквей и золоченых куполов, зато много архитектурного авангарда. В 1920-е годы советская власть хотела сделать из Иваново-Вознесенска образцово-показательный социалистический город. Для большевиков эта территория имела большое значение. Как и в других крупных промышленных центрах, во время первой русской революции в Иваново-Вознесенске проходили крупные забастовки, а в 1905 году именно здесь появился первый в стране Совет рабочих депутатов. К слову, в Иванове до сих пор работает занятный Музей первого Совета: при входе — памятник Ильичу, который тычет в вас рукой, стоит лишь открыть дверь.

Главный памятник ивановского конструктивизма — железнодорожный вокзал, построенный в 1933 году и отреставрированный в 2020-м. Именно сюда прибывает «Ласточка» из Москвы, но вокзал заслуживает отдельного посещения. Во-первых, здание огромно и, чтобы вдумчиво его обойти, потребуется время. Во-вторых, здесь действительно попадаешь в прошлое: выпуклые линии, плавные формы, много стекла — на других станциях подобного не увидишь. В-третьих, вокзал работает и как культурное пространство. До конца ноября здесь проходит выставка современных художников «Станция воображения», организованная в рамках фестиваля «Первая фабрика авангарда». Экспозиция — одна большая инсталляция из работ нескольких авторов, которым предложили поразмышлять о том, способна ли выставка стереть грань между сном и реальностью.
