items.title: Shane Gillis Grades His Own Mediocre 'SNL' Monologue a C Minus
items.description: Shane Gillis hopped on Joe Rogan’s podcast to address his controversial Saturday Night Live monologue last month.
items.author: Charisma Madarang
paragraphs: Shane Gillis hopped on Joe Rogan’s podcast to address his controversial Saturday Night Live monologue last month.

During his mediocre stint on the stage, during which he name drops Rogan’s sauna, the comedian said that women who wear workout clothes at the gym were “dressing like whores.” When recalling the controversy with Rogan, Gillis said that the NBC sketch comedy show didn’t remove the joke from his monologue because they don’t review it before it goes on air. “Not to defend SNL, they don’t approve it. I mean, they could shut it down,” he said on The Joe Rogan Experience. “They could, but you don’t write your set and give it to them. Unless you’re not a comedian. I’m sure non-comics, they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them.”

Notably, most non-comedians have their monologues penned by the staff, with Taylor Swift (who memorably wrote her monologue song in 2009) being the exception. And while SNL did inquire about Gillis’ monologue, he promised them there would be nothing to fuss over. “The funniest part was, they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great but I don’t say anything bad,'” he said. “The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C minus of a monologue but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for fucking 10 minutes. That’s it.'”

Gillis was fired from SNL in 2019 for racist and homophobic comments, but has been invited back to host three times since. During his recent appearance, he not only infuriated viewers but dropped a F-bomb during one of the sketches, a Dr. Seuss-themed bit titled “Green Eggs and Ham.”

Following Gillis’ monologue, several celebrities responded in the aftermath, with many describing him as a misogynist. Among them, Maren Morris gave the comedian the middle finger. The singer posted a video of herself on Instagram with the text “me being a wh0re at the gym,” which was accompanied by her song, “Be a Bitch.” The song features the chorus: “Breaking my neck from turning my cheek/ Killing with kindness only killed me/ If the truth means I’m a little too mean/ Tried to fake nice, but it didn’t quite stick/ I’d rather be a bitch.”

Elsewhere, former SNL star Ego Nwodim posted a gym selfie to her Instagram Stories on Monday with the caption, “whore reporting for duty,” and Dan Levy shared an Instagram video saying he was “speechless that something like that can exist on live national television.”

items.title: ‘Club Kid’ Cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra on Capturing Intimate and Authentic New York Moments
items.description: Cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra enjoys working with directors who also act in their films. This year alone, his work includes “The Invite” with director and actor Olivia Wilde, as well as teaming up with Jordan Firstman on A24’s “Club Kid,” in which Firstma
items.author: Jazz Tangcay
paragraphs: Cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra enjoys working with directors who also act in their films. This year alone, his work includes “The Invite” with director and actor Olivia Wilde, as well as teaming up with Jordan Firstman on A24’s “Club Kid,” in which Firstman directs and stars.

Newport-Berra (Variety’s 10 Artisans to Watch 2026) says, “I tend to enjoy working with actor-directors because we get this dynamic experience on set where they get to direct the film both from outside and from within during the scene, which I think is a special opportunity for a director to be able to be inside the scene, guiding it as it’s happening.”

While “The Invite” challenged him to work with Wilde to be creative within a single space, “Club Kid” — which opens this weekend — is set in New York City. The film stars Firstman, Cara Delevingne, Diego Calva, Kirby Howell-Baptiste and Reggie Absolom. It follows a queer party promoter who has long outgrown his time on the scene. However, his life is upended when he suddenly meets the 10-year-old son (Absolom) he never knew he had, forcing him to grapple with the kind of life he wants to lead. Over time, Peter slowly begins to adjust to life with Arlo, and in one memorable scene, the pair sit at a piano as Newport-Berra’s camera slowly zooms out to capture a perfect evening and moment.

Newport-Berra shares, “Originally, we were going to shoot a whole montage of them spending a day together that would culminate in this moment.” However, time, budget and production priorities led to the montage being scrapped and the focus shifted to moving the piano up a flight of stairs. Newport-Berra recalls that after shooting in the apartment for a few weeks, the crew started feeling claustrophobic. “We were like, ‘What if we were looking at the apartment from this window or from that roof?’” The production team scouted until they found a building willing to let them shoot on the roof.

He continues, “We had this amazing zoom-out shot timed perfectly with a dolly shot inside. It starts with a dolly pulling out, which we lit and set up probably an hour or two before we were ready to shoot so we could get the perfect light. We let them rehearse and play around. There were two cameras rolling at the same time. The camera outside doesn’t see the camera inside because it’s just off the window, hidden behind it. As the dolly camera pulls out, the other camera zooms out, keeping itself out of the shot so we could time everything perfectly to the exact moment of sunset. It became this really magical moment.”

Overall, Newport-Berra appreciated working with Firstman, noting that they had shotlisted the entire film beforehand. “But we were keen to take the temperature on set and figure out what the moment needed. Sometimes it was very clear to us that we wanted a very intimate, simple handheld camera, where I could just be between them — the three of us in the room. Other times, the camera needed to be locked off and observing the pair from a distance. The nuance of everything very much came from being in the moment together in the room.”

As for capturing New York, Newport-Berra felt confident he could help portray an authentic version of the city. He started his career there, working on indie films, student projects and music videos. “I know the city very well. I lived there for over a decade and really fell in love with it.” He adds that he and Firstman wanted to make “Club Kid” feel like an iconic, nostalgic New York movie, but with a fresh perspective. Their familiarity with the city helped immensely, as did Newport-Berra’s connections with local crew members that dated back to his student days.

“It was a very small movie,” he recalls. “We were all carrying camera cases upstairs, cramming into the back of a van to get from one location to another, loading film on the sidewalk and politely asking random bystanders to move out of the way so we could steal a shot.” He concludes, “It was very much a New York indie movie and I love that. I’m proud we got to make that movie there.”

items.title: James Gunn Says ‘No One From Skydance’ Has Seen ‘Superman’ Sequel ‘Man of Tomorrow’ as Rumors Fly After His DC Studios Exit
items.description: James Gunn took to Threads to clarify a rumor about his exit from DC Studios: It had nothing to do with the upcoming “Superman” sequel “Man of Tomorrow” worrying executives at Warner Bros.’ new parent company, Skydance. Rumors have circulated on social media a
items.author: Zack Sharf
paragraphs: James Gunn took to Threads to clarify a rumor about his exit from DC Studios: It had nothing to do with the upcoming “Superman” sequel “Man of Tomorrow” worrying executives at Warner Bros.’ new parent company, Skydance. Rumors have circulated on social media alleging the film’s poor quality is one of the reasons Gunn got the boot after four years as co-CEO of DC Studios alongside Peter Safran. The rumors snowballed into claims Skydance would dump “Man of Tomorrow” onto streaming via HBO Max amid yet another DC Universe overhaul, this time under president and chief creative officer Jeremy Latcham.

“There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen ‘Man of Tomorrow’ and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made,” Gunn posted on his Threads account denying the rumors. “No one from Skydance has even seen the movie — the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false.”

Gunn and Safran’s exits from DC Studios were announced Nov. 9. Their departures came as a shock considering the duo was named as part of Skydance’s business leadership team when Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery closed in October. Gunn and Safran became the heads of DC Studios in 2022 and their four-year stint included film releases like “Superman,” “Supergirl” and “Clayface” and television series like “Creature Commandos” and “Lanterns,” among others.
Soon after the news broke, Gunn took to social media to express his feelings about the job and revealed that he had grown weary of the executive position.

“What only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least,” Gunn wrote. “I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.”

In his statement, Gunn also revealed that he’s “engaged on another DC project which I’m writing” in addition to post-production on “Man of Tomorrow.” The “Superman” sequel is currently on the release calendar for July 9, 2027.

items.title: Shane Gillis Was Surprised by ‘SNL’ Monologue Backlash and Says He Doesn’t ‘Have a Problem’ With How Women Dress at the Gym
items.description: Shane Gillis is reflecting on his “Saturday Night Live” monologue about women’s gym attire that drew controversy.
items.author: William Earl
paragraphs: Shane Gillis is reflecting on his “Saturday Night Live” monologue about women’s gym attire that drew controversy.

On the Oct. 10 episode this season, the comedian’s opening monologue included jokes about how women “dress like whores now” at the gym, which inspired a wave of criticism on social media. Gillis revealed on the Nov. 13 episode of the “Joe Rogan Experience” that he was surprised by the blowback.

“The funniest part was, I was going in going — they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great, but I don’t say anything bad,’” he said. “The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C minus of a monologue, but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for fucking 10 minutes. That’s it.’”
He also said that he thinks the reaction “obviously had a lot to do with the climate” and, with regard to the gym attire, “for the record, [I] don’t have a problem with it.”
Gillis also clarified that “Saturday Night Live” gave no feedback about the joke ahead of time.

“Not to defend ‘SNL,’ they don’t approve it. I mean, they could shut it down,” he said to Rogan. “They could, but you don’t write your set and give it to them. Unless you’re not a comedian. I’m sure non-comics, they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them.”
The original joke ignited criticism online and even a response from Inde Navarrette during her “SNL” monologue.

“I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” Gillis said in the monologue. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe it. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts? Those neon, they’re like artificial bait-colored. And the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combined at the butthole. And don’t look, you’re not allowed to look. For real, don’t look because they are filming. I’m in the background of like 10 TikToks right now.”
Watch Gillis talk about the controversy on Rogan’s show below.

items.title: Ben Stiller Gives Update on His New York Knicks Documentary: “The Pressure Is on”
items.description: Ben Stiller is sharing an update on his forthcoming New York Knicks documentary, and after the team’s historic championship earlier this year, he knows “the pressure is on.”
items.author: Lexi Carson
paragraphs: Ben Stiller is sharing an update on his forthcoming New York Knicks documentary, and after the team’s historic championship earlier this year, he knows “the pressure is on.”

While premiering his next film, Focker-in-Law, slated for a Thanksgiving release, on Wednesday night in New York, Stiller teased the documentary to The Hollywood Reporter, describing it as a multi-part project exploring the Knicks’ history.
“It’s going to be a multi-part documentary about the history of the Knicks, including this team. It’s about what they’ve meant to New York and hopefully capture the spirit of the team,” he said.

“It’s been fun to work on so far,” Stiller added, acknowledging the high expectations surrounding the project, especially after the Knicks won their first NBA championship since 1973 on June 13. The documentary was announced shortly afterward, with Stiller directing the project and following the team’s full arc from the ’90s to its record-breaking championship run this year.
“I feel like Knicks fans really love the Knicks, so the pressure is on to make something that lives up to what they want, but I hope it does,” Stiller said.
As for where the project currently stands, Stiller said it is “in the beginning stages since the playoffs,” adding, “but it’s not gonna be long. We’re full on it.”

Stiller, who was born and raised in New York City, has been a lifelong Knicks fan, dating back to his childhood in the early 1970s. He’s also a staple star to sit courtside at games, alongside other celebrity fans including Timothée Chalamet, Spike Lee, Tracy Morgan, Tina Fey and more.

When asked if any of those superfans, specifically Chalamet, would appear in the documentary, Stiller said, “Yeah, there definitely are Knicks fans, both known and not known Knicks fans, because I love the community, fans in New York, all over New York, such a huge part of what it means to love the Knicks. So that community is really strong.”
Speculation that Stiller is working on a documentary about the NBA team grew after he was spotted filming content during the Knicks’ 2026 Finals run.
Immediately after Game 5 of the 2026 NBA Finals, cameras caught up with Stiller, and the Severance executive producer said he was “as happy as I’ve ever felt.”

Stiller joked with THR that he would check the score of the Knicks’ Wednesday night game against the Cleveland Cavaliers “right after” finishing interviews at the Focker-in-Law premiere and “periodically” throughout the film’s screening following the red carpet. However, the Knicks lost 115-107. Following the loss, Stiller wrote on X, “What happened.”
The Knicks are set to face the Indiana Pacers on Friday night in Indianapolis.

items.title: Chris Harrison Says His Exit From ‘The Bachelor’ Was a “Blessing,” Not a Cancellation
items.description: Chris Harrison is back as host of a TV dating competition, but he won’t be handing out any roses.
items.author: Tony Maglio
paragraphs: Chris Harrison is back as host of a TV dating competition, but he won’t be handing out any roses.

Harrison, the former longtime host of The Bachelor (and its in-universe spinoffs), is launching his own spin on the genre with Chris Harrison’s The Vow from Lionsgate Alternative Television, which streams on Fox News Channel’s companion platform Fox Nation. You’ll remember Harrison from getting fired from The Bachelor for defending 2021 contestant Rachael Kirkconnell for attending an antebellum-themed fraternity formal three years before she appeared on the ABC series.

Five long years later, Harrison is bringing his own (second) bride with him. Lauren Zima, the former Entertainment Tonight host, and Harrison were married in 2023. Harrison and Zima created The Vow together and executive produce it.

“It feels really a little cathartic,” Harrison told The Hollywood Reporter of his Hollywood comeback vehicle, which has more than flicked at his old job in its marketing materials — earning Lionsgate and Fox a cease and desist from The Bachelor studio Warner Bros. Television.

Chris Harrison’s The Vow curates the dates between its hero and his prospects, setting up “real-world compatibility challenges,” according to its synopsis. It’s all pretty faith-based and longterm focused: “At a time when much of modern dating culture is driven by fleeting connections and social media attention, the series offers a different approach by placing the focus on meaningful relationships, commitment and building a life together.”
The six-episode Chris Harrison’s The Vow premieres its first two episodes today on Fox Nation; read more from our interview with Harrison below.
Five years later, how do you now feel about your very public split with The Bachelor?

I know this sounds weird because it was so tumultuous and it was a crazy time in my life, but I look back at it as a bit of a blessing. I was in a contract negotiation with them. I was talking to my wife: “Is it time to move on? What do I do?” And I don’t know if this lightning-bolt moment hadn’t happened, if I would have stepped away. Having that divorce and that breakup was a blessing. It allowed me to step away. However humbling all of that was, it allowed me time to hit the pause button and watch my kids graduate high school, fall in love, get married in my own life — tell my own love story for a minute — and then kind of get the fire burning again and get excited about creating my own show because The Bachelor wasn’t my baby.

Being able to create this with my wife and with the people I choose to do it with, and be there every step of the way to executive produce, host, sit there and go through the post-production process — it is a painstaking process to get something there, and it’s a great achievement. We’re very proud of it and very excited.
Do you believe your contract situation played more of a role in you being let go from The Bachelor than was initially reported?

Probably. But in any divorce, you only know your side, right? The rest is speculation. They have their story, and then somewhere in the middle is probably the truth. I’m guessing it had some impact on it all, but how much I have no idea. It definitely played in it for me, and gave me that chance to break away from that, and come back and be so refreshed and excited and involved from the ground up and create [a new show]. Again, it’s weird to call something like that a blessing, but when you’re humbled and you move forward and you come back bigger and better, feel the excitement in the air — timing is everything, and the timing now is so good.
Do you believe you were “canceled”?

I don’t. I know people say that because of the time, and that term really came on strong then. I don’t say that, and I don’t think that. In my opinion, it makes me seem like a victim, and I wasn’t. I had a messy public divorce with the people I worked for. It was a very humbling moment for me, and I think a little humility and getting knocked down is good in life. Look, as I tell my kids, life’s not a hockey stick — it’s a roller coaster ride. The ups and the downs. I’m glad I don’t define my life by being the host of a certain show. Again, I go back to my faith. I go back to my friends and family, and you carry on and come back bigger and stronger and hopefully smarter. If you don’t learn from something like that, God, you’ve done yourself a disservice. I do feel like a better host, a better producer, a better husband, a better friend because of all that.
Do you feel that the industry has typecast you into this host-of-reality-dating-competition role? Or is this genuinely what you want to be doing right now?

It is. I got to a very blessed place in my life, and it’s very rare you can get there in business. And that is being able to choose the project, and also choose who you would like to do that project with. Going back to The Bachelor, I was a hired host, so I didn’t get to choose who I was working for, with, etc. You go in, you do your job, and you are so happy to get the paycheck in this business. But along the way, I did Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? I hosted Miss America, The Walking Wallendas.

I did a bunch of other shows, and really, what I love is twofold: I love hosting and producing TV. I find it so invigorating, intriguing. I love telling stories, being a part of stories — but I also love love. I’ll admit, I’m a little bit of a hopeless romantic. I love rom-coms — those are my favorite movies — and I love diving into these people’s lives, kind of exposing them and telling their stories and hopefully helping them find love, as romantic and silly as that may sound. I love being a part of those stories. When you see it work, that’s the addiction. When you see it work, you’re just like, man, that lightning in a bottle, that love story that we’re all clamoring for, that we all enjoy. It’s worth it. It makes it all worth it.
Forgive me for not remembering his name, but how did you find this show’s “bachelor”? He’s frustratingly handsome and seems like a good dude too.
Right and he has a cool fucking name. It’s not fair.

He could be a spy. He could be a stunt man. He might be the next James Bond. We we like to say he’s if Tim Tebow and [Rob Gronkowski] had a baby, that’s what Jace looks like. He has the looks, and yes, he has the abs. He really was that diamond in the rough, and that’s what set the tone.

We had this amazing casting director, Lindsay Liles, who was a producer on The Bachelor and left to go do her own casting agency. I had this great relationship with her, but she thinks like a producer, and that was really important to understand— as the kids say, she understood the assignment. She really knocked it out of the park, and we took more time, more energy, probably more money on casting than anything. We really wanted to do our due diligence on every aspect of these people, and make sure that this is who we wanted to launch this show with. In our case that diamond in the rough was from Canby, Oregon, of all places, and he is a man of faith, a man of values, high morals. Not perfect — he’s a human being. And he’s a little bit older. He’s 30 years old. That was important to us as well. The frontal lobe is formed, and he knows what he wants.
Faith is a big part of the show. Jace and his bachelorettes, for lack of a better word, pray together on camera. Fox Nation’s audience should be into that. Tell me about your own faith.

My wife and I — faith very much plays a part in our lives. It’s a big part of our marriage. I think it’s the foundation. Definitely as a man, it’s my foundation. It’s something I always fall back on. But our faith wasn’t the impetus for the show, but what I do think is, it made Lauren and I good stewards of how to create this environment.

That was why we ended up partnering with [Fox Nation] because that is part of their brand. They have other faith-based shows. All of us thought it was important that this wasn’t a cocktail joke. It’s not. “Hey, look, we’re doing a show about faith and look how crazy and silly this can be!” No, I wanted the intention there, and it was important that we understand that world to create the environment so they can actually feel able to let go. Like they— you know, I guess pun intended, they had to put their faith in us to come on this show, talk about their faith, feel comfortable doing that. And I think we were trusted to create that world for them that they could let go and really try to find love and talk about it freely.
So the season is wrapped as we speak. Did any of the 11 participants sort of expose themselves as maybe not being there for the right reasons?

What I was hoping for as a producer was, if we did a show involved that involved people of faith, that if we brought 11 humans on, we’d have 11 different opinions, experiences, and I was hoping that we would get the conversations that we have. And this is one thing I’m really excited about. You are going to see and hear conversations and topics covered you’ve never heard on reality TV, and it is raw. It’s rare. You’re going to see people pray, and you will see people called into question about their faith.

Some people, like the people at Warner Bros., will call this a ripoff of The Bachelor, and I believe it’s a fair criticism. That said, pretty much every dating show since The Bachelor has been, to some degree, a ripoff of The Bachelor. You, more than most people, should get a pass on that. But you’ve removed a bunch of the tropes, like a formal elimination ceremony to end each episode, and Jace is not expected to propose in the finale…

We took all those hurdles and safeguards that honestly, you probably should have as a producer, because it’s smart. Like an elimination ceremony. “OK, it’s 10 o’clock. Kick two girls out, so I know I can end episode one with a break up.” We didn’t do that. We felt any contrived, produced moment is going to [feel like a contrived, produced moment].

Well episode one does kind of end with a break up, but I’ll concede that the elimination feels more authentic. Jace’s marching orders are to eliminate a potential mate when she stops seeming like a potential mate.

It’s what a gentleman should do. It’s what women should expect. If you’re going to break up, look her in the eye. Don’t shoot a text. Don’t go on your keyboard. Don’t just ghost somebody. Let’s raise the level, guys — come on!

But that intentionality is very important to us, but it’s scary because if you take your hand off the wheel, you don’t know what you’re going to get. But what we found was the unpredictability is the drama. You don’t know when those breakups are going to happen, and even as producers, Jace would be talking, and all of a sudden we’d be like, “Whoa, OK, he’s up right now. Here we go.” And it turned out to be great TV.

In the sizzle reel for the remainder of the season, it is revealed to (those of us who don’t watch The Bachelor) that one of the women was on The Bachelor. I’m guessing that was after your time, so did you know?

Yeah, yeah. Yeah. We talked about that in casting, and we had a long talk between all the executive producers and our casting agent. And again, it was very intentional. Why her faith in where she is in her journey and what she wants, and it felt like none of that was really given a fair shake [on The Bachelor], and she wasn’t really able to talk about that and show that. So we thought, “You know what? OK.” And we had a long talk with her, and we felt like that was a very intentional, good choice to add to the mix.
Was it a challenging decision to cast the woman who sells penile implants for a faith-based Fox Nation show?

It’s what she does for a living. I wanted to show what people of faith really look like in this world. This generation, these are women are unbelievably dynamic, incredibly diverse, and come from all walks of life. One is a penile implant salesman. So be it. That’s her job. She’s really — and I mean this sincerely — she’s passionate about it.
No spoilers, but are you happy with the arc of the season and the results, whatever they may be?

I am. I am very proud of the show. We are very proud of the show. We’re proud of what we created. On one side, because this business is so hard, and to get a show created, sold, and produced, and on air…it’s tough right now. And to put people to work and all those things. There’s that side of it that we’re really proud of. But then the product we created, the show, the idea we had — to watch that come to fruition really was a dream. The show’s not predicated on the fact that it’s going to work. It’s not guaranteed.
Chris Harrison’s The Vow streams weekly on Wednesdays on Fox Nation.

items.title: Shane Gillis Addresses ‘SNL’ Monologue Backlash, Says He Promised the Show There Would Be “No Controversy”

“The funniest part was, they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great, but I don’t say anything bad,'” Gillis continued. “The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C minus of a monologue, but I promise there’s no controversy. items.title: MAHERSHALA ALI - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: Revelations over breakfast with the Oscar-collecting actor
paragraphs: Revelations over breakfast with the Oscar-collecting actor

American actor Mahershala Ali received his first Oscar for his electrifying role in ‘Moonlight’. (Remember that crazy ceremony, when the coveted gold statuette for best film was mistakenly awarded to ‘La La Land’, only to revert to its righteous winner a few minutes later?) Just two years on, he scored another Academy Award, this time for his part in ‘Green Book’. What’s even more amazing is Mahershala never originally set out to act in the first place – he was an athlete and a poet. He’s even released a few original rap albums as Prince Ali. In his new film ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ he plays a sword-wielding father of three – a role written especially for him. Over a sandwich in Philadelphia, where he’s shooting for HBO, the actor contemplates his almost cinematic life story and how his world turned upside down on 31 December 1999. What exactly happened?
From Fantastic Man n° 43 – 2026
Photography by TYLER MITCHELL

It is 11.05am. Mahershala Ali’s face is alight with passion and his smooth baritone is cracking. It is a seasonably hot Friday in early July, and we are having breakfast at a quaint cafe nestled along the Schuylkill River, the 135-mile tributary that flows through the heart of Philadelphia. He has barely touched the turkey wrap he ordered. The performer is in the process of telling me what happened on the last New Year’s Eve before the millennium. It was a day that changed the trajectory of his life. As he remembers it, the morning didn’t begin like a typical one. Ali awoke with an urgent urge, a call to be somewhere. Like a tidal wave that builds up before unexpectedly rolling over a stretch of coastline, this moment had been amassing strength for a week. “A light went off,” Ali explains. “It felt weird to me at the time, but there was something that was resonating, and I felt… This felt new.” He trails off before returning to the feeling: “This, this, this is different.”

An hour earlier, the actor and I meet for the first time. He arrives in the restaurant through a side door, entering briskly and immediately greeting me with a firm, enthusiastic handshake. He is wearing a pair of sunglasses with orange-tinted lenses and a green cap which compliments his pastel-dyed chore jacket. The faint noise of conversation continues in the cafe as he settles into his chair. Before I can say anything, he asks, “Where are you from?” I tell him Chicago, although I now live in Manhattan, and Ali takes the opportunity to briefly expound on the benefits of West Coast living. He used to live in New York but left a decade ago, having relocated in 2016 to Los Angeles, where he lives with his wife and daughter in the leafy Mount Washington neighbourhood. “I do so much better outside of the city,” he says. “I think California gives you more opportunity for that.”

The 52-year-old actor was born in Oakland, California, in 1974. He was raised by a single mother, Willicia Goines, from whom he became estranged when he was 16. They have since reconciled. While he was growing up, sports played a pivotal role in his life. “I was always a good athlete,” says Ali, who eventually went to university on a scholarship to play Division I college basketball as a 6-foot-2 guard at Saint Mary’s College of California. The first sport he truly fell in love with, however, was bike racing. His uncle owned a track in Fremont, California. “I started when I was four,” he says, reaching into the pocket of his tan trousers to retrieve his phone. He scrolls through it and finds what he is looking for. He looks at the screen, smiles and then reaches across the table to hand me the phone. I see a scan of a grainy black-and-white news clipping. It shows Ali, his cousins and some friends huddled together victoriously after a bike race. “Between four and ten, we were in the ABA, the American Bicycle Association,” he says proudly. “I was a BMX racer, and I was also on the Schwinn competition team.”

During his childhood Ali would often travel back and forth between the Bay Area and New York City. In 1977, his father, Phillip Gilmore, moved to the latter city to pursue a career as a Broadway dancer. He performed with the Dance Theatre of Harlem, joined the cast of ‘Dream Girls’ and took on small roles in films like Spike Lee’s 1992 biopic, ‘Malcolm X’. Ali tells me his father got to New York by winning a national dance contest on the television programme ‘Soul Train’. “I remember it vividly. It’s clearly one of my earliest memories,” Ali says. “Let me find it!” Seconds later, we are back on his phone, watching an old clip of his father in the competition. Gilmore is lithe, with a perfectly coiffed Afro, and dressed in a brown low-cut tank top and a white pair of ballooning harem pants. It’s all very 1970s Black Arts Movement. Round after round, he dances marvellously with his partner, Linda Lewis, until they are announced as the winners of the $2,500 cash prize and a car. “I remember him coming back to my grandmother’s house, and we were all looking at the car outside,” says Ali. “I grew up kind of just knowing that really impractical things are possible.”

Ali’s father passed away in 1994 at the age of 38 after battling a long-term illness. “I was 20 when he died,” Ali says. “Before he passed away, we spent a summer watching movies on LaserDisc. ‘Reservoir Dogs’; ‘One False Move’ with Michael Beach and Billy Bob Thornton; Ethan Hawke and Winona Ryder in ‘Reality Bites’. Ben Stiller had directed that. And of course, he had taken me to see Spike’s movies in theatres, you know?” The way Ali describes it to me, it is as though his father was racing against time to introduce his son to the things that mattered most to him. “He’s essentially introducing me to indie films five minutes before he passes away,” Ali says.

Ali wasn’t acting at the time. What he had been doing was writing poetry, both as a way of processing his father’s death and to deal with insomnia. He would send his poems to Gilmore to read, and when they were together his father would gather his friends and encourage Ali to perform his pieces. “So I’d do ‘Cool Birth’ or one of my other poems, and I could see the reactions of his friends.” Encouraged by his father, who even got him a directory that listed literary agents, Ali would perform the poems as monologues at school, and eventually at the California Shakespeare Festival. Poetry has continued to be a constant in his life. His poems have helped to anchor him and helped him to find meaning and courage in moments of confusion. In 2024, he performed a reading of the young poet Mohammed al-Qudwa’s ‘Longing for Haifa’ to raise funds for the safe evacuation of the writer’s family from Gaza to Egypt. In a video published online, Ali wears a black dress shirt and a red and orange kufi. The first few lines ring out clearly under the weight of the rich seriousness of his voice. They contain within them the universally binding, yearning sorrow of colossal personal loss:
I comb the seashore with my eyes for the last time
Or even just an orange tree branch
Break through the sea’s barriers
I want my orange tree to bear fruit
For whatever lives in the sea to eat
Maybe it will save me from a shark’s teeth
I smile at the sea one last time
Or maybe the time before last
I watch for Noah’s miracle…

“It was really my poetry that transitioned me into acting,” says Ali. More than two decades into his career, he brings a subtle gravitas and a tender emotional power to each role. He often takes on parts where his skill lies in exhibiting the quiet authority found in the natural warmth of his gaze. He has showcased this in television roles as the suave political lobbyist Remy Danton in Netflix’s ‘House of Cards’ and the hot, thoughtful Sheikh Ali Malik on the second season of comedy-drama ‘Ramy’. He has brought the same intensity to characters in movies like 2017’s ‘Roxanne Roxanne’, about the life of the hip-hop pioneer Roxanne Shanté, in which he played Cross, the rapper’s controlling older boyfriend. Ali tells me the film was “not a fun thing to shoot, because I was abusing a young girl. And it just had a real profound effect on me, so much that I couldn’t sleep.”

Ali’s breakout film role came a year earlier, in 2016, when he played Juan, the Cuban-born drug dealer turned unlikely father figure in Barry Jenkins’s critically acclaimed ‘Moonlight’. He showcases a startling humanity as he shepherds Chiron, an abandoned gay Black boy, on an odyssey back to himself. They travel together through the contradictions of inner-city Miami poverty and the often perilous intersections of sexuality and race. That 2016 performance allowed Ali to pick up his first Oscar, for best supporting actor. The second came with 2018’s ‘Green Book’, an imperfect period film in which he played Dr. Don Shirley, a wealthy, world-class Black pianist, who hires a white driver (Viggo Mortensen) to escort him on a concert tour through the American South in 1962. Ali is the first Black actor to win multiple Academy Awards in the same category and the second (after Denzel Washington) to win more than one acting Oscar.

His latest film, ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’, is set to premiere at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. The genre-blending epic sees Ali in the lead as Latif, a sword-wielding devout Muslim samurai. In the opening scene, Latif, a hitman and an absent father, receives a call as he is finishing a job, informing him that his wife, Khadija (Shakirah DeMesier), has unexpectedly died. As the film unfolds he is confronted with his work, faith and fatherhood in ways both dire and hilarious. The plot is pushed forward by Latif’s quest to protect his three children, one a newborn girl who in the sudden absence of her mother rejects baby formula. Latif’s new mission is a desperate crosstown search for breast milk. Throughout the 111-minute film a bigger question is asked, tenderly and probingly, by his teenage daughter, Adia, who occasionally engages in activities that would definitely be considered haram: “Why did you leave me?” Latif: “So I could find my way back to you.”

I ask Ali, himself a practising Muslim, if the film feels personal. “The role of Latif is personal, but they are all the same,” he says of all the characters he has played over his long career. “I feel what I think is an extraordinarily healthy pressure. To me, acting honestly feels like life or death. I’m sure some firefighter, some military person or police officer could call bullshit on that. But what I’m saying is: for me, artistically, if you look at me and go, ‘I don’t believe you,’ that means I just died.” As he talks, he balls his hands into fists, revealing a silver ring with a giant green quartz inset.

He has developed this view from his experiences, and deeply felt frustrations, as one of very few prominent Black Muslim actors in Hollywood. “What Hollywood does is – especially with Black actors – they ask you to turn water into wine,” he explains. “And once you turn water into wine, instead of giving you a vineyard they just give you another glass of water.” He goes on: “Coming up, especially in television, you get written for in bits. So you learn that: this one-eighth of a page of a scene, this half a page of a scene. I have one response, which is to bring the heart, especially as a Black person, because they’re never gonna focus on your cerebral quality.”

It is odd that an actor of Ali’s calibre has not been given more leading roles in Hollywood. He certainly looks the part, and with multiple major awards, he clearly has the talent. This paradox is not unique to Ali. Black artists are asked to prove themselves time and again in a culture industry that is more concerned with not appearing racist than with addressing the structural inequalities that allow white actors to burn up significantly more screen time than anyone else. Black actors’ unique gifts are often only seen as a way to represent how progressive the industry can be. Ali has dealt with this reality by being patient, being comfortable saying no and waiting for the rare opportunity to display his talents in full. “Eventually, if you’re fortunate enough to end up with a ‘Your Mother’, where I’m getting scene after scene after scene after scene, where not only do I get to bring it but I have to bring it…” He expands: “I’m finally written for in a way where all those things that you learn to do, you have to bring every single moment, or you fail.” He laughs before exclaiming, “Do it or else!”

During the pandemic, when writer and director Bassam Tariq was penning the ‘Your Mother’ script, he wrote in “M” for Mahershala as the lead. He hadn’t met the actor yet but knew he would be perfect for the role. “He carries himself with this incredible dignity,” Tariq tells me over the phone. The film-maker studied Ali’s interviews and films as he developed Latif, who, in the Islamic tradition, is referred to as Al-Latif, “the most gentle,” one of the 99 names of Allah. “I think the thing of a prophetic character – the prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him – in our religion is we never portray him, but the idea is he is portrayed by all of us.”

Tariq first met the actor when he signed on to direct Ali in the now shelved remake of Marvel Studios’ ‘Blade’. The original movies starred Wesley Snipes as a vampire-hunting swordsman with a semi-iconic V-shaped, low-cut fade who is out to avenge his mother’s death. At the time of writing, the new venture seems to have died a slow death in continually stalled pre-production over the last seven years.

“When we started working on ‘Blade’, I was, like, ‘All right, this is the guy,’” Tariq says. “We connected at this really deep spiritual level. When I walked off of ‘Blade’, I reread the draft [of ‘Your Mother’], and the first thing I said was, ‘I have to call Mahershala.’” First, he rewrote parts of the film to include things he picked up on the set of ‘Blade’, like sword fighting, which Ali does to dazzling effect at the end of the film. “You have to be able to carry grief; you have to be a little manic. I mean, the dude is searching for breast milk in all the wrong places. Also, he is having a crisis of faith. He is someone who can be really violent but also loving. So there are all of these things you need to have in a person. And I think knowing what I knew about [Mahershala] and how he was with his family – I have seen the way he looks at his wife and how he talks about his daughter. You can’t act that.”

Ali is here in Philadelphia for pre-production of season two of the HBO crime drama ‘Task’, where he will play respected Drug Enforcement Administration agent Eddie Barnes. He tells me this city is where he began his own journey to find an enduring faith. The process began in the late 1990s, while he was in graduate school at New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts. As someone who had recently started acting, he was being broken down and built back up again. It made him question a lot of things about himself. “You’re being picked apart, and you’re constantly processing other people’s problems, because you’re learning how to take on character. But you’re also starting to really process and look at yourself.” He continues: “In the midst of all that, I was really trying to figure out why I believed what I believed.” He already had what he called “Mama faith”: “I just believed in God.” He had inherited this unquestioned belief as a child from his mother and grandmother, both ordained Baptist ministers. The actor’s full first name is Mahershalalhashbaz, the longest name in the Hebrew Bible. In early adulthood, he questioned everything he’d been taught. He began to read books such as Gary Zukav’s spiritual self-help guide ‘The Seat of the Soul’ and visited a Baháʼí centre in San Francisco and a non-denominational church in nearby Oakland.

On the evening of 24 December 1999, he began to have a personal breakthrough. He was in Philadelphia to hang out with a group of friends, including his future wife, Amatus Sami-Karim, a Muslim former classmate at Tisch, and her friend Questlove, the drummer and co-founder of hip-hop band The Roots. The group went to watch ‘Man on the Moon’, the Jim Carrey biopic of comedian Andy Kaufman. Afterwards, Ali felt an unexplainable need to visit a mosque for the first time and decided to join Sami-Karim and her mother, who were both visiting one that evening. “I went in, and there was this brother named Maneer that took care of me,” he recalls. “I heard the sermon,” he says, laughing softly to himself at the memory. “We go to make the prayer, and they start in Arabic, and I just start crying. I had cried in church, but this feels different.”

And so we arrive at 31 December 1999. Ali was back in New York. His friends were due to arrive from the Bay Area to visit him for the New Year’s weekend. But he awoke that morning in his apartment in the South Slope section of Brooklyn with an unusual thought: “I gotta go to the mosque. It’s Friday.” He didn’t know where a mosque was in New York, but he knew that the bodega on the corner, where he often bought potato chips and toilet paper, was operated by some Muslim men.
“I go to the corner store. I was, like, ‘Hey, peace, brother. Where’s the…mosque?’”
“The mosque?” the man replied.
“Yeah, where’s the mosque?” Ali repeated.
“Well…Omar is going,” the man said, pointing to another man sitting reading a newspaper in the corner of the store.

Ali turned to Omar and asked if he could accompany him. “Yeah, but we have to go soon,” Omar said. Ali borrowed his roommate’s car, and Omar guided him to a mosque on Atlantic Avenue in downtown Brooklyn. It was packed with worshippers there to celebrate the new millennium. In the throng, Omar and Ali got separated, and Ali ended up in the back by a radiator at the start of the opening prayer, Surah al-Fatihah.
Across from me at the table, Ali looks down at the turkey wrap he has barely touched and starts to recite the prayer in Arabic under his breath:
بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ
إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ
اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا الضَّالِّين
At the time, he didn’t understand a word, but the sensation of hearing the prayer made sense. After it ended, Ali sat there, and a stranger came up to him. The guy was around his age, 25.
Guy — “Do you want to be?”

The guy went up to the imam and whispered something to him. The imam stopped everyone and called out, “Allah akbar.” He brought Ali to the front and asked if he wanted to be Muslim, and Ali said he did. He instructed the actor to get on his knees and repeat the Shahada, the Islamic declaration of faith, after him in Arabic. “Once I said that, he said, ‘You’re Muslim now.’” Ali laughs, still struck by the unexpected ease and spontaneity of it all. Eventually, he and Omar found one another again at the end of the service. “He was crying his eyes out,” says Ali.

It is 11.14am. I look over at Ali. He has removed his sunglasses. Underneath the hat he is wearing, I find his eyes. A small tide of water has gathered around his dark brown irises, allowing the hints of amber in his eyes to glisten, as if they are small subdued suns burning with the morning’s light.

Photographic assistance by Zack Forsyth and Brandyn Liu. Styling assistance by Fred Kim. Hair by Roddi Walters at Bryant Artists. Make-up by Nolan Eakin. Tailoring by Tae Yoshida. Set design by Nicole Roosien. Production by Brachfeld.

items.title: An N.B.A. Player Got Hooked on Sports Betting. Soon, He Became the Bet
items.description: When Jontay Porter was ten, his father woke him up most mornings before dawn. He and his siblings piled into the family’s Sprinter van and drove to an empty field house off the highway. Then, while their friends slept, they ran basketball drills with their fat
items.author: Nick Berardini
paragraphs: When Jontay Porter was ten, his father woke him up most mornings before dawn. He and his siblings piled into the family’s Sprinter van and drove to an empty field house off the highway. Then, while their friends slept, they ran basketball drills with their father. “All I remember is it still being pitch-black outside, and the two dreaded double doors on the side of the building that would always be left open for us,” Jontay told me recently. In the bleary moments just before one of his siblings tugged the field-house doors open, Jontay always secretly wished that they’d be locked. And, one morning, they were. Jontay smiled as he climbed back into the van and drifted off to sleep. But his brother Michael, Jr., who was seventeen months older, was furious. “Michael was the opposite,” Jontay said. “He wanted to go.”

Jontay grew up in Columbia, Missouri, the fourth of eight children. His father, Michael, Sr., worked in Christian ministry, and his mother, Lisa, homeschooled the children. Both had played college basketball—Lisa, as a high-school senior, had averaged a nearly impossible fifty-eight points per game—and they saw the sport as their children’s ticket to college. All eight of the kids eventually got basketball scholarships. By the time Jontay was sixteen, he was six feet ten. In most families, as a five-star high-school recruit, Jontay would have been the main attraction. But Michael was Mozart. In 2010, their father got a job on the coaching staff for the women’s team at the University of Missouri. The men’s coach spotted Michael shooting alone in the arena one night and offered him a full scholarship; he was still in seventh grade. When he accepted it, as a high-school senior, he was the top recruit in the country. His highlight reels had racked up millions of views on YouTube. N.B.A. scouts believed that he could be the next Kevin Durant. “He’s a game-changer,” a league executive told the New York Post.

Big state schools turn their best athletes into local celebrities, but the hype that followed Michael to Missouri’s campus on his recruiting visits was closer to Beatlemania. Fans asked for autographs and took selfies. Jontay, who came along, was seduced by the hysteria. “Frat houses are putting up posters, and he’s literally treated like a king,” he recalled. “I wanted to be a part of that circus.” He skipped his senior year of high school to join the team, too. The brothers were best friends. Still, it was sometimes hard to be one of the top players in the country but just the second best in his family. “He got all the attention,” Jontay said. “I was just kind of his biggest fan.”

For a time that first season, Michael was sidelined with a back injury, giving Jontay a turn in the spotlight. “He’s the best player I’ve ever been around,” Chris Hollender, then an assistant coach at Mizzou, told me. “I’ve always said I thought he was a more complete player than Mike.” At eighteen, Jontay led his team to the N.C.A.A. tournament. “For me to finally get a taste of stardom?” Jontay said. “I was the man. I controlled the narrative.”

Michael went to the N.B.A. draft that summer. Jontay planned to enter the following year. Then, during the final scrimmage before his sophomore season, he pushed off his right leg to explode toward the rim. “I felt, like, every crack in that moment, and just crumpled to the ground,” he said. He had torn the major ligaments in his knee. His teammates lifted him off the ground and laid him on a table in the training room. “He was beside himself,” Hollender said. “Couldn’t catch his breath, he was crying so hard.” It wasn’t from the pain; Jontay knew what his injury meant for the team’s chances that season. “The only thing he said to me was ‘I’m so sorry,’ ” Hollender said. “It was gut-wrenching.”

In 2019, while Jontay was in rehab for his knee, he injured it again. “Everybody’s telling me, ‘You’re going to be O.K.,’ ” he said. “I knew it wasn’t true.” By then, Michael was a rookie with the Denver Nuggets. (He went on to win a championship with the team, in 2023.) But Jontay, watching the N.B.A. draft in his parents’ basement, saw sixty picks go by without a team calling his name. Eventually, the Memphis Grizzlies took a chance and signed him to a contract as a free agent. He loved the N.B.A.—luxury travel, assistants to run his errands, last-minute reservations at Michelin-starred restaurants—but he felt that he was a tourist there. He had to take painkillers just to play, and after games he had to stick needles into his knees to drain fluid, in order to keep them from swelling. After just two seasons, he was cut from the roster.

In September, 2021, Jontay was in Memphis, living like any other twenty-one-year-old kid—except for the money. He’d made two million dollars from his N.B.A. salary, and had received an insurance settlement for another $2.7 million (the difference between his projected N.B.A. earnings before his injury and his actual deal). One Sunday, he invited some friends over to watch football. Sports betting had recently been legalized in several states, and apps like FanDuel and DraftKings, which previously hosted fantasy-sports contests, were suddenly the biggest sportsbooks in America. Jontay had always avoided them; it seemed improper for an N.B.A. player to bet even on other sports. But now he was out of the league, and had started dabbling in sports gambling. He opened up FanDuel and placed a hundred-and-twenty-five-thousand-dollar bet that the Kansas City Chiefs would beat the Baltimore Ravens. He put another ten thousand dollars on a parlay—a riskier bet that strings together multiple outcomes to increase the payout—wagering that the Chiefs would win, that their running back would rush more than his expected yards, and that the Ravens’ quarterback, Lamar Jackson, would run for a touchdown himself.

In the fourth quarter, the Chiefs were up eleven points, and Jackson raced along the right edge and into the end zone, clinching the last leg of the parlay. If the Chiefs held on to their lead, Jontay would win hundreds of thousands of dollars. His friends recorded a video of him jumping off his couch, hands in the air, shrieking, “Let’s go! Let’s go!”

But, in the final minutes of the game, the Ravens scored to take the lead. The Chiefs then fumbled while setting up what would have been a game-winning field goal. Ravens 36, Chiefs 35. Jontay slumped into his bed. “Literally, like, the party was over,” he said. That night, he stared at the ceiling, unable to sleep. How could he have been reckless enough to lose six figures on a football game? Then again, he had come so close to winning. In basketball, his body had betrayed him. But in sports betting all he needed was his brain. “That moment where I tore my knee is where everything that is on the news right now kind of started from,” he told me. “That point where I no longer had control.”

In 2015, amid a familiar flood of Bud Light and Allstate commercials, football fans were inundated with cheap-looking testimonials—men in jerseys holding oversized checks and spraying champagne. Some had taglines like “More sports, more winners, more millionaires.” The ads were for FanDuel and DraftKings, which had recently launched as fantasy-sports apps. That year, they spent a combined two hundred million dollars on TV advertising; in September, they ran a national spot every ninety seconds. The C.E.O. of DraftKings, Jason Robins, bragged that his business had signed up two hundred thousand new players in a single day.

The companies were taking advantage of a legal loophole. In 1992, sports betting had been made illegal almost everywhere in the country except Nevada, through the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act. But fantasy sports had been a staple of American fandom going back to the nineteen-eighties—a social activity that the comedian Joey Mulinaro once likened to a “book club for regular guys.” Traditional fantasy sports were slow and methodical. Friends and colleagues got together, forked over twenty dollars or so, and drafted an imaginary team of real players. Then they pored over newspapers and tallied up their players’ stats with pencil and paper. The person with the best record at the end of the season took home the pot. Eventually, leagues moved online so that computers could do the math, but the scrappy ethos remained. In 2006, lawmakers banned online gambling, but they exempted fantasy pools. They didn’t want the F.B.I. kicking down the doors of suburban dads on N.F.L. Sunday.

Nigel Eccles, a sandy-haired former McKinsey consultant, grew up on a dairy farm in Northern Ireland and knew nothing about American sports. But he saw that there was an opportunity to monetize the endless optimism of dudes who think they know ball. Eccles founded FanDuel out of his home in Edinburgh, in 2009, and began offering weekly, or sometimes daily, fantasy competitions. Pay an entry fee, draft a football team to compete against scores of strangers on the internet. If your team is good, you win some money; if it’s terrible, you can try again the next day. The action never stopped. “People love fantasy, and the idea that you could take something they love and make it faster, more exciting, give it real money, and they could play it on their phone was just, like, Yes, yes, definitely yes,” Eccles has said. (He left the company in 2017.) DraftKings launched soon after. In 2011, FanDuel had one U.S.-based salesperson, who worked out of a home office. Four years later, it had a forty-thousand-square-foot headquarters in the Flatiron district, with seats from the original Yankee Stadium. It also had a billion-dollar valuation.

The ad blitz brought in millions of new players, but it also drew scrutiny. To observers, the apps looked a lot like illegal sportsbooks. They collected entry fees that were essentially bets on a player’s performance, and kept a cut of around ten per cent. ESPN reported that FanDuel pitched investors on targeting players with a “higher preponderance to gambling.” In 2015, Jim Leach, a former congressman from Iowa who had co-sponsored the ban with the fantasy-sports carve-out, said he’d had no idea that it would “morph into today’s cauldron of daily betting.” By 2016, states were sending cease-and-desist letters to FanDuel and DraftKings, and both were facing bankruptcy.

That’s when they caught a lucky break. A couple of years before, New Jersey, hoping to revitalize Atlantic City, had attempted to legalize sports betting, eventually arguing in a lawsuit that the national ban violated states’ rights. In 2018, the Supreme Court struck down the ban, permitting states to decide for themselves. Jeremy Kudon, a lobbyist working for FanDuel and DraftKings, then started in on a plan called Project Aftermath. (“I’d just seen the N.W.A. movie, and that’s what Dre names his company after Death Row,” he said, laughing.) He went state to state, leaning into the similarities between sports betting and fantasy competitions. “I’d meet with legislators who were, like, ‘Didn’t we pass this already?’ ” he said.

Kudon had a powerful new ally. In the early nineties, major professional-league commissioners had testified in support of the sports-betting ban. “We should not gamble with our children’s heroes,” Paul Tagliabue, the N.F.L. commissioner at the time, said. The leagues even sued New Jersey to defend the ban. But by 2015 they had also cashed in on fantasy-sports deals. The N.B.A. became a direct investor in FanDuel, and M.L.B. in DraftKings. Twenty-eight of thirty-two N.F.L. teams formed partnerships with at least one of the companies. FanDuel, wooing the leagues, cited research showing that its customers watched forty per cent more sports after becoming members. The year after the Supreme Court ruling, the leagues were prepared to capitalize on the legalization of sports betting; the N.B.A. even advocated for it. “The data is clear,” Adam Silver, the N.B.A. commissioner, said at the time. “If someone has a bet on a game, even a small bet, they’re much more likely to engage in that match.”

Silver became the public face of the leagues’ flip-flop. The day after the N.B.A. closed on its deal with FanDuel, in 2014, Silver wrote an Op-Ed in the Times calling for sports betting to be legalized nationwide. He argued that Americans were already betting huge sums in unregulated markets. “Some estimate that nearly four hundred billion dollars is illegally wagered on sports each year,” he wrote. This figure was later debunked, but the idea allowed the leagues to appeal to the same sentimentality that they’d once used to argue against gambling—the purity of the games was at stake. Kudon began lobbying lawmakers with famous athletes by his side. “Everybody has a pennant for their favorite baseball team,” he said. “Nobody has a pennant for their favorite casino.” The effect was obvious. “We brought Joe Torre to the New York State Legislature,” he said, referring to the former manager of the Yankees. “And I watched grown men cry. I mean, people were weeping.”

Traditional casino giants like MGM and Caesars didn’t see what was coming. Sports gambling is typically a small slice of the betting pie relative to roulette and slots. The big casinos “were kind of almost patting us on the head: ‘What are you guys doing?’ ” Kudon joked. The casinos started building apps, but FanDuel and DraftKings were already on everyone’s phone. MGM and Caesars were like shops at the mall; FanDuel was Amazon.

By the end of 2021, thirty states and Washington, D.C., had legalized sports betting, many crafting legislation with substantial input from industry lobbyists. The companies launched another ad blitz. A study by McKinsey found that just five per cent of fantasy-baseball players were responsible for seventy per cent of the businesses’ profits. In a pitch to investors, according to ESPN, FanDuel noted internal data showing that twenty per cent of its customers would describe themselves as “a bit of an addict.” The companies spent a fortune on promotions, but it was nothing compared with the “customer lifetime value” of the guy who stuck around, day after day, to try his luck.

Strangers have always stared at Jontay Porter because of his height. Recently, I visited him at his brother’s house in Columbia, where he dipped under doorframes and moved through the living room like a parent navigating a child’s play fort. “There’s times where I wish I just lived a normal life,” he said. His size makes it difficult to find clothes that fit, or to squeeze into a commercial-airline seat. Still, he told me that he never once thought about buying a first-class ticket to get extra legroom. He saw himself as a frugal person.

Jontay had been fixated on money since childhood. In seventh grade, he started a side hustle fixing iPhone screens. At fifteen, he got hold of his mom’s driver’s license to create a Coinbase account, and bought bitcoin before most people had any idea what it was. He watched the price soar, and bought his first car with the proceeds. “I felt like, I’m better than these hedge-fund guys,” he said.

After his knee injury, he signed up for a Robinhood account and began day-trading stocks. In the N.B.A., ungodly money was the norm. “You’re just used to guys that are spending three thousand dollars on a bottle of wine at dinner,” he said. Jontay began to enjoy a reputation in the league as a market guru. He went “diamond hands” on meme stocks like Big 5 Sporting Goods and GameStop. This fuelled his belief that he didn’t need basketball to make what he called “N.B.A. F-U money.” (He rarely curses.) Soon, he and a partner were selling stock tips to subscribers on Discord through a company that he started called the Financial Cloud. “We couldn’t technically give financial advice, because we’re not licensed,” Jontay said. “We had automated algorithms that would spit out alerts of stocks to go buy.”

Robinhood’s interface was gamified: digital confetti exploded on the screen after customers placed a trade. “It looks like a casino,” Jontay said. “I’m not a scientist, you know. But that type of thing that gambling fed? Robinhood did the same thing.” He started playing a little blackjack on offshore-casino sites such as Stake, later made famous by the rapper Drake, who regularly streams six-figure bets. Jontay signed up for FanDuel two months shy of his twenty-first birthday. (His account couldn’t actually place bets until he turned twenty-one.)

For Jontay, there was truth to Paul Newman’s iconic line from “The Color of Money”—that money won is twice as sweet as money earned. He made a hundred thousand dollars on an unlikely ten-leg college-baseball parlay. But there were warning signs. He told me about his first big bet, on the Chiefs, yet he had memory-holed the fact that, the same weekend, he’d made a hundred and forty-three other bets for more than a million dollars. When I reviewed his transaction history and texted him about them, he replied, “Omg!!!! No way.”

Jontay’s family gave him the benefit of the doubt. He was bashful, but his brother Michael seemed to enjoy stirring up controversy. Michael had suggested that the COVID vaccine was a means of population control, and once warned that kids who attend public school might one day identify as “a cat.” He recently said that, when he’s dating women, he will “throw on some Andrew Tate and see how they react.” These takes, some offered on his own podcast, “Curious Mike,” have led fans to give him the nickname MAGA Porter, Jr. (More tragically, Jontay’s younger brother Coban, in 2024, pleaded guilty to vehicular manslaughter for driving drunk and causing a crash that killed a young mother. Two weeks after his sentencing, another brother, Jevon, got a D.U.I.) Jontay, by contrast, had never so much as stayed out past curfew.

Around the time Jontay started gambling, he began a long-distance relationship with a woman from Seattle named Kelli Kingma. She hadn’t initially been interested in him, because he played in the N.B.A. “I wanted a normal life,” she told me. But, she added, “I fell for how kind and humble and gentle he was. He seemed so innocent.” In 2021, he decided to sell his house. Kelli hoped to use the money to start a nest egg. What she didn’t know was that Jontay had taken out a five-hundred-thousand-dollar loan against the house, and then lost it all gambling. When he realized that she was sure to learn his secret, he panicked. “I’m instantly, like, I gotta make that five hundred thousand back real quick,” he said. While driving his Tesla from Memphis to his parents’ house, in Missouri, he put the car on Autopilot and spent the whole six-hour trip playing blackjack on his phone. By the end of the drive, he had lost another two hundred thousand dollars.

Later that month, Jontay holed up at his brother’s penthouse in Denver and opened FanDuel. He had discovered that his favorite sport to bet on wasn’t football; it was table tennis. It can take weeks to make money from a stock trade. But “a Ping-Pong match, it takes fifteen minutes,” he told me. FanDuel let players “live bet” a match while it was happening. Starting around midnight, he began repeatedly betting hundreds of thousands of dollars on Russian table tennis. “It’s exhilarating because, in your mind, your whole life rides on how good a serve this Ping-Pong guy has,” Jontay said. “It drives you insane, quite literally. Eyes bloodshot. Staring at the screen. I think you’re addicted to the thrill of the in-between, when you don’t know if it’s going to win or lose.” He bet for nearly three days straight, and won more than a million dollars.

Jontay called Kelli ecstatic. He told her that he’d earned the money trading futures. “I was super proud,” he said. “But she was equally, if not more, hurt.” Kelli was a financial adviser, and the story didn’t add up: what edge could her basketball-player boyfriend possibly have in commodities trading? She pressed him for details, but, ultimately, she backed down. “When you’re close to people, your own perspective makes you cling to things you want to be true,” she said. “I just wanted to get married. And I trusted that it was all O.K.”

Frank Cardenas started a job as a V.I.P. account manager at FanDuel a few months before Jontay began betting. At forty-two, Cardenas is a natural sportsbook host—classically good-looking yet weathered, like an aging frat guy. He had been working in casinos since he was sixteen, when he handled greyhounds at a dog track in Iowa. At FanDuel, part of his job was to scout big bettors. Poring over spreadsheets of fresh betting data, he quickly spotted Jontay. “I looked at his wagering history and I was, like, Damn,” he said. “I know that a guy making this many bets, betting every single game in the world right now, he doesn’t have some edge. He’s just a hard-core gambler.”

Online sportsbooks like FanDuel and DraftKings offer V.I.P. programs modelled on the perks that Vegas casinos provide for high rollers. DraftKings V.I.P.s can win the kinds of prizes one might expect (golf clubs, a Peloton) but also more exotic ones (a thirty-thousand-dollar crystal decanter of rare Cognac, a trip to the Pyramids of Giza). Cardenas regularly hosted clients in box suites for sporting events. He bought them steak dinners and took them to swank night clubs, where bottle-service girls in bikini tops lit sparklers and served alcohol under a banner that read “We bet on FanDuel only!” He took them to parties with Chris Rock, and to a track where they test-drove Porsches. The purpose of it all was to keep them betting.

The irony was that, to be a V.I.P., you had to be a loser. Unlike Vegas casinos, where hosts typically confirm the assets of their mega-rich whales, online sportsbooks don’t typically do so. Some of Cardenas’s clients were wealthy. But a V.I.P. could also be a “Taco Bell manager” who “was betting five hundred dollars a week, and then it goes up to two thousand,” he said. Bettors who show a propensity for winning often face restrictions on the apps, or are sometimes even banned. Isaac Rose-Berman, a professional tennis “sharp” and a gambling researcher, told me that, when he tried to place a bet on FanDuel predicting the winner of a tournament last summer, the app gave him a maximum wager of a hundred and ninety dollars. His friend, a V.I.P., could make the same bet for seventy-six thousand. “These are companies that want to make the most amount of money,” he said. “That’s their prerogative.”

Some pros will make dumb bets just to get V.I.P. status, so that they can unlock higher betting limits. It’s also now a common (though prohibited) practice to pay existing V.I.P.s for access to their accounts. I talked to two of these “straw bettors”—people who loved sports and jumped at the chance to let someone else bet for them as long as they could use the box seats. They expected a raucous atmosphere at the games they attended, with V.I.P.s living like kings. But both found quiet rooms of young men glued to their phones, placing bets. “Every other person in this box must be a gambling addict,” one told me. “It was profoundly joyless.” The other told me that, once his pro started winning, he never heard from his V.I.P. host again.

The real V.I.P.s, Cardenas said, are the people who “just can’t stay away.” I spoke with a former client of his whom I’ll call Chris. He told me that he had bet more than a billion dollars in two decades of relentless gambling, and that he’d tried “every modality of treatment” to quit. “My life’s been an absolute disaster for twenty-one years,” he said. “I’m getting evicted. I have a one-year-old daughter.” But nothing has worked. “I’m a zombie. Sex is whatever. Food is whatever. Everything is so mundane—unless I get a hundred thousand on a parlay.”

Jontay’s habits would have raised a red flag with any mental-health professional. One week, Cardenas told me, Jontay wagered more money than anyone else on FanDuel. Harry Levant, a counsellor and gambling-recovery coach who is one of the country’s leading experts on gambling addiction, and a recovering addict himself, told me, “Here’s a sentence that has never in the history of mankind been uttered. You ready? ‘I know what I want to do with my money for enjoyment purposes today. I’m going to go bet on Ping-Pong from the Czech Republic.’ ”

Cardenas wasn’t directly compensated for his clients’ losses, but, per a job posting, V.I.P. hosts were expected to use their clients to “drive revenue.” “These guys make all our money for us,” Cardenas said. When he first welcomed Jontay to the V.I.P. program, he sent him a bonus of ten thousand dollars to gamble with. For Jontay, it was a rush. He was used to offshore-casino apps in which he had to “beg for a bonus after losing” so that he could keep playing. When Jontay asked for another ten thousand the next night, Cardenas gave it to him. The following day, Cardenas got a call from a supervisor. “I got my ass chewed out,” Cardenas said. “ ‘Don’t you give him another dollar without our say-so!’ ” Cardenas was in trouble not only because he’d exceeded his discretionary-bonus limit but also because he’d given out the extra bonus while Jontay was winning. “Yeah, he might be up off ‘Monday Night Football,’ ” Cardenas said. “But we’re gonna get the money back.” The next day, Jontay lost six hundred thousand dollars. Cardenas’s bosses quit scolding him. Then the company gave Jontay another thirty-five thousand dollars in credit.

FanDuel didn’t ask Jontay for proof of his income. All he needed was his name. “It’s right away known that he’s a basketball player,” Cardenas said. “And it doesn’t take much of a deeper dive to find out he’s M.P.J.’s brother.” Michael had recently signed a contract extension with the Nuggets worth more than two hundred million dollars. “There was certainly a sentiment at some point, like, Well, what’s the big deal if M.P.J. has to break him off a million?” Cardenas said. Early on, the accounts team noticed that Jontay had made more than thirty million dollars’ worth of bets during his first two weeks on FanDuel, and when Jontay didn’t respond to an e-mail asking whether he was “comfortable” with his “level of spending,” his account was briefly suspended. Cardenas berated the employees, pointing out how much money Jontay’s brother had. Cardenas walked Jontay through replying, and FanDuel reactivated the account.

In fact, Cardenas said, the company had evidence to suggest that Jontay couldn’t afford his bets. Deposits from PayPal into Jontay’s FanDuel account were instant, but PayPal took a couple of days to actually withdraw the funds from a bank account. About a month after Jontay began betting on FanDuel, according to Cardenas, PayPal notified the company that Jontay owed half a million dollars in overdrawn deposits, and asked for help retrieving the funds. FanDuel decided to suspend Jontay’s account until receiving proof that he’d paid PayPal back. Cardenas said that the company could have used the incident to investigate how many V.I.P. players were betting with overdrawn deposits, though he speculated that the company didn’t want to know the answer. “A lot of these states don’t allow you to bet on credit,” he said. “But with PayPal you essentially can.”

A former FanDuel V.I.P.-program executive I spoke to defended the company’s actions, saying, of Jontay, “At no point when he was on FanDuel was he in such crazy debt.” When I suggested that FanDuel would have no way to know this without verifying Jontay’s finances, the executive agreed that there should be mandatory income checks and other safeguards, particularly for V.I.P. players. “It was never supposed to be twenty-four hours a day,” he said.

As one of the top V.I.P.s at FanDuel, Jontay was offered all kinds of perks: a new iPhone, courtside seats at N.B.A. games, tickets to the Super Bowl. Jontay and Cardenas became friends. They texted almost every day. Jontay called him the “goat of bonuses.” He told me that, while he was hiding his gambling from everyone else, it felt good to have someone who shared his secret. “Frank became why I stayed,” he said.

The anthropologist Natasha Dow Schüll spent fifteen years studying how casinos developed electronic gambling machines such as slots and video poker. In her book “Addiction by Design,” from 2012, she wrote that executives said the machines were engineered to increase “time on device” by entrancing players into a kind of dissociative state that came to be known as “the zone.” The companies sped games up by increasing the lines in slots or the playable hands in blackjack and poker. They removed “frictions” like pulling levers or depositing coins. The machines flashed with bright lights and played rhythmic sounds. The zone was so hypnotic that some gamblers soiled themselves rather than leave their machines to go to the bathroom. A compulsive gambler named Mollie told Schüll, “The thing people never understand is that I’m not playing to win” but, rather, “to keep playing—to stay in that machine zone where nothing else matters.” One industry consultant admitted that the goal was to keep players so enchanted that they stopped only because they ran out of money: to “play to extinction.”

Traditional sports betting didn’t have much in common with machine gambling. The hypnosis of the zone shared characteristics with the Skinner-box effect. Beginning in the nineteen-thirties, the behavioral scientist B. F. Skinner discovered that, when pigeons were given a lever that dispensed food pellets at random, as opposed to in a predictable pattern, they began to unceasingly peck at it. Unlike slot machines, sports bets were not random. Games were narrative contests. There was a limited number of bets that a player could make, and matches took hours to resolve.
But FanDuel and DraftKings found ways to increase the speed and the volume of sports betting. They offered bets on everything from soccer to jai alai,

items.title: How an Unlikely Charles de Gaulle Bio-Pic Conquered France
items.description: In the summer of 1942, a cash-strapped William Faulkner signed on to work at Warner Bros. as a screenwriter, earning three hundred dollars a week. His first task was to whip up a biographical treatment of General Charles de Gaulle, leading the Free French gove
items.author: Lauren Collins
paragraphs: In the summer of 1942, a cash-strapped William Faulkner signed on to work at Warner Bros. as a screenwriter, earning three hundred dollars a week. His first task was to whip up a biographical treatment of General Charles de Gaulle, leading the Free French government from exile in London. Provisionally titled “The De Gaulle Story,” the project was intended as hagiography—explicitly so, as President Franklin Roosevelt had proposed the idea to Jack Warner, hoping to boost de Gaulle’s credibility with the American public.
