Faulkner gave the gig his best shot, producing some twelve hundred pages and entertaining fussy notes from French consultants. (A memo titled “Observations on Inexact Details” cautioned, “In a cafe in France one does not play dominos but cards or billiard.”) Ultimately, Faulkner found his protagonist so hard to pin down that he purged the bio from the bio-pic, instructing a colleague, “Let’s dispense with General de Gaulle as a living character in the story.” The script was soon relegated to oblivion.

Churchills and Roosevelts—not to mention Hitlers—abound in cinema, but, even in France, bringing de Gaulle to the big screen has historically been a fraught enterprise. As the British historian Julian Jackson has written, postwar filmmakers strove to emphasize the collective nature of resistance rather than focussing on a single great man; yet, when de Gaulle returned to power in 1958, becoming President after more than a decade’s retirement from politics, it was with such command that, as Jackson puts it, “to dare to ask an actor to portray de Gaulle himself would have been an act of lèse-majesté.” (The director Réné Clément solved the problem by using archival footage whenever the General’s presence was required.) Pierre Schoendoerffer and Bertrand Tavernier both tried to make de Gaulle films and failed, the latter surely unhelped by his producer’s insistence that the lead character be played by Gérard Depardieu. Then there was the challenge of de Gaulle’s distinctive physiognomy. Such were the sensitivities surrounding him and his myth that a single actor—the towering, schnozzy, serviceably chinless Adrien Cayla-Legrand—maintained an effective monopoly on the role for decades. It wasn’t until 2020 that the first full-scale feature film devoted to the General, Gabriel Le Bomin’s “De Gaulle,” premièred in French theatres. It closed just ten days later, with COVID-19 advancing like the Panzerjäger-Abteilung 187.

This is all to say that Antonin Baudry knew what he was getting into when he signed on to co-write and direct the most ambitious, improbable de Gaulle movie yet: “La Bataille de Gaulle”—a two-part, five-plus-hour epic, based on Julian Jackson’s nine-hundred-page biography “A Certain Idea of France.” (The book's title alludes to the opening lines of de Gaulle’s own memoirs: “All my life, I have had a certain idea of France.”) The film captivated France this summer, and the first part opened last week in the U.S. Its timing has certainly been fortuitous, with France facing a Presidential election that may put the far right in power for the first time since the Vichy regime. But when we met recently, at a café in the Luxembourg Gardens, Baudry told me he believes that the film has resonated largely because of its human element. He looked chicly rumpled in cream trousers, a button-down, and white leather high-tops decorated with red lightning bolts. He said, of the filmmakers who preceded him, “I understood the malediction—none of them had dared and managed to crack the character.”

Baudry, who is fifty-one, began his career far from the moving image, studying math before earning degrees in engineering and literature from France’s arch-prestigious grandes écoles. (He managed to slip in a film-studies minor, with a thesis on Wong Kar-wai.) After graduating, he entered the French diplomatic corps, where he worked as a speechwriter to the Foreign Minister at the time, Dominique de Villepin, and at least partially authored his famous speech at the United Nations, opposing the Iraq War. After that, he pseudonymously co-wrote a graphic novel called “Quai d’Orsay,” after the seat of the foreign ministry. The book—a juicy look at the inner workings of foreign-policymaking—was a hit, selling more than sixty thousand copies of its first edition. Having proved himself as a sort of beast of the French establishment, devouring the competition in every arena he entered, Baudry volunteered to co-write a film adaptation. Then he decided he wanted to be a director. Casual. So he wangled a meeting with Jérôme Seydoux, the chairman of Pathé film company, and persuaded him to finance a nuclear-submarine thriller called “Chant du Loup,” which premièred in 2019 to warm reviews and respectable takings.

For the de Gaulle project, Pathé gave Baudry carte blanche and an initial seventy-five million euros, an unheard-of budget for a French production. (The film was called “La Bataille de Gaulle” in France but is known as “De Gaulle” in the U.S.) It focusses on the critical years of 1940 to 1944, beginning, in Part 1, with de Gaulle refusing to join the collaborationist Vichy government and ending, in Part 2, with his triumphant return from exile during the Liberation of Paris. Baudry had a breakthrough when he and his co-writer, Bérénice Vila, who is also his wife, started thinking about de Gaulle as a figure spiritually not of the mid-century but of the Middle Ages. “I realized that de Gaulle was a modern Don Quixote,” Baudry recalled, citing the General’s “denial, his stubbornness, his readiness to die rather than admitting the unbearable reality that France had capitulated.” Once the notion of de Gaulle as a knight-errant had clicked, Baudry and Vila came up with a tactic to alleviate the pressure of his legend: as they wrote, they called their hero “Robert” instead of “Charles.” They emphasized the initial lostness of his cause: a mad band of marginals, holding on to France out of unaccountable faith, rather than a reasonable chance of wresting control from Vichy. By that point, Baudry recalled, “I had my character in my veins, and I was going to make these films.”

For the title role, Baudry cast Simon Abkarian, an actor best known for his work on the stage. The film took a hundred and fifty gruelling days to shoot, with reports of delays, quarrels, and a generally trying atmosphere leaking from sets in Paris and Cherbourg. Several months into filming, some twenty crew members quit, including the first assistant director and the director of photography. After filming finally wrapped, in 2024, post-production took more than a year, and Part 1 missed an anticipated release date in 2025. When it finally premièred, in May, at Cannes, reviews were mostly positive. Les Cahiers du Cinema criticized its formal “heavy-handedness” and its “idealized vision” of France, but critics in Le Monde and Le Figaro loved it. “De Gaulle” had won a battle, but it had not won the war.

The first installment hit French theatres in June, to dismal ticket sales. Baudry, meanwhile, was M.I.A., still editing the sound for Part 2. “I honestly didn’t give a shit about the noise outside the mixing room,” he recalled. The film’s producers, hoping for a turnaround, moved up the release of the second installment to coincide with la Fête du Cinema, a nationwide promotion offering discounted tickets. (The films’ full titles—“La Bataille de Gaulle: L’Âge de Fer” and “La Bataille de Gaulle: J’Écris Ton Nom”—were unwieldy enough to cause at least one moviegoer, yours truly, to accidentally see the second part first.) Executives overhauled the marketing campaign. Seydoux told me, “We had a crisis meeting, and I said, ‘We have a rifle with only two shots.’ ”

Then came a third, lucky blast—record-breaking heat, which sent people flocking to the cinema, one of the only reliable places to find air-conditioning. By its fourth week in theatres, “La Bataille de Gaulle” had seen admissions surge by seventy per cent. Word-of-mouth took over, and, suddenly, “La Bataille de Gaulle” was a sensation. I heard chatter about it, in the course of a few days, from both a government minister and my boxing coach. “It’s French panache!” Le Parisien crowed, heralding “a fiasco turned triumph.” The trajectory was almost embarrassingly de Gaullian: a crazy project, flailing and discounted, mounting a gritty comeback that would subsequently be treated as inevitable.

In late September, Jérôme Seydoux was sitting in an orange chair at a huge circular conference table on the top floor of Pathé Palace, his company’s Paris headquarters. He has piercing blue eyes and the plain confidence of a man born to industrial wealth—his mother was a member of the Schlumberger oil dynasty—who managed to conquer another field completely. (He is also grandfather to the actor Léa Seydoux.) At ninety-two, he is something of a cross between Louis B. Mayer and Willy Wonka, confecting France’s major films according to a proprietary formula of market savvy and personal conviction.

Seydoux and Baudry like to say that the “De Gaulle” project took shape out of serendipity: over lunch, they discovered that they were both reading the Julian Jackson biography. But in a way Seydoux has been preparing for much longer to make such a film. “I am an old man, and the story, to some extent, is the story of my life,” he admitted. Seydoux witnessed firsthand the Liberation of Paris, in August of 1944. “We tried to go to the Champs-Élysées, but we didn’t make it, because we were crossing the Tuileries and there were people shooting on the Rue de Rivoli,” he recalled. “The soldiers advised my mother to have us all go under a truck to be protected.” Another day, he and his sister were forbidden to go outside, but they snuck out and saw a German tank. “Kids were able to move because nobody would stop them,” he said.

Making a wildly expensive diptych about a long-dead, famously wooden statesman was a gamble, surely, but it conformed to a strategy that Seydoux has pursued to success in recent years,. This involves taking canonical French stories and turning them into “grandes fresques historiques,” the kind of lavish historical epics at which Hollywood once excelled in the nineteen-fifties and sixties. The movies are old-fashioned, and they are expensive, but they have proved adept at drawing big, cross-generational crowds to physical theatres. Pathé’s “The Three Musketeers: D’Artagnan” was the third-highest-grossing French film of 2023; the next year, its “The Count of Monte Cristo” took second place. “It’s this sort of instinctive I.P.,” the film critic Jordan Mintzer told me. “We have Marvel. They have Dumas.” The advantage of resurrecting a wartime superhero is that the world he saves is our own, though “De Gaulle” would have been a very different proposition if it had followed its protagonist into the years of the Algerian War, decolonization, and student revolt.

Baudry has said that he approached the film from another kind of decolonial perspective—that of a French director “breaking the Atlanticist taboo” and liberating his national history from the clutch of the American cultural empire. He spent years living in the U.S. (where he created Albertine, the French cultural center in Manhattan), and when he came back to France he found “a country that was mentally colonized,” as he told Le Monde. “I saw advertisements in public spaces written in broken English that even Americans wouldn’t have understood.” His de Gaulle is difficult, not because he is a comedy Frenchman but because he is a steadfast believer in the near-hopeless cause of maintaining the sovereignty of la Fraaaaaahnce. (Abkarian’s enunciation is the stuff of epic earworms.) “I embody everything the Americans detest,” de Gaulle once said. “I am weak, and I stand my ground.” In the film, he also says borderline delusional stuff such as, “Mosquitoes don’t bite General de Gaulle!” In the next scene, he’s in bed with malaria. Baudry explained, of the General’s almost mystical self-belief, “You have to be passionate. If you’re reasonable, you leave.”

Roosevelt, played by Campbell Scott, is a far more sour, transactional figure than the morally driven humanitarian we know from American history books. Churchill (Simon Russell Beale) waffles and feints as much as he blusters. Baudry told me, “This is the first time we’re seeing this full history through our own lens.” Call it a reverse Pepé Le Pew, flattening Anglo-American icons to give some space not only to de Gaulle but to his internal antagonists and allies and to the French people themselves. Niels Schneider’s sensational performance makes you long for a spinoff two-part, five-hour bio-pic of the Free French general Philippe Leclerc. Baudry’s dramatization of the Germans' violent crackdown on dozens of mostly young, civilian protesters on November 11, 1940, incorporating real live archival footage, is among the most moving set pieces I’ve seen. And nobody who has seen this film will ever forget the Battle of Bir-Hakeim.

There are many ironies to “De Gaulle”—a great-man bio-pic distinguished by its ensemble cast; an anti-American, or at least American-agnostic, film done in high Hollywood style. But its biggest contradiction might be the fact that it is both avowedly antifascist and profoundly patriotic, a film about resistance that could be seen as almost reactionary in its insistence on the purity of de Gaulle and his cause. During our coffee, I asked Baudry whether he’d had any reservations about making a movie that is so overtly, even unfashionably proud of France. He answered in a sidelong way, saying that he hadn’t anticipated the powerful frissons of pride that many moviegoers had reported feeling. Weeks later, I received a long text: “I keep thinking about our exchange in the Luxembourg Garden,” it began. “I don’t want to sound naïve on this,” Baudry wrote. Part of the problem, he said, was that “the far-right has managed to monopolize patriotism,” confiscating “our flag and our pride.” He brought up American exceptionalism, and said that “De Gaulle” does not try to argue for a French version. “It doesn’t say that the French are better than the Spanish, the British, the Americans,” he said. “It just shows people trying to save their country which is France and which they love.”

“Why now?” is an irksome question to impose on an artist, but with Europe struggling to assert itself against an increasingly aggressive American hegemon, and people all over the world searching for models of resistance against autocratic regimes, Baudry is not oblivious to the film’s broader resonances. “I thought to myself, It’s Trump-Zelensky!” he told Le Grand Continent, of a scene in which Roosevelt and de Gaulle face off at the Anfa Hotel, in Casablanca, in 1943. Baudry told me that the current political situation put him in mind of the words of Edward Grey, the British Foreign Secretary in 1914: “The lamps are going out all over Europe, we shall not see them lit again in our life-time.” He continued, “That was true, and that’s a little bit what we’re fearing now.” “De Gaulle” joins a slew of other recent French movies about the Second World War, including “Notre Salut,” a drama by Emmanuel Marre about his collaborationist great-grandfather, and a starry bio-pic of the French Resistance leader Jean Moulin. But “De Gaulle,” like its hero, stands out for its willingness to be true to itself, and even a little weird. Baudry brought up Don Quixote again. “A knight devoted to his lady isn’t necessarily convinced that she is technically more beautiful than, say, the king’s wife,” he told me. “He just thinks she’s perfect, and he’ll die for her any time if needed.” It’s a certain idea about a certain idea. ♦
An earlier version of this article inaccurately described the dramatization of the November 11, 1940, civilian crackdown.

items.title: What Is Biography For?
items.description: I had occasion, a year ago, to draft my mother’s eulogy. Unable to swallow, with advanced Alzheimer’s, she was being fed by intravenous drip. The end seemed imminent. Helpless and uncertain, I set out to write her life.
items.author: Kieran Setiya
paragraphs: I had occasion, a year ago, to draft my mother’s eulogy. Unable to swallow, with advanced Alzheimer’s, she was being fed by intravenous drip. The end seemed imminent. Helpless and uncertain, I set out to write her life.

My mother grew up in Hull, on the northeast coast of England, the youngest child of a large family. She took care of her mother, who lapsed into dementia; she married my father, quit her hospital job, and raised two children, my brother and me. The outlines of her life were clear but the insides dark, lit up by vivid memories here and there. I recall a newspaper cutting from before I was born, with a glamorous black-and-white photo of my mother as a radiotherapist, beside an impressive-looking medical machine. Later, there were trips to the local library, where I inherited her love of reading, and the speech she gave at my wedding, shaking but determined. My mother never liked to be the center of attention, and those around her generally obliged. If only I’d tried harder to push through her reticence, to ask her more about her life when she still remembered it.

As it turned out, my mother’s eulogy could wait. She recovered, as she had after a similar episode once before. But the biographical imperative rankled like an unpaid debt. Why did telling her story seem so vital and so fraught? And why did my inability to do so foster so much shame?

Clare Carlisle writes her mother into her new book, “Transcendence for Beginners,” three times over: once while teaching her daughter how to write; once as her mother is dying; and once to mourn and memorialize her. Like me, Carlisle is a philosophy professor; unlike me, she’s an award-winning biographer, the author of a life of Søren Kierkergaard that eschews chronology for thematic immersion, as well as a philosophical “biography” of George Eliot’s relationship with her romantic partner George Henry Lewes. If anyone could explain the value of writing a life—what I owed to my mother and why—it would be her.

“Transcendence for Beginners” is not a biography, though many lives are caught up in its weft. Instead, it’s a book about why life-stories matter. Both of Carlisle’s professions grapple with the value of human life, but philosophy veers toward the abstract, and biography toward the specific: a single individual with a mother and a given name. Whereas “Socrates went around Athens asking, ‘What is a human being?,’ ” Carlisle writes, “I want to know who this singular person is.” As a biographer, she attempts to create art, too, “to bring something new and singular into the world”—a world that “the philosophical part of us wants to declutter.”

Some philosophers will balk at that diminutive “declutter,” as though the great thinkers who built visions of the world were nothing more than metaphysical Marie Kondos. Not me. Carlisle is entitled to make fun of her colleagues for overestimating the power of rational argument and for preferring false simplicity to complicated truth. Her contrast is, in any case, provisional: she’s open both to moral philosophy that makes use of the individual and to art that does philosophical work.

But there’s a residual tension in Carlisle’s book, and it has to do with her touchstone, the seventeenth-century philosopher Baruch Spinoza. To those who know his ideas, the notion of a Spinozist biographer will seem about as logical as a vegan butcher or a pacifist contract killer. For Spinoza, there is one substance only, a depersonalized God, and everything else is simply a “mode,” or modification, of that substance, a ripple in the ocean of being. We are all ontological froth. As Carlisle argues:

On its face, biography is the genre of the integral subject—a person interacting with others but distinct from them, not dissolving in a sea of substance. For Carlisle, though, the “metaphysical selfishness” of a world composed of discrete human beings “reinforces moral selfishness, and vice versa.” Spinoza is an antidote to self-conceit. But what room is left, in his metaphysics, for the value of an individual life?

Carlisle finds an answer in the microcosm. If everything is an aspect of God, we can divine the value of the whole—the divine itself—within a single person. This way of looking at human life is radically democratic. Carlisle’s book begins halfway up a mountain in Dharamshala, India, in her twenties, when she meets a man who makes his home in a small cave, tending a stone shrine, selling concessions to tourists for a living. At sixteen or seventeen, he left the temporal world behind for a life of ascetic devotion. What moves Carlisle most is how ordinary he seems. “Over the years I’ve met a few people who exuded a palpable spiritual quality, some rare insight or depth or stillness you could feel in their presence,” she notes. “The man on the mountain was not like that.” Later in the book, we meet another ascetic, Ramana Maharshi, who spent his life on a sacred Himalayan mountain named Arunachala. Maharshi became a renowned spiritual guide, fictionalized by Somerset Maugham in “The Razor’s Edge.” Both lives are noble, both beautifully evoked: for the Spinozist biographer, it makes no sense to prize one over the other, the famous over the nameless, since they are merely different faces of a single peak.

Carlisle argues, then, for the value of unheroic lives. The argument is most overt in relation to works of art: George Eliot’s heroines, for example, or Celia Paul’s attentive portraits of her mother. Eliot, who produced the first English translation of Spinoza’s “Ethics,” lived in a time that idolized “great men”: in 1841, Thomas Carlyle wrote “On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History,” and Ralph Waldo Emerson’s “Representative Men” was published in 1850. Eliot’s riposte was “Middlemarch,” in which Dorothea Brooke devotes herself to her self-deluding husband Edward Casaubon, before discovering that his great work is a fraud. Dorothea lives a smaller life than she had hoped, but her life still matters, as the final lines of “Middlemarch” sing out: “For the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs.”

Daringly, Carlisle reads even Eliot’s more morally ambiguous protagonists as “a manifestation of God. . . . a glimpse of something shining, perhaps not far away at all.” Carlisle guides us to a metaphysical summit from which we survey human lives “under the aspect of eternity,” in Spinoza’s phrase, filled with love for them as facets of a divine reality. It’s a breathtaking prospect, and “Transcendence for Beginners” is both moving and profound. But is its vision true? Or, to make this personal, how far does it illuminate the need I felt to write my mother’s life and the pain of being unable to do it well?

“Above all, Eliot was interested in the moral power of ordinary lives, like Dorothea’s,” Carlisle writes, “whose effects are ‘not widely visible’, though nevertheless ‘diffuse.’ ” My mother died soon after I tried, and failed, to write her eulogy. Like Dorothea Brooke, she lived an unhistoric life, and that things are not so ill with me as they might have been is at least half owing to her. I am grateful for that. Yet to value my mother in these terms, for her diffuse effects on me, or on other people, is not to value her for herself. For the Spinozist, the value of a life is the value of a sequence of events—waves in God’s ocean—not the value of the person living through them. “Even if the self dissolves, or never existed in the first place,” Carlisle insists, “the life remains vivid, its story compelling.” But my mother’s life—everything she did and everything that happened to her—only matters because she matters. The fundamental value of the subject: this is what the Spinozist cannot see.

If what we’re interested in are events, we will gravitate toward dramatic ones, and, though Spinoza reassures us that a small, flawed life is as much an expression of God as a heroic one, that doesn’t mean our interest is misplaced. It’s not an accident that Carlisle has published biographies of Kierkegaard and Eliot, not of her mother or mine: as a rule, we are more intrigued by bigger lives. There’s nothing wrong with that—unless we lose track of the fact that every person has a value independent of the life they happen to live. The “metaphysical selfishness” that Spinoza disdains—the world of discrete human beings—makes room for moral selfishness, true; but it makes room, too, for the dignity of the singular person.

For Carlisle, the artist Celia Paul’s repeated portraits of her mother celebrate the episodes in which they were created, “the beauty of those hours in which two human beings gave one another time.” But what is made in those beautiful hours is not a biography, nor the painting of a chapter in a life, but a picture of a person in time. Painting is not a narrative art in the way that life-writing is. The value of a portrait lies less in telling a life story, or part of one, than in sustained attention to a particular human being, the individual whose substance Carlisle and Spinoza dissolve. “My mother was never properly seen in her daily life,” Paul writes to Carlisle. “She found the attention I gave her healing in some way. She didn’t mind what I made of her, she just needed to be looked at.”

“I’ll see you when I see you”: the last full sentence my mother said to me, over the phone from the hospital, several years ago, before her power of speech fragmented. You could hear it as self-deprecation: I don’t matter so much, no need to rush to my side. You could also hear it as a vow of loving attention. We love people, first, and not their lives; but when we love them well, we look toward them, wanting to see them better. The shame of knowing so little about my mother’s life was not the shame of being blind to the value of a life story, but the shame of failing in love. ♦

items.title: In “The Heart” and “I Became We,” the Rise of the Hive-Mind Musical
items.description: The first image in the poignant, propulsive new E.D.M.-pop musical “The Heart,” at the Roundabout’s Laura Pels Theatre, is of a young surfer, Simon (Nick T. Daly), swaying in solitary bliss, like the only dancer left at a club. Behind him, a neon line pulses—i
items.author: Emily Nussbaum
paragraphs: The first image in the poignant, propulsive new E.D.M.-pop musical “The Heart,” at the Roundabout’s Laura Pels Theatre, is of a young surfer, Simon (Nick T. Daly), swaying in solitary bliss, like the only dancer left at a club. Behind him, a neon line pulses—it’s an ocean swell, an electrocardiogram, a musical beat. Just nineteen, Simon has slipped out early to catch a predawn wave, but on the drive home he’ll be critically injured in a crash.

And, in a flash, Simon is no longer the show’s protagonist—instead, his heart is. As bright grids fill up screens that frame the stage, the musical—smartly directed by the Roundabout’s new artistic director, Christopher Ashley, with lighting by Amanda Zieve, immersive video design by Lucy Mackinnon, and subtly gliding choreography by Mandy Moore (the auteur behind Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour)—becomes a thrilling, thrumming twenty-four-hour countdown to an organ transplant, tracing the path from one person’s tragedy to another’s miracle. We meet Simon’s powerhouse mother, Marianne (a moving Joaquina Kalukango, belting in denial by her son’s bedside); her prickly ex-husband, Sean (Jason Tam); Simon’s girlfriend, a d.j. named Juliette (Max McKenna); and also the medical team, including a warm, no-filter nurse (a fab Bre Jackson) and a cocksure surgeon (Drew Gehling, who, after playing doctors in “Waitress” and “Little Shop of Horrors,” may qualify for a medical degree). Later, we meet the recipient of Simon’s heart, portrayed with rueful glamour by Heidi Blickenstaff. These characters are distinct individuals, but there’s a fungibility to the whole enterprise: we meet each of them briefly but intensely, in passing, the way you do in a hospital. The cast juggles minor roles, so a patient might reappear as a doctor; Simon’s surfboard becomes an operating table.

The central concept, adapted by Kait Kerrigan from a poetic French novel, could easily go gooey or gimmicky, like a musical episode of “Grey’s Anatomy.” At first, there’s an almost bludgeoning pathos to what we witness, as Marianne resists the news that her son—brain-dead, but still with a beating heart—is gone. But, just as her grief becomes unbearable, a jarring image intervenes. At center stage, a fey stranger appears, warbling in a high operatic voice, with bright-blue gel patches under his eyes and a white towel wrapped around his head, diva style. Only after his phone rings do we learn who this person is: Thomas (Lincoln Klauss), the hospital professional assigned to persuade Marianne and Sean to donate Simon’s organs. “They might be divorced?” a colleague tells Thomas, filling him in on the case. “The divorce’ll be fun,” he responds, tartly.

It’s a tonic splash of detachment before Thomas’s mask of professionalism slides back up. Some of the production’s strongest moments feature this sort of tricky tonal pivot, as when a punkish gamer (a terrific Wren Rivera) is unveiled as the gleeful consultant who selects organ recipients using an algorithm. The show’s lyrics are often literal-minded, with rare outliers, such as a wry joke about Juliette becoming “a side piece to his nine-foot slab of fibreglass.” But did that blunt sincerity deliver emotionally? It sure did. Before long, my eyes stung; my chest got tight. If the critical part of my brain sometimes resisted an obvious turn of phrase—“You are my heartbeat,” say—the rest of my body was all in.

There was certainly no resisting the score, an audacious suite of electronic anthems and ballads co-written, with some help from Kerrigan, by the married pop-music wizards Anne and Ian Eisendrath, the latter of whom was an executive music producer for the banger-heavy “KPop Demon Hunters.” Broadway musicals have mined everything from rock and pop to hip-hop and folk. But there’s something bracingly logical about injecting the synthetic jolt of electronic dance music into a hospital environment, where vulnerable bodies are sustained by machines. The score has an exhilarating artificiality, from the breakneck “Keep Up,” which is punctuated by the beeps of hospital monitors, to the kinetic “Strike the Match,” in which layers of slick digital uplift thicken like shellac as the consultant homes in on her match. Any rhythm that repeats becomes fodder—the whoosh of the ocean, the boop-boop of video games. It’s an aural vocabulary that evokes both the cold, invisible workings of neural networks and sticky bodies losing themselves at a rave, united by a heartbeat.

“Was he generous?” is the question that Simon’s parents are forced to answer as they struggle over whether to let the doctors remove their son’s organs. The show itself feels generous, open to feeling as a source of wisdom. As one of the show’s lovelier lines says of surfing—and, implicitly, of nearly everything else in life—“You only get one wave, then you pass it on.” As anyone who has ever been in an emergency room knows, in a crisis some clichés ring true.

There is a ravenousness in midtown right now, after a frustrating few years, for Broadway to get behind some great new musical. Will “Galileo” break through? Lin-Manuel Miranda’s “The Warriors”? “Wanted”? In late October, a hot contender débuted: the London transfer “The Curious Case of Benjamin Button,” which had a celebrated run there. In New York, some critics found it twee, but I adored this small, oddball fable about a man aging backward. The production actually shared a lot with “The Heart,” even though it was scored with Celtic sea chanteys. It, too, is a countdown show obsessed with mortality, a stylized tale in which actors swap roles. It, too, had a lyrical directness that risked cliché in pursuit of elemental feelings.

But what felt most notable about “Button” was its structure, which, like “The Heart,” featured an ensemble telling an individual’s story in unison—in this case, down to the thoughts inside Benjamin’s head. Both plays are part of a cadre of hive-mind musicals, along with an earlier Ashley-directed project, “Come from Away” (which, like “Button,” has a Celtic-folk score). These shows are explicitly focussed on communities, not individuals—a hospital in “The Heart,” a fishing village in “Benjamin Button,” a rural Canadian town in “Come from Away.” They’re romances about systems, riffing off the choral storytelling of such classics as “A Chorus Line” and “Sweeney Todd” or the clever identity-flipping of “Operation Mincemeat.”

There’s another play in town that employs a similar technique, more austerely: the song cycle “I Became We,” written by Mona Pirnot, with soaringly lovely music by Jack D. Coen. At the Linda Gross Theatre, sixteen singers stand on risers, holding green choral folders. There’s a conductor and a piano. It felt like church until we heard the first line, which was sung as solemnly as Handel’s “Messiah”: “I saw a segment on ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live!’ called ‘What Do You Know About the Female Body?’ ”

What followed was the funny, philosophical narrative of a successful New York playwright in her mid-thirties. She’s got friends to dish with; she adores her mother, a math professor, and her “jumpy and nervous” husband; she is certain that she doesn’t want children. When she goes to a boring party in Brooklyn, a friend passes her a baby, who—as the chorus sings, in joyful, slightly frenzied counterpoint—starts “squirming, squirming!” and “screaming, screaming!” And then there’s a sudden, destabilizing shift in tone: a solo soprano begins singing mournfully, “She’s so small / She’s so small.”

It seems, at first, that this will be a story about fertility—or infertility. But the narrative never goes quite where we expect, its idiosyncratic turns intensified by the singers’ communal delivery, like a catechism or a shared consciousness. Nobody “plays” the narrator; nobody acts out her behavior. They just sing her thoughts, without comment.

Why did this pack such a punch? Maybe it was because of the tension between the elevated harmonies and the down-to-earth words. Maybe it was because the performance framed one person’s inner monologue—It is wonderful to see people love my talented mother! Why am I crying at this Adam Sandler movie?—as a grand, even sacred project. When the payoff arrived, it reduced the audience to sobs as heavy as any I’d heard at “The Heart.” I suspect that we were all thinking about our own lives. It was impossible not to. ♦

items.title: J.D. Vance’s ‘Will He, Won’t He’ Story Line Has Begun
items.description: In the aftermath of the GOP’s midterms catastrophe, J.D. Vance is going through a wrestling-with-his-future phase. That’s literally the headline of CNN’s new report, which reveals that the vice-president and supposed heir apparent to Donald Trump’s MAGA empire
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: In the aftermath of the GOP’s midterms catastrophe, J.D. Vance is going through a wrestling-with-his-future phase. That’s literally the headline of CNN’s new report, which reveals that the vice-president and supposed heir apparent to Donald Trump’s MAGA empire “has given serious consideration to not running for president in 2028”:

While Vance has yet to make up his mind, interviews with roughly a dozen allies and advisers reveal a vice president wrestling with his political ambitions, the fracturing of the MAGA coalition and the demands of fatherhood. They described him as deeply committed to rebuilding the movement that won in 2024 but uncertain over whether he should be the one to lead it.

He’s also not at all sure he or any Republican can win in 2028, unnamed Vance insiders told CNN. And there’s more than one way to end up a loser that year, since he might not even be able to win the GOP nomination if people like Florida governor Ron DeSantis challenge him. Vance apparently realizes the only way to win would be to rebuild the change-election-focused coalition he and Trump won in 2024, and per CNN, “Vance’s allies and advisers envision that, if he runs, he would try to recapture the anti-Washington, anti-establishment message that propelled him to the Senate and then the vice presidency.”
The Washington Post, meanwhile, reports that he is in fact leaning toward a run:

Vance is still more likely to run for president than not, according to several close allies with knowledge of his thinking. In interviews, more than a dozen people with a view into the vice president’s orbit, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss his future, described Vance as keenly aware of the headwinds against the Trump administration — but also of the potential for those winds to shift as Democrats increase their power in Washington.

“Two years is such an eternity in politics, and people are very easily prisoners of the moment,” said one person close to Vance, describing the vice president as someone who is largely able to resist “panicky inclinations.”

In both reports, insiders and advisers say the Iran war is Vance’s most significant hurdle, but though Vance has clearly tried to take the lead on resolving that conflict over the past week, there’s little evidence that Trump thinks it’s anywhere near as big a problem as Vance and other GOP realists think — or any problem at all. And, of course, talking about the war in any negative light always risks backlash from the president, who tends to view contradictions of what he says as a betrayal. A day after reports surfaced that Vance had inserted himself into peace negotiations with Iran, Trump indicated that he had told him to bugger off. “I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States,” Trump posted on Truth Social, adding that “we don’t need a deal with Iran.”

Considering how critical ending the Iran war is to Vance’s 2028 chances, Trump might as well have said “we don’t need J.D. Vance, either.” If the vice-president decides he wants to replace Trump, he’s going to have get through him first.

items.title: David Walliams: British Police Open Investigation Into Sexual Misconduct Allegations
items.description: Following the allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams, London police announced Friday they have opened an investigation into the British comedian.
items.author: Daniel Kreps
paragraphs: Following the allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams, London police announced Friday they have opened an investigation into the British comedian.
Earlier this week, The Guardian and ITV News published their report about Walliams, with more than 30 people accusing him of abusing his celebrity and star power to prey on women and teenagers.

Without naming Walliams, the Met Police confirmed to the BBC that they have opened an investigations following “a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offenses involving a man now in his 50s.”

“The allegations are separate from those reported by ITN and The Guardian,” the police added in a statement. “However, as part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offenses.”

Walliams has not yet been charged in connection to the allegations, and denied the accusations in The Guardian and ITN report. However, Walliams admitted that he sometimes “behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships” and “did not always take people’s feelings into proper account. That is something I regret.”

“We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offense to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened,” said Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney, whose team is leading the investigation, added in a statement. “We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process.”

items.title: Hollywood Still Faces Weekend Disruptions After FAA Lifts Flight Ground Stop
items.description: UPDATED: In the wake of a four-hour long flight ground stop, Hollywood can still expect a weekend of disruptions after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the shutdown Friday evening. Travel plans were thrown into question for talent, executives and buy
items.author: Clayton Davis
paragraphs: UPDATED: In the wake of a four-hour long flight ground stop, Hollywood can still expect a weekend of disruptions after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the shutdown Friday evening. Travel plans were thrown into question for talent, executives and buyers headed to and from Los Angeles and New York during one of the busiest stretches on the industry calendar.

The FAA says it grounded flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It marks the most extensive disruption to air travel in the U.S. since the federal government mandated a total shutdown of all activity after the 9/11 attacks in September 2001. Some flights resumed immediately, but hundreds of others were canceled while travelers scrambled to make new plans.

From the Motion Picture Academy’s Governors Awards to an array of premieres, screenings, concerts, among myriad other events, Hollywood’s plans as film award season kicks in to high gear were thrown into total disarray. The same is true for innumerable professional and college football and basketball games. CNN estimated that some 1.5 million travelers were left stranded in airports, on runways or on trips that inevitably had to be extended amid the ground stop.

The cause is not yet clear, but an FAA spokesperson says a communications problem affected the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle flights moving across the country. Preliminary reports indicate it is not a cyberattack, according to law enforcement officials and media outlets. The rare ground stop, which was announced just after 1 p.m. PT, led to more than 7,800 flights across the U.S. being delayed by Friday evening, according to the air travel tracking service FlightAware.

On Sunday, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences is set to hold its 17th Governors Awards at the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood, where honorary Oscars go to eight-time nominee Glenn Close, legendary Director Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman, Disney’s first Black animator. Killer Films producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, longtime champions of independent film, receive the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award.

The evening doubles as one of the season’s most important campaign stops, with contenders working a room filled with the Academy’s governors, three from each of its 19 branches, representing everyone from actors and directors to artisans and executives.
Variety has reached out to the Academy for comment.

The grounding will also affect buyers and sellers at the final days of the American Film Market, which runs Nov. 10-15 at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Century City. With international sales agents, buyers and financiers due to fly home this weekend, many of them could find themselves stuck in Los Angeles.
Numerous FYC events are also taking place around Los Angeles, with awards contenders frequently criss-crossing the country during the busy pre-Thanksgiving period.

On Saturday, Netflix will host the official Academy screening for AMPAS members for David Fincher’s highly anticipated “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” written by Quentin Tarantino, in which Brad Pitt reprises his Oscar-winning role from “Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood” (2019). The

items.title: AFM Dealmakers, Talent Agents and Hollywood Stars Left Stranded by Nationwide Flight Stoppage
items.description: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a halt on all U.S. flights on Friday at around 1 p.m. PT and didn’t lift the order until approximately four hours later. With the American Film Market, the Governors Awards and numerous FYC panels scheduled over the n
items.author: Jack Dunn
paragraphs: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a halt on all U.S. flights on Friday at around 1 p.m. PT and didn’t lift the order until approximately four hours later. With the American Film Market, the Governors Awards and numerous FYC panels scheduled over the next several days, the stoppage left many Hollywood insiders grounded on one of the busiest travel weekends of the year.

AFM was hit hard by the standstill, and several events were canceled as dealmakers were preparing for their final days at the major sales function. Ryan Werner, president of global cinema at Neon, told Variety he was unsure if he could make it to AFM on Saturday for the studio’s party. He mentioned “our flights” when referring to travel plans, likely meaning several members of the Neon team were shut down on the way to Los Angeles.

One agency source told Variety that when the FAA shut down travel, their department broke out in a panic to see if anyone could still make their scheduled appearances at Saturday’s Governors Awards, which take place at the Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood.

“Once the news happened, everyone jumped on the phone to see if anyone is going to be able to make it to L.A. for the Governors Awards,” they said. “One agent has a client traveling through Europe with no idea how he will get back for his next things in the U.S., so they might have to hang out in Canada to at least be close.”

TMZ reported that “Baywatch” star Brooks Nader’s private jet was stopped in New York just before taking off for Louisiana. The outlet also shared a video of “Bachelorette” star Kaitlyn Bristowe stuck in an airport. Flava Flav and Morgan Fairchild both took to social media to share that their travel plans were affected. Variety also confirmed that the Sharpe Family Singers and actor Isaac Robinson Smith were all left stuck at the airport.

News of the flight stoppage broke around 1 p.m. PT. At the time, the FAA said the pause was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin later appeared on Fox News and clarified that it was a “telecommunications outage” that caused the backup and that there was no indication of a “nefarious attack” against the United States.
The FAA announced around 6 p.m. PT that the nationwide ground stoppage was canceled.

items.title: Amid Flight Halt, Trump Meets With Jon Voight to Talk U.S. Film Incentive: ‘Get This Done!’
items.description: As flights across the U.S. came to a halt Friday amid a rare nationwide ground stop, President Donald Trump was in a meeting with actor Jon Voight to talk about jumpstarting support for a federal film incentive.
items.author: Gene Maddaus; Pat Saperstein
paragraphs: As flights across the U.S. came to a halt Friday amid a rare nationwide ground stop, President Donald Trump was in a meeting with actor Jon Voight to talk about jumpstarting support for a federal film incentive.
Voight and his team, Steven Paul and Scott Karol, were at the White House to urge the president to push for the film incentive during the lame duck session of Congress.

“It was exciting to watch,” Karol told Variety, saying the president was getting updates on the flight situation and also the capsized boat in New Orleans. “He’s concerned with different things because he’s the president. He gave us attention while taking care of two emergencies.”
Voight made an impassioned speech in support of the Hollywood tax incentive bill, which would provide a 20%-30% rebate on domestic labor costs for films and TV shows.
“He was telling (Trump) he has a helpful heart and he feels this can get done,” Paul said. Voight “was great. He was crying by the end of the meeting. It was an Academy Award-winning speech.”
While Voight was still in the room, the president sent out a Truth Social post reaffirming his support for the federal incentive and urging Congress to pass it.

“Meetings are being set up, routinely, with the Leaders of both Parties in order to, GET THIS DONE!” Trump wrote. “It is a very Bipartisan undertaking, especially in that so much of the money being lost to other countries is coming out of the Blue States. Hopefully Republicans and Democrats will get together and finalize this already very actively negotiated Legislation.”

He also noted that he was working with Sen. Adam Schiff — “believe it or not.” Karol said the team had met with Schiff earlier in the day, and Schiff told them to tell Trump: “This is Tim Scott’s bill and I’m there to help.”
Schiff responded to Trump’s post on X, saying that the bill should not wait until the Democrats take over in January.
“President Trump and I agree: it’s time for Congress to pass a federal film incentive,” Schiff wrote.
Rep. Laura Friedman, a Democratic co-author, also responded, saying “there’s no excuse to wait.”
“A national film and TV incentive means jobs in California, Georgia, New York, New Jersey and every state across the country,” she wrote. “Let’s get it done.”

Karol said that the challenge is finding a legislative vehicle, in which to include the incentive bill. He said that momentum has not slowed since the Republicans’ defeat in last week’s midterm elections.
“There’s good energy on both sides,” he said. “There’s no indication from either side of the aisle that this is something that is not as important as it was before the election.”

Earlier on Friday, Politico published an article saying “Hollywood’s tax credit push runs into a post-midterm wall.” The story quoted Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., as saying chances were “pretty low” of passing any tax bill during the lame duck session.

Supporters of the incentive hope that Trump’s post will encourage lawmakers to make it a priority. Voight has served as Trump’s ambassador to Hollywood, and has met with the president several times to encourage him to back the tax credit. Those meetings paid off in August, when the president first endorsed the measure, leading to the introduction of the bill on a bipartisan basis in September.

Trump’s comment on the film incentive preceded any public statement on the nationwide ground stop. Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of Homeland Security, did address the public after the ground stop was called, telling the nation, “This isn’t another 9/11. This is a telecommunication outage.”
Read Trump’s Truth Social post below:

“I am working with Senator Tim Scott and, believe it or not, Senator Adam Schiff, and, additionally, Senators John Cornyn, Raphael Warnock, Steve Daines, Bernie Moreno, Tim Sheehy, Alex Padilla, Mark Warner, Thom Tillis, Chris Coons, Katie Britt, and Dick Durbin, together with Representatives Jason Smith, Nathaniel Moran, Brian Jack, Linda Sanchez, and many others, both Republican and Democrat, on the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act. The support and popularity of doing this, and bringing Entertainment back to the United States of America, has been unbelievable! Hollywood, and so many other places, have been virtually ’emptied out’ by the Tax Incentives, and much more, given by other Countries. Everyone feels strongly about the Motion Picture and Television Industry — and so do I, and we all want to save it. It was MADE IN AMERICA, and must STAY IN AMERICA. The Entertainment Industry has largely moved to Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other countries, but the actors, producers, and all others involved want to come back home! Importantly, hundreds of thousands of Blue Collar Workers will be positively affected, BIG TIME, by the passage of this Bill. The amount of money spent on these Tax Incentives will be made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers. Meetings are being set up, routinely, with the Leaders of both Parties in order to, GET THIS DONE! It is a very Bipartisan undertaking, especially in that so much of the money being lost to other countries is coming out of the Blue States. Hopefully Republicans and Democrats will get together and finalize this already very actively negotiated Legislation. It can be done quickly, accurately, efficiently and, importantly, will benefit all of America. MAKE OUR ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP”
Updated with remarks from Karol and Paul.

items.title: Margot Robbie to Star in A24’s ‘The Week of Pain’ From ‘The Drama’ Director Kristoffer Borgli
items.description: Margot Robbie will star in A24 and Square Peg’s “The Week of Pain” from “The Drama” writer-director Kristoffer Borgli, Variety has confirmed. A24 is set to produce and finance the project. Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg banner will also produce alongs
items.author: Jack Dunn
paragraphs: Margot Robbie will star in A24 and Square Peg’s “The Week of Pain” from “The Drama” writer-director Kristoffer Borgli, Variety has confirmed. A24 is set to produce and finance the project. Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg banner will also produce alongside Dilemma Films and Robbie’s LuckyChap.

Plot details for “The Week of Pain” remain under wraps, but considering Borgli’s previous works, which include “Dream Scenario” and “Sick of Myself,” it’s safe to assume it will be another squirmy drama with streaks of cringe-out humor. Square Peg and A24 recently collaborated with Borgli on April’s “The Drama,” which starred Robert Pattinson and Zendaya. The film, an intimate original dramedy about a wedding week derailed by a childhood secret, was a box office smash, grossing $135 million worldwide against a slim $28 million budget.

Robbie most recently appeared in the steamy literary romance “Wuthering Heights” for Warner Bros. Audiences couldn’t resist a big-screen affair between the “Barbie” superstar as Cathy and Jacob Elordi as her mysterious love interest, Heathcliff, and the film rocketed to $241 million worldwide. Coming up for Robbie is an “Ocean’s 11” prequel. She will star alongside Bradley Cooper, who is also directing, presumably as the mom and dad of George Clooney’s Danny Ocean. Robbie revealed at CinemaCon 2026 that the film will follow an “epic heist at the 1962 Monaco Grand Prix.” Clooney, in a completely separate sequel, is getting the band back together from the 2001 original for one last ride.
Robbie is represented by Entertainment 360, CAA, Narrative, Aran Michael Management and attorney Jeff Bernstein. Borgli is repped by UTA.

items.title: ‘The Bachelor’ Casts NFL Quarterback Sam Hartman as Season 30 Star
items.description: After two years off the air, “The Bachelor” is returning for its 30th season with a brand new face: NFL player Sam Hartman will be looking for love on the iconic ABC reality dating series beginning on March 21.
items.author: Selome Hailu
paragraphs: After two years off the air, “The Bachelor” is returning for its 30th season with a brand new face: NFL player Sam Hartman will be looking for love on the iconic ABC reality dating series beginning on March 21.

Hartman is a quarterback for the Washington Commanders, who is also an alumnus of the Wake Forest and Notre Dame football teams, where he set the Atlantic Coast Conference records for most career touchdown passes and 300-yard passing games. He also made an appearance in Season 2 of the Netflix docuseries “QB1: Beyond the Lights.” Hartman is originally from Charlotte, N.C.

Hartman’s casting marks something of a relaunch for the “Bachelor” franchise. When Season 30 premieres, it will have been two years since the last iteration of the flagship series, which starred Grant Ellis, and once year since the failed return of “The Bachelorette,” which was pulled from the air last-minute amid a domestic violence scandal between star Taylor Frankie Paul and her ex-boyfriend, Dakota Mortensen. The most recent entry into the franchise was “Bachelor in Paradise” Season 10, which aired in the summer of 2025.

Also of note for “Bachelor” fans is the return of another scandal-wracked personality: Chris Harrison, who hosted all versions of “The Bachelor” until 2021, when he received major backlash for defending former contestant Rachel Kirkconnell from allegations of racism surrounding an antebellum plantation-themed party she had attended in the past. Harrison is now hosting a new dating series called “The Vow,” which follows contestants seeking a “traditional marriage,” on Fox Nation.
“The Bachelor” is produced by Warner Horizon Unscripted Television. Executive producers include Scott Teti, Jason Ehrlich and Andy Frank.

items.title: Amanda Seyfried Eager to Campaign for ‘You Can See Everything’ as Awards Eligibility Comes Into Focus (Exclusive)
items.description: Can Amanda Seyfried receive awards recognition for her acclaimed portrayal of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s blockbuster documentary You Can See Everything? No performance featured in a doc has ever been nominated by
items.author: Scott Feinberg
paragraphs: Can Amanda Seyfried receive awards recognition for her acclaimed portrayal of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s blockbuster documentary You Can See Everything? No performance featured in a doc has ever been nominated by any major awards group. Many weren’t even sure it was possible. Now, the major awards groups have made their determinations, and The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively report their (split) decisions.

Seyfried has been deemed eligible for a best supporting actress nom by the Critics Choice Awards — but ineligible at the Golden Globe, BAFTA and Actor awards. SAG-AFTRA, which is behind the Actor Awards, encouraged A24 to file a formal appeal to try to qualify Seyfried, but insiders say no appeal will be forthcoming. The studio is focused on an Oscar nom.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ submission deadline is today, after which the executive committees of its various branches will begin to review submissions. Official determinations will go out in early December. But in the meantime, THR has learned that A24 has been given assurances by representatives of its Actors Branch Executive Committee that there is no reason to believe that she won’t be OK’ed.

Per the Academy’s rules governing the best documentary feature Oscar, “Films submitted in this category may also qualify for awards in other categories if they meet the specified requirements.” And per the organization’s rules for acting awards, “The Actors Branch Executive Committee shall have the right and responsibility to resolve all questions of eligibility.” In other words, it’s up to the Actors Branch Executive Committee, which has previously deemed eligible acting noms in docs for those who received onscreen credits, as Seyfried did — and they have no incentive to block their constituents from having the option of voting to nominate someone.

In her first one-on-one interview about the film, Seyfried — who landed an Oscar nom for 2020’s Mank and came close to another for 2025’s The Testament of Ann Lee — tells THR that she’s excited to hit the campaign trail and promote not only her performance but the film itself, which could land another nom in a category that has never previously recognized a doc: best picture. “Now that they’re going to let me loose and show up, I’m down!” Seyfried says.

You Can See Everything blends traditional doc techniques with re-enactments featuring Seyfried. The film is at 96 percent on Rotten Tomatoes and recently became only the fourth documentary to ever top the domestic box office. It has grossed more than $80 million worldwide and is still playing in nearly 2,500 theaters. Last Sunday, it swept the Critics Choice Documentary Awards. And Fielder and Oppenheim are currently in the U.K. participating in a slew of post-screening Q&As for Academy and British Academy members — including one moderated by Olivia Wilde — that have drawn the likes of Richard Curtis, Cate Blanchett, Riz Ahmed, Barbara Broccoli and Alex Garland.

In our conversation below, Seyfried reveals when she first realized the film might have legs and that she’s fully prepared for the demands of an Oscar race. “A campaign is a lot,” she says. “It’s time-consuming. It takes all your energy. And I’m totally willing to do it.”

Amanda, you’ve been in awards contention several times — we spoke when you were in the running for Mank, Long Bright River and The Testament of Ann Lee. When you were shooting those projects, I suspect you realized you might wind up in the awards conversation, no? Was that also the case with You Can See Everything?

With Ann Lee maybe, because I thought it was so special and weird, and special, weird movies get some kind of halo effect sometimes. But I usually have low expectations because I don’t want to get disappointed. With You Can See Everything, I didn’t even know if it was ever going to come out! They [Fielder and Oppenheim] were searching for the story. They said very early on that A24 was like, “See what happens. And if nothing happens, that’s OK.”

I was at that surprise first screening of You Can See Everything at the Telluride Film Festival on Sept. 6. You were out of the country promoting another movie. How did you first learn that people who had seen the film were flipping out for it and for your contributions to it?

I was in Venice and only found out hours before I went to bed that they were screening the movie in Telluride. I had thought [Oppenheim] were going to Telluride to screen Primetime [Oppenheim’s other 2026 film], so I was as aware as everybody else was. Later Nathan was like, “I’m sorry I didn’t tell you.” I was like, “I don’t care, it’s all good news.” They’re super discreet for a reason, and I totally respect that.

Nathan had screened it for me months before, and I was like, “OK, cool. I mean, maybe it’ll come out.” Nobody really knew. So when I found out before I went to bed in Venice that it was screening in Telluride, I got really nervous and excited, because I knew it was industry people. And then I woke up to all this chatter and texts from people involved in the movie, and it was that day that I realized that this was going to be kind of an event piece, something that gets under people’s skin. Whether you love it or not, you’re still thinking about it.

People have been trying to figure out how to describe and recognize your work in the film. It has prompted interesting conversations: “Is the film a documentary? Is what you do in the film a performance? How can there be a performance in a documentary? Is it possible to nominate a performance in a documentary?” My question for you: Do you see it as a performance?

Yeah, I do. The re-enactments were definitely a challenge. But it’s not like I ever considered that I would be up for any kind of accolade. I understand the politics and the luck and the timing of awards stuff. I don’t really know if we can fully consider it a doc — it’s very genre-bending. I have seen a lot of documentaries, but not enough to know if they’ve ever done anything like this. I know people have said they have never seen anything like it.

I didn’t see the re-enactments as anything very special when I watched it — I thought the movie was interesting — but what I have come to understand from actors who I really respect is that the re-enactments feel seamless to people after having spent 100 minutes with Elizabeth Holmes. I come into the film and I’m able to be myself and to have an opinion and to question Nathan — and also to then just disappear by the end in the prison scene. The fact that actors who I respect and love have said that they’ve experienced it almost as if it’s her is the most incredibly flattering thing I’ve ever experienced, and that makes me feel very good. And there are so many actors that want to talk to me about the film, which is so fun because I would talk shop all day!

The experimental feeling that I got when I was part of it and when I was watching it — I feel like that’s why everybody’s talking about it! Does it necessarily need to be celebrated in every way in awards season? No, it’s being celebrated already. But do people want to challenge the awards structure? Probably.

Whether or not the Academy’s documentary branch embraces the film, it seems like a lot of other people in other branches of the Academy love the film and want to recognize it, and A24 seems to be going full speed ahead with an unconventional kind of a campaign that will court that sort of recognition. How much of that are you open to being a part of?

I’m fully present for that. I think the amount of events and the amount of presence you need to have when campaigning for these things is pretty extreme — you saw me go through it last year — but it’s still all very positive because getting a seat at the table is the thing. It’s not necessarily about the win, it’s about getting a seat at the table — even quite literally at The Hollywood Reporter Roundtable, or stuff like that.
We’re so glad that you’ll be part of that, by the way. Thank you.

Oh, God, yeah, for sure! Put me in a room with other actors and I’m very happy. A campaign is a lot. It’s time-consuming. It takes all your energy. And I’m totally willing to do it. A24 is great. They’re excited, and I’m very proud of the film, so I’m fully ready to engage in that. And I love these filmmakers! I had a great time with this tiny crew. And I think because [the experience] is so rare, and it will never happen again, I’m doubled down on it.

That doesn’t mean I’m going to do everything I did last year, because I’ve had a year, an interesting year personally [Seyfried and her husband, Thomas Sadoski, who are the parents of two children, announced in September that they have separated], and as grateful as I am that I am where I am, my priorities are pretty clear. The fact that they [A24] didn’t need me to be involved in the press up until this point has been a godsend, because I’ve been needing to be home.

But I’ll do what I need to do because I support the movie and I support the fact that it is unconventional and I want this to proliferate, if that makes sense? I want [Hollywood] to keep being brave. I want to be part of something that inspires actors to take risks, because yeah, I didn’t know what I was getting into, but I had trust in a few people, and then ended up in a project that changed my life.

I’ve been working for a long time, but I’m having an extraordinary experience with You Can See Everything. It’s just following me around, and it’s great, it’s so fun. I like to talk — you’ve seen me — about stuff that I’m crazy about. And so now that they’re going to let me loose and show up, I’m down!

items.title: ‘Cunk on Cinema’ Review: Michael Bay and Benedict Cumberbatch Join Diane Morgan’s Documentary Presenter for Her Latest Laugh-Filled Netflix Series
items.description: Philomena Cunk is flying close to the sun.
items.author: Daniel Fienberg
paragraphs: Philomena Cunk is flying close to the sun.

The obstinately disinterested host of such Charlie Brooker-created educational programming as Cunk on Britain, Cunk on Earth and Cunk on Life is turning her misdirected fascination at least partially inward to tackle the entertainment industry in the appropriately titled Netflix miniseries Cunk on Cinema.

This means baiting critics, who have a greater knowledge of and investment in the topic that’s under Cunk’s withering gaze, and baiting the experts whose increasingly implausible flummoxitude — not a real word — in the face of Cunk’s probingly incurious curiosity is the comedy franchise’s bread and butter.

Surely Brooker and writer-star Diane Morgan know that Cunk and her gimmick won’t play forever, so Cunk on Cinema may mean they’ve decided to take the premise about as far as it can go without becoming a parody of a thing that’s already a parody.

The seams are certainly showing in the delicately threaded tapestry that is Cunk in this series. At six episodes of under 15 minutes apiece, Cunk on Cinema doesn’t overstay its welcome or entirely strain the credulity of viewers who are more in on the joke than her interview subjects. But the ratio of punchlines that fizzle to punchlines that hit is probably closer to even than at any previous point in the franchise.

Still, Cunk on Cinema offers more laughs than just about anything else you’re likely to watch this month, and I’m prepared to follow the miseducation of Philomena Cunk until the wheels entirely come off.
Cunk on Cinema is structurally simple, as television presenter Cunk (Morgan) takes viewers on a history of filmic media going all the way back to, well, the absence of movies.

“Movies haven’t always been with us. In fact, for centuries Earth was a barren wasteland devoid of entertainment content,” she observes, walking through a sea of classic paintings and noting, “For centuries, eyes were literally useless, because there was nothing worth looking at.”

She traces the advent of photography and then moving pictures, touching on landmarks like The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat (“It’s almost as boring as Ben Affleck,” she notes), The Birth of a Nation (“A typically woke Hollywood fantasy”), and into the comedies of Charlie Chaplin (“To this day, the only homeless person it’s okay to openly laugh at”) and Buster Keaton.

I don’t want to accuse Cunk on Cinema of being intellectually nourishing by any stretch of the imagination, but as bite-sized introductions to film studies go, it has some validity. Working her way through her usual assortment of photogenic backdrops, from film studios to the base of the Hollywood sign to various libraries and repositories, Cunk touches at least briefly on a range of noteworthy, properly contextualized bits of history — from an acceptable definition of the Kuleshov effect to a rudimentary explanation of the Hays Code to an acknowledgement of the impact of TV on the films of the 1950s and 1960s.

Cunk’s droll approach to classic films and the medium’s evolution alternates between willfully ignorant and perceptively counter-logical, going amusingly deep on E.T. as a grooming narrative and resorting to social media-friendly one-liners like, “Do you have to have seen the first 2000 films in the series in order to understand 2001?” It’s possible that some parts of Cunk on Cinema benefit from knowing about the films and industry conventions she’s lampooning. But I’m not sure how knowledgable one need be to find it funny to keep referring to Eisenstein’s Battleship Potemkin as “Batshit Pumpkin” over and over. I found it funny over and over.

As always, Cunk can’t do it alone and she’s assembled a group of experts, from the usual dry British intellectuals to a scattering of film critics to an amusing range of cinematic craftsmen (mostly men) to actual A-listers including Michael Bay and Benedict Cumberbatch.

A key piece of the appeal of Cunk has been tracing how realistic it is for her subjects not to know what she’s doing as she peppers them with questions like “What was The Jizz Slinger?” or, regarding the behavior of Taxi Driver antihero Travis Bickle, remarks that “If they remade it today, he’d be violating Uber’s code of conduct, wouldn’t he?”

I’m guessing the screening process for Cunk on Cinema had to be different from her earlier series and that more people probably had to be rejected for being excessively in on the joke. Moreover, it’s easy to notice that Cunk has needed to shift her style of inquiry in a way that’s interesting, but increasingly repetitive.

If your interview subject is in on the joke, the worst thing you can do is ask a lengthy, ridiculous question based on an absurd premise — the meat and potatoes of her finest moments, previously — because if they laugh or, perish the thought, attempt to counter with a joke of their own, you’ve wasted a lot of rope just to hang yourself. But if you ask a simple question based on a malapropism or misheard or misread title or concept, at the very least you’ll get several seconds of well-earned confusion, and then several more seconds of confusion while the interviewee tries to come up with a sincere response or a joke. That confusion is gold, or as much gold as you happen to find in jokes like “The Jizz Slinger.”

With most of the scholars and scribes, Cunk on Cinema settles for “confusion,” as opposed to the delicious obtuseness that earlier seasons yielded. It’s good for chuckles, but it denies viewers those moments of brilliance from previous series, when Philomena Cunk would actually intrigue an expert with a bizarre supposition or only half-jesting theory.

It’s fairly reasonable to believe that a serious-minded historian or zoologist might not know Philomena Cunk and her thing, but it’s harder to imagine an entertainment journalist or film critic with no awareness of this increasingly long-running franchise. But not impossible!
Some of these interview subjects are performers, or at least people with years of experience talking to the press or appearing in the public eye, which forces viewers to engage in guesswork.

So … Benedict Cumberbatch? Pretty clearly in on the joke and intentionally giving Cunk only stone-faced bafflement. Die Hard scribe Steven E. de Souza? Pretty clearly not in on the joke and being genuine in not understanding what he’s in the middle of.

And Michael Bay? This could be one of the year’s great debates, like a TV equivalent of You Can See Everything. Michael Bay has a team. They must have briefed him and advised him on how to react to certain pieces of obvious bait. At the same time, Michael Bay has an ego, and it’s possible he went in with one goal — not looking like a total fool — and that goal went out the window, or very nearly went out the window, in the face of one rambling trademark Cunk family story. This puts Bay in a liminal space halfway between professional and cool (as his team must’ve wanted him to appear) and thoroughly risible (as schadenfreude-hungry audiences may crave).

(Disclaimer: My guesses could all be off! Cumberbatch might have been sincerely perplexed, de Souza might have been playing Cunk like a fiddle, and Michael Bay? Well, I should know better than to think I know what’s in Michael Bay’s mind.)

Morgan remains a droll genius, never better than in the walk-and-talk monologue on a studio lot in the final episode. The material is so perfectly tailored to her voice that she can get laughs even on flaccid punchlines that sound like outtakes from Brooker’s angry political comedy (see his Wipe shows) rather than from Cunk, who does not feel like the sort of character who would bother with a J.D. Vance joke out of nowhere. Now Cunk’s obsession with AI and Brooker’s contempt for it? Those mesh admirably.

Simply put, the Cunk formula still works, but it probably can’t work forever. Now bring on Cunk on TV. I’m available for talking head segments and I promise to look confused when she mispronounces “Quibi.”

items.title: FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop on Flights That Halted Travel Across the U.S.
items.description: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems.
items.author: The Associated Press
paragraphs: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems.

The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
Certain U.S. flights had already been cleared for departure, including flights within Alaska and Hawaii, as have some international flights that are departing US airspace.

This was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunications outage.”
Multiple NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded following the groundings, throwing a busy sports weekend into chaos.
Duffy says getting planes back in the air will take some time
At the time of the ground stoppage, there were 3,500 airplanes in the sky.
“And last time I looked, we had less than, 400 in the airspace,” Duffy said.
He added, “it’s going to be slow” getting air traffic back to normal.
Transportation secretary says outages caused by overload of old system
The U.S. air traffic control system is “incredibly old” and relies on an analog system that got overloaded with data, said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
“This is an emergency,” he said, calling on Congress for emergency funding for upgrades.
Mullin says no indication FAA communications failure was related to a cyberattack
“There was never any lives at risk,” Mullin added. “There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution.”
The homeland security secretary sought to downplay conspiracy theories about what caused the outage.
“I do understand the internet traffic, and where all these conspiracies are running towards,” he said.
FAA says airplane departures can resume
The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems.

The FAA had grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
JetBlue cancels all remaining domestic flights Friday evening
The airline said only Europe-bound flights out of Boston Logan International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport would be able to depart Friday night.
“We expect disruptions to continue into tomorrow, including additional cancellations,” JetBlue said in a news release.
Air Canada cancels flights between the US and Canada
The airline said that the cancellation of all of its flights to and from the U.S. will last the rest of Friday evening.
The decision was a result of the U.S. ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration.
Air Canada said flights between Canada, the Caribbean and South America that go through U.S. airspace could also be affected.
White House briefing will begin shortly
The White House advised that Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would deliver a briefing Friday evening on the nationwide ground stop.
Pete Buttigieg jokes about helping people rebook flights
The former U.S. transportation secretary briefly referenced the freeze in air transportation at the start of a convention for Democrats in Denver.
“I will be available in the hotel bar following the conference for anybody who needs to rebook their flights or get a refund, per your rights,” Buttigieg said.
He’s speaking at the “What’s Next” conference, where Democrats are gathering to celebrate their successes in last year’s midterms and discuss how to use their new congressional majorities.
This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when Buttigieg was secretary.
Some international flights are being allowed to take off because they are departing US airspace
San Francisco airport said that flights headed across the Pacific Ocean were cleared to leave the airport starting around 5 p.m. Eastern. That includes flights destined for Hawaii and Asia.
Mullin had said earlier that international flights would be handled on a case-by-case basis.
Alaska Airlines says flights within Alaska and Hawaii not impacted
