The airline said its flights within the state of Alaska and its “neighbor island” flights in Hawaii are not impacted by the nationwide grounding of flights.
The airline, in a statement, said that flights from the West Coast to Hawaii also have been able to continue and that international flights from Honolulu have been cleared for departure.
But the airline said it also was feeling the impacts elsewhere, noting that due to the significance of the ground stop it had canceled some flights in the U.S. and diverted others.

“When the ground stop is lifted, it will take time for our operations to get back on track for the rest of the day,” the statement read. It encouraged travelers to check their flight statuses before going to the airport.
National Weather Service says there’s no weather radar outage
The NWS said both its radar and website are fully operational. The agency sought to correct false reports that it, too, was experiencing communication disruptions.
Europe suspends US-bound flights
Europe’s aviation agency has suspended U.S.-bound departures at the request of the FAA from 5 p.m. Eastern on Friday until midnight.
The agency manages air traffic for its 42 member countries across the continent.
Microsoft says outages are unrelated

Microsoft said it has no indication that the FAA nationwide ground stop is related to the service disruption that took Outlook and other services offline Thursday, a spokesperson for the company said.
Hundreds of flights have been diverted
At least 600 flights have been diverted so far as a result of the FAA’s order to ground all air traffic nationwide.
As of 5:50 p.m. Eastern, 496 flights were diverted to the airport from where they originally took off, while 104 were sent to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

Among the airports where many of the flights ended up being diverted are Chicago O’Hare International Airport, Denver International Airport, Dallas Fort Worth International Airport and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. Eastern, raising the likelihood of more cancellations and flight diversions.
Flights from Mexico to US to remain grounded
Mexico’s federal aviation agency said Friday that all scheduled flights from Mexican airports headed to the U.S. are grounded for the time being.
Cargo flights also delayed by FAA ground stop

FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, is among the parcel delivery services that are monitoring the ground stop, saying customers can track the status of their shipments through the company’s website.
“We are prepared to activate contingency plans to minimize service disruptions and will resume normal flight operations as soon as the FAA permits,” said Shannon Davis, a spokesperson for FedEx.
The FAA’s ground stop applies to all departing flights at U.S. airports and therefore affects cargo and package shipping operations that rely on air transport.
U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

FedEx has nearly 700 aircraft that operate around the globe, shipping an average of 17 million packages and 20 million pounds of freight daily, according to the company’s website. Most of those shipments are made in the U.S.
Sports weekend thrown into chaos as teams get stranded in airports

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations, and NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time for them to travel to their games this weekend.

Most college football teams playing Saturday travel the day before their game, and the stoppage left many schools — including No. 2 Utah, eighth-ranked Texas and No. 9 Tennessee — at a standstill as they departed for road games.

Meanwhile, the Nets were among five NBA teams scheduled to fly Friday for games on Saturday. They had just boarded the team plane in New Orleans after playing the Pelicans earlier this week when their flight to Memphis was halted in place.

There are 14 scheduled games in the NHL on Saturday. And while the Panthers made it to St. Louis for their game before the stoppage began, the Sharks were among those that were left waiting to leave for their game in Utah.
Communications problems don’t appear linked to new FAA computer system
The communications problems that led to the nationwide halt to flights don’t appear to be linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there’s no indication yet that the problems are linked to the new computer system or any kind of terrorist attack.

The FAA’s SMART system is based in a single location near Washington, D.C., where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center that relays them to controllers across the country for consideration.
The company that designed the system, ASI, said “the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”
Chicago travelers learn about ground stop as they leave security
Travelers just passing through security at Chicago O’Hare Airport learned about the ground stop when they gazed up at screens that showed flight delays across the board.
Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin sat on a bench nearby, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals. Her friends, she said, had already arrived there.

“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer, who took a week of vacation for the trip. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”
Couple headed to a Denver baby shower get an extended stop in Chicago
Austin Curtis and his wife were rethinking their trip from South Bend, Indiana, to a friend’s baby shower in Denver after getting delayed during a layover in Chicago.
They had boarded their flight to Denver from O’Hare International Airport when they were told to get off the plane.
“We did see them taking luggage off our plane and others, so we’re assuming it’s going to be a pretty substantial delay,” Curtis said.

They were unsure whether to get a hotel room or keep waiting out the delay at the airport. With care already in place for their two young children at home, they might stay the weekend in Chicago, he said.
“We might just make the most of it,” Curtis said.
Pilots are trained how to handle losing communications with air traffic controllers

Aviation professor Skip Bailey said the reason they teach them that is so they will be prepared if the radio on their plane malfunctions. He said no one expects air traffic controllers nationwide to lose the ability to communicate.

Pilots are expected to maintain the headings and vectors that controllers gave them before the problem. And then if the outage continues, they revert to following their filed flight plan. Pilots may also be able to communicate with each other over the radio even if they can’t talk to controllers. And airliners have their own radar systems.

“It’s not mass chaos out there. There’s plenty of ways to try to communicate,” said Bailey, who teaches at the University of Nebraska at Omaha’s aviation institute. “But not letting anybody take off again obviously is extremely important because we don’t want to put more aircraft into a system that’s already having an issue.”
Passenger stuck on plane in L.A. takes delays in stride
Jeff Dubner was still waiting to disembark his plane an hour and a half after leaving the gate at Los Angeles International Airport.
His Alaska Airlines flight to Washington, D.C., was already half an hour late and was taxiing to the runway when the plane came to a halt.
Dubner heard about the nationwide ground stop from somebody behind him, he said by phone from the tarmac.
“It’s frustrating. This certainly sounds like it’s going to be more than the usual run of the mill delay. I look forward to finding out why,” said Dubner, a Washington, D.C., attorney.
But passengers were taking things in stride. Even a baby near him had calmed down, Dubner said.
United and American Airlines warn passengers about the pause
Both airlines said in statements on X that flights already in the air will continue.
United Airlines said while domestic flights will not depart, “international departures are being managed on a case-by-case basis by the FAA.”
American Airlines said it expects disruptions for the rest of the day.
“It will be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible when the FAA lifts this nationwide ground stop,” the airline said.
Passenger shares video of midair announcement
A Delta passenger flying from Detroit to Fort Lauderdale recorded video of the captain explaining the ground stop during a midair announcement.

He tells passengers that other planes will be unable to depart, but they are still on track to land at their destination within the hour, according to footage shared with The Associated Press by passenger Andrew Gillfillan.
A photo also taken by Gillfillan shows rows of passengers watching live broadcasts about the ground stop on their seatback televisions.
Travelers wait at airports as flights are suspended

Sean Carey was waiting for his flight at Chicago O’Hare Airport when his grandparents and other family members called and texted him from Las Vegas to let him know about the ground stop. He was planning to travel there for a family wedding.
“I’m surprised the airport’s not in more disarray,” he said.
If he can’t get on a flight for the wedding Saturday, he only hopes he gets a refund and plans to visit another time.
“I hope everyone gets home safely and gets to where they need to go safely,” he said.
DHS chief says system ‘overwhelmed’ at certain levels
Mullin said communication systems had been affected, triggering the nationwide ground stop, but he provided few other details. He said officials continue to investigate the causes.
They are able to communicate “at certain levels,” he said. “But it’s overwhelmed some of the systems we have.”
Mullin said flights are continuing to land during the stoppage and that, for now, officials are working to “make sure” that “we get the flights down and then we get a normal operations back up.”
Cause of outage is unknown
Mullin said it’s not yet known what caused the communications outages, but “we’re gonna find out what happened.”
He added that he’s not going to make assumptions and encouraged others to do the same.
Asked if there may be a connection to Thursday’s Microsoft outage, Mullin said officials are not ruling anything out.
Officials are dealing with midair flights on a case by case basis and working to help them land safely, he added.
Homeland security secretary says grounding all flights isn’t the same as Sept. 11
“There is no indication — and we had no reason to believe that — as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States,” Mullin said.
“This was a telecommunication outage,” Mullin told reporters outside the White House.
He said details were still emerging, but that the president had been briefed.
Mullin said the immediate priority was ensuring that planes still in the air would be landing safely, but that there was no clear information on how long the stoppage might last.
He also downplayed comparisons to the Sept. 11 attacks of 2001, saying, “This isn’t the same comparison to 9/11. That’s a road I won’t go down.”
FAA says flights halted ‘out of an abundance of caution’
The federal agency said on social media that there has been a temporary telecommunications outage.
All flights have been accounted for and international flights will be “handled on a case by case basis,” the agency said.
Homeland Security secretary says currently no indication of an attack
“There was no indication as of yet this was a nefarious attack against us,” said U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin.
All flights in the air are accounted for, he said during a news conference, adding that the public has no reason to be afraid.
The FAA’s ground stop order runs through at least 11 p.m. ET Friday.
Passengers on boarded plane returned to gate
Passengers on an American Airlines flight from Wichita to Chicago on Friday afternoon received text messages explaining the problem as “air traffic conditions in Chicago.”
The plane sat on the runway for about an hour before the captain announced the air traffic problem seemed to be nationwide, and the plane would return to the gate.
Passengers deboarded and the airline said no one would be rebooked for at least an hour.
Aviation safety expert says issue appears similar to September regional outage

Former United Airlines pilot and aviation expert Steve Arroyo said the problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, except this time on a nationwide scale.
Arroyo said it could be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”
First nationwide ground stop since January 2023
A key FAA computer system malfunctioned, temporarily grounding all flights nationwide and touched off a cascading air traffic jam.
Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Flights halted at airports across US due to air traffic control communications problems, FAA says
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there is a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating.
This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

items.title: There Will Surely Be a Jensen Huang Movie. Will It Be Comedy or Tragedy?
items.description: The CEO of one of the world’s most powerful tech companies, taken down by a suspected Chinese honey trap. The first thought of any self-respecting Hollywood producer upon reading the news about Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who resigned from the multi-trillion-dollar
items.author: Julian Sancton
paragraphs: The CEO of one of the world’s most powerful tech companies, taken down by a suspected Chinese honey trap. The first thought of any self-respecting Hollywood producer upon reading the news about Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who resigned from the multi-trillion-dollar semiconductor company in the wake of revelations of his extramarital affairs with both the aforementioned Chinese spy and an executive who reported to him, was surely: This is a movie.

It would certainly be on trend. This awards season has seen a slew of films about rapacious tech titans flying dangerously close to the sun, including Artificial, Musk, The Social Reckoning and You Can See Everything. Their release coincides with a culture-wide backlash against not only the tech industry but also the Trump administration’s laissez-faire enabling of it, a resentment that likely helped fuel Democrats’ resounding triumph in last week’s midterms.

Of all the tech barons who attended (and funded) Trump’s 2025 inauguration, few (with the exception of on-again off-again toady Elon Musk) have cozied up to the president more than Jensen, who sat next to him at the recent White House AI summit and has been among the most forceful voices urging him to ignore increasingly loud warnings about the technology’s dangers. A Huang movie would benefit from widespread schadenfreude and readymade intrigue in the form of a cookie-cutter espionage plot.

The honey trap is such a Hollywood cliché you have to wonder how Huang didn’t see it coming. Has he not watched The Americans? You would imagine that, as an avowed fan of leather jackets, he’s at least seen Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade. If Harrison Ford, Cary Grant (North by Northwest), Michael Douglas (Disclosure) and even James Bond (every Bond movie) fell for it, some might argue Huang never stood a chance.

The cinematic potential is so obvious that an AI trailer for a yet-to-be-made film about Huang’s downfall, titled Honeypot, has already been posted — likely made using Nvidia’s own GPU microchips, which power the lion’s share of the generative artificial intelligence market.

But for now, at least, viable movies still require actual humans to make creative choices. The first such choice facing any exec contemplating a Huang movie will be what source material to acquire. Yes, Huang is a public figure and the scandal has been widely covered, so there’s technically no need to option anything, but Hollywood has grown so risk-averse that it prefers to plant a stake into any shred of existing IP, if only to change it completely later. In this case, however, it’s hard to know what that property would be. The most notable book on Huang and Nvidia, Stephen Witt’s The Thinking Machine, was written in 2025, well before the latest scandal. And the recent news has been reported piecemeal by publications including The New York Times and the Financial Times, as well as an obscure short-selling firm. So in this case Hollywood may have to face its fears and commission — gasp — an original script.
The exec’s second choice will be whether to play it as comedy or drama.

Judging from the number of late-night punchlines the scandal has generated, comedy would seem the easier choice. Huang, with his obliviousness to what seems to the non-centibillionaires among us to have been an obvious ploy, appears to have had more in common with Austin Powers than James Bond. Picture steamy, nerdy sex scenes in which his seductress Alice Huang fakes an orgasm while Jensen Huang passionately shares industrial secrets. Imagine her complimenting his leather jackets in the same purring tone that Jasmine complimented Jafar’s twisty beard in Aladdin, and Jensen falling for it. The farcical possibilities are endless.

But given the global stakes of the world’s then-most valuable company, pivotal to humanity’s future, being compromised because its leader couldn’t keep his pants on, perhaps drama is more appropriate. That the man who called for American companies to race full speed ahead to beat China to AI domination was bested not just by a Chinese spy but by his own all-too-human impulses is an irony worthy of a Greek tragedy. Ultimately, this is a tale of hubris, of a geeky engineer who grew so powerful that he felt invincible. Why else would he so frequently have allowed himself to be photographed sharing romantic glasses of wine with his paramour?

The real problem for a dramatist, I imagine, would be to make the seduction look more difficult than it actually was. Or to explain why it was so easy. A screenwriter would have to concoct some kind of origin story for Huang. Perhaps we’d find young Jensen recovering from a swirlie or a wedgie, and sniffling to himself, “One day I’ll make a billion dollars and wear leather jackets all the time. That’ll show ‘em!”

items.title: The Hubble Space Telescope Is Sinking. NASA Is Looking for Ways to Keep It Afloat
items.description: As telescopes go, few if any are more famous than the Hubble Space Telescope. Over 30 years of operations, the telescope has been essential to groundbreaking discoveries that have fundamentally transformed humanity’s view of the universe. But like all satellit
items.author: Ritsuko Kawai
paragraphs: As telescopes go, few if any are more famous than the Hubble Space Telescope. Over 30 years of operations, the telescope has been essential to groundbreaking discoveries that have fundamentally transformed humanity’s view of the universe. But like all satellites in low Earth orbit, it’s been gradually descending.

This happens because of atmospheric drag, and the Hubble Space Telescope is not equipped with a propulsion system to adjust its own orbit. According to NASA’s analysis, if left unchecked, the telescope will likely re-enter Earth’s atmosphere in 2033 or 2034, eventually crashing back onto the planet.

Hoping to delay this conclusion, NASA has issued a formal Request for Information seeking proposals from the private sector for “in-space servicing” of the famous telescope. This would likely involve raising Hubble’s altitude to extend its operational lifespan, but the agency is also open to industry’s suggestions for managing a safe and controlled reentry or disposal of the telescope while still in orbit. Space companies can also propose upgrades to enhance the telescope’s functionality in its remaining years.

“Hubble is a national icon,” Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate, said in a statement. “Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated reentry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.”

The telescope was designed with the expectation that astronauts would perform repairs and upgrades in orbit. Since it was launched in 1990, a total of five service missions have been carried out. The last of these missions was canceled after the space shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003. But NASA later determined that the benefits of servicing Hubble outweighed the risks of a final mission, and in 2009 a crew took measures, such as replacing the battery, to extend the telescope’s lifespan.

This is also not the first time NASA has considered private-sector resources for raising the Hubble Space Telescope’s orbit. In September 2022, NASA entered into a nonfunding partnership agreement with SpaceX to investigate the possibility of using the company’s Dragon spacecraft to move Hubble into a more stable orbit. However, according to NASA’s announcement at the time, the agency had no plans to conduct or fund the service mission itself; the study was intended solely to assess commercial feasibility.

Meanwhile, NASA commissioned the private company Katalyst Space Technologies in September 2025 to perform an orbital raise for the Swift Observatory, which was experiencing faster-than-expected orbital decay. However, the company’s spacecraft, launched in July 2026, suffered an attitude control malfunction, forcing the mission to be abandoned. On November 4, Swift reentered the atmosphere over Indonesia.

The problems facing the Hubble Space Telescope are not limited to its drop in altitude. The spacecraft itself is also experiencing malfunctions. In June 2024, NASA announced that it would transition the Hubble Space Telescope to a new operating mode using only one of the six gyros on board to assess the telescope’s orientation. After more than three decades in space, only three of the gyros were operational, and one of those was starting to return abnormal readings. The other remaining functional gyro is now being kept in a ready state for future use.

NASA estimates that a mission to raise the telescope’s orbit will need to be carried out by 2032. In an announcement made in 2022, NASA also explained that if the Hubble Space Telescope could be raised to a higher, more stable orbit, it could continue to observe the cosmos for several more years.

“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” said NASA administrator Jared Isaacman. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already in orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.”
This story was originally published in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

items.title: Synchron Pauses Trials of Its Brain Implant Due to Performance Issues
items.description: Brain implant company Synchron has paused clinical trials of its second-generation device after it failed to perform as expected in initial study participants, WIRED has learned.
items.author: Emily Mullin
paragraphs: Brain implant company Synchron has paused clinical trials of its second-generation device after it failed to perform as expected in initial study participants, WIRED has learned.

The Brooklyn-based startup, a competitor to Elon Musk’s Neuralink, is also undergoing a restructuring, which includes eliminating jobs and scaling back its footprint in New York while building up a team in San Diego to support the development of an entirely new device.

Synchron is one of several companies developing brain-computer interface technology meant to allow people to control digital devices by reading brain signals and translating those signals into output commands. The company has touted its technology, dubbed the Stentrode, as minimally invasive since it does not rest in the brain itself or require brain surgery.

Instead, the stent-like mesh tube is inserted into the jugular vein at the base of the neck, then guided with a catheter to sit on top of the brain’s motor cortex. The company’s first-generation Stentrode connected using an external wire resting on a user’s chest. Ten volunteers across the US and Australia received that device and were able to send emails, text, browse the internet, and do online shopping and banking with their thoughts. Synchron has also enabled volunteers to control an Amazon Alexa and Apple’s iPad and Vision Pro without using their hands or voice.

Synchron’s second-generation device has fewer electrodes and is fully wireless, using Bluetooth to connect. The company launched a multisite trial in the US earlier this spring with sister sites in Australia and Canada to evaluate the newer Stentrode, and some participants have already had it implanted. Those sites have recently paused enrollment, however, because the device is not working as intended, according to sources familiar with the trials who asked to remain anonymous.

In a statement to WIRED, Synchron says it voluntarily paused enrollment “after identifying a performance issue involving the lead, the cable that carries signals from the Stentrode to the implanted electronics.”

“The issue does not involve the Stentrode itself and no safety issues related to the device have been identified. The pause was a company decision, not an FDA-directed action,” the statement continues.

The company says it has since brought lead design and manufacturing in-house. Instead of fixing the lead alone, Synchron says it is upgrading the whole Stentrode system and will resume trial enrollment once the hardware upgrades are complete.
“We will continue to support participants with Stentrode devices across their lifetime. Our commitment to their care and well-being remains unchanged,” Synchron says.

Two of the five US trial sites that WIRED was able to reach confirmed that recruitment is on hold at those locations. A coordinator at one site said the pause was not safety-related and was due to Synchron taking a look at the device to make sure the company is getting the readouts it is looking for.
These trials are key to Synchron advancing the Stentrode into a larger pivotal trial, which is needed for the US Food and Drug Administration to grant marketing approval.
“We still have strong confidence that it has the potential to be a first-line therapy,” CEO Tom Oxley says of the Stentrode.

Synchron’s website and LinkedIn page show around a dozen job openings in San Diego, including electrical and mechanical engineers, microchip designers, and materials scientists. The San Diego team will be designing and manufacturing the upgraded lead and Stentrode, as well as a separate device that the company has not yet revealed that will go “beyond the blood vessels altogether,” according to its website. Oxley previously told WIRED that the company was planning to develop a device that reaches multiple brain regions at once, which could allow more complex and natural functions beyond moving a cursor or making a mouse click.

The brain-computer interface field is expanding rapidly, with money pouring into companies pursuing both implanted devices and wearables. Synchron was estimated to have a nearly $1 billion valuation after closing a $200 million funding round last fall. It is backed by Khosla Ventures and the venture firms of Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos.

Neuralink was reportedly valued as high as $42 billion in secondary market transactions as of this summer. The company had an early problem with its implant in 2024 after it malfunctioned in its first volunteer, Noland Arbaugh. The coin-sized device sits in the skull and has 64 tiny, flexible wires that are threaded into the brain. A few weeks after Arbaugh received the device, several of the wires came out of his brain, leading to a loss of cursor control. Neuralink was able to compensate for the lost threads and restore control by modifying its recording algorithm.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence are fueling the development of brain-computer interfaces since AI models can read brain patterns faster and more accurately than traditional algorithms. Merge Labs, a brain-computer interface company cofounded by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, came out of stealth in January with $252 million in funding. OpenAI provided some of the funding, and the two companies are collaborating on AI models.

While these devices have shown incredible promise for people with severe motor disorders, they remain experimental. Synchron’s setback shows just how far the field still has to go before these systems are commercially available for patients.

items.title: How Do I Teach My Daughter That Robots Are Not Her Friends?
items.description: My daughter was a toddler when we first brought a Google smart speaker into our home. The technology seemed like the way of the future, and we thought it would help teach her empathy. We encouraged her to talk to the speaker kindly, to say ‘please’ and ‘thank
items.author: Elizabeth Endicott
paragraphs: My daughter was a toddler when we first brought a Google smart speaker into our home. The technology seemed like the way of the future, and we thought it would help teach her empathy. We encouraged her to talk to the speaker kindly, to say ‘please’ and ‘thank you’ as if she were asking a real person to play “Let It Go” for the 57th time.

Now my daughter is in fourth grade, and she recently started interacting with AI in her twice-a-week STEM class, using Canva’s Dream Lab, an AI-powered text-to-image generator on a Google Chromebook. The activity — feeding the chatbot information about her interests so it can create cartoons in her likeness — has reignited her interest in STEM, which she had grown bored with. The time goes by so quickly, she says, because she enjoys answering the chatbot’s questions. As an extroverted kid, she sees it as yet another fun pal she gets to interact with. She can’t wait to start the class’s next unit, when they’ll start working on robotics. My daughter has long enjoyed playing with a toy at home that allows kids to build, program, and customize a robot with sensors for eyes and a permanent smile cut into its aluminum body. She constructs mazes for the robot and gently encourages it when it becomes stuck.

In the years since we brought that smart speaker home, however, I’ve started to sour on AI. Beyond the large-scale environmental consequences, there are kid-specific dangers: Teens have died by suicide after being encouraged by chatbots, and eight states just filed suit against OpenAI’s ChatGPT for harming children. AI agents and chatbots are designed to seem relatable, almost as if human, but we are quickly learning they aren’t trustworthy.

On a warm Saturday morning a few weeks ago, as local vendors set up at our nearby farmers’ market here in Denver, a baby blue Waymo circumvented barricades and bumbled down the main artery of the market. Without a driver, no one knew how to get it to stop. Vendors had to clear a path so it could exit. At first, I laughed upon hearing about the wayward Waymo, as it was such a ridiculous situation, but eventually the near-miss of it all hit me. And then I realized that my daughter would have felt bad for the vehicle. It appeared lost and pathetic, its headlights flashing like big worried eyes amid the white tents, its sensors whirring as if sentient. But a robotaxi is not sentient. In a dangerous situation like this, where a full-size vehicle was out of control, would my daughter have known not to trust it? I now think that in teaching my daughter to be polite to robots, chatbots, and AI agents, I may have led her astray.

I don’t want my daughter to be rude or inconsiderate. When her first word was more, my husband and I were careful to model manners to ensure please soon followed. Trust me, I’ve met more than a few of her peers who seem unable to consider the feelings of others. There has not yet been enough research to establish whether the way children interact with AI and robots can affect their empathy skills, and part of me fears that if she stops treating machines with kindness that it could erode her sense of compassion for real people, too.

But it’s not lost on me that girls are socialized to be more polite than boys, starting at young ages. This can lead to compliance, people-pleasing, and habitually bending to social pressure. I’m proud that my daughter has won awards at her school for being kind and considerate, but I can’t help but wonder if she may be more susceptible to big tech. She’s smitten with the kitty-shaped robot serving ramen at our local Japanese restaurant, and she was charmed by the boxy food-delivery apparatus that winked before nearly tripping us on a recent trip to Helsinki. While I’ve been quietly backing away from anything AI generated, she has been drawn in.

It makes sense that these things appeal to her. As Sherry Turkle writes in her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, “As humans, we are vulnerable to things that behave like humans.” My daughter has been raised alongside The Wild Robot, Wall-E, and Lightning McQueen. I grew up with the Pixar lamp, the Microsoft paper clip, and The Brave Little Toaster. I cried when my Tamagotchi died and felt sick to my stomach when Haley Joel Osment’s cyborg character was abandoned in Steven Spielberg’s 2001 dystopian film, A.I. Artificial Intelligence. I remember thinking as an impressionable high-school freshman that I would always help a robot in distress because neither their creation nor their tasking was their fault. Even though I didn’t grow up with this technology in my daily life, it’s hard even now not to anthropomorphize it; I can only imagine how confusing it must be for children today.

This is what tech companies want. They try to take advantage of human empathy by adding features to their products that foster connection, and it is working. Developers intentionally design robots with eyes and other facelike qualities, and a recent study has shown that robots with these features provoke more emotional reactions from humans than those without. The leader of that study, Dr. Elly Konijn, a professor of media psychology at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, told me “we know from research that people easily self-disclose with such humanlike, empathy-simulating robots.” We don’t always know where that sensitive information is going, where it’s stored, and who owns it. Meta just released its new AI assistant, Muse, to early success, despite the fact that it collects much more data than other kinds of chatbots, sometimes without users’ knowledge or permission. When my daughter saw its beige Teletubby-like mascot over my shoulder in the repeated pop-ups trying to convince me to opt in, she squealed over its cuteness, wondering if it was a toy for sale.

My daughter hasn’t yet interacted with many chatbots outside of class, but I wouldn’t be surprised if that time comes sooner than I’d like. These LLMs are designed to persistently reply in a positive way, and their prompt responses mirror the slot-machine effect you get from scrolling on social media. There is no clear end when talking with a chatbot; it always has an idea for further use. Young people are particularly susceptible to robots or chatbots behaving in humanlike ways, Konijn says, especially when they’re emotionally engaging. A recent study showed that children were more likely than adults to abandon their own correct answer if they noticed robots providing a wrong answer.

In a perfect world, I’d love to limit my daughter’s interactions with AI and robots in the same way I do her screen time. We have household rules around what media can be consumed, for how long, and where. But with AI infiltrating more classrooms, and Google’s announcement that any schools banning AI will lose access to its search engine, the technology feels unavoidable. After my daughter first told me about the AI use in her STEM class, a few fellow parents and I discussed our concerns on the playground, wondering if this was something that should have required our consent. Ultimately, we all shrugged off our unease, settling reluctantly into the inescapability of it all. There doesn’t seem to be a way to dodge exposure to AI; I’m not going to pull my daughter from her favorite elective.

So for now, I’m teaching her to be less nice to AI and robots. That definitely does not mean I want her to be unkind or cruel — just to refrain from being courteous. I remind her to be wary of programs using emotional language such as feel, understand, and think, because they cannot do those things. I tell her that robots cannot have emotions but are designed to manipulate ours. I want my daughter to approach these products with skepticism rather than a wide-open heart. Turkle writes, “Whenever a program says ‘I,’ it’s a deception.” When chatbots seem to relate to my daughter, I remind her it’s because they’ve already collected her personal information, and behind every robot there’s a company putting on a performance to pad their own pockets.

The other day, my daughter came home from school, excited to tell me about the AI-generated cartoon she made in her class. Because of her interest in Jimothy, the AI had rendered her as a raccoon who was carrying shopping bags and eating pho. “Oh, and I didn’t say ‘please’ to it,” she added uncertainly. I acknowledged that that must have felt strange. Even though the AI’s prompts were flattering and kind, I told her, she was only speaking to a series of equations that predicted what she wanted to hear and see next. We talked about how and why that was different from an interaction with a friend, a teacher, our cat, or even a tree. Only the AI has a multibillion-dollar company behind it.

She seemed to understand what I was saying, but I’m not naïve enough to think it’s that simple. I’m trying to preserve her humanity by encouraging her to subvert her most natural instincts. If anything, this problem will likely become even harder to manage. But maybe — as her exposure to anthropomorphic AI and robots increases, and assuredly in even more tantalizing ways — she can hold herself back from being quite so nice.

items.title: At 81, I Wanted My Breasts to Look Like They Did in My 40s
items.description: Sagging breasts are a common consequence of aging and weight loss, and a breast-lift can help reshape the breasts and restore a firmer appearance. But what if you want one at 81? While there’s no set age limit for elective plastic surgery, doctors must weigh a
items.author: Jaclyn Smock
paragraphs: Sagging breasts are a common consequence of aging and weight loss, and a breast-lift can help reshape the breasts and restore a firmer appearance. But what if you want one at 81? While there’s no set age limit for elective plastic surgery, doctors must weigh a patient’s overall health and the potential benefits of surgery against the risks of general anesthesia, complications, and a longer recovery.

“Chronological age matters less to me than the patient’s overall health and functional status,” says Peter Andrade, MD, a board-certified plastic and reconstructive surgeon at Andrade Plastic Surgery. When evaluating a patient in her 80s for a breast-lift, he looks at factors like a history of stroke or cardiac disease, diabetes, blood sugar control, and smoking history. He also considers skin quality, which generally declines with age and can affect both healing and the longevity of the results.

“For a patient in her 80s, I would be especially mindful of the increased risk of cardiovascular complications and blood clots, as well as the likelihood of a longer recovery,” Andrade says. Reduced blood flow to the surgical area can also slow wound healing and increase the risk of complications, including infection. Before proceeding, he says, he would want a thorough review of the patient’s cardiac and pulmonary health, appropriate medical clearance when needed, and any existing conditions to be well managed.

I’m 82, and my life is still full of things I want to do. I’m a documentary filmmaker, and my most recent film, about Suiseki, the Japanese art of appreciating naturally formed stones, aired on PBS and received awards at film festivals. I’m working on two more films, and I travel whenever I can. I’ve always taken care of myself, and I didn’t think getting older meant I had to stop caring about how I looked. So last year, I decided it was time to get a breast-lift.

I’d been thinking about it for a while. I’d lost about 20 pounds in my 70s, which made my breasts sag more. I wanted them to look perkier, the way they did in my 40s. I noticed them in intimate settings and in places like nude baths, and ultimately, it was about how I felt looking at myself. I’ve always looked good for my age and maintained a slim, firm figure, and I wanted my breasts to reflect how young I still feel. I probably wouldn’t have considered surgery earlier, before losing the weight.

I found Dr. Maryam Zamani, a dual-board-certified plastic surgeon in Beverly Hills, while looking for someone who understood the kind of result I wanted. I felt comfortable with her immediately. She also seemed to understand that what a woman wants from her body can change over time, and that those preferences don’t suddenly become irrelevant when you get older.

I’d seen my primary-care doctor, too, and my pre-op tests including laboratory testing, an electrocardiogram, a physical examination, and medical clearance from an internist came back well, so I felt good about moving forward. I knew there were potential cognitive risks associated with general anesthesia, but I’d had surgery before without experiencing those effects. My mother stayed youthful into her 90s, and I’ve always felt I had good genes. I was healthy, and I didn’t see my age as a reason not to have the surgery.

I had the operation in October 2025. It took about three hours, and I was under general anesthesia. I went in early in the morning, got prepped, and met the anesthesiologist. I was put under pretty quickly, so I don’t remember anything about the operation itself.

Dr. Zamani lifted and reshaped my breasts using my own tissue rather than implants. My left breast was wider and sagged more than my right one, so she removed additional tissue from that side to make them more symmetrical.

Afterward, I spent a day at a recovery center with nursing support. My boyfriend offered to help me recover at home, but I wanted to do things on my own, so I opted for the extra support. In hindsight, the recovery was so easy that I’m not sure I needed it. I had some pain at first, but after a day or two, I felt fine. I took over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medication as needed.

I’ve had other operations, including a hip replacement and surgery on my wrist after I broke it carrying film equipment to a location. The wrist surgery was really painful. Compared with that, the breast-lift was fairly innocuous.

Dr. Zamani’s team gave me a pre-op cleanser to use before surgery. They also recommended treatments like hyperbaric oxygen therapy, red-light therapy, and lymphatic massage, but I didn’t feel I needed them since I’ve had surgery before and healed fine without them.

For the first couple of days, I took what I call French baths. I washed everywhere except my breasts because they were bandaged. I wore the support bra Dr. Zamani gave me, and my surgical dressings were removed about a week after the operation. When the dressings came off, I thought my breasts looked pretty good.

I was eager to get back to my routine, so after a week, I was back to yoga, and after a couple of weeks, Pilates. I held off on jogging because the bouncing could be painful and put strain on my breasts while they were healing. Otherwise, I was able to get back to my usual activities and schedule fairly quickly, which was important to me.

By around three months, much of the swelling had subsided and the breast tissue had begun to settle into its new position. I was told the results would continue to develop over the following months as my scars healed.

I didn’t tell many people I was having the surgery. I told my boyfriend, and he said, “Oh dear. You don’t have to do that for me.” I think he wanted me to know that it wasn’t something I needed to do to please him. But I made the decision for myself. I didn’t tell anyone else, before or afterward. Why would I? I don’t feel the need to explain every personal decision I make.

I think people sometimes assume that when you reach your 80s, you’re supposed to be kind of frail. And there’s a notion that women in their 80s aren’t interested in sex anymore. I still am. A lot of my peers aren’t, so maybe I’m an outlier in that area. But I don’t feel that being in my 80s means I should stop caring about my body.

For me, confidence comes from accomplishment more than looks. I used to be shy and awkward, but now I can be at ease in the world. I don’t need to look a certain way to feel confident, but that doesn’t mean I can’t have preferences about my body. I wanted my breasts to look perkier, and now they do. When I’m naked, I like what I see. I like them better.

Would I do it again? Yes. The surgery hasn’t made much difference in my everyday life, since I’m usually dressed. But I like knowing that when I’m nude, I’m not focused on something I want to change. I made the decision for myself, I’m happy with the result, and I would do it again.

[Editor’s note: Breast-lifts with Dr. Maryam Zamani typically range from $19,000 to $25,000 or more, depending on the complexity of the procedure. The patient was not comfortable sharing what she paid.]

items.title: 15 Gifts For The Friend Who Collects Perfume Like Memories
items.description: 15 Gifts For The Friend Who Collects Perfume Like Memories
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: 15 Gifts For The Friend Who Collects Perfume Like Memories

At Refinery29, we’re here to help you navigate this overwhelming world of stuff. All of our market picks are independently selected and curated by the editorial team. All product details reflect the price and availability at the time of publication. If you buy or click on something we link to on our site, Refinery29 may earn commission.
Rare Beauty Rare Moments Eau De Parfum Rollerball Mini Duo

As a self-professed perfume snob, I was seriously impressed by Selena Gomez's fragrance debut last year. Then, IMO, she outdid herself with her sophomore release, Rare Beginnings. This adorable rollerball duo lets you experience both scents, each offering a completely different (but equally Rare-coded) fragrance mood: one fresh and fruity, the other warm and comforting. Plus, the miniature bottles are practically made for tossing into your bag for midday touch-ups.
Summer Fridays Sunlit Vanilla Set

Summer Fridays' fragrance debut was one of my favorite beauty launches of 2026, making this gift set a no-brainer for anyone on the hunt for their next favorite vanilla perfume. I'm particularly obsessed with the blend of caramel, coconut, and bergamot, which creates a warm, creamy scent that feels cozy without veering too summery. And considering the full-size bottle alone retails for $82, getting that plus a travel spray and cosmetic case? Girl math at its finest.
Marc Jacobs Daisy 4-Piece Mini Perfume Discovery Gift Set

If you know someone (or are that someone) who’s dreamed of frolicking in a field of wildflowers ever since first seeing Marc Jacobs’ Daisy ads, this festive set is a steal at under $100 — not that your recipient would ever guess. Inside, your lucky giftee will discover a mini garden of different varieties encased in Christmas cracker-inspired packaging.
Tom Ford Private Blend Deluxe Discovery Set

Who doesn't love a little Tom Ford under the tree? This impossibly chic discovery set brings together four of the brand's most iconic fragrances, spanning the decadent, cherry-soaked Lost Cherry, smoky-sweet Tobacco Vanille, beach-resort-coded Soleil Blanc, and bold, woody Oud Wood. Consider this the gift of smelling expensive.
Hermès Barénia Eau de Parfum Gift Set

I treated myself to a similar version of Hermès' Barénia gift set during the Nordstrom Anniversary Sale, but if you missed out, fear not. This duo includes a full-size bottle of the brand's addictive, skin-like Barénia, plus a travel spray for keeping your signature scent close, whether you're commuting, jet-setting, or simply refreshing on the go.
Cyklar The Bestsellers Perfume Oil Gift Set

Without a doubt, perfume oil is one of the most sensual ways to wear fragrance. There's the ritual of applying it, the subtle sheen it leaves on skin, and the bonus of using it as a base to help other fragrances linger longer. Cyklar is quickly mastering the art of the perfume oil, and this quartet of its bestselling scents — Sacred Santal, Vanilla Verve, Sex Musk, and Naked Neroli — offers a little something for every mood, from cozy to come-hither.
Miu Miu Mini Miutine Eau De Parfum Perfume Duo Gift Set

I not-so-secretly love strawberry fragrances, and Miutine is my current favorite. With warm brown sugar and floral gardenia rounding out the juicy fruitiness, it's playful yet ladylike in the most Miu Miu way possible. This duo includes two adorable minis — a travel spray and a Honey, I Shrunk the Kids-sized version of the brand's signature matelassé bottle. All for under $40? A luxury fragrance steal, if you ask me.
Ellis Brooklyn ISLA TIME Mini Perfume Duo Gift Set

We haven't even reached the dead of winter, but for the person who's already dreaming of an island escape, Ellis Brooklyn's tropical perfume duo is just the ticket. It includes teeny-tiny bottles of ISLA SIRENA, a mermaid-coded blend of coconut water, blue java banana, and lime, alongside my personal Ellis Brooklyn favorite, Miami Nectar, a sun-drenched cocktail of pink pineapple, coconut water, and vanilla. OOO mode: activated.
Sephora Favorites Holiday Women's Perfume Sampler Gift Set

I'll say it every year: Gifting fragrance can be tricky unless you're replenishing someone's signature scent or know their tastes really well. Enter Sephora's perfume sampler set, aka my favorite hack for giving someone a fragrance they'll actually love. With 20 scents to choose from, the odds are very much in your favor. The set includes a treasure trove of Sephora bestsellers in sample sizes (which, trust me, last longer than you'd think), plus a voucher to redeem a favorite for a full-size bottle online or in-store. The gift that keeps on giving, indeed.
The 7 Virtues Mini Amber Orchid & Vanilla Woods Eau de Parfum Duo Gift Set

This right here is your ultimate cozy-girl scent combo. Vanilla Woods is an all-time favorite in my fragrance collection, and I'm convinced newcomer Amber Orchid is her long-lost soulmate-slash-bestie — that's how beautifully they complement each other. Together, they're subtly sweet, warm, and inviting, with an airy, skin-like amber floral quality that gives off that "naturally smells good" energy.

Leave it to IYKYK lifestyle brand Sidia to reimagine portable fragrance as an endlessly refillable, keepsake-worthy object. Meet The Strike, a chic scent atomizer that lets you choose from three of the brand's signature fragrances: warm and cozy Braless, earthy Soaked, and sunny Midas. Consider it your new favorite way to take your signature scent everywhere — and make every reapplication feel like a little luxury.
Glossier Mini Glossier You Wardrobe Kit

I audibly squealed when I spotted this Glossier You perfume set in-store — that's how good it is. Perfect for the Glossier obsessive on your list, this quartet of ambroxan-based fragrances is a skin-scent lover's dream, offering four takes on that signature your-skin-but-better magic. (Plus, the tiny bottles are the ultimate beauty-girl keepsakes.)
Sol de Janeiro Cheirosa All the Way Mini Perfume Mist Gift Set

Spread some holiday cheer — or should we say, Cheirosa — with this set of six Sol de Janeiro fragrance mists. The lineup includes fan favorites like caramel-forward '62 and fruity-floral '68, plus the chance to discover a new signature scent in picks like nutty, gourmand '71 and juicy, plum-forward '40. Consider it a one-way ticket to smelling delicious.
Kylie Cosmetics Kylie Jenner Mood Stones 3-Piece Discovery Gift Set

IMO, Kylie Jenner has yet to miss when it comes to her growing fragrance empire. Her first foray beyond the Cosmic collection came in the form of Mood Stones, arguably her most elevated perfume offering yet. This discovery set lets you sample all three scents — Cashmere Muse, Blush Wood, and Velvet Brew — and mix, match, and layer to your heart's content.
NOYZ Only Human Layering Set

There's no shame in knowing what you like — especially when it's as good as NOYZ's Only Human. This set lets you wear the sultry-sweet scent three ways: as an eau de parfum mist, a moisturizing milky lotion, and a solid perfume stick for on-the-go touch-ups. Layer them together for a fragrance ritual that goes the extra mile, or wear each one solo. (The chic faux-leather mini purse is just the cherry on top.)
